name: Age Ayurveda Nighantu Ayurvedic terminology lexicon
description: How Ayurvedic technical terms are rendered into English by the WHO standard terminologies, by the published Samhita translations and by the secondary literature, with an assessment of each rendering and the classical passages that bear on the term. provenance.quotePolicy: A classical quote publishes only if it is Sanskrit mula, which is ancient, or a translation this project has cleared: Kaviratna's Charaka 1896-1913 or Bhishagratna's Sushruta 1907-1916. classical.establishes: The locus classicus: a list of conduct qualities (truthful, free from anger, abstaining from wine and sex, non-violent, calm, pleasant-spoken, etc.) whose possessor 'should be known as one on perpetual rasayana' (nityarasāyanam); the colophon names the section ācāra-rasāyana.
classical.quote: सत्यवादिनमक्रोधं निवृत्तं मद्यमैथुनात्| अहिंसकमनायासं प्रशान्तं प्रियवादिनम्||३०|| जपशौचपरं धीरं दाननित्यं तपस्विनम्| देवगोब्राह्मणाचार्यगुरुवृद्धार्चने रतम्||३१|| आनृशंस्यपरं नित्यं नित्यं करुणवेदिनम् | समजागरणस्वप्नं नित्यं क्षीरघृताशिनम्||३२|| देशकालप्रमाणज्ञं युक्तिज्ञमनहङ्कृतम्| शस्ताचारमसङ्कीर्णमध्यात्मप्रवणेन्द्रियम्||३३|| उपासितारं वृद्धानामास्तिकानां जितात्मनाम्| धर्मशास्त्रपरं विद्यान्नरं नित्यरसायनम्||३४|| गुणैरेतैः समुदितैः प्रयुङ्क्ते यो रसायनम्| रसायनगुणान् सर्वान् यथोक्तान् स समश्नुते||३५|| (इत्याचाररसायनम्)|

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints '52-&' (OCR-damaged; probably 52-56) after the long sentence and 57 after the next; standard numbering 30-34 and 35 per carakasamhitaonline - do not convert by arithmetic
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English for the achara rasayana passage; his aphorism numbers are printed AFTER each passage; OCR text from archive.org item BIUSante_47357, quoted with OCR artefacts normalised only for spacing.
classical.quote: One that is truthful, and free from wrath, that abstains from wine and sexual indulgence, that has no animosity, that undergoes only such labour as involves no fatigue, that is tranquil and of amiable speech, that is accustomed to the silent recitation of sacred texts, and is pure (in body and mind), that is endued with gravity and firmness, that is always charitable and engaged in penances, that honours the deities and kine and Brahmanas and preceptors and spiritual guides and men of advanced years, that is always averse to cruelty, that is always compassionate, that is regular in respect of sleep and wakefulness, that takes milk and ghee, that has knowledge of time and place as also authority, that is conversant with reasons, that is reft of pride, that is of practices which are praiseworthy, that is possessed of a liberal mind, that has senses directed towards the soul, that honours men of advanced years as also those who are endued with faith and who have their souls under control, that is devoted to the scriptures, should be known as a user of 'Rasayana.' ... (Further) he who, endued with these high attributes, uses Rasayana', enjoys all the effects enumerated of 'Rasayana.'

distinguishFrom.why: Code of good conduct for the healthy taught in Ca.Su.8 (Indriyopakramaniya); WHO 2022 gives it a separate entry ITA-10.3.7 'Harmonious way of living'. Achara rasayana is taught inside the Rasayana chapter and is defined by its rasayana (rejuvenative) outcome, not merely as ethics.
Achara rasayana is explicitly non-pharmacological; the text contrasts it with the kutipraveshika/vatatapika drug regimens that precede it.

Restraint of harmful mental/verbal/physical urges (Ca.Su.7.26-29) overlaps in content, and the NIA 2011 draft folds dharaniya vega into its achara rasayana definition, but they are separate concepts in the Samhita.

mistranslations.why: NIA 2011 draft wording; not meaningful English and 'virility' imports vajikarana connotations absent from the text.
Drops the rasayana claim entirely; the text's point is that conduct produces rasayana effects (nityarasāyanam), not merely that it is virtuous.
There is no drug; the Sanskrit colophon and WHO both make it a regimen of conduct.

classical.establishes: Defines the year as six seasons; the sun's northward course (udagayana) = ādāna, comprising the three seasons śiśira to grīṣma; varṣā to hemanta = dakṣiṇāyana = visarga.
classical.quote: इह खलु संवत्सरं षडङ्गमृतुविभागेन विद्यात्| तत्रादित्यस्योदगयनमादानं च त्रीनृतूञ्छिशिरादीन् ग्रीष्मान्तान् व्यवस्येत्, वर्षादीन् पुनर्हेमन्तान्तान् दक्षिणायनं विसर्गं च||४||

classical.establishes: Visarga is saumya (lunar/cooling), ādāna is āgneya (fiery); sun, wind and moon determine season, rasa, dosha and bodily strength.
classical.quote: विसर्गे पुनर्वायवो नातिरूक्षाः प्रवान्ति, इतरे पुनरादाने; सोमश्चाव्याहतबलः शिशिराभिर्भाभिरापूरयञ्जगदाप्याययति शश्वत्, अतो विसर्गः सौम्यः| आदानं पुनराग्नेयं; तावेतावर्कवायू सोमश्च कालस्वभावमार्गपरिगृहीताः कालर्तुरसदोषदेहबलनिर्वृत्तिप्रत्ययभूताःसमुपदिश्यन्ते||५||

classical.establishes: Strength is lowest at the start of visarga and end of ādāna, medium in the middle, highest at the end of visarga and start of ādāna.
classical.quote: भवन्ति चात्र- आदावन्ते च दौर्बल्यं विसर्गादानयोर्नृणाम्| मध्ये मध्यबलं, त्वन्ते श्रेष्ठमग्रे च निर्दिशेत्||८||

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 2, 3, 4 (printed after each passage); standard numbers 4 and 5 per carakasamhitaonline - recorded separately, not converted
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering of ādāna/visarga as 'Taking'/'Giving' periods; his footnote (not the text) supplies the month equivalences of the six seasons.
classical.quote: For the purposes of this lesson, the year should be known as consisting of six portions, divided according to the seasons. Of these, the three seasons commencing with the season of dews and ending with summer constitute the period when the Sun travels in the region lying to the north of the equinoctial. That is again the period when the Sun takes (i. e., sucks up the liquid portion of every earthly object). The three other seasons commencing with the season of rains and ending with Hemanta constitutes the period of the Sun's southerly course. That is, besides, the time when the Sun gives (or yields moisture to all earthly objects). ... Hence the period of Giving is mild (and agreeable). The period of Taking is fiery.

classical.verse: Sushruta Sutrasthana 6.7 (standard numbering; siva.sh Devanagari closes the passage ॥७॥). Bhishagratna Ch. VI, paragraph beginning 'The two Ayanams are ushered in', wisdomlib doc122894; he prints no verse numbers.
classical.establishes: Sushruta's parallel division of the year into two ayanas: śiśira, vasanta and grīṣma belong to uttarāyaṇa, in which the sun strengthens, three rasas grow strong, and the strength of all beings progressively declines (Su.Su.6.7). Two translator's choices to note: 'Summer Solstice' for uttarāyaṇa is Bhishagratna's English, not a doctrine; and his 'sour' is a mistranslation. The Sanskrit reads 'तिक्तकषायकटुकाश्च रसा बलवन्तो भवन्ति', bitter, ASTRINGENT (kaṣāya) and pungent; sour (amla) is assigned in the same sutra to dakṣiṇāyana ('अम्ललवणमधुराश्च रसा बलवन्तो भवन्ति'), which agrees with Caraka Su.6.6 as cited above (Kaviratna: 'dry, bitter, astringent, and pungent').
classical.quote: Winter, spring and summer mark the passing of the sun over the Summer Solstice (Uttarayana). The sun grows stronger in heat and light, and saps (rasas) of bitter, pungent and sour tastes increase in intensity, and all animals gradually begin to lose strength and energy.

classical.verse: opening verses (page gives no verse numbers; conventionally 1-6)
classical.establishes: Vagbhata restates ādāna/visarga with the etymology 'tad ādatte nṛṇāṁ pratidinaṁ balam' (it takes away men's strength day by day). Verse numbers not shown on the retrieved page.

distinguishFrom.why: The complementary half-year (varṣā, śarad, hemanta), saumya, in which strength is 'given back'; the two are defined together in Ca.Su.6.4-5.

Charaka equates ādāna with the sun's northward course, but uttarāyaṇa is an astronomical term; ādāna names the physiological effect (strength-taking). Bhishagratna's 'Summer Solstice' collapses a six-month course into a single day.
The 14-day transition between two seasons (WHO ITA-10.3.4); not a half-year.
Only the last of the three ādāna seasons; ādāna also includes the cold śiśira, so 'hot season' is wrong.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's rendering of Uttarayana; the solstice is an instant/day, whereas ādāna/uttarāyaṇa is a six-month course beginning in śiśira (cold season).
Reduces a three-season period that begins in late winter to its final season.
The text describes environmental absorption of sneha (unctuousness) and rasa changes, not a disease state.

classical.establishes: The list of 13 urges not to be suppressed: urine, faeces, semen, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, belching, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, and breathing from exertion. classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed numbers (page images, archive.org BIUSante_47357 leaves 104-105 = printed pp. 73-74): '1' after '...vomitting and sneezing' (p. 73) and '3' after '...pronounced forms' (p. 74); no '2' is printed, his paragraph covering standard 4 and 5 carries only the closing '3'. His next numbers '*4', '†5', '6', '7' sit on standard 6, 7, 8, 9. Standard address of the quote: Su 7.3-5 (carakasamhitaonline: ||३|| ||४|| and एतान् धारयतो जातान् वेगान् रोगा भवन्ति ये | पृथक्पृथक्चिकित्सार्थं तान्मे निगदतः शृणु ||५||). Recorded separately, not converted.
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English of the 13-urge list and of the transition verse (std 7.5). In this chapter his printed numbers sit two behind the standard (his 1 = std 3, his 3 = std 5, his 4 = std 6), with no '2' printed; this is a measured local fact and must not be generalised to other chapters.
classical.quote: One endued with intelligence should not suppress urgings, that have become pronounced, in respect of urine and faeces ; as also of the semen and the wind, and of vomitting and sneezing. The urgings also in respect of eructations, of yawns, of hunger and of thirst, of tears, of sleep, and of heavy breathing induced by toil (should not to be suppressed). Listen now to me as I discourse (to you) on the topic of treating the several diseases that are generated of the person who suppresses the urgings of these when they appear in pronounced forms.

classical.quote: Udavarta is so called from its origin from the repression of any natural urging such as Vata (flatus), evacuation of bowels, micturition, yawning, lacrimation, sneezing, eructation, vomiting and discharge of semen...

distinguishFrom.why: The urges that SHOULD be restrained (greed, grief, anger, harsh speech, violence, etc.), Ca.Su.7.26-29; the opposite category.
The disease produced by suppressing urges (Su.Ut.55), not the urge itself.
The act of suppressing; adhāraṇīya-vega names the urges.
In toxicology and fever contexts vega means a paroxysm/impulse of poison (NIA 2011: vegāntara 'interval between two attacks'); unrelated.

mistranslations.why: Direct inversion; adhāraṇīya means not-to-be-held.
Hunger, thirst, sleep and tears are not reflexes in the physiological sense; 'urge' is the sense intended.

classical.establishes: Charaka's agantu: bhūta-viṣa-vāyu-agni-samprahāra-ādi-samuttha, arising from spirits, poison, wind, fire, assault and the like. Notably broader than Sushruta's abhighata-only agantu.

distinguishFrom.why: The complementary class. Nija arises from one's own doshas, agantu from an external agent. The complementarity is real but the boundary is not: Charaka's agantu includes bhuta (possessing entities) and Sushruta's does not.

WHO ISTA glosses adhibhautika as 'Extrinsic, exogenous diseases' with a description nearly identical to Charaka's agantu. They belong to different classifications (tapa-traya vs nija/agantu) and must not be merged just because their English descriptions converge.

Sushruta's traumatic class in the seven-fold bala-pravritta scheme of Su.Su.24. Overlaps agantu in extension but sits in a different taxonomy within the same text, so Sushruta classifies trauma twice, in two schemes.
Sushruta's fourth class. 'Natural' processes are not caused by an external agent and are not agantu, though both are sometimes lumped as 'not caused by dosha'.

Specific disease entities (fever of external origin, traumatic ulcer) that carry the agantu qualifier. WHO ISTA codes these individual compounds and not the class term, so retrieving them and treating them as the class definition is an error.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's own choice, and misleading in modern English because 'accidental' implies chance. Agantu means 'arriving, coming from outside'; a deliberate assault and a snakebite are agantu and neither is accidental.

A very common modern over-reading, encouraged by the gloss of bhuta as 'invisible organisms'. Agantu is defined by externality of the agent, not transmissibility. WHO ISTA codes contagious disease separately (ITA-4.2.32, samsargajarogaḥ).

Correct for Sushruta (abhighata-nimitta) and too narrow for Charaka, whose agantu includes poison, fire, wind and bhuta. A single English word cannot serve both texts and the lexicon should say so rather than pick one.
Occasionally seen by confusion with 'of unknown cause'. Agantu is the class with the most conspicuous cause of all.

openQuestions: Do the commentators note the discrepancy between Charaka's broad agantu (bhuta, visha, vayu, agni, samprahara) and Sushruta's narrow abhighata-only agantu, or is it simply left standing?
Where does Sushruta's own agantu class sit relative to his samghata-bala-pravritta class in Su.Su.24? The two taxonomies coexist in one sthana and I did not find a passage reconciling them.

classical.establishes: Agni is the cause of lifespan, complexion, strength, health, exertion, growth, lustre, ojas, tejas and the pranas, all of which Ci.15.3 calls dehagni-hetukah; and Ci.15.4 concludes mulam agnis tasman nirucyate, agni is therefore called the root. Kaviratna prints these as his aphorisms 2 and 3, which is one behind the standard here. HIS OFFSET IN THIS CHAPTER IS NOT CONSTANT and must never be applied by arithmetic: he is level by his 120-121 and runs one ahead from his 195.
classical.quote: The period of life, complexion, strength, health, exertion, growth, lustre, ojas, energy, animal and other kinds of heat, and the life-breaths, have all been said to have the digestive fire for their cause. When this fire becomes extinguished, a person dies. When it burns within the body, one lives long without ailments of any kind. When it becomes vitiated, one becomes afflicted with disease. For these reasons, this fire is said to be the root (of all).
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Sanskrit wording and standard verse number for the 'agni is the root' statement, used to fix Kaviratna's off-by-one numbering.
classical.quote: शान्तेऽग्नौ म्रियते, युक्ते चिरं जीवत्यनामयः। रोगी स्याद्विकृते, मूलमग्निस्तस्मान्निरुच्यते॥४॥

classical.establishes: Charaka's position on the agni-pitta relation: agni is 'within' pitta (pittāntargata), not simply identical with it. Kaviratna renders agni here as 'the heat dwelling in the body' rather than 'digestive fire'.
classical.quote: The son of Marichi said,—The heat dwelling in the body, within the Bile, when excited, produces evil and when in its normal condition leads to beneficial consequences. This is as follows :—In its normal condition it aids digestion, vision, the proper measure of warmth (of body), propriety of complexion, courage, cheerfulness, and free play of the faculties, &c. When excited, it produces indigestion, weakness of vision, an improper measure of warmth, an unhealthy complexion, fear, wrath,

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi's gloss on pittāntargata, in his own voice and not Charaka's: by that word Charaka rules out a flame-bearing fire (jvālādiyukta-vahni) in the body and establishes a fire whose form is the heat of pitta (pittoṣmarūpasya vahneḥ sadbhāvam), while still not asserting its non-difference from pitta (na tu pittād abhedam). His two reasons are that agnimāndya is to be treated in the Grahaṇī chapter without being located in pitta, and that ghee, which reduces pitta, is nonetheless described as increasing agni. This is the key text for the agni/pitta disambiguation and the locus where agnimāndya enters the commentarial layer.
classical.quote: [mūla, Ca.Sū.12.11] marīciruvāca agnireva śarīre pittāntargataḥ kupitākupitaḥ śubhāśubhāni karoti tadyathā paktimapaktiṃ darśanamadarśanaṃ mātrāmātratvam ūṣmaṇaḥ prakṛtivikṛtivarṇau śauryaṃ bhayaṃ krodhaṃ harṣaṃ mohaṃ prasādam ityevamādīni cāparāṇi dvaṃdvānīti // [Āyurvedadīpikā ad loc., Cakrapāṇi's voice, not Charaka's] pittāntargata iti vacanena śarīre jvālādiyuktavahniniṣedhena pittoṣmarūpasya vahneḥ sadbhāvaṃ darśayati na tu pittādabhedaṃ pitte nāgnimāndyasya grahaṇyadhyāye vakṣyamāṇatvāt tathā pittaharasya sarpiṣo'gnivardhanatvenoktatvāt

classical.verse: prose section, pp. 196-197 of Bhishagratna vol. I
classical.establishes: Sushruta's contrary doctrine: agni IS pitta, and there is no separate fire in the body. Charaka/Cakrapāṇi and Sushruta disagree on this point, which is the single most important thing a lexicon entry on agni has to record.
classical.quote: Now it may be asked whether the Pittam is identical with the elemental fire, or is it something other than that ? The question may be answered by stating that the Pittam is the same as fire. Since such symptoms, as a burning sensation, digestion (boiling), and all other characteristics of fire can never exhibit themselves in the human body without the intervention of Pittam. Pittam therefore is called internal fire. ... There is no other fire (heat making factor) in the organism than Pittam.

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Su.Sū.35.27. Bhishagratna dissolves the compound 'jāṭhara ... agni' into 'the fire that burns within a person'; the Sanskrit verse number is fixed independently from sa.wikisource.
classical.quote: The fire, that burns within a person, is godly in its subtle essence, and possesses the divine attributes of atom-like invisibility, weightlessness, etc., and is the digestant of food. It takes up the lymph chyle of different tastes for the purpose of digestion, and is invisible owing to its extremely subtle essence.

distinguishFrom.why: Sushruta Sū.21 says there is no fire in the body other than pitta; Charaka Sū.12.11 says agni is 'within pitta' (pittāntargata) and Cakrapāṇi expressly denies their non-difference. Treating agni and pitta as synonyms silently picks a side in a live classical dispute.
ūṣman is heat as a property or measurable warmth; agni is the functional agent that produces transformation. Kaviratna translates both as 'heat', which loses the distinction.
WHO ISTA gives kāyāgni its own term ID (ITA-2.6.2, 'Metabolic factors of the body') distinct from agni (ITA-2.6.1). Much textbook writing uses the two interchangeably.
agnibala is the strength or capacity of agni — the thing questionnaires actually measure (PMID 27381899) — not agni itself.
Pure homonym. Search results and lay sources routinely conflate the physiological term with the fire god.

mistranslations.why: Reduces a whole-body regulatory concept spanning gut, tissue and elemental levels to a class of proteins. Bhishagratna's own 1907 gloss ('bile and pancreatic secretions') already shows this compression happening, and it does not survive contact with dhātvagni or bhūtāgni.

Drops the specifically digestive/gastrointestinal sense and, more importantly, drops the normative claim (agni as 'root' of lifespan and health) that the classical texts make. WHO's compound 'digestive, metabolic factors' is a deliberate repair of this.
Acceptable as a calque and used by both public-domain translators, but it invites literal thermal readings ('raising body heat'). Su.Sū.35.27 explicitly calls it invisible and subtle, not thermal.
A modern popular equation with no classical warrant; it cannot account for the seven tissue-level agnis.

openQuestions: Does WHO ISTA document why it rejected 'fire' for 'factors'?
Is there a critical edition consensus on whether Ca.Sū.12.11's pittāntargata implies identity or containment?
Which of the three competing Agni/Agnibala/Jāṭharāgni questionnaires, if any, has been validated against an external physiological criterion?

classical.establishes: The word agnimāndya in a retrievable pre-modern source. Glossing Charaka's pittāntargataḥ, Cakrapāṇi argues that the body's fire exists in the form of pitta's heat, a fire without flames, but is not identical with pitta, for two reasons: agnimāndya is to be discussed in the Grahaṇī chapter, and pitta-reducing ghee is described as agni-increasing. Both turn on agni and pitta moving in opposite directions. This is commentarial usage of roughly the 11th century and is what Cakrapāṇi says, not what Charaka says; the mūla of 12.11 does not contain the word.

classical.establishes: Sitagnita stands in Charaka's list of twenty kaphaja disorders at Ca.Su.20, and Kaviratna DOES render it: his footnote on p. 230 reads "17. Citagnita is loss of appetite and inability to take any food", so a public-domain English rendering exists. Note on the locator: NAMASTE cites Ca.Su.20/17, where 17 is the VERSE number and not a position in the list. classical.establishes: The classical aetiology of impaired agni, in public-domain English: dietary, iatrogenic, disease-related, environmental and urge-suppression causes. Verse numbers confirmed against the Sanskrit (Ca.Ci.15.42 'अभोजनादजीर्णातिभोजनाद्विषमाशनात्', Ca.Ci.15.44 'दुष्यत्यग्निः, स दुष्टोऽन्नं न तत् पचति लघ्वपि').
classical.quote: From abstention from all food, from eating food that is indigestible, from eating to excess, from eating food consisting of inharmonious ingredients, from eating food that is not assimilable, or is heavy, or cold, or excessively dry (unoily), or vitiated, from errors in the administration of purgatives, emetics, and oils, from affliction (i. e., weakness, emaciation, &c.,) by diseases, from absence of harmony in respect of place (habitat), time (age), and season, from suppression of the urgings (of nature), the (digestive) fire is vitiated. The vitiated fire cannot digest food that is even light.

classical.establishes: The mechanism linking impaired agni to āma: the vitiated fire cannot digest even light food, and undigested food becomes sour (śukta) and acquires the nature of poison (viṣarūpatā).
classical.quote: दुष्यत्यग्निः, स दुष्टोऽन्नं न तत् पचति लघ्वपि। अपच्यमानं शुक्तत्वं यात्यन्नं विषरूपताम् ॥४४॥

distinguishFrom.why: The central distinction. mandāgni names a state or type of agni; agnimāndya names the condition of agni being dulled. The standards split on which they carry: WHO has only mandāgni, ICD-11 TM2 has only agnimāndya, NAMASTE has mandāgni as a code and agnimāndya only as a gloss. Treating them as one word will break any cross-standard mapping.

ICD-11 SM3B puts them under one code, but ajīrṇa is the failure to digest a particular meal (with its own vātaja/pittaja/kaphaja/āmaja subtypes in NAMASTE, e.g. EB-3.3 Amaja-ajīrṇam) whereas agnimāndya is the standing impairment of capacity.
NAMASTE glosses śītāgnitā as agnimāndya and restricts it to kapha alone (kEvala-kapha). If that restriction is real, agnimāndya is the broader term and the gloss is loose.

Dyspepsia is a symptom complex defined by epigastric pain, fullness and early satiety with duration criteria; agnimāndya is a functional-capacity diagnosis that can exist without any of those symptoms. The National Health Portal's equation is administratively convenient and clinically lossy.
Ca.Ci.15.56 makes weak agni causally prior to grahaṇī vitiation. The disease and the impairment are at different levels.
ICD-11 TM2 has a separate Anorexia disorder (TM2). Loss of desire for food is not the same as loss of digestive capacity.

mistranslations.why: Used by the National Health Portal of India and widespread in clinical writing. It maps a capacity concept onto a symptom cluster, and it makes the condition undiagnosable in an asymptomatic patient with poor digestion — which is precisely the case classical practice cares about.
Same problem as ICD-11's SM3B grouping: it collapses agnimāndya into ajīrṇa, losing the standing-versus-episodic distinction.
Systemic framing for a term whose classical aetiology (Ca.Ci.15.42-44) is almost entirely dietary and behavioural.
No source I retrieved supports this; ICD-11 TM2 keeps Hyperacidity disorder (SM3A) separate.

openQuestions: Where does agnimāndya first appear as a fixed compound — Mādhava Nidāna, Cakrapāṇi, or earlier?
Why does WHO ISTA omit a term that ICD-11 TM2 indexes?
Is NAMASTE right that śītāgnitā is agnimāndya restricted to kapha?
Does Bhāvaprakāśa Ma.28/3 define it?

classical.establishes: Food (anna) is the life of living beings; complexion, clarity, voice, life, intelligence, happiness, contentment, nourishment, strength and intellect all rest on food. Note the verse uses anna, not āhāra.
classical.quote: प्राणाःप्राणभृतामन्नमन्नंलोकोऽभिधावति। वर्णःप्रसादःसौस्वर्यंजीवितंप्रतिभासुखम्॥३४९॥ तुष्टिःपुष्टिर्बलंमेधासर्वमन्नेप्रतिष्ठितम्। लौकिकंकर्मयद्वृत्तौस्वर्गतौयच्चवैदिकम्॥३५०॥

classical.establishes: Use of hita (wholesome) āhāra alone promotes growth of the person; ahita āhāra is the cause of disease.

classical.verse: Kaviratna Sutrasthana Lesson XXVII, printed p. 329 (archive.org BIUSante_47357 leaf 449), his aphorism 2 only (his printed '2' follows 'they become injurious'; his 1 closes the two opening sentences, his 3 the Agnivesa sentence) = standard Sutrasthana 27.3 (carakasamhitaonline ||3||; GRETIL Car_1,27.3). His 1 merges standard 27.1-2.
classical.establishes: Kaviratna renders anna-pāna as 'food and drink': the Sanskrit of this sutra is 'vidhivihitam annapānaṁ' and the chapter title annapānavidhi, which he gives as 'the ordinances relating to food and drink'. The passage says nothing about his rendering of āhāra, which does not occur in it; that half of the earlier claim needs a passage where the mula actually has āhāra.
classical.quote: Physicians skilled in the science of Life say that food and drink that are agreeable in point of color, scent, taste, and touch, and consistent with the ordinances laid down, are the very Life of those living creatures that are said to be animated. This appears from the visible effects thereof. In consequence, again, of the fuel of food and drink is the existence of the (digestive) fire; Food and drink develop strength of both body and mind. If taken according to the measure that is directed, food and drink lead to the growth of the several ingredients of the body, of strength and complexion, and contribute to the cheerfulness of the senses. If taken otherwise, they become injurious.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Sushruta's statement of food as source of strength and the four modes of intake (ashita, pita, lidha, khadita).
classical.quote: Food is the source of the growth, strength, and healthful glow of organic beings. It is food that imparts strength to the organs of sense and makes them operative in their respective fields of action. It is irregularity (Vaishamya) of diet which brings about ill-health. Diet may be divided into four kinds such as, solid food, (Ashitha) drink, Līdham (food taken by licking), and the Khadita (food that is chewn and assimilated only for the enjoyment of a specific taste).

distinguishFrom.why: 'Food/cooked grain'; often interchangeable (Ca.Su.27 uses anna in the key verse) but anna can mean specifically cooked rice/grain.
Pathya is the wholesome subset of āhāra and vihāra; āhāra is the whole category of food.
Medicine; Ayurveda treats food and medicine as a continuum (āhāra as the 'great medicine'), but the categories remain distinct in the texts.
Activities/regimen (WHO ITA-10.2.14), the behavioural counterpart to āhāra.

mistranslations.why: In modern English 'diet' connotes a restrictive or prescribed regimen; āhāra is simply what is eaten. Acceptable only when context makes it neutral.
A biochemical abstraction; āhāra is the ingested substance, and the texts classify it by mode of intake (eaten, drunk, licked, chewed), not nutrient content.

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Vi 8/120.
classical.quote: Next, as to examination (of the patient) in respect of capacity for food. One's capacity for food is to be ascertained from one's capacity for eating as also capacity for digesting; since strength and period of life are both dependent upon food.

classical.establishes: In the same chapter where Sushruta examines the patient, digestive capacity is handled as the four states of agni (sama, viṣama, tīkṣṇa, manda) rather than as a śakti. Sushruta's framework for this domain is agni, not āhāraśakti — a structural difference between the two samhitas. No verse numbers on the retrieved page.
classical.quote: The digestive heat, which fully digests the ingested food at the proper time without the least irregularity, thus reflecting the continuance of the bodily humours in their normal state, is called Samagni .

distinguishFrom.why: The commonest conflation. Agni is the digestive fire with four states; jaraṇa-śakti is the capacity it confers, and āhāraśakti the composite with intake. Sushruta Sutrasthana 35 handles the domain entirely through agni and never uses āhāraśakti.
One limb, not the whole. WHO defines it as the amount of food that does not disturb physiological function — a quantity, not a desire.
The other limb. A patient can have good jaraṇa-śakti and poor abhyavaharaṇa-śakti, which is why Vi 8/120 requires both.
Desire to eat. Neither limb of āhāraśakti is desire; both are capacities.
Bowel type, a different axis of digestive assessment.
Used in later writing for much the same idea, but it folds āhāraśakti back into the agni framework and loses the intake limb.

mistranslations.why: Reduces two capacities to one desire, and the wrong one. The Sanskrit asks how much a person can take in and digest, not how much he wants.
That is agni. Vi 8/120 examines demonstrated capacity, which is evidence about agni, not agni itself.
A modern systemic concept covering far more, and implying measurement methods the term does not have.
Drops the intake limb, which is half the definition.

openQuestions: Is there any validated instrument for assessing āhāraśakti, or does assessment rest entirely on clinical interview? None found.

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English of the vidhāna; here his number runs one AHEAD of the standard (his 25 = std 24), the opposite direction from Su.7.
classical.quote: The following provisions relating to the ordinances of food are beneficial for the hale as also for those that are diseased. As regards some persons these become most beneficial at certain seasons in consequence of the very nature of those persons. Food that is warm, oily, and according to the proper measure, should be taken. It should also be taken after that previously taken has been properly digested. It should also consist of such ingredients as would not form a compound of hostile potencies. One should take one's food in a place that is agreeable, (i. e., not repulsive). The food one takes should, again, consist of dishes every one of which is agreeable One should not eat with haste ; or taking up a long time ; or talking, or laughing the while. While eating, one should eat with attention concentrated thereon. Lastly, one should eat after a proper survey of oneself.

classical.verse: Sanskrit verse number not established (Bhishagratna prints none)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's parallel rules of eating (warm, unctuous, light, timely, erect posture, attentive, neither hurried nor slow) with his own reasons for each.
classical.quote: A man, who is well-read in the Science of medicine (Ayurveda), should sit during his meal in an easy posture on a high seat and partake, at the right time, with his body erect and his whole mind engaged in the act of eating light, wholesome emollient and warm viands, which are congenial to his temperament and abound in fluid preparations, with an adequate quantity of boiled rice, neither too hurriedly nor too slowly, even when feeling the pinch of a keen and piercing hunger. Food eaten with a good appetite tastes pleasant and relishing. The food which is congenial to one's temperament begets no discomfort after the eating. Light food is soon digested. Emollient food gives tone and vigour to the system. Warm food improves the appetite. Food eaten neither too slowly nor too hurriedly is uniformly digested.

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Vi.1.21: prakṛti, karaṇa, saṁyoga, rāśi, deśa, kāla, upayogasaṁsthā, upayoktā - the determinants of a food's effect. The vidhāna (Vi.1.24) is the set of eating rules, which Chakrapani and modern authors place under the single factor upayogasaṁsthā. WHO 2022 encodes only the eight factors.

The vidhāna is about the manner of eating (temperature, pace, attention, setting), not which foods to choose.

distinguishFrom.why: The two negative limbs are not the same. Duḥkhāyu (Su 30.24: asukham) is the reverse of the health-and-circumstances description; ahitāyu is the reverse of the ethical-conduct description. A rich, healthy, happy person living badly is ahitāyu and sukhāyu at once.
Ahita-āhāra, unsuitable food, is a different and much commoner use of the word ahita. Ahitāyu is about the conduct of a life, not about a substance.
Apathya is the contra-indicated regimen for a condition. Ahitāyu is a description of a whole life, and is not prescriptive.

mistranslations.why: Health does not appear in the ahitāyu definition; that content belongs to the duḥkhāyu side of the verse.
Over-translates. The Sanskrit says only viparyayeṇa, by the reverse; the moral colouring comes from the list of virtues in the hitāyu half, not from a separate term.

Ambiguous between harmful to oneself and harmful to others. The Sanskrit derives it by negation and does not specify which, and WHO's description covers both ('disadvantageous for oneself and generally detrimental') without resolving it either.

openQuestions: Whether any classical commentator supplies positive content for ahitāyu rather than leaving it as viparyaya. Chakrapani on Su 30.24 was not retrieved.

Whether the standalone word ahitāyuḥ occurs anywhere in the Brhattrayi as a single word, or whether, as the two verses I retrieved suggest, it is always hitāhita as a compound or ahitam as a predicate. This is checkable against a full Sanskrit corpus and I could not check it: GRETIL's Charaka file covers only Su 1.1-1.43 and a few other blocks, not Su 30.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed numbers here are OCR-garbled ('5*-35' and '*34''); standard numbering 1.27 and 1.29 per Sanskrit at carakasamhitaonline.com: शब्दः स्पर्शश्च रूपं च रसो गन्धश्च तद्गुणाः||२७|| ... खरद्रवचलोष्णत्वं भूजलानिलतेजसाम्| आकाशस्याप्रतीघातो दृष्टं लिङ्गं यथाक्रमम्||२९||
classical.establishes: Ākāśa's guṇa is śabda (sound) and its liṅga is apratīghāta (non-obstruction), the basis of the WHO/NAMASTE 'non-obstruction' definitions. Two passages joined with [...]; OCR spacing collapsed.
classical.quote: The great primal elements are ether (space), air, fire (or light), water, and earth. Their (respective) attributes are sound, touch, form (vision), taste, and scent. Each of the great elements has one of these attributes; while each succeeding one has (in addition) the attribute or attributes of the preceding one or ones. Thus ether has sound; air has touch and sound; fire (or light) has form (or vision) and touch and sound; water has taste and form, and touch and sound; and earth has scent, and taste, and form, and touch and sound. [...] Roughness, liquidity, mobility, and heat are (respectively) seen to be the properties of earth, water, air, and fire; while, of ether the property is non-resistibility.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna section 20 (his numbering). Sanskrit verse 19 per siva.sh: आन्तरिक्षाः- शब्दः शब्देन्द्रियं सर्वच्छिद्रसमूहो विविक्तता च; ... (https://www.siva.sh/sushruta-samhita/sharira-sthana/1/19)
classical.establishes: Suśruta's list of ākāśa-derived features in the body: sound (śabda), the auditory faculty (śabdendriya), the aggregate of all hollows (sarvacchidra-samūha), and distinctness (viviktatā). Bhishagratna renders the fourth as 'differentia evolution of the veins, ligaments etc. into their characterised species (Viviktata)', an expansive gloss of the single word viviktatā; the Sanskrit has no mention of veins or ligaments.
classical.quote: The properties of akasha (ether) are sound, the sense of hearing, porosity and differentia evolution of the veins, ligaments etc. into their characterised species (Viviktata.)

distinguishFrom.why: Bodily hollows are ākāśa-derived (Su.Śā. 1.19 sarvacchidra-samūha; Ca.Śā. 5.4 'the hollow places are Ether'), and the NIA draft even glosses ākāśa as 'synonym of Srotas', but srotas are structures, ākāśa is the bhūta.
19th-century physics concept imported by 'ether' renderings (NIA draft SK0003, Bhishagratna 'Etherion'); Ayurveda's ākāśa is defined by non-obstruction and sound, not as a medium.
Ākāśa is a positive dravya with a guṇa (śabda), not emptiness.
A separate kāraṇadravya (Ca.Sū. 1.48; WHO ITA-1.9.3.1.1), often blurred with 'space' in English.

mistranslations.why: Still used by WHO-era comparators (NAMASTE 'ether/space'), but carries physics connotations; WHO 2022 dropped it for 'Space'. Kaviratna's hedge 'Ether (or Space)' and his gloss 'non-resistibility' show the translators themselves felt the gap.
Bhishagratna's footnote to Su.Sū. 41 (a now-abandoned 1900s hypothetical gas), explicitly a modern-science equivalence by the translator, not the text.
Bhishagratna 'Sky (Vyoma)', 'principle of sky (Akashiyam)': vyoma does mean sky, but as a mahābhūta the referent is space/non-obstruction, not the atmosphere.

openQuestions: Bhishagratna's 'differentia evolution of the veins, ligaments etc.' for viviktatā needs a Sanskritist's check.
Kaviratna's printed numbers for Ca.Śā. 1.27-29 should be read from page scans; the OCR text is unreliable there.

distinguishFrom.why: Prakṛti is the constitutional type assessed in the tenfold examination; ākṛti in the Yogaratnakara is current outward build/appearance read for dosha-predominance. Modern papers fold the two together ('may be considered under Deha prakriti pariksha', IJARSCT review), which is an interpretation, not the text's own equation.
WHO 2022 lists ākṛtiḥ as a synonym of liṅga/lakṣaṇa/rūpa (clinical presentation). In that sense ākṛti means the form the disease takes, not the patient's physique.
The Nirnaya Sagar Yogaratnakara heads the relevant section 'rūpa-parīkṣā' while the enumeration verse says 'ākṛti'; the two words are being used interchangeably in that edition.
Compactness and proportion of the body are separate items in the tenfold examination; 'physique' renderings of ākṛti blur into them.

mistranslations.why: Overstates it: in the Yogaratnakara the item is one of eight sites, a short section on dosha-typed appearance, not a whole-body work-up.
Narrower than the text, whose rūpa/ākṛti verses describe the whole person (hair, limbs, complexion, temperament).

openQuestions: Does the Vidyotini (Chaukhambha) edition head the section 'ākṛti-parīkṣā' or 'rūpa-parīkṣā'? The IJARSCT paper cites Vidyotini 2015 for its ākṛti material but gives page numbers only.

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa agrees with Suśruta on both seat (dṛk-stha) and function (rūpa-ālocana), and gives the explicit etymology: it is called ālocaka FROM rūpa-ālocana. This is the one pitta subtype on which the two authorities do not disagree.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: At Su.Sū. 15.4 the function list gives tejaḥ-kṛt, which Bhishagratna maps to eyesight. But tejas is also the general fire-element and, separately, a name for the subtle essence of pitta. Reading 'tejas' as automatically meaning ālocaka is unsafe.

Dṛṣṭi is the anatomical/functional seat (roughly the pupil and visual apparatus); ālocaka is the pitta operating there. Ophthalmology chapters of the Uttaratantra discuss dṛṣṭi extensively without invoking ālocaka.

Both are 'surface' pittas concerned with appearance — bhrājaka with the complexion being SEEN, ālocaka with the act of SEEING. The Sanskrit roots (bhrāj- to shine, ālocana to look at) are easy to swap in translation.
Prāṇa vāta is also credited with governing the sense organs including the eyes. The division is that vāta carries and enables, pitta apprehends form.

mistranslations.why: A modern speculative correlate presented as a meaning. Nothing in either mūla concerns photochemistry, and I found no peer-reviewed paper that even defends this equation, let alone tests it.

Too thin. Rūpa-grahaṇa is the apprehension of visible FORM AND COLOUR specifically, one of the five viṣayas matched to one of the five bhūtas. 'Eyesight' loses the element-to-sense-object architecture that is the reason ālocaka is a PITTA at all (tejas/agni is the element of rūpa).
An anatomical substitution. The classical seat is dṛṣṭi, the visual apparatus at the front of the eye, not a nerve tract.

openQuestions: Does any classical text distinguish an ālocaka that apprehends from an ālocaka that interprets? Some later commentarial traditions are said to split it into cakṣur-vaiśeṣika and buddhi-vaiśeṣika ālocaka — I could NOT verify this in any retrieved source and have deliberately not recorded it.
What does Suśruta's own Uttaratantra (the ophthalmology section) say about ālocaka, if anything? I did not search it.
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 carries any ālocaka-pitta entry.

renderings.english: Ama, a state of incomplete digestion, transformation or metabolism
renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.assessment: WHO keeps the Sanskrit word in the English term rather than translating it — an explicit judgement that āma is untranslatable. WHO's description, verbatim: 'A transient state of the body wherein the digestive, metabolic processes come to a standstill and do not further transform to end products, by-products or waste products. This standstill leads to various changes in the body such as blockade of channels, excess secretions, unusual accumulation of waste materials, slowing down of movements and catabolic processes. It presents with the following generic symptoms: loss of strength, heaviness, laziness, tastelessness or altered taste, and exhaustion even without physical or mental exertion. The ama phase is an initial stage of almost all disorders, e.g. fever or diarrhoea, which arises due to vitiation of endogenous factors: dosha, fundamental structural components and excretory products. Physiologically, the ama phase denotes early digestion of food in the stomach.' Note WHO calls it a STATE or PHASE, never a substance.

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's only explicit English equation of āma with undigested food, and the causal chain from weak agni through grahaṇī vitiation to āma. Verse number fixed against the Sanskrit (Ca.Ci.15.56 'अग्न्यधिष्ठानमन्नस्य ग्रहणाद्ग्रहणी मता').
classical.quote: The duct called 'Grahani' is the seat of the digestive fire, and because it takes the food that is eaten, therefore is it called 'Grahani' (taker). It is placed above the (region of the) navel. ... It holds the food in its undigested state. After digestion, it lets out the digested food through its lower opening. When the digestive fire is weak, the 'Grahani' becomes vitiated, It then discharges only undigested food (called Ama)

classical.establishes: The transformation: undigested food becomes sour and takes on the nature of poison. The word here is anna, not āma; the āma terminology is applied to this state by the tradition rather than by this verse.
classical.quote: अपच्यमानं शुक्तत्वं यात्यन्नं विषरूपताम् ॥४४॥

classical.establishes: āma is mobile and can spread systemically (śarīrānugate sāme rase), and its management is laṅghana plus pācana. Kaviratna transliterates 'ama Rasa' rather than translating. The Sanskrit at Ca.Ci.15.75 reads 'शरीरानुगते सामे रसे लङ्घनपाचनम्'.
classical.quote: When the 'ama Rasa' (i. e., the undigested juice of the food taken) spreads over the whole body, fasting and the administration of 'Pachana' (i. e., drugs which assist in digesting undigested food, without increasing the appetite) are prescribable.

classical.establishes: Two locations of āma (adherent in the pakvāśaya vs following the rasa through the body) with two different treatments. This is the textual basis for the sthānika/systemic distinction that modern writing usually flattens.
classical.quote: लीनं पक्वाशयस्थं वाऽऽप्यामं स्राव्यं सदीपनैः। शरीरानुगते सामे रसे लङ्घनपाचनम्॥७५॥

distinguishFrom.why: WHO separates āma (ITA-4.6.2, the state) from sāmadoṣa (ITA-4.8.23, a doṣa carrying āma). NAMASTE codes āmadoṣaḥ (DA) as the vitiated condition. āma is the state; āmadoṣa is the pathological entity that state produces.

Ajīrṇa is the failure of a meal to digest. āma is the residue/state that failure creates and which can then travel and lodge. WHO's own gloss makes āma an early phase of almost all disorders, which ajīrṇa is not.

Normal waste products of properly completed digestion (Ca.Ci.15.15 kiṭṭa-prasāda). āma is the product of digestion that did NOT complete. NAMASTE codes sāmamala (CB-3) precisely because mala can additionally carry āma.
The everyday adjective 'raw, unripe' — the same word. Kaviratna's scan has 'āmamāṃsa' (raw meat) in unrelated contexts. Automated term extraction will over-match badly.
A live retrieval hazard rather than a conceptual one: PubMed searches on 'AMA' return hepatology literature. I had to search on compounds (āmavāta, āmadoṣa) to get anything relevant.
See the separate record. āma becoming poison is a further stage, not a synonym.

mistranslations.why: The most consequential error in this whole cluster. Both WHO ISTA and NAMASTE conspicuously decline to translate āma at all rather than use 'toxin'. 'Toxin' implies an identified exogenous or endogenous poisonous substance with a mechanism; āma as WHO defines it is a transient state of arrested transformation. The 'toxin' rendering also feeds directly into detox marketing.

Kaviratna's own rendering, and defensible for the gut-level sense at Ca.Ci.15.56, but it cannot account for āma following the rasa through the body (Ca.Ci.15.75) or for sāmapitta, sāmakapha and sāmamala, where the āma is not food.
A specific biomedical identification with no supporting study. The one paper that goes near it (PMID 22556911) proposes free radicals, not endotoxin, and proposes rather than demonstrates.
Collides with mala/kiṭṭa, which are the normal waste products and are explicitly distinguished from āma in the same chapter.

openQuestions: Is there a classical definitional sentence for āma, or is it defined only ostensively?
Is āma a substance, a state, or deliberately both? WHO and Kaviratna give different answers.
What are the exact Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya Sū.13 verses for sāma/nirāma lakṣaṇa that NAMASTE cites?
Has any study proposed a measurable biomarker for āma that survived replication? I found none.

classical.establishes: The compound āmaviṣa occurs verbatim in the Charaka mūla, as a named disease in the list of conditions caused by viruddha āhāra (incompatible food). Independently corroborated from the GRETIL Charaka text ('pāṇḍvāmayasyāmaviṣasya caiva // car_1,26.102'), retrieved separately this session.

classical.establishes: A second mūla occurrence: the cilicima fish taken with milk 'provokes āmaviṣa'. Confirms āmaviṣa is used in Charaka as something that can be provoked by a specific incompatible combination, not merely as a general state.
classical.quote: sa hi mahābhiṣyanditvāt sthūlalakṣaṇatarān etān vyādhīn upajanayatyāmaviṣam udīrayati ca

classical.establishes: A precision point that matters: the compound in the grahaṇī chapter is ANNAVIṢA ('food-poison'), not āmaviṣa. Much secondary writing quotes this verse as the locus for āmaviṣa. It is not; the āmaviṣa attestations are in Sūtrasthāna 26.
classical.quote: जृम्भाऽङ्गमर्दस्तृष्णा च ज्वरश्छर्दिः प्रवाहणम्। अरोचकोऽविपाकश्च, घोरमन्नविषं च तत्॥४६॥

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for the annaviṣa verse and its symptom list. Kaviratna continues: undigested food combining with excited bile, phlegm or wind produces the corresponding disease families, and 'When it goes into the urine, that poison causes diseases of the urine...' — i.e. the poison is mobile and organ-tropic.
classical.quote: The following are the symptoms of indigestion (of the food taken): flatulence of the stomach, langour of the body, headache, swoons, vertigo, pains in the back and the waist, yawns, lassitude of the limbs, thirst, fever, vomiting, dysentery (white flux), disgust for food, and absence of transformation into healthy stools. The food in the stomach that is not digested is a terrible poison.

classical.establishes: The clearest classical statement of the concept, though not using the compound āmaviṣa: the most terrible āmadoṣa is 'viṣa-saṃjñaka', called by the name of poison, because it acts rapidly like poison and because its treatment is self-contradictory (what relieves one aspect aggravates another). Vāgbhaṭa says such a case is to be refused. Chapter fixed by the file's own internal variant markers (8.11bv, 8.16bv).
classical.quote:
āma-doṣaṃ mahā-ghoraṃ varjayed viṣa-saṃjñakam |
viṣa-rūpāśu-kāri-tvād viruddhopakrama-tvataḥ || 14 ||
classical.translator: none — no public-domain English translation of Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya exists

distinguishFrom.why: āma is the state of arrested digestion; āmaviṣa is the further stage in which that state acts with the rapidity and lethality of poison. Vāgbhaṭa marks the difference prognostically — āmaviṣa/viṣasaṃjñaka āmadoṣa is to be refused as a case.

The compound actually used at Ca.Ci.15.46. Widely misquoted as āmaviṣa. Whether Charaka intended two terms or one is an open philological question; a lexicon should keep them as separate headwords until it is settled.

Classical toxicology treats exogenous poisons as a separate discipline with its own nidāna and cikitsā (NAMASTE codes P, PA, PE series). āmaviṣa is endogenous and is called poison by analogy of behaviour, not by class membership.
Artificial compounded poison and latent residual poison respectively — both exogenous, both distinct from āmaviṣa, and all three are routinely lumped together in popular 'ama = toxin' writing.
NAMASTE's DA-1 'irremediable vitiated-आम' occupies the same prognostic slot Vāgbhaṭa assigns to viṣasaṃjñaka āmadoṣa. It may be the modern code equivalent, but no source I found says so.

mistranslations.why: Compounds the 'ama = toxin' error with redundancy: if āma is already a toxin, āmaviṣa becomes 'toxin-poison'. The whole point of the compound is that āma is NOT ordinarily a poison and becomes one only under specific conditions.

Tempting because of the viruddha-āhāra aetiology at Ca.Sū.26 and the 'annaviṣa' wording, but food poisoning is an acute exogenous microbial or chemical event; Ca.Sū.26.102 lists āmaviṣa alongside chronic conditions such as impotence, blindness, fistula-in-ano and leprosy.
Imports a discredited late-19th-century Western theory. Convenient rhetorically, historically loaded, and not what any source I retrieved says.
A specific biomedical identification with no supporting study of any kind. I found zero peer-reviewed literature on this term.

Which item in Kaviratna's Sūtrasthāna 26 English list renders āmaviṣa? Requires a page-level collation against his Sanskrit base text (Gaṅgādhara's recension).
Does Cakrapāṇi gloss āmaviṣa at Ca.Sū.26.102, and how?
Is NAMASTE's asādhya-āmadoṣa (DA-1) intended as the code equivalent of Vāgbhaṭa's viṣasaṃjñaka āmadoṣa?

classical.establishes: Karma and guna of amla rasa (laghu, ushna, snigdha). Sanskrit as retrieved: अम्लो रसो भक्तं रोचयति, अग्निं दीपयति, देहं बृंहयति ऊर्जयति, मनो बोधयति, इन्द्रियाणि दृढीकरोति, बलं वर्धयति, वातमनुलोमयति, हृदयं तर्पयति, आस्यमास्रावयति, भुक्तमपकर्षयति क्लेदयति जरयति, प्रीणयति, लघुरुष्णः स्निग्धश्च| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya). classical.quote: The Sour Taste adds relish to food ; excites the digestive fire ; gives nutrition to the body ; weakens objects by entering into them, enlivens the mind ; invigorates the senses ; increases the strength ; makes the wind flow in its natural course ; cools and gratifies the heart ; causes the mouth to be filled with saliva ; assists at deglutition ; generates impurities in the body ; and contributes to general cheerfulness. It is light, warm, and oily.

classical.verse: Standard 26.40 (the mahabhuta-origin prose unit ends ||४०|| on carakasamhitaonline); Kaviratna prints 54
classical.establishes: Pañcabhautika constitution of amla: pṛthvī + agni. Agrees with Bhishagratna's Sushruta ('earth and fire').
classical.quote: From a preponderance of the attributes of Earth and Fire, arises the Taste called Sour.

classical.verse: Sanskrit verse number not established; Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers
classical.establishes: Sushruta's perceptual definition (lakshana) of amla. Same chapter, same page: 'An acid taste should be regarded as a digestant of assimilated food, and is endued with resolving, appetising and carminative properties. It sets in the natural emission of flatus and urine, restores the natural movements of the bowels, lessens the tendency to spasms, and gives rise to an acid (digestive) reaction in the stomach, and to a sensation of external shivering.' and 'An acid taste is pre-eminently possessed of attributes, which belong to the elementary principles of earth and fire.'
classical.quote: A taste, which produces tooth-edge and increased salivation, and increases the relish for food, is called acid (Amla).

classical.verse: Standard number NOT established (taste-identification block near chapter end); Kaviratna prints 31
classical.establishes: Charaka's perceptual test for amla rasa. Kaviratna's 31 is his own count in the closing verse block (which restarts); standard verse not verified.
classical.quote: From tenderness of the teeth, the appearance of saliva, of perspiration (on the body), awakening of the mouth, and a burning sensation of both the mouth and the throat, as soon as the object is placed in the mouth, one should say that its taste is Sour.

classical.establishes: Amla as a quality of pitta itself, not of a drug: Su 1/60 lists seven attributes of pitta, sasneha (slightly unctuous), uṣṇa, tīkṣṇa, drava, amla, sara, kaṭu, and says pitta is quickly pacified by substances of opposite qualities. Kaviratna's English matches the Sanskrit on four (hot, keen, sour, liquid) and departs from it on three ('cold' for sasneha, 'soft' for sara, 'bitter' for kaṭu). Only amla and drava are taken from this verse for the entry; the English is kept as a record of Kaviratna's rendering, with the Sanskrit as the authority.
classical.quote: सस्नेहमुष्णं तीक्ष्णं च द्रवमम्लं सरं कटु | विपरीतगुणैः पित्तं द्रव्यैराशु प्रशाम्यति ||६०|| Kaviratna (his 59): "Bile, which may be cold, hot, keen, soft, sour, liquid, and bitter, is speedily cured by objects having adverse attributes."
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: Hindi/commercial 'amla' is the fruit; the Sanskrit guna-term amla is the sour taste. PubMed searches for 'amla' return the fruit almost exclusively.
WHO RS0011 records amla as 'acids' used as media for purification processes, a pharmaceutical sense distinct from the rasa.
Ca.Su.1.60 lists amla among Pitta's gunas; this describes the dosha, not a drug's rasa.
A sour secondary taste perceived late or faintly (Ca.Su.26.28) is not the rasa proper.
'Producing burning' is a karma attributed to excess amla (Ca.Su.26.43) but is not the taste itself.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's Edwardian usage for sour; today it implies chemical pH or 'acidic foods' and misleads.
Conflates the taste term with the fruit āmalakī.
Kaviratna's 'cools and gratifies the heart' adds 'cools'; amla is ushna in the same sentence.

openQuestions: Standard verse numbers for the Charaka taste-identification block (Kaviratna 30-35) and for Sushruta Su.42 passages were not established from a Sanskrit edition.
Whether modern taste-threshold/sensory methods (as attempted for kashaya, PMID 25558164) have been applied to amla was not found.

classical.establishes: Suśruta's root = stomach + food-carrying dhamanīs. Agrees with Caraka on āmāśaya but replaces Caraka's 'left side' with the dhamanīs.
classical.quote: The foodcarrying Srotas (Æsophagus) have their roots in the Amashaya (stomach) and in the food-carrying Dhamanis (intestines). An injury to or piercing of such a duct (Srota), gives rise to tympanites, colic pain, aversion to food, vomiting, thirst, blindness or darkness of vision, or may even end in death.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO defines mahāsrotas (ITA.3.11.1) as 'The major inner cavity of the body from the mouth to anus', which overlaps annavaha srotas almost entirely but is a cavity term, not a transport-channel term; Caraka uses mahāsrotas as a root of prāṇavaha, not annavaha.
These are organs (receptacles) named as roots; annavaha srotas is the conduit system rooted in them.
Both are gut-located, but Caraka roots purīṣavaha in pakvāśaya + sthūlaguda, i.e. the distal gut, and assigns it excretory rather than alimentary function.
The product of annavaha srotas' work (āhāra rasa) enters rasavaha srotas; texts and modern authors slide between them when discussing 'nutrition'.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's parenthetical. The Sanskrit names no oesophagus; both Caraka and Suśruta root the channel in the stomach.

mistranslations.rendering: the digestive system (as a whole, including liver/pancreas)
mistranslations.why: Common textbook expansion. Caraka's named roots are stomach and the left flank only; liver and spleen belong to raktavaha srotas in the same passage.

openQuestions: Does 'vāmaṃ pārśvam' refer to the spleen, the left hypochondrium, or the greater curvature of the stomach?
Is there any classical warrant for including hepatobiliary/pancreatic structures in annavaha srotas, or is that purely a modern biomedical mapping?

classical.verse: Standard 27.325 (prose) as numbered on carakasamhitaonline; Kaviratna's printed number for this prose unit is illegible in the OCR ('*™')
classical.establishes: The anupāna-karma list. Sanskrit as retrieved: अथानुपानकर्मगुणान्प्रवक्ष्यामः- अनुपानं तर्पयति, प्रीणयति, ऊर्जयति, बृंहयति, पर्याप्तिमभिनिर्वर्तयति, भुक्तमवसादयति, अन्नसङ्घातं भिनत्ति, मार्दवमापादयति, क्लेदयति, जरयति, सुखपरिणामितामाशुव्यवायितां चाहारस्योपजनयतीति॥३२५॥ (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Annapanavidhi_Adhyaya). Kaviratna's 'sedative' renders tarpayati (satiates/refreshes), not a CNS effect; his parentheses are glosses.
classical.quote: I shall now speak of the effects of Anupana. Anupanas exercise a sedative and nutritive influence. They make the mind cheerful. They conduce to increase of energy. They produce the sensation of gratification after one has eaten. They moisten what is eaten (and thereby assist at digestion). They disjoin united food. They soften the food in the stomach. They cause the impurities to separate themselves from the food in the stomach. They cause the food to be digested. They contribute to that sensation of pleasure which arises after eating. They cause the food to extend its effects to all parts of the body.

classical.verse: Standard 27.326; Kaviratna's printed number reads '328' in OCR (uncertain)
classical.establishes: Summary verse. Sanskrit as retrieved: अनुपानं हितं युक्तं तर्पयत्याशु मानवम्| सुखं पचति चाहारमायुषे च बलाय च||३२६||
classical.quote: (Here occur some verses.) An Anupana that is suitable is certainly beneficial. It soon exercises a sedative and nutritive influence on the body. It causes easy digestion of the food that has been eaten. It conduces to strength and long life.

classical.verse: Standard 27.319; Kaviratna's printed number OCR'd as 'f821' (likely 321, unverified)
classical.establishes: Selection rule: opposite in guna to the food, not hostile to the dhatus. Sanskrit (IAST as retrieved): yadāhāraguṇaiḥ pānaṁ viparītaṁ tadiṣyatē| annānupānaṁ dhātūnāṁ dr̥ṣṭaṁ yanna virōdhi ca||319||. Kaviratna's footnote here: 'The word 'Anupana,' it should be noted, implies not only fluid food or drink that is taken subsequently, — that is, at the conclusion of a course of eating, — but also such fluids as are used as vehicles of medicines. — T.' (translator's note, not text).
classical.quote: That fluid food or drink should be taken subsequently which in qualities is the reverse of the food taken previously. It should be remembered, however, that the subsequent fluid food should not be hostile to the upholding ingredients of the body.

classical.verse: Standard 27.321; Kaviratna's printed number OCR'd as '*28' (unverified)
classical.establishes: Dosha-wise anupana. Sanskrit (IAST as retrieved): snigdhōṣṇaṁ mārutē śastaṁ pittē madhuraśītalam| kaphē'nupānaṁ rūkṣōṣṇaṁ kṣayē māṁsarasaḥ param||321||
classical.quote: As regards such subsequent fluid food or drink, that which is oily and hot is praised in excitements of the wind ; that which is sweet and cooling is praised in excitements of the bile ; that which is dry and hot is praised in excitements of the phlegm ; while in emaciation and waste, the juice of meat is highly beneficial.

classical.verse: Standard Ca.Su.27.327-328 (carakasamhitaonline Annapanavidhi: nordhvangamarutavishta na hikkashvasakasinah | na gitabhashyadhyayanaprasakta norasi kshatah ||327|| pibeyurudakam bhuktva taddhi kanthorasi sthitam | snehamaharajam hatva bhuyo doshaya kalpate ||328||). Kaviratna prints '329-30' after this paragraph on his p. 387 (the djvu OCR '323-20' is a misread); he is two ahead of standard here (his 327 = std 325, his 328 = std 326).
classical.establishes: Contraindication of drinking water after a meal (Ca.Su.27.327-328). The Sanskrit names four classes who should not: (1) those with vata disturbed in the upper body (urdhvanga-maruta-avishta); (2) sufferers from hiccup, dyspnoea and cough (hikka-shvasa-kasin); (3) those engaged in singing, lecturing or recitation (gita-bhashya-adhyayana-prasakta); (4) those with chest injury (urasi kshata). Reason given: the water lodged in throat and chest destroys the sneha of the food and produces further dosha. Kaviratna's rendering 'asthma and consumption' is his, not the text's: the Samhita says hiccup, dyspnoea and cough, and says nothing of consumption (kshaya/rajayakshma). Parallel in Sushruta Su.46 below.
classical.quote: Those persons the upper parts of whose bodies are afflicted with wind, those persons who are afflicted with asthma and consumption, those persons who are generally engaged in singing or speaking aloud or reading aloud, and those who have sores or wounds on the chest, should not drink water after having taken their food, for, if they drink, that water, remaining in their throat or chest, will destroy the oily secretions of the food previously taken, and generate many faults.

distinguishFrom.why: Its pair, but not its mirror image in every source. Charaka defines only upaśaya; Vagbhata defines anupaśaya by opposition; WHO gives them separate codes with different descriptions, and only the anupaśaya entry states the indication for using the procedure.

Vagbhata and Madhavakara equate the two FOR A GIVEN DISEASE. But asātmya in general Ayurvedic usage means unsuitability to a person, season or region — a constitutional notion — and asātmyendriyārtha-saṃyoga (WHO ITA-4.4.10) is one of the three primary causes of disease. The equation is local to this chapter and the general sense is a different concept.

The obvious modern reading and wrong in purpose. An ADR is harm to be avoided and reported; anupaśaya is information deliberately sought. The physical event can be identical and the epistemic status is opposite.
Treatment failure is the non-attainment of a therapeutic goal. Anupaśaya presupposes there was no therapeutic goal — the agent was given to classify, not to cure.

Charaka's actual usage at Ni. 1.21, 1.24 and 1.27: non-relief from what the stated nidāna would predict, appearing inside a sign list. This is anupaśaya operating as evidence WITHIN rūpa, not as the pentad's fourth member. The two roles are routinely merged.

Charaka's upaśaya definition distinguishes agents opposite to the cause from agents opposite to the disease. Non-relief therefore has at least two different diagnostic meanings depending on which relation the agent bore, and calling both 'anupaśaya' without saying which loses the inference.

mistranslations.why: WHO's own looser phrase at ITA-4.3.2. Turns a physician-initiated probe into a history item, and drops the requirement that the agent stood in a defined viparīta relation.
A contraindication is a prior prohibition. Anupaśaya is a posterior observation, and the agent was deliberately given.
Locates the finding in the patient's constitution. The classical inference is about the DISEASE: non-relief reclassifies the illness, not the person.
WHO's own description phrase, and it imports an outcome-measure framing. The head term at ITA-4.5.15 is better because it names the inference.

Too weak. Vagbhata's asātmya and WHO's 'signs and symptoms of AGGRAVATION' both require a positive worsening, not merely a failure to improve. Nothing happening is a third outcome that neither term covers.

openQuestions: Whether anything at all has been published on this term. PubMed returns ZERO records for the query 'anupashaya' — I ran it and the count was 0. Not one paper. The modern array is empty for that reason and this is a verified negative, not an unsearched gap.

What Charaka's Ni. 1.21/1.24/1.27 formula means precisely — whether 'nidānokta-anupaśaya' there means non-relief on withdrawal of the stated cause, or aggravation on exposure to it. The Sanskrit is compressed and I did not retrieve a commentary. This changes whether the passage is about upaśaya-style probing or about nidāna confirmation, and it should not be resolved by guessing.
Whether a distinct third outcome (no change either way) is recognised anywhere. Neither Charaka's definition nor WHO's two entries provide for it.
Whether Sushruta uses the term. Not located in my full-text search of Bhishagratna's Sūtrasthāna volume.

classical.establishes: The defining verse. Sanskrit as retrieved: व्यक्तः शुष्कस्य चादौ च रसो द्रव्यस्य लक्ष्यते| विपर्ययेणानुरसो रसो नास्ति हि सप्तमः||२८|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya). Kaviratna's footnote (translator's note, not text): 'Literally rendered, the verse, therefore, is this : "of a dry object or (the same when wet), at the outset or (at the end), that taste which is manifest, is (truly) the taste : the taste that is perceptible otherwise is the subordinate taste." Chakrapani goes on to explain : take Piper longum ; when drenched or soaked in water, its taste is sweet ; when dry, it is Pungent. The latter is its taste ; take dried grapes ; when dry, they are sweet ; when drenched, they are sweet. There being no difference, Sweet is its taste. Take any of the liquids, say, kanjika or sour gruel of rice. That taste which becomes perceptible at the outset is its true taste. That which is perceived afterwards is its subordinate taste.'
classical.quote: That taste which becomes manifest, of a dry or wet object, at the outset or at the end, is called its (true) taste. That taste which becomes perceptible otherwise or in succession is called the subordinate or unmanifest taste. classical.establishes: Sushruta seats apāna in the pakvādhāna and gives it five downward expulsions — foetus, faeces, urine, semen and menstrual blood — with its disorders localised to basti (bladder) and guda (anus/rectum). Corresponding Sanskrit, cross-checked at a separate URL: 'पक्वाधानालयोऽपानः काले कर्षति चाप्यधः | समीरणः शकृन्मूत्रं शुक्रगर्भार्तवानि च ||१९|| क्रुद्धश्च कुरुते रोगान् घोरान् बस्तिगुदाश्रयान् |२०|'. Note the Sanskrit adds 'kāle' — it draws these down AT THE PROPER TIME — which Bhishagratna does not render.
classical.quote: The Vayu known as the Apana acts in the lower region of the intestines (Pakvadhana). Its functions consist in bearing down the fetus and the feces and in evacuating the urine, semen and catamenial blood. An enraged condition of this Vayu tends to bring on serious diseases, which are peculiar to the urinary bladder and the distal portion of the large intestine (Guda).

classical.establishes: Charaka gives apāna the widest seat list of any subtype: vṛṣaṇau (testes), basti (bladder), meḍhra (penis), nābhi and ūrū (navel and thighs), vaṅkṣaṇau (groins) and guda (anus); situated in the intestines, it releases semen, urine, faeces, menstrual fluid and the foetus. Verse 11 closes the whole five-subtype passage with the statement that when all five are in their proper seats and functioning, the body is sustained free of disease. NOTE: the retrieved page prints 'नाम्भूरू', which is almost certainly a transcription slip for नाभ्यूरू (nābhi + ūrū, navel and thighs). I have quoted the page exactly as retrieved rather than silently correcting it.

distinguishFrom.term: apāna as the anus / large intestine (the anatomical sense)
distinguishFrom.why: The single most confusing feature of this term. Sanskrit apāna denotes both the vāta subtype AND the lower bowel or anus. Ashtanga Hridaya Su.12.9 opens 'apāno 'pānagaḥ' — 'apāna, which goes in the apāna' — and modern glosses render this as 'Apana Vata is located in the Apana – large intestine'. Reading the second occurrence as the subtype produces a circular definition.

Both operate in the pakvāśaya. The division of labour is that samāna separates the nutrient essence from the waste and apāna expels the waste. Sushruta gives samāna an explicit pakvāśaya range (Ni.1.16), so the two genuinely overlap in that text.

The yogic apāna is the downward current worked with in mūla bandha and aśvinī mudrā, tied to the mūlādhāra cakra. The Ayurvedic apāna is defined by five specific expulsions and a seat list of organs. The overlap is real (both downward, both pelvic) which is why the conflation goes unnoticed.

Sushruta Ni.1.20 pairs them: aggravated together they produce prameha and śukra disorders. Because apāna alone governs śukra expulsion, papers sometimes cite the combined statement as though it were about apāna alone.

Classical Ayurveda calls the pakvāśaya the general seat (sthāna) of the vāta doṣa as a whole. Not every vāta pathology localised to the colon is an apāna pathology, though clinical writing often treats the two as equivalent.

'Adhoga vāta' in clinical usage often just means flatus. Apāna is the agency that moves it downward, not the gas itself. The easyayurveda gloss on Su.Ni.1.19 lists 'flatus' first among what apāna eliminates, which makes the slide easy.

mistranslations.why: Confuses the subtype with one of the substances it expels. 'Apana' is not a synonym for flatus in any of the classical loci retrieved.

mistranslations.rendering: the elimination vata / the excretory vata
mistranslations.why: Drops parturition and menstruation, which are explicit in Charaka Ci.28.10-11, Sushruta Ni.1.19 and AH Su.12.9. Apāna governs downward release generally, including reproductive events that are not excretion. The Kerala Tourism rendering makes exactly this cut.

Bhishagratna's 1911 footnote, 'the Apana is identical with the force of the Hypogastric plexus'. A colonial-era neuroanatomical equation from a translator's note, frequently requoted as if it were Sushruta's own statement.
Imported from yoga. No classical Ayurvedic locus for apāna mentions a cakra; the seat lists are anatomical (testes, bladder, penis, groins, anus, thighs).

An organ-for-agency substitution. The colon is where apāna acts (and, confusingly, is also called apāna). Rendering the subtype AS the colon collapses the very distinction AH Su.12.9's wordplay depends on.

classical.establishes: A live variant-reading dispute: Gangādhara read the añjali entry as ślesman-of-the-ojas kind; Kaviratna rejects it. This is the textual root of the ślaiṣmika ojas name now attached to apara ojas, and it rests on a reading Kaviratna calls evidently incorrect. classical.quote: Some. texts read 'yleshmanajcliaujasah.' Gangadhara-, following this, reading, explains it as meaning 'the particular kind of phlegm known as. ojas.' This can be hardly correct. The 'ojas' has been before described. It is not regarded as any kind of phlegm. On the other hand, it is the blood of blood, the mosjt vital 'dhatu' in the body. The reading is evidently incorrect.

classical.establishes: Body-wide pervasion, and gradual rather than immediate consequence of its loss. Both features are what later tradition assigns to apara rather than para ojas. Sushruta himself makes no such division.
classical.quote: The whole body with its limbs and members is permeated with Ojas, and a loss or diminution in its natural quantity leads to the gradual emaciation (and ultimate dissolution) of organism.

classical.establishes: Ojas can be increased by rasāyana therapy. Treatability is the property most often used to distinguish apara from para ojas, whose loss is held to be irreversible.
classical.quote: The medical treatment in cases of dislodgment or flowing out external secretion) of albumen from its natural seat (Visransha), as well as in the event of it becoming contaminated by the vitiated principles of the body, should consist in improving its quantity by elixirs and remedies possessed of rejuvenating properties, tending to increase the quantity of such fluid (albumen) in the body.

distinguishFrom.why: The counterpart. Apara pervades the body, is the larger quantity, responds to diet, drugs and rasāyana, and its loss is gradual; para is heart-resident, fixed, and its loss is held to be immediately fatal.

The añjali measure and the body-wide pervasion are stated of ojas simpliciter in Charaka and Sushruta. Assigning them to apara ojas is a later reading, and the entry should say so rather than backdate the division.

The name ślaiṣmika ojas rests on Gangādhara's variant reading at Ca.Śā.7, which Kaviratna rejects as evidently incorrect. The identification is contested at the level of the manuscript, not just the interpretation.
Both circulate and both respond to food, and PMID 41289791's lipid argument could be made of either. Apara ojas is the essence carried by the dhātus, not the first dhātu.
Apara ojas is often glossed straight to immunity or strength. WHO assigns those to bala and vyādhikṣamatva (ITA-2.2.27) and gives ojas its own untranslated entry.

mistranslations.why: A calque that appears in several review articles. Apara means the other or the further of a pair; it carries no implication of poor quality, and apara ojas is the larger and the clinically actionable fraction.
Its loss causes gradual emaciation and ultimately death in Sushruta's own account. Nothing about it is non-essential.
Imports a centre/periphery anatomy the texts do not use; Sushruta says the whole body with its limbs and members is permeated, not that it sits at the periphery.
A 2025 hypothesis presented as correlative by its own authors (PMID 41289791). Recording it as a rendering would convert a proposal into a definition.

openQuestions: Whether the ardha-añjali measure belongs to apara ojas specifically or to ojas undivided. Charaka's Śārīrasthāna 7 says ojas without qualification; the assignment to apara is later. No retrieved source shows the classical text making the assignment.
Whether the ślaiṣmika ojas name has any basis beyond Gangādhara's disputed variant reading at Ca.Śā.7.
Where the para/apara division is first made, and by whom. The NIA/WHO-APW list records it as settled; no classical locus for it was verified here.

classical.quote: All that is suitable to the way (of life) and that is agreeable to the mind is said to constitute what is called Pathya (or regimen). What, however, is the reverse of Pathya and is not agreeable to the mind, should never be attended to. classical.verse: Standard Sutrasthana 28.5 (final sentence, हिताहितोपयोगविशेषास्त्वत्र शुभाशुभविशेषकरा भवन्तीति||५||) and 28.6 (Agnivesha's objection, एवंवादिनं भगवन्तमात्रेयमग्निवेश उवाच... ||६||), Atreya's qualification being 28.7 (carakasamhitaonline Vividhashitapitiya_Adhyaya raw); Kaviratna Lesson XXVIII, his printed 8 (the wholesome/unwholesome sentence) and 9 (Agnivesha's objection), p. 394 (page image; the djvu OCR prints '8' for both)

classical.quote: As regards the body, particular administrations (of regimen), wholesome or unwholesome, become productive of good or evil consequences. ... The antonym; also used as a synonym of 'treatment' (WHO ITA-9.1.5), which apathya is not.

classical.establishes: Confirms ārtava as the eleventh and last member of Suśruta's list, and that the list is framed as a SURGICAL (śalya) concern about piercing, not a physiological taxonomy.

distinguishFrom.term: ārtava as menstrual blood vs ārtava as ovum/bīja
distinguishFrom.why: Bhishagratna glosses it both ways within one paragraph ('catamenial blood', 'ovarian product'). Modern authors coin 'artava-bija-vaha srotas' to capture the ovum sense. Which substance the channel carries is unsettled and the whole fallopian-tube identification depends on it.
Often presented as the female counterpart, but Suśruta's śukravaha is rooted in breasts and testes, so they are not symmetrical.
The vagina/uterus are organs, one of which is the root; ārtavavaha srotas is not a synonym for the reproductive tract.

mistranslations.why: NAMASTE's head-term, but the very paper most cited for this mapping (PMID 22131704) states that the fallopian tube is not mentioned in the classics. It is a 20th-century correlation presented as a translation.
WHO's rendering is defensible as a functional gloss but is far wider than the text, which names uterus + ārtava-carrying dhamanīs and nothing else.
Restricts the channel to menstruation when Suśruta's injury signs include sterility and inability to copulate, i.e. reproductive function broadly.

openQuestions: Does ārtava here mean menstrual blood or the ovum/bīja? The fallopian-tube identification stands or falls on this.
Is there any pre-modern text that actually names ārtavavaha srotas outside Su.Śā.9? Aṣṭāṅga Saṅgraha/Hṛdaya should be checked (discussable, not quotable).

classical.quote: As regards curable diseases, they are of two kinds, viz., those that are easily curable and those that are curable with difficulty. Incurable diseases, also, are of two kinds, viz., those that are capable of being suppressed, and those that have no treatment.
