classical.establishes: Features of the pratyākhyeya (to-be-refused) disease: tridoṣaja, beyond the path of treatment, following all channels, causing anxiety/restlessness/confusion, destroying the senses, well-grown in a weak patient, with ariṣṭa signs.
classical.quote: ...तद्वत्प्रत्याख्येयं त्रिदोषजम्| क्रियापथमतिक्रान्तं सर्वमार्गानुसारिणम्||१९|| औत्सुक्यारतिसम्मोहकरमिन्द्रियनाशनम्| दुर्बलस्य सुसंवृद्धं व्याधिं सारिष्टमेव च||२०||

classical.verse: Kaviratna's '12-14' (printed after); corresponds to standard 18-20 read together
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English for the pratyākhyeya features. Note he folds the dvidoṣaja features of standard v.18 (which the Sanskrit assigns to yāpya) into the 'not to be taken up' block; carakasamhitaonline reads 17-18 as yāpya and 19-20 as pratyākhyeya.
classical.quote: When the disease is deeply ingrained (into the marrow and such other constituents of the body), when it affects many of the constituent parts, when it is attached to the vital limbs and joints of the body, when it manifests itself continuously, when it is chronic and very old, when it is born of the derangement of two of the three ingredients (of wind, bile, and phlegm) or of all the three, when it is beyond the operation of treatment, when it affects all the organs, when the patient is thoroughly cheerless and despairing, when the disease is characterised by a stupefaction of the mind, when the disease weakens the strength of all the organs (of knowledge and action), when the disease has reached the highest limit of aggravation and the patient has become entirely strengthless, and lastly when the disease exhibits indications of the patient's dissolution, it should be regarded as one that should not be taken up for treatment.

classical.chapter: 10 (Bhishagratna ch. X, 'Essential qualifications of a physician'); Sanskrit verse number not established (Bhishagratna prints none; no numbered Sanskrit edition was reachable)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's threefold practical stance: cure the curable, palliate the palliable, give up the untreatable.
classical.quote: Having made these observations the physician will try to cure diseases that are curable, adopt palliative measures in cases where palliation is the only remedy that can be offered, and give up a case which is beyond all medical treatment, and mostly those which are of more than a year's standing.

classical.chapter: 35 (Bhishagratna ch. XXXV, 'Examination of the patient'); Sanskrit verse number not established
classical.establishes: Sushruta's threefold prognosis: sādhya, yāpya, asādhya (pratyākhyeya, glossed 'fit to be pronounced as hopeless').
classical.quote: All the diseases, whose names have been specifically enumerated before, may be grouped under any of the three different heads as the curable, the suppressible (Yapya) and the incurable (lit: fit to be pronounced as hopeless).

distinguishFrom.why: In Caraka Su. 10/9 yāpya is a SUB-class of asādhya (palliable but not curable). WHO 2022 lists yāpyarogaḥ as a separate category beside asādhyarogaḥ; Sushruta Su. 35 (Bhishagratna) also lists three parallel heads. The lexicon should not present one scheme as 'the' Ayurvedic one.
The untreatable sub-class of asādhya ('to be refused', 'no treatment'). WHO renders pratyākhyeya 'terminal', which imports a modern end-of-life sense.
Curable with difficulty is still sādhya; conflating 'difficult' with 'incurable' is the commonest error.
Ariṣṭa are fatal signs (Indriyasthana); their presence is one criterion of pratyākhyeya (Su. 10/20 'sāriṣṭam'), not a synonym of asādhya.

mistranslations.why: Asādhya includes yāpya conditions (WHO's own example: persistent diabetes mellitus, bronchial asthma), which are chronic, not terminal.
Kaviratna's commentary note explicitly says incurable diseases may be 'quickly fatal or the reverse'; incurability and fatality are separate axes.

openQuestions: Whether the lexicon adopts Caraka's nested scheme (asādhya ⊃ yāpya, anupakrama) or the flat three/four-way scheme used by WHO and implied by Bhishagratna's Su. 35.
Sushruta Sanskrit verse numbers for the Su. 10 and Su. 35 passages (needs a numbered Sanskrit edition; NIIMH e-Sushruta is JS-driven and could not be read).

classical.establishes: The root statement of the threefold cause: wrong, deficient or excessive yoga of kāla, buddhi and indriyārtha is the cause of diseases resting on both body and mind. The term asātmyendriyārtha-saṃyoga itself does not appear here; this verse supplies the indriyārtha limb of the triad.
classical.quote: kālabuddhīndriyārthānāṁ yōgō mithyā na cāti ca| dvayāśrayāṇāṁ vyādhīnāṁ trividhō hētusaṅgrahaḥ||54||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 53 (= standard 54; confirmed by reading the adjacent aphorisms 41=42, 45=46, 47=48 in this block)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering of Ca.Sū.1.54. He renders buddhi as 'mind' here, which flattens the buddhi/manas distinction the text keeps elsewhere. OCR double-spacing normalised.
classical.quote: Of all diseases, physical and mental, the causes in brief are of three kinds, viz., adverse or excessive correlation or want of correlation of time, mind, and the objects of the senses.

classical.establishes: The locus that names and defines the term: atiyoga, ayoga and mithyāyoga of the five sense-objects (37), the statement that this fivefold, threefold-varied condition is asātmyendriyārtha-saṃyoga and that sātmya here means upaśaya (38), and the summary naming the three causes with the counter-statement that proper conjunction (samayoga) is the cause of health (43). Verse 37 was retrieved in full; only the opening and the operative clause are reproduced here.
classical.quote: त्रीण्यायतनानीति- अर्थानां कर्मणः कालस्य चातियोगायोगमिथ्यायोगाः| ... ||३७|| ... सोऽयमनुपशयात् पञ्चविधस्त्रिविधविकल्पो भवत्यसात्म्येन्द्रियार्थसंयोगः; सात्म्यार्थो ह्युपशयार्थः||३८|| ... इत्यसात्म्येन्द्रियार्थसंयोगः, प्रज्ञापराधः, परिणामश्चेति त्रयस्त्रिविधविकल्पा हेतवो विकाराणां; समयोगयुक्तास्तु प्रकृतिहेतवो भवन्ति||४३||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorisms 42-43 (his 42 spans standard 42 plus the opening clause of 43; his 43 = rest of standard 43)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English for the summary verse and the samayoga counter-statement. His aphorism boundaries do not coincide with the standard 42/43 split; recorded as read. OCR spacing normalised.
classical.quote: Thus are the three subjects treated of, Viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time or Parinama.42 These three, (viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time,) each subdivided into three kinds, constitute the causes of disease. Connection therewith in normal or judicious proportions is the cause of health.

classical.establishes: The three causes are explicitly the aggravators (prakopaṇa) of BOTH classes of doṣa, mental (rajas, tamas) and bodily (vāta, pitta, kapha). Kaviratna's English for the same aphorism: 'there are three kinds of exciting causes, viz., union with disagreeing objects of sense, faults of understanding, and Time.' (his aphorism 10, same archive.org URL).
classical.quote: तत्र खल्वेषां द्वयानामपि दोषाणां त्रिविधं प्रकोपणं; तद्यथा- असात्म्येन्द्रियार्थसंयोगः, प्रज्ञापराधः परिणामश्चेति||६||

classical.establishes: The physiological mechanism: ati/a/mithyā-yoga of a sense with its object derange the sense 'together with the mind' (samanaska) and impair the corresponding indriya-buddhi; sāmarthya-yoga (fit conjunction) restores it. Kaviratna's English (his aphorism 10): 'In consequence again of the excessive correlation, the absence of (judicious) correlation, and the impropriety of correlation, of the senses with their respective objects, the senses including the mind, falling away from their normal condition, become hurtful to the perceptions of which they are the respective sources or channels.'
classical.quote: Tadarthātiyōgāyōgamithyāyōgāt samanaskamindriyaṁ vikr̥timāpadyamānaṁ yathāsvaṁ buddhyupaghātāya sampadyatē, sāmarthyayōgāt punaḥ prakr̥timāpadyamānaṁ yathāsvaṁ buddhimāpyāyayati||15||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

distinguishFrom.why: The second of the three causes: misuse of karma (speech, mind, body) arising from error of buddhi/dhṛti/smṛti (Ca.Sū.11.39-41). Asātmyendriyārtha-saṃyoga concerns the senses meeting their objects, prajñāparādha concerns action. Both are 'misuse', and secondary literature often folds sensory misuse into prajñāparādha.
The third cause: time, defined in Ca.Sū.11.42 as the seasonal year and its ati/a/mithyā manifestation. Not a sensory contact at all.

Sannikarṣa (Ca.Sū.8.12, Śā.1.18) is the normal proximity of indriya, artha, sattva and ātmā that produces perception. Asātmya-saṃyoga is the pathological variant of the same contact. Kaviratna's footnote at Śā.1 insists sannikarṣa is 'not samyoga or union'.
Asātmya is used of diet, climate, habit. Here it is specialised by Ca.Sū.11.38: 'sātmyārtho hy upaśayārthaḥ', so the sātmya intended is upaśaya, that which agrees.
The parent class (WHO ITA-4.4.9). Asātmyendriyārtha-saṃyoga is one member of the triad, not the triad.

mistranslations.rendering: improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind
mistranslations.why: Kaviratna (Sū.11.42). The compound is indriya-artha, sense-with-object; manas is implicated only secondarily (samanaska, Sū.8.15). Putting 'Mind' in the headline rendering turns a sensory-hygiene doctrine into a psychological one.
Common shorthand that drops saṃyoga. The text locates the fault in the conjunction (over-, under-, mis-use), not in the object: Sū.11.37 counts even total non-use (ayoga) as a cause.
Captures only atiyoga; the text gives three modes, and the WHO description 'underuse, overuse and abuse' is closer.

openQuestions: Whether Ca.Sū.11.38's 'pañcavidhas trividhavikalpaḥ' (fivefold, each threefold) is the intended count, i.e. fifteen species, as Cakrapāṇi reads it; commentary not retrieved.
Whether Suśruta uses the compound at all.

distinguishFrom.why: Three METHODS of examining (Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya Su. 1/22); aṣṭavidha lists eight SITES/objects. Not a subset relationship.
Sushruta's examination by five senses plus interrogation (WHO ITA-4.7.3; Bhishagratna Su. 10: 'the five sense-organs of hearing, sight, etc. and oral enquiry'); methods, not sites.
Caraka Vi. 8/94: ten attributes of the PATIENT (prakṛti, vikṛti, sāra ...) assessed to gauge strength, not eight sites of disease signs.
Same scheme, different head-word; WHO 2022 and the Yogaratnakara section title use sthāna (site), modern Indian literature uses vidha (kind). Record both as names of one scheme.
WHO ITA-4.3.1 'rogaparīkṣā' is disease assessment by nidāna, pūrvarūpa, rūpa, upaśaya, samprāpti; the eightfold scheme belongs to rogī-parīkṣā (patient examination, ITA-4.7).

mistranslations.why: The Yogaratnakara verb is nirīkṣayet (inspect); it lists what to look at, not a diagnostic algorithm.

Several teaching notes render śabda as 'speech'; WHO reads it as 'voice and other body-sounds such as breathing and heart', and the Yogaratnakara śabda-parīkṣā verse (OCR) speaks of heavy/clear/hoarse voice by dosha. 'Speech' (content/language) is too narrow and misleading.

openQuestions: Standard verse numbering for the Yogaratnakara parīkṣā sections across editions (Nirnaya Sagar vs Vidyotini vs Suresh Babu).
Whether the lexicon's head-word should be aṣṭavidha or aṣṭasthāna given WHO uses the latter.

classical.establishes: Asthi's two functions, dhāraṇa (supporting the body) and the production of majjā. WHO ISTA gives dhāraṇam its own term ID (ITA-2.2.3) and notes there that it 'is also the specific function of bone'.
classical.quote: The bones, in their turn, support the body, and contribute to the formation of marrow.

classical.establishes: Asthi-kṣaya presenting as bone and joint pain, dental and gum loss, and general dryness. The inclusion of teeth is textual evidence that asthi extends beyond the skeleton. Note that this is not the presentation of osteoporosis, which is typically silent until fracture.
classical.quote: The degeneration of the bones is marked by an aching pain in the bones and bone-joints, a wasting of teeth and gums, and a general dryness of the body.

classical.establishes: Asthi-vṛddhi recognised by supernumerary teeth and bony overgrowth. Again teeth are treated as asthi.
classical.quote: An excessive formation of bone (abnormal ossification) is attended with such symptoms as the cutting of additional teeth and the abnormal development of any of the bone-structures.

classical.establishes: Hair as the waste fraction of asthi. A doctrinally important and biomedically unsupported claim, and the reason hair loss is treated in the tradition as a bone problem.
classical.quote: The 'Kitta' of bones is hair (of the head and the body)

classical.verse: 120 in Kaviratna's marginal numbering; sara section cited as Vi 8/102 ff by carakasamhitaonline
classical.establishes: Asthi-sāra. The list of sites explicitly includes nails and teeth alongside bones and joints, which fixes the classical extension of asthi wider than 'bone tissue'.
classical.quote: They who have bones for the predominating element in their constitution have these parts of the body, viz. the heels, ankles, knees, the portion of the arm from the elbow-joint to the fingers'-ends, shoulder-joint, chin, head, and joints, and bones, nails, and teeth, thicker than those of other people. They are possessed of great energy and perseverence, addicted to acts, capable of bearing pain and fatigue, endued with bodies firm and compact, and possessed of longevity of life.

classical.establishes: Asthi's position in the chain in verified Sanskrit: from medas comes asthi, from asthi comes majjā.

distinguishFrom.why: Marrow, the next dhātu, contained within asthi. WHO ISTA lists asthisāram as a Sanskrit SYNONYM of majjā-dhātuḥ at ITA-2.2.16, which means 'asthi-sāra' denotes marrow in one part of the standard and a bone-predominant constitution in another (ITA-2.8.1.6). This is a genuine collision inside a single standard and any index must handle it.
Two incompatible senses, both in WHO ISTA: (a) marrow, as a synonym of majjā (ITA-2.2.16); (b) the constitutional type in which bone predominates (ITA-2.8.1.6). The lexicon must carry both.
Joints. WHO gives these separate term IDs (ITA-2.2.13). Asthi-kṣaya signs include joint pain, so the two are clinically entangled but terminologically distinct.
The skeleton as a whole (ITA-2.2.14), distinct from asthi as tissue class.

Asthi is the classical seat (āśraya) of vāta, and the two have an inverse relationship (āśraya-āśrayi bhāva). This is why asthi disorders are treated with basti. The doṣa and the dhātu are constantly co-mentioned and are categorically different.
Hair, the mala of asthi per Charaka Chikitsasthana 15. A waste product, not part of the dhātu, though it is diagnostic of it.

mistranslations.rendering: bone, read as bone tissue only
mistranslations.why: The classical asthi includes teeth and nails in both the sāra description (Charaka Vimanasthana 8) and the kṣaya/vṛddhi signs (Sushruta Sutrasthana 15). WHO's closing sentence 'It refers to bone tissue' narrows it further than WHO's own dhāraṇa entry implies.

An equation, widely used in clinical papers (PMID 23049194), that the classical signs do not support: Sushruta's asthi-kṣaya presents with bone and joint pain, dental and gum wasting, and generalised dryness, whereas osteoporosis is typically asymptomatic until fracture. The two populations have never been compared.
That is asthipañjara (WHO ITA-2.2.14), a distinct headword.

Bhishagratna's own gloss for asthi-vṛddhi. A nineteenth-century pathological category imposed on a sign list whose content is supernumerary teeth and bony overgrowth. Quotable as a period document; not a translation.

openQuestions: The asthi-sāra collision inside WHO ISTA (marrow at ITA-2.2.16, bone-predominant constitution at ITA-2.8.1.6) is unexplained and may be an error in the standard or a real double usage. It should be raised with whoever maintains ISTA.
Why hair is the mala of asthi is nowhere explained in the retrieved sources and has no published discussion that this search located.

Whether patients meeting classical asthi-kṣaya criteria overlap with patients meeting densitometric osteoporosis criteria has never been studied, so far as PubMed searches for 'asthi dhatu' (1 hit) and 'asthi ayurveda bone' (4 hits) reveal.

The Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 11 reference is carried forward from an earlier project record and was not re-verified in this pass; since no public-domain translation exists it can only ever be a located reference.

distinguishFrom.why: Caraka inverts the expected relation: asthivaha is rooted in medas, while majjāvaha is rooted in asthi and sandhi. The two are frequently swapped in secondary sources.

medas is the ROOT of asthivaha srotas and the dhātu served by medovaha srotas; the same word occupies two different structural positions in one passage.

classical.establishes: atipravṛttiḥ as the first-named of the four signs of srotodushti. This is the only verified classical occurrence of the term in this technical sense that I found.
classical.quote: अतिप्रवृत्तिः सङ्गो वा सिराणां ग्रन्थयोऽपि वा| विमार्गगमनं चापि स्रोतसां दुष्टिलक्षणम्||२४||

classical.establishes: Charaka's channel-specific signs use the paired terms atisṛṣṭa (over-released) and atibaddha (over-bound) rather than atipravṛtti and saṅga. The same pairing recurs verbatim for the mutravaha srotas. This shows the excess/obstruction polarity is worked out in the prose BEFORE the summary verse names it, and under different vocabulary.
classical.quote: तद्यथा- अतिसृष्टमतिबद्धं कुपितमल्पाल्पमभीक्ष्णं वा सशब्दशूलमुच्छ्वसन्तं दृष्ट्वा प्राणवहान्यस्य स्रोतांसि प्रदुष्टानीति विद्यात्|

classical.establishes: A public-domain English example of the excess-versus-stoppage polarity as Charaka actually applies it channel by channel ('stoppage of sweat, or copiousness of sweat'). OCR artifact 'pr' for 'or' is in the source.
classical.quote: Beholding the stoppage of sweat, pr copiousness of sweat, or roughness ( of the skin ), or excessive oiliness ( of the skin ), or burning sensation ( all over the body ), or a general horripilation ( of the skin ), the physician should understand that the sweat-bearing ducts of the individual have become vitiated.

distinguishFrom.why: Charaka's own prose word for the same phenomenon in Ca.Vi.5/8, paired with atibaddha. atipravṛtti is the term of the summary verse. A lexicon that indexes only atipravṛtti will fail to find the passage where the concept is actually deployed.
Increase in the QUANTITY of a dosha or dhatu. atipravṛtti is excess of FLOW or activity through a channel. A dhatu can be increased without its channel being in atipravṛtti, and vice versa.

Excessive administration of a therapy (e.g. over-purgation), a treatment-outcome category in the panchakarma context. Shares the ati- prefix and the sense of excess but is iatrogenic and procedural, not a channel sign.

distinguishFrom.term: vega / pravṛtti in the sense of natural urges
distinguishFrom.why: pravṛtti also names the natural urges (mutra-pravṛtti etc.). 'atipravṛtti of the urges' is not the srotodushti sense.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's own lead rendering, but pravṛtti is proceeding/flowing, not producing. Over-production is closer to vṛddhi or to dhatu-vṛddhi and should not be carried forward as the primary gloss.
These are instances in particular channels, not the meaning. The term is channel-neutral.
Imports a glandular/endocrine reading. Atipravṛtti applies equally to purishavaha and pranavaha channels where secretion is not the operative function.

classical.establishes: Ātmā is the fourth constituent of āyu alongside body, senses and sattva (mind). Kaviratna (his 41): 'The union of body, senses, mind, and soul is called Life.'
classical.quote: śarīrēndriyasattvātmasaṁyōgō dhāri jīvitam| nityagaścānubandhaśca paryāyairāyurucyatē||42||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: The tridaṇḍa: sattva, ātmā and śarīra together constitute puruṣa, the subject of Ayurveda. Sanskrit (Charak Samhita Online 46-47): 'sattvamātmā śarīraṁ ca trayamētattridaṇḍavat' ... 'sa pumāṁścētanaṁ tacca taccādhikaraṇaṁ smr̥tam'. OCR spacing normalised.
classical.quote: Mind, soul, and body, this trinity, called person, resteth on union like three sticks (standing with one another's support.) Upon that (trinity) everything rests. That is also called purusha or Being. It is also animate. That is also regarded as the subject matter of this Science; and it is also for the sake of that, that this Science is promulgated.

classical.establishes: Ātmā is one of the nine dravyas (five bhūtas, ātmā, manas, kāla, diś). Kaviratna (his 47): 'Those having ether for the first (i.e., ether, air, fire, water, and earth), soul, mind, and the quarters, are constituent elements (of all things).'
classical.quote: khādīnyātmā manaḥ kālō diśaśca dravyasaṅgrahaḥ| sēndriyaṁ cētanaṁ dravyaṁ, nirindriyamacētanam||48||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: Ātmā is nirvikāra (unchanging), para, the cause of consciousness only in conjunction with sattva, bhūta-guṇas and indriyas, eternal, and a witness (draṣṭā). Kaviratna: 'The Soul is immutable (incapable of being affected by anything) and eternal; faculties, the attributes of matter, and the senses, are the causes of consciousness. The Soul is the eternal witness, for it views all actions (without being itself affected by any of them).' His printed number for this aphorism is illegible in the OCR (reads 56 twice); by sequence it is his 55.
classical.quote: nirvikāraḥ parastvātmā sattvabhūtaguṇēndriyaiḥ| caitanyē kāraṇaṁ nityō draṣṭā paśyati hi kriyāḥ||56||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: The ṣaḍdhātu puruṣa: five bhūtas plus cetanā-dhātu; the cetanā-dhātu alone is also called puruṣa. This is the medical (cikitsya) puruṣa in which ātmā appears as the sixth, conscious constituent. Kaviratna (his 23): 'Some regard that Purusha is made up of six ingredients, viz, those begining with ether, and consciousness. Others regard that only one of the ingredients, viz., consciousness is called Purusha.'
classical.quote: khādayaścētanāṣaṣṭhā dhātavaḥ puruṣaḥ smr̥taḥ| cētanādhāturapyēkaḥ smr̥taḥ puruṣasañjñakaḥ||16||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.verse: 70-73 (standard; Kaviratna prints 76-78 and a second 78 in the OCR)
classical.establishes: The liṅgas (inferential marks) of the embodied ātmā: breathing, blinking, life, movement of mind, passage of mind between senses, impulsion, retention, dreaming, dying, cross-ocular recognition, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, effort, consciousness, steadiness, buddhi, memory, ego-sense; absent in the dead. Kaviratna's English (his 76-78): 'The vital breaths called Prana and Apana, the opening and closing of the eye (and other similar motions), the period of time called Life, the movements of the mind, the passing of the mind from one sense to another, the despatch of the mind (to a particular object), and holding the mind thereto. Sojourns (of the mind) to other places in dreams, as also the acceptance of death, the perception by the left eye of objects seen by the right eye. Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, will, consciousness, apprehension, understanding, memory, and the idea of personal identity, these are the indications of the Supreme Soul (when invested with a body).' Both the Sanskrit and English were retrieved; the English is at the archive.org URL given in the other entries.
classical.quote: prāṇāpānau nimēṣādyā jīvanaṁ manasō gatiḥ| indriyāntarasañcāraḥ prēraṇaṁ dhāraṇaṁ ca yat||70|| dēśāntaragatiḥ svapnē pañcatvagrahaṇaṁ tathā| dr̥ṣṭasya dakṣiṇēnākṣṇā savyēnāvagamastathā||71|| icchā dvēṣaḥ sukhaṁ duḥkhaṁ prayatnaścētanā dhr̥tiḥ| buddhiḥ smr̥tirahaṅkārō liṅgāni paramātmanaḥ||72|| yasmāt samupalabhyantē liṅgānyētāni jīvataḥ| na mr̥tasyātmaliṅgāni tasmādāhurmaharṣayaḥ||73||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 16-17; Sanskrit verse number not established
classical.establishes: Suśruta's medical position on the self: not all-pervading (against Sāṃkhya), real, eternal, transmigrating, known by inference; the karma-puruṣa (self plus five bhūtas) is the object of medicine. Bhishagratna's section numbers are his own, not verse numbers.
classical.quote: The Science of medicine does not lay down that the self-conscious Selves (Kshetrajna) are all pervading, but on the contrary it asserts that they are real and eternal and are born in the planes of divine, human or animal existence according to their good or evil deeds in life. The existence of these self-conscious entities can be ascertained duly by inference inasmuch as they are extremely subtle in their essence. ... Purusha (individual) is nothing but a combination of a self-conscious self and the five kinds of matter (Maha- bhutas) formed into an organic body. This Purusha or individual, which is called Individual of action (Karma- Purusha), falls within the scope of the science and art of medicine.

distinguishFrom.why: In Ca.Śā.1.16 puruṣa is either the six-dhātu compound (five bhūtas plus cetanā) or the cetanā-dhātu alone; in Sū.1.46-47 it is the sattva-ātmā-śarīra triad. Ātmā is the conscious constituent of puruṣa, not a synonym, though Śā.1.16b and Bhishagratna's 'Purusha (self-conscious subjectivity)' use puruṣa for ātmā.
Listed separately from ātmā in every enumeration retrieved (Sū.1.42, 1.48, Śā.1.17). Ātmā is nirvikāra and a witness; manas is an instrument with guṇas (aṇutva, ekatva) and objects.
Buddhi is a liṅga (mark) of ātmā (Śā.1.72) and in Sū.1.49 a guṇa of ātmā; it is not the self.
WHO separates jīvaḥ (ITA-1.9.3.2.3) and bhūtātmā (1.9.3.2.2, the embodied self) from ātmā; Kaviratna uses 'Jiva-Soul' for the living embodied self in Śā.1.73.

Śā.1.72 says the liṅgas are of paramātman; Kaviratna renders 'the Supreme Soul (when invested with a body)'. Whether Caraka intends a cosmic self or the individual self qualified as supreme is a commentarial question not resolved here.

mistranslations.why: Not wrong but loaded; Kaviratna himself flags it as 'misleading' (footnote, Sū.8) because it imports a theological entity where the text means the principle that unifies consciousness. Bhishagratna avoids it in favour of 'self-conscious self'.
NIA SV0009 offers 'Soul or spirit'. 'Spirit' in English overlaps with prāṇa and with ghosts; the texts never make ātmā a breath or a spectre.
Ātmā is the CAUSE of consciousness only in conjunction (Sū.1.56: caitanye kāraṇam ... sattvabhūtaguṇendriyaiḥ); cetanā is a mark of ātmā, not its definition.

openQuestions: Whether paramātman in Ca.Śā.1.72 means the individual self or a cosmic one (commentaries not retrieved).
How Suśruta's denial that selves are vibhu (all-pervading) squares with WHO ITA-1.9.3.2.15 vibhu 'an attribute of atma'; WHO appears to follow the Caraka/Sāṃkhya line.

renderings.sourceName: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda (2022), term ID ITA-2.1.3.2
renderings.locator: ITA-2.1.3.2; printed p. 35 (PDF p. 53). Sanskrit term 'avalambaka-kaphaḥ'. Description: 'Subtype of kapha seated in the chest region which supports and sustains the heart and other sites of kapha.'
renderings.assessment: WHO follows VĀGBHAṬA here: chest seat, supports the heart AND the other kapha sites. That second clause is AH Sū 12.15-16a; in Suśruta it belongs to the āmāśaya kapha instead. WHO lists avalambaka FIRST among the five kaphas, matching AH's order.

renderings.sourceName: Suśruta Saṃhitā tr. Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (public domain)
renderings.locator: Sūtrasthāna ch. 21, Wikisource text: 'The Avalamvaka:—The Kapham, located in the region of the chest, protects the joints of the arms, the neck and the sternum, and enables the heart to perform its natural functions with the help of the lymph-chyle derived from the assimilated food and its own intrinsic potency.'
renderings.assessment: Note the spelling 'Avalamvaka' (v for b) — Bengali-influenced transliteration, consistent across Bhishagratna. As with kledaka, the NAME is Bhishagratna's supplied heading; the mūla at 21.14 does not contain it. Bhishagratna's 'protects the joints of the arms, the neck and the sternum' is his reading of trika-sandhāraṇa.

renderings.sourceName: Suśruta Saṃhitā tr. Bhishagratna, footnote at Sūtrasthāna ch. 15
renderings.locator: 'They are known as Shleshmaka, Kledaka, Vodhaka, Tarpaka, Avalamvaka.'
renderings.assessment: Listed last in Bhishagratna's footnote, first in WHO's ordering. Ordering of the five kaphas is not stable across sources.

renderings.english: situated in the heart and is responsible for its structural integrity
renderings.sourceName: J Ayurveda Integr Med (2025), atherosclerotic CVD review
renderings.locatorWithheld: "J Ayurveda Integr Med (2025), atherosclerotic CVD review" is not a source this project has cleared for quotation
renderings.assessment: MISLOCATION. Both mūlas place avalambaka in the chest (uras/trika) SUPPORTING the heart — avalambana OF the hṛdaya. Saying it is 'situated in the heart' collapses the supporter into the supported, and the paper says this while citing the very verses that contradict it.
renderings.licenceNote: "J Ayurveda Integr Med (2025), atherosclerotic CVD review" is not a source this project has cleared for quotation

classical.establishes: Seat = chest (uras); functions = holding the trika, and supporting the heart with the aid of anna-rasa and its own potency. The heading name is the translator's.
classical.quote: The Avalamvaka:—The Kapham, located in the region of the chest, protects the joints of the arms, the neck and the sternum, and enables the heart to perform its natural functions with the help of the lymph-chyle derived from the assimilated food and its own intrinsic potency.

classical.establishes: The word 'avalambaka' does not appear; what appears is the verbal phrase 'hṛdaya-AVALAMBANAṂ karoti' — it performs the supporting of the heart. The later NAME is derived from this function word. Seat is uraḥ-stha; second function is trika-sandhāraṇa. Crucially, Suśruta does NOT here give it the 'supports the other kapha seats' role.
classical.quote: उरःस्थस्त्रिकसन्धारणमात्मवीर्येणान्नरससहितेन हृदयावलम्बनं करोति;

classical.text: Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya (Sanskrit mūla; no public-domain English translation exists, so no translation is quoted)
classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa supplies the NAME and its etymology explicitly ('ato'valambakaḥ śleṣmā' — hence it is called avalambaka) and ADDS the function of supporting the remaining kapha abodes (kapha-dhāmnāṃ ca śeṣāṇām), which Suśruta gave to the āmāśaya kapha. Corroborated: PMID 40972327 cites 'Ashtanga Hridaya Sutra Sthana 12/15-16'.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: The principal confusion, and a real textual conflict. 'The kapha that supports the other kapha seats' is the ĀMĀŚAYA kapha (kledaka) in Suśruta 21.14 but AVALAMBAKA in AH 12.15-16a. Any claim about which kapha supports the others is unstatable without naming the authority.

Both are cardiac and are invoked together in the same papers (PMID 29153383, PMID 40972327). Avalambaka is the structural/sustaining component at the chest; sādhaka is the functional/mental-drive pitta within the heart.
Avalambaka supports the heart (hṛdaya-avalambana); it is not the heart and is not seated in it. PMID 40972327 makes exactly this error in print.

Suśruta gives avalambaka the job of trika-sandhāraṇa — holding the trika, a joint region. That looks like joint work, which is śleṣaka's general domain. The distinction is regional: avalambaka holds the specific uras/trika complex, śleṣaka acts at all sandhis.

mistranslations.why: Published in PMID 40972327 and contradicted by both mūlas, which place it in uras/trika and have it SUPPORT the heart. The name itself (avalamb- to hang upon, to support) encodes the relation, so the mistranslation erases the etymology.
A proposed correlate, not a meaning, and it does not account for either trika-sandhāraṇa (Suśruta) or the support of the remaining kapha seats (Vāgbhaṭa).
Common in popular and teaching material because the seat is the chest. Neither mūla assigns avalambaka any respiratory function; the chest here is the seat, not the organ of action.

mistranslations.rendering: Citing Suśruta for 'supports the other sites of kapha'
mistranslations.why: That clause is AH Sū 12.15-16a. Suśruta 21.14 gives that role to the āmāśaya kapha. WHO ISTA's description combines both clauses and is therefore following Vāgbhaṭa.

openQuestions: The retrieved AH text reads 'यत्करोत्यबलम्बनम्' where the sense and the following etymology require 'अवलम्बनम्'. Is this a typographical error on the retrieved page or a genuine variant reading? Needs a critical edition.
How do Dalhaṇa and Aruṇadatta handle the Suśruta/Vāgbhaṭa swap of the 'supports the other kaphas' function?

What exactly does 'trika' denote here — the sacral region, or the shoulder/neck/upper-back junction? Bhishagratna reads 'the joints of the arms, the neck and the sternum'; EasyAyurveda reads 'meeting place of shoulder, neck and back'. Other traditions read trika as sacroiliac. Unresolved.

classical.establishes: Defines āyu as the conjunction (saṃyoga) of body, sense organs, mind (sattva) and self (ātman), and gives dhāri, jīvita, nityaga and anubandha as its synonyms. This is the locus classicus for the term.
classical.quote: शरीरेन्द्रियसत्त्वात्मसंयोगो धारि जीवितम्| नित्यगश्चानुबन्धश्च पर्यायैरायुरुच्यते||४२||

classical.establishes: The only lawfully quotable English rendering of the āyu definition: Kaviratna gives 'Life' for āyu and leaves the four synonyms untransliterated. Double spacing in the quote is the archive.org OCR, reproduced as retrieved.
classical.quote: The  union  of  body,  senses,  mind,  and  soul  is  called  Life.  The  latter  is  known  again  by  the  names  of  Dhari, Jivita,  Nityaga,  and  Anubandha *41

classical.establishes: States that āyu is fourfold - hita, ahita, sukha, duḥkha - and that the science which declares these, plus its measure (māna), is called āyurveda. This single verse is the source of four of the nine terms in this group.
classical.quote: हिताहितं सुखं दुःखमायुस्तस्य हिताहितम्| मानं च तच्च यत्रोक्तमायुर्वेदः स उच्यते||४१||

classical.verse: within the passage printed up to Kaviratna's aphorism-marker 18
classical.establishes: A second, independent synonym-list for āyu in Charaka, this one headed by cetanānuvṛtti (continuation of consciousness) rather than by the body-senses-mind-self conjunction. 'Chetanci' and 'Anubandka' are OCR corruptions of Chetana and Anubandha; quoted exactly as retrieved. Kaviratna's own footnote on this passage confirms the correct reading is 'Chetananuvrittih'.
classical.quote: As  to  Life  :  that  in  which  (or,  by  which)  Chetanci  exists  or  follows),  Jivitam,  Anubandka,  and  Dhari,  are  words  expressive  of  the  same  meaning.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata's opening chapter is titled for the desire for āyu (Āyuṣkāmīya) and grounds the four puruṣārthas on it. Recorded as a location only: no quotation is given because Ashtanga Hridaya has no public-domain English translation, and the Sanskrit line I saw on the retrieved page carried a verse number I could not check against a critical edition.

distinguishFrom.why: Listed in Su 1.42 as one of several synonyms (paryāya) of āyu, not as an equivalent term in its own right. Treating jīvita as interchangeable with āyu loses the point of the verse, which is that āyu has several aspects each named separately.

Prāṇa is vital breath / a vāta subtype, a physiological entity. Āyu is the conjunction of body, senses, mind and self as a whole. English 'life' covers both, which is precisely why the English is unsafe.
Āyu is the object; āyurveda is the knowledge of it. Su 1.41 and 1.42 are consecutive and define the pair in that order.
A separate WHO-listed term (ITA entries āyuṣyam / anāyuṣyam appear in the WHO index), meaning life-promoting or conducive to longevity - an adjective of things, not the noun for life itself.

mistranslations.why: Su 1.42 defines āyu structurally (a conjunction of four constituents), not temporally. Kaviratna's own footnote concedes 'Ayush' can mean period of life but says that 'generally, however, it stands for Life'. Rendering it as lifespan silently picks the minority sense.
Conflates āyu with vayas (age/stage of life), a distinct term.
Ātman is one of the four constituents of āyu, not āyu itself.

openQuestions: Does NAMASTE carry a code for āyu, and what English term does it assign? The portal is a single-page app that returns a shell to a plain fetch and its API paths 302-redirect; the underlying terminology table was not retrievable.

I confirmed the offset by matching his English against the Devanagari of 1.41, 1.42 and 1.43 individually. Whether the offset holds across the whole chapter is unverified.

classical.establishes: The definition of āyurveda by its contents: the knowledge in which hita, ahita, sukha and duḥkha forms of life, what is beneficial and harmful to life, and the measure of life are declared.
classical.quote: हिताहितं सुखं दुःखमायुस्तस्य हिताहितम्| मानं च तच्च यत्रोक्तमायुर्वेदः स उच्यते||४१||

classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of the definitional verse. Note Kaviratna renders the fourfold āyu as 'Good, evil, happy and unhappy' - hita/ahita become good/evil, not salutary/unsalutary.
classical.quote: Good,  evil,  happy  and  unhappy  is  Life.  That  (  knowledge)  in  which  are  declared  its  nature,  and  measure,  and  what  is  beneficial  to  it  and  what  injurious,  is  called  the  Science  of  Life.40

classical.establishes: Names āyurveda the most sacred veda of that āyu, beneficial to men in both worlds - the verse that grounds the claim that āyurveda is a veda, not merely a śāstra.
classical.quote: तस्यायुषः पुण्यतमो वेदो वेदविदां मतः| वक्ष्यते यन्मनुष्याणां लोकयोरुभयोर्हितम्||४३||

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English for Su 1.43. 'ivith' is the archive.org OCR for 'with'; reproduced exactly as retrieved.
classical.quote: The  sacred  Science  of  Life,  approved  by  persons  conversant  ivith  the  Vedas,  and  beneficial  to  both  ( this  and  the  other)  region  of  men,  is  being  expounded  (as  follows.)42

classical.verse: within the passage printed up to Kaviratna's aphorism-marker 18
classical.establishes: Charaka's own etymological justification of the name in Sutrasthana 30 (āyurvedayati iti āyurvedaḥ). The hyphenation artefact and the stray ']' are OCR; reproduced as retrieved.
classical.quote: It  is  called  the  Science  of  Life  because  it  explains  (the  condi¬  tions  of]  Life.

classical.establishes: The prayojana (purpose) verse: preservation of the health of the healthy and pacification of disorder in the diseased. The most-quoted single line about what āyurveda is for.
classical.quote: प्रयोजनं चास्य स्वस्थस्य स्वास्थ्यरक्षणमातुरस्य विकारप्रशमनं च ॥२६॥

classical.verse: 15 as printed on the retrieved page
classical.establishes: Sushruta's two-way etymology of the name: the science in which āyu is found, or by which one obtains āyu. The verse number 15 is as printed on this secondary page and was NOT cross-checked against a critical edition.
classical.quote: आयुरस्मिन् विद्यते, अनेन वाऽऽयुर्विन्दन्ति' इत्यायुर्वेदः ||१५||

classical.verse: no verse number printed on the retrieved page
classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for the same etymology. Wisdomlib's Sushruta is the Bhishagratna translation and is therefore quotable; its Charaka is the 1949 Gulabkunverba and is not.
classical.quote: The etymological meaning of the term 'Ayurveda' may be interpreted to denote either a science in the knowledge of which life exists, or which helps a man to enjoy a longer duration of life.

classical.verse: no verse number printed on the retrieved page
classical.establishes: Sushruta's statement of purpose, corresponding to the Sanskrit printed as Su.Su 1.14 on the easyayurveda page (व्याध्युपसृष्टानां व्याधिपरिमोक्षः, स्वस्थस्य रक्षणं च ||१४||). Note the order is inverted relative to Charaka Su 30.26: Sushruta puts cure first, Charaka puts preservation first.
classical.quote: The object or utility of the science which forms the subject of our present discussion, may be grouped under two distinct sub-heads such as (1) the cure of diseased persons, and (2) the preservation of health in those who are not afflicted with any sort of bodily distempers.

classical.verse: no verse number printed on the retrieved page
classical.establishes: Sushruta's placement of āyurveda as an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda, and the eight-branch division that follows. Relevant to whether 'Ayurveda' names a veda, a branch of one, or a secular science - a disagreement the sources do not settle.
classical.quote: The Ayurveda (which forms the subject of our present discourse), originally formed one of the subsections of the Atharva Veda; and even before the creation of mankind, the self-begotten Brahma strung it together into a hundred thousand couplets (Shlokas), divided into a thousand chapters.

classical.establishes: Charaka gives śākhāvidyā, sūtrajñāna, śāstralakṣaṇa and tantra as synonyms of āyurveda - a synonym set almost never reported in modern entries. Kaviratna's transliteration uses C for ś; reproduced as retrieved.
classical.quote: As  regards  these,  (it  should  be  answered  that)  Ayurveda,  Cakhavidya,  Sutrajnana,  Castralakshmanam,  and  Tantram  are  words  expressive  of  the  same  meaning.*

distinguishFrom.why: The object of the knowledge, not the knowledge. Su 1.41 defines āyurveda; Su 1.42 defines āyu; they are consecutive and deliberately separated.
Treatment, one limb of āyurveda. Kaviratna in Sutrasthana 30 translates cikitsā as 'the Science of Treatment' and distinguishes it from the Science of Life in the same paragraph.

Sushruta calls āyurveda a subsection (upāṅga) of the Atharvaveda; Charaka Su 1.43 calls it a veda in its own right. The two founding texts do not agree, and a lexicon entry that asserts either is taking a side.
WHO gives this a separate term ID (ITA-1.4.1, 'Eight clinical specialities of Ayurveda'); it is the eightfold division of the subject, not a synonym for the whole.

mistranslations.why: Selects only Sushruta's second etymological alternative and drops Charaka's definition by content (Su 1.41), which is about hita/ahita and sukha/duḥkha rather than duration.
A category label from outside the tradition. It carries no relation to the compound and cannot support the classical claim that āyurveda covers the healthy as well as the sick (Su 30.26).
An English back-formation. It makes āyurveda an adjective qualifying 'medicine', which inverts the compound: veda is the head, not the modifier.
Marketing vocabulary with no textual anchor; it also imports therapeutic connotations that the definitional verses do not carry.

openQuestions: Whether Sushruta Su.Su 1.14 and 1.15 carry those numbers in a critical edition. The Bhishagratna page I quoted prints no verse numbers at all, and the numbers come from a secondary site (easyayurveda).
Whether NAMASTE codes āyurveda as a term at all, and with what English.

classical.establishes: The three-fold classification and its address. sahaja bala is prākṛta to BOTH śarīra and sattva, and kālaja is explicitly both ṛtu-derived and vayas-derived, so 'seasonal strength' alone is incomplete.
classical.quote: त्रिविधं बलमिति- सहजं, कालजं, युक्तिकृतं च| सहजं यच्छरीरसत्त्वयोः प्राकृतं, कालकृतमृतुविभागजं वयःकृतं च, युक्तिकृतं पुनस्तद्यदाहारचेष्टायोगजम्||३६||

classical.establishes: Sets the context: the three-fold bala is announced in a list of triads at verse 34 and expounded at 36, immediately after the three upastambhas.
classical.quote: अथ खलु त्रय उपस्तम्भाः, त्रिविधं बलं, त्रीण्यायतनानि, त्रयो रोगाः, त्रयो रोगमार्गाः, त्रिविधा भिषजः, त्रिविधमौषधमिति||३४||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Su 11/36, preserving the body-and-mind scope of sahaja bala.
classical.quote: There are three kinds of strength, viz., that which is due to one's nature, that which is due to a particular season ( of life or the year ) ; and that which is due to exertion ( such as physical exercise, the use of invigorating food and spices and liquors, &c). Natural strength implies that kind of strength which inheres to the very nature of one's body and mind.

classical.establishes: Why bala anchors this whole term group: the stated purpose of the entire ten-fold examination is grasping the particular measure of strength. Bala is not one of the ten items; it is what the ten items are for. Ellipsis marks the ten-item list quoted in full in the prakriti record.
classical.quote: tasmādāturaṁ parīkṣēta … balapramāṇaviśēṣagrahaṇahētōḥ||94||

classical.establishes: Confirms the same purpose clause for sāra specifically: the eight sāras are taught for knowing the measure of strength.
classical.quote: sārataścēti sārāṇyaṣṭau puruṣāṇāṁ balamānaviśēṣajñānārthamupadiśyantē||102||

distinguishFrom.why: WHO both merges them (ITA-2.2.27) and separates them (ITA-4.8.25). Su 11/36 defines bala without reference to disease resistance at all: sahaja bala is what is natural to body and mind. Treating them as one word is a modern move WHO has half-adopted.
A distinct WHO headword. Ojas is a substance; bala a capacity. Their classical relation is a live question, not a settled identity.
Vi 8/121 says bala is inferred from karmaśakti; vyāyāmaśakti is evidence for bala, not bala.
Vi 8/102 says the sāras are taught in order to know bala. Indicator, not identity.
WHO ITA-2.2.26, whose criteria include 'increase in strength' — so bala is a sign of dhātusāmya, hence distinct from it.
Vi 8/101 grades vyādhi-bala, the strength of the DISEASE, with the same word. A bare 'bala' in a nidāna passage may be the illness's strength, not the patient's.

mistranslations.why: WHO's own first word at ITA-2.2.27, and the most consequential error in this group. Su 11/36 defines bala by what is natural to body and mind, by season and age, and by diet and activity — none of which is an immune mechanism. 'Immunity' licenses infection-resistance claims the classical definition does not support.
Incomplete. Su 11/36 says kālaja bala is ṛtu-vibhāgaja AND vayaḥkṛta. WHO's description catches this even though its English term does not.
Loses the specificity. yukti means rational contrivance; Su 11/36 says it arises from the yoking of āhāra and ceṣṭā. 'Acquired' could equally describe kālaja.
sahaja bala is explicitly prākṛta to śarīra AND sattva; restricting bala to the body contradicts the defining verse.

openQuestions: Is bala a headword in this lexicon or a cross-cutting concept? Vi 8/94 makes it the purpose of the examination rather than an item in it, which argues for a concept record rather than a term record.
What is the classical relation between bala and ojas, and do Chakrapani and Gangadhara agree?
Why does WHO carry vyādhikṣamatvam twice, once merged with balam and once alone?

classical.quote: बलवृध्दिकरास्त्विमे भावा भवन्ति| तद्यथा- बलवत्पुरुषे देशे जन्म बलवत्पुरुषे काले च, सुखश्च कालयोगः, बीजक्षेत्रगुणसंपच्च, आहारसंपच्च, शरीरसंपच्च, सात्म्यसंपच्च, सत्त्वसंपच्च, स्वभावसंसिध्दिश्च, यौवनं च, कर्म च, संहर्षश्चेति||१३||

classical.establishes: The four śarīra-vṛddhikara factors, immediately preceding the bala list. Quoted so the two can be told apart; WHO standardises this one and not the other.
classical.quote: कार्त्स्न्येन शरीरवृध्दिकरास्त्विमे भावा भवन्ति; तद्यथा- कालयोगः, स्वभावसंसिध्दि:, आहारसौष्ठवम्, अविघातश्चेति||१२||

classical.establishes: The public-domain English of the list. The ellipsis marks a page break in the scan occupied by a translator's footnote; no list item was omitted.
classical.quote: The following are means of increase of strength; They are — Birth in a country of strong men; Birth in an age of strong men; Happy conjunction of time; Wealth of attributes of both seed and soil; Wealth of food and drink; Wealth of body; Wealth of assimilability; Wealth of Mind; ... Dispensation of Nature; Youth; Acts; and Cheerfulness or joy.

distinguishFrom.why: Bala is the capacity; bala-vṛddhi is its augmentation. WHO classifies bala into sahaja/yuktikṛta/kālaja (ITA-2.2.28/29/30); the Śā. 6.13 list cuts across that classification — 'birth in a strong region' is sahaja-adjacent, 'karma' is yuktikṛta, 'yauvana' is kālaja.

CS Śā. 6.12 lists FOUR factors for body growth; 6.13 lists TWELVE for strength. WHO standardises only the former (ITA-3.1.3). Citing 'the four factors' when you mean strength, or vice versa, is a common slip and the two sūtras are adjacent.
Rasāyana is a therapeutic modality producing yuktikṛta bala; bala-vṛddhi as given in Śā. 6.13 is overwhelmingly non-therapeutic (birth, region, era, seed and soil, youth).

The NIA glossary's bala entry runs them together ('As long as the patient has good strength he can resist all sorts of diseases'), and WHO puts balam and vyādhikṣamatvam under one ID. But CS Sū. 28.7 predicates vyādhikṣamatva of śarīras with particular constitutions, while Śā. 6.13 is a causal list for bala. They are not interchangeable.
The same word names doṣa/dhātu excess (e.g. WHO ITA-5.2.2.4 pittavṛddhi-lakṣaṇam, rasavṛddhiḥ, raktavṛddhiḥ). In bala-vṛddhi it is desirable; in rakta-vṛddhi it is a disorder.

mistranslations.why: Collapses bala-vṛddhi into vyādhikṣamatva and then into a product claim. Eight of the twelve factors in Śā. 6.13 are not modifiable at all.
Reads karma as exercise and drops the other eleven items. The NIA glossary itself renders karma as 'physical exercise' where Kaviratna has 'Acts', so even the glossaries disagree on that single item.
Confuses the bala list (Śā. 6.13) with the śarīra-vṛddhi list (Śā. 6.12), and imports a biochemical sense of 'growth factor'.

openQuestions: Whether 'bala-vṛddhi' is a headword anywhere in the samhitas at all. What is attested is the adjectival compound balavṛddhikara ('strength-increasing') qualifying bhāvāḥ. The lexicon should decide whether to head the entry balavṛddhikara bhāva instead.
How Chakrapāṇi glosses karma and saṃharṣa in this list — the divergence between Kaviratna's 'Acts'/'Cheerfulness' and the NIA glossary's 'physical exercise'/'cheerfulness' turns on it. Not checked.
Whether the Śā. 6.13 list has any relation to the three-fold bala classification, or is an independent scheme.

distinguishFrom.why: Same word; WHO ITA.3.11.13 'Urinary bladder' is a different entry from ITA-9.2.71 bastikarma. The procedure is named from the animal bladder used as the enema bag (Bhishagratna's note on Dallana).
The decoction (non-unctuous) enema, the cleansing type; Sushruta Chi.35.19 'nirūhaḥ śodhano lekhī'; Kaviratna 'dry enemata'; WHO ITA-9.2.75.
The unctuous enema, nourishing (Chi.35.19 'snaihiko bṛṁhaṇo mataḥ'); WHO ITA-9.2.72/73 distinguish half-dose anuvāsana from full snehabasti.
Urethral or vaginal route (WHO ITA-9.2.85); WHO's bastikarma definition folds these routes in, classical usage treats them as a named sub-type.
Charaka's five count two bastis (nirūha and anuvāsana) separately (Kaviratna's footnote, Lesson II); Vāgbhaṭa's five count nirūha once and add bloodletting (AH Su.14.5, GRETIL).
The nozzle/pipe; Sushruta Chi.35 is titled for both Netra and Vasti, so 'vasti' in that chapter often means the bag, not the procedure.

mistranslations.rendering: colonic irrigation / colon cleanse / detox enema
mistranslations.why: Imports hydrotherapy and pop-wellness toxin models; classical basti is a dosed medicated preparation retained or expelled on a schedule, with a nourishing (anuvāsana) class that has no cleansing aim at all.
Collapses nirūha, anuvāsana, mātrā, yāpana and uttara basti into one biomedical procedure; the Sanskrit sources treat the classes as having opposite actions (śodhana vs bṛṁhaṇa).

Whether Kaviratna's translation reaches Siddhisthana at all was not checked; the BIUSante copy used runs Sutra through Chikitsa.
Charaka's own definition of basti by route (Siddhisthana 1.41 region, 'सम्यक् सुखेनैति च यः स बस्तिः') was seen only as a half-line; the full verse was not transcribed.

Recorded to show the range WHO assigns to the same root elsewhere: classification of diseases, and surgical incision (ITA-9.6.65 'Incision and drainage — The procedure of incising a fluid-filled cavity for drainage'; ITA-9.6.133 'Incision — Incision procedure for wound management'). Neither is the sixth kriyakala, and both are live sources of confusion.

classical.establishes: Critical point, parallel to vyakti and re-confirmed this session: the prose of the sixth stage does not use the word bheda. It speaks of lesions that have BURST (avadīrṇānām) and become ulcers (vraṇabhāvam āpannānām), and of long-standing sequelae (dīrghakālānubandhaḥ) for fever and diarrhoea, ending in incurability if untreated. The name 'bheda' comes only from the summary verse 21.36.
classical.quote: अत ऊर्ध्वमेतेषामवदीर्णानां व्रणभावमापन्नानां षष्ठः क्रियाकालः, ज्वरातिसारप्रभृतीनां च दीर्घकालानुबन्धः । तत्राप्रतिक्रियमाणेऽसाध्यतामुपयान्ति ॥३५॥

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for the sixth stage. Note that his prose here is about bursting and chronicity, while his gloss on the summary verse is 'differentiating traits' — the same translator gives the stage two different senses in one chapter, which is the clearest evidence that the ambiguity is in the source, not in later readers.
classical.quote: The sixth occasion for the calling in of medical aid should be considered to have arisen when a swelling (abscess, tumour, etc.) would burst and exhibit the characteristic symptoms of an open ulcer. A persistent lingering or continuance of a fever or dysentery, etc., should be considered as marking, or forming one of its particular stages, and which may run into one of an incurable type, if neglected or not sufficiently cared for at the outset.

classical.establishes: The only occurrence of bheda as the stage-name in the retrieved verses, and again governed by doṣāṇām — bheda of the doshas.
classical.quote: व्यक्तिं भेदं च यो वेत्ति दोषाणां स भवेद्भिषक् ॥३६॥

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ITA-4.5.24 defines upadrava as 'A factor, event or condition complicating a disease or condition' (printed p. 112) — the dedicated word for complication. If bheda simply meant complication, upadrava would be redundant. Practitioner sources that gloss bheda as 'stage of complications' are collapsing these.

WHO ITA-4.2.3: 'Types of disease — The categorization of diseases based on various established criteria.' A taxonomic term, not a stage. The overlap with WHO's 'differentiates into subtypes' sense of bheda at ITA-4.6.12 makes this a real trap.

A surgical procedure — WHO ITA-9.6.65 renders it 'Incision and drainage' and ITA-9.6.133 'Incision'. Same root, and the sixth-stage prose is about a lesion bursting, so the two can be confused, but bhedana is something the surgeon does and bheda is something the disease does.

distinguishFrom.term: bhedana (a drug action) and bhedaka (a pain quality)
distinguishFrom.why: Bhedana also names a class of drug action (breaking up, deobstruent). Bheda/bhedaka additionally names a splitting or breaking type of pain in symptom lists — WHO's own vata-aggravation list at ITA-5.2.1.2 includes 'breaking type of pain'. Neither is the stage.
21.35 says untreated cases 'attain incurability' (asādhyatām upayānti). Incurability is a consequence of neglect at this stage, not a synonym for the stage.

mistranslations.why: True of the surgical cases Sushruta names (a shopha or vidradhi bursting into a vrana) but false for the systemic cases in the same sentence, where the criterion is dīrghakālānubandhaḥ, long-term persistence. A rendering that covers only the surgical half misreads half the verse.
Drops the differentiation-into-subtypes sense that both WHO and Bhishagratna record, and duplicates upadrava, which WHO codes separately at ITA-4.5.24.
Overstates. 21.35 says untreated cases become incurable, not that the stage is itself terminal. The whole framing of kriyakala is that a sixth occasion for treatment still exists.
Confuses bheda the stage with bhedana the procedure. WHO codes the procedure separately at ITA-9.6.65 and ITA-9.6.133.
Captures the dīrghakālānubandha half and misses the bursting half. The mirror image of the 'rupture' error.

openQuestions: Whether Dalhana reconciles the two senses (bursting versus differentiation) or licenses one of them.
Whether WHO's 'differentiates into subtypes based on dosha' reading has a textual basis in Su.Su. 21 or is imported from the vyādhibheda tradition.

Whether the stray 'kālaḥ' at WHO ITA-4.6.12 is an erratum in WHO's own copy: it is now confirmed present in the PDF text, so it is not a mirror artefact, but whether WHO has since issued a correction is unchecked.

classical.establishes: Seat = skin (tvak); two functions — absorption/digestion of topically applied substances, and manifestation of complexion; designation = bhrājakāgni.
classical.quote: The Bhrajakagni:-The Pittam, which has its seat in the skin, is called the Bhrajakagni (illuminating or irradiating heat) inasmuch as it absorbs the substances used in the shape of unguents. lubrications, etc. and irradiates the glow of one's natural complexion.

classical.establishes: The mūla is explicit and specific: bhrājaka is the 'paktā' (digester) of the kriyā-dravyas of abhyaṅga (oil massage), pariṣeka (pouring), avagāha (tub bath) and ālepana (paste application), AND the 'prakāśaka' (revealer) of chāyā (complexion/hue). Both clauses are in the same sentence; dropping either misrepresents the term.
classical.quote: यत्तु त्वचि पित्तं तस्मिन् भ्राजकोऽग्निरिति सञ्ज्ञा, सोऽभ्यङ्गपरिषेकावगाहालेपनादीनां क्रियाद्रव्याणां पक्ता छायानां च प्रकाशकः ||१०||

distinguishFrom.why: Three distinct classical terms for aspects of appearance that bhrājaka is said to govern. Chāyā is what Su.Sū. 21.10 actually names (bhrājaka is its prakāśaka). Varṇa is complexion/colour proper. Prabhā is radiance and has its own WHO entry (ITA-2.1.2.8, 'Lustre') as a FUNCTION of pitta generally, not of bhrājaka specifically. English collapses all three into 'complexion' or 'glow'.
Both are 'appearance' pittas and their Sanskrit roots are confusable in transliteration. Bhrājaka makes the skin visible to others; ālocaka makes visible forms apprehensible to the self.
Both are colouring functions. Rañjaka colours rasa internally; bhrājaka manifests colour at the skin surface. Papers on skin pigmentation routinely invoke both and rarely say which is doing what.

distinguishFrom.term: tvak (the seven skin layers) and the avabhāsinī layer
distinguishFrom.why: Tvak is the anatomical seat; avabhāsinī is the outermost of Suśruta's seven layers and is where bhrājaka is conventionally localised by commentators. Bhrājaka is the functional pitta there, not the layer itself.

mistranslations.why: The dominant modern equation (the AYUSHDHARA review builds its whole second half on it) but it is a hypothesis, not a meaning. Melanin does not digest topically applied oils, which is the FIRST function Suśruta assigns. The equation keeps one clause of the source and discards the other.

mistranslations.rendering: "Pitta for complexion" used as a complete definition
mistranslations.why: This is WHO ISTA's own English term, and as a definition it is incomplete: it silently drops the absorption/digestion of abhyaṅga, pariṣeka, avagāha and ālepana substances. Since that clause is the classical justification for the entire transdermal-therapy tradition, the omission is consequential, not cosmetic.

mistranslations.rendering: "governs skin sensation" / "sensory function of the skin"
mistranslations.why: Function creep (seen in PMID 40837116). Touch is the domain of the sparśanendriya and of vāta; neither mūla gives bhrājaka a sensory role.

This attribution comes from Cakrapāṇidatta's commentary on Caraka, not from Su.Sū. 21.10, whose bhrājaka clause says nothing about thermoregulation. Suśruta gives the heat-maintenance role to PĀCAKA ('it keeps up the temperature in its other distant locations').

openQuestions: Cakrapāṇidatta's Āyurveda Dīpikā on Ca.Sū. 12.11 is reported to explain bhrājaka pitta as governing body temperature and skin colour. I did NOT retrieve the commentary itself and have not recorded it as a citation — a human should verify it directly.
Aṣṭāṅga Saṅgraha Sūtrasthāna 19 is cited by the AYUSHDHARA review as also naming bhrājaka. Unverified by me.
Does AH state the absorption function for bhrājaka anywhere outside 12.14? The half-verse I verified gives only the shining function.

It acts at two levels: 1. together with digestive fire during digestion; and 2. together with metabolic factors located in structural components during fundamental structural component level metabolism. There are five types: transforming factors of earth element, water element, fire element, air element and space element.' WHO's two-level account is notable and not universal in the textbooks.

This is Bhishagratna's own commentary, not Sushruta's text — but it is public domain and is a documented rendering.

classical.establishes: The five elemental heats are named as 'pañcoṣmāṇaḥ' — five ūṣmans — not as bhūtāgni. Each cooks its own corresponding elemental quality in the food.
classical.quote: भौमाप्याग्नेयवायव्याः पञ्चोष्माणः सनाभसाः। पञ्चाहारगुणान्स्वान्स्वान्पार्थिवादीन्पचन्ति हि॥१३॥

classical.establishes: The only public-domain English for the bhūtāgni doctrine, including the like-nourishes-like principle that is its whole point.
classical.quote: Since the five heats, viz., that appertaining to earth, that to water, that to fire, that to air, and that to ether, digest earth and the other properties, respectively, numbering five, of the food eaten, Therefore, the material properties in the body (that is, those that relate to the five material substances already named) are nourished, respectively, by their correlative elements. The earthy properties (in food) nourish the earthy elements in the body. The rest nourish the rest, in detail.

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa's technical triad names the elemental level 'bhautika', the adjectival form, alongside anna- and dhātv-agni.
classical.quote: anna-bhautika-dhātv-agni-karmeti paribhāṣitam || 70 ||
classical.translator: none — no public-domain English translation of Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya exists

distinguishFrom.why: Different level and different count (five vs seven). WHO adds a wrinkle by saying bhūtāgni acts together with dhātvagni during tissue-level metabolism as well as with jāṭharāgni during digestion, which blurs a boundary most textbooks keep sharp.
The bhūtas are the elements themselves; bhūtāgni is the transforming agent assigned to each. Writing that treats 'bhūtāgni' as 'the five elements' has lost the agent.
Names the process of elemental conversion; bhūtāgni names the agent.
Genuine homonym inside the same terminologies — every NAMASTE hit on the 'bhūta' stem is possession-related (bhūtagraha, bhūtābhiṣaṅgajvara). A term-matching pipeline will collide on this.

mistranslations.why: Imports catalytic specificity with no textual or experimental basis; there is no candidate enzyme for a 'space-element fire'.

Traceable to PMID 22556911 and repeated in lay sources. The paper offers a correlation essay, not evidence, and the mapping reverses the valence — bhūtāgni is a normal physiological agent, free radicals are framed as damaging.
Drops the agent and leaves only the substrate.

openQuestions: Is bhūtāgni a commentarial coinage, and if so whose?
Is WHO's claim that bhūtāgni acts at two levels (with jāṭharāgni and with dhātvagni) sourced to a specific classical passage, or is it a committee harmonisation?
Does any classical text enumerate the five bhūtāgnis individually by name, or is the naming (pārthivāgni etc.) entirely modern?

renderings.sourceName: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda (2022), term ID ITA-2.1.3.4
renderings.locator: ITA-2.1.3.4; printed p. 36 (PDF p. 54). Sanskrit term 'bodhaka-kaphaḥ'. Description: 'Subtype of kapha seated in the tongue which assists with the perception of taste.'
renderings.assessment: WHO says 'seated in the tongue', which is VĀGBHAṬA's rasanā-sthāyī. Suśruta's seat is broader: jihvāmūla and kaṇṭha (root of tongue AND throat). WHO's narrowing is a silent choice between authorities and removes the throat.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.sourceName: Suśruta Saṃhitā tr. Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (public domain)
renderings.locator: Sūtrasthāna ch. 21, Wikisource text: 'The Vodhakam:—The Kapham, situated in the throat and at the root of the palate, lends its aid to the perception of tastes by maintaining the moist or humid character of the tongue.'
renderings.assessment: Note the spelling 'Vodhakam' (v for b), consistent with Bhishagratna's transliteration habits. Note also that he renders jihvāmūla as 'the root of the palate' rather than 'the root of the tongue' — arguably an error, and worth flagging to anyone quoting him. The NAME is his supplied heading; the mūla at 21.14 does not contain it.
renderings.licenceNote: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Samhita, 1907-1916

renderings.sourceName: Suśruta Saṃhitā tr. Bhishagratna, footnote at Sūtrasthāna ch. 15
renderings.locator: 'They are known as Shleshmaka, Kledaka, Vodhaka, Tarpaka, Avalamvaka.'
renderings.assessment: Same v/b spelling. Anyone searching a 19th-century corpus must search both 'Bodhaka' and 'Vodhaka'.
renderings.licenceNote: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Samhita, 1907-1916

renderings.english: one of the types of Kapha which resides in oral cavity
renderings.sourceName: J Ayurveda Integr Med (2025), tongue carcinoma case report
renderings.assessment: Broadens the seat from tongue/throat to 'oral cavity' and drops the taste function entirely, using bodhaka purely as a site marker to justify a kapha-directed treatment rationale.
renderings.licenceNote: "J Ayurveda Integr Med (2025), tongue carcinoma case report" is not a source this project has cleared for quotation

classical.establishes: Seat = throat and root of the (palate/tongue); the MECHANISM is explicit — it enables taste perception BY maintaining moisture of the tongue. The heading name is the translator's.
classical.quote: The Vodhakam:—The Kapham, situated in the throat and at the root of the palate, lends its aid to the perception of tastes by maintaining the moist or humid character of the tongue.

classical.establishes: The word 'bodhaka' does NOT appear. Seat is jihvāmūla-kaṇṭha-stha (root of the TONGUE and throat — note Bhishagratna's 'palate' is a slip). The mechanism is 'jihvendriyasya saumyatvāt' — by the watery/soft quality of the tongue-organ — enabling 'samyag rasa-jñāna', correct knowledge of taste.
classical.quote: जिह्वामूलकण्ठस्थो जिह्वेन्द्रियस्य सौम्यत्वात् सम्यग्रसज्ञाने वर्तते;

classical.text: Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya (Sanskrit mūla; no public-domain English translation exists, so no translation is quoted)
classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa supplies the NAME with its etymology — called bodhaka FROM rasa-bodhana (making taste known) — and narrows the seat to rasanā (the tongue) alone, dropping Suśruta's kaṇṭha. WHO ISTA follows Vāgbhaṭa.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: A serious homonym trap running right through this record. Bodhaka enables rasa-jñāna = knowledge of TASTE. Rañjaka colours rasa = PLASMA. English 'rasa' in an untranslated citation can mean either, and automated processing will conflate them.

Both are moisture-providing kaphas in the upper digestive tract. Kledaka moistens the food in the stomach; bodhaka keeps the tongue-organ moist so taste can be apprehended. Different site, different purpose.
The tongue and the taste-organ are the seat and instrument; bodhaka is the kapha operating there. Saying 'bodhaka is the tongue' confuses agent with organ.

Saliva is the most common modern correlate, but salivary function spans bolus formation (closer to kledaka), enzymatic digestion (pitta/agni territory) and taste dissolution (bodhaka's part). Equating bodhaka with saliva wholesale imports all three.

mistranslations.why: A substitution, not a translation, and it overshoots: saliva does several things the classical texts distribute across different subtypes. Bodhaka's specific job is making taste KNOWABLE by keeping the taste-organ moist — a perceptual enabling role, not a secretion.
Anatomical substitution. Bodhaka is the condition of perception (moisture of the organ), not the receptor. The classical mechanism is explicitly 'jihvendriyasya saumyatvāt'.

mistranslations.rendering: "seated in the tongue" cited to Suśruta
mistranslations.why: Suśruta gives jihvāmūla AND kaṇṭha — root of tongue and throat. The tongue-only seat is Vāgbhaṭa's rasanā-sthāyī and is what WHO records. Citing 'tongue' to Suśruta drops the throat.
The Sanskrit is jihvā-mūla — root of the TONGUE. This looks like a slip in the 1907-1916 translation. Flagged because the translation is public domain and therefore heavily reused.

openQuestions: Does Dalhaṇa name this kapha 'bodhaka' in his gloss on Su.Sū. 21.14, or is Bhishagratna importing the name from Vāgbhaṭa?
Is 'the root of the palate' a genuine variant reading Bhishagratna followed, or simply his error for jihvāmūla?
Where does the association of bodhaka with cognitive qualities (seen in PMID 39114320) come from? Neither mūla supports it; possibly a later or popular source.
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 carries any bodhaka-kapha entry.

renderings.assessment: WHO's pair is internally odd: the privative a-brahmacarya is defined as 'appropriate indulgence ... in moderation', i.e. positively, while the upastambha itself is defined as total non-indulgence. Also ITA-10.2.1 trayopastambhaḥ describes the third pillar as 'moderation in sensual indulgence including sexual activity', contradicting 10.2.12.

renderings.sourceName: Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita (1896-1913)
renderings.locator: Sutrasthana Lesson XI, his aphorism 30: 'The three stays (of the body regarded as a column) are eating, sleep, and restraint of the senses.' Footnote: 'By Brahmacharyya as used here, is meant a judicious indulgence or use of our faculties and powers.'
renderings.assessment: The gloss 'judicious indulgence' is the TRANSLATOR'S footnote, not the text. Elsewhere (Lesson I) Kaviratna renders it 'continence', and in a later footnote: 'Brahmacharyya means the observance of sexual continence by young men during the period of pupillage ... Those who never indulge in sexual congress save with their wedded wives in the proper season, are regarded as observing Brahmacharyya.'

classical.establishes: Brahmacarya is the third upastambha (support) of the body with food and sleep; the qualifier yuktiyuktaiḥ ('properly/judiciously applied') is the textual hook for the 'regulated, not absolute' reading.
classical.quote: त्रय उपस्तम्भा इति- आहारः, स्वप्नो, ब्रह्मचर्यमिति; एभिस्त्रिभिर्युक्तियुक्तैरुपस्तब्धमुपस्तम्भैः शरीरंबलवर्णोपचयोपचितमनुवर्तते यावदायुःसंस्कारात् संस्कारमहितमनुपसेवमानस्य , य इहैवोपदेक्ष्यते||३५||

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 29 and 30 (printed after each passage); standard 34-35 per carakasamhitaonline - recorded separately, not converted
classical.establishes: Kaviratna renders brahmacarya here as 'restraint of the senses' and 'upastambha' as 'stays'; his footnote explains 'upastambha is used to express the stays which support a column'.
classical.quote: There are three stays (of the body) ; three kinds of strength ; three kinds of causes of disease ; three kinds of disease ; three seats of disease ; three kinds of physicians ; and lastly three kinds of medicines. The three stays (of the body regarded as a column) are eating, sleep, and restraint of the senses. In consequence of the three stays (mentioned above) supporting the body, the latter receives accession of strength and complexion and nourishment.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ITA-10.2.13 defines it as 'Appropriate indulgence ... (in moderation)', which makes the WHO pair read as regulated-vs-unregulated rather than celibate-vs-sexual; flag this when citing WHO.
Aphrodisiac/reproductive therapy; the texts prescribe both, which itself shows brahmacarya is not lifelong celibacy in the medical context.
In Yoga Sutra and Dharmashastra it is a vow or life-stage (student); in Ayurveda it is one of three bodily supports, read by commentators as regulated sexual conduct.
General sense-control; Kaviratna's 'restraint of the senses' blurs brahmacarya into this broader idea.

mistranslations.why: The upastambha verse qualifies all three supports with yuktiyuktaiḥ (properly applied); Kaviratna's footnote and WHO's own ITA-10.2.1 ('moderation in sensual indulgence') read it as regulated conduct. WHO ITA-10.2.12 nevertheless prints 'Celibacy'.
Kaviratna's rendering widens brahmacarya to all sense-control; the Sanskrit term's primary reference in this context is sexual conduct.
Imports a moral/religious register; the Ayurvedic frame is physiological (support of bala, varṇa, upacaya).

openQuestions: How does Chakrapani gloss brahmacarya at Ca.Su.11.35? Not retrieved; secondary sources claim a 'regulated' reading.
Does Sushruta or Vagbhata define brahmacarya anywhere? Not located.

classical.verse: 10 (carakasamhitaonline numbering; the number closes the verse whose first half defines bṛṁhaṇa). Kaviratna prints 7-9 for the block containing it.
classical.establishes: Definition: whatever produces bṛhattva (largeness/bulk) of the body is bṛṁhaṇa.
classical.quote: बृहत्त्वं यच्छरीरस्य जनयेत्तच्च बृंहणम्| रौक्ष्यं खरत्वं वैशद्यं यत् कुर्यात्तद्धि रूक्षणम्||१०||

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed 7-9 (standard 22.9-11 per carakasamhitaonline; he is two behind here and aligned at 18)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering and spelling 'Vring-hana'; the parenthesis is his gloss.
classical.quote: Any thing that lightens or attenuates (the aggravated humours and altered constituents) in the body has been said to be a Langhana. That which promotes nutrition and bulk of the body is known as Vring-hana.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (OCR text; spacing normalized)

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed 26 (standard 22.27-28 region; the half-verse ending in bṛṁhaṇam is numbered 28)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's list of universal bṛṁhaṇa measures, including the oily enema.
classical.quote: Baths, gentle rubbing of the body (with medicated oils), sleep, honey and other sweets, oily enemata, sugar, and milk and ghee, know, are Vring-hanas for all persons.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (OCR text; spacing normalized)

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed 24 (standard number not independently established; the Sanskrit 22.26 ends 'बृंहणीया नराः स्मृताः')

classical.verse: 1-2 (GRETIL e-text numbering; chapter confirmed by '14.14cv' variant markers in the same block)
classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa makes treatment twofold (santarpaṇa/apatarpaṇa) and names bṛṁhaṇa and laṅghana as their synonyms, defined by bṛhattva and lāghava.
classical.quote: upakramyasya hi dvi-tvād dvi-dhaivopakramo mataḥ | ekaḥ saṃtarpaṇas tatra dvitīyaś cāpatarpaṇaḥ || 1 || bṛṃhaṇo laṅghanaś ceti tat-paryāyāv udāhṛtau | bṛṃhaṇaṃ yad bṛhat-tvāya laṅghanaṃ lāghavāya yat || 2 ||

classical.establishes: Sushruta applies bṛṁhaṇa as the action of the unctuous enema, contrasting it with the cleansing nirūha.
classical.quote: निरूहः शोधनो लेखी स्नैहिको बृंहणो मतः  / :निरूहशोधितान्मार्गान् सम्यक् स्नेहोऽनुगच्छति १९

distinguishFrom.why: The nourishing half of the twofold scheme (WHO ITA-9.1.40); Vāgbhaṭa calls bṛṁhaṇa its synonym (AH Su.14.2), WHO keeps them as separate entries.
Oleation is one of the six upakramas with its own definition (Ca.Su.22.11); it is often bṛṁhaṇa in effect but defined by unctuousness, not bulk.
Strength-promoting and rejuvenative categories of drug action; bṛṁhaṇa is defined only by increase of body bulk (Ca.Su.22.10).
Its defined opposite (lāghava vs bṛhattva, Ca.Su.22.9-10).
Heaviness is a property of substances; Ca.Su.22.13-14 lists guru among the properties that make a substance bṛṁhaṇa, the therapy is the effect.

mistranslations.why: Bṛhattva covers bulk and strength in the indications (emaciated, wounded, aged); Kaviratna's 'excessive Vring-hana results in corpulency' shows corpulence is the overdose sign, not the aim.
Victorian pharmacological category; it does not map to the six-fold upakrama scheme and is also used for rasāyana and balya.
Biomedical nutrition is about intake; bṛṁhaṇa includes sleep, baths, massage and oily enema (Kaviratna's printed 26).

openQuestions: The standard verse numbers for Kaviratna's printed 23-24 (bṛṁhaṇīya persons) were not independently established; carakasamhitaonline shows 22.25-26 ending in बृंहणमुच्यते / बृंहणीया नराः स्मृताः, which suggests his offset here is two behind, but this was not confirmed line by line.
WHO's reason for separating bṛṁhaṇa (9.1.43) from santarpaṇa (9.1.40) is not stated in the entries read.
