classical.verse: 21-23 (standard; Kaviratna prints 28-30, the last two garbled to '25' in the OCR)
classical.establishes: The cognitive sequence: sense-with-mind grasps the object; manas deliberates (kalpyate) as to merit or fault; then buddhi, which is niścayātmikā (of the nature of certainty), arises about the object, and one speaks or acts buddhi-pūrvakam. This is the text's functional definition of buddhi as the determinative stage after manas. Kaviratna: 'By the organs of sense, with the mind working with them, are all sensuous objects apprehended. The mind then works upon those objects, rightly or wrongly. The Intellect then, having certitude for its essence, becomes manifested in connection thereto. Aided (thus) by the Intellect, one then sets about to speak or act.' His footnote: 'The mind doubts, saying, Is this so, or, Is this not so? Then comes the Intellect which discriminates ... Hence, the Intellect is said to have certitude for its essence.' English at https://archive.org/stream/BIUSante_47357/BIUSante_47357_djvu.txt
classical.quote: indriyābhigrahaḥ karma manasaḥ svasya nigrahaḥ| ūhō vicāraśca, tataḥ paraṁ buddhiḥ pravartatē||21|| indriyēṇēndriyārthō hi samanaskēna gr̥hyatē| kalpyatē manasā tūrdhvaṁ guṇatō dōṣatō'thavā||22|| jāyatē viṣayē tatra yā buddhirniścayātmikā| vyavasyati tayā vaktuṁ kartuṁ vā buddhipūrvakam||23||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: Buddhi is classed as a guṇa, heading the series buddhi ... prayatna (the ātma-guṇas), alongside the sense-objects (sārthā), the gurvādi and the parādi guṇas. This is the textual root of WHO filing buddhi under 'Qualities of the soul or self'. Kaviratna: 'the intellect, pleasure and pain, and desire and aversion and will ... are called attributes'.
classical.quote: sārthā gurvādayō buddhiḥ prayatnāntāḥ parādayaḥ| guṇāḥ prōktāḥ prayatnādi karma cēṣṭitamucyatē||49||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: Buddhi is the second member of the etiological triad (its misuse is later named prajñāparādha, Sū.11.41). Kaviratna renders buddhi here as 'mind'.
classical.quote: kālabuddhīndriyārthānāṁ yōgō mithyā na cāti ca| dvayāśrayāṇāṁ vyādhīnāṁ trividhō hētusaṅgrahaḥ||54||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: Two senses of buddhi in one chapter: (12) the five indriya-buddhis, momentary and determinative, born of the sannikarṣa of indriya, artha, sattva and ātmā; (13) buddhi as one of the four adhyātma-dravyaguṇas with manas, manortha and ātmā. Kaviratna (his 7): 'Mind, the functions of the mind, the Understanding, and the Soul constitute, in brief, the substances and qualities that are known by the name of Adhyatma.'
classical.quote: Pañcēndriyabuddhayaḥ- cakṣurbuddhyādikāḥ; tāḥ punarindriyēndriyārthasattvātmasannikarṣajāḥ, kṣaṇikā, niścayātmikāśca, ityētat pañcapañcakam||12|| Manō manōrthō buddhirātmā cētyadhyātmadravyaguṇasaṅgrahaḥ śubhāśubhapravr̥ttinivr̥ttihētuśca ...||13||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: Buddhi is one of the liṅgas (marks) of the embodied self, between dhṛti and smṛti. Kaviratna renders the triad dhṛti-buddhi-smṛti as 'apprehension, understanding, memory'.
classical.quote: icchā dvēṣaḥ sukhaṁ duḥkhaṁ prayatnaścētanā dhr̥tiḥ| buddhiḥ smr̥tirahaṅkārō liṅgāni paramātmanaḥ||72||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 2-3 and 7; Sanskrit verse numbers not established
classical.establishes: Suśruta's Sāṃkhya framing: buddhi = mahat/mahān, the first evolute of prakṛti, triguṇa in nature, presided over by Brahmā. Different from Caraka's functional account in Śā.1.21-23.
classical.quote: Out of that latent unmanifest (Avyakta) or original nature (impregnated by the atoms or elemental units of consciousness or Purushas) Intellection or Mahan has been evolved, and out of Mahan egoism. This Mahan or intellection should be likewise considered as partaking of the three fundamental attributes (Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas) of the latent (Avyakta) or original nature. ... The tutelary god of intellection (Buddhi) is Brahma.

distinguishFrom.why: In Ca.Śā.1.21-23 manas deliberates (ūha, vicāra, kalpanā) and buddhi determines (niścaya). Kaviratna's footnote to Śā.1 is explicit that 'Manas excludes Buddhi. With Buddhi, Manas is Mind.' English 'mind' habitually covers both.

The triad dhī-dhṛti-smṛti whose failure is prajñāparādha (Ca.Sū.11.39-41; Kaviratna: 'faults of the Understanding'). Prajñā is wider than buddhi, embracing dhṛti and smṛti; the standards (WHO ITA-4.4.11) render prajñāparādha as 'erroneous judgement'.
The five sensory cognitions of Ca.Sū.8.12, momentary (kṣaṇikā). Same word, different referent: a perception, not the faculty.

Suśruta Śā.1 and the Sāṃkhya-style 24-tattva list use mahat for the cosmic first evolute; Bhishagratna glosses it 'intellection (Buddhi)'. Caraka's functional buddhi is individual and post-perceptual.
Not retrieved here, but the clinical literature on 'intelligence' (e.g. PMID 26730140, medhā enhancement RCT) uses medhā, not buddhi; the two should not be merged in a lexicon.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna, Sū.1.54 ('time, mind, and the objects of the senses'). Buddhi is not manas; the same translator's Śā.1 footnote condemns the conflation.
Modern clinical papers (PMID 29403134) equate buddhi with intelligence quotient. The classical buddhi is a determinative act or faculty (niścayātmikā), not a measurable trait.
Kaviratna's Lockean term. Not wrong, but opaque to modern readers and carries the capital-U faculty psychology he also imposes via Kant.

openQuestions: Whether Caraka's buddhi in Sū.1.49 (a guṇa of ātmā) and in Śā.1.23 (a determinative cognition) are reconciled by the commentators as faculty versus act.
Whether WHO's four-tier antaḥkaraṇa (buddhi, manas, ahaṃkāra, citta) has any Bṛhattrayī basis; the NIA list gives manas, buddhi, indriya, ahaṃkāra instead, and citta is a Yoga term.

classical.establishes: Definition by agency: the activity of the four excellent factors (physician etc.) aimed at dhātu equilibrium when the dhātus are deranged is called cikitsā.
classical.quote: चतुर्णां भिषगादीनां शस्तानां धातुवैकृते| प्रवृत्तिर्धातुसाम्यार्था चिकित्सेत्यभिधीयते||५||

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed 3 (standard 9.5 per carakasamhitaonline; he leaves the opening prose unnumbered)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering of 9.5; 'ingredient humours' = dhātu.
classical.quote: In Disease, the well-known tale of four commencing with Physician has active agency. The course that is adopted for restoring the harmony of the ingredient humours is called Treatment.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (OCR text; spacing normalized)

classical.establishes: Definition by result: the actions by which the dhātus become equal in the body are the cikitsā of disorders; that is the physician's work.
classical.quote: याभिः  क्रियाभिर्जायन्ते शरीरे धातवः समाः| सा चिकित्सा विकाराणां कर्म तद्भिषजां स्मृतम्||३४||

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed 31 (standard 16.34; three behind in this chapter)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering of 16.34.
classical.quote: Those acts by which the constituent elements of the body become harmonious are said to constitute what is called (medical) treatment of disorders or disease. Those acts constitute the duty of men called physicians.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (OCR text; spacing normalized)

classical.establishes: The purpose of the treatise is dhātusāmya-kriyā, the action that restores dhātu equilibrium; the frame within which cikitsā is defined.
classical.quote: इत्युक्तं कारणं कार्यं धातुसाम्यमिहोच्यते| धातुसाम्यक्रिया चोक्ता तन्त्रस्यास्य प्रयोजनम्||५३||

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering of dhātusāmyakriyā as 'modes of restoring the ingredient humours to their normal state'.
classical.quote: The modes of restoring the ingredient humours to their normal state have been said to be the object of this Science.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (OCR text; spacing normalized)

classical.establishes: Disease = dhātu disequilibrium, health = equilibrium; the premise that makes cikitsā 'dhātusāmyārthā'.
classical.quote: विकारो धातुवैषम्यं, साम्यं प्रकृतिरुच्यते| सुखसञ्ज्ञकमारोग्यं, विकारो दुःखमेव च||४||

distinguishFrom.why: The clinical speciality (WHO ITA-1.4.3 'General medicine'); cikitsā unqualified is the act or principle of treatment, and WHO's ITA-1.4.2 lists cikitsā itself among specialities, which is a classification choice of that standard.
Medicine or remedy, the means; Ca.Su.11.54 classifies auṣadha threefold (daiva-, yukti-vyapāśraya, sattvāvajaya), while cikitsā is defined by the aim (dhātusāmya).
A treatment approach or procedure; Ca.Su.22 counts six (ṣaḍ upakrama) and AH Su.14 two; cikitsā is the genus.
Past participle used for chapter titles ('the treatment of X'); Bhishagratna renders these as 'medical treatment of'.
The purpose of the whole tantra (Ca.Su.1.53); cikitsā is the physician's activity toward it (Ca.Su.9.5, 16.34).

mistranslations.why: Ca.Su.9.5 and 16.34 define cikitsā by aim and action, not outcome; WHO's ITA-9.1.4 vyādhiharam 'Cure of disease' is a separate synonym entry.
Conflates cikitsā with āyurveda or with kāyacikitsā; Kaviratna uses 'Science' for the tantra and 'Treatment' for cikitsā.

mistranslations.rendering: restoring the harmony of the humours (Kaviratna, read as the three doṣas)
mistranslations.why: The Sanskrit is dhātu; Kaviratna's own footnote narrows 'ingredient humours' to Wind, Bile and Phlegm, which is the translator's gloss, not the verse.

openQuestions: Whether WHO intends ITA-1.4.2 'Treatment' (under Specialities) and ITA-9.1.3 'Treatment' as one concept or two was not determined from the entries.
No peer-reviewed paper offering an operational or measurable definition of cikitsā was found in the searches run.

classical.verse: Standard Sutrasthana 11.54 (carakasamhitaonline / Trikamji, unit closed ||५४||); Kaviratna prints 55 (Lesson XI, his p. 130, archive.org BIUSante_47357 leaf 193), ONE ahead here
classical.establishes: The locus classicus: auṣadha is threefold; daivavyapāśraya comprises mantra, herbs (auṣadhi), gems (maṇi), auspicious rites, offerings (bali, upahāra), oblation (homa), observances (niyama), expiation (prāyaścitta), fasting (upavāsa), benedictions (svastyayana), prostration (praṇipāta), pilgrimage (gamana) and the like.
classical.quote: त्रिविधमौषधमिति- दैवव्यपाश्रयं, युक्तिव्यपाश्रयं, सत्त्वावजयश्च| तत्र दैवव्यपाश्रयं- मन्त्रौषधिमणिमङ्गलबल्युपहारहोमनियमप्रायश्चित्तोपवासस्वस्त्ययनप्रणिपातगमनादि,युक्तिव्यपाश्रयं- पुनराहारौषधद्रव्याणां योजना, सत्त्वावजयः- पुनरहितेभ्योऽर्थेभ्यो मनोनिग्रहः||५४||
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Kaviratna Lesson XI, printed aphorism 55 (his p. 130, archive.org BIUSante_47357 leaf 193), the number placed after the third-kind sentence = standard Sutrasthana 11.54 (carakasamhitaonline / Trikamji)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering of 11.54; his 'herbs and plants of invisible virtue (if kept in contact with the body)' expands auṣadhi with a gloss; 'libations of meat and ghee' expands homa.
classical.quote: Medicines are of three kinds; those that depend for their action upon the deities and invisible influences; those that depend for their application and action upon knowledge and reason; and those that appertain to the subjugation of the mind. Among these, mantras, herbs and plants of invisible virtue (if kept in contact with the body), gems, auspicious rites, offerings in sacrifices, offers of articles to the deities in course of worship or religious rites, libations of meat and ghee on the sacred fire, practice of vows, expiatory ceremonies and rites, fasts, propitiatory rites, bows to the deities, and pilgrimage to sacred waters and shrines, constitute medicines of the first kind.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (OCR text; spacing normalized)
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.sthana: Uttarasthana (GRETIL file section containing bhūtavidyā/graha chapters)
classical.verse: Not established; GRETIL line reads 'śāpātharvaṇa-mantrotthe vidhir daiva-vyapāśrayaḥ' and a variant note '5.83dv ... daiva-vyapāśrayaṃ tat tad atharvoktaṃ ca pūjitam'
classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa uses the compound and ties it to Atharvan rites; chapter and verse not determined from the plaintext in this pass.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: The second of the three auṣadhas in Ca.Su.11.54: rational combination of diet and drugs (WHO ITA-9.1.26 'Structured therapy based on clinical reasoning').
The third: restraint of the mind from harmful objects (Ca.Su.11.54); not a ritual and not a drug.
Disease classified by cause (WHO ITA entry 'daivabalapravṛttarogaḥ'); daivavyapāśraya is a class of treatment, not of disease.
These are items in the daivavyapāśraya list, not synonyms for it; WHO gives them separate sub-entries (e.g. ITA-9.1.15 'Chanting of auspicious hymns').
The speciality dealing with graha/possession; daivavyapāśraya is a treatment mode available across specialities.

mistranslations.why: Imports a Christian/evangelical practice; the Charaka list is a set of ritual actions (homa, prāyaścitta, upavāsa, gamana) rather than belief as the agent.
Daiva in Ca.Su.11 contrasts with yukti (human reasoning) and is close to 'fate' or 'the unseen'; the list includes fasting and pilgrimage, which are not interventions by a deity.
Widely used (WHO description, NIA gloss) but it absorbs sattvāvajaya, which Charaka keeps separate as mind-control.

openQuestions: The AH Uttarasthana locus for daiva-vyapāśraya was seen only as plaintext lines in GRETIL; chapter and verse need establishing against a printed edition.
Whether Sushruta uses the compound was not checked in this pass.

classical.quote: the physician should view the body of his patient, touch it with his own hands, and enquire (about his complaint). Several authorities hold that these three, (inspection, touch and questioning) largely form the means of our ascertaining the nature of a disease. But that is not correct, inasmuch as the five sense-organs of hearing, sight, etc. and oral enquiry materially contribute to a better diagnosis.

Eight sites of disease signs (Yogaratnakara) versus ten attributes of the patient gauged for strength (Caraka).

Sushruta Su. 35 (Bhishagratna: 'the nature of the disease, the country and season ... state of digestion, age, body, strength, disposition, habit, previous medicine, natural temperament and the power of endurance') is a different, longer list often called twelvefold; not Caraka's ten.
Only item 1 of the ten; popular usage sometimes treats 'dashavidha pariksha' as a constitution test.
Item 10 is vaya (age); āyu (lifespan) is assessed separately (Indriyasthana, Su. 35) per PMID 28273996.

mistranslations.why: The stated purpose (Vi. 8/94) is to gauge the patient's measure of strength (bala), to calibrate treatment, not to diagnose the disease.
Not wrong but opaque; 'homologation' is a WHO coinage not found in older English renderings. Record as a disagreement rather than an error.
Popular rendering; Kaviratna gives 'mental disposition', WHO 'psychic condition'. The text grades sattva as pravara/madhya/avara, so 'strength' is a partial reading.

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English; his footnote (translator's note, not text): 'As an example of ill-regulated courage the Commentator gives the instance of one's approaching an infuriate elephant.' In this chapter his numbers run two behind the standard.
classical.quote: One desirous of one's good both here and hereafter should suppress these impulses also, viz., those of (ill-regulated) courage and all fruitless impulses of thought, word, and deed. The man of intelligence should also suppress the impulses of cupidity, grief, fear, wrath, pride, shamelessness, envy, violent propensities of every kind, and covetousness. One should also suppress the rising impulses of harshness, of doing anything that is disagreeable to others, of untruthfulness of speech, of speech that is inopportune, of whatever tendencies that exist for giving pain to others, of sexual congress, of appropriating the property of others, and of all wrongful propensities. Through sinlessness of thought, word, and deed, a person earns righteous fame, and lives happily, acquiring and enjoying religious merit, wealth, and (sources of) pleasure.

distinguishFrom.why: The bodily urges that must NOT be suppressed (Ca.Su.7.3-4); the opposite category, and the pair is often inverted in student writing.
Positive code of conduct in Ca.Su.8; dhāraṇīya-vega is framed negatively (what to restrain) and sits inside the chapter on urges.
Conduct that produces rasayana effects (Ca.Ci.1.4.30-35); the NIA 2011 draft folds dhāraṇīya vega into achara rasayana, but the texts keep them apart.
The three subdivisions mānasika/vācika/kāyika are commentarial labels; the Samhita text itself lists by mind, speech and body without naming subtypes.

mistranslations.why: The standard rendering (WHO) but misleading in English: 'suppressible' means 'capable of being suppressed', whereas dhāraṇīya is a gerundive, 'to be restrained / that ought to be held'. The Sanskrit is an injunction, not a possibility.

Over-reads v.27: the text targets vegas (impulses to act) of greed, grief, anger etc., and includes speech and bodily acts, not emotional experience as such.

classical.establishes: That Charaka's enumeration at this point runs to EIGHT and ends in ojas, not seven. It also names a further category, the 'essence of the Dhatus' (dhātu-prasāda), which supplies the sense organs. Directly complicates the standard 'seven dhatus' formula.
classical.quote: From, however, that juice which springs from food grow the fluids, blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, vital seed, and that which has been called Ojas ; as also those substances that are requisite for the functions of the five senses. These latter are called the essence of the Dhatus.

classical.establishes: The prasāda/kiṭṭa split at the level of food, upstream of any dhātu. OCR renders āhāraprasāda as 'Aharaprasdda'.
classical.quote: From that, (viz., the food thus taken), arises a juice which is called Aharaprasdda or food-substance, as also a Refuse called dregs or dross.

classical.establishes: The seven-fire (dhātvagni) model and the prasāda/kiṭṭa split. Note that Kaviratna's own parenthetical enumeration here puts adeps and marrow BEFORE bones, contradicting the chain he translates one verse later.
classical.quote: They who sustain the body, viz., the 'dhatus' (i. e., 'Rasa' or juice, blood, flesh, adeps, marrow, bones, and vital seed), are cooked by their seven respective fires. This process of cooking which they undergo is of two kinds in consequence of the 'Kitta' (refuse) and the 'Prasada' (pure substance) Which results from it.

distinguishFrom.why: Doṣa are the regulatory functional factors that vitiate; dhātu are what gets vitiated. Sushruta's own framing at Sutrasthana 15 separates doṣa, dhātu and mala as three categories of bodily constituent. Rendering both as 'element' or both as 'constituent' erases the distinction the texts build the whole pathology on.

Mala are the excretory fraction (kiṭṭa) thrown off at each stage of dhātu formation. Kaviratna, however, translates Charaka Sutrasthana 28 as calling the malas themselves 'Dhatus' ('Of the Dhatus of both classes, viz, those called Malas and those called Prasadas'), so the boundary is not as clean in the source as in modern teaching.

The same word names the medicinal metals. WHO ISTA carries it twice with different English headwords: 'Fundamental structural component' (ITA-2.2.1) and 'Metal' (ITA-7.2.5.1). An index built on the Sanskrit alone will merge two unrelated entries.

In Paninian grammar dhātu is a verbal root. Su.Su.14.13 actually uses the word in this grammatical sense in the same chapter that defines the bodily dhātu ('तत्र रस गतौ धातुः'), so the two senses sit adjacent in the source text.
Upadhātu are produced from dhātu but are held not to transform further into a following tissue. They are not members of the seven.

Standardly the essence (sāra) of all seven, not an eighth member. But Charaka Sutrasthana 28 as translated by Kaviratna enumerates ojas as the eighth item in the list, and Bhishagratna's footnote to Su.Su.14 records that 'certain authorities hold albumen (protoplasmic matter) to be the eighth or the culminating principle of the body'. The disagreement is in the sources, not only in the secondary literature.
The five great elements. Both are routinely Englished as 'element'; dhātu are formed from food by digestion, mahābhūta are ontological constituents of all matter.

mistranslations.why: Imports a histological category that the classical term does not carry. Rasa is a fluid, ojas is sometimes counted, and the dhātus are defined functionally (by what they hold and what they produce) rather than by cellular architecture. WHO ISTA specifically avoided 'tissue' in favour of 'fundamental structural component'.

Belongs to doṣa, and is contested even there. Applying it to dhātu compounds the error. Note that Bhishagratna's chapter title rendering, 'the humoral constituents of the body and excrements', does blur exactly this line.

Collides with mahābhūta, which most translators also call 'element'. Kaviratna uses 'constituent elements of the body' for dhātu and 'the five material substances' for mahābhūta, but not consistently.
Correct only in the Rasashastra sense (WHO ISTA ITA-7.2.5.1). Applied to the bodily dhātu it is simply the wrong lemma.

Fixes the count at seven when two of the three public-domain passages retrieved here list eight, the eighth being ojas. The number is treated as settled in modern teaching and is not settled in the source texts.

openQuestions: Whether ojas is an eighth dhātu or the sāra of the seven is stated both ways inside the public-domain translations of the two samhitas; no retrieved source resolves it.

Kaviratna's verse markers in the OCR do not align with the numbering used by carakasamhitaonline (see gatheringNotes). A Sanskrit Charaka with verse numbers is needed before any Charaka verse number in this record set can be called verified.

Whether Charaka's 'essence of the Dhatus' (dhātu-prasāda) supplying the sense organs is a distinct technical category or a commentarial reading of Kaviratna's own could not be established from the retrieved text alone.
No retrieved source gives a criterion by which a proposed English rendering of dhātu could be judged adequate; the choice is currently made by convention.

alternates: dhātvāgni (spelling used in the NIA/WHO-APW list)
rasāgni, raktāgni, māṃsāgni, medo-agni, asthyagni, majjāgni, śukrāgni (the seven members)

classical.establishes: The seven dhātu-level fires and their two-fold product, prasāda and kiṭṭa. This is the core locus for the concept. Kaviratna's footnote here remarks on the awkwardness of moving from five bhūtāgnis to seven fires.
classical.quote: They who sustain the body, viz., the 'dhatus' (i. e., 'Rasa' or juice, blood, flesh, adeps, marrow, bones, and vital seed), are cooked by their seven respective fires. This process of cooking which they undergo is of two kinds in consequence of the 'Kitta' (refuse) and the 'Prasada' (pure substance) which results from it.

classical.establishes: The bhūtāgni layer immediately preceding the dhātvagni verse, which is why the two are so often conflated. The five elemental fires act on the five elemental properties of food; the seven tissue fires act on the dhātus.
classical.quote: Since the five heats, viz., that appertaining to earth, that to water, that to fire, that to air, and that to ether, digest earth and the other properties, respectively, numbering five, of the food eaten, Therefore, the material properties in the body (that is, those that relate to the five material substances already named) are nourished, respectively, by their correlative elements.

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi glosses the mūla phrase yathāsvenoṣmaṇā ('by its own respective heat') at Ca.Sū.28.3 as dhātvagni: food that has become rasa, on reaching rakta and the rest, is cooked by the heat of rakta and the rest. This is a second, independent classical anchor for the term, in Sūtrasthāna rather than Cikitsāsthāna.
classical.quote: kiṃvā yathāsvenoṣmaṇeti yasya rudhirāder ya ūṣmā dhātvagnirūpastena samyagvipacyamānamaśitādi rasatām āpannaṃ yadā raktādidhātūn pratipadyate tadā raktādyūṣmaṇaiva pacyate

classical.establishes: Jāṭharāgni is primary and the dhātvagnis are dependent on it. This subordination is the textual basis for treating jāṭharāgni disorder as upstream of dhātvagni disorder.
classical.quote: That heat which cooks (digests) the food eaten is the prince of all heats whose function is cooking. Indeed, all the other heats have the food-cooking heat for their root. Their increase or decrease depends on its increase or decrease.

distinguishFrom.why: The gastric/central digestive fire, one in number, acting on ingested food. Ca.Ci.15 makes it the root on which all other fires depend. Dhātvagni acts later and within tissue.

Five elemental fires acting on the five elemental properties of food. WHO gives it a separate entry (ITA-2.6.7) and notes it acts at two levels, alongside jāṭharāgni during digestion and alongside dhātvagni during tissue-level metabolism. The five/seven mismatch is exactly what Kaviratna's footnote flags.
The pitta subtype seated in the gastrointestinal tract. Agni and pitta overlap but are not identical categories; agni is a functional principle, pitta a doṣa subtype.
The product of impaired agni, not a kind of agni.
Dhātvagni is the agency; poṣaṇa is the process and outcome. The nyāyas concern routing of nutrient, not the fire.

mistranslations.why: Names a molecular class the texts do not have, and loses the doṣa-linked functional states (sama, tīkṣṇa, viṣama, manda) that WHO itself records at ITA-2.6.8 to ITA-2.6.11. Enzymes have no such states.
Agni's four states are qualitative and doṣa-linked, not a single scalar; and dhātvagni is tissue-specific in a way BMR is not.
A popular modern correlation with no basis in the classical description and no empirical support in the retrieved literature.
Correct for jāṭharāgni, wrong for dhātvagni, which acts after digestion is complete.

openQuestions: Whether the standard list is six or seven fires. The NIA/WHO-APW entry SK0062 says 'seven' and then lists six, omitting majjāgni. WHO ISTA ITA-2.6.6 lists seven but writes five of them as -āgniḥ and two as -dhātvagniḥ, an inconsistency worth flagging.

No peer-reviewed operational definition or biomarker of dhātvagni was found. Searches on EuropePMC for 'dhatvagni' returned 55 hits, none offering a measurable definition. This appears to be a real gap, not a search failure.

Kaviratna's Cikitsāsthāna 15 verse numbers run one behind Chakrapani-based editions (his v.14 is the verse universally cited as Ci.15/15). The offset should be confirmed chapter-wide before publishing his numbers.

alternates: ekakāla dhātu poṣaṇa (a fourth named model)

classical.establishes: The mūla text states only the ORDER of derivation of the seven dhātus, not a mechanism. All three nyāyas are commentarial attempts to supply the missing mechanism.
classical.quote: From 'Rasa' (juice) arises blood ; from blood is flesh ; from flesh is adeps ; from adeps is bone ; from bone is marrow ; from marrow is vital seed : from the vital seed arises the fcetus.

classical.establishes: The mūla itself reports the six-day transformation period as an opinion ('some are of opinion'), i.e. the text does not settle the timing question either.
classical.quote: Some are of opinion that the transformation (of one 'dhatu' into another) takes place in six days and nights. Of food and the 'dhatus' this transformation goes on eternally like (the motion of) a wheel.

classical.establishes: Sushruta gives the same succession independently of Charaka. Secondary sources cite this as Su.Sū.14/10; Bhishagratna's text carries no verse numbers, so the verse number is not verified here.
classical.quote: The chyle produces blood. From blood is formed flesh. From flesh originates fat which gives rise to bones. From bones originate marrow, which, in its turn, germinates semen.

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi's commentary on Ca.Sū.28.4 is the primary locus where the competing nourishment models are set out and weighed. This is the anchor citation for the whole dhātu-poṣaṇa topic.
classical.quote: anye tv āhuḥ khalekapotanyāyenāyam annarasaḥ pṛthak pṛthag dhātumārge gataḥ san rasādīn poṣayati na tv asya dhātupoṣako rasabhāgo dhātvantareṇa samaṃ sambandham apyanubhavati

distinguishFrom.why: Pariṇāma is transformation of one dhātu into the next, which is only ONE of the competing accounts of poṣaṇa. Treating them as synonyms silently commits the entry to the kṣīra-dadhi model that Cakrapāṇi rejects.
Dhātvagni is the transforming agency; poṣaṇa is the process and its result. The nyāyas are about routing and selection of nutrient, not about the fire that acts on it.
Sāra is the qualitative excellence of a fully-nourished dhātu, used in constitutional assessment. Poṣaṇa is the supply process.
The nutrient fraction in transit (poṣaka) versus the settled tissue (sthāyi). Cakrapāṇi's argument turns entirely on this distinction; collapsing it makes the khale-kapota position incoherent.
Secondary tissues produced as by-products of the main sequence, not stages in it.

mistranslations.why: Metabolism covers catabolism and energy turnover; poṣaṇa is specifically the supply-and-incorporation side, and the classical debate is about routing, not about chemical turnover.
Imports a biochemical category that the classical accounts do not make. None of the three nyāyas is about synthesis reactions.
Correct only for the kedārī-kulyā model and wrong for khale-kapota, which is explicitly about selection rather than delivery.

openQuestions: Whether dhātu-poṣaṇa occurs as a fixed compound in any mūla text, or is a modern textbook headword for a topic the texts discuss without naming. Nothing retrieved settles this.
The fourth model, ekakāla dhātu poṣaṇa (simultaneous nourishment), is named only in PMID 32855015 among sources retrieved here. Its classical locus was not established.

Kaviratna's verse numbers in Cikitsāsthāna 15 run one behind the numbering used by Chakrapani-based editions (his v.15 = the verse everyone cites as Ci.15/16). This offset needs confirming across the whole chapter before any Kaviratna verse number is published.

classical.chapter: 8 (the Vimana of how disease is to be conquered by the physician; Rogabhishagjitiya)
classical.establishes: The eightfold enumeration, with SKIN (tvak) first, not rasa, and MIND (sattva) eighth. Also the stated purpose: sāra examination measures strength (bala), not tissue quality in the abstract. Chapter located by the heading 'We shall next expound the Vimanam called how disease is to be conquered by the physician' in the retrieved file.
classical.quote: Next, as to examination according to Sara (predominating essence or element) : there are eight Saras of human beings. We shall lay down instructions about them for exact knowledge of the measure of one's strength. They are i. skin, 2. blood, 3. flesh, 4. fat, 5. bones, 6. marrow, 7. vital seed, and 8. mind,

classical.establishes: A translator reasoning explicitly about how to render sāra, and coining 'pith'. Also attests the compound forms twak-sāra and rakta-sāra, and the negative asāra. OCR has 'baken' for 'taken'.
classical.quote: It will be seen that the word "sara" has been rendered "predominance of (constituting) element." This long periphrasis becomes inconvenient in rendering such short compounds as 'Twak-sara', 'Rakta-sara,' &c. The fact is, if 'sara' be baken as equivalent to 'pith' in the sense of 'essence,' the periphrasis may be abandoned with this explanation. 'Twak-sara' may be rendered as 'Skin-pithed ;' so 'Rakta-sara' as 'Blood-pithed,' &c. Hence 'Asara' implying the absence of 'Sara,' may be rendered as 'having no pith'

classical.establishes: Sarva-sāra, the all-round type, which WHO records at ITA-2.8.1.10 with oja-sāraḥ as a synonym.
classical.quote: Now, those men in whose constitutions all the elements exist in a large and harmonious measure, become endued with great strength and great honors (in every direction). They become capable of enduring toil and pain in all kinds of acts : they are inspired with confidence in their own abilities

classical.establishes: That sāra is graded (pravara, madhyama, avara) rather than binary, that asāra is a recognised category, and again that the purpose is assessing strength.
classical.quote: Those men that are possessed of attributes which are the reverse of these, are regarded as possessed of no pith. Persons endued with a predominance, in a middling measure, of any of the eight elements, have attributes, corresponding with the above, in a middling measure. Thus have been explained the eight different kinds of pith as regards human beings. These explanations are given for a knowledge of the differences in respect of the measure of strength of different men.

classical.establishes: The stated RATIONALE for sāra examination: body size is an unreliable index of strength, so a different measure is needed. This is the text arguing for its own method, and it is the passage a lexicon entry should be built around. OCR has 'btearing' for 'bearing'.
classical.quote: It has been said that a person should be examined by the test of his pith. This has been laid down for preventing a physician from arriving at an erroneous conclusion by a sight of the body alone of the patient. Such conclusions should never be formed, viz., that this one is endued with strength because this one's body is large ; ... It is, indeed, seen that men whose bodies are of small dimensions or whose bodies are lean are still possessed of strength. In this connection, a proof is offered by ants (which are very diminutive creatures) btearing away large weights.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's only use of the sāra idea: ojas as the essence of all seven dhātus. There is NO eightfold sāra examination in Sushruta Sutrasthana 15; the constitutional method is Charaka's. This is a real difference between the two samhitas.
classical.quote: The quintessence of all the fundamental principles of the body, starting with lymph chyle and ending with semen, is called the Ojas, which is identical with what is termed "vital power."

distinguishFrom.why: Constitution by doṣa predominance, determined at conception and fixed. Sāra is predominance by dhātu and is assessed at examination. PMID 42161239 records both separately for each participant, which is the clearest demonstration that they are different instruments.
Strength, which sāra examination exists to estimate. Charaka Vimanasthana 8 states the purpose explicitly. WHO gives balam its own headword at ITA-2.2.27. Sāra is the index; bala is what is indexed.
Equilibrium of the dhātus (WHO ITA-2.2.26), a state of health. Sāra is a constitutional predominance, present in health. A person can be dhātu-sāmya and also asthi-sāra.

WHO gives oja-sāraḥ as a synonym of sarva-sāraḥ (ITA-2.8.1.10), and Sushruta calls ojas the quintessence of all dhātus. So ojas is both the all-round sāra type and the substance that is the sāra of every dhātu. Two related but distinct uses.

Collides inside WHO ISTA: at ITA-2.2.16 asthisāram is a Sanskrit synonym for majjā ('bone marrow'), at ITA-2.8.1.6 asthi-sāraḥ is the bone-predominant constitution. Same string, two referents, one standard.
In dravyaguna sāra is the heartwood of a tree; in general Sanskrit it is essence, pith or wealth. Kaviratna's 'pith' rendering deliberately exploits this.

The eighth sāra is mind, not a dhātu at all (WHO ITA-2.8.1.9, 'Person with predominance or essence of strong willpower'). So the 'eight saras' are not eight dhātus, and calling the construct dhātu-sāra is already slightly inaccurate.

mistranslations.why: Introduces a quality judgement. Charaka's construct is predominance for the purpose of estimating strength, and it includes a negative category (asāra, 'having no pith') and a middling grade. 'Excellence' cannot accommodate the grading.
Too bare. It loses the constitutional and diagnostic function entirely, and collides with the separate use of sāra for ojas as the essence of all dhātus.

mistranslations.rendering: dhātu-sāra as though it were the classical term
mistranslations.why: Charaka's phrase as translated is simply sāra, and the compounds attested in Kaviratna's footnote are twak-sāra, rakta-sāra and so on, not dhātu-sāra. WHO ISTA likewise has sāraḥ, not dhātusāra. Citing 'dhātusāra' to Ca.Vi.8 would attribute a compound to the text that the retrieved sources do not show there.
The eighth is sattva (mind), which is not a dhātu. Charaka's list is skin, blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, vital seed and mind.

mistranslations.rendering: treating rasa-sāra and tvak-sāra as one type because WHO does
mistranslations.why: WHO merges them at ITA-2.8.1.2. Kaviratna's Charaka lists skin first and never mentions rasa in the eightfold list. The variant is real and WHO has resolved it in one direction without marking that it did.

openQuestions: The tvak-sāra / rasa-sāra variant is unresolved. WHO ISTA merges them under one term ID titled by rasa; Kaviratna's Charaka lists skin. Which the mula gives, and whether commentators differ, needs a Sanskrit Charaka and Chakrapanidatta.

Kaviratna's marginal verse numbers in this section run 116-128 while carakasamhitaonline cites the sāra section as Vi 8/102 ff. Roughly a fourteen-verse offset in this chapter alone. No verse number in this record should be treated as verified.

No study reports interrater reliability for sāra assessment. Given that the project's own reconnaissance records kappa of 0.28 for prakriti assessment, the prior for sāra is poor and nobody has measured it.

Whether sāra classification predicts anything independent of body habitus has not been tested. Charaka's own argument is that it should, since he explicitly rejects body size as an index of strength - which makes it a testable claim that has never been tested.
Sushruta has no eightfold sāra examination in the chapter retrieved. Whether it appears elsewhere in Sushruta was not checked.

classical.establishes: The seven-fold tissue-level cooking, stated as 'agnibhiḥ' in the plural rather than as the compound dhātvagni; and the two-fold output (kiṭṭa / prasāda, waste and essence).

classical.establishes: The only public-domain English for the seven dhātvagnis. Kaviratna adds a footnote noting that the text has just said there are five fires and now says seven, and explains the discrepancy — evidence that the bhūtāgni and dhātvagni counts were already felt as awkward.
classical.quote: They who sustain the body, viz., the 'dhatus' (i. e., 'Rasa' or juice, blood, flesh, adeps, marrow, bones, and vital seed), are cooked by their seven respective fires. This process of cooking which they undergo is of two kinds in consequence of the 'Kitta' (refuse) and the 'Prasada' (pure substance) which results from it.

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa names the three levels together as a technical triad — anna(-agni), bhautika(-agni), dhātv-agni. This is the earliest compound form of dhātvagni I could actually retrieve. Chapter/verse fixed by the file's own internal variant markers around this passage.
classical.quote:
doṣāṇām api caivaṃ syād eka-deśa-prakopaṇam |
anna-bhautika-dhātv-agni-karmeti paribhāṣitam || 70 ||
classical.translator: none — no public-domain English translation of Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya exists

distinguishFrom.why: bhūtāgni acts on the five elemental fractions of food; dhātvagni acts on the already-assimilated tissue. Vāgbhaṭa names them as separate members of a triad (AH Śā.3.70). Popular writing frequently merges them.
jāṭharāgni is prior and governing (Ca.Ci.15.39); dhātvagni is downstream and dependent. Weak dhātvagni with intact jāṭharāgni is a distinct clinical picture from mandāgni.
These name the process; dhātvagni names the agent. Texts that define dhātvagni as 'tissue metabolism' collapse agent into process.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's 1907 gloss. Protoplasm is a substance, dhātvagni is a transforming agent; the gloss also makes his own sentence ('the Dhatvagnis (protoplasm) of the muscle are not of the same kind as that of the arteries') incoherent as physiology.
The modern successor to 'protoplasm'. It imports specificity (named catalysts, measurable activity) that the concept does not have, and there is no study identifying any enzyme with any dhātvagni.
Conflates a seven-fold, tissue-specific, directional transformation series with a single scalar quantity.

openQuestions: Does Aruṇadatta or Cakrapāṇi give the first explicit seven-fold dhātvagni list, and with what wording?
Why does WHO mix two naming conventions inside ITA-2.6.6?
Has any study attempted a measurable proxy for any individual dhātvagni?

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English for the tooth-stick rule (astringent, pungent or bitter stick, end chewed to a brush, used twice daily without hurting the gums; removes bad odour and taste, clears sordes, restores appetite). His footnote 'To this day many Hindus wash their teeth twice a day ... A brush once used should not be used again.—T.' is the translator's note, not the text. In Su.5 his numbers run about eight BEHIND the standard (his 63-64 = std 71-73).
classical.quote: The stick for brushing the teeth should be either astringent or pungent or bitter. One of its ends should be chewed into the form of a brush. It should he used twice a day, taking care that the gums be not injured. The process (of washing the teeth thus) destroys bad odor and bad taste. It removes sordes from the tongue, teeth, and mouth, and quickly produces appetite and purifies the teeth.

classical.quote: Now we shall discourse on the rules of hygiene and the prophilactic measures in general ... A man should leave his bed early in the morning and brush his teeth. The tooth-brush should be made of a fresh twig of a tree or a plant grown on a commendable tract and it should be straight, not worm-eaten, devoid of any knot or at most with one knot only ... What is (popularly) known as physical exercise is (nothing but) a sense of weariness from bodily labour, and it should be taken every day. After taking physical exercise, the whole body should be shampooed, until it gives rise to a comfortable sensation in the limbs.

distinguishFrom.why: Night regimen (WHO ITA-10.3.2); dinacaryā in the texts actually runs from waking to sleep, so textbooks sometimes fold night into day.
Seasonal regimen (Ca.Su.6, AH.Su.3); varies by season rather than by day.
Code of conduct (Ca.Su.8), ethical rather than hygienic, though AH.Su.2 mixes conduct rules into its dinacaryā chapter.
The umbrella discipline (WHO ITA-10.1.3 'Routine(s) for health maintenance': 'Daily, seasonal and ethical regimens'); dinacaryā is one of its parts.
Charaka's chapter containing the daily-regimen rules is named for food quantity; citing it as 'Charaka's dinacharya chapter' is a modern relabelling.

mistranslations.why: Popular usage reduces dinacaryā to pre-noon practices; the texts and WHO run it from waking to sleep.
Bhishagratna's 'rules of hygiene' captures only part; dinacaryā includes exercise, massage, diet, conduct and sleep.
Imports a religious frame; the texts give physiological rationales (e.g. tooth-stick 'produces appetite and purifies the teeth').

classical.establishes: The doṣa set is explicitly partitioned: vāyu, pitta and kapha are the bodily (śārīra) doṣas, while rajas and tamas are the mental ones. 'Dosha' therefore does not mean 'the three humours' without qualification.
classical.quote: वायुः पित्तं कफश्चोक्तः शारीरो दोषसङ्ग्रहः| मानसः पुनरुद्दिष्टो रजश्च तम एव च||५७|| / vāyuḥ pittaṁ kaphaścōktaḥ śārīrō dōṣasaṅgrahaḥ| mānasaḥ punaruddiṣṭō rajaśca tama ēva ca||57||

classical.establishes: The only lawfully quotable English rendering of the foundational Charaka doṣa verse. Shows Kaviratna translating the triad as 'wind, bile, and phlegm' and narrowing doṣa to 'causes of disease', which the Sanskrit does not do.
classical.quote: Wind, bile, and phlegm have been said to be the causes of all bodily diseases. The qualities of Passion and Darkness have, again, been indicated to be the causes of mental diseases.

classical.establishes: Repeats the bodily/mental doṣa partition in prose and introduces the doṣa-dūṣya relation: the doṣas are what vitiates (dūṣayanti), not what is vitiated.
classical.quote: tatra trayaḥ śarīradoṣā vātapittaśleṣmāṇaḥ, te śarīraṁ dūṣayanti; dvau punaḥ sattvadoṣau rajastamaśca, tau sattvaṁ dūṣayataḥ| tābhyāṁ ca sattvaśarīrābhyāṁ duṣṭābhyāṁ vikr̥tirupajāyatē, nōpajāyatē cāpraduṣṭābhyām||34||

classical.establishes: Sushruta treats the doṣas as constitutive supports of the healthy body, not as pathogens, and adds blood as a fourth factor. Wisdomlib's Sushruta is Bhishagratna and is quotable; it does not carry verse numbers, only chapters.
classical.quote: The Vayu, Pitta and Shleshma should be considered as the primary and the most essential factors in the constitution of human organism. These fundamental and vital humours, occupying respectively the lower, middle, and upper parts of the body, maintain its integrity. The human body is supported by the three fundamental humours in the same way as a dwelling house is propped up by three supporting poles or stays; from which fact, the body is called the three-supported one (Tristhuna) by certain authorities.

classical.establishes: The text's own etymology of the three names, grounded in function (moving, burning, cohering) rather than in substance.
classical.quote: The terms Vata (Vayu), Pitta and Shleshma (Kapha) are respectively derived from the roots ‘Va’, to move or smell, ‘Tapa,’ to burn or to heat, and “Shlisha,” to embrace, with the suffix ‘Ta’ thereto added.

distinguishFrom.why: The doṣas vitiate; the dūṣyas (dhātus, malas, srotas) are what gets vitiated. Charaka Sharirasthana 4/34 states this directly ('te śarīraṁ dūṣayanti'). Treating dosha as 'the thing that is diseased' inverts the grammar of the system.
Charaka Sutrasthana 1/57 makes rajas and tamas doṣas too. 'Dosha' unqualified in English writing almost always means śārīra doṣa only; the classical term is broader.

Prakṛti is the individually fixed proportion of doṣas at conception; doṣa is the factor itself. 'Vata type' is a prakṛti claim, not a doṣa claim, and the two are routinely collapsed in popular writing.
Vikṛti is the current deviation from one's prakṛti. A doṣa reading taken today is a vikṛti observation unless explicitly constitutional.

distinguishFrom.term: doṣa in general Sanskrit / Nyaya usage
distinguishFrom.why: Outside medicine doṣa means fault, blemish, or a flaw in an argument. This is the sense Kaviratna translated by, and it is why 'fault' entered English Ayurvedic writing.

Malas are the excreta (faeces, urine, sweat). Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 treats doṣa, dhātu and mala as three parallel categories, so 'dosha = waste product' is a category error, though Charaka Sutrasthana 17/117 does call vitiated kapha a mala.

mistranslations.why: Imports the Galenic four-humour scheme, which has different members, a different number, a different theory of mixture and a different pathology. The public-domain translator who used it most, Bhishagratna, himself appended a note that the terms 'differ in their meaning from their usual English synonyms'.
Kaviratna's rendering. Substitutes three material substances for three functional factors; it cannot accommodate prāṇa-vāta governing cognition or sādhaka-pitta governing decision-making.
Etymologically the ordinary Sanskrit sense, but in the medical texts the doṣas in their normal state constitute and maintain the body (Sushruta Sutrasthana 21). Only the vitiated state is a fault.
Conflates doṣa with āma and with viṣa. No classical text equates them, and the conflation is the main route by which 'detox' marketing language enters translated Ayurveda.
Popular-wellness rendering with no classical or standardised warrant. WHO ISTA, ICD-11 and both public-domain translators all avoid it.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's aphorism numbering in Sutrasthana runs one behind the Jamnagar/ITRA numbering (his 43 = Cha.Su.1/44, his 56 = Cha.Su.1/57). Is the offset constant across all sthanas, or only in Sutrasthana 1?
Does any WHO ISTA entry define doṣa in its normal state as against its deranged state, or does the standard rely wholly on the 5.2 'Derangement of dosha' block for that contrast?
NAMASTE's English headword for doṣa itself could not be retrieved.

classical.establishes: This is the shat-kriyakala verse, the classical locus modern writers point to when they use 'dosha-dushya-sammurchana'. It names six stages including sthana-samshraya; it does NOT contain the compound dosha-dushya-sammurchana, and Bhishagratna's English contains no word for the dosha-dushya union.
classical.quote: The physician, who fully knows about the accumulation (Sancaya), disturbance or aggravation (Prakopa), expansion (Prasara), and differentiating traits of the deranged humours (Bheda), and is well conversant with the specific localities in which they are respectively confined in the course of their expansion (Sthana-samshrayam), and with the symptoms which they respectively exhibit in connection with the incidental disease (Vyakti), is alone worthy of that epithet.

classical.establishes: Opening of the Sthana-Samshraya section. Establishes that the classical text describes doshas lodging in a site and producing site-specific diseases, i.e. the mechanism the modern compound names, expressed without any term for the union itself.
classical.quote: Now we shall enumerate the names of the peculiar diseases, which are originated by the deranged and expanded humours, incarcerated in the different parts of the body.

classical.establishes: Charaka's definition of samprapti and its synonyms jati and agati. Recorded here to bound the claim: Charaka's treatment of pathogenesis names samprapti and its six subdivisions (Ni.1/12) and never uses sammurchana. Sanskrit quoted; the English on that page is the 2020 CSRTSDC translation and is not quoted.
classical.quote: सम्प्राप्तिर्जातिरागतिरित्यनर्थान्तरं व्याधेः||११|| / samprāptirjātirāgatirityanarthāntaraṁ vyādhēḥ||11||

distinguishFrom.why: Samprapti is the whole causal sequence from nidana to bheda and is a defined classical term with its own synonyms (Cha.Ni.1/11) and six subdivisions (Cha.Ni.1/12). Sammurchana, as used today, names one event inside that sequence. Treating them as equivalents collapses a process into a moment.

Sthana-samshraya is the fourth kriyakala, a classical stage named in Sushruta Su.21 with a retrievable verbatim text. Dosha-dushya-sammurchana is a later descriptor for what is said to happen at that stage. The stage has classical standing; the descriptor does not, on the evidence gathered.

Khavaigunya is the pre-existing defect or weakness in a channel or tissue that permits the lodging. Sammurchana is the lodging/union itself. Modern sources sometimes run them together; khavaigunya is the precondition, not the event.
A pharmaceutical processing operation on oils and ghee, from the same root. Entirely unrelated to pathogenesis, and a live collision risk in any glossary that indexes on the string 'murchana'.

Sannipata is the coming-together of the three doshas with one another. Sammurchana as used here is the coming-together of dosha with dushya (tissue). Both are 'combination' words and are routinely conflated in English summaries.

mistranslations.why: Implies an irreversible material merging. The classical mechanism (Su.Su.21) is lodging and localisation of a mobile dosha in a susceptible site, which the same chapter says can be reversed at an earlier stage. 'Fusion' overstates the physical claim.

A dictionary-driven error. Sammūrcchanā shares a root with mūrcchā, which does mean fainting or stupor, and that sense is what a general Sanskrit dictionary returns first. It is not the sense in this compound.
Flattens the term to mere co-occurrence. The point of the concept in modern usage is a pathological interaction at a defective site, not that dosha and dushya are both present, which they always are.

'Pathogenesis' is the standard English for samprapti, which is the whole sequence. Using it for sammurchana loses the distinction between the process and the event and makes the two terms indistinguishable in English.

openQuestions: Is the compound doṣa-dūṣya-sammūrcchanā attested in any samhita mula text, or does it first appear in a commentary (Chakrapani on Charaka, Dalhana on Sushruta, Vijayarakshita/Madhukosha on Madhava Nidana)? Nothing retrieved settles this.
If commentarial, which commentator and at which verse? Search summaries repeatedly attributed it to 'Charaka Nidana Sthana chapter 1' but no retrieved page showed the compound in that chapter.
Does the term properly belong to sthana-samshraya (4th kriyakala) or to vyakti (5th)? One single modern source uses it for both.
Is the term in NAMASTE? The portal could not be queried.

classical.establishes: The core passage. THREE distinct threefold gatis are given: (1) kṣaya, sthāna, vṛddhi; (2) upward, downward, transverse; (3) koṣṭha, śākhā, marma-asthi-sandhi. 'Dosha gati' is a family of three unrelated classifications, not one concept, and only the second and third are movement in any spatial sense.
classical.quote: क्षयः स्थानं च वृद्धिश्च दोषाणां त्रिविधा गतिः| ऊर्ध्वं चाधश्च तिर्यक्च विज्ञेया त्रिविधाऽपरा||११२|| त्रिविधा चापरा कोष्ठशाखामर्मास्थिसन्धिषु| इत्युक्ता विधिभेदेन दोषाणां त्रिविधा गतिः||११३|| / kṣayaḥ sthānaṁ ca vr̥ddhiśca dōṣāṇāṁ trividhā gatiḥ| ūrdhvaṁ cādhaśca tiryakca vijñēyā trividhā'parā||112|| trividhā cāparā kōṣṭhaśākhāmarmāsthisandhiṣu| ityuktā vidhibhēdēna dōṣāṇāṁ trividhā gatiḥ||113||

classical.establishes: Charaka announces the three gatis of doṣa in the chapter's opening list of topics, confirming that Sutrasthana 17 (Kiyantaḥśirasīya) is the locus classicus.
classical.quote: दोषाणां त्रिविधा चोक्ता गतिर्विस्तरतः शृणु||७|| / dōṣāṇāṁ trividhā cōktā gatirvistarataḥ śr̥ṇu||7||

classical.establishes: Two further gatis beyond the three threefold ones: the time-made (seasonal caya-prakopa-praśama) gati, and the twofold prākṛta/vaikṛta gati. Five classifications in total in this one chapter. Any definition of doṣagati as 'the movement of vitiated dosha' captures at most one of them.
classical.quote: गतिः कालकृता चैषा चयाद्या पुनरुच्यते|११५| गतिश्च द्विविधा दृष्टा प्राकृती वैकृती च या||११५|| / gatiḥ kālakr̥tā caiṣā cayādyā punarucyatē|115| gatiśca dvividhā dr̥ṣṭā prākr̥tī vaikr̥tī ca yā||115||

classical.establishes: Sushruta's account of prasara, the movement stage, in lawfully quotable English. Note Sushruta frames doṣa movement through the kriyākāla scheme rather than through Charaka's gati classifications; the two texts organise the same phenomenon differently.
classical.quote: As a vast and mighty expanse of water, which has been divided into two expanses by a dam or barrier, will sweep away the latter and unite again to form one sheet of water; so the deranged humours, sometimes singly, sometimes in combination with two or all of their species, or in unison with blood, expand and over-run the organism in all directions.

classical.establishes: The therapeutic consequence of doṣa movement: treat by the site occupied, not by the doṣa that moved. This is the clinical payload of the gati doctrine and it is quotable.
classical.quote: The deranged and aggravated Vayu, having moved into any specific seat of Pitta, should be medicinally treated as a case of Pittaja aggravation. Similarly, the deranged and aggravated Pitta, or Kapha, changing their respective places with each other, should be medicinally treated as the humour in whose location it is found.

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's own gloss on śākhā and asthi-sandhi, the terms in Charaka Sutrasthana 17/113's third gati. Quotable in English and useful because it shows śākhā means the dhātus and skin, not 'the limbs' as is often assumed. The sthana and chapter of the passage this footnote attaches to were not pinned down in the OCR and are left blank rather than guessed.
classical.quote: ‘Cakha’ literally means branch. As a techinacal word in medical science, it implies, as explained in the text, blood and the like, the humours and the skin. Of course, it includes flesh, marrow, fat, bones, and seminal fluid. ... ‘Asthi-sandhi’ is, literally, bone-joints.

distinguishFrom.why: In WHO ISTA itself, bare gatiḥ (ITA-2.1.1.12) means gait, a normal function of vāta. A search for 'gati' in the standard hits this before doṣagatiḥ.

Prasara is the third kriyākāla stage (WHO ITA-4.6.9); doṣagati in Charaka's sense is a classification scheme that is not stage-indexed. ICD-11 codes prasara ('Spreading of vata pattern', SR13) and does not code gati at all.
WHO ITA-4.8.20, the destinations rather than the movement. Separately standardised.

The three disease pathways (śākhā, marmāsthisandhi, koṣṭha) look identical to Charaka's third gati but are a classification of DISEASES by site, not of doṣa movement. The overlap in vocabulary is total and the referents differ.
The pulling of one doṣa from its seat by another, dealt with at Charaka Sutrasthana 17/45-47 per the retrieved chapter page. A specific mechanism, not a gati class.
This 'gati' involves no movement at all — it is the three quantitative states. Calling it a movement is a translation artefact of rendering gati as 'movement' across all three of Charaka's triads.

mistranslations.rendering: movement of dosha (as the whole meaning)
mistranslations.why: WHO's headword. It fits two of Charaka's five gatis and actively misdescribes the kṣaya/sthāna/vṛddhi triad, which is about quantity, and the prākṛta/vaikṛta pair, which is about normality.
Implies a continuous transport system analogous to blood circulation. Nothing in Charaka Sutrasthana 17 supports it.
Takes śākhā as 'limbs'. Kaviratna's own footnote gives śākhā as blood, the doṣas, skin, flesh, marrow, fat, bone and semen — the tissue compartment, not the extremities.
This is one of five gatis. Presenting it as the meaning of doṣagati is the commonest error in secondary literature.
Conflates doṣagati with roga-mārga, which is a classification of diseases rather than of doṣa states.

openQuestions: Charaka Sutrasthana 17/113 has 'trividhā gatiḥ' twice in two lines while enumerating three separate threefold schemes; whether the commentators read this as three parallel classifications or as a single one with three aspects was not established and materially affects the entry.
The Kaviratna footnote on śākhā and asthi-sandhi could not be located to a sthana and chapter in the OCR; a human should find the corresponding passage in a paginated copy.
Whether Sushruta anywhere uses gati as a technical term, or organises this material solely through kriyākāla, was not established.
Neither WHO ISTA nor ICD-11 has any term for the kṣaya/sthāna/vṛddhi gati or the prākṛta/vaikṛta gati. Whether this is deliberate scope limitation or an omission is unknown.

classical.establishes: Charaka announces eighteen kṣayas as a topic in its own right, alongside the three gatis of doṣa. Kṣaya is a named division of the doctrine, not an afterthought to vṛddhi.
classical.quote: दशाष्टौ च क्षयाः सप्त पिडका माधुमेहिकाः| दोषाणां त्रिविधा चोक्ता गतिर्विस्तरतः शृणु||७|| / daśāṣṭau ca kṣayāḥ sapta piḍakā mādhumēhikāḥ| dōṣāṇāṁ trividhā cōktā gatirvistarataḥ śr̥ṇu||7||

classical.establishes: The eighteen kṣayas are distributed across doṣas, dhātus, malas and ojas — so 'kshaya' unqualified is ambiguous in the source text itself and must always be qualified.
classical.quote: वातादीनां रसादीनां मलानामोजसस्तथा| क्षयास्तत्रानिलादीनामुक्तं सङ्क्षीणलक्षणम् ||६३|| / vātādīnāṁ rasādīnāṁ malānāmōjasastathā| kṣayāstatrānilādīnāmuktaṁ saṅkṣīṇalakṣaṇam ||63||

classical.establishes: The diagnostic criterion for kṣaya: the depleted doṣa abandons its own signs. Kṣaya is recognised by absence of function, which is why it is systematically under-diagnosed relative to vṛddhi. (Site prints 'कुवेते' for 'कुर्वते'.)
classical.quote: क्षीणा जहति लिङ्गं स्वं, समाः स्वं कर्म कुवेते||६२|| / kṣīṇā jahati liṅgaṁ svaṁ, samāḥ svaṁ karma kuvētē||62||

classical.establishes: The three kṣaya sign-lists and the treatment principle (supply what was lost) in lawfully quotable English. The single most useful passage for this term.
classical.quote: The loss of the bodily Vayu (nerve-force) is followed by a state of languor, shortness of speech, uneasiness or absence of hilarity, and loss of consciousness. The loss of (Pitta) is marked by a dulness of complexion, diminution of the bodily heat and an impaired state of internal fire (digestive heat). The loss of phlegm (Kapha) is marked by dryness, a sensation of internal burning, a feeling of emptiness in the stomach and other cavities or chambers of the body, looseness of the joints (a feeling as if the joints were all broken), thirst, weakness, and insomnia. In such cases the medical treatment should consist of remedial agents which are capable of directly contributing to the growth or formation of the humour so lost or deteriorated.

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's footnote 5 giving the causes of kṣaya, and naming overtreatment by śodhana and śamana first. Directly relevant to dosha-prashamana: excessive pacification is itself a cause of doṣa depletion.
classical.quote: Such a loss or perceptible deterioration of any of them should be ascribed to the use of excessive cleansing or cathartic (Samshodhana) and pacifying (Samshamana) measures, or to a repression of the natural urgings of the body, or to a course of violent or overfatiguing physical exercise, or to amorous excesses, or to the use of unwholesome and unsuitable food, or to, grief, etc.

distinguishFrom.why: Charaka Sutrasthana 17/63 lists kṣaya of doṣas, dhātus, malas and ojas together. Dhātu-kṣaya (tissue wasting) drives a different pathology — Charaka Nidana 4 uses it for one type of madhumeha — and is not interchangeable.

Enumerated in the same eighteen but treated separately and prognostically worse; Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 says a patient who has lost consciousness through loss of ojas 'should be given up by a physician'.

distinguishFrom.term: kṣaya / rājayakṣmā as a disease name
distinguishFrom.why: Kṣaya standing alone commonly denotes phthisis/consumption in classical and colonial-era Indian medical writing. Another genuine homograph trap.

Praśamana is the deliberate therapeutic reduction of an aggravated doṣa toward normal; kṣaya is depletion below normal. Sushruta's footnote makes excessive śamana a cause of kṣaya, so they are causally linked and conceptually opposite.
Post-purification doṣa reduction is an expected therapeutic state, not a kṣaya diagnosis, unless it exceeds the target.
WHO ITA-5.2.1 doṣavaiṣamyam, 'Derangement of dosha', is the umbrella term covering both vṛddhi and kṣaya.

mistranslations.why: Borrows the nutritional-deficiency frame, which implies a measurable shortfall against a reference intake. No doṣa has a reference range.
Laboratory register again, and it also invites the inference that raising the doṣa is straightforwardly good.
Bhishagratna's rendering, and it overstates: kṣaya is diminution, not absence, and the texts describe it as recoverable.
Imports the disease kṣaya (phthisis). Correct for one homograph, wrong for this one.
Collapses kṣaya with vṛddhi; the two have opposite treatments and opposite diagnostic criteria.

openQuestions: The eighteen kṣayas are announced at Charaka Sutrasthana 17/7 but the full enumeration across verses 63-72 was only partly read; a complete list of which eighteen was not compiled here.
WHO ISTA and ICD-11 TM2 disagree ('Diminution' vs 'Depletion') for the same Sanskrit; whether either instrument documents the choice was not established.
The Devanagari compound दोषक्षय was not attested verbatim; क्षय and दोष were each verified (Cha.Su.17/7, 17/63).

classical.establishes: Caya, prakopa and praśama occur individually and in sequence for each doṣa across the six seasons. Prakopa here is a normal seasonal event, not a disease — decisive against rendering it as a purely pathological 'aggravation'.
classical.quote: चयप्रकोपप्रशमाः पित्तादीनां यथाक्रमम्| भवन्त्येकैकशः षट्सु कालेष्वभ्रागमादिषु||११४|| / cayaprakōpapraśamāḥ pittādīnāṁ yathākramam| bhavantyēkaikaśaḥ ṣaṭsu kālēṣvabhrāgamādiṣu||114||

classical.establishes: The six kriyākāla stages named in Sanskrit inside a lawfully quotable English translation, with prakopa as the second. The only quotable English source located for the six-stage scheme.
classical.quote: The physician, who fully knows about the accumulation (Sancaya), disturbance or aggravation (Prakopa), expansion (Prasara), and differentiating traits of the deranged humours (Bheda), and is well conversant with the specific localities in which they are respectively confined in the course of their expansion (Sthana-samshrayam), and with the symptoms which they respectively exhibit in connection with the incidental disease (Vyakti), is alone worthy of that epithet.

classical.establishes: Prakopa is time-indexed and circadian as well as seasonal, and Bhishagratna's word for it here is 'naturally aggravated' — again a normal process.
classical.quote: The bodily Vayu is naturally aggravated in a cold, cloudy or windy day, in winter, during the rains, in the morning and evening and especially at the close of digestion.

classical.establishes: The clinical rationale for the kriyākāla scheme: intervention at sañcaya forestalls prakopa. This is why the stages are called 'occasions for treatment' rather than stages of disease.
classical.quote: The deranged humours, checked or subdued in their accumulating stage, fail to exhibit any further or subsequent development, but, if left unremedied, they gain in strength and intensity in the course of their further development.

classical.establishes: A representative prakopa aetiology list, showing that emotional states are given equal standing with diet.
classical.quote: The Pitta is aggravated by anger, grief, fear, fatigue, fasting, acid transformation (reaction) of the assimilated food, or deficient gastric digestion, unnatural sexual indulgence, partaking of a food consisting of pungent, acid or saline, keen, heat making or light substances, as well as of those whose digestion is followed by a reactionary acidity.

distinguishFrom.why: See the dosha-vriddhi record. Vṛddhi is increase; prakopa is the threshold-crossing stage. WHO ISTA keeps them apart at ITA-4.6.8 and merges them at ITA-5.2.1.2, so the standard cannot be cited as settling the question.
The preceding stage, accumulation within the doṣa's own seat (WHO ITA-4.6.7). Sushruta's whole clinical point is that these are different treatment occasions.
The following stage, overflow beyond the seat (WHO ITA-4.6.9). Sushruta attributes prasara specifically to vāta's mobility.
WHO ITA-5.2.1, 'Derangement of dosha' — the general state, not a stage.
WHO ITA-6.2.6.6 kōpanam is a pharmacological property of a substance, not a state of a patient.
Charaka Sutrasthana 17/114 makes seasonal prakopa a normal cycle; Sushruta Sutrasthana 21 lists behavioural and dietary causes. Only the latter is a clinical finding on its own.

mistranslations.why: Standard in both WHO ISTA and ICD-11, but it carries a pathological connotation in English that the seasonal prakopa of Charaka Sutrasthana 17/114 does not have. WHO itself notes the term 'may also indicate physiological aggravation'.
Used by WHO for kopanam and by ICD-11 for SR10/SR15/SR1A. Vitiation maps better to doṣa-duṣṭi or vaiṣamya; using it for prakopa loses the stage information.
Clinical English shorthand. It implies symptomatic disease, whereas prakopa by definition precedes vyakti (manifestation).
Literal from the root kup. Occasionally seen in older translations ('enraged humours' in Bhishagratna); anthropomorphic and misleading.
Erases the six-stage structure entirely, which is the main thing prakopa contributes.

openQuestions: WHO ISTA is internally inconsistent: ITA-4.6.8 defines prakopa as a stage, ITA-5.2.1.2 uses it as a synonym of vṛddhi-lakṣaṇa, and ITA-6.2.6.6 renders kopana as 'vitiating'. Whether this was deliberate was not established.
Whether the six-stage kriyākāla scheme is Sushruta's alone or is also stated as such in Charaka was not verified; Charaka Sutrasthana 17 gives caya-prakopa-praśama (three seasonal states), not six.
The compound दोषप्रकोप was not attested verbatim; प्रकोप is verified within चयप्रकोपप्रशमाः at Cha.Su.17/114.

mistranslations.why: Exactly backwards. doṣaprakṛti is the individual's balanced baseline; imbalance is vikṛti (Vi 8/101).

Vi 8/95 says the doṣa attaches to the four causal factors and the foetus is bound in consequence — a claim about causes, not about a doṣa in the embryo.

classical.establishes: The crucial and usually missed sense: praśama occurs by itself, seasonally, with no therapeutic agent. Doṣa pacification is a natural process before it is a treatment category.
classical.quote: चयप्रकोपप्रशमाः पित्तादीनां यथाक्रमम्| भवन्त्येकैकशः षट्सु कालेष्वभ्रागमादिषु||११४|| / cayaprakōpapraśamāḥ pittādīnāṁ yathākramam| bhavantyēkaikaśaḥ ṣaṭsu kālēṣvabhrāgamādiṣu||114||

classical.establishes: The verb praśāmyati is applied to the bodily doṣas (pacified by drugs) and, in the same breath, to the mental doṣas (pacified by knowledge, discernment, fortitude, memory and concentration). Praśamana is not restricted to pharmacology.
classical.quote: प्रशाम्यत्यौषधैः पूर्वो दैवयुक्तिव्यपाश्रयैः| मानसो ज्ञानविज्ञानधैर्यस्मृतिसमाधिभिः||५८|| / praśāmyatyauṣadhaiḥ pūrvō daivayuktivyapāśrayaiḥ| mānasō jñānavijñānadhairyasmr̥tisamādhibhiḥ||58||

classical.verse: 58 (Kaviratna prints this as aphorism 67, an OCR corruption)
classical.establishes: The same verse in lawfully quotable English. Kaviratna renders praśāmyati as 'is cured by', which overstates: praśamana is pacification toward normalcy, not cure of a disease.
classical.quote: The first kind (i.e., bodily disease) is cured by medicines founded upon acts in respect of the deities and upon reason* Mental disease is cured by knowledge of the soul, knowledge of the scriptures, (exercise of) patience and memory, and the abstraction of the mind from all worldly objects.

classical.establishes: Sushruta sets a floor on reduction: abnormal excesses of the humours and bodily principles are to be checked or remedied "so as not to reduce them to a smaller quantity than that in which they are found in the normal and healthy state of a body." The floor is stated for corrective (cleansing, śodhana) and pacifying (śamana) measures together, so it binds praśamana without being distinctive to it, and the sentence governs vṛddhi only. The sentence does not itself name kṣaya as the result of overshooting the floor.
classical.quote: These abnormal excesses of the aforesaid humours and principles, etc. of the body should be checked or remedied with corrective (cleansing) or pacifying measures as would be indicated by their respective natures, so as not to reduce them to a smaller quantity than that in which they are found in the normal and healthy state of a body.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: The viparīta (opposite-quality) mechanism of praśamana in lawfully quotable English, stated guṇa by guṇa rather than substance by substance.
classical.quote: Wind, which may be dry, cold, light, subtile, unstable, clear, keen, is cured by objects which have adverse attributes.

classical.establishes: Susruta's closing mandate for Sutrasthana 15: the physician preserves health in the healthy, and in the sick reduces or increases the dosas, dhatus and malas as the case requires, until the patient is free of disease, which is the mark of samya (equilibrium). This sets restoration of the normal quantity, not reduction as such, as the endpoint of treatment, and so fixes the floor below which pacification must not go. It does not make prasamana bidirectional: the mula (Su. Su. 15.40) names the two directions ksapayet and brmhayet, and the increasing arm is brmhana, a separate upakrama from samana. What 'pacifying' conceals is therefore the equilibrium target, not an increasing sense of prasamana.
classical.quote: An intelligent physician should preserve the state of health in a healthy individual, while he should increase or decrease the quantity of the bodily humours, vital fluids, or excrements in a sick patient according to the exigencies of the case until his health is perfectly restored.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: Śodhana expels the doṣa from the body (WHO ITA-9.2.1, 'Cleansing therapy', of which pañcakarma is the five-fold form). Śamana pacifies it where it is. The two are the primary division of Ayurvedic treatment and are constantly merged in English writing as 'detox'.
Charaka Sutrasthana 17/114 uses praśama for the natural seasonal subsidence of a doṣa with no therapy involved. A published entry that defines praśamana only as a drug action is incomplete.
WHO ITA-6.2.6.9 defines this as the drug that neither eliminates nor aggravates but restores. Narrower than praśamana, which covers regimen and non-material means too (Cha.Su.1/58).
The diagnostic trial — relief on applying an antagonistic measure, used to confirm a diagnosis. Therapeutically identical in form to praśamana, epistemically opposite in purpose.
WHO ITA-9.1.62. The full dosha-specific management plan, of which praśamana is one arm.
Praśamana pursued past the normal quantity produces kṣaya; Bhishagratna's footnote to Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 names excessive śodhana and śamana as the first causes of doṣa depletion.

mistranslations.why: The dominant wellness rendering. It has no classical counterpart term, obscures the śodhana/śamana division, and implies a symmetrical operation where the texts specify a directional one with a floor.
Renders śodhana, not śamana, and imports a toxin model absent from the texts.
Kaviratna's 'is cured by'. Praśamana returns a doṣa toward normalcy; it is not coextensive with curing a disease.
Reads the root śam as psychological calm. Correct for the mānasa doṣas at Cha.Su.1/58, wrong as a general gloss.
Actively misleading: the texts distinguish pacification from suppression of urges (vegadhāraṇa), which is itself a cause of doṣa derangement.
