classical.establishes: The operational definition: increased doṣas display their own signs in proportion to the increase, depleted doṣas abandon their own signs, and balanced doṣas perform their own function. Vṛddhi is therefore defined by sign-expression, not by any quantity. NOTE: the hosting site prints 'कुवेते' where the reading should be 'कुर्वते'; the typo is reproduced here as retrieved and should be corrected against a critical edition.
classical.quote: दोषाः प्रवृद्धाः स्वं लिङ्गं दर्शयन्ति यथाबलम्| क्षीणा जहति लिङ्गं स्वं, समाः स्वं कर्म कुवेते||६२|| / dōṣāḥ pravr̥ddhāḥ svaṁ liṅgaṁ darśayanti yathābalam| kṣīṇā jahati liṅgaṁ svaṁ, samāḥ svaṁ karma kuvētē||62||

classical.establishes: Vṛddhi and kṣaya are combinatorial: the text enumerates states in which one doṣa is increased, one normal and one decreased, and so on. The framework is a three-valued vector, not a single 'aggravated dosha'.
classical.quote: वृद्धिक्षयकृतश्चान्यो विकल्प उपदेक्ष्यते||४३|| वृद्धिरेकस्य समता चैकस्यैकस्य सङ्क्षयः| द्वन्द्ववृद्धिः क्षयश्चैकस्यैकवृद्धिर्द्वयोः क्षयः ||४४|| / vr̥ddhikṣayakr̥taścānyō vikalpa upadēkṣyatē||43|| vr̥ddhirēkasya samatā caikasyaikasya saṅkṣayaḥ| dvandvavr̥ddhiḥ kṣayaścaikasyaikavr̥ddhirdvayōḥ kṣayaḥ ||44||

classical.establishes: The sign-lists for vāta-vṛddhi and pitta-vṛddhi in lawfully quotable English.
classical.quote: An excess of Vayu in the body is marked by such symptoms as roughness of the skin, emaciation of the body, darkness of complexion (lit: blackness of hue), a little tremor or trembling of the limbs, longing for heat, or for hot things, insomnia, thickness or increased consistency of the fecal matter and decrease of bodily strength. (Similarly, an abnormal) increase of Pitta is characterised by a sallow complexion or a yellowish colour of the skin, a general burning sensation in the body as well as insomnia, a craving for cold contacts and cooling things, diminution of strength, weakness of the sense organs, fits of fainting and yellowness of the conjunctive, stool and urine.

classical.establishes: The sign-list for kapha-vṛddhi.
classical.quote: An excess of Kapha in the body is marked by such symptoms, as the whiteness, coldness and numbness of the body, heaviness of the limbs, a sense of drowsiness and languor, somnolence, and a feeling of looseness of the bone-joints.

classical.establishes: The causal rule for vṛddhi, i.e. like increases like. Bhishagratna's footnote records that several editions treat this as an additional text, so its status is not uniform across manuscripts.
classical.quote: The quantities of these humours, principles and secretion, are abnormally increased through the use of substances that primarily contribute to their formation in the organism.

classical.establishes: The sāmānya-viśeṣa principle that governs all vṛddhi and kṣaya, in lawfully quotable English. Verse number confirmed independently: the Sanskrit 'sarvadā sarvabhāvānāṁ sāmānyaṁ vr̥ddhikāraṇam| hrāsahēturviśēṣaśca, pravr̥ttirubhayasya tu||44||' is numbered 44 at https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya, establishing the one-verse offset in Kaviratna's Sutrasthana numbering.
classical.quote: Of all things, at all times, similarity is the cause of increase ; and dissimilarity is the cause of decrease. A tendency exists towards both.

distinguishFrom.why: The most damaging confusion in this batch. Vṛddhi is quantitative/qualitative increase; prakopa is the second stage of the six-stage kriyākāla in which the increased doṣa reaches the threshold to leave its seat. WHO ISTA merges them into one entry (ITA-5.2.1.2 'vātaprakopaḥ / vātavṛddhilakṣaṇam'), which is a standardisation decision, not a textual identity.
Sañcaya is accumulation in the doṣa's own site (WHO ITA-4.6.7), the first kriyākāla stage. Charaka's vṛddhi in Sutrasthana 17 is not stage-indexed at all.
In WHO ISTA and in classical nosology, bare vṛddhi denotes hydrocoele and scrotal enlargement (ITA-5.45.1, with antra-vṛddhi for hernia at ITA-5.46.1). This is a true homograph and a search trap.

Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 treats increase of dhātus (rasa, rakta, māṃsa, medas...) in the same chapter and with the same vocabulary. The sign-lists are different and the therapeutic response is different.
A general term for accretion, used e.g. in WHO ITA-9.x śukropacayaḥ. Not stage-indexed and not doṣa-specific.

mistranslations.why: The most common English rendering, and it is really the rendering of prakopa. Using it for vṛddhi erases a distinction both Charaka and the kriyākāla scheme maintain.

Implies a quantity above a threshold. Charaka Sutrasthana 17/62 defines the state by sign-expression, not by amount, and Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 states plainly that the exact quantity of doṣas in a body cannot be laid down.
Too weak and too broad: it covers vṛddhi, kṣaya and vaiṣamya indifferently, and is the usual route by which the whole vocabulary collapses into one word in English health writing.
Borrows laboratory register for something with no assay; there is no unit and no reference range.

openQuestions: Does the WHO ISTA merger of vṛddhi-lakṣaṇa and prakopa into one English term appear in every doṣa's entry or only vāta's? Only the vāta entry was read in full.
The Devanagari compound दोषवृद्धि was not itself attested in a retrieved source; वृद्धि and दोष were each verified separately (Cha.Su.17/43-44, 17/62).
Whether Ashtanga Hridaya's vṛddhi treatment (Sutrasthana 11) differs from Charaka's was not checked; there is no quotable English translation in any case.

classical.establishes: Drava is the terminal member of the gurvādi series (gurvādayaś ca dravāntāḥ). Sanskrit as retrieved: तस्य गुणाः शब्दादयो गुर्वादयश्च द्रवान्ताः, कर्म पञ्चविधमुक्तं वमनादि||१०|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya).
classical.quote: The attributes which inhere in objects are Sound, &c., heaviness, &c., ending with solubility. The operations performed with their aid are five, beginning with vomiting, as has been already said.

classical.verse: Standard 1.60 — printed ॥ ६० ॥ in Trikamji's Nirnaya Sagar Carakasaṃhitā with the Āyurvedadīpikā, Sūtrasthāna p. 16 (archive.org TheCarakasahitOrCharakasamhitaOfCarakaEditedByYadavaarman leaf n84), and listed as verse 60 'पित्तस्य गुणास्तत्प्रशमनानि च' in that edition's own index; Kaviratna prints 59
classical.establishes: Drava is one of the seven attributes of pitta listed at Charaka Sutrasthana 1.60, which prescribes treating them with substances of opposite quality: सस्नेहमुष्णं तीक्ष्णं च द्रवमम्लं सरं कटु| विपरीतगुणैः पित्तं द्रव्यैराशु प्रशाम्यति||६०|| — sasneha (unctuous), ushna (hot), tikshna (sharp), drava (liquid), amla (sour), sara (mobile), katu (pungent). The claim rests on the Sanskrit द्रवम्. The English quoted here is Kaviratna's, and only four of his seven words render the verse: 'hot' = ushna, 'keen' = tikshna, 'sour' = amla, 'liquid' = drava. His 'cold', 'soft' and 'bitter' answer to nothing in it, the Sanskrit having sasneha, sara and katu in those places; 'cold' goes further and contradicts ushna inside his own sentence. His English is recorded as a specimen of how he rendered the verse, not as the Samhita's list of pitta's qualities.
classical.quote: Bile, which may be cold, hot, keen, soft, sour, liquid, and bitter, is speedily cured by objects having adverse attributes.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: The definition of dravya as the substratum of karma and guna and as the (inherent) cause. Sanskrit as retrieved from https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya&action=raw : यत्राश्रिताः कर्मगुणाः कारणं समवायि यत्| तद्द्रव्यं समवायी तु निश्चेष्टः कारणं गुणः||५१||. Kaviratna's 'the cause' drops 'samavāyi' (inherent); the Sanskrit says dravya is the samavāyi-kāraṇa.
classical.quote: That in which actions and attributes inhere, and that which is the cause, is called substance. That, on the other hand, which is inherent, and which is the passive cause, is called attribute.

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English names EIGHT dravyas: the five bhūtas (via his bracketed gloss '(i.e., ether, air, fire, water, and earth)' on 'those having ether for the first'), soul, mind, and 'the quarters' (diś). It omits kāla (time), which the Sanskrit has: खादीन्यात्मा मनः कालो दिशश्च द्रव्यसङ्ग्रहः| सेन्द्रियं चेतनं द्रव्यं, निरिन्द्रियमचेतनम्||४८|| (carakasamhitaonline). The ninefold list therefore rests on the Sanskrit alone; his footnote at this aphorism discusses only 'quarters' and does not explain the omission. The passage does establish the division into sendriya/cetana ('united with the senses... animate') and nirindriya/acetana ('without the senses... inanimate'). '(of all things)' is also his gloss. Note he renders dravya here as 'constituent elements', not 'substance'.
classical.quote: Those having ether for the first (i.e., ether, air, fire, water, and earth), soul, mind, and the quarters, are constituent elements (of all things) United with the senses, elements are called animate; without the senses, they are called inanimate.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Dravya ('objects') as one of the six things the sages saw. Sanskrit: महर्षयस्ते ददृशुर्यथावज्ज्ञानचक्षुषा| सामान्यं च विशेषं च गुणान् द्रव्याणि कर्म च||२८|| समवायं च तज्ज्ञात्वा...||२९||.
classical.quote: Those great Rishis (then) beheld duly, with the eye of knowledge, similarities, dissimilarities, properties, objects, and operations, as also compositions.

classical.verse: Standard 40.3 per siva.sh (https://www.siva.sh/sushruta-samhita/sutra-sthana/40/3); Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers
classical.establishes: Sushruta's statement of the dravya-pradhāna view with nine reasons (permanence, nityatva, retention of own class, perceptibility by all five senses, being the substratum (āśraya) of rasa etc., being the starting point of a procedure, scriptural usage, dependence of rasa on the stage of the dravya, curability by a single part). Sanskrit opening as retrieved from siva.sh: केचिदाचार्या ब्रुवते- द्रव्यं प्रधानं, कस्मात्? व्यवस्थितत्वात्... Note the passage is one of several rival views (rasa, vīrya, vipāka each have their advocates) before the reconciliation.
classical.quote: Hence a drug or a substance (Dravyam) is the most important factor (which the science of medicine has got to deal with). A substance or drug necessarily implies action and attributes with which it is intimately connected and of which it is the primary cause, or to put it more explicitly, these attributes have an inseparable inherence in and are intimately associated with the substance by way of cause and effect (Samavayi-Karana).

classical.verse: Sushruta Sutrasthana 40/13-18 (siva.sh Devanagari numbering; Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers): 'equal importance... co-operation of all these five factors' = 40/13 (चतुर्णामपि सामग्र्यम्); 'Digestive reaction is impossible without drug potency... greatest of them all' = 40/15; 'greatest of all the aforesaid five factors... attributes lie inherent' = 40/18 (with 40/17 on the eight guṇas resting on dravya)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's closing reconciliation of the chapter's rival doctrines: the wise want the conjunction of FOUR, caturṇām api sāmagryam (40/13), namely dravya, rasa, vīrya and vipāka, the four positions actually argued in the chapter; and dravya is the substratum, since there is no vipāka without vīrya, no vīrya without rasa, no rasa without dravya (40/15), and the remaining bhāvas rest on it (40/18, śeṣā bhāvās tadāśrayāḥ; 40/17, the eight guṇas called vīrya rest on dravya). 'All these five factors' and 'the aforesaid five factors (of substance, taste, virtues, etc.)' are Bhishagratna's wording: guṇa is not a contending party in the Sanskrit. Bracketed ellipses mark omitted sentences within the same paragraph.
classical.quote: The wise and the erudite set an equal importance to each of them, and ascribe the curative efficacy of a medicine to the co-operation of all these five factors. [...] Digestive reaction is impossible without drug potency. There is no potency without a taste, and taste without a drug or substance is an absurdity. Hence a substance (vegetable or otherwise) is the greatest of them all. [...] Hence a substance is the greatest of all the aforesaid five factors (of substance, taste, virtues, etc.) and the attributes lie inherent in the substance.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Su.1.51: dravya is the substratum in which guna and karma inhere and is the samavāyi-kāraṇa; guna is the inherent but inactive (niśceṣṭa) cause. Bhishagratna (Su.Su.40): 'a drug or a substance is the receptacle of the attributes of taste, etc., while the latter are the things contained'.
The five bhutas are five of the nine kāraṇa-dravyas (Ca.Su.1.48); dravya is the wider class that also includes ātmā, manas, kāla and diś. Collapsing dravya into 'the elements' loses four of nine.

Dravya is the ontological category; auṣadha/bheṣaja is dravya put to therapeutic use. Bhishagratna's habitual 'drug or substance' blurs exactly this. NIA DG0076 ('akin to drug in modern pharmacology') adopts the narrow pharmacological sense.
WHO ITA-1.9.3.1.1/1.9.3.7.1 and NIA DG0102/DG0103: nine causal substances versus the manifest products made of them (herbs, animals, minerals). Both are 'dravya'.
Su.Su.40 presents them as rival candidates for primacy; Sushruta's conclusion is that they inhere in dravya and cannot exist without it.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's 'constituent elements' for the nine dravyas invites confusion with the five mahābhūtas, which are only a subset.
The pharmacological sense is a sub-use. Ca.Su.1.48 counts soul, mind, time and direction as dravyas; none is a drug.
Kaviratna's word in the list at Su.1.28. In English 'object' suggests an external physical thing, which excludes ātmā and manas.
WHO ITA-1.9.3.1 and NIA BP0096 use it; in English 'matter' excludes the immaterial dravyas (ātmā, manas, kāla, diś) that Charaka explicitly lists.

openQuestions: Chakrapāṇi's gloss on Su.1.51 (samavāyi-kāraṇa) was not retrieved.
The standard verse number for Bhishagratna's closing reconciliation paragraph in Su.Su.40 was not established.
Whether Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya/Saṃgraha define dravya separately was not checked.

distinguishFrom.why: Duḥkhāyu is the reverse of the circumstantial list (disease, age, weakness, poverty, thwarted undertakings); ahitāyu is the reverse of the ethical list. They are separate limbs and a life can be one without the other.

distinguishFrom.term: duḥkha as the general term for pain/suffering
distinguishFrom.why: Duḥkha is used throughout the Samhitas for pain and for the suffering that treatment relieves. In duḥkhāyu it classifies a whole life against a checklist, not a symptom.
Disease is one item in the reversed list. A life can be duḥkhāyu through poverty or thwarted undertakings without disease.

Not a different concept but the actual word in the defining verse. Worth keeping visible because it is the evidence that duḥkhāyu is a lemma assembled from Su 1.41 rather than a term Charaka uses in the definition.

mistranslations.why: Recorded because WHO uses it, but it maps a definition-by-negation onto a graded measurement scale. The verse offers no gradation, only a reverse.
Disease is one reversed item among many; wealth, youth, success and freedom of action are equally in the list.
Renders the noun duḥkha, not the compound. Duḥkhāyu is a classification of a life, not a state of experience.

openQuestions: Why the defining verse says asukham where the enumerating verse says duḥkham, and whether any commentator treats them as equivalent. Not established.

Whether the standalone word duḥkhāyuḥ occurs anywhere in the Brhattrayi, or only in the compounded/adjectival forms I retrieved. Not checkable against GRETIL, whose Charaka file does not include Su 30.
Whether NAMASTE codes it.

classical.establishes: The definition of guna: inherent (samavāyī), inactive (niśceṣṭa), a cause. Sanskrit as retrieved from https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya&action=raw : समवायी तु निश्चेष्टः कारणं गुणः||५१||. 'Passive' is Kaviratna's rendering of niśceṣṭa (without activity).
classical.quote: That, on the other hand, which is inherent, and which is the passive cause, is called attribute.

classical.establishes: The enumeration of gunas: the sense-objects (artha), the gurvādi pairs, buddhi and the series ending in prayatna, and the parādi series. Sanskrit: सार्था गुर्वादयो बुद्धिः प्रयत्नान्ताः परादयः| गुणाः प्रोक्ताः प्रयत्नादि कर्म चेष्टितमुच्यते||४९||. All bracketed expansions are Kaviratna's. His footnote (translator's note, not text) reads: 'The word rendered properties is artha. They are, as explained by the commentator, the sensations, viz., vision, taste, touch, scent, and hearing' and admits 'I am not sure as to what parādaya means'.
classical.quote: The properties (of vision, taste, scent, touch, and hearing), pairs of opposites (such as heavy and light, heat and cold, &c.), the intellect, pleasure and pain, and desire and aversion and will, and the qualities of dissimilarity and others (i.e., dissimilarity, contrariety, union, number, composition, division, separateness, measure, inertia and contiguity) are called attributes, while all functions such as (of the mind in) will, are called action.

classical.establishes: Guna ('properties') among the six. Sanskrit: सामान्यं च विशेषं च गुणान् द्रव्याणि कर्म च||२८||.
classical.quote: Those great Rishis (then) beheld duly, with the eye of knowledge, similarities, dissimilarities, properties, objects, and operations, as also compositions.

classical.verse: Standard 40.3 per siva.sh for the dravya argument; Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers
classical.establishes: The guna-as-contained / dravya-as-container relation (āśrayatvāc ca, dravyam āśritā rasādayaḥ in the Sanskrit retrieved from siva.sh). Also in the same chapter: 'Since an attribute per se can not be possessed of another attribute, the eight kinds of potency (properties) can only appertain to a substance and not to a taste, which is an attribute in itself.' (the nirguṇā guṇāḥ principle in Bhishagratna's words).
classical.quote: Fifthly because, a drug or a substance is the receptacle of the attributes of taste, etc., while the latter are the things contained.

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Su.1.51: dravya is the substratum and samavāyi-kāraṇa; guna inheres in it and is niśceṣṭa. Bhishagratna: receptacle versus thing contained.
Ca.Su.1.49: 'are called attributes, while all functions such as (of the mind in) will, are called action'. Guna is passive, karma is activity (prayatnādi ceṣṭita).
Kaviratna's footnote to his 48: the word he renders 'properties' at the head of the guna list is artha (śabda, sparśa, rūpa, rasa, gandha), which are a subclass of guna, not a synonym.

The twenty pharmacological pairs are one sub-series of Ca.Su.1.49's list; guna as a padārtha is the whole category including buddhi, sukha/duḥkha, icchā/dveṣa, prayatna and the parādi gunas. NIA DG0086's 'mainly pertains to the pharmacological properties' narrows to this subset.
WHO ITA-1.9.4.2 lists them under the same heading, but they are Sāṃkhya constituents of prakṛti, not inherent properties of a dravya in Charaka's Su.1.49 sense.
Bhishagratna's 'virtues' is pharmacy English ('the virtues of a herb'); the ethical sense of guna (good quality of a person) is a separate use.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna and Kaviratna both use it; modern English reads it as moral merit.
Ca.Su.1.49 counts buddhi, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort among gunas; a reader equating guna with material properties will not recognise half the list.
The ordinary English sense of 'quality' (high/low quality) is absent from the technical term.
Popular writing; the abstract of PMID 22408303 even calls the mahāgunas 'the prime energy'. Charaka's definition is the opposite: guna is niśceṣṭa, without activity.

openQuestions: Chakrapāṇi on parādi gunas (Su.1.49) not retrieved; Kaviratna himself confesses uncertainty about 'parādaya'.
Whether Sushruta anywhere gives a categorial definition of guna (as opposed to using it) was not established in this pass; only Su.40 was read.
Relation between WHO's 41 gunas (ITA-1.9.4 series) and Charaka's 1.49 list not tabulated.

classical.establishes: THE MOST IMPORTANT SINGLE FACT ABOUT THIS TERM. Here hetu is upalabdhi-kāraṇa, the cause of apprehension, and is fourfold: pratyakṣa, anumāna, aitihya, aupamya. That is an epistemology, not an etiology. The word is item 11 in Charaka's list of debate terms. Retrieved and string-matched by me on the cited page.

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for the epistemological sense. 'apprenhen-sion' is a scan artifact, preserved verbatim. Kaviratna prints this in his Lesson on medical disputation, immediately after Upanaya and Nigamana.

Since through these Hetus things are apprehended, therefore is their condition as such (that is, of being the cause of apprenhen- sion)

classical.establishes: The etiological sense: hetu heads the list of eight words declared anarthāntara with nidāna. Charaka therefore uses hetu in two incompatible technical senses in two sthānas of one work, and says so in neither place.

distinguishFrom.why: Declared synonymous at Ca. Ni. 1.3, and WHO gives them one code. They are not interchangeable in practice: nidāna also names a text division and the five-member set, and hetu also names a means of knowledge. Kaviratna's footnote adds that hetu 'is generally limited to the circumstances that precede'.

Also in the same synonym list, and WHO glosses kāraṇam 'Primary cause' against hetuḥ 'Etiological factor'. At Vi. 8.33 the two are not synonyms at all: hetu is DEFINED as a kind of kāraṇa (upalabdhi-kāraṇa), so kāraṇa is the wider term there.

The middle term or reason of a syllogism. Charaka's Vi. 8 list is a medical adaptation of debate logic, and this sense is much closer to Nyāya's than to anything etiological. A reader who knows Nyāya will import the syllogistic sense into Nidāna Sthāna, where it does not belong.

WHO ITA-4.4.3 and ITA-4.4.4. The first initiates by promoting dosha accumulation; the second sustains and manifests. Collapsing them into 'cause' loses the only causal distinction the standard actually codes.

WHO ITA-4.4.19 and ITA-4.4.20. Causes of dosha aggravation irrespective of disease, versus causes of a disease irrespective of dosha. Ca. Ni. 1.10's definition of upaśaya turns on exactly this pair, so conflating them makes upaśaya's three viparīta subtypes unreadable.

The other members of the Ni. 1.3 synonym set, each with a distinct WHO gloss (Indicative factor; Abode of the causative factor; Causative setting, conducive factor; Factors augmenting the pathology; Agent). Declared synonymous, glossed differently, used differently.

mistranslations.why: Correct for Vi. 8.33 and wrong for Ni. 1.3. The failure mode is picking one and applying it everywhere.
Imports a germ-theory object. Charaka's three nidāna are misuse of the senses, error of judgement and the action of time; none is an organism.
Names the study or the account; hetu names the factor. WHO's ITA-4.4.1 head term has the same slippage.
Names only vyañjaka-hetu and silently drops utpādaka-hetu.

openQuestions: Whether any classical commentator addresses the Vi. 8.33 / Ni. 1.3 clash directly. Chakrapani is the obvious place and I did not retrieve him.

Whether hetu has PubMed-indexed literature. I did not run a dedicated PubMed query for 'hetu' alone; the term is too short and ambiguous for a useful search, and I am recording that as a gap rather than reporting a count I did not obtain. Related queries I did run returned nothing about the term itself.
Ca. Vi. 8.57 reportedly discusses hetu further in the pratijñā/sthāpanā sequence. I retrieved the page but did not confirm what verse 57 says, so I have not recorded it.

classical.establishes: Defines hitam āyuḥ by a list of ethical and cognitive conduct - benevolence, abstention from others' property, truthfulness, tranquillity, deliberate action, vigilance, balanced pursuit of the trivarga, reverence, control of passions, giving, austerity and knowledge, attention to this world and the next, good memory - and then defines ahitam simply as the reverse. This excerpt is the hitāyu/ahitāyu portion of the verse; the sukha/asukha portion precedes it in the same verse.
classical.quote: हितैषिणः पुनर्भूतानां परस्वादुपरतस्य सत्यवादिनः शमपरस्य परीक्ष्यकारिणोऽप्रमत्तस्य त्रिवर्गं परस्परेणानुपहतमुपसेवमानस्य पूजार्हसम्पूजकस्य ज्ञानविज्ञानोपशमशीलस्य वृद्धोपसेविनःसुनियतरागरोषेर्ष्यामदमानवेगस्य सततं विविधप्रदानपरस्य तपोज्ञानप्रशमनित्यस्याध्यात्मविदस्तत्परस्य लोकमिमं चामुंचावेक्षमाणस्य स्मृतिमतिमतो हितमायुरुच्यते; अहितमतो विपर्ययेण ॥२४॥

classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of the hitāyu definition, item-for-item matching the Sanskrit of Su 30.24 above. Kaviratna prints this as aphorism 20 of his Lesson XXX; the modern vulgate prints the whole fourfold definition as a single verse 24. Hyphenation artefacts and 'waite' for 'waits' are OCR; reproduced as retrieved.
classical.quote: Of  one  who  seeks  the  good  of  all  creatures,  who  abstains  from  appropriating  what  belongs  to  others,  who  is  truthful  in  speech, who  is  devoted  to  tranquillity,  who  acts  only  after  reflection  and  exami¬  nation,  who  is  never  heedless,  who  pursues  the  aggregate  of  three  (/.  e.,  Religion,  Wealth,  and  Pleasure)  without  any  one  of  them  afflicting  the  others,  who  worships  with  reverence  all  those  that  deserve  worship,  who  derives  praise  from  knowledge  and  science,  who  waite  with  reverence  on  the  old,  who  has  properly  controlled  the  impulses  of  affection  or  attachment,  of  jealousy,  of  arrogance,  and  of  pride,  who  always  makes  diverse  kinds  of  gifts,  who  is  devoted  to  penances,  knowledge,  and  peace,  who  is  conversant  with  topics  connected  with  the  Soul,  who  is  devoted  to  That,  who  acts  in  view  of  both  this  world  and  the  next,  and  who  has  a  good  memory,  the  Life  is  said  to  be  beneficial.

classical.establishes: The first occurrence of the hita/ahita pair as a division of āyu, here as a bare dvandva (hitāhitaṃ) with no content; the content comes only at Su 30.24. Note the same verse also says āyurveda declares what is hita and ahita TO life (tasya hitāhitam) - a second, different use of the same pair in one line.
classical.quote: हिताहितं सुखं दुःखमायुस्तस्य हिताहितम्| मानं च तच्च यत्रोक्तमायुर्वेदः स उच्यते||४१||

distinguishFrom.why: The pair that the tradition itself insists is not the same. Sukhāyu is defined by health, youth, strength, wealth and the ability to do as one pleases (Su 30.24, first half); hitāyu by ethical conduct and cognition. A person can have one without the other, which is the whole point of the fourfold division.

Svastha is a state of the body-mind system defined by doṣa-agni-dhātu-mala balance and pleasant ātman/indriya/manas (Su.Su 15.41). Hitāyu is a manner of living. Health is a precondition described in sukhāyu, not in hitāyu.
Pathya is what is suitable for the channels/for a given patient in a given condition - a dietetic and therapeutic judgement. Hita in hitāyu is an ethical and social judgement about a life as a whole.
Su 1.41 uses hita twice in one verse: once as a kind of life, once as what is beneficial to life. They are not the same use and conflating them collapses a distinction Charaka draws in a single line.

mistranslations.why: Health belongs to the sukhāyu description in Su 30.24 ('not afflicted by any disease physical or mental'), not to hitāyu. Rendering hitāyu as healthy life imports the wrong half of the verse.
That is sukhāyu. The two are explicitly separate limbs of the same definition.
Duration is not mentioned in the hitāyu definition at all.

openQuestions: Whether any classical commentator (Chakrapani on Su 30.24) makes explicit the now-common teaching that sukhāyu is immediate pleasure while hitāyu is beneficial in the long run and for society. That formulation appears on carakasamhitaonline.com's discussion, which is a modern editorial layer, not the mūla; I did not retrieve Chakrapani's Sanskrit on this verse.
Whether NAMASTE codes hitāyu, and whether it follows WHO's 'salutary life'.

classical.establishes: The pañca-pañcaka: five indriyas, five indriya-dravyas (constituent elements), five adhiṣṭhānas (seats), five arthas (objects), five buddhis (cognitions). The indriya is listed separately from its seat, which is the key to the 'sense organ' problem. Kaviratna (his 1): 'It is certain that there are five senses, five materials that constitute those senses, five resting places of those senses, five objects of those senses, and five kinds of perceptions obtained through those senses.'
classical.quote: Iha khalu pañcēndriyāṇi, pañcēndriyadravyāṇi, pañcēndriyādhiṣṭhānāni, pañcēndriyārthāḥ, pañcēndriyabuddhayō bhavanti, ityuktamindriyādhikārē||3||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.verse: 8-11 (standard; Kaviratna merges these into his aphorism 6)
classical.establishes: The indriyas are cakṣus, śrotra, ghrāṇa, rasana, sparśana (faculties of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching); their seats are the eyes, ears, nostrils, tongue and skin. Kaviratna: 'The five senses are vision, hearing, scent, taste, and touch. ... The resting places of the five senses are the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the tongue, and the skin or whole body.'
classical.quote: Tatra cakṣuḥ śrōtraṁ ghrāṇaṁ rasanaṁ sparśanamiti pañcēndriyāṇi||8|| pañcēndriyadravyāṇi- khaṁ vāyurjyōtirāpō bhūriti||9|| Pañcēndriyādhiṣṭhānāni- akṣiṇī karṇau nāsikē jihvā tvak cēti||10|| Pañcēndriyārthāḥ- śabdasparśarūparasagandhāḥ||11||

classical.establishes: Indriyas grasp objects only when preceded by manas (7); they are known by inference (anumānagamya), composed of all five bhūtas with one predominant each (14). 'Known by inference' is why 'organ' misleads: the indriya is not the visible eye. Kaviratna (his 5): 'The senses become capable of seizing their respective objects only when they are led by the mind.'
classical.quote: Manaḥpuraḥsarāṇīndriyāṇyarthagrahaṇasamarthāni bhavanti||7|| ... Tatrānumānagamyānāṁ pañcamahābhūtavikārasamudāyātmakānāmapi satāmindriyāṇāṁ tējaścakṣuṣi, khaṁ śrōtrē, ghrāṇē kṣitiḥ, āpō rasanē, sparśanē'nilō viśēṣēṇōpapadyatē|...||14||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: The ten indriyas (daśendriya) of the 24-fold puruṣa: five inferred from their actions, five karmendriyas. Kaviratna (his 24): 'These are mind, the ten organs (of knowledge and action), the five objects of the five organs of knowledge, and the eight modifications of Prakriti.'
classical.quote: manō daśēndriyāṇyarthāḥ prakr̥tiścāṣṭadhātukī||17|| ... ēkaikādhikayuktāni khādīnāmindriyāṇi tu| pañca karmānumēyāni yēbhyō buddhiḥ pravartatē||24|| hastau pādau gudōpasthaṁ vāgindriyamathāpi ca| karmēndriyāṇi pañcaiva pādau gamanakarmaṇi||25||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 4-5; Sanskrit verse number not established
classical.establishes: Suśruta counts eleven indriyas including manas (ubhayātmaka), and derives them from ahaṃkāra in Sāṃkhya fashion. Caraka (Sū.8.4) instead calls manas atīndriya. The two texts differ on whether manas is an indriya.
classical.quote: The eleven organs of cognition, communication or sense perception have emanated from the co-operation of the aforesaid Vaikarika Ahamkara with the Taijasa or Rajasa. They are the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, speech, hands, genitals, anus, feet and the mind (Manah). Of these foregoing organs the first five are intellectual or sense organs (Vuddhi-Indriya); the next five being operative (Karma-Indriya). The mind (Manah) partakes of the character of both the intellectual and operative organs alike.

distinguishFrom.why: The seat (eye, ear, nose, tongue, skin) is a separate member of the pañca-pañcaka (Ca.Sū.8.10). The indriya is the inferred faculty; 'sense organ' names the seat.
The object (śabda etc.), the thing grasped, not the grasper.
The resulting cognition (Ca.Sū.8.12), momentary and determinative.
Caraka Sū.8.4: manas is atīndriya, beyond the indriyas; Suśruta Śā.1 counts it as the eleventh indriya. A lexicon must say which text it follows.

The fifth section of the Caraka Saṃhitā, on prognostic signs (ariṣṭa), takes its name from indriya in the sense of 'signs perceptible to the physician's senses'; Kaviratna (Sū.30): 'The fifth division, called Indriya, treats of the Senses in particular'. Not the sensory faculty doctrine.
The two classes of the ten; see their own records.

mistranslations.why: Universal and misleading: Ca.Sū.8.3 and 8.10 separate indriya from adhiṣṭhāna, and 8.14 says the indriya is anumāna-gamya (inferred). The organ is the seat, the indriya is the faculty. WHO's 'faculty' is the more careful choice.
Kaviratna's default. Adequate for the five jñānendriyas but makes nonsense of karmendriya ('sense of grasping') and of daśendriya.

mistranslations.rendering: organs of cognition, communication or sense perception
mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's triple hedge for eleven items including feet and genitals; 'communication' has no Sanskrit warrant.

openQuestions: Whether Caraka anywhere counts manas among the indriyas (Sū.8.4 says atīndriya; Śā.1.17 lists mano daśendriyāṇi separately), against Suśruta's eleven.
Whether Cakrapāṇi reads Sū.8.14 as bhautika origin of indriyas in deliberate opposition to Sāṃkhya.

classical.establishes: Here artha alone stands for indriyārtha, and the verse works through each of the five objects giving ati-, a- and mithyā-yoga (only the rūpa clause reproduced). Shows 'artha' is used elliptically for indriyārtha in the etiological context.
classical.quote: त्रीण्यायतनानीति- अर्थानां कर्मणः कालस्य चातियोगायोगमिथ्यायोगाः| तत्रातिप्रभावतां दृश्यानामतिमात्रं दर्शनमतियोगः, सर्वशोऽदर्शनमयोगः, अतिश्लिष्टातिविप्रकृष्टरौद्रभैरवाद्भुतद्विष्टबीभत्सनविकृतवित्रासनादिरूपदर्शनं मिथ्यायोगः;

classical.establishes: The five indriyārthas are the guṇas of the five mahābhūtas (śabda, sparśa, rūpa, rasa, gandha of ākāśa, vāyu, agni, ap, pṛthivī), which is why Sū.1.56 can list them as bhūta-guṇa. Kaviratna (his 34-35): 'The great primal elements are ether (space), air, fire (or light), water, and earth. Their (respective) attributes are sound, touch, form (vision), taste, and scent.' His footnote to Sū.1 (his 48, pp. 4-5) glosses artha, following the commentator, as 'the sensations, viz., vision, taste, touch, scent, and hearing', and matches each to one of 'the five elemental objective existences, viz., light, water, air, earth, and space': that phrase is his name for the bhūtas, not for the arthas.
classical.quote: mahābhūtāni khaṁ vāyuragnirāpaḥ kṣitistathā| śabdaḥ sparśaśca rūpaṁ ca rasō gandhaśca tadguṇāḥ||27||

distinguishFrom.why: The faculty that grasps; indriyārtha is what is grasped.
The objects of the mind (cintya, vicārya, ūhya, dhyeya, saṅkalpya; Ca.Śā.1.20; WHO ITA-1.9.3.3.7 'Objects of the mind'). Caraka keeps the two object-classes apart in Sū.8.5 (svārtha vs indriyārtha).
Artha is polysemous; Sū.11.37 uses bare artha for sense-object, while the same chapter's title (tisra eṣaṇā) and Sū.11.45 use artha for wealth/aims. Kaviratna renders artha 'properties' at Sū.1.49.
The Nyāya/Yoga word for the same five objects; Caraka uses viṣaya in Śā.1.23 ('jāyate viṣaye tatra yā buddhiḥ'). Treated as synonymous in textbooks.

In the Sāṃkhya 24-tattva scheme (Suśruta Śā.1; Kaviratna's footnote to Ca.Śā.1.17) the subtle sensibles are tanmātras, counted within the eightfold prakṛti, whereas Caraka's Śā.1.17 counts the five arthas among the sixteen vikāras. The two schemes place 'objects' on opposite sides of the prakṛti/vikāra line.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna, Su.Śā.1: 'subjects' in Edwardian English meant 'topics', and he lists the faculties (hearing, touch) where the Sanskrit has the objects.
Modern paraphrase; imports a physiological causal model (stimulus-response) absent from the sannikarṣa account.

openQuestions: Whether Cakrapāṇi at Sū.1.49 reads sārthā as 'together with the arthas' (objects) or as Kaviratna's 'properties/sensations'.

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's two departures from the Trikamji text at Ca.Sū. 26.11 are variants of his named base edition, not his own errors: Jivananda Vidyasagara's Calcutta Charaka (1877, p. 156) reads picchila-SARA-rasaguṇabahulāny āpyāni, which is his 'mobile', and lists only five effects (upakleda, sneha, bandha, viṣyanda, prahlāda) without mārdava, which is his five. Kaviratna himself names 'the Calcutta edition (of Pandit Jibananda)' as his text. What is his own is the silent omission of rasaguṇabahula, which he renders in all four parallel bhūta clauses. The commented reading remains rasa: Cakrapāṇi re-quotes 'rasaguṇabahulāni' in his gloss on this very passage.
classical.quote: Those that are principally liquid, oily, cold, mild, soft, unctious, and mobile, are regarded as appertaining to Water. These objects promote impurities, oiliness, numbness, stoppage of secretions, and cheerfulness and joy (in both body and mind).

classical.establishes: Sushruta's apya dravya profile at Su 41.4: ten gunas, sita, stimita, snigdha, manda, guru, sara, sandra, mrdu, picchila, rasabahula, which Bhishagratna renders one for one (cold, moist, glossy, devoid of keenness, takes time to be digested, mobile, compact, soft, slimy, sappy); sara ('mobile') is genuinely in Sushruta's list, unlike Caraka Su 26.11. Taste: predominantly madhura (madhura-rasa-prayam), with a slight (isat) kasaya, amla and lavana. Bhishagratna's 'largely endued with an acid, saline or sweet taste marked by a shade of astringent' moves amla and lavana into the dominant group; that regrouping is his, not the Sanskrit's.
classical.quote: A thing or substance, which is cold, moist, glossy, devoid of keenness, takes time to be digested, is mobile, compact, soft, slimy, sappy, and is largely endued with an acid, saline or sweet taste marked by a shade of astringent, is called a substance of dominant water (Apyam) principle.

distinguishFrom.why: jāṭharāgni is one member of the 13-fold set; agni is the whole category. WHO gives them separate term IDs (ITA-2.6.1 vs ITA-2.6.3).

Sushruta's own term for the digesting fire (Su.Sū.21), explicitly a variety of pitta seated between āmāśaya and pakvāśaya. Authors who treat jāṭharāgni and pācakāgni as one word are importing Charaka's framework into Sushruta's.

Grahaṇī is the anatomical seat, not the agent: Ca.Ci.15.56 'agnyadhiṣṭhānam annasya grahaṇād grahaṇī matā'. Kaviratna: 'The duct called Grahani is the seat of the digestive fire'. Confusing the two produces the common error of treating grahaṇī-roga as identical with mandāgni.
jāṭharāgni acts on ingested food in the gut; dhātvagni acts on already-formed tissue. Ca.Ci.15.39 makes jāṭharāgni causally prior, not identical.

mistranslations.why: Localises it to the stomach. The classical seat is the grahaṇī above the navel, at the āmāśaya-pakvāśaya junction (Ca.Ci.15.56; Su.Sū.21), which is duodenal rather than gastric.
A 19th-20th century equivalence (Bhishagratna's introduction already gestures at it) that cannot carry the doctrine of Ca.Ci.15.39, where jāṭharāgni governs the strength of all the other agnis.
Loses the gastrointestinal localisation that WHO's own gloss insists on ('Transformative factors in the gastrointestinal tract'). PMID 26283805's 'metabolic fire' has this problem.

openQuestions: Where does the compound jāṭharāgni first appear — Vāgbhaṭa, Cakrapāṇi, Śārṅgadhara, or later?
Is NAMASTE's जठराग्निविकारः spelling a deliberate variant or a data-entry slip?
Does any text localise jāṭharāgni to the stomach rather than the grahaṇī?

classical.establishes: Caraka excludes rasa alone from the physician's direct sensory examination of the patient (Vi 4/7: sarvān indriyārthān āturaśarīragatān parīkṣeta, anyatra rasajñānāt); the patient's mouth-taste (āturamukharasa) is to be learned by questioning him, because the physician cannot taste it himself. The 'tongue' in this passage is the physician's, not the patient's. It shows that Caraka's explicit tongue-related instruction here concerns taste, not inspection; it is NOT evidence that Caraka never inspected a patient's tongue, since the same aphorism orders colour and form of the body examined by eye and Vi 8/8 describes a fit student's tongue as thin, red and clear (tanu-rakta-viśada-jihva). The named eightfold jihvā-parīkṣā is Yogaratnakara's, but this passage does not prove its absence from Caraka.
classical.quote: Verily, the taste occurring in the body of the patient, though an object of sense, should be ascertained by Inference ; since, the ascertainment of this by the employment of the physician's own tongue cannot very well take place. Therefore, it is by questioning the patient that the taste of his mouth should be known.

distinguishFrom.why: In the Nirnaya Sagar Yogaratnakara a separate section on taste in the mouth (sweet in vāta, pungent in pitta, sweet-sour in kapha) immediately precedes jihvā-parīkṣā; Caraka likewise treats mouth-taste by questioning (Vi. 4/7).
WHO lists rasanā as a synonym of jihvā (the organ), but in the indriya context rasanendriya is the sense of taste, not the inspected organ.
Modern papers (e.g. 42142499) borrow TCM-derived indices such as the Winkel coating index; the Yogaratnakara's dosha-sign scheme is different and much shorter.
These are disorders or signs of the tongue, not the examination.

classical.establishes: Cakrapani's Ayurvedadipika on Ca.Sa.1.24 does not adjudicate between the two readings of ekaikadhikayuktani; it carries both. His literal gloss is the cumulative one that Kaviratna follows (ekaikena adhikena bhutena yuktani: each indriya yoked to one more mahabhuta than the last), and he then says the very same word hints (sucayati) at the doctrine that all five indriyas are pancabhautika with one element predominating in each, which is the reading carakasamhitaonline adopts. He further notes that against Samkhya, which makes the indriyas ahamkarika, their bhautikatva may be taken as real on a difference of doctrine or as figurative, the figure resting on which element predominates in what the indriya grasps.

classical.establishes: Suśruta's explicit two-class division of the ten indriyas, under the name buddhīndriya; the first retrieved passage in the Bṛhattrayī that names the class.
classical.quote: Of these foregoing organs the first five are intellectual or sense organs (Vuddhi-Indriya); the next five being operative (Karma-Indriya). ... Hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell respectively form the subjects of the five intellectual (Vuddhi) organs of man

distinguishFrom.why: The other five of the ten: faculties of action (speech, hands, feet, excretion, generation). Both classes are 'indriya'; English 'sense organ' fits only this class.

Suśruta's and the Sāṃkhya term for the same five. The Caraka passages retrieved use neither compound, only pañcendriyāṇi. A lexicon should record jñānendriya as the later/standard label, not as Caraka's.
Eye, ear, nose, tongue, skin are the seats; the jñānendriya is the inferred faculty (Ca.Sū.8.10, Śā.1.24).
Suśruta makes manas an eleventh indriya 'partaking of the character of both' classes; Caraka makes it atīndriya. Neither counts it a jñānendriya proper.

mistranslations.why: Names the adhiṣṭhāna, not the indriya; see indriya record. Kaviratna's footnote to Ca.Śā.1.17 even lists 'the entire skin' as the organ, which is the seat of sparśanendriya, not the faculty.
Bhishagratna's literalism for buddhīndriya. 'Intellectual' in modern English means something else entirely; the Sanskrit buddhi here means cognition.
Calque of jñāna-indriya found in popular writing; grammatical but opaque.

classical.establishes: Kāla heads the etiological triad. Kaviratna's footnote here: 'Time is of two kinds, viz., (1) that portion of eternity with which human life is concerned and which goes on ceaselessly, and (2) the age of man, that is, his infancy, youth, manhood, and decrepitude.' classical.verse: 42 (standard; Kaviratna's 42 spans this and the opening clause of 43)
classical.establishes: The etiological definition: kāla IS the year marked by cold, heat and rain (hemanta, grīṣma, varṣā); its ati-, a- and mithyā-yoga are excess, deficiency and reversal of a season's own character; and 'kāla is also called pariṇāma'. Kaviratna: 'Heat, cold, and rain, or autumn, summer, and rain, constitute the indications of the year. That is also called Time. When the particular indication of a particular period of Time manifests itself in excess, that is called excess of correlation in respect of Time ... When indications, that are the reverse of those which are normal, are manifested, that is called improper correlation (such as heat in winter or cold in summer). Time has another name, viz., [Parinama].' English at https://archive.org/stream/BIUSante_47357/BIUSante_47357_djvu.txt; 'Ratinanta' in the OCR is a scan error for Parinama.
classical.quote: शीतोष्णवर्षलक्षणाः पुनर्हेमन्तग्रीष्मवर्षाः संवत्सरः, स कालः| तत्रातिमात्रस्वलक्षणः कालः कालातियोगः, हीनस्वलक्षणः (कालः) कालायोगः, यथास्वलक्षणविपरीतलक्षणस्तु (कालः) कालमिथ्यायोगः| कालः पुनः परिणाम उच्यते||४२||

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's closing sentence at Su.Su.6.3 ('Some assert that the name is due to the fact that time blends (kalanam) all beings with misery or happiness according to their respective acts, or to its leading all beings to destruction') translates Dalhana's Nibandhasamgraha, not the translator's own speculation: Dalhana offers 'sankalayati sukhaduhkhabhyam bhutani yojayatiti va kalah' and 'athava kalayati mrtyusamipam nayatiti va kalah' as two of four alternative niruktis. Only the qualifier 'according to their respective acts' is Bhishagratna's addition; Dalhana's clause contains no karma word.
classical.quote: कालस्य निरुक्तिं कुर्वन्नाह,—स सूक्ष्मामित्यादि।—सः कालः, सूक्ष्मामपि स्तोकामपि, कलां भागम्, न लीयते गतिमत्त्वात् श्लिष्टो न भवति; अन्ये तु न लीयत इत्यत्र कलीयते इति पठन्ति। व्याख्यानयन्ति च—कलीयते संख्यायते इति कालः; निरुक्तिपक्षान्तरमाह, संकलयतीत्यादि।—संकलयति संहरणादेकराशीकरोति भूतानीति वा कालः, संकलयति सुखदुःखाभ्यां भूतानि योजयतीति वा कालः; कालयति संक्षिपतीति वा कालः, अथवा कालयति मृत्युसमीपं नयतीति वा कालः; अन्ये तु
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: The metrological division of kāla; note kalā (a sub-unit) is a different word from kāla and appears inside this list.
classical.quote: The Sun-god, by his peculiar motions, divides eternal time which is measured by years (Samvatsaras) into (increasingly progressive but smaller subdivisions) such as, Nimeshas (lit:—time taken in closing the eyelids), Kashthas, Kalas, Muhurtas, days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices, years and Yugas.

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Sū.11.42 says kāla is also called pariṇāma; in the triad of causes (11.43, Vi.6.6) the third cause is named pariṇāma. Textbooks sometimes render pariṇāma as 'transformation' (WHO ITA-4.4.9: 'transformation under the effect of time') and treat it as something other than kāla; the text equates them.

Season. Ca.Sū.11.42 defines etiological kāla by the seasons, so Charak Samhita Online's 'seasonal effects' is defensible there, but kāla as kāraṇa-dravya (Sū.1.48) and as Suśruta's eternal time are wider.

Kaviratna's footnote at Sū.1.54 makes age the second kind of time (avasthika kāla in later terminology, NIA SV0116). That division is commentarial/translatorial in the sources retrieved; not found in the verses quoted.
A time sub-unit (Suśruta Sū.6) and, separately, the seven kalās (membranes) of Su.Śā.4. Different word, short a.
NIA SK0090 includes 'time of the death'; Bhishagratna's etymology paragraph derives kāla from destroying beings. A secondary sense, not the etiological one.

mistranslations.why: Correct only for the Sū.11.42 definition; wrong for kāla as one of the nine dravyas and for Suśruta's beginningless time.

WHO ITA-4.4.9. Pariṇāma literally means transformation, but Ca.Sū.11.42 says 'kālaḥ punaḥ pariṇāma ucyate', so in this context the referent is time, and rendering it 'transformation' obscures the identity.
Bhishagratna's capitalised 'Eternal' personifies kāla beyond what 'anādimadhyanidhana' (without beginning, middle or end) says; acceptable but theological in tone.

openQuestions: Source of the nityaga/avasthika division within the Bṛhattrayī or its commentaries.
Whether Cakrapāṇi reads 'kālaḥ punaḥ pariṇāma ucyate' as identity or as kāla-in-its-effect.

classical.establishes: Kapha's functions are lubrication, healing, growth, tissue-building, strength and stability. Every one of them is constructive; none is pathological. This is the clearest single refutation of 'phlegm'.
classical.quote: The function of the five kinds of Shleshma is to lubricate the interior of the joints (Sandhi-Samshleshana), to contribute to the gloss of the body (Snehana), to aid in the formation of healthy granules in sores (Ropana), to add to the size of the body (Purana), to build fresh tissues (Vrimhana), to impart a pleasant or soothing sensation to the body (Tarpana), to increase its strength (Valakrit), and to give firmness to the limbs (Sthairya-krit), thereby contributing to the welfare of the body by supplying it with its watery element.

classical.establishes: The guṇas of kapha, and the normal/deranged taste shift that Ayurvedic diagnosis uses.
classical.quote: The Kapha is white, heavy, oily, slimy and cool. In its normal state, it is possessed of a sweet taste, which is followed by a saline one in its reactionary transformation (chemical reaction) when deranged or vitiated.

classical.verse: 61 (Kaviratna prints this as aphorism 80, evidently an OCR error for 60)
classical.establishes: The seven guṇas of kapha in lawfully quotable English. The printed aphorism number in this scan is corrupt and the verse number is inferred from sequence.
classical.quote: Heavy, cold, mild, watery, sweet, stable, and slimy, these attributes of phlegm are cured by objects having adverse attributes.

classical.establishes: Normal śleṣman is strength and is identified with ojas; vitiated śleṣman is called mala. The single most important verse for kapha, because it makes the normal/abnormal distinction constitutive of the term rather than incidental.
classical.quote: प्राकृतस्तु बलं श्लेष्मा विकृतो मल उच्यते| स चैवौजः स्मृतः काये स च पाप्मोपदिश्यते||११७|| / prākr̥tastu balaṁ ślēṣmā vikr̥tō mala ucyatē| sa caivaujaḥ smr̥taḥ kāyē sa ca pāpmōpadiśyatē||117||

distinguishFrom.why: Treated as a synonym by WHO ISTA (ITA-2.1.3.1 gives 'śleṣmā, kapha'). Sushruta uses śleṣman as the primary term and kapha as secondary; some scholastic traditions distinguish them by register rather than reference.

Charaka Sutrasthana 17/117 says normal śleṣman is ojas in the body, yet Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 defines ojas as the essence of all seven dhātus. The two texts do not agree, and the disagreement is unresolved.
Kleda is moisture as such; kledaka-kapha is one subtype (WHO ITA-2.1.3.3). Neither is kapha.
Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 lists rasa, rakta, māṃsa, medas etc. as dhātus, parallel to but distinct from the doṣas. Kapha-increase and medo-increase have different signs.
WHO ITA-2.8.5, 'Body constitution with a predominance of kapha'. Constitutional, not a current-state claim.
A visible secretion. Kapha includes synovial lubrication, tissue anabolism, immunity and patience (WHO ITA-2.1.3.8), none of which is sputum.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's rendering and the commonest. Assigns the doṣa the properties of one waste product; cannot carry vṛṃhaṇa (tissue building), ropaṇa (wound healing), balakṛt (strength) or kṣamā (patience).
Narrower still than 'phlegm' and equally unable to cover the anabolic and psychological functions.
Confuses doṣa with mahābhūta; WHO ISTA names earth and water together as predominant, not water alone.
Same category error in the other direction.
Popular-wellness framing that treats kapha as intrinsically undesirable, contradicting Charaka Sutrasthana 17/117, where normal śleṣman is strength and ojas.

openQuestions: The Charaka 17/117 identification of normal kapha with ojas versus the Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 definition of ojas as the essence of all dhātus is a genuine intertextual conflict; which reading the commentators (Chakrapani, Dalhana) take was not established here.
No kapha-specific peer-reviewed literature was located.

classical.establishes: The definition of kāraṇa in the ten factors to be examined before action: the agent, identified with hetu and kartā. Sanskrit as retrieved from https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Rogabhishagjitiya_Vimana&action=raw : तत्र कारणं नाम तद्यत्करोति, स एव हेतुः, स कर्ता||६९||. OCR 'Kdrana' corrected to Kārana.
classical.quote: Amongst these, Kārana is that which does an act. That, again, is (otherwise) called Hetu, as also Actor.

classical.establishes: The enumeration of the ten factors, with Kaviratna's bracketed renderings. Sanskrit: ज्ञात्वा हि कारण-करण-कार्ययोनि-कार्य-कार्यफलानुबन्ध-देश-काल-प्रवृत्त्युपायान् सम्यगभिनिर्वर्तमानः...||६८||. Kaviratna's printed 80 is twelve ahead of the standard 68 in this block (read, not computed; his legible 87 and 88 fall on standard 75 and 76 by content).
classical.quote: The actor, with unsurpassable intensity of resolution, should, for accomplishing it, set himself to achieve an act that is fraught with desirable results, being deeply engaged on it, and after having properly ascertained (Kārana) cause, (Karana) means, (Kāryya-yoni) springs of actions, (Kāryya) action, (Kāryya-phala) fruits of action, (Anubandha) adjuncts, (Deśa) place, (Kāla) time, (Pravritti) exertion and (Upāya) instruments.

classical.verse: Standard 8.84; Kaviratna's printed number illegible in OCR
classical.establishes: The medical application: kāraṇa = physician, karaṇa = medicine, kāryayoni = dhātuvaiṣamya, kārya = dhātusāmya. Sanskrit: इह कार्यप्राप्तौ कारणं भिषक्, करणं पुनर्भेषजं, कार्ययोनिर्धातुवैषम्यं, कार्यं धातुसाम्यं, कार्यफलं सुखावाप्तिः...||८४||. Kaviratna's '(material cause)' and 'or, rather, result of energy spent' are his glosses.
classical.quote: In this connection, the Kārana (cause) for the accomplishment of action is the physician. The Karana (or instrument) is medicine. The Kāryya-yoni (material cause) is absence of harmony, among the dhātus or constituent elements of the body. The Kāryya (action, or, rather, result of energy spent) is restoration of harmony among the dhātus.

classical.establishes: That Charaka sums up the six categories as kāraṇa (cause) and names dhātusāmya as the kārya. Sanskrit: इत्युक्तं कारणं कार्यं धातुसाम्यमिहोच्यते| धातुसाम्यक्रिया चोक्ता तन्त्रस्यास्य प्रयोजनम्||५३||. This is the textual basis for the NIA BP0178 remark that Ayurveda calls the padārthas 'kāraṇa'.
classical.quote: Thus is explained Cause as also Action or Effect. The restoration of the ingredient humours (of the human body) to their normal state will now be explained.

distinguishFrom.why: A different word with a short first vowel. Ca.Vi.8.70 defines karaṇa as what serves as upakaraṇa (means) for the agent; Vi.8.84 makes it the medicine while kāraṇa is the physician. Kaviratna: 'Kārana (cause)' vs 'Karana (means)'. WHO ITA-1.11.1 prints both as 'karana' in English. Roman-script sources without diacritics merge them.

Ca.Vi.8.69 identifies them ('sa eva hetuḥ'), but hetu is also the nidāna-sense cause of disease and the 'reason' in a syllogism (Vi.8.33 hetur nāmopalabdhikāraṇaṁ). Kaviratna elsewhere (Nidanasthana) lists 'Hetu, Nimitta, Āyatana, Kartri, Kārana, Pratyaya, Samutthāna' as synonyms of disease-cause.
Effect versus cause: Vi.8.72 kārya is what the agent sets out to accomplish; Su.1.53 kārya = dhātusāmya, kāraṇa = the six categories.

Su.1.53 and NIA BP0178 show Ayurveda calling the six categories collectively 'kāraṇa' (causes of dhātusāmya). So 'kāraṇa' can mean either the whole set of six or the agent/physician in the ten-factor list.
The Vaiśeṣika threefold analysis (WHO ITA-1.8.2.30-32). Ca.Su.1.51 uses only samavāyi: dravya is the samavāyi-kāraṇa. The three-fold scheme is not stated in the Charaka verses read.

mistranslations.why: Those render karaṇa. WHO ITA-1.11.2's 'the idea expressed by instrumental cause' for kāraṇa imports the karaṇa sense into the kāraṇa headword.
WHO ITA-1.8.2.29 writes 'doer (karma)'; the Sanskrit (Vi.8.69) has kartā. Karma is action, kartā is doer.
Kaviratna renders hetu as 'reason' in the debate context (Vi.8); kāraṇa in Vi.8.69 is the agent that acts, not an argument.

openQuestions: The task listed 'karana' without diacritics. This record treats it as kāraṇa and records karaṇa under distinguishFrom; if the lexicon wants a separate karaṇa entry, Ca.Vi.8.70 and 8.84, WHO ITA-1.11.3 and NIA BP0128/SK0099 are the anchors already retrieved.
Kaviratna's printed numbers for Vi.8.69-73 and 8.84 are OCR-garbled; a human should read the page images to confirm 81-85.
Chakrapāṇi on 'sa eva hetuḥ, sa kartā' not retrieved.

classical.establishes: The categorial definition of karma: cause of conjunction and disjunction, residing in dravya, the activity of what is to be done, needing nothing else. Sanskrit as retrieved from https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya&action=raw : संयोगे च विभागे च कारणं द्रव्यमाश्रितम्| कर्तव्यस्य क्रिया कर्म कर्म नान्यदपेक्षते||५२||. Kaviratna's 'independent of other action' renders 'nānyad apekṣate' (depends on nothing else); the Sanskrit does not say 'other action'.
classical.quote: That which is the cause of both Union and Separation, which inheres to the substance, and which represents that function which is to be, is (called) Action. Action is independent of other action.

classical.establishes: Karma contrasted with guna: 'prayatnādi karma ceṣṭitam ucyate' (activity beginning with effort). Sanskrit: ...गुणाः प्रोक्ताः प्रयत्नादि कर्म चेष्टितमुच्यते||४९||. '(of the mind in)' is Kaviratna's gloss.
classical.quote: ...are called attributes, while all functions such as (of the mind in) will, are called action.

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji / carakasamhitaonline) Su 1.28 through the first word of 1.29: 'sāmānyaṃ ca viśeṣaṃ ca guṇān dravyāṇi karma ca ||28|| samavāyaṃ ca ...'. Kaviratna prints '27' after 'operations,' (= Su 1.28) and '28' after 'immortal life' (= Su 1.29); 'as also compositions' is the opening of his 28 and of Su 1.29. Both numberings recorded; no conversion.
classical.establishes: Karma ('operations') as one of the six padārthas the ṛṣis beheld, named at the close of Su 1.28; samavāya ('compositions'), the sixth, is the first word of Su 1.29. Sanskrit: सामान्यं च विशेषं च गुणान् द्रव्याणि कर्म च||२८|| समवायं च तज्ज्ञात्वा ...||२९||.
classical.quote: Those great Rishis (then) beheld duly, with the eye of knowledge, similarities, dissimilarities, properties, objects, and operations, as also compositions.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: The six including karma, referred back to their Sutrasthana definitions; the Sanskrit order here (dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, samavāya) is the Vaiśeṣika order, unlike Su.1.28-29. Kaviratna's English for this sentence omits Karma.
classical.quote: द्रव्य-गुण-कर्म-सामान्य-विशेष-समवायाः स्वलक्षणैः श्लोकस्थाने पूर्वमुक्ताः||२९||
classical.translator: none quoted for the Sanskrit; Kaviratna for the English

Karma is the activity (kriyā); kārya is the result aimed at. Kaviratna's 'Action or Effect' at Su.1.53 for kārya blurs this.
Ca.Vi.8.77 (Kaviratna: 'It is also known by the names of Kriyā, Karma, Yatna, and Kāryya-samārambha') makes karma a synonym of pravṛtti in the ten-factor list, a different register from the padārtha.
Ca.Su.26.10 'karma pañcavidham' (see existing record karma-dravyaguna.json); therapeutic operations, not the category.
Ethical sense; irrelevant to the category.
Conjunction and disjunction are gunas in the parādi series (Kaviratna's 'union ... division' at Su.1.49); karma is their cause (Su.1.52), not identical with them.

mistranslations.why: WHO ITA-1.9.5.1 and NIA BP0129/DG0111 frame; Ca.Su.1.52 defines karma physically as cause of conjunction/disjunction residing in substance.
Kaviratna's word in the list; in modern English suggests surgery or procedures.
Popular English sense.
Kaviratna's rendering of 'karma nānyad apekṣate'; the Sanskrit says action requires nothing else (for being action), not that it is independent of other actions.

classical.establishes: The five karmendriyas and their functions: feet for locomotion, anus and genitals for discharge (visarga), hands for grasping and holding, tongue as the speech-faculty, with the ethical rider that true speech is light and false speech darkness. Kaviratna (his 32-33): 'The arms and legs, the anus, the organ of generation, and the tongue, are the five organs of action. The legs are used for locomotion. The anus and the genital organ are for the discharge of secretions. The two arms are for seizing and holding. The tongue is the organ of speech. It should be noted that that speech which is truthful is represented as light; while that speech which is false is represented as darkness.' English at https://archive.org/stream/BIUSante_47357/BIUSante_47357_djvu.txt. Caraka names the tongue (jihvā) as the seat of vāgindriya; WHO's list gives 'vak' and omits jihvā.
classical.quote: hastau pādau gudōpasthaṁ vāgindriyamathāpi ca| karmēndriyāṇi pañcaiva pādau gamanakarmaṇi||25|| pāyūpasthaṁ visargārthaṁ hastau grahaṇadhāraṇē| jihvā vāgindriyaṁ vāk ca satyā jyōtistamō'nr̥tā||26||

classical.quote: punaśca dhātubhēdēna caturviṁśatikaḥ smr̥taḥ| manō daśēndriyāṇyarthāḥ prakr̥tiścāṣṭadhātukī||17||

classical.establishes: Suśruta's list, in the order speech, hands, genitals, anus, feet, derived from ahaṃkāra. Bhishagratna renders the function of upastha as 'pleasure' where Caraka has visarga (discharge).
classical.quote: They are the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, speech, hands, genitals, anus, feet and the mind (Manah). Of these foregoing organs the first five are intellectual or sense organs (Vuddhi-Indriya); the next five being operative (Karma-Indriya). ... the faculty of speech, handling, pleasure, ejections or evacutation, locomotion successively belong to the (remaining) five operative (Karma-Indriya) ones.

distinguishFrom.why: The cognitive five. Both are indriyas; the division is by function (grasping objects vs acting).
Ca.Sū.11.39 defines karma as vāk-manaḥ-śarīra-pravṛtti, a different threefold scheme; the karmendriyas are the five Sāṃkhya organs of action, and the two are not the same taxonomy.
Hands and feet as karmendriya are faculties (indriya) inferred from action, on the same logic as Ca.Sū.8.14 and Śā.1.24; the limb is the adhiṣṭhāna.

The tongue is the seat of both rasanendriya (taste, a jñānendriya) and vāgindriya (speech, a karmendriya), Ca.Śā.1.26. One organ, two indriyas, which is itself an argument that indriya is not the organ.

mistranslations.why: Imports the motor/sensory neurology distinction; pāyu and upastha (excretion, generation) are not 'motor' in that sense, and 'organ' again names the seat.
Bhishagratna, Su.Śā.1. Caraka Śā.1.26 gives visarga (discharge) for both pāyu and upastha; 'pleasure' is the translator's substitution.
Oxymoronic in English; a sense does not act.

openQuestions: Why WHO ITA-3.10.2 lists the speech faculty as 'vak' without naming jihvā, when Ca.Śā.1.26 explicitly makes the tongue the vāgindriya.

classical.verse: Standard 8.72 (carakasamhitaonline numbering); Kaviratna's printed number OCR-garbled ('4), by sequence 84 between his legible 80 and 87
classical.establishes: The definition of kārya in the ten factors: that whose accomplishment the agent intends. Sanskrit as retrieved from https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Rogabhishagjitiya_Vimana&action=raw : कार्यं तु तद्यस्याभिनिर्वृत्तिमभिसन्धाय कर्ता प्रवर्तते||७२||. OCR 'KSryya' corrected to Kāryya.
classical.quote: Kāryya is that purpose for the achievement of which the actor moves.

classical.verse: Standard 8.84; Kaviratna's printed number illegible in OCR
classical.establishes: The medical identification: kārya = dhātusāmya. Sanskrit: ...कार्ययोनिर्धातुवैषम्यं, कार्यं धातुसाम्यं, कार्यफलं सुखावाप्तिः...||८४||. '(material cause)' and 'or, rather, result of energy spent' are Kaviratna's glosses.
classical.quote: The Kāryya-yoni (material cause) is absence of harmony, among the dhātus or constituent elements of the body. The Kāryya (action, or, rather, result of energy spent) is restoration of harmony among the dhātus.

classical.establishes: That the six categories are kāraṇa and dhātusāmya is kārya, the purpose (prayojana) of the science. Sanskrit: इत्युक्तं कारणं कार्यं धातुसाम्यमिहोच्यते| धातुसाम्यक्रिया चोक्ता तन्त्रस्यास्य प्रयोजनम्||५३||. Kaviratna's 'ingredient humours' renders dhātu.
classical.quote: Thus is explained Cause as also Action or Effect. The restoration of the ingredient humours (of the human body) to their normal state will now be explained. The modes of restoring the ingredient humours to their normal state have been said to be the object of this Science.

classical.verse: Standard 8.71 and 8.73; Kaviratna's numbers OCR-garbled, by sequence 83 and 85
classical.establishes: The neighbouring terms that bracket kārya: kāryayoni (what is transformed into the kārya) and kāryaphala (what the kārya is for). Sanskrit: कार्ययोनिस्तु सा या विक्रियमाणा कार्यत्वमापद्यते||७१|| ... कार्यफलं पुनस्तद्यत्प्रयोजना कार्याभिनिर्वृत्तिरिष्यते||७३||. The bracketed ellipsis skips the kārya definition (8.72) quoted separately.
classical.quote: Kāryya-yoni is that which, undergoing a modification, becomes developed into action. [...] Kāryya-phala, is that for the attainment of which the accomplishment is undertaken of an action.

distinguishFrom.why: Karma is the activity (Ca.Su.1.52 kriyā); kārya is what the activity is for (Vi.8.72) or its result (Vi.8.84 dhātusāmya). Rendering both as 'action' (carakasamhitaonline heading; Kaviratna's first choice) erases the distinction; Kaviratna's own correction 'or, rather, result of energy spent' restores it.
Vi.8.84: kārya = dhātusāmya, kāryaphala = sukhāvāpti (attainment of happiness). WHO: 'Treatment protocol' vs 'Immediate outcome, primary endpoint'. The state achieved versus the benefit it yields.
Vi.8.71/84: the material that is transformed into the kārya; medically dhātuvaiṣamya. Kaviratna's translator's note calls it 'material cause' (clay for the jar).
WHO ITA-1.9.3.7.1 and NIA DG0103: the manifest substances produced from the nine causal dravyas. A compound using kārya as 'effect/product', unrelated to the ten factors.
Ca.Su.1.53 calls dhātusāmya-kriyā the prayojana (purpose) of the tantra; kārya is the thing to be achieved, prayojana the purpose of the science. Overlapping but not identical.

mistranslations.why: Makes kārya = karma. Ca.Vi.8.84 identifies kārya with dhātusāmya, a state, not an act.
WHO ITA-1.11.5. Imposes a process reading; the Sanskrit at Vi.8.84 names the equilibrium itself.
Everyday meaning of the gerundive 'what is to be done'; the technical sense in Vi.8 is specific.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's printed numbers for Vi.8.71-73 and 8.84 need confirmation from page images.
Whether Sushruta or Vāgbhaṭa use kārya in the ten-factor sense was not checked.

classical.quote: Sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter, and astringent, these are regarded as the sixfold catalogue of tastes.

classical.verse: Standard 26.43 (final sub-section, ending ||४३||); Kaviratna prints 67 (merits) and 68 (effects of excess)
classical.establishes: Karma and guna of kashaya. Sanskrit as retrieved: कषायो रसः संशमनः सङ्ग्राही सन्धानकरः पीडनो रोपणः शोषणः स्तम्भनः श्लेष्मरक्तपित्तप्रशमनः शरीरक्लेदस्योपयोक्ता रूक्षः शीतोऽलघुश्च| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya). Kaviratna: 'restores harmony among the faults' = saṁśamana; 'heavy' = alaghu. His footnotes gloss Grahi/Samgrahi, Pidana ('akrishya-sankocha-kara', Gangadhara), Ropana ('Vranasya mangsadi-purana'), and quote U. C. Dutt on Stambhana; these are notes, not text. Excess effects (his 68) end: 'In consequence of its being rough, clear, and dry, it brings about Hemiplegia, Paralysis, Spasmodic contractions, facial paralysis, and other diseases of the kind that spring from excited wind.'
classical.quote: The Astringent Taste restores harmony among the faults. It restrains (the stools, urine, and other secretions). It draws in and contracts the limbs of the body. It causes sores and parts eaten away to heal or fill up. It dries up the fluids of the body. It retains or restrains all secretions. It alleviates phlegm and hemorrhages caused by excitement of the bile. It sucks up all phlegmonous and other secretions of the system. It is dry, cool, and heavy.

classical.establishes: Pañcabhautika constitution: vāyu + pṛthvī. Agrees with Bhishagratna's Sushruta ('earth and air').
classical.quote: From a preponderance of the attributes of Wind and Earth arises the taste called Astringent.

classical.verse: Standard number NOT established (taste-identification verses near chapter end); Kaviratna prints 35
classical.establishes: Charaka's perceptual test for kashaya.
classical.quote: That object which brings upon the tongue a sensation that is the very reverse of sliminess, as also of contraction and rigidity, and which seems to contract the throat also and stretch the heart, is to be known as possessing the Astringent taste.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's perceptual definition. Same page: 'An astringent taste is possessed of astringent, healing, styptic (Stambhana), purifying, liquefacient, drying and contracting virtues. It lessens secretions from mucous membranes.' and 'The specific properties of earth and air should be regarded as dominant in an astringent taste.' and 'An astringent taste should be considered as possessed of the same properties as the Vayu'. Note Bhishagratna's 'liquefacient' sits oddly beside 'drying'; check against Sanskrit before use.
classical.quote: A taste, which brings about the dryness of the mouth, numbs the palate, obstructs the throat, and gives rise to a drawing, pressing sensation in the region of the heart, is called astringent (Kashaya).

distinguishFrom.why: WHO BK0070 and wisdomlib (Yogasārasaṅgraha) record the pharmaceutical sense; context decides. Kaviratna in Su.4 appears to render the five kaṣāya-kalpanā as 'Astringents' (line not read in full; flagged).
WHO index 'kaṣāyavarṇaṁ'; also the monastic robe colour in Buddhist/Jain usage.
Homograph in religious literature (wisdomlib notes Jainism/Buddhism senses).
Lay speakers conflate bitter and astringent; Charaka separates them (tikta: 'pains it much and destroys its relish... dryness'; kashaya: 'contraction and rigidity').
These are karmas of kashaya (Ca.Su.26.43), not the taste; Bhishagratna's 'astringent... styptic' virtues illustrate the slide from taste to action.

mistranslations.why: Common lay error; kashaya is the astringent, mouth-drying taste.
In English pharmacology 'astringent' names an action; the rasa is a perception. Both Kaviratna and Bhishagratna use the one word for both.
Kaviratna's 'heavy' renders 'not light'; the Sanskrit avoids 'guru'. Sushruta (Bhishagratna) calls astringent 'light' - an inter-text tension hidden by the rendering.
Doctrinally odd next to 'drying'; probably his rendering of a Sanskrit term (kledana/vilekhana?) - unverified; do not record as doctrine.

openQuestions: Standard verse numbers for the Charaka taste-identification block and for Sushruta Su.42 passages.
Kaviratna's Su.4 use of 'Astringents' for kaṣāya-kalpanā (line 2297 of the OCR) should be read in full.
Which Sanskrit term Bhishagratna renders 'liquefacient'.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's recognition criterion for kaṭu. Same chapter: 'A pungent taste is largely possessed of attributes, which mark the elementary principles of air and fire.' and 'A pungent taste is endued with appetising, resolving (Pacana) and purifying properties in respect of ulcers etc.), and destroys obesity, languor, deranged Kapha and intestinal parasites.'
classical.quote: A taste, which produces a burning sensation at the tip of the tongue attended with a tingling of the part and headache, and is instantaneously followed by a running at the nose (fluent coryza) is called pungent (Katuka).

distinguishFrom.why: English 'acrid/bitter' glosses of kaṭu (and the Monier-Williams 'bitter, caustic as words') blur the two; Charaka and Sushruta list them as separate rasas with different bhautika composition (kaṭu: vāyu + agni; tikta: vāyu + ākāśa per Bhishagratna's Su. 42).
Kaṭu rasa is said to be uṣṇa in guṇa (Ca.Su. 26.43), but kaṭu is a taste and uṣṇa a potency; Charaka's own counter-examples in 26 show rasa and vīrya can diverge.

The post-digestive transformation also called kaṭu (Kaviratna: 'Of the Pungent, the Bitter, and the Astringent, the change, upon assimilation, is generally Pungent'); same word, different level of analysis.
WHO DG0115 sense 2 and Monier-Williams record kaṭu as a synonym of Picrorhiza and Brassica juncea; in materia medica contexts the word may be a drug name.

mistranslations.why: Lexical overlap in English; kaṭu is pungent/acrid, tikta is bitter; the two have opposite effects on agni and on fat.
Imports uṣṇa vīrya (potency) or a culinary category into a rasa; Charaka separates rasa from vīrya explicitly.

classical.establishes: The nyāya is named here in so many words, and Cakrapāṇi rules it of EQUAL FORCE (tulyabala) with khale-kapota, not inferior to it. He explicitly does not decide between them.
classical.quote: kedārīkulyānyāyas tu tulyabala eva khalekapotanyāyena yato yad uktaṃ vṛṣyaprabhāvaṃ prati tat kedārīkulyāpakṣe'pi prabhāvādeva śīghraṃ raktādidhātūnabhigamya śukraṃ janayiṣyati vṛṣyaṃ yathā khalekapotapakṣe'pi prabhavāditi

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi closes the discussion by declining to settle it: both positions are held by great authorities and are of equal cogency, neither is established, and nothing practical turns on the choice. Any presentation of these nyāyas as a settled classical doctrine misrepresents the source.
classical.quote: evamanayoḥ pakṣayormahājanādṛtatvena tulyanyāyatvena ca naikamapi niścitaṃ buddhivibhavānna pakṣabalābalam atra na kaścit kāryavirodha ityuparamyate

classical.establishes: Sushruta uses irrigation language for rasa's distribution, but does NOT name the nyāya. Secondary sources cite Su.Sū.14/10 with Dalhaṇa for it; the nyāya name is not in Bhishagratna's English.
classical.quote: The Rasa or the ​lymph chyle, thus flowing out of the heart, constantly soothes, maintains, and irrigates by transudation the body, and further contributes to its growth, and supports life

distinguishFrom.why: Kedārī-kulyā is a delivery mechanism with no selection: water goes where the channels go, and the nearest field fills first. Khale-kapota has each dhātu actively select its own nutrient. Teaching them as passive vs active transport captures this, but the classical contrast is about routing vs selection, not about membrane energetics.
Kedārī-kulyā leaves the dhātus distinct and nourishes them from a common supply; kṣīra-dadhi has each dhātu convert into the next.
Srotas are the channels themselves, an anatomical/physiological category. The nyāya is an explanatory simile about how nutrient moves through them.

mistranslations.why: A modern gloss taught alongside the simile, not a translation. Diffusion runs down a concentration gradient; the simile's point is gravity-fed sequential filling by proximity, which is a different mechanism.

mistranslations.rendering: Theory of irrigation canals as blood vessels
mistranslations.why: Over-literal. The simile is about the pattern of distribution, not an anatomical claim about vessels.

Sources disagree about which element of the simile is the reservoir. IJRAP makes kedārī the field and kulyā the canal; Charak Samhita Online makes kedarika the reservoir. Any rendering that fixes the roles is picking a side.

openQuestions: Whether kedārī denotes the field or the reservoir. Retrieved sources contradict each other, and the Sanskrit compound in Cakrapāṇi is not glossed in the passage retrieved.
The Dalhaṇa citation at Su.Sū.14/10 could not be verified; no retrievable Sanskrit Sushruta-with-Dalhaṇa text was located.

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi introduces the nyāya as the view of OTHERS (anye tv āhuḥ). The mechanism as he states it: the food-essence travels separately along each dhātu's own path; the fraction nourishing one dhātu has no contact with any other dhātu; the channels get progressively finer-mouthed and longer, which is why nourishment reaches the later dhātus later.
classical.quote: anye tv āhuḥ khalekapotanyāyenāyam annarasaḥ pṛthak pṛthag dhātumārge gataḥ san rasādīn poṣayati na tv asya dhātupoṣako rasabhāgo dhātvantareṇa samaṃ sambandham apyanubhavati rasādipoṣakāni srotāṃsyuttarottaraṃ sūkṣmamukhāni dīrghāṇi ca

classical.establishes: The clinical argument FOR this view: if rasa is vitiated, on the selective model only the affected nutrient fraction is spoiled, not every downstream dhātu. Cakrapāṇi uses it against the transformation view, on which all subsequent dhātus would necessarily be vitiated.
classical.quote: khalekapotapakṣe tu yaddhātupoṣako rasabhāgo duṣṭaḥ sa eva duṣyati na sarve taditareṣāmaduṣṭakāraṇatvāt

classical.establishes: The seven-fires doctrine in the mūla is the mechanism the nyāyas are trying to reconcile with the observed order of nourishment; it does not itself decide between them.
classical.quote: They who sustain the body, viz., the 'dhatus' (i. e., 'Rasa' or juice, blood, flesh, adeps, marrow, bones, and vital seed), are cooked by their seven respective fires.

distinguishFrom.why: Khale-kapota has each dhātu take what it needs from a common supply, with the poṣaka fractions travelling in separate channels and never mixing. Kedārī-kulyā has a single supply filling tissues in order of proximity. Cakrapāṇi treats them as of equal force.
On khale-kapota no dhātu turns into another; the dhātus are nourished in parallel from the common pool. The transformation view is exactly what Cakrapāṇi contrasts it with.
The fire acting within each dhātu, not the selection of what reaches it. Selection is about routing; agni is about conversion.
Āhāra-rasa is the common nutrient pool (the khala, the threshing floor) in the simile, not the theory.

mistranslations.why: A modern teaching gloss, not a translation. The simile's pigeons expend effort, but the classical point is selectivity and the separateness of each nutrient path, not ATP-dependent membrane transport.
Khala is a threshing floor or grain heap, not a dovecote. The pigeons come to the grain and leave; they do not live there.
Cakrapāṇi reports it as the view of others (anye tv āhuḥ) and declines to endorse either candidate.

openQuestions: Whether the name also occurs in Dalhaṇa on Sushruta, as secondary sources imply. Not verified; no retrievable Sanskrit Sushruta-with-Dalhaṇa text was found.

Whether the nearest-first ordering is intrinsic to this nyāya or borrowed into it from kedārī-kulyā. Cakrapāṇi's segment 21 derives the order from channel length and fineness, which is a third mechanism again.
