classical.establishes: THE locus classicus, and the ONLY mula-text occurrence of the word khavaiguṇya that I was able to verify anywhere. Of the aggravated doshas coursing through the body, disease arises at the place where they are arrested BECAUSE OF khavaiguṇya (defect of the kha, i.e. of the channel-space). This single verse is the entire textual basis of the concept; everything else in the literature is inference from it or from the sthana-samshraya stage of shatkriyakala.
classical.quote: भवति चात्र- कुपितानां हि दोषाणां शरीरे परिधावताम् | यत्र सङ्गः खवैगुण्याद्व्याधिस्तत्रोपजायते ||१०||

classical.establishes: The only lawfully quotable English of the locus classicus. It also demonstrates that Bhishagratna did not recognise khavaiguṇya as a term of art: he renders it as 'an obstruction in their natural passage', which reads it as a second description of saṅga rather than as its cause.
classical.quote: The deranged and aggravated humours, freely coursing through the body, give rise to a disease at the place in which they are incarcerated owing to an obstruction in their natural passage.

classical.verse: the shatkriyakala passage; sthana-samshraya is the fourth stage
classical.establishes: Where the concept operates in the six-stage model: sthana-samshraya, the lodgement of the disseminated doshas in a particular site. The secondary literature (IRJAY 2023, IJRAP 2020, IJFMR 2023, CSNE) is unanimous that khavaiguṇya is what determines WHERE lodgement occurs. I located the chapter and confirmed it contains the six-stage sequence, but I could NOT verify a verse number or obtain a clean verbatim sentence tying khavaiguṇya to it, and the word does not appear in the English I retrieved. Recorded as located, not quoted.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: The tradition orders them in time: khavaiguṇya is the pre-existing defect or susceptibility in the channel; srotoduṣṭi is the vitiation that then occurs there when dosha meets dushya. The CSNE article states this explicitly. WHO ISTA, by giving srotovaiguṇyam and srotoduṣṭihetuḥ the SAME English term, erases the distinction. A lexicon should preserve it and flag the WHO collision.

Treated as a synonym throughout the modern literature, and it is the form WHO standardised. But note it is srotovaiguṇya, not khavaiguṇya, that WHO carries — so the two words are not interchangeable at the level of a standards lookup even if they are in clinical usage.
The fourth stage of shatkriyakala, the EVENT of lodgement. khavaiguṇya is the pre-condition that determines where lodgement happens. Stage versus mechanism.
Defect in the reproductive seed or in a specific part of it, Charaka's mechanism for congenital disease. Reviews treat bija dushti as one CAUSE of khavaiguṇya, not as the same thing.

In Su.Su.24/10 saṅga is the arrest of the doshas and khavaiguṇya is its cause ('yatra saṅgaḥ khavaiguṇyāt'). They appear in one clause and are routinely collapsed — Bhishagratna himself collapses them.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's own rendering, and the reason English readers of Sushruta never encounter the term. It reads khavaiguṇya as a restatement of saṅga, whereas the ablative khavaiguṇyāt makes it the CAUSE of saṅga.

A Latin tag imported by twentieth-century Ayurvedic writers. It is a reasonable analogy but it is not a translation, it carries specific connotations from European pathology, and presenting it as an equivalent gives the concept a spurious biomedical pedigree.

One proposed subtype (IJRAP 2020) offered as the whole. The classical verse says nothing about heredity; the hereditary/congenital/acquired classification is explicitly labelled a hypothesis by its own author.

mistranslations.rendering: khavaigunya as a stage of shatkriyakala
mistranslations.why: It is not one of the six. The six are sanchaya, prakopa, prasara, sthanasamshraya, vyakti, bheda. Khavaiguṇya is the condition that makes the fourth possible.
Loses the channel reference. 'Kha' is the space or lumen of the srotas; the defect is in the channel-space, not in a tissue mass or an organ generally.

openQuestions: Whether khavaiguṇya occurs anywhere in the Charaka Samhita mula. I could not run an exhaustive negative check: the GRETIL Caraka e-text I searched covers only selected chapters. The dedicated reviews give no Charaka citation containing the word, which is suggestive but not proof.
Whether Dalhana's commentary on Su.Su.24/10 or on Su.Su.21 supplies the definition that the secondary literature attributes to him. This is the single highest-value next step.
Whether Chakrapani uses the term anywhere, and whether the equation of 'kha' with 'srotas' is his.
Whether the sirā/dhamanī-level defect and the dhatvagni-level defect are two distinct classical mechanisms or one.

classical.verse: 4 (standard/Trikamji numbering as printed on carakasamhitaonline, the whole prose unit is ||4||)
classical.establishes: The defining passage. Food yields two products: rasa 'called āhāra-prasāda' and kiṭṭa 'called mala'. From kiṭṭa are nourished sweat, urine, faeces, AND vāta, pitta, śleṣman, plus the secretions of ear, eye, nose, mouth, hair follicles and genitals, and hair, beard, body hair, nails. Kiṭṭa is thus the source-fraction; mala is its name/class; the doṣas themselves are listed among what kiṭṭa nourishes.
classical.quote: तत्राहारप्रसादाख्यो रसः किट्टं च मलाख्यमभिनिर्वर्तते| किट्टात् स्वेदमूत्रपुरीषवातपित्तश्लेष्माणः कर्णाक्षिनासिकास्यलोमकूपप्रजननमलाः केशश्मश्रुलोमनखादयश्चावयवाःपुष्यन्ति| / tatrāhāraprasādākhyō Rasaḥ kiṭṭaṁ ca malākhyamabhinirvartatē| kiṭṭāt svēdamūtrapurīṣavātaPittaślēṣmāṇaḥ karṇākṣināsikāsyalōmakūpaprajananamalāḥ kēśaśmaśrulōmanakhādayaścāvayavāḥ puṣyanti|
classical.translator: none quoted (Sanskrit mula only; site's English is CC BY-NC-SA and not reproduced)

classical.verse: 4 (standard); Kaviratna's printed aphorism numbers here are unreadable in OCR (the passage is bracketed by a '4', a '3' and another '4'), so his number is NOT established
classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of Su 28/4. 'Aharaprasdda' is an OCR artefact for Aharaprasada. Kaviratna renders kiṭṭa as 'Refuse ... dregs or dross' and the derived malas as 'excrements'. Note that he, like the Sanskrit, lists 'wind, bile, and phlegm' among the products of the Refuse.
classical.quote: From that, (viz., the food thus taken), arises a juice which is called Aharaprasdda or food-substance, as also a Refuse called dregs or dross. From the Refuse arise urine, sweat, faeces* wind, bile, and phlegm ; as also those excrements which have for their sources the ears and eyes and nose and mouth, the hair-cells of the body and the genital organs, and such limbs of the body as hair, beard, bristles, nails, &c.

classical.verse: 18-19 (standard, as printed on carakasamhitaonline); Kaviratna prints 17 and 18 for the same two units, i.e. one behind here
classical.establishes: Kiṭṭa is used at the dhātu level too: faeces and urine are the kiṭṭa of food; kapha of rasa; pitta of rakta; the orifice-wastes (khamala) of māṁsa; sweat of medas; hair of asthi; the unctuousness of eyes, faeces and skin of majjā. Verse 18 uses kiṭṭa and mala interchangeably within one line.
classical.quote: किट्टमन्नस्य विण्मूत्रं, रसस्य तु कफोऽसृजः| पित्तं, मांसस्य खमला, मलः स्वेदस्तु मेदसः||१८|| स्यात्किट्टं केशलोमास्थ्नो, मज्ज्ञः स्नेहोऽक्षिविट्त्वचाम्| प्रसादकिट्टे धातूनां पाकादेवंविधर्च्छतः ||१९|| / kiṭṭamannasya viṇmūtraṁ, rasasya tu kaphō'sr̥jaḥ| Pittaṁ, māṁsasya khamalā, malaḥ svēdastu mēdasaḥ||18|| syātkiṭṭaṁ kēśalōmāsthnō, majjñaḥ snēhō'kṣiviṭtvacām| prasādakiṭṭē dhātūnāṁ pākādēvaṁvidharcchataḥ ||19||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English of the dhātu-mala list. 'sweet' is a misprint/OCR error for 'sweat'; 'Prasfida' for Prasada. His 'that of the skin is the secretions flowing from the eyes' does not match the Sanskrit 'majjñaḥ snēhō'kṣiviṭtvacām' (the unctuousness of eyes, faeces and skin comes from majjā); flag before relying on his construal of verse 19.
classical.quote: That which Is called the ‘Kitta’ (refuse) of the food taken, consists of stools and urine ; the ‘Kitta’ of ‘Rasa is phlegm ; that of blood is bile ; that of flesh are the filths of the body, including the secretions (from the nose, the ears, &c.) ; while sweet forms the ‘Kitta’ of adeps, [17] The ‘Kitta’ of bones is hair (of the head and the body) ; that of marrow is the oily-substance in the body ; that of the skin is the secretions flowing from the eyes. From digestion (of the food eaten) thus arise, it is said, both ‘Prasfida’ and ‘Kitta’ of the ‘Dhatus.’ [18]

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa pairs kiṭṭa with sāra (not prasāda) for the two products of digested food, and specifies that the liquid (accha) kiṭṭa of food is urine and the solid (ghana) kiṭṭa is faeces — a distinction Charaka 28/4 does not make. Verse 64 then reverts to prasāda-kiṭṭau.
classical.quote: kiṭṭaṃ sāraś ca tat pakvam annaṃ saṃbhavati dvi-dhā | tatrācchaṃ kiṭṭam annasya mūtraṃ vidyād ghanam śakṛt || 61 || ... kaphaḥ pittaṃ malāḥ kheṣu prasvedo nakha-roma ca || 63 || sneho 'kṣi-tvag-viṣām ojo dhātūnāṃ krama-śo malāḥ | prasāda-kiṭṭau dhātūnāṃ pākād evaṃ dvi-dharcchataḥ || 64 ||
classical.translator: none (no public-domain English exists; Sanskrit only)

distinguishFrom.why: Charaka Su 28/4 makes kiṭṭa the waste FRACTION of digested food and mala the CLASS NAME ('kiṭṭaṁ ca malākhyam'); the malas (sweat, urine, faeces...) are nourished FROM kiṭṭa. WHO (ITA-2.4.1 vs 2.4.2) and NAMASTE (SAT-B.457 vs 458) keep two headwords but near-identical definitions, and Charaka Chi 15/18 itself uses the two words interchangeably, so the distinction is real but soft.
The complementary nutritive fraction. Charaka Su 28/4 says prasāda; Charaka Chi 15/15 says kiṭṭa-prasāda; Ashtanga Hridaya Sha 3/61 says sāra. Same pair, three labels.

Āma is incompletely digested food that has not undergone pāka; kiṭṭa is a normal product of completed pāka. WHO separately codes sāmamalaḥ (ITA-5.4.8) for waste associated with incomplete digestion, which is the pathological overlap of the two.
WHO ITA-2.4.6 'Metabolic waste'. In Charaka Chi 15/18-19 the dhātu-level wastes are also called kiṭṭa, so kiṭṭa is the broader word and dhātumala a subclass.

mistranslations.why: Popular rendering; no classical source calls kiṭṭa toxic. Charaka Su 28/4 says kiṭṭa nourishes (puṣyanti) the malas and, by Kaviratna's footnote, restores them to measure. 'Toxin' imports a modern biochemical claim and contradicts the nutritive verb.
Kaviratna reserves 'excrements' for the malas that arise FROM the Refuse; kiṭṭa is the pre-excretory fraction. Using 'excreta' for kiṭṭa collapses the source and its products.
Drops the primary sense: in Su 28/4 kiṭṭa is first the waste of FOOD digestion (āhāra), and only secondarily dhātu-level waste. WHO's 'either digestion or metabolism' is the more faithful comparator.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's printed aphorism number for Su 28/4 could not be read from OCR (the passage shows '4', then '3', then '4'); a human should check the page image (archive.org BIUSante_47357, scan p. 392-393).
Whether Chakrapāṇi treats 'kiṭṭaṁ ca malākhyam' as making kiṭṭa and mala synonyms or as naming a class was not checked; Kaviratna's footnote reads it the latter way.
Dalhana / Arunadatta on accha-kiṭṭa vs ghana-kiṭṭa (AH Sha 3/61) not checked.

classical.quote: The Kledakam:—The Kapham, even though principally located in the stomach, permeates its four other distant localities with its peculiar watery or humid essence in virtue of its inherent attributes.

classical.establishes: MAJOR FINDING: the word 'kledaka' does NOT occur here. The mūla identifies this kapha only by location (implicitly āmāśaya, from 21.12-13) and by function — 'anugrahaṃ karoti' to the remaining kapha seats by udaka-karma. classical.quote: स तत्रस्थ एव स्वशक्त्या शेषाणां श्लेष्मस्थानानां शरीरस्य चोदककर्मणाऽनुग्रहं करोति;

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa is where the NAME and the moistening function both come from: seated in āmāśaya, called kledaka FROM anna-saṅghāta-kledana (moistening the compacted food mass). Vāgbhaṭa moves the 'supports the other kapha seats' role to AVALAMBAKA (12.15-16a). Corroborated: PMID 40972327 cites 'Ashtanga Hridaya Sutra Sthana 12/16'.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: THE central confusion for this term, and it is a genuine textual conflict, not a reader's error. Suśruta gives the āmāśaya kapha the job of supporting the remaining kapha seats (Su.Sū. 21.14); Vāgbhaṭa gives that same job to avalambaka in the chest (AH Sū 12.15-16a) and gives the āmāśaya kapha the moistening job instead. So 'the kapha that supports the other kaphas' means kledaka in Suśruta and avalambaka in Vāgbhaṭa.

Kledana (moistening, liquefying) is not snehana/saṃśleṣa (unctuousness, binding, lubrication). PMID 42492167 glosses kledaka as 'food lubrication', which is śleṣaka's function applied to the wrong subtype.

Co-located in the āmāśaya and both act on ingested food, with opposite qualities. Kledaka prepares (moistens, loosens the bolus); pācaka transforms (cooks, splits sāra from kiṭṭa). Grahaṇī/agnimāndya discussions invoke both.

Āma is undigested/improperly processed residue, a pathological product. Kledaka is a physiological doṣa subtype. Excess kledaka is implicated in āma formation, but the two are not the same thing and English texts sometimes slide from one to the other.
Kleda is the watery waste/moisture as a substance; kledaka is the agent that produces the moistening. Same root, different grammatical role.

mistranslations.rendering: "gastric mucus" / "mucin" / "the mucous lining of the stomach"
mistranslations.why: A proposed correlate, not a meaning. Gastric mucus is protective; kledaka's classical role is preparative (loosening the bolus) and, in Suśruta, supportive of the other kapha seats. No paper has operationalised or measured the equation.
Published in PMID 42492167 and wrong. 'Lubricating kapha' is WHO ISTA's English term for ŚLEṢAKA (ITA-2.1.3.6). Using it for kledaka collides head-on with the standards terminology.

mistranslations.rendering: Citing Suśruta for 'kledaka moistens the food bolus'
mistranslations.why: Su.Sū. 21.14 does not say this, and does not use the word kledaka at all. The moistening function and the name are both Vāgbhaṭa's (AH Sū 12.16).

openQuestions: Does Dalhaṇa name the five kaphas in his gloss on Su.Sū. 21.14, and is he the proximate source of Bhishagratna's supplied section headings? This would settle how the names attached to Suśruta's unnamed passage.
Do any classical or commentarial sources attempt to reconcile the Suśruta/Vāgbhaṭa swap of the 'supports the other kaphas' function between kledaka and avalambaka?
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 carries any kledaka-kapha entry.

distinguishFrom.why: Koṣṭha is the site; agni is the transformative capacity. Mṛdu/krūra koṣṭha is classified by stool consistency and doṣa dominance, not by digestive power — though the NIA glossary entry for krūra koṣṭha does fold in 'irregular digestive ability', blurring the two.

Charaka lists mahāsrotas as a SYNONYM of koṣṭha (Sū. 11.48), which is why the two are interchangeable there — but mahāsrotas is also the name of a srotas, and srotas elsewhere is a distinct category from rogamārga.

These are parts of koṣṭha (āmapakvāśaya is one of its synonyms as a dvandva), not the whole. WHO ITA.3.11.1's description, which names only stomach and large intestine, effectively reduces koṣṭha to this pair.

Koṣṭha type (mṛdu/madhya/krūra) is doṣa-determined and is often called a constitutional feature, but it is assessed from present stool behaviour and can be altered; it is not the same as janma-prakṛti.
The viscera contained in the koṣṭha (WHO ITA.3.11.2), not the cavity itself.

mistranslations.why: The commonest single-word error. Koṣṭha's synonym list is a set of cavities and a body-region; āmāśaya alone is the stomach.
Narrower still, and drives a false equation of krūra koṣṭha with constipation as a bowel disease rather than a physiological type.

WHO's choice. It is a legitimate secondary sense, but a reader who meets koṣṭha first in CS Sū. 11.48 as the ābhyantara rogamārga and then looks it up in WHO will find only a description of stool frequency.
Confuses koṣṭha with agni; nothing in Sū. 11.48 mentions agni.

openQuestions: Does koṣṭha include the thoracic cavity? The NIA glossary says yes; WHO's 'mouth to anus' description says effectively no. Charaka's śarīramadhya is indeterminate on the point.
The primary classical locus for the mṛdu/madhyama/krūra triad — which text states it first, and in which verse. I located it in Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya via a secondary page but did not verify.
Whether any study has tested inter-rater agreement on koṣṭha classification, which is used to dose purgatives. None found.

classical.establishes: kṛcchrasādhya is the second sub-class of sādhya (curable), alongside sukhasādhya.
classical.quote: सुखसाध्यं मतं साध्यं कृच्छ्रसाध्यमथापि च| द्विविधं चाप्यसाध्यं स्याद्याप्यं यच्चानुपक्रमम् ||९||

classical.verse: standard 10/14-16 (Sanskrit; first and last confirmed independently: 14 begins 'निमित्तपूर्वरूपाणां', 16 ends 'कृच्छ्रसाध्यं द्विदोषजम्'). Kaviratna's block printed '8-11' covers 14-17 (his 11 includes the yāpya verse 17).
classical.establishes: The defining features of kṛcchrasādhya: moderate strength of cause/prodrome/symptoms; one of kāla, prakṛti, dūṣya shared with the dosha; in pregnant women, the old, children; not very complicated; requiring śastra/kṣāra/agni; not new; arising in a difficult place; single-pathway with incomplete four requisites, or two-pathway, not very old, dvidoṣaja.
classical.quote: निमित्तपूर्वरूपाणां रूपाणां मध्यमे बले| कालप्रकृतिदूष्याणां सामान्येऽन्यतमस्य च||१४|| गर्भिणीवृद्धबालानां नात्युपद्रवपीडितम्| शस्त्रक्षाराग्निकृत्यानामनवं कृच्छ्रदेशजम्||१५|| विद्यादेकपथं रोगं नातिपूर्णचतुष्पदम्| द्विपथं नातिकालं वा कृच्छ्रसाध्यं द्विदोषजम्||१६||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English of the kṛcchrasādhya criteria. Note divergences from the Sanskrit worth flagging: Kaviratna has 'elderly woman' where the Sanskrit has garbhiṇī (pregnant woman); he renders kṛcchradeśajam loosely ('affecting some vital limb or some joint ... only one part') and 'anavam' as 'chronic'. The final sentence is the yāpya verse (10/17) which he runs into this block.
classical.quote: The characteristics of diseases that are curable with difficulty are as follows : when the causes, premonitory indications, and present symptoms, are of force neither slight nor very grave ; when any of these, viz., the season of the disease, its nature, and the character of those ingredients of the body which are known by the name of Dushya, is sympathetic with the derangement that induces the disease ; when the disease appertains to an elderly woman, an old man, and an infant ; when the disease is not characterised by excessively violent symptoms ; when the disease is such that it should be treated with the aid of operations by (surgical) instruments, by caustic alkali, and by fire ; when the disease is chronic ; when the disease, affecting some vital limb or some joint of the body, affects only one part; when the four principal requisites of treatment are wanting in some particular and the disease affects two parts; when the disease is not very old; and lastly when the disease has been induced by a double derangement ; such diseases should be known as curable with difficulty. Even diseases that are incurable in consequence of the exhaustion of one's allotted period of life may be kept in a suppressed state by means of regulated diet and (proper) nursing.

classical.chapter: 35 (Bhishagratna ch. XXXV); Sanskrit verse number not established
classical.establishes: Sushruta's criterion for the hard-to-cure class: mixed features of the curable and incurable types.
classical.quote: A disease, which is marked by features other than those described above, should be regarded as incurable, while the one exhibiting traits common to both the abovesaid types, should be looked upon as extremely hard to cure.

distinguishFrom.why: Yāpya is a sub-class of ASĀDHYA (10/9): not curable, only maintainable. Kṛcchrasādhya is curable, with difficulty. Kaviratna's running of 10/17 into his kṛcchrasādhya block (his 8-11) makes this confusion easy.
The alpa/madhya/utkṛṣṭa grading is by the magnitude of MEANS required; kṛcchra/sukha is by the disease's features. They overlap but are distinct schemes in consecutive verses.
Several kṛcchrasādhya features (dvidoṣaja, needs śastra/kṣāra/agni, in the old or very young) are shared by yāpya and pratyākhyeya in greater degree; the gradation is by degree, not by kind.
Common modern synonym; not seen in Caraka 10 or WHO, which both use kṛcchra.

mistranslations.why: That is yāpya; kṛcchrasādhya diseases are expected to be cured.
The Sanskrit of 10/15 reads garbhiṇī-vṛddha-bālānām (pregnant women, the old, children); the translator's word is wrong, and should not be recorded as what the text says.
anavam means 'not new', i.e. not of recent onset; 'chronic' overstates duration, and Caraka reserves dīrghakālam avasthitam for yāpya (10/18).

openQuestions: Whether to record Kaviratna's grouping (10/17 within the kṛcchrasādhya block) as a reading or as an error; the Sanskrit yāpya verse begins 'śeṣatvād āyuṣo yāpyam asādhyam'.

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi names this position pariṇāma-pakṣa, NOT kṣīra-dadhi-nyāya, and raises an objection to it: on the transformation view an aphrodisiac would take a very long time to become śukra, yet milk and the like are seen to act as aphrodisiacs at once. CRITICAL: the string 'kṣīradadhi' does not occur anywhere in this commentary file.

classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi explicitly REFUTES the total-transformation view by reductio: if every part of a dhātu were transformed, three or four days of fasting would empty the body of rasa and kill it, and a month's fast would leave a body made entirely of śukra. This is the single most important and most often omitted fact about this nyāya.
classical.quote: eṣu ca pakṣeṣu sarvātmapariṇāmavādo viruddha eva yena sarvātmapariṇāme tricaturopavāsenaiva nīrasatvāccharīrasya maraṇaṃ syāt māsopavāse kevalaṃ śukramayaṃ śarīraṃ syāt
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: The transformation account, with a stated period, is reported in the mūla as one opinion among others.
classical.quote: Some are of opinion that the transformation (of one 'dhatu' into another) takes place in six days and nights.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Sushruta gives the one-month serial-transformation timetable, and Cakrapani quotes exactly this Sushruta passage in his commentary on Ca.Su.28.4 when setting out the transformation view. This is the textual basis MODERN writing invokes for the name ksira-dadhi-nyaya; Sushruta does not use that name and neither does Cakrapani when quoting him. Note Sushruta's timetable differs from the six days reported in Ca.Ci.15.
classical.quote: The Rasa is successively transformed into each of the six remaining fundamental principles of the body, and continues in the shape of each for the period of three thousand and fifteen kalas five days according to our modern computation . Thus the Rasa is converted into semen, or into the menstrual blood (ovum) in women, in the course of a month.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: Kṣīra-dadhi has the whole preceding dhātu convert into the next; khale-kapota has a common nutrient pool from which each dhātu draws its own fraction, with the dhātus never converting into one another. They are mutually exclusive as stated, which is why Cakrapāṇi weighs them against each other.

Kedārī-kulyā is about the route and order of delivery; kṣīra-dadhi is about the identity of the substance being nourished. Cakrapāṇi says kedārī-kulyā is of equal force with khale-kapota, and treats both as alternatives to the transformation view.
Pariṇāma is the doctrine; kṣīra-dadhi-nyāya is a later label naming it by its simile. Using the label where the sources say pariṇāma-pakṣa obscures that Cakrapāṇi argued against it.

mistranslations.rendering: milk to curd to butter to ghee
mistranslations.why: The name contains only kṣīra and dadhi. The extension to navanīta and ghṛta is a later elaboration, though WHO ISTA itself adopts it (ITA-2.6.19). Recording the four-stage version as 'the' simile misstates the compound.
'Law' implies a settled doctrine. In the commentary it is one contested pakṣa, and the strong form of it is refuted.
Cakrapāṇi reports and criticises this position; he does not hold it. Attributing it to him inverts the source.

openQuestions: Whether Dalhaṇa on Su.Sū.14 uses the name. No retrievable Sanskrit Sushruta-with-Dalhaṇa text was found.
Which timetable the lexicon should record: Sushruta's one month, or the six days reported in Ca.Ci.15.

nameAttestation.finding: The doctrine is classical. The name is not, so far as the retrievable corpus goes.
nameAttestation.detail: The four citations here document the DOCTRINE and not the NAME. Checked directly against GRETIL's Agnivesa Carakasamhita-parts with the Ayurvedadipika (328,448 characters, ed. Trikamji, Chaukhambha 1994, data entry Oliver Hellwig): ksiradadhi occurs ZERO times in any form, joined or hyphenated, and ksira and dadhi never fall within sixty characters of one another anywhere in the file. What Cakrapani does use, in his commentary on Ca.Su.28.4, is parinamapaksa and parinamavada for this position, and he reserves nyaya for its two RIVALS: khalekapota appears five times and kedarikulyanyayas once. The whole file contains only five nyaya compounds and none of them is ksiradadhi. So the passage supports the transformation doctrine under the name Cakrapani actually gives it, and the refutation was right that it does not support the term this record is filed under.

classical.establishes: Suśruta reporting the view of 'some' (kecid āhuḥ) at Su 42.7: within a two-fold Saumya/Āgneya division of the rasas, madhura, amla and lavaṇa are snigdha and guru, while kaṭu, tikta and kaṣāya are rūkṣa and laghu. Bhishagratna's 'According to certain authorities' marks the same framing. This is a cited opinion, not Suśruta's own siddhānta; in his own voice at 42.8 he assigns lāghava to kaṣāya (vāyu-samānayoni) and to kaṭu (pitta-samānayoni), and does not there list tikta. classical.establishes: THE CIRCULARITY, visible in one verse. The definiens is prādurbhūta-LAKṢAṆA, the manifested lakṣaṇa; the definiendum is liṅga; and the second half then declares lakṣaṇa a synonym of liṅga. If they were strictly synonymous the definition would say nothing. Retrieved and string-matched by me.

classical.establishes: The same word doing the same job one verse earlier: pūrvarūpa is the pre-manifestation lakṣaṇa of the disease. So in Ni. 1.8-9 lakṣaṇa is the GENUS of which pūrvarūpa and liṅga are the temporally-divided species — and is simultaneously listed as a synonym of one of the species.

classical.establishes: Two uses on one page. At 1.7 lakṣaṇa is a synonym of rūpa; in the chapter title Pañca Nidāna Lakṣaṇa it means the definition or characterisation of the five. The retrieved page prints both.

distinguishFrom.why: Declared anarthāntara at Ca. Ni. 1.9, yet liṅga is what one infers FROM (Kaviratna: root 'ligi', to go, hence to proceed to an inference) while lakṣaṇa is what one observes BY (root 'laksha', to see). Sign-as-evidence versus mark-as-criterion.
The headword of the pentad's third member in Vagbhata and Madhavakara. Lakṣaṇa is a synonym of it there, but lakṣaṇa alone carries the definitional sense that rūpa does not.

THE DISTINCTION THIS RECORD IS FOR. Across Sanskrit systematic literature lakṣaṇa means the defining characteristic, the definiens — as in Madhava Nidana's own chapter title. Reading every occurrence as 'symptom' mistranslates chapter headings and definitional passages throughout the corpus.
Not a contrast but a containment: Ca. Ni. 1.8 makes pūrvarūpa a KIND of lakṣaṇa (the pre-manifestation kind). A reader who treats lakṣaṇa as equal to liṅga will find Ni. 1.8 incoherent.
Kaviratna glosses cihna as 'literally a mark'. Closest to lakṣaṇa of the seven, and the pair is where an actual semantic distinction, if any survives, would have to be argued.

mistranslations.why: The default rendering and wrong wherever the word is doing definitional work, which includes Ca. Ni. 1.8, the definiens of Ca. Ni. 1.9, and the title of Madhava Nidana chapter 1. It also imports the modern sign/symptom split, which the Sanskrit does not make.
Better than 'symptom' but still one-sided: it renders the evidential half and drops the definitional half.
WHO's gloss, and the best of the short ones, but by placing lakṣaṇa inside the ITA-4.5.5 'Signs and symptoms' block WHO commits it to the clinical sense and makes the definitional sense uncodeable.
Seen in older translations influenced by pathological anatomy. A lakṣaṇa need not be structural at all.

openQuestions: Whether any classical commentator addresses the circularity of Ni. 1.8-9 directly, where lakṣaṇa is both the genus and a synonym of one species. Chakrapani is the place to look and I did not retrieve him.

Whether the definitional sense has ever been given a terminology code by anyone. WHO has not; I could not check NAMASTE (the terminologies path 302-redirects) and could not query ICD-11 TM2 (search endpoints returned 404).

Whether any Sanskrit lexicographic study treats the seven Ni. 1.9 synonyms as genuinely distinct. Kaviratna's footnote glosses six of them separately, which implies he thought so, but he does not argue it.

Modern literature: none found. I did not locate any peer-reviewed paper on the semantics of lakṣaṇa, and I did not run a dedicated PubMed query because the term is too ambiguous for a useful search. That is a gap in this record, honestly stated rather than filled.

distinguishFrom.why: The depleting half of the twofold scheme (WHO ITA-9.1.41); Vāgbhaṭa treats laṅghana as its synonym (AH Su.14.2), WHO keeps separate entries.
One of the ten laṅghanas (Ca.Su.22.18), not the whole; WHO ITA-9.1.47 'Therapeutic sustained hunger' is a separate entry.
Charaka counts the fourfold saṁśuddhi inside laṅghana (22.18); Vāgbhaṭa makes śodhana one of laṅghana's two divisions (AH Su.14.4).
Another of the six upakramas, defined by dryness and roughness (Ca.Su.22.10); Kaviratna notes its over- and under-dose signs are those of laṅghana.
Digestive drugs are one laṅghana method (22.18) and are paired with laṅghana in the recurrence verse (Ca.Su.16.20; AH Su.4.26).

mistranslations.why: Reduces ten methods (including exercise, sun, wind, purification) to one.
The defined aim is lāghava (lightness), the signs of success are elimination, appetite and mental clarity (22.34-35), not weight.
Only the four saṁśuddhis within laṅghana remove doṣa; the rest (thirst, wind, sun, pācana, fasting, exercise) do not expel anything.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's offset in Lesson XXII shifts from two behind (7-9 for 9-11) to aligned (18) to two behind again (32-33 for 34-35); the exact point of each shift was not mapped.
The 'ten laṅghanas' count depends on reading catuṣprakārā saṁśuddhi as four items; the Sanskrit of 22.18 does not enumerate them, so any list of the four is gloss (Kaviratna supplies one).

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji/carakasamhitaonline) 3.43-44; Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 59 (list of three) and 60-61 (explanation), his p. 490
classical.establishes: The locus classicus: laṅghana-pācana is the second of three grades of apatarpaṇa, indicated for doṣa of middling strength (madhyabala), between laṅghana alone (alpabala doṣa) and doṣāvasecana (bahudoṣa). The simile: a moderate body of water dried by sun and wind plus dust and ashes. Numbering note: Kaviratna's printed numbers here run 16 AHEAD of the standard numbering (his 59 = std 43; his 60-61 = std 44, one standard prose unit split across two of his paragraphs); both were read directly, not converted.
classical.quote: Sanskrit (carakasamhitaonline, v.43-44): अपतर्पणमपि च त्रिविधं- लङ्घनं, लङ्घनपाचनं, दोषावसेचनं चेति||४३|| तत्र लङ्घनमल्पबलदोषाणां , लङ्घनेन ह्यग्निमारुतवृद्ध्या वातातपपरीतमिवाल्पमुदकमल्पो दोषः प्रशोषमापद्यते; लङ्घनपाचने तु मध्यबलदोषाणां, लङ्घनपाचनाभ्यां हि सूर्यसन्तापमारुताभ्यां पांशुभस्मावकिरणैरिव चानतिबहूदकं मध्यबलो दोषः प्रशोषमापद्यते; बहुदोषाणां पुनर्दोषावसेचनमेव कार्यं, न ह्यभिन्ने केदारसेतौ पल्वलाप्रसेकोऽस्ति, तद्वद्दोषावसेचनम्||४४|| — Kaviratna (p. 490, numbers printed after each aphorism): "Apatarpana is of three kinds ; (1) Langhana, (2) Langhana-Pāchana, and (3) Doshāvasechana.59 Of these, Langhana is prescribable for faults slightly provoked. A fault slightly provoked and of little strength becomes dried up through the increase of the (digestive) fire and of the wind brought about by Langhana, even as a piece of shallow water is dried up by heat and wind.60 A fault that is provoked a little more than what would be called slight and that possesses middling strength, is dried up by (the administration of) both Langhana and Pāchana, even as a quantity of water that is not large is dried up by the wind and the hot rays of the sun as also by (clouds of) dust and ashes falling upon it.61"
classical.translator: Sanskrit: carakasamhitaonline.com; English: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna

classical.verse: Standard 16.20; Kaviratna's printed aphorism 17, his p. 181
classical.establishes: Doṣa subdued by laṅghana-pācana may flare up again, whereas doṣa removed by saṃśodhana do not recur: positions laṅghana-pācana as a palliative (non-evacuative) management relative to śodhana. Numbering note: Kaviratna's printed 17 = standard 20 (three behind in this chapter, read directly).
classical.quote: Sanskrit (carakasamhitaonline, v.20): दोषाः कदाचित् कुप्यन्ति जिता लङ्घनपाचनैः| जिताः संशोधनैर्ये तु न तेषां पुनरुद्भवः||२०|| — Kaviratna: "The faults of the system, if subjugated by fasts and Pāchanas, may reappear. If subjugated by correctives, they cannot reappear.17"
classical.translator: Sanskrit: carakasamhitaonline.com; English: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna

classical.verse: Standard 22.18; Kaviratna's printed aphorism 16, his p. 245
classical.establishes: Pācana is itself one of the ten laṅghana measures (pācanāni among the ten). So 'laṅghana-pācana' in Vi. 3.43 is not laṅghana plus something outside laṅghana, but a grade of laṅghana in which pācana drugs are added to the lighter measures; Kaviratna's footnote here glosses Pāchana as 'an infusion or decoction of various drugs which promotes digestion or brings bad humours into maturity'. Numbering note: Kaviratna's printed 16 = standard 18 (two behind here, read directly).
classical.quote: Sanskrit (carakasamhitaonline, v.18): चतुष्प्रकारा संशुद्धिः पिपासा मारुतातपौ। पाचनान्युपवासश्च व्यायामश्चेति लङ्घनम्॥१८॥ — Kaviratna: "The four kinds of corrective processes (viz., administration of emetics, of purgatives, of errhines or cerebral purgatives, and dry enemata), as also bearing thirst and wind and the heat of the Sun, drinking the medicines called Pāchana, fast, and physical exercise,—these are all included under Langhana.16"
classical.translator: Sanskrit: carakasamhitaonline.com; English: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna

classical.verse: Standard 22.20-21; Kaviratna's printed '18-19' (read from the archive.org OCR text, not from the page image)
classical.establishes: The indication for pācana within the laṅghana scheme: diseases of middling strength (madhyabala) arising from kapha and pitta are to be treated first with pācana. This is the Sutrasthana counterpart of Vi. 3.44's 'madhyabala' indication for laṅghana-pācana.
classical.quote: Sanskrit (carakasamhitaonline, v.20-21): येषां मध्यबला रोगाः कफपित्तसमुत्थिताः। वम्यतीसारहृद्रोगविसूच्यलसकज्वराः॥२०॥ विबन्धगौरवोद्गारहृल्लासारोचकादयः। पाचनैस्तान् भिषक् प्राज्ञः प्रायेणादावुपाचरेत्॥२१॥ — Kaviratna (OCR): "...such as vomiting, diarrhoea, thoracic diseases, choleraic diarrhoea, tympanites, fever, suppression of stools and urine, heaviness of the limbs, eructations, hiccup, nausea or disgust for food; and other diseases of the kind, are generally treated at the outset, by the wise physician, with the aid of Pachana.18-19"
classical.translator: Sanskrit: carakasamhitaonline.com; English: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorism 74, his p. 1421. Standard verse number NOT established: carakasamhitaonline was unreachable (database error) and easyayurveda groups the passage as verses 73-76 without a one-to-one mapping.
classical.establishes: Clinical application in grahaṇī: when āma has spread systemically (as opposed to adhering in the pakvāśaya, which gets dīpana, or lodged in the āmāśaya, which gets emesis), the indicated management is laṅghana plus pācana. Shows the pair is the standard answer to systemic sāma states.
classical.quote: Kaviratna: "When the 'āma Rasa' (i.e., the undigested juice of the food taken) spreads over the whole body, fasting and the administration of 'Pāchana' (i.e., drugs which assist in digesting undigested food, without increasing the appetite) are prescribable. 74"

classical.verse: Verse number not given by Bhishagratna; not established from a Sanskrit edition
classical.establishes: Sushruta pairs fasting with pācana (and dīpana) as the treatment of a sāma-type presentation (heaviness, anorexia, nausea, fever) in a specific disease, but does not use laṅghana-pācana as a named grade of therapy as Charaka does. Bhishagratna prints no Sanskrit verse numbers.
classical.quote: "Fastings and employment of digestive (Pacana) and appetising (Dipaniya) remedies should be the medical treatment in cases of Pinasa (nasal catarrh) accompanied by such distressing symptoms as vomiting, aching, heaviness in the limbs, feverishness, non-relish for food, apathy, and Atisara (diarrhea)."

distinguishFrom.why: Laṅghana alone is the first grade of apatarpaṇa, for alpabala doṣa (Ca.Vi. 3.44). Laṅghana-pācana adds pācana drugs for madhyabala doṣa. Confusing the two collapses Charaka's three-grade scheme. Note also that laṅghana is not only fasting: Ca.Su. 22.18 lists ten laṅghana measures, of which upavāsa is one and pācana another.

Third grade of apatarpaṇa, for bahudoṣa. Ca.Su. 16.20 explicitly contrasts the two: doṣa subdued by laṅghana-pācana may recur, those evacuated by saṃśodhana do not. Laṅghana-pācana is therefore a non-evacuative (śamana-type) management.

WHO ISTA ITA-6.2.6.7 vs 6.2.6.8: dīpana kindles agni without acting directly on āma; pācana acts directly on āma without kindling agni. Kaviratna's notes make the same distinction ('drugs which assist in digesting undigested food, without increasing the appetite'). Many drugs are both (dīpana-pācana), but the therapeutic grade 'laṅghana-pācana' is named for the pācana action, and Ca.Ci. 15 (Kaviratna 74-75) sequences pācana during the sāma phase and dīpana afterwards.

A drug/action term (digestion of āma) rather than a grade of therapy. Laṅghana-pācana is the regimen (lightening measures plus pācana drugs) in which āma-pācana is the intended pharmacological effect. Modern reviews often use the two interchangeably.
Upavāsa is one of the ten laṅghana measures (Ca.Su. 22.18), not a synonym of laṅghana. 'Upavasa plus Pachana' (Rajani 2010) is one concrete instantiation of laṅghana-pācana, not the definition of it.

WHO ISTA also lists pācanam as a method of haemostasis by chemical cautery (ITA-9.6.109), vraṇapācanakarma as induction of suppuration (ITA-9.6.127) and pācanakarma as removal of a foreign body by suppuration (ITA-9.6.205), plus cooking-process senses (ITA-8.3.2, 8.3.3). None of these is the pācana of laṅghana-pācana.
The genus. Apatarpaṇa (depletion) is threefold: laṅghana, laṅghana-pācana, doṣāvasecana (Ca.Vi. 3.43). Laṅghana-pācana is one species of it, not a synonym.

mistranslations.why: Reduces laṅghana to upavāsa, which is only one of its ten measures (Ca.Su. 22.18), and reads pācana as the physiological process of digestion rather than the class of drugs/measures that ripen āma. Kaviratna himself uses 'fasts and Pāchanas' at Su.16 but warns elsewhere that laṅghana 'does not mean fast only'.

Marketing gloss. Laṅghana-pācana is defined by Charaka as the non-evacuative grade; it is specifically the grade that does NOT remove doṣa from the body (Ca.Su. 16.20), so 'detox' inverts its position relative to doṣāvasecana.

Over-reads laṅghana as deprivation; the classical criterion is laghutā (lightness) and the measures include exercise, sun, wind and pācana drugs. Also carries a connotation of harm that the text guards against (Ca.Su. 22 lists signs of excessive laṅghana).

'Carminative' (relieving flatulence) is a pharmacological subset at best; pācana is defined by its action on āma (WHO ITA-6.2.6.8; Kaviratna's notes 'brings bad humours into maturity'). Kaviratna's and carakasamhitaonline's use of 'carminative' is a convenience, not a definition.
Modern biomedical substitution; pācana drugs in the classics are hot, light, dry herbal decoctions and powders (e.g. Shunthi in Rajani 2010), chosen for their action on āma, not enzyme preparations.

Too broad: the classical indication is doṣa of middling strength (madhyabala, Ca.Vi. 3.44; Ca.Su. 22.20-21), and the carakasamhitaonline gloss 'digestion of ama dosha' is an interpretive addition. Sāma states with bahudoṣa go to śodhana, and with alpabala doṣa to laṅghana alone.

classical.establishes: Lavaṇa is the third of Atreya's six rasas. Kaviratna: 'They are sweet, sour, saltish, pungent, bitter, and astringent.'
classical.quote: षडेव रसा इत्युवाच भगवानात्रेयः पुनर्वसुः, मधुराम्ललवणकटुतिक्तकषायाः|

classical.verse: 43 sub-paragraph (3) standard; Kaviratna prints 61 after the actions and 62 (inferred from sequence, OCR unclear) after the excess-effects
classical.establishes: Actions of lavaṇa and its guṇas (not excessively guru, snigdha, uṣṇa). Kaviratna: 'The Saline Taste digests (the bad humours), generates impurities, promotes the appetite, expels stools, cuts away and removes by force (adherent phlegm and other humours), and purges the intestines after making the stools watery. ... It overwhelms all other Tastes. ... It is heavy, oily, and warm, but not excessively so.' His footnote admits 'There are many words in this aphorism that are, rather, of doubtful import.'
classical.quote: लवणो रसः पाचनः क्लेदनो दीपनश्च्यावनश्छेदनो भेदनस्तीक्ष्णः सरो विकास्यधःस्रंस्यवकाशकरो वातहरः स्तम्भबन्धसङ्घातविधमनः सर्वरसप्रत्यनीकभूतः, ... नात्यर्थं गुरुः स्निग्ध उष्णश्च|

classical.establishes: Sushruta's recognition criterion. Same chapter: 'A saline taste is mostly endued with attributes which characterise the elements of water and fire.' and 'A saline taste is possessed of corrective (purgative and emetic) virtues, favours the processes of suppuration and spontaneous bursting of swellings, brings about the looseness or resolution of any affected part (ulcer), is heat-engendering in its property and proves incompatible with all other tastes.'
classical.quote: A taste, which imparts a greater relish to food, produces salivation and softness of a part, is called saline (Lavana).

distinguishFrom.term: lavaṇa (salt, the substance) and lavaṇa varga
distinguishFrom.why: WHO splits DG0146 (taste) from DG0147 (salt). Charaka's exceptions make the point: 'Rock-salt, though saline in taste, is not of heating energy' (Kaviratna, standard 26.42 region), so a salt need not carry the rasa's typical vīrya.
Ca.Su. 26.9 explicitly denies kṣāra the status of a rasa ('क्षरणात् क्षारः, नासौ रसः'); it is a substance, chiefly kaṭu-lavaṇa, not a seventh taste (Nimi's view, rejected).
Both are uṣṇa and vāta-pacifying and often paired; Sushruta assigns amla to pṛthvī + agni and lavaṇa to jala + agni.

mistranslations.why: Modern clinical papers read lavaṇa as dietary sodium; the rasa is a sensory-pharmacological category covering several salts and non-salt substances.

renderings.sourceName: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda (WHO, 2022)
renderings.assessment: Verified absence, not an assumption. I searched the full extracted text of the WHO document for 'sāmya', 'loka', 'macrocosm' and 'microcosm': the only sāmya entry is dhātusāmyam, 'microcosm' occurs once and only inside the description of caturviṃśati-puruṣaḥ (ITA-1.9.3.2.12, glossing avyakta as 'unmanifested microcosm'), and there is no loka entry at all. The doctrine has no WHO term ID.

renderings.english: The human body is an epitome of the universe. It is in every respect a microcosm. Everything existing in the macrocosm is shown to exist in this microcosm.

classical.establishes: The actual textual basis of the doctrine: Punarvasu Atreya says 'this puruṣa is lokasammita' (commensurate with / measured by the loka). Note what this verse does NOT contain: the word sāmya, and the compound loka-puruṣa-sāmya. The text says lokasammita.
classical.quote: 'पुरुषोऽयं लोकसम्मितः' इत्युवाच भगवान् पुनर्वसुरात्रेयः|

classical.establishes: The substantive ground of the comparison: the same six dhatus, aggregated, receive the name loka and equally the name puruṣa. The correspondence is asserted at the level of constituents before any of the deity-faculty correlations that follow.
classical.quote: षड्धातवः समुदिताः 'लोक' इति शब्दं लभन्ते; तद्यथा- पृथिव्यापस्तेजो वायुराकाशं ब्रह्म चाव्यक्तमिति, एत एव चषड्धातवः समुदिताः 'पुरुष' इति शब्दं लभन्ते||४||

classical.verse: unnumbered in Kaviratna's text at this point, printed p. 764, immediately after his aphorisms 1-2
classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of the doctrine's founding statement, including the bidirectionality (universe to puruṣa AND puruṣa to universe) that modern one-directional 'man is a miniature universe' paraphrases lose. Kaviratna prints no aphorism number on this passage; the next numbered marker in his text is 4.
classical.quote: Purusha  is  like  unto  the  Universe.  As  many  particular  entities  endued  with  form  occur  in  the  Universe,  so  many  occur  in  Purusha.  As  many  occur  in  Purusha  so  many  occur  in  the  Universe.

classical.establishes: Quotable English for the six-dhatu correspondence and its item-by-item mapping onto the body. It matches the Devanagari of Sha 5.4 retrieved separately, which is the check that the two citations are the same verse. The 'f' and hyphenation artefacts are OCR.
classical.quote: The  universe  is  made  of  six  ingredients.  This  is  what  is  generally  heard.f  They  are  as  follows:  Earth,  Water,  Heat,  Air,  Ether  (or  Space),  and  Brahma  which  is  unmanifest.  Purusha  is  made  up  of  six  ingredients.  This  is  what  is  gene¬  rally  heard.  Of  that  Purusha,  the  form  is  Earth  ;  the  liquid  secre¬  tions  are  Water  ;  the  animal  heat  is  Heat ;  the  life-breaths  are  Air  ;  the  hollow  places  are  Ether  (or  Space) ;  and  the  Inner  Self  is  Brahma.4

classical.establishes: That the correspondence is extended beyond material constituents to deity-faculty pairs (Prajapati/mind, Indra/consciousness, Aditya/adana, Rudra/wrath, Soma/satisfaction, Vasus/pleasure). The ellipsis marks a parenthetical gloss omitted from the middle of the passage; everything on either side is verbatim. Relevant because modern 'ecological' readings of the doctrine usually drop this half entirely.
classical.quote: Verily,  as  there  is  in  the  universe  the  manifestation  of  Brahma,  so  there  is  in  Purusha  also  the  manifestation  of  the  Inner  Self.  In  the  universe  the  manifestation  of  Brahma  is  Prajapati  ... In  Purusha  the  manifestation  of  the-  Inner  Self  is  the  Mind.  He  who  is  Indra  in  the  universe  is  Consciousness  in  Purusha.

classical.establishes: Sushruta is frequently cited for a parallel loka-puruṣa statement. I identified the chapter but did NOT retrieve a passage in it making the correspondence claim, so no quotation is recorded and this reference is location-only. A human must verify before any Sushruta parallel is asserted.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: The word Charaka actually uses at Sha 5.3. Sammita means commensurate with, measured by, of the same measure. Sāmya means equality or balance. The doctrinal name in circulation is not the text's word, and this is the single most important thing this record establishes.
The like-increases-like principle of Su 1.44-45. It is the mechanism by which the correspondence has therapeutic consequences, but it is a separate doctrine with its own verses.
The only sāmya compound WHO codes. It means equilibrium of the bodily constituents and has nothing to do with the loka correspondence, but the shared word invites confusion.
The five-element theory. Charaka Sha 5.4 uses SIX dhatus (the five plus unmanifest brahman), not five, and the sixth is what makes the loka/puruṣa identity of names possible.
The Rgvedic hymn of the cosmic person from whom the world is made. That is a creation account running world-from-person; Charaka Sha 5 is a structural comparison running both ways.

mistranslations.why: One-directional and quantitative. Kaviratna's text states the correspondence in both directions in consecutive sentences, and 'miniature' adds a scale claim the Sanskrit (sammita, commensurate) does not make.

mistranslations.rendering: as is the macrocosm, so is the microcosm
mistranslations.why: Recorded because Kaviratna's own footnote introduced the microcosm/macrocosm vocabulary into English, but it is Greek-derived and imports Hermetic associations. The text's vocabulary is loka and puruṣa.
Identity, where the text asserts commensurability. Sha 5.4 says the same six dhatus 'receive the name' loka and 'receive the name' puruṣa, which is co-constitution, not identity.

A modern recruitment. The chapter's correspondences are largely deity-faculty and constituent pairs; the ecological reading is imported from outside and should be recorded as a modern claim, not as the doctrine.

openQuestions: Whether the compound loka-puruṣa-sāmya occurs in Charaka at all, or whether it is entirely a post-classical doctrinal label built from lokasammita. I retrieved the Devanagari of Sha 5.3 and 5.4 and the word sāmya is in neither. This should be settled against a full Sanskrit corpus search, which I could not run: GRETIL's Charaka file covers only Sutrasthana 1, 12, 26-28 and a few other blocks and does not include Sharirasthana 5.
Whether Sushruta states a parallel. Sharirasthana 5 is commonly cited for it; I located the chapter and did not find the claim, so the citation is recorded as located-only.

The Devanagari form लोकपुरुषसाम्यम् recorded above is the standard modern spelling of the doctrinal label, not a form retrieved from a classical text. It should be treated as the name of the doctrine, not as an attested textual word.

classical.establishes: Actions of madhura and its guṇas (snigdha, śīta, guru). Kaviratna: 'the Taste that is Sweet, in consequence of its being well-adapted to the body, increases the juices, blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, Ojas, and vital seed. ... It is exceedingly liked by bees and ants. It is oily, cool, and heavy.' Excess: 'generates corpulency, softness of the body, idleness or aversion to labour, excessive sleep, heaviness ... and such other diseases as are born of (the excitement of) the Phlegm.'
classical.quote: तत्र, मधुरो रसः शरीरसात्म्याद्रसरुधिरमांसमेदोस्थिमज्जौजःशुक्राभिवर्धन आयुष्यः षडिन्द्रियप्रसादनो बलवर्णकरः पित्तविषमारुतघ्नस्तृष्णादाहप्रशमनस्त्वच्यः केश्यः कण्ठ्यो बल्यः प्रीणनो जीवनस्तर्पणो बृंहणः स्थैर्यकरः क्षीणक्षतसन्धानकरो ... स्निग्धः शीतो गुरुश्च|

classical.verse: 61 (standard; Kaviratna's printed number read as 60 by sequence, OCR shows '80')
classical.establishes: Madhura listed among the attributes of kapha. Kaviratna: 'Heavy, cold, mild, watery, sweet, stable, and slimy, these attributes of phlegm are cured by objects having adverse attributes.' Note his 'watery' for snigdha and 'mild' for mṛdu.
classical.quote: गुरुशीतमृदुस्निग्धमधुरस्थिरपिच्छिलाः| श्लेष्मणः प्रशमं यान्ति विपरीतगुणैर्गुणाः||६१||

classical.establishes: Sushruta's recognition criterion. Same chapter: 'A sweet taste is largely endued with attributes which specifically appertain to the material principles of earth and water.' and 'the sweet taste is possessed of the virtue of increasing the quantity of lymph-chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone marrow, albumen (ojas), semen, and milk in a parturient woman.' (Wikisource scan prints 'Kapham'.)
classical.quote: A taste, which is pleasant, proves comfortable to, and contributes to the life-preservation of a man, keeps his mouth moist, and increases the quantity of bodily Kapha, is called Sweet (Madhura).

distinguishFrom.why: Post-digestive 'sweet' (Kaviratna: 'The Sweet and the Saline change into the Sweet') is a different level from madhura rasa; lavaṇa is madhura in vipāka but not in rasa.

distinguishFrom.term: madhu (honey) and madhura as plant name
distinguishFrom.why: Monier-Williams lists madhura as names of specific plants and drugs (jīvaka, sugarcane); honey is madhu, which is itself madhura-kaṣāya in rasa.
The rasa covers staple grains, milk, ghee and many meats (Bhishagratna's Su. 42 groups), not just sugary foods; kapha-promoting effects attach to the whole class.

mistranslations.why: Reduces a broad nutritive class to refined sweeteners; most madhura dravyas are not sweet to a modern palate.

classical.establishes: Majjā's functions: production of shukra, filling the bone cavities (pūraṇa), and being the source of strength, sexual feeling and cheerfulness. The affective functions are not properties of haematopoietic marrow and are quietly dropped by the 'bone marrow' rendering.
classical.quote: The marrow contributes towards the formation and increase of semen, and fills in the internal cavities of the bones, and forms the chief source of strength, amorous feelings and hilarity.

classical.establishes: Majjā-kṣaya presenting as reduced semen and bone/joint pain. Not cytopenia. A reader expecting the haematological referent will find nothing here about blood counts.
classical.quote: the loss or waste of marrow is characterised by the formation of a lesser quantity of semen, aching pain in the bones and breaking pain in the bone-joints which have become marrowless.

classical.establishes: Majjā-vṛddhi as heaviness of the eyes and limbs. Again no haematological content.
classical.quote: An excessive formation of marrow gives rise to a heaviness of the eyes and to the members of the body.

classical.establishes: The mala of majjā is the body's oily secretion. Bhishagratna's parallel footnote to Su.Su.14 attributes the eye-corner deposits and skin oils to majjā, so the two translators divide these products differently.
classical.quote: that of marrow is the oily-substance in the body ; that of the skin is the secretions flowing from the eyes.

classical.verse: 121 in Kaviratna's marginal numbering; sara section cited as Vi 8/102 ff by carakasamhitaonline
classical.establishes: Majjā-sāra, recognised by soft limbs, oily voice and complexion, and thick round joints, and associated with learning and longevity. WHO ISTA's own ITA-2.8.1.7 description tracks this closely.
classical.quote: They who have the marrow for the predominating element in their constitution have limbs that are soft, as also great strength, oily complexion and voice, and joints that are thick, long, and round. They become long-lived, endued with great strength, knowledge of the scriptures, science, and offspring. They become entitled to the respect of all.

classical.verse: footnote to the prose section on successive transformation
classical.establishes: The three-fraction account of majjā's metabolism. This is Bhishagratna's own explanatory footnote, not the mula, and is recorded as such: it is quotable because he wrote it in 1907, but it is the translator speaking, not Sushruta.
classical.quote: The marrow, in its nascent state, enters into the organic principle of that name ; and there matured under the native heat of that principle, it is resolved into three factors, viz, its excreted portion contributes towards the formation of gelatinous matter deposited in the corners of the eyes, and the oily secretions of the skin, its condensed portion is assimilated into the organic principle of marrow, and its subtile portion is metamorphosed into semen.

classical.establishes: Majjā from asthi, and shukra from majjā, in verified Sanskrit with verse number.
classical.quote: ततो मज्जा मज्ज्ञः शुक्रं तु जायते (within रसाद्रक्तं ततो मांसं मांसान्मेदः प्रजायते । मेदसोऽस्थि ततो मज्जा मज्ज्ञः शुक्रं तु जायते ॥१०॥)

distinguishFrom.why: The preceding dhātu, which contains majjā. Clinically they are so often paired ('asthi-majjakshaya', 'asthimajjadhatu') that the compound risks becoming the unit and the distinction being lost.

WHO ISTA lists asthisāram as a Sanskrit synonym for majjā-dhātu (ITA-2.2.16) while separately defining asthi-sāraḥ as the bone-predominant constitution (ITA-2.8.1.6). Same string, two referents, one standard.

Brain matter. Modern teaching often folds brain and spinal cord into majjā; no passage retrieved here does so, and WHO's definition (soft material filling bone cavities) excludes it. The extension needs its own evidence.
Both are unctuous and both are often called 'fat-like'. Medas is two steps earlier in the chain and its excess obstructs channels; majjā fills cavities.
Another unctuous substance with a distinct classification (WHO: upadhātu of māṃsa). The three unctuous substances medas, vasā and majjā are routinely blurred in English.
The next dhātu, produced from majjā. Sushruta ties majjā-kṣaya directly to reduced semen, so depletion of the one presents as depletion of the other.

mistranslations.rendering: bone marrow, read as the haematopoietic organ
mistranslations.why: Nothing in the retrieved classical material connects majjā to the formation of blood. Rakta is formed from rasa in spleen and liver per Sushruta Sutrasthana 14, several steps earlier in the chain. The modern reader who sees 'bone marrow' will import haematopoiesis, which the tradition assigns elsewhere.

mistranslations.rendering: nervous tissue / brain and spinal cord
mistranslations.why: A common teaching extension with no support in any passage retrieved here, and in conflict with WHO's cavity-filling definition. It may be defensible from other sources; it is not established by these.

mistranslations.rendering: marrow, as a purely structural filler
mistranslations.why: The opposite error. Sushruta makes majjā 'the chief source of strength, amorous feelings and hilarity' - affective and constitutional functions that a filler reading discards.

mistranslations.rendering: majjā-kṣaya = aplastic anaemia or marrow failure
mistranslations.why: Occasionally proposed. The classical sign list is reduced semen plus bone and joint pain, with no cytopenic feature at all.

openQuestions: Whether majjā includes nervous tissue is the central unresolved question for this term. No retrieved classical passage supports the extension; modern teaching asserts it routinely. The relevant evidence would be in Sushruta Sharirasthana and in the Laghu Trayi, neither searched here.
The WHO asthi-sāra collision (marrow vs bone-predominant constitution) is unexplained.
Kaviratna and Bhishagratna assign the eye-corner and skin secretions differently between majjā and tvak. Which reflects the mula could not be determined without Sanskrit.
PubMed 'majja dhatu' returns zero records. There is no peer-reviewed operational definition of majjā, and no study measures anything and calls it majjā. This is the emptiest modern record in the set.

alternates: majjavaha srotas (मज्जवह-, the form in Ca.Vi.5/8)

classical.establishes: Root = asthīni (bones) and sandhi (joints). Note the text reads majja-vahānām (short stem), whereas WHO, NAMASTE and most textbooks head the term majjā-vaha.

classical.establishes: Causes: crushing, excessive abhiṣyanda, trauma, compression, and incompatible food.
classical.quote: उत्पेषादत्यभिष्यन्दादभिघातात् प्रपीडनात्| मज्जवाहीनि दुष्यन्ति विरुद्धानां च सेवनात्||१८||

distinguishFrom.why: The two are mirror images and are constantly swapped: asthivaha is rooted in medas + jaghana; majjāvaha in asthi + sandhi.

distinguishFrom.term: majjā (as marrow) vs majjā (as nervous tissue)
distinguishFrom.why: A large modern literature reads majjā as including nervous tissue/brain, which would make majjāvaha srotas a neural channel. Neither WHO nor NAMASTE endorses this; both say 'bone marrow'.
If majjā is read as nervous tissue, majjāvaha and manovaha begin to overlap. Keeping them apart matters: manovaha is rooted in hṛdaya, majjāvaha in bone.
Three distinct fatty/marrow substances; only majjā has this srotas.

mistranslations.why: Rests on reading majjā as nervous tissue. The classical root is bones and joints, and both international standards render majjā as bone marrow. Recording it as 'nervous system' imports a conclusion the sources do not make.
They are the same word; Caraka uses the short stem, the standards use the long one.

openQuestions: Does majjā in the srotas context include nervous tissue, and if so on whose authority?
Why are joints (sandhi) a root of the marrow channel rather than of the bone channel?

renderings.locator: ITA-2.4.1 malaḥ; description: 'Waste products formed during various stages of digestion and metabolism; one of the fundamental constituents of the human body along with dosha (regulatory functional factors) and fundamental structural components; there are two categories: waste products from digestion of food and waste products from transformation of structural components. The waste products from digestion of food comprise urine and faeces. The waste products from transformation of structural components are: phlegm (excretory form of kapha) from the primary product of digestion (the primary circulating nutrient fluid), bile (excretory form of pitta) from blood, mucus of nose and ear wax from muscle, perspiration from fat, nails and hair from bone, and rheum of the eye from bone marrow.'
renderings.assessment: WHO's headword is plural-sense 'Excretory products' and the definition tracks Charaka Chi 15/18-19 (dhātumala list) rather than Su 28/4. Note WHO's āhāramala are urine and faeces only; sweat is placed under dhātumala (from fat), consistent with Chi 15/18 but not with the 'trimala' textbook grouping.

classical.verse: 4 (standard; carakasamhitaonline prints the whole prose unit as ||4||)
classical.establishes: Three things: (1) mala is the name of the kiṭṭa-derived class; (2) its members include sweat, urine, faeces AND vāta-pitta-śleṣman AND the orifice secretions, hair and nails; (3) Charaka calls both malas and prasāda-products 'dhātavaḥ', and says malas that exceed their measure are to be excreted (utsargiṇaḥ) and, properly handled, keep the dhātus in equilibrium. Mala is therefore a functional constituent, not inert waste.
classical.quote: तत्राहारप्रसादाख्यो रसः किट्टं च मलाख्यमभिनिर्वर्तते| किट्टात् स्वेदमूत्रपुरीषवातपित्तश्लेष्माणः कर्णाक्षिनासिकास्यलोमकूपप्रजननमलाः केशश्मश्रुलोमनखादयश्चावयवाःपुष्यन्ति| ... ते सर्व एव धातवो मलाख्याः प्रसादाख्याश्च रसमलाभ्यां पुष्यन्तः स्वं मानमनुवर्तन्ते यथावयःशरीरम्| ... स्वमानातिरिक्ताः पुनरुत्सर्गिणः शीतोष्णपर्यायगुणैश्चोपचर्यमाणा मलाः शरीर धातुसाम्यकराः समुपलभ्यन्ते||४|| / tatrāhāraprasādākhyō Rasaḥ kiṭṭaṁ ca malākhyamabhinirvartatē| kiṭṭāt svēdamūtrapurīṣavātaPittaślēṣmāṇaḥ karṇākṣināsikāsyalōmakūpaprajananamalāḥ kēśaśmaśrulōmanakhādayaścāvayavāḥ puṣyanti| ... tē sarva ēva dhātavō malākhyāḥ prasādākhyāśca Rasamalābhyāṁ puṣyantaḥ svaṁ mānamanuvartantē yathāvayaḥśarīram| ... svamānātiriktāḥ punarutsargiṇaḥ śītōṣṇaparyāyaguṇaiścōpacaryamāṇā malāḥ śarīra Dhātusāmyakarāḥ samupalabhyantē||4||

classical.verse: 4 (standard); Kaviratna's printed numbers for this passage unreadable in OCR
classical.establishes: Public-domain English for the malākhya-dhātu and utsargin clauses. Kaviratna preserves the Sanskrit's startling classification of malas as 'Dhatus'.
classical.quote: The Refuse operates similarly with respect to those Dhatus which are called by the name of Malas. ... As regards the latter Dhatus, viz., Malas, which have the virtue of being excreted, when they increase beyond their normal measure, being treated alternately by regimen of cooling and warm properties, they regain their position of restoratives of the elements of the body to harmony.

classical.verse: 63 (standard Trikamji numbering; carakasamhitaonline prints ||६३||); Kaviratna prints 62 for this aphorism (Part VII, p. 192, archive.org BIUSante_47357 leaf n290, superscript *62 after 'of wind and the others'), one BEHIND the standard; the djvu OCR misreads his 62 as 63
classical.establishes: Mala is one of four classes whose kṣaya Charaka enumerates (doṣa, dhātu, mala, ojas). Kaviratna's rendering of mala here is 'the impurities evacuated by the system'.
classical.quote: वातादीनां रसादीनां मलानामोजसस्तथा| क्षयास्तत्रानिलादीनामुक्तं सङ्क्षीणलक्षणम् ||६३|| / vātādīnāṁ rasādīnāṁ malānāmōjasastathā| kṣayāstatrānilādīnāmuktaṁ saṅkṣīṇalakṣaṇam ||63|| — Kaviratna: 'Attenuation is in respect of the wind and the others ; of the (seven) elements beginning with Rasa or humour and the others; of the impurities evacuated by the system ; and of the element called Ojas.'

classical.verse: 3 (Sanskrit verse number from siva.sh e-text; Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers)
classical.establishes: The body is rooted in doṣa, dhātu and mala. Bhishagratna renders mala 'excretions' and re-orders the triad in English (doṣa, mala, dhātu).
classical.quote: दोषधातुमलमूलं हि शरीरं, तस्मादेतेषां लक्षणमुच्यमानमुपधारय ॥३॥ — Bhishagratna: 'Since the human body is constituted of humours, (Doshas), excretions (Mala), and the fundamental principles (Dhatus) of blood, marrow, etc., hear me discourse on the features which are peculiar to each of them.'
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (English); Sanskrit from siva.sh

classical.verse: 41 (siva.sh numbering); Bhishagratna, closing metrical text of chapter XV
classical.establishes: The famous svastha definition includes 'sama-dhātu-mala-kriya'. Bhishagratna paraphrases mala-kriyā as 'the normal processes of secretion'; the word mala does not surface in his English.
classical.quote: समदोषः समाग्निश्च समधातुमलक्रियः । प्रसन्नात्मेन्द्रियमनाः स्वस्थ इत्यभिधीयते ॥४१॥ — Bhishagratna: 'A person with an uniformly healthy digestion, and whose bodily humours are in a state of equilibrium, and in whom the fundamental vital fluids course in their normal state and quantity, accompanied by the normal processes of secretion, organic function, and intellection, is said to be a healthy person.'
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (English); Sanskrit from siva.sh

classical.establishes: Treatment is framed as increasing or decreasing doṣa, dhātu and mala; here mala = 'excrements'.
classical.quote: An intelligent physician should preserve the state of health in a healthy individual, while he should increase or decrease the quantity of the bodily humours, vital fluids, or excrements in a sick patient according to the exigencies of the case until his health is perfectly restored.

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa opens Doṣādivijñānīya with the same triad as Sushruta 15/3: doṣa, dhātu, mala are always the root of the body.
classical.quote: doṣa-dhātu-malā mūlaṃ sadā dehasya taṃ calaḥ | utsāhocchvāsa-niśvāsa-ceṣṭā-vega-pravartanaiḥ || 1 ||

distinguishFrom.why: Kiṭṭa is the waste fraction produced by digestion; mala is the name of the class it nourishes (Charaka Su 28/4 'kiṭṭaṁ ca malākhyam'). WHO and NAMASTE keep both headwords with overlapping definitions.

Routinely opposed to mala in textbooks, yet Charaka Su 28/4 lists vāta, pitta and śleṣman among the products of kiṭṭa, and Chi 15/18 calls kapha and pitta the malas of rasa and rakta. The doṣa/mala boundary is drawn by function (doṣas regulate; malas are excreted when in excess), not by substance.

Charaka Su 28/4 explicitly calls malas 'dhātavaḥ malākhyāḥ'; Kaviratna keeps this ('those Dhatus ... called ... Malas'). The modern tripartition doṣa/dhātu/mala should not be read back as Charaka saying malas are not dhātus.
Āma is undigested; mala is the normal product of digestion. WHO ITA-5.4.8 sāmamalaḥ codes the pathological overlap.
WHO ITA-5.4.1 / NAMC C: the disorder-class, not the substance.

Retention of stool; found as an index term under ICD-11 TM2 SM7Y 'Other specified gastro-intestinal disorders (TM2)'. Here mala is used in the narrow sense of faeces, as it often is in Sanskrit; the lexicon must say which sense is meant.

mistranslations.why: Common in popular and some clinical writing. No classical source retrieved calls mala toxic; Charaka Su 28/4 says malas within their measure are dhātusāmyakarāḥ (keep the dhātus in equilibrium), and Sushruta Su 15/5 (Bhishagratna) says faeces are 'indispensably necessary for the preservation of the body'.
Edwardian English with a moral charge; the Sanskrit mala in these passages is a physiological constituent with assigned functions.

Not wrong, but 'waste' in English implies worthless residue, whereas Charaka and Sushruta assign functions to each mala and count mala among the three roots of the body. Both WHO and NAMASTE use 'waste products' and immediately qualify it as 'one of the fundamental constituents'.
True in colloquial and some clinical Sanskrit (cf. mala-apravṛtti, mala-pravṛtti), but as a technical term in Su 28/4 it is the whole class. Entries must disambiguate the two senses.

openQuestions: Why do WHO and NAMASTE place sweat under dhātumala (from fat) while the common 'trimala' teaching groups it with urine and faeces as āhāramala? Charaka Chi 15/18 supports the WHO placement; the source of the trimala grouping was not located in a primary text in this pass.
Kaviratna's footnote counts seven malas (stools, urine, five orifice secretions) in the eighteen kṣayas; Chakrapāṇi's enumeration not checked.
Whether any ICD-11 TM2 code addresses mala as a class: none found in my searches; only the index term mala-apravṛtiḥ under SM7Y.

classical.verse: 70-72 (standard, as printed on carakasamhitaonline: 70 purīṣa, 71 mūtra, 72 other malāyana). Kaviratna prints 70, 71, 72 for the same units (aligned here, though he is one behind at 64-65 in the same chapter)
classical.establishes: Charaka's mala-kṣaya signs: faeces depleted → vāta presses the intestines and moves obliquely/upward in a dry patient; urine depleted → dysuria, discoloured urine, thirst, dry mouth; the OTHER mala-seats (malāyana) → empty, light, dried. The compound used is malasaṅkṣaya. Charaka gives NO sveda-kṣaya verse here (verified by searching the page for स्वेदक्षय).
classical.quote: क्षीणे शकृति चान्त्राणि पीडयन्निव मारुतः| रूक्षस्योन्नमयन् कुक्षिं तिर्यगूर्ध्वं च गच्छति||७०|| मूत्रक्षये मूत्रकृच्छ्रं मूत्रवैवर्ण्यमेव च| पिपासा बाधते चास्य मुखं च परिशुष्यति||७१|| मलायनानि चान्यानि शून्यानि च लघूनि च| विशुष्काणि च लक्ष्यन्ते यथास्वं मलसङ्क्षये||७२|| / kṣīṇē śakr̥ti cāntrāṇi pīḍayanniva mārutaḥ| rūkṣasyōnnamayan kukṣiṁ tiryagūrdhvaṁ ca gacchati||70|| mūtrakṣayē mūtrakr̥cchraṁ mūtravaivarṇyamēva ca| pipāsā bādhatē cāsya mukhaṁ ca pariśuṣyati||71|| malāyanāni cānyāni śūnyāni ca laghūni ca| viśuṣkāṇi ca lakṣyantē yathāsvaṁ malasaṅkṣayē||72||

classical.establishes: Lawfully quotable English of Su 17/70-72 (OCR shows his 70 as '-]*701' and his 71, 72 clearly; OCR spacing normalised). 'Strangury' = mūtrakṛcchra.
classical.quote: When the stools decrease below the quantity that is normal, the wind in the constitution of the patient who has become dry, becomes provoked or aggravated and afflicting his entrails forces them upwards and penetrates the abdomen in transverse and upward directions. [70] When the urine decreases below the normal quantity, the symptoms that appear are strangury, and loss of color of the urine itself. Besides this, the patient suffers from thirst, and his mouth becomes dry. [71] As regards the other organs or outlets of the body, when their secretions decrease below the normal measure, all of them seem to be empty, light, and dry. [72]

classical.verse: 11 (Sanskrit verse number from siva.sh; Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers)
classical.establishes: Sushruta gives all three mala-kṣaya pictures in one sūtra, INCLUDING sveda-kṣaya (which Charaka Su 17 lacks), with the treatment principle 'svayoni-vardhana' (supply what builds that mala) and, for sweat, abhyaṅga and svedana. Bhishagratna's 'liver and the intestines' and 'dribble ... thin and scanty jets' are expansions beyond the Sanskrit (basti-toda, alpa-mūtratā).
classical.quote: पुरीषक्षये हृदयपार्श्वपीडा सशब्दस्य च वायोरूर्ध्वगमनं कुक्षौ सञ्चरणं च, मूत्रक्षये बस्तितोदोऽल्पमूत्रता च; अत्रापि स्वयोनिवर्धनद्रव्योपयोगः । स्वेदक्षये स्तब्धरोमकूपता त्वक्शोषः स्पर्शवैगुण्यं स्वेदनाशश्च; तत्राभ्यङ्गः स्वेदोपयोगश्च ॥११॥ — Bhishagratna: 'The loss absence, suppression or scanty formation of fecal matter is attended with a sensation of pain at the sides and the region of the heart, and the upward coursing of (the incarcerated) wind or flatus, accompanied with a rumbling sound about the region of the liver and the intestines. Similarly, the loss, (absence or scanty formation) of urine is marked by an aching pain in the bladder, causing it dribble or to come out in thin and scanty jets. Here, as in the foregoing instances, the remedial agents should consist of drugs which directly contribute to the formation of urine. Similarly the waste, absence or scanty formation of perspiration is followed by such symptoms as numbness about the pores of the hair, and dryness of the epidermis (skin). The sense of touch is perceptibly affected, and perspiration is entirely stopped. The medical treatment in such a case consists in the application of medicated unguents, lubrications, diaphoretics, and adoption of measures (that tend to produce a copious perspiration).'
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (English); Sanskrit from siva.sh

classical.establishes: The general kṣaya rule (craving for what rebuilds the depleted item) is stated for mala as much as for doṣa and dhātu. Bhishagratna's 'Ojah (albumen)' is his own biomedical gloss; the Sanskrit says bala.
classical.quote: दोषधातुमलक्षीणो बलक्षीणोऽपि वा नरः । स्वयोनिवर्धनं यत्तदन्नपानं प्रकाङ्क्षति ॥२९॥ — Bhishagratna: 'A person suffering from a wasting of any of the constituent humours or fundamental principles or excrements of the body, as well as one suffering from loss of Ojah (albumen) naturally craves for drink and food that tend to contribute directly to the formation of the matter (or bodily principle) so lost or wasted.'
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (English); Sanskrit from siva.sh

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa's consolidated mala-kṣaya list (faeces, urine, sweat, and the subtle malas recognised by dryness, pricking, emptiness and lightness of their seats). Matches NAMC's references Ah.Su.11/21-22.
classical.quote: purīṣe vāyur antrāṇi sa-śabdo veṣṭayann iva | kukṣau bhramati yāty ūrdhvaṃ hṛt-pārśve pīḍayan bhṛśam || 21 || mūtre 'lpaṃ mūtrayet kṛcchrād vi-varṇaṃ sāsram eva vā | svede roma-cyutiḥ stabdha-roma-tā sphuṭanaṃ tvacaḥ || 22 || malānām ati-sūkṣmāṇāṃ dur-lakṣyaṃ lakṣayet kṣayam | sva-malāyana-saṃśoṣa-toda-śūnya-tva-lāghavaiḥ || 23 ||

classical.establishes: Aetiology and prognosis: mala-vṛddhi arises from retention (saṅga), mala-kṣaya from excessive discharge (ati-visarga); because the body is accustomed to its malas, kṣaya is more distressing than vṛddhi. This is the clearest classical statement that mala depletion is clinically worse than mala excess.
classical.quote: vṛddhiṃ malānāṃ saṅgāc ca kṣayaṃ cāti-visargataḥ | malocita-tvād dehasya kṣayo vṛddhes tu pīḍanaḥ || 25 ||

distinguishFrom.why: Both are among Charaka's eighteen kṣayas (Su 17/63) but have different sign-lists; mala-kṣaya is recognised by emptiness/dryness of the mala's seat (malāyana), dhātukṣaya by loss of the dhātu's function.
AH Su 11/25: vṛddhi comes from retention, kṣaya from over-discharge; kṣaya is the more painful. Not mirror images in prognosis.
WHO codes mūtrakṣayaḥ both as a mala-disorder (ITA-5.4.3) and as a urinary disease (ITA-5.39.16); NAMC likewise CA-1 vs EJ-3.4. A lexicon entry must say which coding it means.
Non-passage of stool is retention (saṅga), which AH 11/25 makes a cause of mala-VṚDDHI, not kṣaya. 'Scanty stool' in English covers both and must be disambiguated.
Charaka Su 17 has no sveda-kṣaya verse; Sushruta Su 15/11 and AH Su 11/22 do. 'Charaka's three mala-kṣayas' would be a misstatement.

mistranslations.why: These are biomedical sign-terms and are only part of the classical picture; mūtrakṣaya in Ca.Su.17/71 also includes discoloration, thirst and dry mouth, and svedakṣaya in Su.Su.15/11 includes skin dryness and altered touch. Substituting the biomedical term loses the syndrome.
Constipation is retention/difficulty of passage; purīṣakṣaya is reduced formation of faeces with vāta signs. AH 11/25 assigns retention to vṛddhi.

mistranslations.rendering: loss of waste = detoxification / a good thing
mistranslations.why: Popular inversion. Every classical source retrieved treats mala-kṣaya as a disorder requiring the mala to be rebuilt (svayoni-vardhana), and AH 11/25 calls it more distressing than mala excess.

openQuestions: Standalone compound: Charaka Su 17/72 uses malasaṅkṣaya; WHO and NAMASTE have no generic malakṣaya headword, only per-mala codes. Whether a generic 'malakṣaya' appears as a headword in any standard was not established.
Whether Chakrapāṇi reads the 'malāyanāni cānyāni' of Su 17/72 as the five sense-orifice malas (as Kaviratna's footnote at 17/63 implies) was not checked.

Bhishagratna's section numbering within chapter XV was not captured from wisdomlib; a human citing him by page should use the archive.org Vol. I scan (b24758619_0001), which did not download in this session.
