classical.establishes: Stool signs by dosha, read from the Nirnaya Sagar page images rather than OCR: hard and dry in vata, yellow in pitta, white in kapha (v.1); all signs together in sannipata, and broken-up, frothy, rough and smoke-coloured (trutitam phenilam ruksam dhumalam) in vata-kopa, ash-grey (kapisa) in a combined vata-kapha disorder (v.2); bound, finely broken, yellow-dark from pitta with anila, slightly thick and slimy from kapha with pitta (v.3); dark, broken and yellowish, bound and white in tridosa, and when the stool passed is foul-smelling and cold (v.4) the physicians who know the dosas call it jirna, digested (v.5); tawny and lumpy stool indicates depleted mala-dosa (v.5-6); white, large and putrid-smelling in jalodara (v.6); dark in ksaya, raw-and-undigested, yellow with pain in the flank (v.7); extremely black, extremely white, extremely yellow or ruddy stool portends death, and stool that is intensely hot certainly so (v.7 and the unnumbered half-line); then a second series introduced by anyac ca: black for vata, yellow for pitta, somewhat red, white from kapha (v.8), raw in indigestion and well-formed when digested (v.9); and finally the asadhya signs, lumpy and dry in excessive agni, liquefied in weak agni, and foul-smelling with a sheen (candrika-yukta), which is the mark of the incurable (v.10). The section is attributed by the Yogaratnakara to the Rudra-tantra (rudratantrat), not to Harita.
classical.quote: अथ मलपरीक्षा । रुद्रतन्त्रात्—वातान्मले तु दृढता शुष्कता चापि जायते । पीतता जायते पित्ताच्छुक्लता श्लेष्मतो भवेत् ॥ १ ॥ संनिपाते च सर्वाणि लक्षणानि भवन्ति हि । त्रुटितं फेनिलं रूक्षं धूमलं वातकोपतः । वातश्लेष्मविकारे च जायते कपिशं मलम् ॥ २ ॥ बद्धं सुत्रुटितं पीतश्यामं पित्तानिलाद्भवेत् । पीतश्यामं श्लेष्मपित्तादीषत्सान्द्रं च पिच्छिलम् ॥ ३ ॥ श्यामं त्रुटितपीताभं बद्धश्वेतं त्रिदोषतः । दुर्गन्धः शीतलश्चैव विष्ठोत्सर्गो यदा भवेत् ॥ ४ ॥ तदा जीर्णं मलं वैद्यैर्दोषज्ञैः परिभण्यते । कपिलं गुटियुक्तं च यदि वर्चोऽवलोक्यते ॥ ५ ॥ प्रक्षीणमलदोषेण दूषितः परिकथ्यते । सितं महत्पूतिगन्धं मलं ज्ञेयं जलोदरे ॥ ६ ॥ श्यामं क्षये त्वामवति पीतं सकटिवेदनम् । अतिकृष्णं चातिशुभ्रमतिपीतं तथाऽरुणम् ॥ ७ ॥ मरणाय मलं किंतु भृशोष्णं मृत्यवे ध्रुवम् ॥ अन्यच्च—वातस्य च मलं कृष्णं ततः पित्तस्य पीतविट् । रक्तवर्णं मलं किंचिन्मलं श्वेतं कफोद्भवम् ॥ ८ ॥ आमं वा श्लेष्मजं प्राहुर्मिश्रितं द्वंद्वजं वदेत् । अपक्वं स्यादजीर्णे तु पक्वं स्वच्छमलं भवेत् ॥ ९ ॥ अत्यग्नौ पिंडितं शुष्कं मन्दाग्नौ तु द्रवीकृतम् । दुर्गन्धं चन्द्रिकायुक्तमसाध्यं मललक्षणम् ॥ १० ॥ इति मलपरीक्षा ।

distinguishFrom.why: In Ayurvedic physiology mala includes urine, sweat and dhātu-malas (NIA draft SK0121). In the eightfold scheme mala means stool only because mūtra is a separate site.
Urine examination is the second site and has its own elaborate oil-drop prognostic test; the two are often lumped as 'mala-mūtra parīkṣā'.
The specific word for faeces (WHO uses purīṣa compounds for stool signs, e.g. 'makṣikākrāntaṁ purīṣaṁ'); modern reviews use purīṣa-parīkṣā and mala-parīkṣā interchangeably.
Assessment of bowel habit (mṛdu/madhya/krūra koṣṭha) for purgation dosing is a different examination.

mistranslations.why: Over-broad; the Yogaratnakara section is specifically about faeces.
The classical examination is by naked-eye colour, consistency, smell and a water-immersion test, not microscopy or chemistry (PMID 27011711 makes the same point).

openQuestions: The attribution marker at the start of the Yogaratnakara mala-parīkṣā (OCR 'र्दतच्रात्', possibly 'हारीतात्', citing Hārīta) needs confirming from the page image.
Verse numbering of the section across editions.

classical.quote: अत ऊर्ध्वमतिवृद्धानां दोषधातुमलानां लक्षणं वक्ष्यामः । वृद्धिः पुनरेषां स्वयोनिवर्धनात्युपसेवनाद्भवति । ... [13] पुरीषमाटोपं कुक्षौ शूलं च; मूत्रं मूत्रवृद्धिं मुहुर्मुहुः प्रवृत्तिं बस्तितोदमाध्मानं च; स्वेदस्त्वचो दौर्गन्ध्यं कण्डूं च ॥१५॥ — Bhishagratna: 'Now we shall describe the symptoms which mark the excess (excessive accumulation in the body) of any of the fundamental humours, principles and excrements of the body. The quantities of these humours, principles and secretion, are abnormally increased through the use of substances that primarily contribute to their formation in the organism.' ... 'An abnormal increase in the formation of fecal matter is attended with distension of the abdomen and colic pains in the loins and the intestines. An excessive formation of urine is manifest by constant urging for micturition and distension of the bladder, attended by a kind of gnawing or aching pain. Similarly, an increased secretion of perspiration is attended with an itching of the skin which emits a bad odour.'
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (English); Sanskrit from siva.sh

classical.verse: 4 (standard); Kaviratna's printed number for this clause unreadable in OCR
classical.establishes: Charaka's general principle for mala in excess of its measure: it is to be excreted, and managed by alternating cold and hot regimen, after which the malas again maintain dhātu-equilibrium. Charaka Su 17 gives no per-mala vṛddhi sign-list (that chapter's vṛddhi section is for the doṣas only).
classical.quote: स्वमानातिरिक्ताः पुनरुत्सर्गिणः शीतोष्णपर्यायगुणैश्चोपचर्यमाणा मलाः शरीर धातुसाम्यकराः समुपलभ्यन्ते||४|| / svamānātiriktāḥ punarutsargiṇaḥ śītōṣṇaparyāyaguṇaiścōpacaryamāṇā malāḥ śarīra Dhātusāmyakarāḥ samupalabhyantē||4|| — Kaviratna: 'As regards the latter Dhatus, viz., Malas, which have the virtue of being excreted, when they increase beyond their normal measure, being treated alternately by regimen of cooling and warm properties, they regain their position of restoratives of the elements of the body to harmony.'
classical.translator: Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline; English by Avinash Chandra Kaviratna

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa's mala-vṛddhi list, adding 'urge even after voiding' (kṛte 'py akṛta-saṃjñatā) for urine, which WHO 5.4.4 and NAMC CA-2 reproduce, and extending vṛddhi to the minor malas (dūṣikā etc.) by abundance and heaviness.
classical.quote: kukṣāv ādhmānam āṭopaṃ gauravaṃ vedanāṃ śakṛt | mūtraṃ tu vasti-nistodaṃ kṛte 'py a-kṛta-saṃjña-tām || 13 || svedo 'ti-sveda-daurgandhya-kaṇḍūr evaṃ ca lakṣayet | dūṣikādīn api malān bāhulya-guru-tādibhiḥ || 14 ||

classical.establishes: Mala-vṛddhi arises from retention (saṅga); it is less distressing than mala-kṣaya because the body is habituated to its malas.
classical.quote: vṛddhiṃ malānāṃ saṅgāc ca kṣayaṃ cāti-visargataḥ | malocita-tvād dehasya kṣayo vṛddhes tu pīḍanaḥ || 25 ||

distinguishFrom.why: AH Su 11/25 gives opposite causes (retention vs over-discharge) and says vṛddhi is the less distressing of the two.

Retention is the CAUSE of vṛddhi in AH 11/25, not the state itself; NAMASTE SAT-D.5095's 'accumulation of feces' blurs this. ICD-11 TM2 lists mala-apravṛtiḥ as an index term under SM7Y, a gastro-intestinal disorder, not a mala-vṛddhi.
Charaka Su 17 gives vṛddhi signs for doṣas only; mala-vṛddhi signs come from Sushruta Su 15/15 and AH Su 11/13-14. Citing Charaka Su 17 for mala-vṛddhi would be wrong.
Polyuric diseases with their own nidāna; NAMC codes mūtravṛddhi (CA-2) separately from them, but renders it 'polyuria', inviting confusion.
Induced sweating (WHO ITA-9.2.36 'Fomentation') is a treatment, not svedavṛddhi; WHO codes svedana-atiyogaḥ (ITA-5.76.8) for over-sudation as a separate iatrogenic disorder.

mistranslations.why: Biomedical sign-words standing for syndromes that in Su.Su.15/15 and Ah.Su.11/13-14 include pain, distension, odour and itching; and 'polyuria' names a quantity whereas the Sanskrit lists frequency and residual urge.
Conflates the state (vṛddhi) with its cause (saṅga) per AH 11/25.
Charaka Su 28/4 says malas in excess are simply to be excreted and managed by regimen, after which they resume their equilibrating role; nothing in the retrieved texts frames vṛddhi as poisoning.

openQuestions: No generic malavṛddhi headword exists in WHO or NAMASTE (both code per mala); whether any standard has one was not established.
WHO's inconsistency ('Morbid increase' for malas, 'Excess formation' for ojas) may be deliberate; the editorial rationale was not found.
Bhishagratna's own section numbers for the vṛddhi passage were not captured (wisdomlib shows footnote markers [8]-[10] only).

classical.establishes: Māṃsa's two functions: bulk/roundness of the limbs (lepana in the mula tradition) and production of medas. Neither is contraction. The verse's Sanskrit opening was verified separately as रसस्तुष्टिं प्रीणनं रक्तपुष्टिं च करोति...
classical.quote: The flesh contributes towards the stoutness or rotundity of the limbs and occasions the formation of fatty matter in the system.

classical.establishes: The classical presentation of māṃsa-kṣaya, defined entirely by regional wasting at named sites. The sites listed (buttocks, cheeks, lips, breasts) are not all muscle, which is direct textual evidence that māṃsa is broader than muscle.
classical.quote: The loss of flesh is marked by emaciation of the buttocks, cheeks, lips, thighs, breasts, armpits, neck, and the calves of the legs. The arteries seem loose and flabby, and the body seems to be dry and inert, accompanied by an aching or gnawing pain in its members.

classical.establishes: Māṃsa-vṛddhi, again by regional fullness at named sites including lips and penis. Reinforces that the referent is soft bodily bulk, not skeletal muscle.
classical.quote: An increase of flesh is marked by the rotundity and fullness of the buttocks and the lips, as well as of the penis, arms, and the thighs, and an increased heaviness of the whole body.

classical.verse: 16 in Kaviratna's marginal numbering (cited as 15/17 by carakasamhitaonline)
classical.establishes: That māṃsa yields skin (six layers) as a secondary product, and that Kaviratna renders a DIFFERENT word as 'muscles' here, derived from adeps, not from flesh. Decisive evidence that 'flesh' and 'muscles' are not interchangeable in this translation.
classical.quote: from flesh is fat or adeps and six varieties of skin ; and from adeps is the origin of the tendons and muscles.

classical.establishes: The kiṭṭa (waste fraction) of māṃsa is the bodily secretions from the orifices. A claim with no biomedical analogue whatever, and one that a 'muscle' rendering makes unintelligible.
classical.quote: that of flesh are the filths of the body, including the secretions (from the nose, the ears, &c.)

classical.verse: 118 in Kaviratna's marginal numbering; carakasamhitaonline cites the sara section as Vi 8/102 ff
classical.establishes: Māṃsa-sāra, the constitutional type in which flesh predominates, again defined by named regions being well covered rather than by strength.
classical.quote: Of men that have the flesh as the predominating element in their constitution, the symptoms are these : viz., their temples, forehead, throat, eyes (or rather, eye-lids), cheeks, jaws, neck, shoulders, chest, armpits, breast, and the joints of the arms and the legs, are covered with compact, heavy and agreeable-looking flesh.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ISTA lists peśī as a Sanskrit synonym of māṃsa-dhātu (ITA-2.2.8), but in the Sharira literature peśī is a counted anatomical unit (the enumerated muscles) while māṃsa is the tissue class. Treating them as synonyms, as WHO does, is a decision that the lexicon should record rather than adopt.

Intramuscular fat, classed by WHO as the upadhātu of māṃsa (ITA-2.3.5). Bhishagratna renders it 'fatty matter (Vasa)' and gives it a distinct description in Sutrasthana XV, including that it predominates in the female organism.

The next dhātu, produced from māṃsa. Since both contribute to bodily bulk, māṃsa-vṛddhi and medo-vṛddhi are clinically confusable, and Sushruta's separate sign lists are the means of distinguishing them.

Skin. Charaka Chikitsasthana 15 derives the six layers of skin from māṃsa as a secondary product, so skin is downstream of māṃsa, not a separate primary dhātu - though tvak-sāra is nonetheless the first of the eight saras.
Ligament/sinew. Kaviratna derives 'the tendons and muscles' from adeps in Chikitsasthana 15, not from flesh, which cuts across the modern assignment of snāyu as an upadhātu of medas.

The same word is the ordinary Sanskrit for meat, and Charaka's dietetics chapters use it constantly in that sense (e.g. the comparative heaviness of the flesh of different animals). A concordance search will merge the two.

mistranslations.why: WHO's own headword, and it is too narrow. The classical wasting signs are at the cheeks, lips, breasts and buttocks; the excretory product is the secretions of the nose and ears; and Kaviratna's Charaka reserves the English 'muscles' for a different Sanskrit word derived from adeps. 'Muscle' also quietly imports contraction, which no retrieved passage ascribes to māṃsa.
Correct for the dietetic sense, wrong for the dhātu. The collision is real and unavoidable in the source language.
Compounds the narrowing of 'muscle' with the histological import of 'tissue'. Now standard in the journals (PMID 42161239) and likely to become self-reinforcing.
'Flesh' is the older rendering but is the more accurate one. Replacing it with 'muscle' for the sake of modern idiom loses information rather than updating it.

openQuestions: Whether peśī is a synonym of māṃsa (WHO) or a subordinate anatomical unit (Sharirasthana usage) is unresolved and has consequences for any coded terminology.

Charaka derives skin from māṃsa and tendons from medas; the modern upadhātu tables usually assign vasā and tvak to māṃsa and snāyu to medas. Whether the modern table is a faithful reading of Ci.15.16 could not be settled from the retrieved text.

No study has measured body composition in māṃsa-kṣaya, so whether the classical entity tracks lean mass, total soft tissue, or neither is unknown. PMID 27833368 used BMI, which cannot distinguish them.
The kiṭṭa of māṃsa being the orifice secretions is unexplained anywhere retrieved and, so far as this search found, has never been discussed in the indexed literature.

classical.establishes: Causes of vitiation: abhiṣyandi, bulky and heavy foods, and sleeping by day after eating.
classical.quote: अभिष्यन्दीनि भोज्यानि स्थूलानि च गुरूणि च| मांसवाहीनि दुष्यन्ति भुक्त्वा च स्वपतां दिवा||१५||

classical.establishes: Suśruta's roots = snāyu, tvak, plus the blood-carrying dhamanīs. Quoted exactly as printed, including Bhishagratna's garbled glossing; I confirmed the identical wording in the independent archive.org scan of the 1911 edition (https://archive.org/stream/b24758619_0002/b24758619_0002_djvu.txt), so this is the edition's text, not a transcription error by wisdomlib.
classical.quote: The two muscle-carrying Srotas (ducts or channels) have their roots in the ( Snayu ), nerves Tvak (serum), and the blood-carrying Dhamanis (capillaries). An injury to any of these channels is characterised by swelling, loss or atrophy of the muscles, appearance of varicose veins or may (ultimately) result in death.

distinguishFrom.why: snāyu is the root, and is itself contested: Bhishagratna glosses it 'nerves', WHO and NAMASTE read 'tendons'. It is not the channel.
māṃsa and medas are consecutive dhātus and their srotas are adjacent in every list; the roots are wholly different (snāyu/tvak vs vṛkka/vapāvahana).
The tissue and its membrane are separate concepts from the conduit.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's 1911 gloss, printed in the retrieved text as 'the ( Snayu ), nerves'. Both WHO (ITA-2.5.13 'tendons and skin') and NAMASTE read snāyu as tendon/ligament. The 'nerves' reading is a 19th-century artefact.

The retrieved 1911 text reads 'Tvak (serum)'. tvak is skin. This is an outright error in the public-domain translation and must not be propagated; it is quotable as evidence about Bhishagratna, not usable as a meaning.
The roots named are tendon and skin, not muscle; the channel is defined by what it nourishes, not by where it lies.

openQuestions: Does snāyu here mean tendon/ligament (WHO, NAMASTE) or nerve (Bhishagratna, Ḍalhaṇa-influenced readings)?
Is NAMASTE's 'Su.Sa.9/13' a typo or a real edition variant?

classical.establishes: Manas is atīndriya (beyond/other than the indriyas), named sattva, by some cetas; its activity depends on its objects and on ātma-sampad; it is the cause of the indriyas' activity (4). It appears manifold but is one; hence the senses cannot all act at once (5). Kaviratna (his 2-3): 'The mind is regarded as something different from the senses. It is sometimes called satwa, and some again call it chetas. Its functions are regulated by the contact of its objects with the soul. Some regard the mind as the cause of the functions of the senses. ... In reality, however, there is no multiplicity of minds. ... Therefore, all the senses are incapable of acting at one and the same time.' English at https://archive.org/stream/BIUSante_47357/BIUSante_47357_djvu.txt. Kaviratna's 'Some regard' for ceṣṭāpratyayabhūtam has no 'some' in the Sanskrit.
classical.quote: Atīndriyaṁ punarmanaḥ sattvasañjñakaṁ, 'cētaḥ' ityāhurēkē, tadarthātmasampadāyattacēṣṭaṁ cēṣṭāpratyayabhūtamindriyāṇām||4|| Svārthēndriyārthasaṅkalpavyabhicaraṇāccānēkamēkasmin puruṣē sattvaṁ, rajastamaḥsattvaguṇayōgācca; na cānēkatvaṁ, nahyēkaṁ hyēkakālamanēkēṣu pravartatē; tasmānnaikakālā sarvēndriyapravr̥ttiḥ||5||

classical.establishes: The fullest Caraka account: manas is inferred from the presence and absence of knowledge when ātmā, indriya and artha are already in proximity (18); its two guṇas are aṇutva and ekatva (19); its objects are the thinkable, considerable, conjecturable, meditable and resolvable (20); its karma is control of the senses, self-restraint, conjecture and consideration, after which buddhi proceeds (21). Kaviratna (his 25-28): 'The attributes by which one may define mind are the presence and absence of knowledge ... Subtility and oneness have been regarded as the two attributes of the mind. That which is remembered, that upon which reason (or comparison) works, that upon which ratiocination is employed, that which after reproduction is held fast in consciousness, that which is resolved upon, and that which is known, form what is called the objects of the mind. Seizure of objects by means of the senses, subjecting them to control, comparison, and ratiocination, are the functions of the mind. After this the understanding begins to work.' Note Kaviratna's 'That which is remembered' for cintya is loose; the Sanskrit has no smṛti here.
classical.quote: lakṣaṇaṁ manasō jñānasyābhāvō bhāva ēva ca| sati hyātmēndriyārthānāṁ sannikarṣē na vartatē||18|| vaivr̥ttyānmanasō jñānaṁ sānnidhyāttacca vartatē| aṇutvamatha caikatvaṁ dvau guṇau manasaḥ smr̥tau||19|| cintyaṁ vicāryamūhyaṁ ca dhyēyaṁ saṅkalpyamēva ca| yatkiñcinmanasō jñēyaṁ tat sarvaṁ hyarthasañjñakam||20|| indriyābhigrahaḥ karma manasaḥ svasya nigrahaḥ| ūhō vicāraśca, tataḥ paraṁ buddhiḥ pravartatē||21||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.establishes: Manas (as sattva) is one leg of the tridaṇḍa with ātmā and śarīra (46); one of the nine dravyas (48); and the seat of the two mānasa doṣas rajas and tamas (57). Kaviratna: 'Mind, soul, and body, this trinity ... like three sticks'; 'The qualities of Passion and Darkness have, again, been indicated to be the causes of mental diseases.'
classical.quote: sattvamātmā śarīraṁ ca trayamētattridaṇḍavat| (46) ... khādīnyātmā manaḥ kālō diśaśca dravyasaṅgrahaḥ| (48) ... mānasaḥ punaruddiṣṭō rajaśca tama ēva ca||57||
classical.translator: Sanskrit text as printed on Charak Samhita Online

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 4-5; Sanskrit verse number not established
classical.establishes: Suśruta classes manas as the eleventh indriya, ubhayātmaka, following Sāṃkhya; this is the direct opposite of Caraka's atīndriya (Sū.8.4). The 'moon god is that of the mind (Manah)' in section 7 gives its presiding deity.
classical.quote: The eleven organs of cognition, communication or sense perception ... They are the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, speech, hands, genitals, anus, feet and the mind (Manah). Of these foregoing organs the first five are intellectual or sense organs (Vuddhi-Indriya); the next five being operative (Karma-Indriya). The mind (Manah) partakes of the character of both the intellectual and operative organs alike.

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Śā.1.21-23: manas deliberates, buddhi determines. Kaviratna's Śā.1 footnote: 'Manas excludes Buddhi. With Buddhi, Manas is Mind.' English 'mind' spans both.

Ca.Sū.8.4 makes sattva a NAME of manas (sattvasañjñaka), and Sū.1.46 uses sattva for the mental leg of the tridaṇḍa; but sattva is also one of the three guṇas (Sū.8.6). Kaviratna: 'Sattwa is the mind as understood in Hindu philosophy.' The lexicon must flag the two senses.

Cetas is an alternative name for manas (Sū.8.4, 'some call it cetas'; WHO lists 'manaḥ, cetaḥ'); cetanā is consciousness, a liṅga of ātmā (Śā.1.72) and the sixth dhātu of the puruṣa (Śā.1.16). Not the same.
Manas is an instrument with guṇas and objects; ātmā is nirvikāra witness. Caraka lists them separately everywhere (Sū.1.42, 1.48, Śā.1.17).
Caraka: manas is atīndriya (Sū.8.4). Suśruta: manas is the eleventh indriya. Any English gloss 'the sixth sense' follows Suśruta, not Caraka.
A class term (WHO ITA-1.9.3.3.34: buddhi, manas, ahaṃkāra, citta; NIA SR0066: manas, buddhi, indriya, ahaṃkāra). Manas is a member, and the two lists disagree on membership.
None of the passages retrieved locates manas anatomically; PMID 42453143 reviews the brain question. A lexicon should not assert a seat from these sources.

mistranslations.why: Not wrong, but Kaviratna's own footnote says manas 'has not for its equivalent Mind'. English 'mind' includes buddhi and often ātmā-functions; manas in Ca.Śā.1.21 stops where buddhi begins.
Bhishagratna, Su.Śā.1 section 18. Manas is a cognitive instrument, not feeling.
Popular gloss. Follows Suśruta's eleven-indriya count against Caraka's atīndriya, and 'sense' imports the English sensory meaning.
WHO offers 'Mind, psyche'. 'Psyche' in English carries Greek soul/Jungian connotations that overlap ātmā rather than manas.

openQuestions: Whether Caraka's atīndriya means 'not an indriya' or 'beyond the reach of the indriyas' (imperceptible); Kaviratna's Vi.5 footnote takes the second reading ('beyond the ken of the five organs of sense').
Whether the triguṇa psychometrics (PMID 40774071 and predecessors) measure manas, mānasa prakṛti, or neither, in classical terms.

classical.establishes: Closes the seven pure sattva types at verse 37 and names brāhma the purest.
classical.quote: इत्येवं शुद्धस्य सत्त्वस्य सप्तविधं भेदांशं विद्यात् कल्याणांशत्वात्; तत्संयोगात्तु ब्राह्ममत्यन्तशुद्धं व्यवस्येत्||३७||

classical.establishes: The full sixteen-type scheme and its address: seven śuddha, six rājasa, three tāmasa. The classical locus for what moderns call mānasaprakṛti — and the text calls it sattva throughout.
classical.quote: शुद्धस्य सत्त्वस्य सप्तविधो ब्रह्मर्षिशक्रयमवरुणकुबेरगन्धर्वसत्त्वानुकारेण, राजसस्य षड्विधो दैत्यपिशाचराक्षससर्पप्रेतशकुनिसत्त्वानुकारेण, तामसस्यत्रिविधः पशुमत्स्यवनस्पतिसत्त्वानुकारेण||४०||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Sha 4/37; Kaviratna renders sattva-bheda as varieties of mind, not as a constitution.
classical.quote: Thus should be known the seven varieties of mind called Pure. Amongst these that which has been called the ' Brahmya ' mind is regarded as the Purest in consequence of its perfect (or complete) union with what is good and auspicious.

classical.establishes: Body follows mind and mind body — the warrant for WHO calling the type mental AND physical, and the reason a clean deha/mānasa split is not classical.
classical.quote: शरीरं ह्यपि सत्त्वमनुविधीयते, सत्त्वं च शरीरम्||३६||

classical.establishes: Sushruta's parallel sixteen-type scheme with the same 7/6/3 division at Sharirasthana 4/73-76; his rājasa list is not in the same order as Charaka's.
classical.quote: These seven types of men should be considered as belonging to the Sattvika group (of Sattvika mental temperament). Now hear me describe the features of men of Rajasika stamp (of mind).

distinguishFrom.why: The decisive one. Charaka never calls the sixteen types mānasaprakṛti; he calls them sattva-bheda (Sha 4/36-40), and at Vi 8/119 defines sattva as manas graded only pravara/madhya/avara.
The three universal guṇas (WHO ITA-1.9.4.2). The sixteen types derive from them but are not identical; a person is not 'a rajas'.
Fixed at conception and per Sushruta Sha 4/70-71 unalterable; WHO says mental type can be refined. Different mutability, different kind of thing.
Mental type is a baseline description, not a diagnosis. ICD-11 TM2 codes mental disorders but no constitution.

mistranslations.why: Conflates guṇas with doṣas. Vi 6/5 calls rajas and tamas the mental doṣas but pointedly excludes sattva, so there is no 'sattva dosha'.
WHO uses it, but it drops the explicitly moral and ritual content of the classical descriptions, which no personality inventory measures.
Only wrong when paired with the immutability claim borrowed from doṣaprakṛti.

openQuestions: Is mānasaprakṛti attested as a compound in any classical samhita, or entirely a modern coinage? Not found in the chapters retrieved.
Do Charaka's and Sushruta's sixteen-type lists agree item for item, or only in shape?

classical.establishes: Charaka's manasa as the third class, defined by non-attainment of the desired and encounter with the undesired. Note the form is मानस, not मानसिक.
classical.quote: त्रयो रोगा इति- निजागन्तुमानसाः| तत्र निजः शारीरदोषसमुत्थः, आगन्तुर्भूतविषवाय्वग्निसम्प्रहारादिसमुत्थः, मानसः पुनरिष्टस्यलाभाल्लाभाच्चानिष्टस्योपजायते||४५||

classical.establishes: Charaka's prescribed management of manasa roga, immediately after the definition at 11/45: it is dharma/artha/kama counselling and self-knowledge, not dravya therapy. Verse number is not legible in the scan at this point, so the verse field is left empty; the passage sits between the 11/45 definition and the rogamarga passage on the same printed page.
classical.quote: The treatment for all mental diseases is attention to the considerations of Religion, Wealth, and Pleasure, and the knowledge of how to reverentially wait upon persons that are well-conversant with those three topics, as also the knowledge of how to attend to the considerations connected with one's own self (viz., consideration in respect of one's own country, race, time, physical strength, and mental energy).

classical.establishes: The twofold psychic division rajasa/tamasa, the direct source of WHO ISTA ITA-4.2.4 to 4.2.6.
classical.quote: अतस्त्रिविधा व्याधयः प्रादुर्भवन्ति- आग्नेयाः, सौम्याः,वायव्याश्च;-द्विविधाश्चापरे- राजसाः, तामसाश्च||४||

classical.establishes: Sushruta's manasa class enumerated as affects (krodha, shoka, bhaya, harsha, vishada, irshya, asuya, dainya, matsarya, kama, lobha) arising through iccha and dvesha. Content-identical to Bhishagratna's English.
classical.quote: मानसास्तु क्रोधशोकभयहर्षविषादेर्ष्याभ्यसूयादैन्यमात्सर्यकामलोभप्रभृतयः इच्छा द्वेषभेदैर्भवन्ति

classical.establishes: Sattva (mind) as one of the two ashrayas of disease. Note Charaka's word here is sattva, not manas, which is a further lemma problem for this headword.
classical.quote: शरीरं सत्त्वसञ्ज्ञं च व्याधीनामाश्रयो मतः| तथा सुखानां, योगस्तु सुखानां कारणं समः||५५||

classical.establishes: dvayāśrayāṇāṃ vyādhīnām, diseases of the two seats, share a single threefold cause. Establishes that Charaka does not give manasika diseases a separate etiology from sharirika ones.
classical.quote: कालबुद्धीन्द्रियार्थानां योगो मिथ्या न चाति च| द्वयाश्रयाणां व्याधीनां त्रिविधो हेतुसङ्ग्रहः||५४||

distinguishFrom.why: The complementary seat. But Cha.Su.1/54 gives both seats the SAME threefold etiology, so the split is by seat and not by cause, which is the opposite of how the modern 'psychological vs physical' opposition is usually understood.

WHO ISTA ITA-1.9.3.3.13 defines mānasika-bhāvaḥ as 'Psychological or mental attributes', i.e. normal features of the mind (dhi, dhriti, smriti and the rest). These are the substrate, not the disorder, and the two are routinely conflated in English writing because both come out as 'mental factors'.
Named psychiatric NOSOLOGICAL entities in the samhitas. Manasika-roga is the class; these are members of it. ICD-11 TM2 codes entities of this kind, not the class term.

The two mental doshas are the causal factors; rajasa-roga and tamasa-roga are the resulting classes. WHO ISTA codes the disease classes (ITA-4.2.5, 4.2.6) but has no mānasadoṣa headword at all, which I confirmed by searching the full text.

Disorders attributed to possessing entities. In Charaka these fall under AGANTU (bhuta is listed in the agantu causes at Su.11/45), not under manasa, even though their presentation is psychiatric. This is one of the most consequential misfilings in English Ayurvedic writing.

mistranslations.why: Imports a clinical specialty and a diagnostic apparatus that the classification does not carry. Sushruta's manasa list at 1/25 is a list of ordinary affects including joy (harsha), which no psychiatric nosology treats as a disorder.
Wrong on both sides. Manasika is seated in manas; the psychosomatic category in WHO ISTA sits under a different headword, ādhyātmikarogaḥ (ITA-4.2.11).

Defensible but carries a modern implication of persistent pathology. Charaka's definition at Su.11/45 (non-attainment of the desired, encounter with the undesired) covers ordinary situational distress, and his prescribed management is counselling on dharma, artha and kama.
Too narrow for Charaka, whose manasa class is defined by a desire relation rather than by affect, and too narrow for the rajasa/tamasa scheme of Cha.Ni.1/4, which classifies by guna dominance.

openQuestions: Is mānasika (with -ika) attested as a disease-class term in the samhitas, or only mānasa? Every classical instance retrieved uses मानस/मानसाः. The -ika form is what WHO ISTA and modern textbooks use.

How do Charaka's two mental schemes relate: manasa as a third class alongside nija and agantu (Su.11/45), versus rajasa/tamasa as a twofold psychic division (Ni.1/4)? No retrieved source reconciles them.
Where do bhutonmada and the graha disorders sit, given that bhuta is listed under agantu causes?

classical.establishes: Manda is an attribute of both pṛthvī- and jala-dominant substances. Kaviratna: 'Amongst objects those that are principally heavy, sharp or pungent, hard, mild, immobile, clear, thick, gross, and possessed of scent, are regarded as appertaining to Earth.'
classical.quote: तत्रद्रव्याणिगुरुखरकठिनमन्दस्थिरविशदसान्द्रस्थूलगन्धगुणबहुलानि पार्थिवानि, तान्युपचयसङ्घातगौरवस्थैर्यकराणि; द्रवस्निग्धशीतमन्दमृदुपिच्छिलरसगुणबहुलान्याप्यानि, तान्युपक्लेदस्नेहबन्धविष्यन्दमार्दवप्रह्लादकराणि;

classical.verse: 521 (printed ५२१ in the Trikamji/Nirnaya Sagar ed., Su.Sū.46; the manda half-line shares the number with the vyavāyī half-line. The web texts' 522 reflects a different hemistich pairing, not a different text.)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's one-line karma of manda: 'mando yātrākaraḥ smṛtaḥ'. Dalhaṇa (Nibandhasaṅgraha, ad loc.) glosses it 'yātrākara iti śarīrasthāyitvād dehasya yātrāṃ vartanaṃ karoti' — manda is yātrākara because, by making the body persist, it carries on the body's course (vartana). The record's working gloss 'sustaining the body's course' is now the commentator's own, not an inference; and the verse number is 521 in the printed edition, 522 only in the web Sanskrit texts.
classical.quote: सरोऽनुलोमनः प्रोक्तो, मन्दो यात्राकरः स्मृतः ॥ व्यवायी चाखिलं देहं व्याप्य पाकाय कल्पते ॥५२१॥
classical.sourceUrl: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.327618 (page image leaf n292, printed p. 232; Dalhaṇa leaf n293, printed p. 233)
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Manda is the second named guṇa in Vagbhata's list of ten-with-opposites (guru, manda, hima, snigdha, ślakṣṇa, sāndra, mṛdu, sthira, sūkṣma, viśada). No public-domain English; no quotation.

distinguishFrom.why: The most important distinction in this cluster and the one most often lost. mandāgni is the state or type of agni; agnimāndya is the condition of that state obtaining. WHO codes mandāgni (ITA-2.6.11, ITA-5.11.1) and has no entry for agnimāndya at all; ICD-11 TM2 carries agnimāndyam as an index term and no mandāgni. They are not interchangeable across standards.
manda is uniformly slow; viṣama alternates. WHO's viṣamāgni definition unhelpfully includes 'diminished', which erodes the boundary.
NAMASTE treats it as a synonym under DB-1. Some textbook traditions treat agnisāda as a distinct, deeper exhaustion of agni. The synonymy is a NAMASTE editorial decision, not a classical given.

Listed at Ca.Sū.20 as one of the twenty kaphaja disorders, and glossed by NAMASTE as agnimāndya. Whether it is a synonym of mandāgni or a specifically kaphaja subtype is not settled in the sources I saw.
Ajīrṇa is the event of non-digestion of a given meal; mandāgni is the standing capacity. ICD-11 SM3B groups them under one code, which erases the distinction.
Ca.Ci.15.56 makes weak agni the cause of grahaṇī vitiation; the disease is the sequel, not the state.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's 1890s choice. In modern English 'mild' reads as benign or moderate, the opposite of the intended deficiency. An obsolete rendering that should not be revived.

Systemic-metabolic framing for what both Sushruta and WHO's disorder entry define by gastrointestinal performance and a specific symptom list.
Usable for ajīrṇa, but as a rendering of mandāgni it drops the standing-capacity sense and makes the term an event.

classical.establishes: THE locus classicus: aggravated doṣas, having approached the hṛdaya, OBSTRUCT the manovaha srotāṃsi and produce unmāda. This is Caraka's only substantive use of the term, and it is pathological — the channel is named in the account of a disease, never enumerated among the thirteen. I quoted the closing clause; the full sentence on the retrieved page is a long etiological list.
classical.quote: ...अभ्युदीर्णा दोषाः प्रकुपिता हृदयमुपसृत्य मनोवहानि स्रोतांस्यावृत्य जनयन्त्युन्मादम्||४||

classical.establishes: Decisive for the entry: immediately after listing the thirteen, Caraka says that for the supra-sensory entities beginning with sattva (i.e. mind), it is the ENTIRE sentient body that is the passage and the seat — not any particular srotas. This is why manovaha is not in the list, and it is an argument against localising it.
classical.quote: वातपित्तश्लेष्मणां पुनः सर्वशरीरचराणां सर्वाणि स्रोतांस्ययनभूतानि, तद्वदतीन्द्रियाणां पुनः सत्त्वादीनां केवलं चेतनावच्छरीरमयनभूतमधिष्ठानभूतं च|

classical.establishes: Suśruta's parallel: saṃjñāvaha srotas obstructed by doṣas produces loss of consciousness and memory in apasmāra. I confirmed the chapter is LXI by locating the surrounding chapter headings in the retrieved scan. Like Caraka's, this is a pathological, not a taxonomic, mention.
classical.quote: The sense-carrying Srotas (channels) of the body overwhelmed by the concerted action of the deranged Doshas bring in a predominance of Rajas and Tamas (Nescience) causing the patient unconscious and forgetful of all past memories.

distinguishFrom.why: The faculty, not a channel. Caraka's Vi.5/4 warning applies with special force here: what a srotas is, what it carries, and where it sits are all distinct.

Suśruta's term (Uttara 61 and, per secondary sources, Uttara 46/7). Bhishagratna renders it 'sense-carrying', i.e. consciousness/sensation rather than mind. Treating the two as identical is an interpretive move, not a translation.
Both are rooted in the hṛdaya; the secondary literature links manovaha specifically to the 'ten dhamanīs' of the heart that Ca.Vi.5/8 assigns to rasavaha. If that link holds they share a substrate.
Authors who read majjā as nervous tissue end up with two candidate 'neural' channels. Classically majjāvaha is rooted in bone and joints; manovaha in the heart.

distinguishFrom.term: hṛdaya as anatomical heart vs seat of mind
distinguishFrom.why: The whole localisation of manovaha depends on which hṛdaya is meant, and the texts do not disambiguate.

mistranslations.why: Neither text names the head or brain here; both name the hṛdaya. The brain identification is a modern overlay and would contradict the classical root.
manovaha is not in any classical enumeration. Caraka's Vi.5/7 explicitly gives the mind the whole sentient body as its seat instead of a channel.

mistranslations.rendering: 'psychic channels' / 'channels of consciousness' presented as a defined anatomical structure
mistranslations.why: Both classical mentions are pathological (obstruction producing unmāda / apasmāra). There is no classical description of the channel's root, course or normal function.

classical.establishes: The count of 107, the five structural classes with their exact numbers (11+41+27+8+20 = 107), and the closure claim that there are no others. OCR artefacts in the scan are preserved above as retrieved.
classical.quote: There are one hundred and seven Marmas (in the human organism), which may be divided into five classes, such as the Mansa-Marmas, Sira-Marmas, Snayu-Marmas, Asthi-Marmas and the Sandhi-Marmas. Indeed there are no other Marmas (vulnerable or vital parts) to be found in the body than the preceding ones. 2. ... There are eleven Mansa-Marmas (vulnerable muscle-joints); forty-one Sira-Marmas (similar veins, anastomosis); twenty-seven Snayu-Marmas (vital ligament-unions); eight Asthi-Marmas (bone-unions) and twenty Sandhi-Marmas (vulnerable joints). 3.

classical.establishes: The definition proper: marma = firm union (sandhāna) of the five structure types, constituting seats of prāṇa. 'Pratna' in the quote is an OCR corruption of 'Prana' and is reproduced verbatim as it appears in the scan.
classical.quote: Firm unions of Mansa (muscles), Sira (veins), Snayu (ligaments), bones or bone-joints are called Marmas (or vital parts of the body) which naturally and specifically form the seats of life (Pratna), and hence a hurt to any one of the Marmas invariably produces such symptoms as arise from the hurt of a certain Marma.

classical.establishes: Charaka's trimarma doctrine (prāṇa established in hṛdaya, mūrdhan, basti) AND his prescription for marma care: avoidance of injury, adherence to healthy regimen, and treatment of arising affliction. Note that 'paripālana' here is protection, not stimulation.
classical.quote: हृदये मूर्ध्नि बस्तौ च नृणां प्राणाः प्रतिष्ठिताः| तस्मात्तेषां सदा यत्नं कुर्वीत परिपालने||९|| आबाधवर्जनं नित्यं स्वस्थवृत्तानुवर्तनम्| उत्पन्नार्तिविघातश्च मर्मणां परिपालनम्||१०||

classical.establishes: That marma is a constituent of the madhyama rogamārga, and that Charaka's exemplary marmas are basti, hṛdaya and mūrdhan — the trimarma, not Sushruta's 107.
classical.quote: मर्माणि पुनर्बस्तिहृदयमूर्धादीनि, अस्थिसन्धयोऽस्थिसंयोगास्तत्रोपनिबद्धाश्च स्नायुकण्डराः, स मध्यमो रोगमार्गः

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ITA-3.16.1 lists TEN 'seats of vital life force' (temporal regions, heart, urinary bladder, head, throat, rectum, blood, semen, ojas). Marmas number 107. Both are called 'seats of life' in English, and Charaka's Sū. 28.7 passage on grave disease distinguishes prāṇāyatana-arising from marma-injuring as separate aggravating factors.
Charaka's three (hṛdaya, mūrdhan, basti); Sushruta's 107 is a different enumeration in a different text. 'The three most vulnerable' (WHO ITA-3.16.3) is not a subset ranking Sushruta endorses.

The comparison is a live research question (PMID 37494833), not an identity. Marmas are defined by anatomical confluence and sized in aṅgulas; acupoints sit on a meridian system that has no counterpart in Sushruta.
The Tamil Siddha tradition's vital-spot system, historically related but with its own enumeration and literature. Routinely conflated in English-language writing.
Sandhi-marma is only one of the five classes (twenty of the 107). Not every joint is a marma and not every marma is a joint.

mistranslations.why: Sushruta assigns each marma a dimension in aṅgula (finger-widths) — they are areas, not points. 'Point' is an import from acupuncture vocabulary and drives the false equation with acupoints.
No classical text assigns prāṇa-flow channels to marmas in the way the popular literature implies; VI.22 grounds them in structural confluence.
Reverses the classical polarity entirely. Both Sushruta (injury produces death, deformity or pain) and Charaka (Si. 9.10: ābādhavarjana, avoidance of injury) treat marmas as things to PROTECT.
Used loosely for trimarma. Basti, hṛdaya and mūrdhan are organs/regions in that triad, but the 107 are mostly junctional soft-tissue sites, not organs.

openQuestions: Whether Charaka anywhere accepts the 107 enumeration, or works only with trimarma plus scattered references.

The relationship between the five FUNCTIONAL classes (sadyaḥprāṇahara, kālāntaraprāṇahara, viśalyaghna, vaikalyakara, rujākara — described at Su.Śā. VI.16-21 in Bhishagratna) and the five STRUCTURAL classes at VI.2. Both are fivefold and are frequently confused.
Whether marma locations have been mapped to modern anatomical landmarks with any published inter-observer reliability.

classical.establishes: Medas' two functions: snehana (unctuousness/glossiness) and the nourishment of asthi. The second is the one that gets lost when medas is read as adipose tissue, since adipose tissue is not held to build bone.
classical.quote: The fat gives rise to the glossiness (formation of oily or albuminous matter) of the body and primarily contributes towards the firmness and growth of the bones.

classical.establishes: Medo-kṣaya presenting as splenomegaly and empty joints. Neither has any relation to loss of adipose tissue, and the passage is strong evidence against the simple equation.
classical.quote: The loss of fat is followed by such symptoms as the enlargement of the spleen, a sense of emptiness in the joints, and a peculiar dryness of the skin and a craving for cold and emollient meat.

classical.establishes: Medo-vṛddhi: central adiposity plus body odour plus cough and breathlessness. The nearest a classical sign list in this set comes to a recognisable modern syndrome.
classical.quote: An excess of fat in the body imparts an oily gloss to the skin. The sides of the abdomen are increased in bulk, and the body emits a fetid smell, and the person is assailed with cough and dyspnoea.

classical.establishes: The srotorodha (channel-obstruction) account of obesity: excess medas physically blocks the channels and starves the later dhātus. This is the mechanism by which the tradition explains why the obese can be simultaneously overnourished and depleted.
classical.quote: the growth of the rest of the root-principles of the body such as, lymph chyle, albumen, semen, etc., is considerably arrested owing to the deposit of fatty matter within the channels of the internal passages of the body, thus seriously affecting his bodily strength. An obese or excessively corpulent person is likely to be afflicted with any of the following diseases such as, urethral discharges, eruptions, boils, carbuncles, fever, fistula in ano, or with any of the diseases which are caused by a deranged state of the bodily Vayu ; and such attacks are invariably found to terminate in death.

classical.establishes: Vasā as a distinct substance from medas, with its own functions and a stated sex difference. WHO classes vasā as the upadhātu of māṃsa (ITA-2.3.5), not of medas; Sushruta discusses it in the medas section.
classical.quote: This fatty matter (Vasa) predominates in the female organism and produces its peculiar softness, beauty and pleasing shape, causes the growth of scanty but soft hair on its surface. It strengthens the eyesight and increases the energy of the body, improves its power of digestion and heightens its glow and complexion.

classical.establishes: Sweat is the waste fraction of medas. The OCR has 'sweet' for 'sweat'; the reading is unambiguous from context and from the parallel lists, but the misprint is left visible here rather than silently corrected.

classical.establishes: Medo-sāra as a constitutional type recognised by unctuousness across many sites, including voice and excreta - not by body fat.
classical.quote: Of men that have the fat as the predominating element in their constitution, the symptoms are a complexion that is oily, a voice that is so, and eyes and hair and bristles and nails and teeth and lips and urine and faeces that are oily.

distinguishFrom.why: Muscle fat / intramuscular fat. Classed by WHO as upadhātu of māṃsa (ITA-2.3.5) but discussed by Sushruta within the medas section, with its own functions and a stated female predominance. The classification differs between sources.
Marrow, the fat-like content of bone. Both are unctuous, and the two are adjacent in the chain via asthi. The distinction is site, not substance.
Unctuousness as a quality, and also the oleaginous medicines used in oleation therapy. Medas is the bodily substance; sneha is a property and a drug class.

Shares unctuousness, coldness and heaviness with medas and is routinely implicated with it in sthaulya. A doṣa, not a dhātu, and Sushruta's obesity account runs through channel obstruction and vāyu, not through kapha alone.
The disease of excess medas, not the dhātu itself. Modern writing often uses 'medas' where it means the disorder.
Brain matter, sometimes described as fat-like and occasionally conflated with both medas and majjā in secondary literature.

mistranslations.why: Too narrow, and WHO's own gloss says so ('adipose tissue and other lipids'). It also makes Sushruta's claim that medas nourishes bone, and that medo-kṣaya presents as splenomegaly and empty joints, unintelligible.

mistranslations.rendering: fat, read as body fat percentage
mistranslations.why: Medo-sāra is recognised by unctuousness of voice, nails, urine and faeces, not by fatness. Reading medas as an amount of fat discards the entire quality dimension the sāra examination depends on.
Kaviratna's Latin pharmacopoeial term for lard. Quotable as a period rendering; unusable now, and it wrongly suggests a purified substance.

Occasionally used in clinical papers on the strength of the dyslipidaemia analogy. No classical passage retrieved supports a biochemical class reading, and the analogy is the researcher's, not the text's.

openQuestions: Whether vasā belongs to māṃsa (WHO ISTA) or to medas (Sushruta's placement) is a live discrepancy between an international standard and a mula text. Neither was retrieved in a form that settles it.
Sushruta's medo-kṣaya sign of splenomegaly has no explanation in any retrieved source and does not appear to have been discussed in the indexed literature.
The mechanism by which medas is said to nourish asthi is asserted and never explained. It is the single least intuitive link in the dhātu chain.
No study has tested whether people classified as medo-sāra differ in any measurable lipid or body-composition variable from those who are not.

distinguishFrom.why: The omental root, not the channel. Note it is also the only srotas root that WHO/NAMASTE render with a confident single biomedical structure.

Caraka gives BOTH channels a root in medas (medovaha: vṛkka+vapāvahana; svedavaha: medas + hair follicles), so sweat and fat channels are linked through the same dhātu — a frequent source of conflation.
Three different fatty substances in Ayurveda; medas is the dhātu this channel serves, vasā is muscle fat, majjā is marrow with its own srotas.
The disorder (obesity) NAMASTE associates with this srotas, not the channel.

mistranslations.why: Collapses a transport concept into a tissue. Neither text describes fat storage; both describe roots and injury signs.
A modern extrapolation from sthaulya and prameha associations, with no textual warrant in either locus.

vṛkka appears here as the root of the FAT channel, not the urine channel (which is rooted in basti and vaṅkṣaṇa). Reading vṛkka as 'kidney = renal excretion' imports the wrong physiology into this entry.

openQuestions: Why do WHO and NAMASTE adopt Caraka's vapāvahana and drop Suśruta's kaṭi without comment?
Is vṛkka in this passage the kidney, or (as some commentators argue) perirenal fat?

distinguishFrom.why: The channel, not the substance; separate lexicon record (Ca.Vi.5/8).
Urinary diseases (retention, dysuria); WHO ITA-5.39.10 mūtrāghātaḥ. Mūtrakṛcchra is a SIGN of mūtra-kṣaya at Ca.Su.17/71 as well as a disease name.
WHO ITA-5.4.3 (mala-disorder) and ITA-5.39.16 (urinary disease) carry the same Sanskrit; NAMC CA-1 vs EJ-3.4 likewise.
The watery waste that urine carries (AH Su 11/5 kleda-vāhana); urine is the vehicle, kleda the load. The kleda paper (PMID 42127454) treats this distinction.
The bladder that urine fills (Su.Su.15/5 basti-pūraṇa); frequently conflated with 'urine' in loose English ('basti disorders').
Medieval urine examination (Basavarājīyam, Yogaratnākara); not in the Bṛhattrayī and not part of the definition of mūtra.

mistranslations.rendering: 'washing or draining off the waste or refuse matter of the organism' (Bhishagratna, Su.Su.15/5)
mistranslations.why: Over-translation of vikleda-kṛt; the Sanskrit assigns moistening/kleda-production, and the 'carrying away of kleda' wording actually comes from AH Su 11/5. Quote Bhishagratna as his rendering, not as Sushruta's doctrine.
WHO 2.4.4 and Charaka Chi 15/18 class urine as āhāramala (waste of food digestion), not dhātumala; NAMASTE SAT-B.458's 'metabolism-only' definition of kiṭṭa sits awkwardly with its own SAT-B.460.

openQuestions: Charaka's own statement of urine's function (as distinct from its origin) was not located in this pass; the function clause in modern standards traces to AH Su 11/5 and Su.Su.15/5. A human should check Ca.Su.28 and Ca.Vi.5 commentaries.
Dalhana on vikleda in Su.Su.15/5 not checked.

classical.establishes: That Yogaratnakara has a titled mūtraparīkṣā section: urine collected at the last watch of night, held in a glass vessel, first stream discarded and middle stream kept; a drop of oil placed on it with a grass stalk; spreading quickly = sādhya, not spreading = kṛcchrasādhya/asādhya. classical.quote: ॥ अथ मूत्रपरीक्षा ॥ अथातः संप्रवक्ष्यामि मृजस्य च परीक्षणम्‌ । सेन विज्ञातमात्रेण रोगचिन्हं पर कार्यते ॥ १ ॥ निशान्तया्म घटिकाचतष्टये उत्याप्य वेद्यः किरु रोगिणं च। मूत्र धृतं काचमये च पात्रे इूयादयं तत्सततं परीक्ष्य ॥ २ ॥ ... परीक्षा वि- धिवत्काया रोगिगत्रस्य तत्त्वतः | तृणेन दापयेत्तेखविन्दुं तत्रातिरूधवात्‌ ॥ ॥ ९ ॥ विकासित तंरुपथाशु मत्रे साध्यः सरोग न विकासित चत्‌ । स्यात्क- एसाध्यस्तछरगे त्वसाध्यो नागाज्ञेनेनेव कृता परीक्ना ॥६॥

Channels carrying urine, not the examination of urine.

classical.establishes: Caraka's causes of vitiation for the urine-carrying channels: taking water or food, or approaching a woman, while under the urge to urinate; suppression of the urge; and the state of one who is emaciated or injured. Vi.5 gives the vitiating causes for thirteen srotas across verses 10 to 22, and mutravaha is the eleventh of the thirteen, at verse 20, between sukravaha at 19 and varcovaha at 21.

classical.establishes: Suśruta's root = bladder + penis/urethra, against Caraka's bladder + groins. 'constipation or epistaxis in the bladder' is Bhishagratna's own odd English and should be flagged, not relied on.
classical.quote: The two urine carrying Srotas (channels) have their roots in the bladder and the penis (urethra). An injury to any of these is marked by constipation or epistaxis in the bladder, retention of urine, and numbness of the genitals.

distinguishFrom.why: basti is the bladder (the root organ) and also the name of the enema therapy — a standing ambiguity in Ayurvedic English.
Caraka's second root; rendered 'groin' by WHO but read as the ureters/inguinal region by others. It is not the same as Suśruta's śepha.
Modern writers map udakavaha to 'fluid balance' and then to renal function; the texts keep water homeostasis (palate/kloma) separate from urine (bladder/groin).
vṛkka (kidney) is the root of MEDOVAHA in Caraka, not of mūtravaha — the most counter-intuitive fact in the whole srotas scheme and a constant source of error.

mistranslations.why: Neither text names the kidney as a root of this channel. In Caraka the kidneys (vṛkka) are the root of the FAT channel. Rendering mūtravaha srotas as 'kidneys' silently rewrites the text.
Bhishagratna's phrasing is garbled English for obstruction/haemorrhage; quoting it as a clinical sign misrepresents both the Sanskrit and the translator.
A plausible modern reading but not what WHO ('groin') or the Sanskrit says; presenting it as settled is unwarranted.

openQuestions: What is vaṅkṣaṇa anatomically — inguinal region, ureters, or both?
Why does Caraka place the kidneys under medovaha rather than mūtravaha? Is this a physiological claim about perirenal fat or a different vṛkka?

classical.establishes: Yogaratnakara's nāḍīparīkṣā: palpate below the thumb root of the right hand with the physician's right hand; the pulse reveals vāta, pitta, kapha, dual and triple involvement and the distinction sādhya/asādhya; synonyms snāyu, nāḍī, haṃsī, dhamanī, dharaṇī, dharā, tantukī, jīvanajñānā.
classical.quote: नारीमङषठम्राधः र्एशेदक्षिणके करे । ज्ञानां रोगिणो वेथो निजदक्तिण- पाणिना ॥ १ ॥ ... वातं पित्तं कफं न्द्रं त्रितयं सानिपासिकम्‌ । साध्यासाध्यविवेकं च स्वं नादी प्रकारयेत्‌ ॥ ७ ॥ ्नायुर्नादी ततो हंसी धमनी धरणी धरा । तन्वु- की जीवनज्ञाना शब्दाः पर्यायवाचकाः ॥ ८ ॥ ... अङ्षटमूरमागे या धमनी जीवसाक्िणी । तचेष्टया सुखं दःखं ज्ञेयं कायस्य पण्डितेः ॥ १० ॥

distinguishFrom.why: In Charaka/Sushruta nāḍī is a tubular structure (nāḍīvraṇa = sinus, nāḍīsveda = tube fomentation, nāḍīyantra = tubular instrument), not the pulse; the pulse sense is post-classical.

Sharngadhara calls the pulsating vessel a dhamanī; nāḍī in his usage is the felt pulse, and Yogaratnakara lists dhamanī among its synonyms, so the words overlap but are not interchangeable in anatomical contexts.
Pulse examination is one application of sparśana (touch), the second of the AH trividhā parīkṣā; sparśana is the broader act.
Modern coinage used by branded schools (e.g., 'Maharishi Nādi-Vigyān'); not a classical title.
Independent system with different positions, depths and theory; cross-mapping is speculative.

mistranslations.why: Rests on the yogic/tantric sense of nāḍī as subtle channel; Sharngadhara explicitly names an artery (dhamanī) at the thumb root.
Overstates: Yogaratnakara says the pulse 'reveals' dosha involvement and prognosis; the texts do not present it as a stand-alone diagnostic of disease entities.
No Vedic or Brihattrayi source; earliest located text is 13th-century Sharngadhara.

classical.establishes: The compound nasyakarma in Charaka's daily-regimen chapter: one who uses it in season and as prescribed gains the benefits listed in 57-62 (sense organs, hair, head and neck).
classical.quote: वर्षे  वर्षेऽणुतैलं च कालेषु त्रिषु ना चरेत्||५६|| नस्यकर्म यथाकालं यो यथोक्तं निषेवते||५७||

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed 48-49 (standard 5.56-57 per carakasamhitaonline; he runs eight behind in this block)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering of Su 5.56-57, evidence of his English, not of Charaka's directive: he renders nasyakarma (5.57) as 'snuff (of oil)', keeps 'anutaila', and in his footnote reports the Commentator's gloss ('oil that is good for the anu or the senses'), which he also folds into his running text as 'or such oils as are beneficial to the senses'. His first sentence prints the opposite of the Sanskrit: वर्षे वर्षेऽणुतैलं च कालेषु त्रिषु ना चरेत् | प्रावृट्शरद्वसन्तेषु गतमेघे नभस्तले (ना = नरः) prescribes anutaila every year in the rainy season, autumn and spring when the sky is clear; Kaviratna read ना चरेत् as न आचरेत् and printed 'These should not, however, be used when the sky remains cloudless in these three seasons'.
classical.quote: One should at all times use anutaila or such oils as are beneficial to the senses. These should not, however, be used when the sky remains cloudless in these three seasons, viz., the rainy season, the autumn, and the spring. He who uses snuff (of oil) in proper times and as directed will have his eyes and nose and ears uninjured.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (OCR text; spacing normalized)
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed 51-54 (page image leaf 90, printed p. 59: '51' after 'become relieved', '52' and '53' after 'acquire great strength', '*54' after 'decrepitude does not prevail in such parts'; the quote stops before that last sentence of 54). Standard Su 5.59b-62 (carakasamhitaonline): मन्यास्तम्भः शिरःशूलमर्दितं हनुसङ्ग्रहः ||59|| ... न चास्य रोगाः सहसा प्रभवन्त्यूर्ध्वजत्रुजाः ||62||; the omitted sentence is 63a जीर्यतश्चोत्तमाङ्गेषु जरा न लभते बलम्. His printed 50 / standard 58 (eyes, hair and beard) is not quoted.
classical.establishes: Benefits Charaka attaches to nasya with anutaila in the daily-regimen chapter, in Kaviratna's English: relief of stiff-neck, headache, ardita, lock-jaw, coryza, hemicrania and head tremor (5.59b-60a); strength to the sira, joints, snayu and kandara of the head (60b-61a); a clear, full face, a smooth firm deep voice, purified and strengthened senses (61b-62a); 'parts above the clavicle' = urdhvajatru (62b). The passage does not call this pratimarsa; the procedure the chapter prescribes for this oil (5.68-69; Kaviratna's printed 60-61) is half a pala by cotton wick after oiling and fomenting the head, repeated over seven days, i.e. a marsa-dose nasya.
classical.quote: By the use of such snuff, stiff-neck, headache, hemiplegia (or paralysis of the muscles on one side of the face and neck), lock-jaw, coryza, hemicrania, and trembling of the head, become relieved. Moistened by such snuff, the nerves, the joints, and the tendons and longer arteries of the head and skull of such a person acquire great strength. The face becomes lighted and full; the voice becomes smooth, steady, and deep; and all the organs become purified (of defects) and acquire great strength. Diseases of parts above the clavicle do not easily appear in such a person.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's two-fold and five-fold typology of nasya in Bhishagratna's words; 'Nasya' is both the genus and one species.
classical.quote: The term “Nasya” (Snuff) is so called from the fact of its being composed of the powders of any drugs or of any Sneha (oleaginous substance) cooked with such drug or drugs, to be stuffed into the nostrils. It may be broadly divided into two kinds, viz. :— Shiro-Virecana (errhines) and Snehana (contributor of oleaginous principles); and may, however, be further grouped under five specific heads, viz. :— Nasya, Shiro-Virecana, Pratimarsha (a medicated Sneha poured into the nostrils to be discharged into the mouth), Avapida (the expressed juice of any drug put into the nostrils in drops by pressing it with the palms then and there) and Pradhamana (a medicinal snuff blown into the nostrils with the help of a blowpipe). Of these, the Nasya (snuff) Shiro-Virecana (errhines) are pre-eminently the most effective. Pratimarsha is a Nasya while Avapida and Pradhamana are Shiro-Virecana (errhines).
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1911); the parentheses are his glosses

Medicated smoke inhaled through nose or mouth; Sushruta Chi.40 and Charaka Su.5 treat it in the same chapter as nasya, but it is a separate procedure.

Biomedical delivery forms with a local aim; nasya's stated aim is action on ūrdhvajatru (above the clavicle) disorders and sense organs (Ca.Su.5.57-62).
An errhine provokes sneezing and discharge; that is only the śirovirecana type. WHO's own ITA-9.2.2 uses 'errhine therapy' while ITA-9.2.86 uses 'Intranasal administration'.

The word 'nidana' is explained as 'something by which disease is ascertained correctly.'

distinguishFrom.why: The five-member set. Nidāna is its first member AND its name, which is the single commonest confusion in this vocabulary. Kaviratna's footnote states the double sense outright.

Declared anarthāntara with nidāna at Ca. Ni. 1.3, and WHO gives both the same code. But Kaviratna's footnote says 'Hetu is generally limited to the circumstances that precede', and Charaka uses hetu in a wholly different epistemological sense at Vi. 8.33 (a means of knowing), where nidāna is never used.
The section of a saṃhitā. A textual division, not a concept. 'Nidāna of fever' in a chapter title means the whole diagnostic account of fever, not its cause alone.
Nidāna is what acts on the body from outside the pathology; samprāpti is the process inside it. WHO separates them into different sub-chapters (4.4 Etiology, 4.5 Pathology).

A disease acting as the cause of another disease (WHO ITA-4.8.34; MN 1.15-20 gives the chain jvara to raktapitta to śoṣa). Not a kind of nidāna in the ordinary sense: the causative item here is itself a disease.
Withdrawal of the causative factor, a treatment principle (WHO ITA-9.1.56). Frequently cited as though it were part of the diagnostic nidāna, which it is not.

mistranslations.why: Reads the section-title sense into the term sense. Charaka's Ni. 1.7 defines nidāna as kāraṇa. Diagnosis is rogaparīkṣā / rogaviniścaya, which WHO codes separately at ITA-4.3.1 and ITA-4.1.1.
Confuses cause with process. WHO puts nidāna in 4.4 Etiology and samprāpti in 4.5 Pathology.
A risk factor is a statistical association in a population. Ca. Ni. 1.3's three nidāna are a causal taxonomy (misuse of the senses, error of judgement, the action of time), not population-derived.
Loses the distinction WHO codes at ITA-4.4.3 and ITA-4.4.4 between utpādaka-hetu (originating) and vyañjaka-hetu (aggravating/manifesting). 'Trigger' names only the second.

openQuestions: Whether Sushruta has a corresponding synonym list. I searched Bhishagratna's Sutrasthana volume (OCR full text) and found the kriyākāla framework at Sūtra 21 but no nidāna-synonym verse. That negative needs proper confirmation against the Sanskrit.
How Chakrapani's commentary reconciles the two senses. Not retrieved.
Whether NAMASTE codes nidāna and under what English. namaste.ayush.gov.in returns 200 at root but 302 on the terminologies path; the machine-readable data was not reachable.

distinguishFrom.why: Its first member and also its name. The set has no standalone name in Charaka's verse; nidāna-pañcaka is a later coinage.

Sushruta's six-stage temporal scheme (sañcaya to bheda). The pañcaka is a checklist of evidence types to be gathered; kriyākāla is a sequence of stages in time. Bhishagratna's Sūtra 21 develops the second with no mention of the first.

Methods of examination — how the physician obtains information (perception, inference, testimony; ten factors of the patient). The pañcaka is what the information is about. Charaka keeps them in different sthānas.

The eightfold clinical examination (pulse, urine, stool, tongue, and so on). A later scheme, not classical in Charaka, and routinely presented alongside the pañcaka as though the two were the same kind of thing.
The activity and its endpoint. WHO codes these separately at ITA-4.3.1 and ITA-4.1.1. The pañcaka is the instrument, not the act or the conclusion.

mistranslations.why: WHO's own head term, but 'criteria' implies each member is a test with a threshold. Four of the five are descriptive categories of evidence; only upaśaya involves anything like a decision rule.
Suggests five kinds of diagnosis rather than five sources of evidence for one diagnosis.
Only upaśaya is differential in operation. The other four are not comparative.
Reads as a fixed obligatory set, which the Ashtanga Hridaya commentary tradition denies: the retrieved AH page states that knowledge of all five is not essential for every disease.

openQuestions: Where the compound nidāna-pañcaka first appears. It is NOT in Charaka Ni. 1: I searched the retrieved Sanskrit page for निदानपञ्च and पञ्चक and got zero occurrences. WHO's ITA-4.3.2 gives it as a Sanskrit headword, so it is established usage somewhere. Madhava Nidana's chapter is titled Pañca Nidāna Lakṣaṇa, which is close but not the same compound. Someone should trace the first attestation.

Whether the third member is liṅga or rūpa. Charaka Ni. 1.6 says liṅga; Ashtanga Hridaya Ni. 1.2 says rūpa; Ca. Ni. 1.9 then declares them synonymous. The modern name of the member follows Vagbhata, not Charaka.
Whether anupaśaya is a sixth member or the negative half of the fourth. Sources split, and Madhava Nidana chapter 1 treats the pair together at 1.8-9 while the set is still called five.

The Devanagari निदानपञ्चक is given here from the WHO index entry, whose Devanagari column extracted with damaged glyphs from the PDF. I did not sight clean Devanagari for the compound in a Sanskrit source.

classical.establishes: The locus classicus: in brief, the application of treatment (kriyāyoga) is nidānaparivarjana; in detail it is the counteraction of vāta and the other doṣas.

classical.translator: Sanskrit text (no translator); wikisource line breaks shown as ' / :'

classical.chapter: I (Diseases of the eye and its appendages)
classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 12-13 (his numbering; corresponds to Sanskrit 1.24-25 in the Hari Sastri edition)
classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's rendering of Ut.1.25; note that it appears inside the eye-disease chapter, which is where Sushruta states the general maxim.
classical.quote: The simple maxim or principle to be followed in the treatment of a disease is simply to forego the primary pathological causes of that disease. The special remedial measures that would pacify the different Doshas, Vayu, etc. have been described in detail.

distinguishFrom.why: Nidāna means both cause and the science of diagnosis; nidānaparivarjana is avoidance of causes, not of diagnosis. Bhishagratna's 'Nidana' references in vol. 3 are to Madhava's Nidāna text.

Treatment opposed to the cause (Charaka's three-fold scheme hetu-, vyādhi-, ubhaya-viparīta); nidānaparivarjana removes exposure, hetuviparīta counteracts its effect. The Charaka locus was not verified in this pass.
Breaking the pathogenesis once established; nidānaparivarjana acts before or alongside, on the inputs.
WHO ITA-9.1.55 'Creating conditions hostile to cause', a neighbouring entry that is active opposition rather than avoidance.
Wholesome and unwholesome regimen; apathya-tyāga overlaps nidānaparivarjana but is framed as diet-and-conduct rather than cause.

mistranslations.why: Parivarjana is abandoning or keeping away from; Sushruta's own detailed counterpart ('pratīghāta' of the doṣas) is the active counteraction, kept separate in the same verse.
Sushruta states it as the compendious form of treatment (kriyāyoga), i.e. for the diseased; WHO's description makes it a prerequisite for cure and for preventing recurrence.

mistranslations.rendering: 'forego the primary pathological causes' (Bhishagratna) read as a technical term
mistranslations.why: It is his paraphrase; 'pathological causes' imports 1900s pathology into nidāna.

openQuestions: Whether Charaka uses the compound nidānaparivarjana anywhere was not established; a grep of the local Charaka Sanskrit corpora found no hit, but the corpora are incomplete and a single spelling was searched.
Whether Ashtanga Hridaya or Madhava Nidana carry the maxim was not checked.

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji, as printed on carakasamhitaonline.com) 21/35; Kaviratna prints his aphorism number 31 after this passage
classical.establishes: The definition of when sleep occurs. Sanskrit seen at carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Ashtauninditiya_Adhyaya: यदा तु मनसि क्लान्ते कर्मात्मानः क्लमान्विताः | विषयेभ्यो निवर्तन्ते तदा स्वपिति मानवः||३५||. Kaviratna's footnote (his own, not the text): 'Sleep, according to this definition, is a total suspension of mental faculties as also the senses'.
classical.quote: When, the mind being fatigued, they that are the souls of action (viz., the senses), becoming fatigued, recede from their objects, it is then that one sleeps.

classical.establishes: Effects dependent on sleep. Sanskrit seen: निद्रायत्तं सुखं दुःखं पुष्टिः कार्श्यं बलाबलम्| वृषता क्लीबता ज्ञानमज्ञानं जीवितं न च||३६||. Note '(judicious and injudicious)' is Kaviratna's parenthetical gloss, not in the Sanskrit.
classical.quote: Happiness and misery, growth and waste, strength and weakness, virility and sterility, knowledge and ignorance, life and death, all depend upon (judicious and injudicious) sleep.

classical.establishes: Akāla, atiprasaṅga and absence of sleep as harmful. Sanskrit seen: अकालेऽतिप्रसङ्गाच्च न च निद्रा निषेविता| सुखायुषी पराकुर्यात् कालरात्रिरिवापरा||३७||.
classical.quote: Sleep, when indulged on improper occasions or in excess, or not at all, does not contribute to either happiness or longevity, for it is even like the Last Night.

classical.verse: Standard 21/58-59; Kaviratna's printed numbers OCR as '64' and '*66' which cannot be right given his 31-34 above; his actual printed numbers here were NOT reliably established
classical.establishes: The six/seven-fold classification of sleep and bhūtadhātrī ('Nurse of all creatures'). Sanskrit seen: तमोभवा श्लेष्मसमुद्भवा च मनःशरीरश्रमसम्भवा च| आगन्तुकी व्याध्यनुवर्तिनी च रात्रिस्वभावप्रभवा च निद्रा||५८|| रात्रिस्वभावप्रभवा मता या तां भूतधात्रीं प्रवदन्ति तज्ज्ञाः| ...||५९||.
classical.quote: Sleep arises from Tamas, from phlegm also, from the weariness of both mind and body, from hurts and wounds; it is induced also by disease; it arises also from the very nature of Night. [...] Amongst these, that sleep which arises from the nature of Night is called the Nurse of all creatures. The sleep that arises from Tamas is regarded as the root of evil. The sleep that arises from the other causes is regarded as due to Disease.

(prose) = Bh 36; 4/39-41 = Bh 37-39, not quoted.

classical.establishes: The threefold classification nija / agantu / manasa, and Charaka's definition of nija as śārīra-doṣa-samuttha, arising from the bodily doshas. This is the primary classical anchor for nija-roga. Sanskrit quoted with its printed verse number; the English on that page is the 2020 CSRTSDC translation and is not quoted.
classical.quote: त्रयो रोगा इति- निजागन्तुमानसाः| तत्र निजः शारीरदोषसमुत्थः, आगन्तुर्भूतविषवाय्वग्निसम्प्रहारादिसमुत्थः, मानसः पुनरिष्टस्यलाभाल्लाभाच्चानिष्टस्योपजायते||४५|| / trayō rōgā iti- nijāgantumānasāḥ| tatra nijaḥ śārīradōṣasamutthaḥ, āganturbhūtaviṣavāyvagnisamprahārādisamutthaḥ, mānasaḥ punariṣṭasya lābhāllābhāccāniṣṭasyōpajāyatē||45||

classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of the same verse. Establishes the 1892-1913 English rendering of the triad as Physical / Accidental / Mental. Quoted from the OCR text of the scanned volume (pages 126-127 of the printed book); the printed verse number is not legible in the scan, so 45 is carried over from the verified Sanskrit rather than read off this page.
classical.quote: Diseases are of three kinds, viz. Physical, Accidental, and Mental. Physical diseases are those that arise from some abnormal condition of the body. Accidental are those that arise from the action of spirits, of poison, of wind, of fire, of acts of violence done to the body, such as beating, &c. Mental diseases are those that arise from non-attainment of objects desired or coveted, or from accession of those that are disliked.

classical.establishes: Under vidhi-samprapti, Charaka gives a TWOFOLD nija/agantu division of diseases, distinct from the threefold nija/agantu/manasa of Su.11/45. Two different classifications in one text, and a lexicon must carry both rather than harmonise them.
classical.quote: विधिर्नाम- द्विविधा व्याधयो निजागन्तुभेदेन,त्रिविधास्त्रिदोषभेदेन, चतुर्विधाः साध्यासाध्यमृदुदारुणभेदेन|१२| / vidhirnāma- dvividhā vyādhayō nijāgantubhēdēna, trividhāstridōṣabhēdēna, caturvidhāḥ sādhyāsādhyamr̥dudāruṇabhēdēna|12|

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English for the vidhi-samprapti classification. NUMBERING WARNING: Kaviratna prints this as aphorism 9 of his Nidana Lesson I, while the modern editions number it 12. The chapter and sthana are certain; the verse number given here is the modern one, taken from the verified Sanskrit, not from this page.
classical.quote: Kind (or Order) is as follows : — Diseases are of two kinds, as natural and accidental. They are of three kinds, according to the particular fault that has been excited among the three that exist (viz., wind, bile, and phlegm). They are of four kinds, considering curability, incurability, mildness, and violence.

distinguishFrom.why: Charaka defines nija as śārīra-doṣa-samuttha (Su.11/45), so nija is defined BY reference to sharira, but the two are not the same category. Nija is a cause-based class (arising from one's own doshas) and stands against agantu; sharirika is a seat-based class (located in the body) and stands against manasika. A manasika disease can be nija; an agantu injury is located in the sharira.

Sushruta's fourth class, the natural processes (hunger, thirst, ageing, sleep, death). Kaviratna's rendering of nija as 'natural' collides head-on with svabhavika and will mislead anyone reading the two translations side by side.

WHO ISTA glosses adhyatmika as 'Intrinsic or endogenous diseases', the same English most people use for nija. They are different classifications: adhyatmika/adhibhautika/adhidaivika is the three-fold suffering (tapa) scheme used in Sushruta Su.24, while nija/agantu is a cause scheme in Charaka. Two Sanskrit terms sharing one English word is a hazard, not a synonymy.

'Congenital' and 'hereditary' classes. 'Nija' literally means 'one's own, innate', which invites a reading as 'congenital'. It does not mean congenital in Charaka; it means arising from one's own doshas, which can begin at any age.

mistranslations.why: Driven by the literal sense of nija ('own, innate'). Charaka's definition is śārīra-doṣa-samuttha, arising from the bodily doshas, with no claim about presence at birth. Charaka has separate machinery for congenital conditions (and Sushruta has adi-bala- and janma-bala-pravritta).

Kaviratna's own choice at Nidana 1, and wrong for a modern reader because 'natural disease' is the established English for svabhavika, which is the class of processes NOT treated as disease in the ordinary sense.

Kaviratna's choice at Sutrasthana 11, and wrong because it reads as a seat claim (in the body) when nija is a cause claim (from the doshas). It also makes the nija/manasa contrast look like a body/mind contrast, which it is not: Charaka lists manasa as a third item alongside nija, not inside it.

Seen when 'endogenous' is over-read. WHO ISTA reserves 'Idiopathic diseases' for a different Sanskrit headword entirely (ITA-4.2.33, ākasmikarogaḥ, 'manifest suddenly in the body without any apparent cause'). Nija diseases have a stated cause; they are not causeless.

openQuestions: Is there a classical passage that explicitly reconciles the twofold (Cha.Ni.1/12) and threefold (Cha.Su.11/45) schemes, or do the commentators simply let them stand?
What verse number does Kaviratna's printed Nidana Sthana use, and why does his aphorism numbering run three behind the modern editions? This affects every citation taken from his Nidana volume.

distinguishFrom.why: THE critical disambiguation. WHO ITA-4.8.24 states explicitly that a nirāma doṣa 'is still in a vitiated state and has not returned to normal state'. Nirāma means āma-free, not healthy. Treating nirāma as 'normal' would license stopping treatment at the wrong point.
WHO ITA-4.6.5. A stage of a disease, not a state of a doṣa. Both are rendered with 'devoid of ama' in the same standard.

WHO ITA-5.6.39, a specific stage of fever with its own symptom set. Not generalisable to doṣas.
The complement. Note that the sāma/nirāma pair is a property of a doṣa that is already vitiated; a normal doṣa is described by neither term.

mistranslations.why: Directly contradicted by WHO ITA-4.8.24, which says the nirāma doṣa is still vitiated. The most consequential error available for this term, because it implies treatment is finished.
Imports the toxin model that WHO's āma entry avoids, and carries the same false completion implication.
Wellness register with no standardised or classical warrant.
A common clinical shorthand — sāma = acute, nirāma = chronic — which is a heuristic about timing, not what either term means.

openQuestions: All three classical locators in this record are secondary: they were read on carakasamhitaonline's Ama page, not in Ashtanga Hridaya or Bhavaprakasha themselves. They are recorded as 'located' and MUST be verified before publication.
Sushruta Sutrasthana 17 (Āmapakvaiṣaṇīya) is lawfully quotable and was not read; it is the most likely source of a quotable English passage for this family of terms.
Whether any classical text gives nirāma doṣa positive signs rather than defining it as the negation of sāma signs was not established; Bhavaprakasha appears to, per the secondary source.
