It is cooling, oleaginous, and firm (Sthira), contributes to the formation and growth of flesh, maintains its integrity or holds it firm, and is mobile or capable of moving about from one place to another within the organism.

classical.establishes: The threefold ojo-doṣa: visraṃsa, vyāpad, kṣaya. This is the classical basis for WHO ISTA entries ITA-5.3.34, 5.3.35 and 5.3.36, and the mapping is clean.
classical.quote: A deranged or vitiated albumen (Ojas) is characterised firstly by its dislodgment from its proper seat or locality (Visransha), secondly, by a change or modification of its native virtues in contact with the deranged humours or disordered organs (Vyápad) and thirdly, by wasting away (Kshaya).

classical.establishes: Charaka's characterisation of ojas as a slightly yellowish pure blood resident in the heart, whose loss is fatal. Note this differs from Sushruta's white and cooling ojas; the two texts do not agree on its colour.
classical.quote: There resides in the heart a quantity of pure blood, which is slightly yellowish. This blood in the body is called Ojas. Through attenuation of this, blood or its loss, even death may overtake the man.

classical.establishes: The identification of normal ślesman with ojas, which is the textual root of the 'ojas is a form of kapha' position and of the term ślaiṣmika ojas. Charak Samhita Online cites this same statement as Ca.Sū.17/117; Kaviratna numbers it 114.
classical.quote: When the phlegm changes its normal condition, it becomes those impurities that are evacuated by the system. It is the phlegm that is also called the Ojas in the system. When its normal condition becomes altered, it becomes a source of evil.

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi states that although ojas is the essence of the seven dhātus and so is already included when the dhātus are named, it is listed separately because it sustains prāṇa; and that for those who hold ojas to be produced from śukra, ojas would be an EIGHTH dhātu. The eighth-dhātu question is thus explicitly a contested position, not a settled doctrine.
classical.quote: atra yadyapyojaḥ saptadhātusārarūpaṃ tena dhātugrahaṇenaiva labhyate tathāpi prāṇadhāraṇakartṛtvena pṛthak paṭhitaṃ ye tu śukrajanyamoja icchanti teṣāmaṣṭamo dhāturojaḥ syāditi

classical.establishes: Independent confirmation, in a public-domain English source, that the eighth-dhātu status of ojas is attributed to 'certain authorities' rather than being the standing view. This is Bhishagratna's footnote, not mūla text.
classical.quote: Semen, like gold a thousand times purified, casts off no dregs. Hence certain authorities hold albumen (protoplasmic matter) to be the eighth or the culminating principle of the body.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO gives bala a separate entry (ITA-2.2.27, 'Immunity, strength, physical endurance') with three subtypes. Ojas and bala are closely linked in the texts but are not the same term, and the NIA list says ojas 'also indicates Bala', which is a gloss, not an identity.
Resistance to disease; WHO pairs it with bala at ITA-2.2.27. It names a capacity; ojas names a substance said to underlie it.

Ca.Sū.17 (Kaviratna's v.114) says normal ślesman is called ojas, and Gangādhara read a variant at Ca.Śā.7 as 'the particular kind of phlegm known as ojas'. Kaviratna rejects that reading outright: 'This can be hardly correct ... It is not regarded as any kind of phlegm.' A live classical disagreement, not a translation problem.
Ojas is said by some to be produced from śukra, which would make it the eighth dhātu; Cakrapāṇi records this as one position among others.
Sāra is the excellence of any individual dhātu, assessed per tissue. Ojas is the single essence of all seven taken together.
Ojas is listed among the ten āyatanas of prāṇa in Ca.Sū.29 (Kaviratna: 'the blood, the semen, ojas'), which makes it a substratum of prāṇa, not prāṇa itself.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's own 1907 rendering, and the one most likely to be copied from a public-domain text without noticing its date. It equates ojas with a specific protein class on the strength of Victorian protoplasm theory. Bhishagratna's footnote already flags that authorities disagreed.
Reduces ojas to one of its functions. WHO deliberately does not translate the term, and assigns 'immunity' to bala/vyādhikṣamatva instead (ITA-2.2.27).
Assimilates ojas to prāṇa-type vitalism. The classical descriptions are consistently of a material substance with colour, taste, smell, quantity and a location, not of an energy.

mistranslations.rendering: essence of the seven tissues, therefore semen
mistranslations.why: Conflates ojas with śukra by running the dhātu sequence one step too far. Cakrapāṇi records that as a minority position which would make ojas an eighth dhātu.

openQuestions: Charaka calls ojas slightly yellowish and heart-resident; Sushruta calls it white and body-pervading. Neither public-domain translator reconciles them, and no retrieved source treats the disagreement as anything but a footnote. It deserves its own contested entry.
Whether ojas is the eighth dhātu. Cakrapāṇi and Bhishagratna both record it as a contested position; no source retrieved settles it.
Kaviratna's verse numbering in Sūtrasthāna 17 diverges from modern editions (his v.114 versus the commonly cited 17/117). The whole chapter's offset needs checking.

ICD-11 TM2 (Chapter 26, Module 2, released on the ICD-11 browser February 2025) classifies disorder patterns, not physiological concepts. No TM2 code for ojas or its disorders was verified. Recorded as unverified, not as absent.

Note WHO glosses the FUNCTION (digesting) rather than transliterating; WHO also preserves the 'supports other subtypes of pitta' clause, which is faithful to both Suśruta 21.10 and AH 12.12.

classical.establishes: Seat between āmāśaya and pakvāśaya; functions of digesting the four kinds of food, separating waste, and maintaining heat at the other pitta seats; and that the designation is 'pācakāgni'.
classical.quote: The Pachakagni:—By the ordination of fate or necessity (unfathomable natural cause),  the Pittam, located in the region between the stomach (Amashaya) and the intestines (Pakvashaya), helps the (digestion of the four kinds of food such as drink and edibles etc.) partaken of by a living subject, and purges off the residue or impure morbiferous matter in the shape of urine and excreta after the completion of the process. Even thus located, it keeps up the temperature in its other distant locations (skin, etc.) in virtue of its native heat-giving attribute. Hence this Pittam is called the Pachakagni (digestive fire or heat) in an animated organism.

classical.establishes: Fixes the verse number as Su.Sū. 21.10 and shows the mūla names it 'pācako'gniḥ' (pācaka AGNI), not 'pācaka pitta'. Retrieved with the verse marker ||१०|| visible on the page.
classical.quote: तच्चादृष्टहेतुकेन विशेषेण पक्वामाशयमध्यस्थं पित्तं चतुर्विधमन्नपानं पचति, विवेचयति च दोषरसमूत्रपुरीषाणि; तत्रस्थमेव चात्मशक्त्या शेषाणां पित्तस्थानानां शरीरस्य चाग्निकर्मणाऽनुग्रहं करोति, तस्मिन् पित्ते पाचकोऽग्निरिति सञ्ज्ञा; ||१०||

classical.establishes: Su.Sū. 15.4 states pitta is divided fivefold and lists six functions (rāga, pakti, ojas, tejas, medhā, ūṣma) but does NOT name the five. The names appear only at 21.10. Several secondary sources cite '15/4' for the five pittas; that citation is for the fivefold division, not the names.
classical.quote: रागपक्त्योजस्तेजोमेधोष्मकृत् पित्तं पञ्चधा प्रविभक्तमग्निकर्मणाऽनुग्रहं करोति; |४|

classical.text: Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya (Sanskrit mūla; no public-domain English translation exists, so no translation is quoted)
classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa names it 'pācaka', calls it 'anala' (fire) because it is devoid of the liquid quality, and assigns it the role of strengthening (bala-dāna) the remaining pittas. Independently corroborated: J Ayurveda Integr Med 2025 (PMID 40972327) cites 'Ashtanga Hridaya Sutra Sthana 12/10-12' for pācaka pitta.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: Frequently treated as a straight synonym. They overlap but are not identical: jāṭharāgni is the general digestive fire of the koṣṭha as a functional principle, whereas pācaka-pitta is one of five named locational divisions of the pitta doṣa. Suśruta's own framing at Su.Sū. 21.9 argues pitta IS the body's only agni, which is why the mūla names the subtype 'pācakāgni' and why the two terms collapse together in practice. The distinction is real in the commentarial literature and is routinely lost in English.

These are the elemental and tissue-level digestive fires. Both Suśruta (21.10) and Vāgbhaṭa (12.12) make pācaka the fire that SUPPORTS the others; it is not a superset of them and not interchangeable with them.

Both are seated in the āmāśaya and both are described as acting on ingested food. Pācaka does pāka (cooking/splitting into sāra and kiṭṭa); kledaka does kledana (moistening/loosening the bolus). They are antagonistic in quality and co-located, which is exactly why they get conflated.

Also seated at the digestive fire and also credited with separating sāra from kiṭṭa. Classical division of labour: samāna fans and regulates the fire and moves the contents; pācaka performs the transformation.

mistranslations.why: A substitution, not a translation. It silently discards the clause both Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa make load-bearing, that pācaka supplies strength to the other four pitta seats (skin, eye, heart, liver/spleen). No enzyme does that. The equation is a modern hypothesis and should never be presented as what the term means.

mistranslations.rendering: "Pachaka Pitta" presented as the classical Suśrutan form
mistranslations.why: Suśruta's mūla reads 'pācako'gnir iti saṃjñā' — the designation is pācaka-AGNI. Bhishagratna correctly translates it as 'Pachakagni'. The '-pitta' compound is Vāgbhaṭa-flavoured and modern; using it while citing Su.Sū. 21.10 misreports the source.

mistranslations.rendering: "metabolic fire" used interchangeably at tissue level
mistranslations.why: Conflates pācaka with dhātvagni. Pācaka is explicitly koṣṭha-located (between āmāśaya and pakvāśaya) in both texts.

openQuestions: Does Caraka Saṃhitā use the word pācaka for a pitta subtype anywhere in the mūla, or only in Cakrapāṇidatta's Āyurveda Dīpikā commentary? I found secondary claims that Caraka does not name the subtypes but did not verify this by searching the Caraka mūla myself.
Suśruta 21.10 says the seat is 'between āmāśaya and pakvāśaya'; Vāgbhaṭa 12.10 says 'pakvāmāśaya-madhyaga'. Are these identical, or does Dalhaṇa read a difference? Needs the commentary.
Whether NAMASTE's Ayurveda 'Standard Terms' list carries an entry for pācaka-pitta, and under what code.

It also denotes the procedure for preparing mercury to amalgamate other substances.' WHO thus records a third, rasaśāstra sense of dīpana.

classical.establishes: THE canonical definition, and a clean triple contrast. dīpana does not digest āma but kindles agni (example: miśi/fennel). pācana digests āma but does not kindle agni (example: nāgakeśara). citraka is both. This is the source WHO's ITA-6.2.6.7 and 6.2.6.8 descriptions reproduce almost word for word, and the source Kaviratna's 1890s glosses independently match.
classical.quote:
तत्र दीपनद्रव्यलक्षणम्
पचेन्नामं वह्निकृच्च दीपनं तद्यथा मिशिः १
पाचनदीपनपाचनद्रव्ययोर्लक्षणे
पचत्यामं न वह्निं च कुर्याद्यत्तद्धि पाचनम्
नागकेशरवद्विद्याच्चित्रो दीपनपाचनः २
classical.translator: none — no public-domain English translation of Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā exists

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for the clinical rule: dīpana for localised āma in the gut, laṅghana plus pācana for āma that has spread systemically. The Sanskrit reads 'शरीरानुगते सामे रसे लङ्घनपाचनम्'.
classical.quote: If undigested food adheres to the 'Pakkaçaya' (that part of the stomach where digestion takes place), it should be expelled by such drugs as are called 'Dipana.' When the 'ama Rasa' (i. e., the undigested juice of the food taken) spreads over the whole body, fasting and the administration of 'Pachana' (i. e., drugs which assist in digesting undigested food, without increasing the appetite) are prescribable.

classical.establishes: Sanskrit fixing the verse number and showing that pācana is prescribed as a compound with laṅghana (laṅghana-pācana), not as a standalone action.
classical.quote: लीनं पक्वाशयस्थं वाऽऽप्यामं स्राव्यं सदीपनैः। शरीरानुगते सामे रसे लङ्घनपाचनम्॥७५॥

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa prescribes pācana-dīpana as the first step for patients presenting with constipation, heaviness, eructation and nausea, before other measures. Chapter fixed by the file's own internal variant markers (14.14cv, 14.14dv) immediately following.
classical.quote:
vibandha-gauravodgāra-hṛl-lāsādibhir āturān |
madhya-sthaulyādikān prāyaḥ pūrvaṃ pācana-dīpanaiḥ || 13 ||
classical.translator: none — no public-domain English translation of Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya exists

classical.verse: prose, p. 353 of Bhishagratna vol. I
classical.establishes: Public-domain English attestation of pācana as a drug-group property in Sushruta's gaṇa chapter. Bhishagratna renders it 'digestant' and does not distinguish it from dīpana anywhere I could find.
classical.quote: The group under discussion destroys the deranged Shleshma, cures uterine and vaginal disorders, purifies the breast milk of a mother, and acts as a good digestant (Pachana).

distinguishFrom.why: The defining contrast, and the one the whole Śārṅgadhara chapter exists to draw. dīpana kindles agni without acting on āma; pācana acts on āma without kindling agni. Kaviratna, Śārṅgadhara and WHO all agree. Clinical writing that uses 'dīpana-pācana' as a single hyphenated action erases it — though Śārṅgadhara himself names citraka as a drug that is both, so the compound is legitimate for some dravyas.
WHO ITA-2.6.30 uses the same lemma for the bodily process of digestion, not a therapeutic action. Two senses, two term IDs.

A third sense entirely: WHO ITA-9.6.109 'Haemostasis by chemical cautery', and Bhishagratna's 'process of setting up suppuration in the wound'. In a surgical context the word means ripening or cauterising, not digesting. Note WHO's and Bhishagratna's glosses of this surgical sense do not agree with each other.
Fasting/lightening. Ca.Ci.15.75 prescribes them together (laṅghana-pācana) for systemic āma, but they are distinct measures; laṅghana withholds, pācana acts.

Usually treated as a synonym, but it specifies the object. Since Śārṅgadhara's definition already makes āma the object, the compound is pleonastic — worth noting rather than treating as a separate action.

Śārṅgadhara Pū.Kh.4.4 defines anulomana separately ('having effected pāka of the malas, breaking the obstruction, it carries them downward'). It includes a pāka step and is therefore easily confused with pācana.

mistranslations.why: A pharmacological class defined by relief of flatulence. It has no relation to the Śārṅgadhara criterion (digests āma, does not kindle agni), and many classical pācana dravyas are not carminative. Common in older Indian materia medica in English.

'Digestive stimulant' is precisely dīpana, the contrast term. Using it for pācana inverts the one distinction the classical definition exists to make. Bhishagratna's 'digestant' has the same ambiguity.
WHO explicitly attaches 'appetizing action' to dīpana (ITA-6.2.6.7), not pācana, and Kaviratna's gloss says pācana works 'without increasing the appetite'.
Follows from the 'āma = toxin' error and turns a specific digestive action into a marketing category.

openQuestions: Does WHO's ITA-9.6.109 gloss of surgical pācana as 'chemical cautery' match the Sanskrit, or is Bhishagratna's 'suppuration' the better reading?
Is there any assay or biomarker by which a candidate drug could be classed as pācana rather than dīpana?

Does any text earlier than Śārṅgadhara give the pācana/dīpana definitional contrast, or is Śārṅgadhara its origin? Kaviratna's Charaka gloss reproduces it but is a 19th-century translator's note, not the mūla.

classical.verse: 10 (Sushruta, Uttara-tantra 65.10; printed ॥ १० ॥ in the Trikamji/Nirnaya Sagar 2nd ed. 1931, p. 757. Bhishagratna's unnumbered English runs this as his section 7.)
classical.establishes: Padārtha as a tantrayukti at Su.Ut.65.10 in the printed Sanskrit: the meaning conveyed by a sūtra or a word — of one word, two words or several — and such meanings are unlimited; where a word admits two or three senses (sneha, sveda, añjana), the sense established by what precedes and follows is the one to be taken. This is the interpretive device, distinct from the six ontological categories, and it is Bhishagratna's section 7.
classical.quote: योऽर्थोऽभिहितः सूत्रे पदे वा स पदार्थः, पदस्य पदयोः पदानां वाऽर्थः पदार्थः; अपरिमिताश्च पदार्थाः । यथा—स्नेहस्वेदाञ्जनेषु निर्दिष्टेषु द्वयोस्त्रयाणां वाऽर्थानामुपपत्तिर्दृश्यते, तत्र योऽर्थः पूर्वापरयोगसिद्धो भवति स ग्रहीतव्यः ... एष पदार्थः ॥ १० ॥

classical.establishes: The six categories as Charaka lists them (sāmānya, viśeṣa, guṇa, dravya, karma, samavāya), without using the word padārtha. Sanskrit: महर्षयस्ते ददृशुर्यथावज्ज्ञानचक्षुषा| सामान्यं च विशेषं च गुणान् द्रव्याणि कर्म च||२८|| समवायं च तज्ज्ञात्वा तन्त्रोक्तं विधिमास्थिताः| लेभिरे परमं शर्म जीवितं चाप्यनित्वरम्||२९||.
classical.quote: Those great Rishis (then) beheld duly, with the eye of knowledge, similarities, dissimilarities, properties, objects, and operations, as also compositions. Knowing these, and conforming to the ordinances of that Science, they obtained great felicity and even immortal life.

classical.establishes: That Charaka's own collective name for the six just defined is kāraṇa, not padārtha. Sanskrit: इत्युक्तं कारणं कार्यं धातुसाम्यमिहोच्यते||५३||.
classical.quote: Thus is explained Cause as also Action or Effect.

classical.establishes: The philosophical source: the six named explicitly as padārthas, in the order dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, samavāya. This is the verification the earlier shad-padartha.json flagged as missing.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO separates ITA-1.8.3.5 (meaning/referent of a word, any nameable entity) from ITA-1.9.1 (the six categories). The simplex is semantic, the compound ontological.
Su.Ut.65 (Bhishagratna): 'the meaning implied by a word or an aphorism'. A reading device for the text, not a category of being. Both uses occur inside Ayurveda.
Ca.Su.1.53 and NIA BP0178: Ayurveda calls the six 'kāraṇa' (causes of dhātusāmya). Charaka's verses never use 'padārtha' for them; the word enters via the commentators and Vaiśeṣika.
WHO ITA-1.8.3.4 'Object of knowledge'. Prameya is what is to be known by a pramāṇa; padārtha is what exists and is nameable.

Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.4 (retrieved) gives six in the order dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, samavāya; Charaka Su.1.28-29 leads with sāmānya/viśeṣa; later Vaiśeṣika adds abhāva (WHO ITA-1.9.7.1 'Nonexistence' under 'Miscellaneous ontological categories').
Five elements, which are dravyas; constantly conflated with the six categories in popular writing.

mistranslations.why: Dravya is one of the six.
Confuses with pañcamahābhūta.
NIA BP0265's calque; 'matters' has no technical content in English.
The etymological sense (pada + artha) is WHO ITA-1.8.3.5 and Su.Ut.65; applying it to the ontological six is a category error, although the etymology is real.

openQuestions: Whether any Ayurvedic mūla text uses the compound ṣaṭpadārtha was not established; the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra uses 'padārthānām' with the six named.
Standard verse number for the Su.Ut.65 padārtha passage not established; Bhishagratna's '7' is his own section number.
The Chakrapāṇi gloss 'ṣaṇṇāṃ padārthānāṃ' recorded in the project's shad-padartha.json was not re-retrieved this session.

On this page he runs two behind standard: his 10 (langhana gunas) = std 12-13a, 11 = 13b-14a, 12 = 14b-15a, 13 = 15b-16a, 14 = 16b-17a, 15 = 17b, 16 = 18.
classical.establishes: Charaka's fourfold saṁśuddhi (Sanskrit 'चतुष्प्रकारा संशुद्धिः', unnamed) is glossed by Kaviratna as four of the five karmas, omitting anuvāsana; shows that Charaka's own counts are four (śuddhi) and five (karma) in different places.

distinguishFrom.why: The principle of expelling doṣa (WHO ITA-9.2.1); pañcakarma is one enumeration of its procedures. Charaka Su.22.18 counts four saṁśuddhis, Su.2.15 five karmas, AH Su.14.5 five śodhanas with bloodletting.

Bloodletting is Vāgbhaṭa's fifth śodhana (AH Su.14.5) and is absent from Charaka's five and WHO ITA-9.2.2. Any claim that 'Sushruta's panchakarma includes raktamokṣaṇa' was not verified against a Sushruta passage in this pass.
Preparatory (snehana, svedana) and follow-up (saṁsarjana krama) phases; Ca.Su.2.15 requires oleation and sudation before the five, so they are not among the five.
The section of Charaka dealing with the successful administration of the five karmas; sometimes loosely called 'the panchakarma sthana'.
In PMID 19412555 the word names a 5-day programme including massage and diet; in the classics it names five specific evacuative procedures.

mistranslations.why: Imports a toxin model and, in wellness use, a package of massages and diet; the five are defined evacuative procedures with specified doṣa targets (Ca.Su.25.40: vamana for kapha, virecana for pitta, basti for vāta).

Correct etymology but tells the reader nothing; Kaviratna's 'five kinds of action or evacuation' at least signals the evacuative sense.

openQuestions: The Sanskrit of Charaka's Su.2 verses preceding 15 (Kaviratna's printed 12, the drug summary) was not transcribed, so the standard number of that half-verse is unestablished.
Whether Sushruta anywhere lists five karmas including raktamokṣaṇa was not checked; the attribution is common in textbooks and should be traced to a verse before being repeated.
Whether Kaviratna's translation covers Siddhisthana at all was not checked in the BIUSante copy.

classical.establishes: The actual home of the doctrine, and its actual form: a recursive 'another self within' (anyo antara ātmā) sequence, annarasamaya → prāṇamaya → manomaya → (continuing to vijñānamaya and ānandamaya). Note that the mūla does NOT say 'five' and does not use the word kośa in these lines; the section heading on this edition reads पञ्चकोशोविवरणम् ('exposition of the five sheaths'), which is an editorial heading, not text.

distinguishFrom.why: The seven-tissue scheme is Ayurveda's own account of bodily constitution. It is ontologically different: dhātus are material constituents in series, kośas are nested selves. Popular writing that equates annamaya kośa with the dhātus imports a Vedāntic hierarchy into a physiological one.

Charaka's own four-fold analysis of the puruṣa (the 'caturviṃśati puruṣa' and related schemes) is the Ayurvedic counterpart to a layered account of the person. If a lexicon needs an Ayurvedic multi-level model, this is it, not pañcakośa.
Sushruta Śārīra 1 opens with the Sāṅkhya enumeration (avyakta, mahat, ahaṅkāra, the tanmātras, the indriyas, the bhūtas). That, not pañcakośa, is the metaphysics the Samhitās actually adopt.

distinguishFrom.term: kośa in its Ayurvedic anatomical senses
distinguishFrom.why: WHO's only kośa entries are eyelid (netrakośa), scrotum (aṇḍakoṣa/phalakośa) and a bandage type (kośabandha). A text search for kośa in Ayurvedic sources will return these, not sheaths.
Five of each, both foundational, entirely unrelated. Confused surprisingly often in secondary writing.

mistranslations.why: The framing in the supplied term itself ('panchakosha-ayurveda') is the error to be documented. The doctrine is Upaniṣadic and is transmitted into modern practice through YOGA therapy, not through the Ayurvedic Samhitās. Neither WHO ISTA nor the NIA glossary records it as an Ayurvedic term.
Reifies each kośa as a separate body. The Upaniṣad's construction is 'another self within this one, filled by it' — nesting, not a stack of bodies.

Convenient but lossy: annarasamaya is 'made of the essence of food', which is a claim about causation and sustenance (the surrounding anuvāka argues that creatures are born from, live by, and return to anna), not an anatomical designation.

'Energy' is a modern physical concept. The text assigns prāṇamaya a structure of prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, ākāśa and pṛthivī as its head, wings, self and foundation — a liturgical anatomy, not an energetic one.

openQuestions: Does ANY classical Ayurvedic text (Charaka, Sushruta, Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya/Saṅgraha, Bhāvaprakāśa, Śārṅgadhara) use pañcakośa or the annamaya/prāṇamaya series? I found no occurrence in the GRETIL Charaka corpus, but that file is 'selected parts' only, so this is suggestive, not proof. Someone should search a complete Charaka and a complete Sushruta.

When and by whom the pañcakośa model was first presented as an Ayurvedic framework — the modern integrative literature treats it as such without citation. A history-of-ideas question worth settling before the lexicon publishes the entry.

Whether any instrument claiming to measure kośa-level outcomes has undergone psychometric validation as a pañcakośa measure (as opposed to validating an intervention that is merely framed by it). None found.

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints '21' after this aphorism; standard numbering 26.10 per the Sanskrit at carakasamhitaonline.com: सर्वं द्रव्यं पाञ्चभौतिकमस्मिन्नर्थे; तच्चेतनावदचेतनं च||10||. Both recorded; not converted by arithmetic.

classical.establishes: A rejected view within the rasa debate linking rasa count to the five bhūtas; shows the Sanskrit adjectival set bhauma/audaka/āgneya/vāyavya/āntarikṣa. Note this is an opinion Caraka records, not his conclusion.
classical.quote: There are five tastes, said Kumarasiras-Bharadwaja. They appertain to Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Ether (or Space).

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints '47' (OCR reads '4T') after this aphorism; standard 1.48 per Sanskrit at carakasamhitaonline.com: खादीन्यात्मा मनः कालो दिशश्च द्रव्यसङ्ग्रहः| सेन्द्रियं चेतनं द्रव्यं, निरिन्द्रियमचेतनम्||४८||
classical.establishes: The nine kāraṇa-dravyas (khādi = the five bhūtas, ātmā, manas, kāla, diś). Kaviratna's rendering omits kāla (time), which the Sanskrit has; the parenthetical list of five is his gloss.
classical.quote: Those having ether for the first (i.e., ether, air, fire, water, and earth), soul, mind, and the quarters, are constituent elements (of all things) United with the senses, elements are called animate; without the senses, they are called inanimate.

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints '5' (with footnote asterisk) after this unit; standard 4.6 per Sanskrit at carakasamhitaonline.com: गर्भस्तु खल्वन्तरिक्षवाय्वग्नितोयभूमिविकारश्चेतनाधिष्ठानभूतः| एवमनया युक्त्या पञ्चमहाभूतविकारसमुदायात्मको गर्भश्चेतनाधिष्ठानभूतः; स ह्यस्य षष्ठो धातुरुक्तः||६||
classical.establishes: The garbha as a modification of the five mahābhūtas with cetanā as sixth dhātu; the Sanskrit uses the compound पञ्चमहाभूत here. OCR stray punctuation removed; words unchanged.
classical.quote: Verily, the foetus is a modification of Ether, Air, Fire, Water, Earth. Such modification becomes the seat (or abode) of the Chetana (or Self). Agreeably to this consideration, the foetus has for its essence an aggregate that consists of a modification of all the five great elements. That aggregate is the seat (or abode) of another element, viz., Chetana (or Self). This Chetana (or Self) is said to be the sixth element (of the foetus).

classical.verse: Sharirasthana 5.4-5. Kaviratna prints '4' after 'and the Inner Self is Brahma.' on his p. 765 (archive.org leaf n976). Standard (carakasamhitaonline Purusha_Vichaya_Sharira): ||4|| closes at 'eta eva cha shaddhatavah samuditah purusha iti shabdam labhante' (the six-dhatu enumeration prithivyapastejo vayurakasham brahma chavyaktam is in 4); the sentence 'tasya purushasya prithivi murtih, apah kledah, tejo'bhisantapah, vayuh pranah, viyat sushirani, brahma antaratma' is the first sentence of standard 5. So the first five sentences of the quote are 5.4 and the last sentence ('Of that Purusha, the form is Earth ... the Inner Self is Brahma') is 5.5.
classical.establishes: Loka-puruṣa sāmya: the five bhūtas plus avyakta Brahman as the six dhātus of both universe and person, with each bhūta's bodily correlate.
classical.quote: The universe is made of six ingredients. This is what is generally heard. They are as follows: Earth, Water, Heat, Air, Ether (or Space), and Brahma which is unmanifest. Purusha is made up of six ingredients. This is what is generally heard. Of that Purusha, the form is Earth; the liquid secretions are Water; the animal heat is Heat; the life-breaths are Air; the hollow places are Ether (or Space); and the Inner Self is Brahma.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers. Sanskrit verse 3 per siva.sh: तत्र पृथिव्यप्तेजोवाय्वाकाशानां समुदायाद्द्रव्याभिनिर्वृत्तिः, उत्कर्षस्त्वभिव्यञ्जको भवति- इदं पार्थिवमिदमाप्यमिदं तैजसमिदं वायव्यमिदमाकाशीयमिति ॥३॥ (https://www.siva.sh/sushruta-samhita/sutra-sthana/41/3)
classical.establishes: Suśruta's statement that dravyas arise from the aggregate of the five bhūtas and are classified by the predominant one. Translator's footnote (NOT the text): 'These may be translated as Solid, Liquid, Gas, Ether, and Etherion in the parlance of modern science.'
classical.quote: The five fundamental principles such as the earth (Kshithi), water (Apa), fire (Teja), air (Marut) and Sky (Vyoma) enter into the composition of all substances in the world

classical.verse: Bhishagratna section 6 (his own numbering). Sanskrit verse 4 per siva.sh: तेषां विशेषाः- शब्दस्पर्शरूपरसगन्धाः; तेभ्यो भूतानि- व्योमानिलानलजलोर्व्यः (https://www.siva.sh/sushruta-samhita/sharira-sthana/1/4)
classical.establishes: Sāṃkhya-style derivation of the five mahābhūtas from the five tanmātras in Suśruta.
classical.quote: From the combination of the aforesaid five Tanmatras (Bhutadi) taken one at a time, have successively emanated the five gross matters of space such as ether, air, heat, (fire,) fluid (water), and earth (solid).

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ITA-1.9.3.1.8: 'Subtle physical state of all five elements from which a gross element (mahabhuta) is produced.' Suśruta Śā. 1.4 derives the bhūtas from the tanmātras; the two are routinely merged in popular writing.
The five bhūtas are a subset; ātmā, manas, kāla, diś complete the nine (Ca.Sū. 1.48; WHO ITA-1.9.3.1.1; NAMASTE SAT-A.177).
Doṣas are derived from and classified by bhūta predominance (e.g. NIA draft describes vāta as predominant in Vāyu and Ākāśa mahābhūtas) but are physiological agents, not the bhūtas themselves.
Buddhist Abhidharma counts four (earth, water, fire, air) without ākāśa as a mahābhūta; PMID 31795591 uses 'Mahābhūta (四大)' in that sense. Not interchangeable with the Ayurvedic five.
Different set (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) and a cyclical-transformation logic; sharing the English word 'five elements' is the only link.
Mahābhūtas are categories of perceptible quality (sound, touch, form, taste, smell; Ca.Śā. 1.27), not substances in the periodic-table sense.

mistranslations.rendering: 'the five elements' used as if equivalent to Western classical or chemical elements
mistranslations.why: Imports Greek/modern physics; the Ayurvedic bhūtas are defined by sense-object and quality (Ca.Śā. 1.27-29, Su.Sū. 41.3-4), not by substance chemistry.
Bhishagratna's own footnote on Su.Sū. 41, offered 'in the parlance of modern science' of 1907; states of matter are not what the text says.
Coinage of the 2011 NIA/WHO-APW draft (BP0151); not in the Sanskrit and dropped from the 2022 WHO ISTA, which uses 'five elements'.

classical.establishes: The five pentads: indriya, indriya-dravya, indriya-adhiṣṭhāna, indriya-artha, indriya-buddhi. Indriya is distinguished from its seat (adhiṣṭhāna), so 'sense organ' is strictly the adhiṣṭhāna. Kaviratna's 1 = standard 3 by content (his chapter numbering begins after the two opening sentences).
classical.quote: Sanskrit: "इह खलु पञ्चेन्द्रियाणि, पञ्चेन्द्रियद्रव्याणि, पञ्चेन्द्रियाधिष्ठानानि, पञ्चेन्द्रियार्थाः, पञ्चेन्द्रियबुद्धयो भवन्ति" (IAST as printed: "Iha khalu pañcēndriyāṇi, pañcēndriyadravyāṇi, pañcēndriyādhiṣṭhānāni, pañcēndriyārthāḥ, pañcēndriyabuddhayō bhavanti"). Kaviratna (his 1): "It is certain that there are five senses, five materials that constitute those senses, five resting places of those senses, five objects of those senses, and five kinds of perceptions obtained through those senses. This has been said (by the learned of old) in discourses on the senses.*1"
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna; Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline.com

classical.verse: Standard 8 (carakasamhitaonline ||८||; the remaining pentads are standard 9-12, pañcapañcakam closes at ||१२||). Kaviratna prints a single aphorism numbered 6 (not 8) covering standard 8-12, at printed p. 86 (archive.org BIUSante_47357 page image, leaf 117, '‡6' after 'five and twenty topics'); his 5 = standard 7, his 7 = standard 13.
classical.establishes: The enumeration of the five indriyas as cakṣus, śrotra, ghrāṇa, rasana, sparśana (named by faculty, in that order) and their seats, elements, objects and cognitions. Kaviratna's single number 6 spans five standard units (8-12); no one-to-one mapping for 9-12.
classical.quote: Sanskrit: "तत्र चक्षुः श्रोत्रं घ्राणं रसनं स्पर्शनमिति पञ्चेन्द्रियाणि||८||" (IAST as printed: "Tatra cakṣuḥ śrōtraṁ ghrāṇaṁ rasanaṁ sparśanamiti pañcēndriyāṇi||8||"). Kaviratna (his 6): "The five senses are vision, hearing, scent, taste, and touch. The materials that enter into the composition of the five senses are space, wind, light, water, and earth. The resting places of the five senses are the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the tongue, and the skin or whole body. The five objects of the five senses are sound, touch, form, taste, and scent. The five perceptions derived from the five senses are the perception of form through vision, &c. These perceptions spring from a union of the senses, the objects of the senses, mind, and the soul, and are of two kinds, viz., transitory and durable or leading to certitude. This about the five and twenty topics (of knowledge or enquiry).6"
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna; Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline.com
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Manas is atīndriya, beyond/other than the five indriyas, so pañcendriya in Charaka excludes manas (contrast Sushruta's eleven).
classical.quote: Sanskrit: "अतीन्द्रियं पुनर्मनः सत्त्वसञ्ज्ञकं, 'चेतः' इत्याहुरेके, तदर्थात्मसम्पदायत्तचेष्टं चेष्टाप्रत्ययभूतमिन्द्रियाणाम्||४||". Kaviratna (his 2): "The mind is regarded as something different from the senses. It is sometimes called satwa, and some again call it chetas. Its functions are regulated by the contact of its objects with the soul. Some regard the mind as the cause of the functions of the senses.2"
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna; Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline.com

classical.verse: Sanskrit Su.Sa. 1.4 (eleven indriyas; five buddhindriya, five karmendriya, manas ubhayatmaka), 1.5 (their visayas) and 1.7 (the adhidaivata list). Numbering confirmed against a printed edition: Susrutasamhita with Dalhana's Nibandhasangraha, ed. Jadavji Trikamji Acharya, Nirnaya Sagar Press, 2nd ed. 1931, pp. 283-284. Bhishagratna's 4-5 and 7 are his own section numbers.
classical.establishes: The easyayurveda numbering the record relied on is the standard Trikamji numbering; no renumbering is needed. The record's openQuestion 'Sanskrit verse number for the Sushruta Sharirasthana 1 enumeration of buddhindriya was not established' can be closed.
classical.quote: Bhishagratna: "The eleven organs of cognition, communication or sense perception have emanated from the co-operation of the aforesaid Vaikarika Ahamkara with the Taijasa or Rajasa. They are the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, speech, hands, genitals, anus, feet and the mind (Manah)." "Of these foregoing organs the first five are intellectual or sense organs (Vuddhi-Indriya); the next five being operative (Karma-Indriya). The mind (Manah) partakes of the character of both the intellectual and operative organs alike." "Hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell respectively form the subjects of the five intellectual (Vuddhi) organs of man, whereas the faculty of speech, handling, pleasure, ejections or evacutation, locomotion successively belong to the (remaining) five operative (Karma-Indriya) ones."
classical.sourceUrl: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.327618 (page images: leaf343 = printed p. 283, leaf344 = printed p. 284)
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: The seat/organ (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin). Ca.Su.8.3 lists it as a separate pentad from the indriya itself; 'five sense organs' as a rendering of pañcendriya merges the two.
The sense OBJECTS (sound, touch, form, taste, smell), not the organs; PMID 23723664 glosses it as 'sense organs', which is wrong.
The five cognitions (visual cognition etc.) arising from indriya + artha + manas + ātman (Ca.Su.8.8 block); not the senses themselves.

The five motor faculties (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals); pañcendriya in the Charaka Su.8 sense means only the five cognitive senses, whereas Sushruta's 'eleven indriyas' include karmendriya and manas.
Ca.Su.8.4 calls manas atīndriya; it is not one of the five. Sushruta counts it as the eleventh indriya 'partaking of the character of both' (Bhishagratna).
Synonyms used by WHO (jñānendriyam ITA-3.10.4) and Sushruta/Bhishagratna (buddhīndriya); Charaka Su.8 uses plain pañcendriya. Same referent, different terminological traditions.
A proprietary oil formulation name (PMID 41056389); search collisions on 'panchendriya' will return it.

mistranslations.why: Charaka separates indriya (faculty) from indriya-adhiṣṭhāna (its seat). Kaviratna's 'five senses' with 'resting places' preserves the distinction; 'sense organs' erases it. WHO likewise chooses 'faculty'.
Bhishagratna's 'eleven organs' is Sushruta's count including karmendriya and manas; applying it to pañcendriya conflates two schemes.
Inverted gloss found in PMID 23723664; indriyārtha are the objects.

openQuestions: Sanskrit verse number for the Sushruta Sharirasthana 1 enumeration of buddhīndriya was not established; Bhishagratna prints only his own section numbers (4-6).

Whether WHO ISTA has any pañcendriya head term under a chapter not grepped (search of the full text layer for 'pañcendriy' returned nothing; 'five senses' appears only in descriptive text, e.g. ITA on physician's examination).
ICD-11 TM2: not checked in the browser; a structural term like this is unlikely to be coded.

classical.establishes: The heart as seat of the foremost/supreme ojas. This is the passage most often cited (as Ca.Sū.30/7 in Chakrapani-based numbering) for para ojas, and the public-domain English does support a superlative reading. Chapter identity confirmed from the colophon: 'Thus ends the Thirtieth Lesson called Arthe Dapa Mahamuliya'.
classical.quote: The heart is the seat (or receptacle) of the foremost Ojas. It is also the seat of supreme Brahman. For these reasons the heart is called Mahat (Great) and Artha (precious possession), by physicians.

classical.establishes: Total dependence of life on this heart-resident ojas. This is the textual basis for the claim that loss of para ojas is immediately fatal.
classical.quote: All embodied creatures, vivified by the Ojas, move about or act. Without it, the life of all creatures becomes extinct.

classical.establishes: Death cannot occur without loss of this ojas; it is the irreducible substratum of life and of the prāṇas. Together with v.6 and v.8 this is the strongest public-domain support for the para ojas concept.
classical.quote: Without its loss or destruction, there can be no destruction (or death). Dwelling in the heart, it sustains or supports life. The Ojas is the strength of the body. The body and the life-breaths are established in it.

classical.establishes: A second heart-resident ojas passage. Secondary sources cite Ca.Sū.17/74-75 with Cakrapāṇi's commentary as the source of the eight-drop measure, but the mūla as Kaviratna renders it gives no quantity.
classical.quote: There resides in the heart a quantity of pure blood, which is slightly yellowish. This blood in the body is called Ojas.

classical.establishes: Cakrapāṇi quotes the definition 'that which is the supreme tejas of rasa through śukra, that indeed is ojas'. CAUTION: para here is adjectival ('supreme'), qualifying tejas. This is NOT an occurrence of the technical term para ojas, and mistaking it for one is an easy and consequential error.
classical.quote: rasādīnāṃ śukrāntānāṃ yat paraṃ tejaḥ tat khalvojaḥ iti

distinguishFrom.why: The counterpart term. Para is heart-resident, fixed in quantity and its loss is immediately fatal; apara pervades the body, is larger in quantity and varies with diet and disease. The pair is recorded in the NIA/WHO-APW list but not in WHO ISTA.

WHO ISTA and both public-domain translators treat ojas as one thing. The two-fold division is a commentarial and textbook refinement. An entry for para ojas must not be written as though the division were the standard classical position.

An adjectival phrase in the classical definition of ojas ('the supreme essence of the dhātus'). It looks like the technical term and is not. Cakrapāṇi's segment 34 quotes exactly this phrase while discussing undivided ojas.
The seat, not the thing seated. Ca.Sū.30 identifies the heart as mahat and as the root of the ten great vessels; ojas is what it holds.

mistranslations.why: Doubles the error: translates ojas as immunity and then grades it. Para ojas is described as a quantity in a place, not as a degree of a capacity.
Reads para as a value ranking on a spiritual scale. In the texts it distinguishes location and criticality, not refinement.
Apara does not mean non-essential; it means the other, the further, the lower in a pair. Neither member is optional.

openQuestions: THE ashta-bindu (eight drops) measure could NOT be verified and is deliberately not recorded as a citation. Retrieved secondary sources give three mutually incompatible loci for it: Cakrapāṇi on Ca.Sū.17/74-75, Cakrapāṇi on Ca.Sū.30/7, and Cakrapāṇi on Ca.Sū.15/9, with a fourth attribution to Dalhaṇa. None was checked against Sanskrit. GRETIL's Āyurvedadīpikā selection does not include Sūtrasthāna 15, 17 or 30, and the string 'bindu' does not occur anywhere in the portion it does cover. A human must resolve this against a printed Āyurvedadīpikā before any eight-drop claim is published.
Whether the para/apara division is Cakrapāṇi's, Dalhaṇa's, or a later textbook systematisation. Not established.

Whether Kaviratna's Sūtrasthāna 30 v.6 corresponds to the 30/7 of Chakrapani-based editions. His numbering runs one behind elsewhere, which would fit, but the offset was not verified for this chapter.

classical.verse: Standard 42 (carakasamhitaonline). Kaviratna prints 41-42 for this block (his 41 closes the prajñāparādha sentence; the Time sentence runs to his 42).
classical.establishes: The defining statement: the year, marked by cold, heat and rain, is kāla; kāla 'is again called pariṇāma'; its ati-, a- and mithyā-yoga are the third cause of disease. Note Kaviratna's parenthetical examples are his own insertions (printed in parentheses).
classical.quote: Sanskrit (numbered 42, two fragments as retrieved, ellipsis is the retrieval's): "शीतोष्णवर्षलक्षणाः पुनर्हेमन्तग्रीष्मवर्षाः संवत्सरः, स कालः ... कालः पुनः परिणाम उच्यते". Kaviratna (pp.125-126): "Heat, cold, and rain, or autumn, summer, and rain, constitute the indications of the year. That is also called Time. When the particular indication of a particular period of Time manifests itself in excess, that is called excess of correlation in respect of Time, (as excess of cold in winter or excess of heat in summer, or excess of rain in the rainy season). When such indication manifests itself in a measure less than normal, that is called want or absence of correlation ... When indications, that are the reverse of those which are normal, are manifested, that is called improper correlation (such as heat in winter or cold in summer). Time has another name, viz., Ratinanta [OCR: Parinama]. Thus are the three subjects treated of, viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time or Parinama.42"
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna; Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline.com

classical.establishes: Kāla (which Su.11.42 equates with pariṇāma) as first-named of the three causes. Kaviratna's footnote (his own): "Time is of two kinds, viz., (1) that portion of eternity with which human life is concerned and which goes on ceaselessly, and (2) the age of man, that is, his infancy, youth, manhood, and decrepitude."
classical.quote: Sanskrit: "कालबुद्धीन्द्रियार्थानां योगो मिथ्या न चाति च| द्वयाश्रयाणां व्याधीनां त्रिविधो हेतुसङ्ग्रहः||५४||". Kaviratna: "Of all diseases, physical and mental, the causes in brief are of three kinds, viz., adverse or excessive correlation or want of correlation of time, mind, and the objects of the senses.*53"

classical.establishes: Pariṇāma of kāla produces the 'natural' (svābhāvika) disorders of ageing and death, which have no counter-measure. Shows pariṇāma covers lifespan/age, not only season. Kaviratna's footnote on his 117-120 ('kalasamprapti') is a translator's exposition and should not be quoted as text.
classical.quote: Sanskrit: "कालस्य परिणामेन जरामृत्युनिमित्तजाः। रोगाः स्वाभाविका दृष्टाः स्वभावो निष्प्रतिक्रियः॥११५॥". Kaviratna (pp.680-681): "With the development of Time, decrepitude, death and such diseases as are not due to known and defined causes, are seen to come naturally. That which is brought about by Nature has no remedy.122"

classical.verse: Standard Vimanasthana 6.6 (carakasamhitaonline Roganika_Vimana, unit closing ||६||); Kaviratna Vimanasthanam Lesson VI, his printed 10, p. 515, which merges standard 6 to 9 into one numbered paragraph.
classical.establishes: Vi. 6.6 names the three prakopana (exciting causes) of both classes of dosha as asātmyendriyārtha-saṁyoga, prajñāparādha and pariṇāma (असात्म्येन्द्रियार्थसंयोगः, प्रज्ञापराधः परिणामश्चेति). Kaviratna renders pariṇāma as "Time", and his footnote on the same page states the equation outright. The footnote is the translator's voice, so what it establishes is how he read the term, not what the Samhita says.
classical.quote: Kaviratna: "there are three kinds of exciting causes, viz., union with disagreeing objects of sense, faults of understanding, and Time." Footnote (translator's note): "By 'Parinama' is meant Time."
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Standard Nidanasthana 1.3 (carakasamhitaonline Jwara_Nidana, unit closing ||३||). Kaviratna Nidanasthanam Lesson I, printed p. 928, inside the unit his printed number 2 closes (the 2 is printed on p. 929). Measured mapping for this chapter: Kav 1 = Std 1-2, Kav 2 = Std 3-4.
classical.establishes: Ni. 1.3 names the same three nidanas as Vi. 6.6, and Kaviratna's footnote at Nidana I names parinama in so many words, so the lexicon can carry a Nidana citation for parinama on its own retrieval. Worth recording as a divergence in the same translator: at Vi. 6 he renders parinama flatly as 'Time', but at Ni. 1.3 he renders it 'the developments in course of time, of evil acts (done in this life or previous ones)', importing karma that the Sanskrit परिणाम does not carry — a translator's expansion, not a variant reading, since the mula word is the same in both places.
classical.quote: Kaviratna (inside his aphorism 2, printed p. 928): "Nidana' is of three kinds, viz., union with such objects of the senses as are not assimilable, faults of judgment, and the developments in course of time, of evil acts (done in this life or previous ones)." Translator's footnote on the same page: "The three general causes of disease, viz., 'asatmasamyoga', 'prajnaparardha', and 'parinama' have been fully explained in the previous divisions of the work." Sanskrit (standard Ni. 1.3): "इह खलु हेतुर्निमित्तमायतनं कर्ता कारणं प्रत्ययः समुत्थानं निदानमित्यनर्थान्तरम् तत्त्रिविधम्- असात्म्येन्द्रियार्थसंयोगः, प्रज्ञापराधः, परिणामश्चेति||३||"

distinguishFrom.why: Charaka equates them ('kālaḥ punaḥ pariṇāma ucyate', Su.11.42), but kāla is the broader word (time as such, also time of dosing, time of day); pariṇāma names time in its transforming/ageing aspect as a disease cause.
NAMASTE SAT-C.77 reduces pariṇāma to season; Ca.Sa.1.115 and Kaviratna's notes include age and lifespan (jarā, mṛtyu). Season is one face of it.
Transformation of food (digestion); NAMASTE SAT-J.63 āhārapariṇāmakara-bhāvaḥ 'factors responsible for proper digestion'. Same word, metabolic not etiological sense.
A named disease (NAMASTE EB-10.10 'duodenal ulcer'; WHO ITA-5.34.9), pain arising during the pariṇāma (digestion) of food. Unrelated to the three-cause doctrine.
Sāṃkhya doctrine of real transformation (NAMASTE SAT-A.111 'theory of transformation'), a philosophical position, not an etiological factor.
Kaviratna's Sa.1 block (his 123-124) treats diseases from past deeds separately from those from pariṇāma of Time; both are 'kālasamprāpti' topics in his footnote but distinct in the text.

mistranslations.rendering: seasonal effects / seasonal variation (as the whole meaning)
mistranslations.why: Drops age and lifespan, which Ca.Sa.1.115 explicitly brings under kālasya pariṇāmena (jarā-mṛtyu). NAMASTE SAT-C.77 does this; its own SAT-C.74 does not.
Lexically valid for pariṇāma in general Sanskrit, but in the three-cause context the texts define it as kāla; 'consequence' would make the third cause tautological.
Not a rendering: an OCR corruption of 'Parinama' in the archive.org text of Kaviratna (p.126). Anyone grepping the scan will miss the passage.

openQuestions: Standard verse number for the Nidanasthana 1 statement (listed 1/3) not verified against Sanskrit.
Whether WHO ISTA has any separate entry for kāla as a cause (only pariṇāmaḥ ITA-4.4.12 and doṣahetuḥ ITA-4.4.13 'seasonal variations leading to natural accumulation' were read).
Ashtanga Hridaya Su.1/19 'kālārthakarmaṇāṃ yogo...' (seen only on Dharmawiki) replaces buddhi with karma; worth recording as a parallel once a Sanskrit edition is checked.

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's rendering 'After-measures (Paschat-karma)'; he scopes the triad to 'the entire course of medical treatment'.
classical.quote: The entire course of medical treatment in connection with a disease may be grouped under three subheads, as the Preliminary measures (Purva- karma ); the Principal therapeutical or surgical appliances (Pradhana-karma); and the After-measures (Paschat-karma). These measures will be discussed under the head of each disease as we shall have occasion to deal with t
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907); quote truncated at page extraction boundary

distinguishFrom.why: The preparatory phase (Su.Su.5.3; WHO ITA-9.2.4); paścātkarma is the after phase of the same triad.
The main procedure (WHO ITA-9.2.68) that paścātkarma follows.

The graded diet after vamana/virecana; often described as the paścātkarma of those procedures (Bhishagratna's footnote places 'rice meal' under paścāt-karma), but it is one content of the phase, not its name.
The period and the things to be avoided after a procedure (Ca.Si.1.4 asks 'किं वर्जनीयं प्रतिकर्मकाले, कृते कियान् वा परिहारकालः'); restrictions during paścātkarma rather than the phase itself.
NIA 2011 has only 'mūtrayutaḥ pāk paścāt' (a symptom description); the therapeutic compound is absent there.

mistranslations.why: Correct for Shalya, but Sushruta scopes the triad to all treatment of disease and WHO scopes it to panchakarma aftercare.

mistranslations.rendering: follow-up (in the biomedical sense of review visits)
mistranslations.why: Paścātkarma is an active regimen (diet, restrictions, further procedures), not monitoring.
Suggests a lesser treatment given afterwards; the phase is part of the one karma that the triad divides.

openQuestions: Whether Charaka uses the compound paścātkarma; the Siddhisthana speaks of parihāra-kāla and saṁsarjana without this term in the lines read.
The commentary (Dalhana) behind Bhishagratna's footnote assignments was not consulted.

classical.verse: Standard 25/45; Kaviratna's printed number for this aphorism is not legible in the OCR (the next aphorism, standard 25/46, carries an OCR'd '8' which is clearly truncated)
classical.establishes: The definition of pathya. Sanskrit seen at carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Yajjah_Purushiya_Adhyaya: पथ्यं पथोऽनपेतं यद्यच्चोक्तं मनसः प्रियम्। यच्चाप्रियमपथ्यं च नियतं तन्न लक्षयेत्॥४५॥. '(of life)' is Kaviratna's gloss of pathaḥ.
classical.quote: All that is suitable to the way (of life) and that is agreeable to the mind is said to constitute what is called Pathya (or regimen). What, however, is the reverse of Pathya and is not agreeable to the mind, should never be attended to.

classical.establishes: Pathya is relative to mātrā, kāla, kriyā, bhūmi, deha, doṣa, guṇa. Sanskrit seen: मात्राकालक्रियाभूमिदेहदोषगुणान्तरम्। प्राप्य तत्तद्धि दृश्यन्ते ते ते भावास्तथा तथा॥४६॥.
classical.quote: Combined with measure, time or season, the nature of the operation, place, the constitution of the body, the faults that have been provoked, and the other attributes, both what is Pathya and what is its reverse are seen to be this or that (i.e., baneful or beneficial)

classical.verse: Sanskrit verse numbers not established (Bhishagratna prints none)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's position that some substances are absolutely hita/ahita, against the view that wholesomeness is purely conditional; the chapter is about hita/ahita, closely allied to pathya/apathya.
classical.quote: clarified-butter, water, milk and boiled-rice, etc. may be denominated as absolutely beneficial [...] fire, alkali and poison, may be designated as unconditionally harmful.

distinguishFrom.why: Hita (beneficial) is the broader category used in Cha.Su.30 and Su.Su.20; pathya in Cha.Su.25/45 adds the criterion 'agreeable to the mind' (manasaḥ priyam) and relativity to dose/time etc.
Sātmya is habitual suitability acquired by use (what one is accustomed to); pathya is wholesomeness by effect, which may be contrary to habit.

Pathyā is also a Sanskrit name of Harītakī (chebulic myrobalan); Kaviratna repeatedly renders 'Pathya (chebulic myrobalans)' in Chikitsasthana recipes, so drug-name occurrences must not be read as 'wholesome diet'.

mistranslations.why: Cha.Su.25/45 defines pathya as whatever (yad yat) is not off the path and pleasing to the mind, covering food and conduct; WHO also says 'Food or conduct'.
Serviceable but imports an English prescriptive sense; the Sanskrit is an adjective 'suited to the path/channels'.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's printed aphorism number for 25/45 should be read from the scan (p. 290 of the Sutrasthana part).

classical.establishes: Picchila is the last-named attribute of kapha. Kaviratna: '...stable, and slimy, these attributes of phlegm are cured by objects having adverse attributes.'
classical.quote: गुरुशीतमृदुस्निग्धमधुरस्थिरपिच्छिलाः| श्लेष्मणः प्रशमं यान्ति विपरीतगुणैर्गुणाः||६१||

classical.establishes: Picchila is one of the six gunas (drava, snigdha, śīta, manda, mṛdu, picchila, plus the rasa-guna) that mark jala-dominant substances, whose actions include bandha (binding). Kaviratna (Su. Lesson XXVI, his 23, p. 300) renders the list 'liquid, oily, cold, mild, soft, unctious, and mobile': 'unctious', after 'oily' (snigdha), is his word for picchila, so he does render it distinctly; it is the rasa-guna that has no counterpart, 'mobile' standing in its place. He renders bandha as 'stoppage of secretions'.
classical.quote: द्रवस्निग्धशीतमन्दमृदुपिच्छिलरसगुणबहुलान्याप्यानि, तान्युपक्लेदस्नेहबन्धविष्यन्दमार्दवप्रह्लादकराणि;

The quality of absorption (Vishad) is the opposite of sliminess. It absorbs or soaks up all mucous secretions and helps the process of healing a sore or ulcer.'

classical.establishes: Picchila/viśada as a kapha-vs-kaṭu axis.
classical.quote: A pungent taste is endued with properties which are contrary to those of the Kapha, hence the sweetness, oiliness, heaviness, coldness and sliminess of the latter, are respectively destroyed by the pungency, dryness, lightness, heat and non-sliminess of the former.

distinguishFrom.why: Both kapha attributes often glossed 'oily/sticky'; snigdha opposes rūkṣa (dry), picchila opposes viśada (clear/non-slimy). Sushruta separates their karmas (snigdha: lubrication, strength, complexion; picchila: binding, kapha, heaviness).
Sushruta 46.521 says ślakṣṇa is 'to be known like picchila' (श्लक्ष्णः पिच्छिलवज्ज्ञेयः), i.e. similar in karma but a distinct guṇa opposing khara/karkaśa.
Its opposite; rendered 'clear' by Kaviratna (Ca.Su. 1.59) and 'absorption'/'non-sliminess' by Bhishagratna, so the English for the pair is unstable.
A channel-clogging action often attributed to picchila foods; an effect, not the guṇa.

mistranslations.why: Imports snigdha; WHO's own search snippet gloss 'oily, sticky' blurs the two. Picchila is about adhesion/viscosity, not lipid content.
His seven-word list for the eight-word Sanskrit drops picchila; do not cite that line as his rendering of picchila.

classical.establishes: Pitta's functions include pigmentation, vision and intellection as well as digestion and heat. No reading of pitta as bile can carry medhā-kṛt.
classical.quote: Pigmentations or colouring (Ragakrit), the digestion of food and metabolism of tissues (Paktikrit), the vitalisation and nutrition of the protaplasmic cells (Ojakrit), the origination and preservation of eye-sight (Teja-Krit), the germination of heat and maintenance of the temperature of the body (Ushma-Krit), and the origination of the faculty of intellection (Medha-Krit) should be regarded as the functions of the five kinds of Pitta, which contribute to the preservation of the body through its thermogenetic potency (Agni-Karma).

classical.establishes: Sushruta explicitly identifies pitta with agni and denies any other heat-producing factor in the body. This is the textual basis for the pitta/agni conflation and for the later scholastic effort to separate them.
classical.quote: Now it may be asked whether the Pitta is identical with the elemental fire, or is it something other than that? The question may be answered by stating that the Pitta is the same as fire. Since such symptoms, as a burning sensation, digestion (boiling, and all other characteristics of fire can never exhibit themselves in the human body without the intervention of Pitta. Pitta therefore is called internal fire. ... There is no other fire (heat making factor) in the organism than Pitta.

classical.establishes: Gives pitta physical properties (liquid, coloured, odorous, tasting) — the strongest classical support for a substance reading, and the reason 'bile' is a tempting though inadequate rendering.
classical.quote: The Pitta is a keen, sharp and warm liquid, of a blue colour (in its normal state), or yellowish (in its deranged condition). It emits a kind of fleshy smell and is possessed of a pungent taste which is transformed into an acid one when deranged or vitiated.

classical.verse: 60 (Kaviratna prints this as aphorism 69, evidently an OCR or typesetting error for 59)
classical.establishes: The guṇas of pitta in lawfully quotable English. Note the printed number is unreliable in this scan; the verse number here is inferred from sequence and should be re-checked against a clean copy.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.establishes: The prākṛta/vaikṛta duality applied to pitta: the same pitta that digests, when provoked, produces many disorders.
classical.quote: पित्तादेवोष्मणः पक्तिर्नराणामुपजायते| तच्च पित्तं प्रकुपितं विकारान् कुरुते बहून्||११६|| / pittādēvōṣmaṇaḥ paktirnarāṇāmupajāyatē| tacca pittaṁ prakupitaṁ vikārān kurutē bahūn||116||

distinguishFrom.why: Sushruta Sutrasthana 21 identifies pitta with fire and denies any other heat source, yet later tradition and WHO ISTA treat agni as a separate entry (WHO ITA-2.6.x, samāgniḥ ITA-2.6.8). Whether pitta and agni are one thing is a live scholastic question, not a settled equivalence.
Sushruta says the factors that derange pitta vitiate blood as well and gives rakta its own constitutive standing. Pittaja and raktaja disorders are separately enumerated.

distinguishFrom.term: pācaka, rañjaka, sādhaka, ālocaka, bhrājaka pitta
distinguishFrom.why: The five subtypes are separately coded (WHO ITA-2.1.2.2 to 2.1.2.6) and are not interchangeable with pitta as a whole.
A constitutional category (WHO ITA-2.8.4, 'Body constitution with a predominance of pitta'), not a statement about current pitta level.
A physical secretion with a measurable concentration. Pitta has no assay; equating them turns a functional category into a lab value and invites false clinical inference.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's rendering and the standard 19th-century one. Cannot carry medhā-kṛt (intellection), ālocaka (vision) or bhrājaka (complexion), all of which Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 and 21 assign to pitta.
Defensible from Sushruta Sutrasthana 21 but incomplete: WHO ISTA names fire and water as the predominant elements, and pitta is repeatedly described as a liquid.
Imports the specific Galenic humour, adding a Greek taxonomy on top of an already inadequate substance reading.
Modern clinical shorthand in Indian practice. Takes the amla-vidagdha state of vitiated pitta as the definition of pitta.
Common modern gloss (including in the Ayurgenomics literature). Better than 'bile', but it silently drops the thermal, visual and cognitive functions.

Not a rendering of the term but of its guna list, and the clearest case in this corpus of a translator's word choice being mistaken for a doctrine. Kaviratna gives Ca. Su. 1.60 as 'Bile, which may be cold, hot, keen, soft, sour, liquid, and bitter'. The mula reads sasneham usnam tiksnam ca dravam amlam saram katu: unctuous, hot, keen, liquid, sour, mobile, pungent. 'Cold' stands where the text has sasneham (unctuous), 'soft' where it has saram (mobile) and 'bitter' where it has katu (pungent). Pitta is hot in every reading of the Sanskrit and no commentator supports a cold pitta, so a reader meeting 'cold' first in a public-domain English text meets the opposite of the doctrine. The citation is kept at classical[3] marked superseded, with the mula beside it, because the error is itself evidence of how the text was read in 1896.

openQuestions: No peer-reviewed literature was found that treats pitta specifically, as opposed to tridosha or prakriti collectively. Whether this is a real gap or an artefact of PubMed indexing is unresolved.

The relation of pitta to agni is the single largest unresolved question in this record and cannot be settled from the two public-domain translations alone; Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 12-13 and Sharngadhara are the places to look, and neither has a quotable English translation.

Citation #3 refuted: Quote and location both check out, but the English misstates pitta's qualities and should not be published as 'the gunas of pitta'. Retrieved: the sentence appears verbatim in the Kaviratna OCR at offset 31,335 -- 'Bile,

classical.verse: 67 (standard; Kaviratna prints 23 after the passage in his restarted Lesson XXVI numbering)
classical.establishes: The defining verse: where rasa, vīrya and vipāka are the same but the action differs, that is prabhāva. Kaviratna: 'Where uniformity is observed (between two objects) in respect of taste, energy, and assimilation, but a difference or distinction occurs in their operation or effect, such distinction is said to arise from what is called the potency of the objects.'
classical.quote: रसवीर्यविपाकानां सामान्यं यत्र लक्ष्यते| विशेषः कर्मणां चैव प्रभावस्तस्य स स्मृतः||६७||

classical.verse: 68-70 (standard; Kaviratna 24-26; first and last confirmed separately)
classical.establishes: The stock examples (citraka vs dantī; poison as antidote; emetic vs purgative direction; worn gems) and the dictum that prabhāva is acintya. Kaviratna: 'Chitraka (Plumbago Zeylanica, Linn.) is pungent in taste, and pungent in assimilation, and hot in energy. So is Danti ... But Danti operates as a purgative (while Chitiaka does not). This occurs through the potency of Danti.' ... 'Potency is said to be inconceivable.'
classical.quote: कटुकः कटुकः पाके वीर्योष्णश्चित्रको मतः| तद्वद्दन्ती प्रभावात्तु विरेचयति मानवम् ||६८|| विषं विषघ्नमुक्तं यत् प्रभावस्तत्र कारणम्| ऊर्ध्वानुलोमिकं यच्च तत् प्रभावप्रभावितम्||६९|| मणीनां धारणीयानां कर्म यद्विविधात्मकम्| तत् प्रभावकृतं तेषां प्रभावोऽचिन्त्य उच्यते ||७०||

classical.establishes: The hierarchy: vipāka overrides rasa, vīrya overrides both, prabhāva overrides all. Kaviratna: 'Taste is subjugated by Assimilation ; both of them, again, are subjugated by Energy ; and all three are subjugated by Potency. Even such is the natural force of each of these.'
classical.quote: किञ्चिद्रसेन कुरुते कर्म वीर्येण चापरम्||७१|| द्रव्यं गुणेन पाकेन प्रभावेण च किञ्चन| रसं विपाकस्तौ वीर्यं प्रभावस्तानपोहति||७२||

classical.establishes: A non-technical use of prabhāva in the same chapter ('their powers are beneficial and non-beneficial'; Kaviratna: 'Beneficial and Not-beneficial are their powers'), showing the word is not reserved for the technical sense even within Ca.Su. 26.
classical.quote: हिताहितौ प्रभावौ

classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: Kaviratna renders prabhāva as 'potency' and vīrya as 'Energy'; modern English reverses this ('potency' = vīrya). Charaka 26.72 places prabhāva above vīrya in the override hierarchy, so they are distinct levels.
Prabhāva is the explanatory residual for a karma, not the karma itself (26.67: viśeṣaḥ karmaṇāṃ... prabhāvaḥ).
Ca.Su. 26.9 uses 'hitāhitau prabhāvau' non-technically; the dictionary senses (might, majesty, supernatural power) are general.
Also a non-sensory inferred principle; vipāka is the post-digestive rasa with three (Charaka) outcomes, while prabhāva is by definition what vipāka and the others fail to explain.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's term; in current English 'potency' denotes vīrya, so quoting him without a gloss inverts the hierarchy.

Monier-Williams' 'supernatural power' sense and the gem example (26.70) tempt this reading; the text's point is unexplained but observed drug action, declared acintya (not inferable), not supernatural.

mistranslations.why: WHO DG0230's 'characteristic therapeutic effect' drops the condition 'given sameness of rasa, vīrya, vipāka', which is what makes prabhāva a residual category rather than a synonym for efficacy.

classical.verse: Not numbered by Bhishagratna; corresponds to the sentence numbered 3 on siva.sh (see previous entry). Do not cite as 'Su.Su. 5.3 (Bhishagratna)'.
classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for the three terms; he frames them as covering 'the entire course of medical treatment', not surgery only.
classical.quote: The entire course of medical treatment in connection with a disease may be grouped under three subheads, as the Preliminary measures (Purva-karma); the Principal therapeutical or surgical appliances (Pradhana-karma); and the After-measures (Paschat-karma).

distinguishFrom.why: The preparatory phase (e.g. snehana, svedana before panchakarma; pre-operative preparation in surgery); pradhānakarma is the main act itself.
After-measures (e.g. saṁsarjana krama, wound care); frequently lumped with pradhānakarma in loose descriptions of 'the procedure'.
Pañcakarma names five specific pradhānakarmas; pradhānakarma is a phase label that applies to any procedure, surgical or purificatory.
'pradhāna' alone means chief/principal; only the compound with karma denotes the procedural phase.

mistranslations.why: Both Sushruta's framing and WHO scope the term to any treatment course including panchakarma; restricting it to surgery loses the panchakarma usage.
Imports the biomedical sense of treatment hierarchy; pradhānakarma is a temporal phase, not a priority ranking.

openQuestions: Which Sanskrit edition siva.sh follows for Su.Su. 5.3 (not stated on the page); verify against Trikamji/Acharya edition before publishing the verse number.
Whether Charaka uses the compound pradhānakarma at all; carakasamhitaonline Kalpana Siddhi page did not formally use the three terms (fetched 2026-10-07).
