classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji-type, as printed on carakasamhitaonline) 11/43 prose; Dharmawiki numbers the same prose 11.44. Kaviratna prints his aphorisms 41, 42, 43 for this block.
classical.establishes: Prajñāparādha is named as the second of the three causes (hetu) of disorders, alongside asātmyendriyārtha-saṃyoga and pariṇāma. Kaviratna's number 42 matches standard 43 by content here (one behind), but his 41 is a different prose unit from standard 42; do not convert by offset.
classical.quote: Sanskrit (carakasamhitaonline, numbered 43): "इत्यसात्म्येन्द्रियार्थसंयोगः, प्रज्ञापराधः, परिणामश्चेति त्रयस्त्रिविधविकल्पा हेतवो विकाराणां". Kaviratna (his 41-42, p.125-126): "Correlation, as shown above, is of three kinds. These three kinds of acts or exertions are regarded as faults of the Understanding.41 ... Thus are the three subjects treated of, viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time or Parinama.42 These three, (viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time,) each sub-divided into three kinds, constitute the causes of disease."
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (English); Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline.com

classical.establishes: The verse names 'buddhi' (not prajñāparādha by name) as the middle member of the three-fold cause; Kaviratna renders buddhi here as 'mind', which obscures the link to prajñāparādha. Kaviratna's footnote (his own, not the text): "Time is of two kinds, viz., (1) that portion of eternity with which human life is concerned and which goes on ceaselessly, and (2) the age of man".
classical.quote: Sanskrit (numbered 54): "कालबुद्धीन्द्रियार्थानां योगो मिथ्या न चाति च| द्वयाश्रयाणां व्याधीनां त्रिविधो हेतुसङ्ग्रहः||५४||". Kaviratna (his 53): "Of all diseases, physical and mental, the causes in brief are of three kinds, viz., adverse or excessive correlation or want of correlation of time, mind, and the objects of the senses.*53"

classical.establishes: Restates the three causes of suffering in Sarirasthana, with dhī-dhṛti-smṛti-vibhraṃśa as the first. Kaviratna's own footnote (not text): "I render 'dhi' the equivalent of 'buddhi,' as Understanding; 'dhriti' as firmness ... and lastly 'smriti' as Memory or the retentive power." In this chapter Kaviratna runs seven ahead of the standard numbering (105/98, 109/102, 116/109), verified by content at each of those three points.
classical.quote: Sanskrit (numbered 98, first line only as retrieved): "धीधृतिस्मृतिविभ्रंशः सम्प्राप्तिः कालकर्मणाम्". Kaviratna (his 105, p.677): "Loss of Understanding, of Firmness, and of Memory, time in respect of the accession of disease and of the administration of correctives as also the accession of objects unaccordant with the senses, — these should be known as the causes of sorrow.105"

classical.establishes: Defines the three component failures (buddhi/dhī-vibhraṃśa, dhṛti-bhraṃśa, smṛti-bhraṃśa) that together constitute prajñāparādha.
classical.quote: Sanskrit: "विषमाभिनिवेशो यो नित्यानित्ये हिताहिते। ज्ञेयः स बुद्धिविभ्रंशः समं बुद्धिर्हि पश्यति॥९९॥ विषयप्रवणं सत्त्वं धृतिभ्रंशान्न शक्यते। नियन्तुमहितादर्थाद्धृतिर्हि नियमात्मिका॥१००॥ तत्त्वज्ञाने स्मृतिर्यस्य रजोमोहावृतात्मनः। भ्रश्यते स स्मृतिभ्रंशः स्मर्तव्यं हि स्मृतौ स्थितम्॥१०१॥". Kaviratna (his 106-108, p.678): "An injudicious attention to what is unchangeable and what is changeable, as also to good and evil, is regarded as loss of understanding, since the understanding implies a judicious application to things.*106 The mind that is prone to earthly objects is incapable of being restrained from evil courses owing to loss of firmness, for firmness implies restraint of inclinations.107 The swerving of the mind of a person who is overwhelmed by passion and heedlessness from the knowledge of truth, is known as loss of memory, for that which should be remembered (viz., the knowledge of truth) dwells in memory.108"

classical.verse: Standard 102 (carakasamhitaonline; Dharmawiki cites the same verse as 'Char. Samh. 1.102'). Kaviratna prints 109.
classical.establishes: The canonical definition: unwholesome action done by one whose dhī, dhṛti and smṛti are deranged is prajñāparādha, and it provokes all doṣas. Kaviratna's footnote (his own): "'Dosha' in 'sarvadoshaprakopanam' has reference as much to the faults, (wind, bile and phlegm) as to all trangressions from duty."
classical.quote: Sanskrit: "धीधृतिस्मृतिविभ्रष्टः कर्म यत् कुरुतेऽशुभम्। प्रज्ञापराधं तं विद्यात् सर्वदोषप्रकोपणम्॥१०२॥". Kaviratna (his 109, p.678): "The evil acts which a man who has lost understanding, firmness, and memory, perpetrates, should be known to constitute what is called fault of judgment. This (fault of judgment) is provocative of all the faults.109"

classical.establishes: Second definition: wrong cognition by the intellect and wrong action; prajñāparādha is located in the domain of manas (manaso gocaram). Kaviratna's footnote: "Acts have two elements, viz., mental and physical. The physical element is excluded. Acts that are faults of judgment are, the Rishi says, all mental." The list of acts (standard 103-107 / Kaviratna 110-114) sits between these two quotes.
classical.quote: Sanskrit: "यच्चान्यदीदृशं कर्म रजोमोहसमुत्थितम्। प्रज्ञापराधं तं शिष्टा ब्रुवते व्याधिकारणम्॥१०८॥ बुद्ध्या विषमविज्ञानं विषमं च प्रवर्तनम्। प्रज्ञापराधं जानीयान्मनसो गोचरं हि तत्॥१०९॥". Kaviratna (his 115-116, p.679): "These and such other acts which arise from passion and stupefaction, are regarded by sages as disease-producing faults of judgment.115 Injudicious apprehension of things by the understanding, as also a setting of one's self to injudicious acts, should be known as fault of judgment. That which is called fault of judgment really concerns the mind.*116"

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints 23 (OCR reads '28!' between his 22 and 24, so 23). carakasamhitaonline lists this as Vi. 3/20; standard number NOT verified against a Sanskrit source in this session.
classical.establishes: Prajñāparādha as the root of adharma, which in turn is the root of the vitiation of air, water, place and time that destroys communities (epidemic causation).
classical.quote: Kaviratna (p.477): "Unto him the illustrious son of Atri said, — O Agniveca, the perversity that arises of all these, viz., air and the rest, has unrighteousness for its root. That unrighteousness has for its root sinful acts committed before. The source of both these (viz., unrighteousness and sinful acts), is faults of the understanding.23" Footnote (translator's note, not text): "By 'prajnaparadhah' is meant faults of the understanding. 'Prajna' means wisdom, or, rather, the faculty by which one judges of things correctly. 'Aparadha' of this, therefore, must imply all instances of erroneous judgment or incorrect apprehension."

classical.verse: Standard Vimānasthāna 6/6 (Trikamji; carakasamhitaonline Roganika Vimana prints ||६|| after 'परिणामश्चेति'). Kaviratna: Vimanasthana Lesson VI, printed p. 515, inside the block closed by his printed 10 (his 10 covers standard 6-9; number printed after). Not Nidānasthāna: Kaviratna's Nidanasthana Lesson I (printed p. 928) renders Ni 1/3 as a different sentence.
classical.establishes: The three causes, asātmyendriyārtha-saṃyoga, prajñāparādha and pariṇāma, restated in Vimānasthāna 6/6 as the threefold provokers (trividhaṃ prakopaṇam) of both classes of doṣa, the mental (rajas, tamas) and the bodily (vāta, pitta, kapha). The gloss 'By Parinama is meant Time' is Kaviratna's footnote, not the text. The same triad is the definition of nidāna at Ni 1/3 (tat trividham: asātmyendriyārthasaṃyogaḥ, prajñāparādhaḥ, pariṇāmaś ceti), which Kaviratna renders differently.
classical.quote: Kaviratna: "Amongst them, verily, of these two kinds of Faults (viz., mental and bodily), there are three kinds of exciting causes, viz., union with disagreeing objects of sense, faults of understanding, and Time." Footnote (translator's note): "By 'Parinama' is meant Time."
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints 13 (OCR 'r3', p.994). carakasamhitaonline lists prajñāparādha as cause of unmāda at Ni. 7/10; standard number NOT verified against Sanskrit in this session.
classical.establishes: Prajñāparādha named as the cause of āgantu (exogenous) unmāda, over against the 'past deeds' view.
classical.quote: Kaviratna: "Some say that the evil acts of previous lives are the cause of this variety of Insanity (viz., that which is called Accidental). But the illustrious Punarvasu of Atri's race declared that fault of judgment is the cause.13" Footnote (translator's note): "'Prajnaparadha,' as explained previously, is fault of judgment, i.e., errors of the understanding. Almost all diseases are born of such errors."

distinguishFrom.why: The first of the three causes: wrong (excess, deficient, perverse) contact of senses with their objects. Kaviratna himself notes (Sa.1 footnote) that the first and third 'are scarcely exclusive of each other'; the texts nonetheless keep them as separate heads.
The third cause, time and its transformations (season, age). Prajñāparādha is volitional; pariṇāma is not.

The derangement of intellect, restraint and memory is the mechanism; prajñāparādha is the unwholesome ACT that results from it (Ca.Sa.1.102). Kaviratna's footnote says the compound 'is otherwise called Prajnaparadha', collapsing cause and effect; the Sanskrit of 102 keeps them distinct.
Ca.Vi.3 makes prajñāparādha the ROOT of adharma, not a synonym for sin. Kaviratna's Su.11 footnote (translator's view) frames the doctrine in terms of 'sin', which is his gloss.

In Sutrasthana 11 the three kinds of wrong exertion of speech, mind and body are what is 'regarded as' prajñāparādha; in Sarirasthana 1 the definition is cognitive. The two chapters define it at different levels (act vs. faculty).
Kaviratna renders buddhi in Ca.Su.1.54 as 'mind', so a reader of his translation will not see that this verse is the seed of the prajñāparādha doctrine.

mistranslations.why: Still the head rendering in NAMASTE (SAT-C.76, SAT-J.49). 'Blasphemy' imports a theological register absent from aparādha (offence, fault, transgression); the Sanskrit concerns erroneous judgement and volitional wrong action, not sacrilege. Even the carakasamhitaonline page calls it 'a more Victorian style'.
WHO ITA-4.8.36 head term; an inversion of 'error of judgement' that reads as a judgement ABOUT error.

Popular Western rendering; 'crime' over-criminalises aparādha and 'wisdom' mystifies prajñā, which Kaviratna glosses as 'the faculty by which one judges of things correctly'. Not retrieved in a source this session; flagged as circulating.

mistranslations.rendering: fault of judgment = all mental (Kaviratna footnote)
mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's note that 'the physical element is excluded' is his reading of manaso gocaram; the text itself lists bodily acts (suppression of urges, overindulgence) as prajñāparādha. Treat the note as translator's opinion.

openQuestions: Standard (Trikamji) verse numbers for Ca.Vi.3 (listed as 3/20), Ca.Ni.1 (1/3) and Ca.Ni.7 (7/10) were taken from carakasamhitaonline's reference list and not verified against a numbered Sanskrit page; Kaviratna's printed numbers (23, 10, 13) are what was read.
Sutrasthana 11 prose numbering differs between editions: carakasamhitaonline prints 43 for the 'ity asātmyendriyārtha...' sentence, Dharmawiki cites 11.44 for the same sentence.

Whether Ashtanga Hridaya Su.1/19 (kālārthakarmaṇāṃ yogo hīnamithyātimātrakaḥ, cited by Dharmawiki) should be recorded as a parallel: no public-domain English exists and the Sanskrit was seen only on Dharmawiki.
ICD-11 TM2 coverage: a search found no evidence that prajñāparādha is coded (it is a cause, not a disorder); not checked in the ICD-11 browser itself.

classical.establishes: Gives the signs of prakopa (pricking and wandering pain in the koṣṭha, sour eructation, thirst, burning, aversion to food, nausea) and marks it the second kriyākāla.
classical.quote: तेषां प्रकोपात् कोष्ठतोदसञ्चरणाम्लीकापिपासापरिदाहान्नद्वेषहृदयोत्क्लेदाश्च जायन्ते । तत्र द्वितीयः क्रियाकालः ॥२७॥

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for the prakopa stage, including his rendering of the stage-marker as 'the second occasion which calls for medical aid'.
classical.quote: The aggravated condition of the humours gives rise to pain and moves the wind Vayu) in the bowels; it further occasions acid eructations, thirst, burning sensations, aversion to food, vomiting and nausea. Any of these symptoms should be regarded as the second occasion which calls for medical aid.

classical.establishes: Verses 19-26 are a long catalogue of prakopaṇa — the causes that provoke each dosha and blood, plus the times and seasons of spontaneous provocation. Important lexicographically: prakopaṇa (the provoking cause) is a distinct word from prakopa (the stage), and the bulk of the chapter's prakopa material is aetiological, not staging. Only the section-opening sentence is quoted; the verse range is a description of what follows it, not a quotation claim.
classical.quote: अत ऊर्ध्वं प्रकोपणानि वक्ष्यामः ।

classical.chapter: Lesson III (Jwara / Treatment of Fever), as numbered in Kaviratna's translation
classical.establishes: Kaviratna renders the prakopa idea as 'provoked' or 'excited' rather than 'aggravated', and shows the accumulation-to-provocation sequence operating seasonally in Charaka. Re-verified this session: the sentence sits inside a block closed by the inline number '41-42', which is confirmed adjacent in the retrieved text; the quoted sentence is one sentence within that numbered block, not the whole of it.
classical.quote: The  accumulated  bile  becomes  provoked  in  the  season  of  autumn through  the  heat  of  the  sun,  and  quickly  generates  fever  (that  is characterised  by  excited  bile).

distinguishFrom.why: Su.Su. 21.19-21.26 uses prakopaṇa for the CAUSES that provoke a dosha (diet, conduct, season). Prakopa is the resulting state. English 'aggravation' is used for both in most sources, which destroys the distinction.

Vṛddhi is quantitative increase. Prakopa in the kriyakala sense is a change of state — the dosha reaches a threshold and is about to overflow. WHO's chapter 5 equates vātaprakopaḥ with vātavṛddhilakṣaṇam (confirmed in the Sanskrit column this session), so even WHO is inconsistent between its own chapters; treat any source that equates them as making a substantive claim, not just a wording choice.
In the three-fold seasonal scheme, kopa is followed by spontaneous praśama. In the six-fold scheme, prakopa is followed by prasara. Same root, different downstream commitment.

Both occur in the dosha's own seat. The distinguishing claim in the sources is degree or threshold: WHO says prakopa is when the dosha 'increases to reach the threshold at its own location'. The boundary is not operationally defined in anything I could retrieve.

mistranslations.why: Imports a specific modern histopathological process. Prakopa is a state of a dosha, and the signs Sushruta lists (sour eructation, thirst, nausea, aversion to food) are not inflammatory signs.
A literal reading of the root kup-. Doshas are described figuratively as enraged, but in a lexicon this reads as an emotion and is wrong.

mistranslations.rendering: 'flare-up' meaning a clinical exacerbation of an existing disease
mistranslations.why: Prakopa in kriyakala precedes disease. Borrowing 'flare' from rheumatology or dermatology puts it at the wrong end of the sequence.

openQuestions: Where exactly sources place the sañcaya/prakopa boundary, and whether any of them defines it by anything other than severity of the same signs.
Whether WHO intends ITA-4.6.8 (stage) and ITA-5.2.x (disorder) to be the same referent under two headings, or two distinct entities.
What Dalhana says on 21.27 about how the threshold is characterised — no public-domain English of Dalhana was located.

classical.establishes: Prakṛti is the first of the ten examination items, and this fixes verse 94 for the whole list. Every verse number in this term group was read off this same retrieved page.
classical.quote: tasmādāturaṁ parīkṣēta prakr̥titaśca, vikr̥titaśca, sārataśca, saṁhananataśca, pramāṇataśca, sātmyataśca, sattvataśca, āhāraśaktitaśca, vyāyāmaśaktitaśca, vayastaścēti, balapramāṇaviśēṣagrahaṇahētōḥ||94||

classical.establishes: Prakṛti is set from conception; five classes named. Note the text's own word is doṣaprakṛti.
classical.quote: tataḥ sā sā dōṣaprakr̥tirucyatē manuṣyāṇāṁ garbhādipravr̥ttā| tasmācchlēṣmalāḥ prakr̥tyā kēcit, pittalāḥ kēcit, vātalāḥ kēcit, saṁsr̥ṣṭāḥ kēcit, samadhātavaḥ kēcidbhavanti||95||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Vi 8/95. Kaviratna numbers this passage 111 in his own scheme (printed p. 594); the verse number above comes from the Sanskrit and the two were matched by content, not by number. Note that "thie" is Kaviratna's own printed typo, visible on the page image at p. 594 line 3, and not an OCR artefact as this record previously said.
classical.quote: Some persons, by nature, have the wind predominating in thie constitutions ; Some have the bile predominating in their constitutions ; Some have the phlegm predominating in their constitutions ; Some have any two of the three faults or all the three faults combined together in predominant measure ; and Some have all the three faults combined in harmonious proportions.

classical.establishes: Closes the prakṛti section at verse 100 and defines the samadhātu type as having all qualities together.

classical.establishes: Sushruta counts seven prakṛtis where Charaka Vi 8/95 names five classes. The two samhitas disagree and modern summaries rarely say so.
classical.quote: The temperaments ( Prakriti ) of persons may be of seven different types, according as the deranged Doshas of the body are involved therein, either severally, or in combination of two or of all the three together.

classical.establishes: The classical immutability claim, i.e. the textual basis for WHO's 'It is immutable and does not change during a lifespan' at ITA-2.8.2.
classical.quote: The temperament of a man is never altered, nor does it suffer any deterioration or abatement. A change, abatement or deterioration in any particular case should be regarded as the harbinger of death.

classical.establishes: The Samkhya sense inside the same samhita. Verse left blank: the page prints '3' but that was not checked against a Sanskrit edition.

distinguishFrom.why: Consecutive items in Vi 8: prakṛti is the conception-set baseline, vikṛti (Vi 8/101) the present morbid state. Not two readings of one scale.
The term Vi 8/95 actually uses. WHO subordinates it to prakṛti; treating them as synonyms drops that distinction.
Mental type is a separate examination item at Vi 8/119. Folding it into 'prakriti' collapses two of the ten items.
Sushruta Sharirasthana 1 uses prakṛti for unmanifest primordial Nature. Nothing clinical follows from it.
WHO ITA-4.8.17 defines prakṛti as the normal state simpliciter. An uncontextualised citation is genuinely ambiguous.
Both are baseline traits assessed for strength, but sāra grades tissue excellence, not doṣa dominance.

mistranslations.why: Reduces a doṣa configuration to somatotype. Vi 8/115 explicitly rejects reading strength off body size.
Merges prakṛti with current derangement, i.e. with vikṛti, which the texts keep separate.
Over-claims discreteness. The reliability literature (24191170, 27257530) argues against it.
Bhishagratna's 1911 word; reads as Galenic humoral temperament and loses the conception-fixed sense.
Right only for the Samkhya passages; simply wrong in a clinical one.

classical.chapter: 1 (Vatavyadhi Nidana; Bhishagratna's title: 'Diagnosis of diseases of nervous system')
classical.establishes: Sushruta's prāṇa is seated in the MOUTH (vaktra) and its defining act is driving food downward into the stomach, plus supporting the vitalising principles. Corresponding Sanskrit, cross-checked at a separate URL: 'यो वायुर्वक्त्रसञ्चारी स प्राणो नाम देहधृक् | सोऽन्नं प्रवेशयत्यन्तः प्राणांश्चाप्यवलम्बते ||१३|| प्रायशः कुरुते दुष्टो हिक्काश्वासादिकान् गदान् |१४|'. Bhishagratna's footnote [4] to this passage adds: 'The field of its action includes the regions of the heart, throat, head and the nose.'
classical.quote: The Vayu, that courses in (governs) the cavity of the mouth, is called the Prana, its function being to force down the food into the cavity of the stomach, and to assist the different vitalising principles of the body (such as the internal heat or fire etc.) in discharging their functions in life, and to contribute to the general sustenance of the body. A deranged condition of this particular kind of Vayu (Prana) is usually followed by hiccough, dyspnea and other kindred distempers. 7.

classical.establishes: Charaka's prāṇa is seated in mūrdhā (head), uras (chest), kaṇṭha (throat), jihvā (tongue), āsya (mouth) and nāsikā (nose); its karma is ṣṭhīvana (spitting), kṣavathu (sneezing), udgāra (belching), śvāsa (respiration) and āhāra (ingestion of food), etc. The enumeration verse 28.5 reads 'प्राणोदानसमानाख्यव्यानापानैः स पञ्चधा | देहं तन्त्रयते सम्यक् स्थानेष्वव्याहतश्चरन् ||५||'. This is the single richest classical locus for the five subtypes and it has NO public-domain English translation (see gatheringNotes).
classical.quote: स्थानं प्राणस्य मूर्धोरःकण्ठजिह्वास्यनासिकाः [१] | ष्ठीवनक्षवथूद्गारश्वासाहारादि कर्म च ||६||

classical.establishes: The ONLY passage naming all five subtypes that exists in a lawfully quotable English Charaka. It establishes the fivefold division and its ordering (prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna, apāna) but gives no seat or function for any individual subtype.

distinguishFrom.why: In Charaka's own translator's footnote 'prāṇāḥ' means the life-winds collectively, and elsewhere prāṇa means life/vitality or the lifespan. WHO's own entry ITA-2.1.1.2 fuses the two senses in one definition ('Also denotes life or vitality'). The subtype prāṇa vāta is one of five functional divisions of the vāta doṣa; prāṇa-as-vitality is not.

distinguishFrom.term: prāṇa vāyu of yoga / the pañca-vāyu scheme
distinguishFrom.why: Yoga and Vedanta use the same five names for breath-currents used in prāṇāyāma, and add five upa-prāṇas (nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, dhanañjaya). Charaka Ci.28.6 gives prāṇa a seat-and-organ definition, not a breath-current one. Sources that say prāṇa vāta 'is the inhaled breath' have imported the yogic sense.

Both operate above the clavicles and both are placed in chest and throat. Charaka separates them by seat (prāṇa: head/chest/throat/tongue/mouth/nose; udāna: navel/chest/throat) and by function (prāṇa: ingestion, respiration, sneezing, belching; udāna: speech, effort, strength, complexion). Ashtanga Hridaya draws the line differently again.

Both are assigned mental and cognitive function and both are located at or near the heart in some texts. Prāṇa vāta is a vāta subtype governing the movement of cognition; sādhaka pitta is a pitta subtype governing its transformation. Conflating them collapses the doṣa distinction.
A channel (srotas), not a doṣa subtype. WHO lists srotas separately (section 2.5). Papers sometimes use 'prana vata dysfunction' and 'pranavaha srotodushti' interchangeably; the texts do not.

mistranslations.rendering: life force / vital air / vital breath
mistranslations.why: Translates prāṇa in its yogic/Upanishadic sense and drops the vāta-subtype sense entirely. WHO's own head-term does this and gives no functional English name, which is why textbooks copying WHO end up with no usable label.

mistranslations.rendering: the medulla oblongata / the energy of the nerve centre in the medulla
mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's 1911 footnote, repeated uncritically for a century. It is a colonial-era attempt to map Ayurvedic physiology onto Victorian neuroanatomy, not a translation of anything Sushruta wrote. Bhishagratna's own footnote is internally corrupt — it names Udana twice and never mentions Vyana.

Respiration (śvāsa) is one item in Charaka's list of prāṇa's karma at Ci.28.6, alongside spitting, sneezing, belching and ingestion. Reducing the subtype to respiration deletes most of its classical remit and collides with udāna, which Sushruta ties to voice.
An organ substitution. Charaka gives a seat list, not an organ; 'head' (mūrdhā) is a region. The brain as such is not the referent in any of the loci retrieved.

classical.establishes: Suśruta's root for prāṇavaha srotas = heart + rasa-carrying dhamanīs, and treats it as a PAIR (two), unlike Caraka's unnumbered plural. Directly disagrees with Caraka's 'hṛdaya + mahāsrotas'.
classical.quote: The two Srotas (channels) of Prana (bronchi) have their roots in the heart and the Rasa-carrying Dhamanis (pulmonary arteries). An injury to any of these Srotas (vessels) produces groaning, bending down of the body, loss of consciousness (Moha), illusion, and shivering, or may ultimately prove fatal.

distinguishFrom.why: prāṇa vāyu is one of the five subtypes of vāta (a functional force); prāṇavaha srotas is the channel system it moves in. Confusing them collapses substance/conduit.

WHO codes these as two separate terms (ITA-2.5.6 vs ITA-2.5.7). The respiratory tract is defined anatomically 'from the external nares to the alveoli'; prāṇavaha srotas is defined functionally and, in Caraka, is rooted in heart + mahāsrotas, which is not the airway.

mahāsrotas is one of prāṇavaha srotas' two roots in Caraka, not a synonym. WHO (ITA.3.11.1) defines mahāsrotas as 'The major inner cavity of the body from the mouth to anus', i.e. the gut, not the airway.

In Suśruta both are rooted in the heart and both, when injured, produce overlapping signs; Suśruta explicitly says injury to rasavaha produces 'symptoms identical with those developed by a hurt to the Prana-vaha channels'.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's 1911 parenthetical gloss, not the Sanskrit. It imports a 19th-century anatomical identification and is inconsistent with Caraka, who roots the channel in the heart and the gut.

A workable clinical shorthand (NAMASTE adopts it) but not a translation. WHO deliberately keeps 'respiratory tract' as a separate term. Using it as the entry definition erases Caraka's mahāsrotas root.

mistranslations.rendering: pranic channels / channels of life force (as an esoteric energy)
mistranslations.why: Popular-Ayurveda rendering that assimilates prāṇa to yogic/New-Age prāṇa and to nāḍīs. Classical srotas are material conduits with named anatomical roots and named injury signs.

openQuestions: Does mahāsrotas in Ca.Vi.5/8 mean the gut (as WHO's mahāsrotas entry implies) or the thoracic 'great channel'? Commentators differ and this decides whether the Caraka channel is respiratory at all.
Is Suśruta's 'two' a real dual anatomy or a convention of the Śārīra chapter (which pairs all eleven)?

classical.establishes: Three load-bearing points: the fermentation simile (kiṇva + udaka + piṣṭa) for how doshas overflow; the doctrine that VAYU is the agent of prasara because it alone has motion (vāyur gatimattvāt prasaraṇahetuḥ satyapy acaitanye); and the explicit fifteen-fold enumeration, now quoted in full, ending एवं पञ्चदशधा प्रसरन्ति — 'thus they spread in fifteen ways'. The fifteen count is the text's own, not a commentator's.
classical.quote: अत ऊर्ध्वं प्रसरं वक्ष्यामः- तेषामेभिरातङ्कविशेषैः प्रकुपितानां किण्वोदकपिष्टसमवाय इवोद्रिक्तानां प्रसरो भवति । तेषां वायुर्गतिमत्त्वात् प्रसरणहेतुः सत्यप्यचैतन्ये । ... तद्यथा- वातः, पित्तं, श्लेष्मा, शोणितं, वातपित्ते, वातश्लेष्माणौ, पित्तश्लेष्माणौ, वातशोणिते, पित्तशोणिते, श्लेष्मशोणिते, वातपित्तशोणितानि, वातश्लेष्मशोणितानि, पित्तश्लेष्मशोणितानि, वातपित्तकफाः, वातपित्तकफशोणितानीति; एवं पञ्चदशधा प्रसरन्ति ॥२८॥

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for the prasara definition, the fermentation simile and the vayu-as-agent doctrine.
classical.quote: Now we shall describe the expansion ( Prasara ) of the deranged humours. The deranged humours, aggravated by the above mentioned causes, expand and overflow the limits of their respective localities in the same manner as, cakes, soaked in any ferment or enzyme and kept standing over night, ferment and rise through the acquisition of new and unseen attributes. The Vayu, which is possessed of locomotion or extreme mobility, should be looked upon as the cause of their expansion or over-flowing.

classical.establishes: Gives the dosha-wise signs of prasara and marks it the third kriyākāla. Note the stage-marker sits at verse 32, four verses after the prasara section opens at 28 — so citing 'Su.Su. 21/28' or 'Su.Su. 21/32' for prasara are both defensible and published sources differ.
classical.quote: एवं प्रकुपितानां प्रसरतां वायोर्विमार्गगमनाटोपौ, ओषचोषपरिदाहधूमायनानि पित्तस्य, अरोचकाविपाकाङ्गसादाश्छर्दिश्चेति श्लेष्मणो लिङ्गानि भवन्ति; तत्र तृतीयः क्रियाकालः ॥३२॥

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for the dosha-wise prasara signs and the third-occasion marker.
classical.quote: The Vayu, thus aggravated and expanded, tends to deviate from its right passage and gives rise to a swelling or distention of the abdomen, accompanied by a rumbling sound in the intestines. The Pitta, under the similar condition, gives rise to heat, and a sort of sucking, burning pain in the affected part, together with a sensation of radiation or evaporation of heat from its surface. The Kapha, under the circumstance, would usher in a complete aversion to food, inertness of the limbs, vomiting and impaired digestion. The preceding symptoms, caused by the aggravation and expansion of the bodily humours, should be the third occasion for medical treatment

classical.establishes: The rain-cloud simile (29): a dosha strongly provoked in the whole body, half of it, or one part 'rains down' disorder there like a cloud in the sky. Verse 30, now quoted in full rather than described, is the latency verse: a not-excessively-provoked dosha stays LATENT (līno) in the channels (mārgeṣu) and, unopposed, is provoked later on meeting a cause. This is the classical basis for a gap between prasara and sthānasaṃśraya.
classical.quote: कृत्स्नेऽर्धेऽवयवे वाऽपि यत्राङ्गे कुपितो भृशम् । दोषो विकारं नभसि मेघवत्तत्र वर्षति ॥२९॥ नात्यर्थं कुपितश्चापि लीनो मार्गेषु तिष्ठति । निष्प्रत्यनीकः कालेन हेतुमासाद्य कुप्यति ॥३०॥

distinguishFrom.why: Prasara is doshas in motion, not yet settled. Sthānasaṃśraya is the same doshas coming to rest in a site and producing prodromes. WHO's own wording is the cleanest statement of the difference: 'migrates outside its own location' versus 'lodges in a different location ... and gives rise to prodromal symptoms'. Sources that gloss prasara as 'localization' have collapsed the two.
Srotas are the channels through which prasara happens — 21.30 says the latent dosha stays mārgeṣu — and srotodusti is their vitiation. Prasara names the dosha's movement, not the channel pathology.
General Sanskrit words for pervasion and scattering, with no kriyakala staging sense. Do not treat as synonyms.

WHO classifies this as a DISORDER 'characterized by abnormal movements of air; gurgling intestinal sounds or borborygmi' — a symptom cluster, not the third stage of the kriyakala sequence. Same root, different WHO entity.

mistranslations.why: A recurring move in Ayurveda-and-cancer writing. Metastasis is dissemination of neoplastic cells; prasara is overflow of doshas and can occur with no disease present at all. The analogy may be pedagogically useful but it is not a translation.

Imports a vascular mechanism. The text's agent is vayu's mobility, and the fifteen enumerated combinations include doshas spreading with or without śoṇita — blood is one participant among fifteen combinations, not the medium.
A gloss derived from the fermenting-dough simile that has hardened into a translation in some practitioner sources. The word prasara does not mean liquefaction.

openQuestions: Whether any source defines a clinical test that distinguishes prasara from prakopa in a patient.
Whether the fifteen-fold enumeration in 21.28 is used anywhere in modern classification or is purely scholastic.
What Dalhana says about the fifteen-fold enumeration — not checked.

classical.establishes: Caraka's pārthiva dravya profile: guru, khara, kaṭhina, manda, sthira, viśada, sāndra, sthūla, gandha-guṇa-bahula. Kaviratna's 'sharp or pungent' for khara (rough) is a word-choice oddity, not doctrine.

classical.establishes: Pṛthvī-derived bodily features: gandha, olfactory organ, mūrti (embodiment), gurutā.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed number OCR-garbled; standard 1.29 per Sanskrit at carakasamhitaonline.com: खरद्रवचलोष्णत्वं भूजलानिलतेजसाम्| आकाशस्याप्रतीघातो दृष्टं लिङ्गं यथाक्रमम्||२९||
classical.establishes: Kharatva (roughness) as the liṅga of pṛthvī (bhū), the textual basis for NAMASTE's 'responsible for hardness'.
classical.quote: Roughness, liquidity, mobility, and heat are (respectively) seen to be the properties of earth, water, air, and fire; while, of ether the property is non-resistibility.

distinguishFrom.why: Suśruta's Sū. 37 (bhūmipravibhāga) and the NIA draft's 'Place (Bhumi/soil)' use bhūmi for terrain; the same word names the bhūta in Ca.Śā. 4.6. Context decides.
Kapha is pṛthvī-jala predominant (NIA draft p.149); not the bhūta.
NAMASTE's hierarchy places pṛthvī as parent of the formed substances; mūrta is the category, pṛthvī one member.
Bhishagratna's 'earth (solid)', 'earth matter or solid' and footnote 'Solid'; the bhūta is defined by gandha (smell) and kharatva/gurutva, and covers e.g. sweet-tasting foods, not only solids.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's period-science equivalence; a pārthiva dravya is identified by smell-predominance and heaviness, not phase.
Kaviratna's Sū. 26 rendering of khara as 'sharp or pungent' reads as a taste; the Sanskrit means rough/coarse.
WHO 2022's gloss has no classical warrant seen in retrieved sources; it is a modern explanatory addition and should not be recorded as the text's definition.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's Śā. 1 printed aphorism numbers should be confirmed from scans.
Whether WHO's 'force of attraction' derives from a specific commentator (Cakrapāṇi?) was not checked.

classical.establishes: Purīṣa is nourished from kiṭṭa.
classical.quote: किट्टात् स्वेदमूत्रपुरीषवातपित्तश्लेष्माणः ... पुष्यन्ति| / kiṭṭāt svēdamūtrapurīṣavātaPittaślēṣmāṇaḥ ... puṣyanti| — Kaviratna: 'From the Refuse arise urine, sweat, faeces* wind, bile, and phlegm'
classical.translator: Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline; English by Avinash Chandra Kaviratna

classical.establishes: Faeces (here viṭ) are the kiṭṭa of food; Charaka uses the synonym viṭ in this verse and śakṛt at Su 17/70, purīṣa at Su 28/4.
classical.quote: किट्टमन्नस्य विण्मूत्रं / kiṭṭamannasya viṇmūtraṁ — Kaviratna: 'That which Is called the ‘Kitta’ (refuse) of the food taken, consists of stools and urine'
classical.translator: Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline; English by Avinash Chandra Kaviratna

classical.establishes: Purīṣa-kṣaya signs (vāta-dominated); source of WHO ITA-5.4.6 and NAMC CB-1 (which cites Ca.Su.17/70). Kaviratna's 'provoked or aggravated' is an addition; the Sanskrit says vāta presses the intestines and moves obliquely and upward.
classical.quote: क्षीणे शकृति चान्त्राणि पीडयन्निव मारुतः| रूक्षस्योन्नमयन् कुक्षिं तिर्यगूर्ध्वं च गच्छति||७०|| — Kaviratna: 'When the stools decrease below the quantity that is normal, the wind in the constitution of the patient who has become dry, becomes provoked or aggravated and afflicting his entrails forces them upwards and penetrates the abdomen in transverse and upward directions.'
classical.translator: Sanskrit from carakasamhitaonline; English by Avinash Chandra Kaviratna

classical.verse: 5 (siva.sh numbering); Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers
classical.establishes: The functions of faeces: upastambha (support) and holding vāyu and agni. This is the source of the 'support the body ... vata and agni' clause in WHO 2.4.3 and NAMASTE SAT-B.459. Bhishagratna's 'indispensably necessary for the preservation of the body' is an expansion of upastambha; his parenthesis is his own gloss.
classical.quote: पुरीषमुपस्तम्भं वाय्वग्निधारणं च / purīṣam upastambhaṁ vāyvagnidhāraṇaṁ ca — Bhishagratna: 'The excreta or the fecal matters of a man are indispensably necessary for the preservation of the body. They contain the wind and digestion (being primarily connected with the movements of the bodily Vayu and the feeling of hunger).'
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (English); Sanskrit from siva.sh

classical.establishes: Sushruta's purīṣa-kṣaya and -vṛddhi signs. 'liver' is Bhishagratna's addition (Sanskrit: kukṣi).
classical.quote: पुरीषक्षये हृदयपार्श्वपीडा सशब्दस्य च वायोरूर्ध्वगमनं कुक्षौ सञ्चरणं च [11] ... पुरीषमाटोपं कुक्षौ शूलं च [15] — Bhishagratna: 'The loss absence, suppression or scanty formation of fecal matter is attended with a sensation of pain at the sides and the region of the heart, and the upward coursing of (the incarcerated) wind or flatus, accompanied with a rumbling sound about the region of the liver and the intestines.' ... 'An abnormal increase in the formation of fecal matter is attended with distension of the abdomen and colic pains in the loins and the intestines.'
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (English); Sanskrit from siva.sh

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa reduces the function of faeces to avaṣṭambha (support).
classical.quote: avaṣṭambhaḥ purīṣasya mūtrasya kleda-vāhanam | svedasya kleda-vidhṛtir vṛddhas tu kurute 'nilaḥ || 5 ||

classical.establishes: Faeces (śakṛt) is the solid kiṭṭa of food.
classical.quote: tatrācchaṃ kiṭṭam annasya mūtraṃ vidyād ghanam śakṛt || 61 ||

distinguishFrom.why: Attested synonyms used interchangeably by Charaka himself (purīṣa Su 28/4; śakṛt Su 17/70; viṭ Chi 15/18; varcas Vi 5/21). WHO codes all under ITA-2.4.3; NAMASTE gives śakṛt (SAT-B.461) and viṭ (SAT-B.463) their own codes, with viṭ glossed more broadly as 'excreta'.
In clinical Sanskrit and ICD-11 TM2 index terms (mala-apravṛtiḥ under SM7Y) 'mala' means stool; in Su 28/4 it is the whole class. Entries must say which.
The channel (Ca.Vi.5/8); separate record.
Retention or constipation diseases; not the same as purīṣa-kṣaya (reduced formation) or purīṣa-vṛddhi (AH 11/25 derives vṛddhi from retention).
Stool examination (one of the aṣṭasthāna parīkṣā; NAMASTE SAT-C.154 'examination of the excreta (mala)'); a diagnostic act, not the substance.

mistranslations.rendering: 'indispensably necessary for the preservation of the body' (Bhishagratna) read as doctrine
mistranslations.why: The Sanskrit says upastambha (support); the emphatic phrasing is Bhishagratna's. Quote it as his rendering.

Bhishagratna uses 'excreta' for faeces here but 'excretions/excrements' for mala as a class elsewhere in the same chapter; NAMASTE uses 'excreta' for viṭ. The English word floats between the narrow and broad senses.
Su.Su.15/5 and AH Su 11/5 assign faeces a supportive function (upastambha, vāyv-agni-dhāraṇa) and both WHO and NAMASTE copy that clause.

openQuestions: Charaka's own statement of purīṣa's FUNCTION (as opposed to origin and kṣaya) was not located; the standards' function clause traces to Sushruta/Vāgbhaṭa. Check Ca.Su.28 commentary and Ca.Chi.15.
Whether purīṣa and śakṛt are ever distinguished by any commentator (e.g. formed vs unformed) was not checked.

classical.establishes: Root = pakvāśaya (colon) and sthūlaguda (rectum/anorectum); vitiation signs = difficult, scanty, noisy, painful, watery, hard-knotted or excessive defaecation.

classical.establishes: Caraka uses varco-vāhīni (from varcas, faeces) in the metrical section — an attested synonym stem not carried by WHO or NAMASTE. Causes: suppression of the urge, overeating, eating on indigestion, weak agni, emaciation.

classical.establishes: Suśruta's roots = guda and pakvāśaya, essentially agreeing with Caraka. ('ententes' is an OCR corruption in the retrieved page, evidently for 'enteritis'.)
classical.quote: The two stool-carrying Srotas (ducts) have their roots in the Guda (anus) and the Pakvashaya (intestines); an injury to any of these is characterised by complete retention of stool (in the bowels), accompanied by a distention of the abdomen, foul smell and intussusception of the intestine (as in a case of ententes).

distinguishFrom.why: Both are gut channels. annavaha is rooted proximally (āmāśaya + left flank) and concerns food in digestion; purīṣavaha is rooted distally (pakvāśaya + sthūlaguda) and concerns the mala.
WHO defines mahāsrotas as the whole cavity 'from the mouth to anus'; purīṣavaha is only its distal, excretory segment.

distinguishFrom.term: purīṣa as mala vs purīṣa-dhara kalā
distinguishFrom.why: The waste product and its retaining membrane are distinct from the conduit.
Not a separate channel — Caraka's own metrical synonym at Vi.5/21.

mistranslations.why: Names one root organ as if it were the channel. WHO and NAMASTE both keep 'channels in which faeces is formed and excreted' precisely to avoid the organ equation.
Bhishagratna's interpretive gloss; the Sanskrit sign is grathita-āntratā (knotted/hardened bowel), which is not intussusception.
Conflates purīṣavaha with mūtravaha and svedavaha, which Caraka enumerates as three separate channels with three separate roots.

openQuestions: Why does NAMASTE nest purīṣavaha srotodushti under the annavaha (EB) code block?
Does sthūlaguda mean the rectum specifically or the whole large bowel?

classical.establishes: The tridaṇḍa (three-stick) definition: puruṣa is the union of sattva (mind), ātman (soul) and śarīra (body), and it is explicitly named the subject matter (adhikaraṇa) of āyurveda and the reason the science exists. This is the single most load-bearing statement about the term. The 'f' before 45 is the OCR of a footnote dagger.
classical.quote: Mind,  soul,  and  body,  this  trinity,  called  person,  resteth  on  union  like  three  sticks  (standing  with  one  another’s  support.)  Upon  that  (trinity)  everything  rests.f45  That  is  also  called  purusha  or  Being.  It  is  also  animate.  That  is  also  regarded  as  the  subject  matter  of  this  Science ;  and  it  is  also  for  the  sake  of  that,  that  this  Science  is  promulgated.46

classical.establishes: The six-dhatu definition: the elements beginning with kha (ether) with consciousness as the sixth are called puruṣa. A different enumeration from the Su 1.46-47 triad, in the same text.
classical.quote: खादयश्चेतनाषष्ठा धातवः पुरुषः स्मृतः।

classical.establishes: The 24-fold definition: this aggregate (rāśi) of twenty-four is designated puruṣa. A third distinct enumeration, and the one WHO codes separately as ITA-1.9.3.2.12.
classical.quote: बुद्धीन्द्रियमनोर्थानां विद्याद्योगधरं परम्| चतुर्विंशतिको ह्येष राशिः पुरुषसञ्ज्ञकः।।

classical.establishes: A fourth enumeration: the same six dhatus (earth, water, fire, air, space, and unmanifest brahman) aggregated get the name 'loka' and, equally, the name 'puruṣa'. This is the verse that makes puruṣa and loka co-extensive, and it is the hinge between this record and loka-puruṣa-sāmya.
classical.quote: षड्धातवः समुदिताः 'लोक' इति शब्दं लभन्ते; तद्यथा- पृथिव्यापस्तेजो वायुराकाशं ब्रह्म चाव्यक्तमिति, एत एव चषड्धातवः समुदिताः 'पुरुष' इति शब्दं लभन्ते||४||

classical.verse: 16-17 as printed on the retrieved page
classical.establishes: Sushruta's karma-puruṣa: the six-component individual (five mahabhutas plus the conscious self) is the puruṣa that medicine treats, as distinct from the Samkhya puruṣa discussed in the same chapter. The verse numbers 16-17 are printed on the retrieved page alongside the passage. Wisdomlib's Sushruta is Bhishagratna and quotable.
classical.quote: The view is further corroborated by a dictum of the Sruti which holds that Purusha (individual) is nothing but a combination of a self-conscious self and the five kinds of matter (Maha- bhutas) formed into an organic body. This Purusha or individual, which is called Individual of action (Karma- Purusha), falls within the scope of the science and art of medicine.

classical.verse: 22-23 as printed on the retrieved page
classical.establishes: The Samkhya sense of puruṣa in the same chapter of the same text: the 25th tattva. Sushruta holds both senses at once and distinguishes them, which is direct textual evidence that the ambiguity is original, not an artefact of translation.
classical.quote: The Purusha forms the twentyfifth principle. These twentyfive fundamental principles of cosmogony have been dealt with in the present treatise (Shalya-Tantra) as well as in the other treatise (Shalaky-Tantra and Sankhya Philosophy).

classical.verse: 10 as printed on the retrieved page
classical.establishes: The metaphysical puruṣa as nirguṇa witness, in the same chapter that later gives the treatable karma-puruṣa. Bhishagratna's syntax here is awkward but the passage is quoted exactly as printed.
classical.quote: But the Purusha (units or atoms of consciousness), devoid of the threefold virtues of Sattva etc. are nonconcerning hence non-producing and bereft of the seed- attributes of lying inherent in all as the primary cause of evolution. They are mere witnesses to the joys and miseries of life, and do not participate in their enjoyment though imprisoned in the human organism.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's own internal back-reference, confirming that the treatable puruṣa definition sits in Sutrasthana chapter 1 as well as Sharirasthana 1. Read from the archive.org OCR of Bhishagratna vol. III; 'livng' and 'wc' are OCR corruptions, reproduced as retrieved. The URL given is the item page for the volume I read; the plain-text stream is at the same item.
classical.quote: it  is  said  in  the  chapter  on  Vedotpatti  (Chapter  I,  Sutra-Sthana)  that  "Purusha"  (livng  organism)  is  the  sum-total  of  the  "Maha-bhutas"  (or  the  five  primary  elements— wc,  earth,  water,  fire,  air  and  ether)  and  the  Sariri  (or  the  soul),  that  medical  treat-  ment  should  be  made  of  him  (Purusha)  and  that  he  is  the  subject  matter  of  every  action)

distinguishFrom.why: Ātman is one constituent of the Charaka triad (Su 1.46) and the sixth dhatu of Sha 1.16. WHO's description of puruṣa ends with 'the soul', which risks collapsing the two. The whole force of Su 1.46-47 is that puruṣa is a union, not a component.
The body alone. Puruṣa includes mind and self, which is why cikitsā is said to be of the puruṣa and not of the śarīra.

Sushruta's own narrowing: the six-component individual that medicine treats, as opposed to the 25th-tattva puruṣa of Samkhya. Sushruta Sha 1 uses both in one chapter and names the narrower one explicitly.
The patient. Puruṣa is the subject of the science whether healthy or ill (Su 1.47 says the science exists for its sake), so it is not a clinical role term.
The inactive, attribute-free conscious witness (Sushruta Sha 1.10, 22-23). Identical word, different referent, in the same chapter as the medical sense.
Charaka Sha 5.4 says the same six aggregated dhatus receive both names. They are co-referential in that verse and distinct everywhere else, which is the ambiguity loka-puruṣa-sāmya rests on.

mistranslations.why: Puruṣa in these definitions is not gendered; the definitions are of a living individual. 'Man' also invites the archaic generic, which obscures that Sushruta's karma-puruṣa is a technical composite.
Renders ātman, one constituent. Directly contradicted by Su 1.46, where mind, soul and body together are called person.
Renders śarīra. Loses the mind and self that make puruṣa the object of treatment.
Imports the Puruṣa Sukta / Vedic macranthropos. Charaka Sha 5 does compare puruṣa to loka, but it defines puruṣa as the individual composite, not as a cosmic being.
Narrows to the clinical encounter. Su 1.47 makes puruṣa the subject matter of the science as such.

openQuestions: Whether Charaka's four enumerations of puruṣa (the tridaṇḍa triad of Su 1.46-47, the six-dhatu of Sha 1.16, the 24-fold of Sha 1.35, and the six-dhatu-shared-with-loka of Sha 5.4) are meant as alternative descriptions of one thing or as four different technical senses. Charaka Sharirasthana 1 opens by asking 'katidhā puruṣaḥ' (in how many ways is puruṣa?), which suggests the plurality is deliberate, but I did not retrieve a commentator on it.
The Sanskrit of Charaka Su 1.46-47 was not retrieved in this pass - only Kaviratna's English. The Devanagari should be added from carakasamhitaonline.com before publication.
Whether NAMASTE codes puruṣa.

classical.establishes: Charaka's definition, and it is purely temporal: pūrvarūpa is the lakṣaṇa of a disease prior to its utpatti. Nothing about mildness, dosha-indifference or number — those criteria come from Vagbhata and Madhavakara, not from this verse. Note also that Charaka uses LAKṢAṆA in the definiens, which is the same word he lists as a synonym of liṅga one verse later.
classical.quote: पूर्वरूपं प्रागुत्पत्ति लक्षणं व्याधेः||८||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English. The parenthesis is Kaviratna's own addition and has no counterpart in the Sanskrit.
classical.quote: 'Purvarupa' implies those indications which manifest themselves before the appearance of the disease. (These are the symptoms of the period of incubation).

classical.establishes: THE STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO SAṂHITĀS, in public domain. For Sushruta pūrvarūpa is not one of five evidence types; it is the fourth of six kriyākāla, i.e. a point in time at which intervention is still possible. 'lor' is a scan artifact for 'for', preserved verbatim. Retrieved and string-matched by me.
classical.quote: The aggravated and expanded humours, thus firmly ensconced in the different parts of the body, exhibit the premonitory symptoms of diseases which will be fully dealt with under their respective heads. The manifestation of these premonitory symptoms should be considered as the fourth occasion lor medical treatment.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata adds three criteria Charaka's verse lacks: the sign is prāgrūpa (he uses that term), it is 'not assignable to any dosha specifically', and it is aspaṣṭa/alpa — indistinct because slight. This is the source of the mildness criterion that most modern definitions treat as classical-in-general. Devanagari mūla and verse numbers sighted on the retrieved page; not quoted per the rule for this text.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

classical.establishes: Madhavakara follows Vagbhata: not specifically assignable to dosha, mild, few in number. Verse number from the modern English rendering on the retrieved page.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: Separated by one thing only in Charaka: prāg-utpatti versus prādurbhūta, before versus after manifestation. Vagbhata and Madhavakara add that pūrvarūpa is dosha-indifferent and mild, and that the same signs become rūpa on becoming clear — which makes the boundary a matter of degree, not kind.
A cause acting on the body; pūrvarūpa is already the body responding. The mistake is easy because both precede the disease in time.

The kriyākāla stage at which dosha lodges in a site (WHO ITA-4.6.10). Sushruta's Sūtra 21 puts the display of premonitory symptoms AT that stage, so the two are adjacent, not identical: one is the lodging, the other is what the lodging shows.

The nearest modern analogue, but a biomedical prodrome is the early phase OF a disease already present; Vagbhata's pūrvarūpa is of a disease 'yet to be manifested' and is dosha-unassignable. The two also differ in what follows: Ayurveda treats pūrvarūpa as a point where the disease can be forestalled, which WHO's ITA-4.5.1 preserves.
Rastogi 2021 makes this mapping explicitly for prameha. It is a proposal in the literature, not an established equivalence, and the record should not present it as one.
WHO ITA-4.5.3 and ITA-4.5.4. Dosha-specific versus general. This division sits awkwardly with Vagbhata's criterion that pūrvarūpa is precisely what is NOT assignable to a dosha.

mistranslations.rendering: symptoms of the period of incubation
mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's own parenthesis, and it presupposes an infectious agent and a latent period. Nothing in Ca. Ni. 1.8 supports it.
Loses the criterion that matters. Charaka's line is drawn at utpatti, not at earliness; and Vagbhata's criterion is indistinctness, not timing alone.
Imports intent. The signs are read by the physician; they do not warn.
Occasionally used by analogy with migraine. Far too narrow and specific to one neurological phenomenon.
A category error in the opposite direction from 'early symptoms': risk factors are causes, and these are already effects.

openQuestions: Whether any study reports operating characteristics for any specific pūrvarūpa. Rastogi 2021 proposes the programme and does not carry out the measurement; PubMed returns only two records for 'purvarupa' and zero for 'poorvarupa', both verified through the API. I found no sensitivity, specificity or predictive value for any premonitory sign of any Ayurvedic disease.
How the two-type division (sāmānya / viśeṣa) is grounded classically, given that Vagbhata's defining criterion is dosha-indifference. WHO codes the division without a source.
Why WHO has two entries (ITA-4.5.1 and ITA-4.8.37) for one word. Possibly a chapter-scoping artifact; possibly deliberate. Worth asking WHO.
Whether Sushruta defines pūrvarūpa as a term anywhere, or only uses it inside kriyākāla. My full-text search of Bhishagratna's Sūtrasthāna volume found the kriyākāla passage and no definition.

classical.establishes: Rajas and tamas are the two mental doṣas, parallel to vāta/pitta/kapha as bodily doṣas; their vikāras are named. Sattva is pointedly absent from the mental doṣas. Verse number 5 printed inline on the retrieved page.

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Vi 6/5. The stray full stop after 'Heedlessness' is an OCR artefact. Kaviratna's aphorism marker here is 7, not 5; the verse number comes from the Sanskrit, matched by content.

classical.establishes: Rajas and tamas never occur apart — a structural claim with no parallel among the bodily doṣas. 'Ta?nas' is OCR corruption of 'Tamas'. Verse blank: Kaviratna marks this 10 but the corresponding Sanskrit verse number was not located.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's rājasa trait list. 'over winning' is the retrieved page's spelling of 'overweening'.
classical.quote: Feeling of much pain and misery, a roving spirit, noncomprehension, vanity, untruthfulness, nonclemency, pride, an over winning confidence in ones own excellence, lust, anger and hilarity are the attributes which mark a mind of the Rajashika cast .

classical.establishes: Maps the three guṇas onto the five mahābhūtas — rajas to vāyu and, with sattva, to tejas. Rarely cited, and it cuts against the popular rajas/pitta equation.
classical.quote: Of these the ether or Akasa abounds in attributes of the Sattvika stamp, the Vayu or etherin (ether?) in Rajashika, the Teja in Sattvika and Rajashika, the water in Sattvika and Tamashika and the earth in Tamasha attributes.

distinguishFrom.why: A live homonym that WHO itself carries (rajaḥsrāvaḥ). An uncontextualised 'rajas' in a gynaecological chapter almost certainly means menstrual flow.
The ordinary Sanskrit sense and the etymological root of the guṇa's agitation; appears in dravyaguṇa and nidāna contexts.
Both principles of motion and both called doṣa, but vāta is bodily and rajas mental (Vi 6/5). The texts do not equate them.
Popular writing pairs rajas with pitta on shared heat. No retrieved classical passage makes that equation, and Sushruta Sharira 1/21 assigns rajas to vāyu and tejas.

mistranslations.why: Reduces a principle of motion and initiation to an emotion, and makes Vi 6/5 read as moralising.
Category error: guṇas and doṣas are different schemes, kept explicitly separate at Vi 6/5.
Flattering rather than false; it drops WHO's own qualification that rajas is capable of vitiating the mind.

openQuestions: What is the Sanskrit verse number for the 'no tamas without rajas' statement Kaviratna marks as aphorism 10 in Vimana 6? Not located.

classical.establishes: Charaka's core statement of rakta's function: life itself depends on it. This is the source of the jīvana function WHO gives its own term ID. Chapter located by its heading 'LESSON XXIV ... Vidhi-Sonitiya' in the retrieved file.
classical.quote: Verily, it is pure blood that brings about strength and complexion and (the) happiness (of health) and longevity, for the very life of living creatures is dependant on blood.

classical.establishes: Rakta as a diagnostic residual category: whatever does not answer to doṣa-directed treatment is attributed to blood. A striking piece of clinical reasoning that gets no mention in the usual 'rakta = blood' gloss.
classical.quote: All those diseases that are curable but that cannot be cured by the application of cool, hot, oily, and dry methods of treatment, should be ascribed to diseased blood as their cause.

classical.establishes: That rakta is defined by acquisition of colour from rasa, i.e. by a transformation, not by composition. Sushruta places the colouring in spleen and liver.
classical.quote: The Rasa or the lymph chyle, coloured through the effect of the healthy normal dyeing heat of the body, obtains the name of blood.

classical.establishes: Rakta as pāñcabhautika, with each of five observable properties assigned to one mahābhūta. The nearest thing in the sources to a compositional analysis of a dhātu.
classical.quote: In blood the properties such as, a raw or fleshy smell, fluidity, redness, lightness and mobility, which respectively characterise the fundamental principles (of earth, water, fire, air, and sky) are to be found thus representing those specific elements in its composition.

classical.establishes: A purely observational normality criterion for rakta, based on colour and consistency. Contrasts with modern operationalisation by haemoglobin.
classical.quote: The blood in its healthy and natural state is possessed of a vivid red colour like that of an Indragopa (Cochineal) insect, and is neither too thin nor too transparent.

classical.establishes: Rakta's three functions: complexion (varṇa-prasāda), nourishment of mamsa, and maintenance of life. The Sanskrit of this verse was verified separately: रक्तं वर्णप्रसादं मांसपुष्टिं जीवयति च.
classical.quote: The blood, in its turn, increases the healthful glow of the complexion, leads to the increased formation of flesh and muscles and maintains vitality in the organism.

classical.establishes: The classical clinical signs of raktakshaya and raktavriddhi. Note these are not the signs of anaemia and polycythaemia; the craving for acid and for cool places has no biomedical counterpart, which is precisely the point at issue when 'rakta' is operationalised as haemoglobin.
classical.quote: The loss of blood is attended with such symptoms as roughness of the skin, and a craving for acid food or drink. The patient longs to be in a cool place and asks for cool things, and the veins become loose and flabby. ... A plethora of blood in the system gives a reddish glow to the complexion and the white of the eyes, and imparts fullness to the veins.

classical.establishes: Rakta's place in the chain, from rasa and yielding mamsa, in verified Sanskrit with verse number.
classical.quote: रसाद्रक्तं ततो मांसं मांसान्मेदः प्रजायते । मेदसोऽस्थि ततो मज्जा मज्ज्ञः शुक्रं तु जायते ॥१०॥

distinguishFrom.why: Treated as a synonym by WHO ISTA (both listed under ITA-2.2.5) and by both public-domain translators, who render both as 'blood'. But śoṇita is also WHO's Sanskrit for menstrual blood at ITA-2.3.3, so the synonymy is not clean and an index will mis-merge.

Menstrual blood, classed as an upadhātu of rasa by WHO (ITA-2.3.3). Bhishagratna writes that ārtava 'is endued with the same properties as its arterial namesake', so the sources themselves relate them closely while keeping them distinct.
The precursor. Rakta is rasa that has acquired colour. Translating rasa 'plasma' and rakta 'blood' inverts the relation, since plasma is part of blood rather than its antecedent.

Pitta is the kiṭṭa (waste fraction) of rakta according to Charaka Chikitsasthana 15, and rañjaka pitta is the agent that colours rasa into rakta. Closely coupled but categorically a doṣa, not a dhātu.
The channel system, not the substance. Diseases are attributed to the srotas as well as to the dhātu and the distinction matters for coding.
'Life blood' in Bhishagratna, flagged in the retrieved text as a distinct topic to be treated separately. Not simply rakta.

mistranslations.rendering: blood, taken as identical with the biomedical referent
mistranslations.why: The word is right and the concept is not coextensive. Classical rakta is formed in spleen and liver from rasa, has fleshy smell listed as its earthy property, and its depletion presents as craving for sour food and for cool places. None of that is a statement about haemoglobin.

Introduced by operational convenience in clinical research (see PMID 24250128). No classical source supports the narrowing, and it silently discards the complexion and mamsa-nourishing functions that Sushruta gives as rakta's defining work.

Imports the Greek humoral scheme, in which blood IS one of the four humours. In Ayurveda blood is a dhātu and not a doṣa, and the confusion is made worse by Bhishagratna's own chapter-heading language about 'humoral constituents'.

openQuestions: Whether rakta and śoṇita are true synonyms or carry a distinction (e.g. śoṇita for extravasated or menstrual blood) is not settled by anything retrieved; WHO lists śoṇitam under both rakta-dhātu and ārtava.

The trial evidence (PMID 24250128) assumes rather than tests the rakta/anaemia equation. No retrieved study asks whether patients meeting classical raktakshaya criteria are the same patients as those meeting anaemia criteria. That would be a straightforward and unperformed study.
Whether Sushruta's attribution of rakta formation to spleen and liver reflects observation or inference is not addressable from the translation alone.
Charaka Sutrasthana 24's residual-category rule (anything curable but unresponsive to cool/hot/oily/dry treatment is blood-caused) has no modern discussion that this search located.

renderings.english: Bloodletting. It means the procedure of blood-letting for the therapeutic purposes for removing morbid Doṣa/ poisons with blood. Blood can be eliminated through scraping, application of horn or leech or venesection. It is practiced in poisoned blood and blood born diseases in pitta (billeous) predominant diseases and also in a few vāta (neurological) disorders.

classical.establishes: Instrumental bloodletting is of two kinds: pracchāna (scarification) and sirāvyadhana (venesection).
classical.quote: शस्त्रविस्रावणं द्विविधं- प्रच्छानं , सिराव्यधनं च ॥२५॥

classical.verse: Unnumbered in Bhishagratna; corresponds to the sentence numbered 25 on siva.sh
classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's renderings of the two instrumental subtypes.
classical.quote: Blood-letting, with the help of a surgical instrument, may be grouped under two distinct heads, according as scarification (Pracchana) or venesection (Sira-Vyadhana) is resorted to for the purpose.

classical.verse: 33-34 (as displayed on siva.sh; edition unstated). Both ends of the range read independently.
classical.establishes: Signs of correctly performed bloodletting (lightness, relief of pain, abatement of disease, mental clarity) and the claim that habitual raktamokṣaṇa prevents skin disorders, granthi, śopha and blood-borne diseases. Verse 34 verifies the Devanagari रक्तमोक्षण.
classical.quote: लाघवं वेदनाशान्तिर्व्याघेर्वेगपरिक्षयः । सम्यग्विस्राविते लिङ्गं प्रसादो मनसस्तथा ॥३३॥ त्वग्दोषा ग्रन्थयः शोफा रोगाः शोणितजाश्च ये । रक्तमोक्षणशीलानां न भवन्ति कदाचन ॥३४॥

classical.verse: Unnumbered in Bhishagratna; matches siva.sh 33 and 34
classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for Su.Su. 14.33-34. His 'sarcomata, aneurism' both render granthi, 'oedema' renders śopha, and the appended 'Ovarian tumour, Carbuncle, Erysipelas' are his biomedical examples of rogāḥ śoṇitajāḥ; none of these English disease names is in the Sanskrit.
classical.quote: An act of complete and successful blood-letting is followed by a feeling of lightness and alleviation of pain in the affected part, by an abatement of the disease, and a general sense of cheerfulness. [...] A person, accustomed to blood letting, enjoys a kind of immunity from all types of skin diseases, sarcomata, aneurism, oedema, and diseases brought about by a vitiated condition of the blood such as, Ovarian tumour, Carbuncle, Erysipelas, etc.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Leech application is the gentlest means of śoṇitāvasecana (a synonym for bloodletting), for kings, the rich, children, the aged, the timid, the weak, women and the delicate.
classical.quote: नृपाढ्य बालस्थविरभीरुदुर्बलनारीसुकुमाराणामनुग्रहार्थं परमसुकुमारोऽयं शोणितावसेचनोपायोऽभिहितो जलौकसः ॥३॥

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's rendering of the leech indication; the quote is two fragments of one sentence as returned by the fetch, so re-read the page before publishing it as a continuous sentence.
classical.quote: old or imbecile, or a woman, or an infant, or a person of an extremely timid disposition, or a person of a delicate constitution [...] the gentlest that can be possibly devised

classical.establishes: Venesection (a subtype of raktamokṣaṇa) is declared 'half of treatment' in śalyatantra. Often misattributed to Sutrasthana 14; it is in Sharirasthana 8.
classical.quote: सिराव्यधश्चिकित्सार्धं शल्यतन्त्रे प्रकीर्तितः

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's own section number 55 (NOT a Sanskrit verse number); Sanskrit verse 23 per siva.sh
classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for Su.Sha. 8.23; the comparison to basti is in the verse's second line, which was not separately verified in Sanskrit.
classical.quote: Venesection (bleeding) properly performed is half of the treatment described in surgery like the application of Vasti-karmas (enematic measures) in therapeutics.

classical.verse: 18 (carakasamhitaonline, Trikamji numbering); Kaviratna prints 16 for this aphorism (Lesson XXII, p. 245, archive.org BIUSante_47357 leaf n347, superscript §16 after 'included under Langhana'), two BEHIND the standard; his footnotes on p. 246 also cite it as 'Verse 16'
classical.establishes: Charaka counts saṁśuddhi under laṅghana as fourfold (catuṣprakārā saṁśuddhiḥ) alongside thirst, wind, sun, pācana, fasting and exercise, but the verse does not name the four. Their identification as emesis, purgation, errhine and (dry) enema, with raktamokṣaṇa therefore absent, is the commentators' and Kaviratna's reading (his bracketed gloss 'viz., administration of emetics, of purgatives, of errhines or cerebral purgatives, and dry enemata'); raktamokṣaṇa is not mentioned in the chapter's Sanskrit. Relevant to the distinction between Charaka's and Sushruta's śodhana sets on that commentary-dependent basis.
classical.quote: चतुष्प्रकारा संशुद्धिः पिपासा मारुतातपौ। पाचनान्युपवासश्च व्यायामश्चेति लङ्घनम्॥१८॥
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: Venesection; one instrumental subtype of raktamokṣaṇa (Su.Su. 14.25), not a synonym for the whole category.
Leech application; the non-instrumental (anuśastra) subtype, indicated for the delicate and for pitta-vitiated blood (Su.Su. 13.3 and Bhishagratna ch. XIII).
Scarification; the other instrumental subtype.

Charaka's fourfold saṁśuddhi in Su. 22.18 is vamana, virecana, śirovirecana, niruha; raktamokṣaṇa is counted as the fifth śodhana in the Sushruta/Shalya tradition. WHO 2022 ITA-9.2.2 likewise defines Panchakarma without bloodletting (its fifth is unctuous enema).
Modern phlebotomy is sampling; raktamokṣaṇa is therapeutic removal of 'vitiated' blood.

mistranslations.why: The procedure removes blood; it does not purify the remaining blood in any mechanistic sense. The doctrinal claim is removal of duṣṭa rakta, which is a different statement.
Narrows the term to venesection and imports the diagnostic sense.
'immunity' in Su.Su. 14.34 is Edwardian English for 'do not occur'; it is not an immunological claim.

openQuestions: Confirm siva.sh verse numbers (13.3, 14.25, 14.33-34, Sha. 8.23) against the Trikamji/Acharya Nirnaya Sagar edition; the site does not name its edition.
Whether a systematic review of raktamokṣaṇa/leech therapy exists in PubMed; the bounded search found case reports and small trials only.

classical.establishes: Root = yakṛt (liver) and plīhā (spleen). Crucially, Caraka's word here is śoṇita-vaha, NOT rakta-vaha — the head-term of the modern lexicon is not the term of the locus classicus.
classical.quote: शोणितवहानां स्रोतसां यकृन्मूलं प्लीहा च|

classical.establishes: Caraka uses rakta-vāhīni in the metrical section, confirming rakta- and śoṇita- as interchangeable stems within one chapter.
classical.quote: विदाहीन्यन्नपानानि स्निग्धोष्णानि द्रवाणि च| रक्तवाहीनि दुष्यन्ति भजतां चातपानलौ||१४||

classical.establishes: Suśruta agrees with Caraka on liver+spleen and adds the blood-carrying dhamanīs. One of the clearest Caraka/Suśruta agreements in the set.
classical.quote: The blood-carrying Srotas (channels) are two in number and have their roots in the spleen and the liver, and the blood-carrying Dhamanis (capillaries in general). An injury to any of these channels is attended with pallor, bluishness of complexion, fever, burning sensations, excessive hemorrhage, and redness of the eyes.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO codes asṛgvahā ('blood vessels') separately at ITA-2.5.12. Caraka at Vi.5/9 lists sirā and dhamanī among the NAMES for body spaces generally, so 'srotas = blood vessel' is a category error even where they overlap.
The tissue versus its conduit.
A disease of bleeding, listed by NAMASTE among the diseases involving this srotas; not the channel itself.
Consecutive in the dhātu chain but with different roots (heart/dhamanīs vs liver/spleen).

mistranslations.why: Neither text names heart or vessels as the root — the roots are liver and spleen, i.e. haematopoietic/haemolytic organs. WHO keeps 'blood vessels' as a separate term precisely to avoid this.
Bhishagratna's 1911 gloss on 'blood-carrying Dhamanis'. An imported histological category with no basis in the Sanskrit.
rakta is a dhātu — the whole blood tissue including its formative and nutritive role — not a cell type.

openQuestions: Is the śoṇita/rakta alternation purely metrical convenience, or do commentators read a distinction?
Why do both texts root a blood channel in liver and spleen rather than the heart, when the heart is the root of rasavaha in both?

renderings.locator: ITA-2.1.2.3; printed p. 35 (PDF p. 53). Sanskrit term 'rañjaka-pittam'. Description: 'Subtype of pitta seated in liver, spleen and its pigment in blood.'
renderings.assessment: WHO's description is grammatically broken as printed ('seated in liver, spleen and its pigment in blood') — worth flagging to anyone quoting it. Substantively WHO follows SUŚRUTA's seat (liver and spleen), not Vāgbhaṭa's (āmāśaya). That is a silent editorial choice between two disagreeing classical authorities.

classical.establishes: THE KEY CLASSICAL DISAGREEMENT: Vāgbhaṭa seats rañjaka in the ĀMĀŚAYA (stomach), directly contradicting Suśruta's yakṛt-plīhan (liver and spleen). Same name, same function (rasa-rañjana), different organ. Corroborated: PMID 40972327 cites 'Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutra Sthana 12/13' for 'Ranjaka Pitta does Rasa Ranjana'.

distinguishFrom.why: Rañjaka acts ON rasa to colour it; it is not blood and not the blood tissue. English texts that render rañjaka pitta as 'the blood-forming pitta' quietly promote it from a colouring agent to a haematopoietic organ.

Because Vāgbhaṭa puts rañjaka in the āmāśaya, in his scheme rañjaka and pācaka are near-neighbours in the same region, which they are not in Suśruta. Any statement about rañjaka's seat is meaningless without naming which authority is being followed.
A disease (a bleeding disorder), not a doṣa subtype. The similar shape of the compound causes genuine confusion in search and in indexing.

mistranslations.why: A hypothesis dressed as a definition. The Suśrutan mūla claims only that it colours rasa. Erythropoiesis happens in red marrow, which no classical text assigns to rañjaka. The equation also has to pick a side in the liver/spleen vs stomach disagreement and usually does so without saying so.

Bhishagratna's own gloss, and historically interesting, but it imports the Galenic identification of pitta with bile. Bile pigments colour faeces, not rasa, so the gloss does not even fit the function it is glossing.

mistranslations.rendering: Citing 'liver and spleen' while citing Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya
mistranslations.why: Extremely common and simply wrong. AH Sū 12.13 reads 'āmāśayāśrayaṃ pittaṃ rañjakam'. The liver/spleen seat is Suśruta's.

WHO ISTA chose the Suśrutan seat. Is that choice documented anywhere in the WHO drafting process, or was it undiscussed?
Is the WHO description's broken grammar ('seated in liver, spleen and its pigment in blood') an erratum? Check whether a corrected reprint exists.

classical.establishes: The dhātu sense: rasa is the subtle essence (sāra) of fully digested food, its seat (sthāna) is the heart, and from the heart it enters the twenty-four dhamanīs to nourish the whole body (Su.Su.14.3: 'तस्य हृदयं स्थानं, स हृदयाच्चतुर्विंशतिधमनीरनुप्रविश्य'). The lymph chyle (Rasa), though running through the whole organism, has its primary seat in the heart, whence it flows through the twenty-four vessels which branch off from the latter (heart) to the remotest parts and extremities of the body.

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Su.26.8 records Varyovida calling heavy/light/cold/hot/unctuous/dry 'six rasas'; Atreya rejects this (26.9). Rasa is perceived by the tongue; gunas are inferred from action.
The first of seven dhatus (WHO ITA-2.2.4; Su.Su.14 'lymph chyle'). Same word, different category; WHO ITA-6.2.1.1 explicitly warns of the overlap.
The secondary or after-taste (Ca.Su.26.28 व्यक्तः शुष्कस्य चादौ च रसो द्रव्यस्य लक्ष्यते| विपर्ययेणानुरसो रसो नास्ति हि सप्तमः||२८||).

Post-digestive taste; a separate member of the rasapañcaka (WHO ITA-6.2 'rasapañcakam').
Rejuvenative therapy; Kaviratna's notes gloss it separately. Not the taste or the dhatu.

mistranslations.why: Common in popular writing; rasa in the texts is a defined gustatory category with pharmacological entailments (Ca.Su.26), not aroma-plus-taste.
