classical.establishes: The text's own etymology: rasa from the root ras/gati, 'to go', because it goes constantly. Note the word dhātu is used here in its GRAMMATICAL sense (verbal root), in the same chapter that defines the bodily dhātu.
classical.quote: तत्र 'रस' गतौ धातुः, अहरहर्गच्छतीत्यतो रसः ॥१३॥

classical.establishes: The quotable English of the etymology. Constant motion and pervasion, not a compartment, is what the name asserts - which is the strongest textual argument against equating rasa with any single named fluid.
classical.quote: The term Rasa is derived from the root "Ras", to go, and the substance is so called from the fact of its continually flowing through and permeating every vital principle of an animated organism.

classical.establishes: Rasa as the immediate product of digestion, defined by fineness of consistency.
classical.quote: The food is fully digested with the help of the internal heat and ultimately assimilated in the system, giving rise to lymph chyle (Rasa) which is extremely thin or attenuated in its consistency and which forms the essence of the assimilated food.

classical.establishes: Rasa's seat in the heart and its distribution through twenty-four named vessels - the passage most often cited in support of a circulatory reading.
classical.quote: The lymph chyle (Rasa), though running through the whole organism, has its primary seat in the heart, whence it flows through the twenty-four vessels which branch off from the latter (heart) to the remotest parts and extremities of the body. Of the aforesaid twenty-four vessels, ten are up-coursing, ten are down-coursing, and four have a lateral direction.

classical.establishes: Rasa's qualities as saumya, and the mechanism by which it becomes rakta - colouring in spleen and liver. This is the join between rasa and rakta and is stated in Sushruta but not in the Charaka passages retrieved here.
classical.quote: since the Rasa or lymph chyle is a fluid, and possessed of lubricating, vitalising, moistening, and nutritive (lit :- supporting) properties, it must be included within the class of Saumya (cooling) substances. The Rasa, though a Saumya fluid, obtains its characteristic pigment (Ragam) in its passage through the spleen and liver.

classical.establishes: 3,015 kalas per dhātu, hence one month from rasa to shukra. Verified Sanskrit with verse number.
classical.quote: स खलु त्रीणि त्रीणि कलासहस्राणि पञ्चदश च कला एकैकस्मिन् धाताववतिष्ठते; एवं मासेन रसः शुक्रं स्त्रीणां चार्तवं भवति ॥१४॥

classical.establishes: Simultaneous whole-body diffusion of rasa by vyāna vāyu. Sits in tension with the strictly serial reading of the dhātu chain, and is the textual basis for the later eka-kāla dhātu poṣaṇa model.
classical.quote: The 'dhatu' called 'Rasa' (that is, the juicy matter into which food is first converted) is continuously diffused through every part of the body simultaneously, by the life-breath called 'Vyana' whose function it is to diffuse.

distinguishFrom.why: The nutrient essence coming out of digestion, before it has become the rasa dhātu proper. Bhishagratna's footnote to Su.Su.14 distinguishes 'the immature Rasa, or the Rasa in its nascent stage' from the matured bodily rasa it then enters. Modern writing frequently collapses the two.

The six tastes. Entirely different technical sense of the same word, and the commoner one in the dietetics and dravyaguna chapters. Charaka's Vimanasthana opens with Rasa-vimana, which is about taste, not tissue.
In the pharmaceutical literature rasa means mercury and by extension the whole metallurgical branch. Yet another collision on the same lemma.

The next dhātu. Sushruta makes rasa become rakta by acquiring colour in spleen and liver, so the two are stages of one material in the source, which is exactly why translating rasa as 'plasma' and rakta as 'blood' misrepresents the relation: plasma is a component of blood, not its precursor.
Usually taken as the lymph proper in Ayurvedic anatomy. If rasa is translated 'lymph', lasika has nowhere to go.

Ojas is the sāra of all seven dhātus, not the first of them, though Bhishagratna's chapter-XV rendering ('The quintessence of all the fundamental principles of the body, starting with lymph chyle and ending with semen, is called the Ojas') makes clear it is derived from the whole chain including rasa.

mistranslations.why: An equation dressed as a translation. Plasma is a fraction of blood; classical rasa is the precursor of blood, is said to be distributed simultaneously to the whole body by vyāna vāyu, and yields breast milk and menstrual blood. No retrieved source establishes the equation; it is asserted in teaching.
Incompatible with 'plasma', yet both circulate widely, including in Wikipedia's dhātu article, which uses 'lymph'. Also strands lasika, which is the term lymph usually translates.
Bhishagratna's rendering, and a Victorian physiological category. 'Lymph chyle' is not an English medical term at all. Quotable as a period document, not usable as a gloss.
Occasionally seen. Serum is plasma minus clotting factors, a still narrower biomedical fraction, and nothing in the retrieved sources supports it.
Loses the fact that rasa is a defined bodily constituent with a seat, a set of vessels, a timetable and named products.

openQuestions: Whether the sources intend rasa as a single substance or a class of circulating fluids is not resolved by anything retrieved. The etymology (that which goes) supports the second reading; the anatomical passage (seat in the heart, twenty-four vessels) supports the first.

No retrieved study measures anything and calls it rasa. There is no operational definition of rasa dhātu in the peer-reviewed literature, and PubMed searches for 'rasa dhatu' (12 hits) and 'rasa dhatu plasma' (0 hits) return no study that attempts one.
The relation between rasa and lasika is not addressed in the passages retrieved and needs a targeted search of Sushruta Sharirasthana.

Charaka's simultaneous-diffusion statement (Ci.15.35) and Sushruta's five-days-per-dhātu timetable (Su.Su.14.14) cannot both describe the same process straightforwardly; no retrieved source reconciles them.

classical.establishes: Root = hṛdaya and the TEN dhamanīs. Caraka gives no separate vitiation signs here, referring instead to the dhātu-pradoṣa signs of Sūtrasthāna 'Vividhāśitapītīya'.
classical.quote: रसवहानां स्रोतसां हृदयं मूलं दश च धमन्यः|

classical.establishes: Caraka explicitly defers the vitiation signs of the seven dhātu-carrying srotas (rasa onwards) to the Vividhāśitapītīya chapter, and equates dhātu-pradoṣa signs with dhātu-srotas signs. This is why Ca.Vi.5 is NOT a complete source for rasavaha/raktavaha/etc. symptomatology.
classical.quote: प्रदुष्टानां तु खल्वेषां रसादिवहस्रोतसां विज्ञानान्युक्तानि विविधाशितपीतीये; यान्येव हि धातूनां प्रदोषविज्ञानानि तान्येव यथास्वं प्रदुष्टानां धातुस्रोतसाम्|

classical.establishes: Suśruta's root = heart + rasa-carrying dhamanīs (not 'ten'); injury yields śoṣa plus prāṇavaha-type signs.
classical.quote: The serumcarrying (Rasa-vaha) ducts are two in number and have their roots in (the viscus of) the heart and the serum-carrying Dhamanis (vessels). An injury to or piercing of any of these ducts gives rise to Sosha (consumption) and symptoms identical with those developed by a hurt to the Prana-vaha channels of the body, ending in death.

distinguishFrom.why: rasa is the substance; rasavaha srotas is its conduit. Caraka's own Vi.5/4 warns that what the srotas are, what they carry, and where they sit are all different from the srotas themselves.
Caraka lists rasāyanī and rasavāhinī at Vi.5/9 as SYNONYMS in the general list of names for body spaces, not as a distinct channel. Treating them as separate structures is an error.
Suśruta gives both the same root (heart) and says injury to rasavaha produces prāṇavaha-type signs; they are separated by what they carry, not by location.
rasa is converted to rakta; the channels are consecutive in the dhātu chain but have different roots (heart/dhamanīs vs liver/spleen).

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's 'lymph-chyle' gloss and the fluid-transport imagery drive this, but the named root is the heart and the ten dhamanīs — a vascular, not lymphatic, anatomy. WHO deliberately avoids 'lymph'.

Convenient but reductive: rasa is the whole post-digestive nutrient fluid and the first of seven dhātus, not the acellular fraction of blood. WHO's 'primary circulating nutrient fluid' is the more careful rendering.
Bhishagratna's 1911 choice; he uses 'lymph-chyle' for the same word elsewhere in the same chapter, so the rendering carries no authority.

openQuestions: What are the 'daśa dhamanyaḥ' of Ca.Vi.5/8, and are they the same ten that Cakrapāṇi (on Ca.Indriya 5/41-42) associates with manovaha srotas?
Why does WHO use two different English head-terms for the anatomy (2.5.10) and the disorder (5.5.5) of the same channel?

classical.verse: Standard Ci. 1.1.4 (carakasamhitaonline, Trikamji numbering). Kaviratna prints '2-3' after the corresponding English ('The medicine is of two kinds. Some medicine has for its purpose the increase of the ojos of a healthy person. Some, again, has for its purpose the alleviation of disease by which one is affected. 2-3'); his '2-3' covers standard 3 (the synonyms of bheṣaja, which he prints unnumbered with a footnote) and standard 4. His '5' belongs to standard 5b, not to this verse. Both numbers recorded, no conversion applied.
classical.establishes: Medicine (bheṣaja) is twofold: some promotes vigour (ūrjaskara) in the healthy, some removes disease in the afflicted. This verse does not name rasāyana; the next verse (Ci. 1.1.5, svasthasyorjaskaraṁ yattu tadvṛṣyaṁ tadrasāyanam) is where the vigour-promoting kind is divided into vṛṣya and rasāyana.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed numbers 5 and 7-8 (printed after the passages, archive BIUSante_47357 leaves 1296-1297). classical.establishes: Kaviratna's rendering of the definition and benefits of rasāyana; 'ojos' is his spelling of ojas.
classical.quote: That which increases the ojos of a healthy person is of two kinds viz., 'Vrishya' (aphrodisiacs), and 'Rasayana (tonics). 5 [...] From the administration of 'Rasayana' one obtains longevity of life, memory, apprehension, health, youth, brightness, complexion, excellence of voice, great strength of body and the senses, power of making speech true, bows (from others), and comeliness of features. These drugs (or preparations) are called 'Rasayana' because of their capacity to impart superior 'Rasa' and other 'dhatus' (or ingredients of the body). 7-8

classical.establishes: Six ṛtus and the ādāna ('Taking') / visarga ('Giving') division. Sanskrit seen at carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Tasyashiteeya_Adhyaya: इह खलु संवत्सरं षडङ्गमृतुविभागेन विद्यात्। तत्रादित्यस्योदगयनमादानं च त्रीनृतूञ्छिशिरादीन् ग्रीष्मान्तान् व्यवस्येत्, वर्षादीन् पुनर्हेमन्तान्तान् दक्षिणायनं विसर्गं च॥४॥.
classical.quote: For the purposes of this lesson, the year should be known as consisting of six portions, divided according to the seasons. Of these, the three seasons commencing with the season of dews and ending with summer constitute the period when the Sun travels in the region lying to the north of the equinoctial. That is again the period when the Sun takes (i.e., sucks up the liquid portion of every earthly object). The three other seasons commencing with the season of rains and ending with Hemanta constitutes the period of the Sun's southerly course. That is, besides, the time when the Sun gives (or yields moisture to all earthly objects).

classical.verse: Sushruta Sutrasthana 6.6, number confirmed as printed ॥६॥ in Susrutasamhita with Dalhana, ed. Jadavji Trikamji Acharya, Nirnaya Sagar Press 2nd ed. 1931, p. 24 (the second scheme is ॥१०॥, p. 25). Bhishagratna vol. 1 (1907): p. 46 for the quoted sentence and the month table; chapter VI opens on p. 45.
classical.establishes: Sushruta's first ṛtu scheme (Su.Su. 6.6): the twelve months from Māgha are taken two to a season, giving six seasons in the order śiśira (Māgha-Phālguna), vasanta, grīṣma, varṣā, śarad, hemanta (Agrahāyaṇa-Pauṣa). The passage makes no comparison with Charaka, and none should be drawn from it: Charaka Su 6.4 likewise begins the ādāna half with śiśira. The scheme that does differ is Sushruta's own second one at 6.6-10, six seasons for doṣa accumulation reckoned from Bhādrapada, varṣā first and prāvṛṭ last, which Bhishagratna renders with 'According to some, the rainy season consists of two months known as Bhadra and Ashvina ...'.
classical.quote: Sanskrit as printed in Trikamji (Su.Su. 6.6, p. 24): "तत्र माघादयो द्वादश मासाः संवत्सरः, द्विमासिकमृतुं कृत्वा षड्ऋतवो भवन्ति, ते शिशिरवसन्तग्रीष्मवर्षाशरद्धेमन्ताः; तेषां तपस्तपस्यौ शिशिरः, मधुमाधवौ वसन्तः, शुचिशुक्रौ ग्रीष्मः, नभोनभस्यौ वर्षाः, इषोर्जौ शरत्, सहःसहस्यौ हेमन्त इति ॥६॥" (Haranacandra omits संवत्सरः, per the edition's own footnote.) And Su.Su. 6.10, p. 25: "इह तु वर्षाशरद्धेमन्तवसन्तग्रीष्मप्रावृषः षड्ऋतवो भवन्ति, दोषोपचयप्रकोपोपशमनिमित्तं, ते तु भाद्रपदाद्येन द्विमासिकेन व्याख्याताः; तद्यथा—भाद्रपदाश्वयुजौ वर्षाः, कार्तिकमार्गशीर्षौ शरत्, पौषमाघौ हेमन्तः, फाल्गुनचैत्रौ वसन्तः, वैशाखज्येष्ठौ ग्रीष्मः, आषाढश्रावणौ प्रावृडिति ॥१०॥" The English in the record stays as it is; it is verbatim Bhishagratna.

classical.establishes: Charaka's explicit statement that roga names both the doshas and the disorders, with a note that it applies to disorders 'especially'. The chapter and aphorism number come from the volume's own printed Abstract of Contents, which lists for Vimana Lesson VI 'The absence of difference between diseases and faults, and the synonymous character of the two terms (aphorisms 4 and 5)'.
classical.quote: There are things that differ in meaning though named by the same words. There are also things that do not differ in meaning though named by different words. The same word Roga ( disease ) is applied to faults ( wind, bile, and phlegm ) as also to disorders affecting the body. Again, the faults receive these different appellations, viz., Roga, Atanka, Yakshma, Doshaprakriti, and Vikara. Diseases are also called by those very designations, viz., Roga, Atanka, Yakshma, Doshaprakriti, and Vikara. Thus, the word Roga applies equally to the faults and diseases. To the last, however, it applies especially.

classical.establishes: The one criterion Charaka gives for separating roga-as-disease from roga-as-dosha: countability. Diseases are innumerable, the doshas are few.
classical.quote: It should be stated that diseases are countless in consequence of their very large number. The faults, however, are countable, in consequence of their not being many.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's principle of disease naming: by dhatu of seat. Relevant to how roga-names are formed (rasaja, raktaja and so on). Quoted verbatim including the retrieved page's line-break artifact in 'bod y'.
classical.quote: The nomenclature of a disease depends upon where the affection of the several elementary principles of the bod y by the deranged bodily humours lies, and which is accordingly styled as it is seated in the lymph-chyle, or in the blood or the flesh, or it is in fat, bone, or in the semen.

distinguishFrom.why: Declared synonymous at Cha.Ni.1/5. The only observable difference is distributional: WHO ISTA builds disease-class names on -roga and meta-terms on vyādhi-, and the classical texts use vyādhi in the ashraya verse (Cha.Su.1/55) and roga in the classification verse (Cha.Su.11/45). Distribution, not denotation.

Cha.Vi.6/5 says roga names the doshas too. This is the most counterintuitive fact in the record and it means 'roga' cannot be safely glossed as 'disease as opposed to its cause' without qualification.
Another Cha.Ni.1/5 synonym, but vikara is also the term in the dhatu-vaishamya definition of disease and carries a general sense of 'modification'. It is the least safe of the eight to swap in.

Listed as a synonym of disease at Cha.Ni.1/5 while also being a specific disease (fever). WHO ISTA preserves this oddity at ITA-4.2.1 sense 6, glossing it 'Fever as a generic term for disease'. A term index that does not handle this will collide.
'Antidote', literally a-gada, not-disease. Built from gada, one of the eight synonyms. An easy false friend for anyone matching on substrings.

mistranslations.why: WHO ISTA's own sense line for roga is 'Disorder, ailment' while vyādhi gets 'Disease'. Readers then infer a classical disease/disorder distinction. Cha.Ni.1/5 says there is none. WHO's split is an artifact of needing nine distinct sense lines in one entry.

In medical anthropology 'illness' is the experienced condition as against 'disease' the biomedical entity. Mapping roga to illness and vyadhi to disease invents a distinction the texts do not make, in the direction opposite to WHO's.
Same problem; 'sickness' carries a social-role sense in medical sociology.

An over-literal reading of Kaviratna's etymology (roga from ruj, to pain). The etymology is his note; the term denotes the condition, not the sensation. Ayurveda has ample vocabulary for pain itself (shula, vedana, ruja).

openQuestions: Does the Sanskrit of Cha.Vi.6/4-5 use roga in the way Kaviratna's English implies, or is his 'the same word Roga is applied to faults' an interpretive expansion? I retrieved only his English for this passage, never the Sanskrit. This needs checking before the claim is published.

Kaviratna's aphorism numbering in Vimana Sthana is taken from his own Abstract of Contents, not from a numbered verse in the body text. The chapter is certain; the verse numbers 5 and 6 should be confirmed against a numbered edition.
Is WHO ISTA's roga/vyādhi distribution deliberate editorial policy or an accident of how the term list was assembled?

classical.establishes: The enumeration in which rogamārga first appears — one of a set of triads, alongside three upastambhas, three kinds of bala, three āyatanas, three rogas, three physicians, three therapies.
classical.quote: अथ खलु त्रय उपस्तम्भाः, त्रिविधं बलं, त्रीण्यायतनानि, त्रयो रोगाः, त्रयो रोगमार्गाः, त्रिविधा भिषजः, त्रिविधमौषधमिति||३४||

classical.establishes: The full definition of all three rogamārgas, including the fact that koṣṭha is defined by a list of synonyms (mahāsrotas, śarīramadhya, mahānimna, āmapakvāśaya) and śākhā by rakta-and-other-dhātus plus skin. Note the Sanskrit as printed on this page has irregular spacing, preserved above as retrieved.
classical.quote: त्रयो रोगमार्गा इति- शाखा, मर्मास्थिसन्धयः, कोष्ठश्च| तत्र शाखा रक्तादयो धातवस्त्वक् च, स बाह्यो रोगमार्गः; मर्माणि पुनर्बस्तिहृदयमूर्धादीनि, अस्थिसन्धयोऽस्थिसंयोगास्तत्रोपनिबद्धाश्च स्नायुकण्डराः, स मध्यमो रोगमार्गः; कोष्ठः पुनरुच्यते महास्रोतः शरीरमध्यं महानिम्नमामपक्वाशयश्चेति पर्यायशब्दैस्तन्त्रे, स रोगमार्ग आभ्यन्तरः||४८||

distinguishFrom.why: Srotas are the channels that carry and transform; rogamārga is a partition of the body into three regions where disease manifests. A dhātu can belong to śākhā (a rogamārga) while its srotas is named separately. Conflating them is the commonest error in review articles.

Doṣagati is the MOVEMENT of doṣa (koṣṭha to śākhā and back, CS Sū. 28.31-33); rogamārga is the static topography. The two are related in Charaka's own text but are distinct concepts and distinct verses.
Marma is one constituent of the madhyama rogamārga (together with asthi-sandhi, snāyu and kaṇḍarā). It is not a synonym for the middle pathway.
Samprāpti is the process of pathogenesis over time; rogamārga is where it lands. A prognosis claim built on rogamārga is a claim about site, not about mechanism.

mistranslations.why: Imports an epidemiological sense of 'route'. Rogamārga is internal topography, not how disease passes between people.

Collapses rogamārga into srotas. Charaka names them separately and defines koṣṭha by synonyms that are cavities, not channels — though mahāsrotas is one of those synonyms, which is exactly why the confusion persists.
Depth is the wrong axis. Koṣṭha, the 'internal' mārga, is the most accessible to śodhana therapy; madhyama, the 'middle' one, is the gravest. A depth reading inverts the prognostic ordering.

openQuestions: Does Sushruta have an equivalent tripartition? Not located; the term rogamārga appears to be Charaka's.
Is there any published inter-rater reliability study for assigning a patient's disease to a rogamārga? None found on PubMed/Europe PMC.

Whether the Baghel Prakash Prognosis Scoring System (PMID 36403500), which generates prognosis items from the classics, includes a rogamārga item — its abstract does not say, and the full text was not retrieved.

classical.establishes: Summary verse of roga-parīkṣā by the three means. Sanskrit (siva.sh 4/9): 'आप्ततश्चोपदेशेन प्रत्यक्षकरणेन च। अनुमानेन च व्याधीन् सम्यग्विद्याद्विचक्षणः ॥९॥'
classical.quote: By Instruction (obtained) from the wise, by acts of Observing, as also by Inference, a physician of wisdom should ascertain (diagnose) disease.

classical.establishes: Parīkṣā is twofold (pratyakṣa, anumāna) for the knowledgeable, threefold with upadeśa; Kaviratna's prose version appears at Vi 4 'Hence, with persons possessed of knowledge, there are two methods of examination: Observation, and Inference. Counting Instruction, the methods are three.'
classical.quote: द्विविधातुखलुपरीक्षाज्ञानवतां- प्रत्यक्षम्, अनुमानंच। एतद्धिद्वयमुपदेशश्चपरीक्षास्यात्। एवमेषाद्विविधापरीक्षा, त्रिविधावासहोपदेशेन ॥८३॥

classical.establishes: Examination of the disorder (kārya-yoni = dhātu-vaiṣamya) means observing whether its signs are deficient/excessive and whether it is sādhya/asādhya, mṛdu/dāruṇa; links roga-parīkṣā to prognosis.

classical.quote: रोगं निदानप्राग्रूपलक्षणोपशयाप्तिभिः||२२||

classical.establishes: The fourfold parīkṣā (āptopadeśa, pratyakṣa, anumāna, yukti) of Su 11, versus the threefold of Vi 4 and Vi 8. Sanskrit (siva.sh 11/17): 'द्विविधमेव खलु सर्वं सच्चासच्च; तस्य चतुर्विधा परीक्षा- आप्तोपदेशः, प्रत्यक्षम्, अनुमानं, युक्तिश्चेति ॥१७॥'
classical.quote: All things are of two kinds, viz., Sat and Asat. Their perception (or knowledge) is of four kinds, viz., Testimony or affirmation of trustworthy teachers, Direct cognisance, Immediate Inference, and Argumentative Inference or Reasoning.

distinguishFrom.why: Examination of the patient (prakṛti, bala, sattva, vayas...) versus examination of the disease (nidāna, rūpa, prognosis); AH Su 1/22 separates them in one verse.
The content examined (five factors), not the act of examining; WHO folds the two together.
Epistemological 'means of valid knowledge' (fourfold incl. yukti) versus the clinical act; same word, different level.
The diagnostic conclusion (used by Yogaratnakara), not the process.

mistranslations.why: Acceptable, but WHO's definition restricts it to nidānapañcaka and omits Charaka's āptopadeśa/pratyakṣa/anumāna framing.
Conflates process (parīkṣā) with result (viniścaya/nirṇaya).

distinguishFrom.why: Reducing/lightening therapy; a separate upakrama in Su. 22.4. Both reduce, but rūkṣaṇa is defined by dryness/roughness, laṅghana by lightness.
Its direct opposite among the six (Su. 22.11 defines snehana by sneha, viṣyanda, mārdava, kleda).
The quality 'dry' (one of the gurvādi guṇas; NIA 2011 rukṣa entry); rūkṣaṇa is the procedure that produces it.
Powder massage, a technique often performed as rūkṣa udvartana; a method, not the category.
Arresting/astringent therapy; Kaviratna's property list for stambhana also includes 'dry', inviting confusion.

mistranslations.why: Implies water loss; the Sanskrit targets sneha/kleda (unctuousness/moistness) and produces kharatva and vaiśadya, not fluid depletion.
Doctrinally odd; vaiśadya is clarity/non-sliminess. Translator's word choice, not doctrine.
Fasting (upavāsa) is a laṅghana method (Su. 22.18), not rūkṣaṇa.

classical.establishes: Two separate claims in one verse. First, the definition, and its headword is LIṄGA, not rūpa: the manifested lakṣaṇa is liṅga. Second, seven words are anarthāntara: liṅga, ākṛti, lakṣaṇa, cihna, saṃsthāna, vyañjana, rūpa. So in Charaka rūpa is a synonym of the defined term, not the defined term. Retrieved and string-matched by me.

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for both halves. 'lak-shana' carries a line-break hyphen from the scan, preserved verbatim.
classical.quote: By 'Linga' is meant those symptoms which manifest themselves on the appearance of the disease. In this connection it should be stated that 'Linga', 'akriti', 'lak-shana', 'chihna', 'samsthana', 'vyanjana', and 'rupa', are words of the same import.

classical.establishes: Public-domain etymology making the inferential structure explicit: a liṅga is what one reasons FROM. This is the semantic content that 'sign' preserves and 'symptom' loses.
classical.quote: 'Linga' comes from the root 'Ligi' to go. Hence, anything by which one can go to or proceed to an inference is called 'Linga.' It is a sign or symptom by which disease is to be inferred.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's vyakti: full manifestation as the fifth kriyākāla. Again a stage, not an evidence type. 'symp-toms' carries a line-break hyphen, preserved verbatim.
classical.quote: The full manifestation of a disease, such as a swelling, tumour, aneurism (Granthi), Vidradhi (abscess) and erysipelas (Visarpa) etc., fever or dysentery, signifies the complete development of the characteristic symp- toms, which should be regarded as the fifth occasion for medical treatment.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata reverses Charaka's headword: the premonitory signs, on attaining clear manifestation (vyaktatā), are called RŪPA, and saṃsthāna, vyañjana, liṅga, lakṣaṇa, cihna and ākṛti are its synonyms. This is why the modern member of the pentad is called rūpa rather than liṅga. Devanagari mūla and verse number sighted on the retrieved page; not quoted per the rule for this text.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

classical.establishes: Madhavakara follows Vagbhata's headword and gives five synonyms (vyañjana, liṅga, lakṣaṇa, cihna, ākṛti), omitting saṃsthāna. The three texts therefore give three different synonym lists for one concept.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: Charaka's headword for this concept, with rūpa as one of its synonyms; Vagbhata's synonym, with rūpa as the headword. The modern pentad follows Vagbhata. A citation of 'rūpa, Ca. Ni. 1.9' is therefore slightly wrong: the verse defines liṅga.

Divided from rūpa by manifestation (prādurbhūta versus prāg-utpatti), and by Vagbhata's additional criteria of clarity and dosha-assignability. Vagbhata's Ni. 1.5 makes them continuous: the same signs, on becoming clear, are rūpa.

Listed as a synonym in all three texts and coded under the same WHO ID, but Charaka uses lakṣaṇa in the DEFINIENS of both pūrvarūpa (Ni. 1.8) and liṅga (Ni. 1.9), which a true synonym could not do without circularity. See the lakṣaṇa record.
The kriyākāla stage of manifestation (WHO ITA-4.6.x). Vyakti is when the signs appear; rūpa is what appears. Bhishagratna's Sūtra 21 passage is about the stage.
Form, or the object of the visual sense. A reader coming from philosophy will import that sense; Kaviratna's three-word footnote 'Rupa is form' is the bridge between the two and is easy to over-read.
Complications arising during the course of a disease. Distinguished from rūpa by dependence on the primary disease, and by arising later. Not covered in this record; it belongs in its own.

mistranslations.why: Halves the concept. Modern usage reserves 'symptom' for what the patient reports and 'sign' for what the examiner finds; WHO's ITA-4.5.5 description spans both explicitly ('as experienced by the patient or observed by the physician'). Kaviratna's liṅga etymology ('by which one can go to an inference') is closer to 'sign'.
The general Sanskrit sense of rūpa, and wrong here. In Ni. 1.9 the word is a technical synonym of liṅga.
Suggests the whole presentation as a gestalt. Rūpa in the pentad is enumerable — texts list the rūpa of a disease as discrete items.
Over-specifies. Nothing in the definition requires a rūpa to be specific to one disease; upaśaya exists precisely because it often is not.

openQuestions: Whether WHO's six glosses at ITA-4.5.5 are intended to map one-to-one onto the seven Sanskrit terms in order. My mapping is read off the PDF table and could be wrong. This should be checked against the printed edition before the mapping is published.

Whether any classical source distinguishes the seven synonyms in use, as Kaviratna does for the nidāna synonyms. He gives brief etymologies for six of them in the footnote to Ni. 1.9 but does not say they differ in application.

Modern literature: EMPTY, and I did not find any. There is no peer-reviewed work I located on the reliability of Ayurvedic sign elicitation as such. The nearest reliability data I retrieved concerned prakriti assessment (e.g. PMID 33750638, ICC 0.72 vata / 0.58 pitta / 0.44 kapha for AyuSoft versus clinicians), which is a different object and is not recorded here as evidence about rūpa.

classical.establishes: Seat = heart (hṛdaya); function = realisation/fulfilment of desires; designation = sādhakāgni. Notably NOT framed as intellect.

classical.establishes: Confirms the seat hṛdaya-stha and the function 'abhiprārthita-manoratha-sādhana-kṛt' — accomplisher of longed-for wishes. The mūla contains no word for intellect, memory or cognition.

classical.text: Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya (Sanskrit mūla; no public-domain English translation exists, so no translation is quoted)
classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa keeps the heart seat but ADDS the explicit cognitive triad buddhi (intellect), medhā (retentive intelligence) and abhimāna (self-regard), as the means by which the desired end is accomplished. This is the source of the modern 'intellect/emotion' framing and of WHO's description.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: CRITICAL retrieval hazard. 'Sadhaka' as an ordinary Sanskrit noun means an aspirant or practitioner. PMID 22557690 ('Place of nutrition in yoga') is returned by a 'sadhaka'[TIAB] PubMed search purely because it discusses diet for the 'Yoga Sadhaka' — it has nothing to do with the doṣa subtype. Any automated literature harvest on this term will pick up false positives of this kind.

All three are credited with mental function and all three are associated with the hṛdaya. Sādhaka is the pitta component (drive, ambition, discrimination, accomplishment); prāṇa vāta governs the mind's movement and grasping; manas is the mental faculty itself, not a doṣa.

Bhishagratna's Su.Sū. 15 footnote maps sādhaka onto both medhā-kṛt AND ojas-kṛt, which blurs sādhaka into ojas production. Later systematisations usually do not, so the footnote should not be read as settled doctrine.

Both are seated at or around the heart and both are invoked together in cardiac and hypertension papers (PMID 29153383, PMID 40972327). Sādhaka is the functional/mental-drive component; avalambaka is the structural/supportive one.

mistranslations.rendering: "the pitta of the intellect" applied to Suśruta
mistranslations.why: Suśruta 21.10 says only 'accomplisher of longed-for wishes'. The intellect content (buddhi, medhā, abhimāna) is Vāgbhaṭa's addition at AH Sū 12.13. Attaching it to a Suśruta citation misreports the source.

A proposed correlate, never a translation. The classical function is teleological (bringing an intended end about); neurotransmitters are a mechanism. No study has operationalised, let alone measured, sādhaka pitta.
Neither text mentions emotion. Sādhana is about accomplishment and resolve. 'Emotional' is a Western-psychology import that also collides with the entirely separate classical treatment of the manas.

openQuestions: Does Suśruta's 'accomplishment' sense and Vāgbhaṭa's 'buddhi-medhā-abhimāna' sense represent a real doctrinal development, or is Dalhaṇa already reading the cognitive sense into Suśruta? Needs the commentary.
Bhishagratna's footnote pairs sādhaka with ojas-kṛt. Is that his own inference or does it follow Dalhaṇa?
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 carries any sādhaka-pitta entry.

classical.establishes: Charaka's four-way scheme: sukhasādhya, kṛcchrasādhya; yāpya and anupakrama as subdivisions of asādhya. Sanskrit (siva.sh 10/9): 'सुखसाध्यंमतंसाध्यंकृच्छ्रसाध्यमथापिच। द्विविधंचाप्यसाध्यंस्याद्याप्यंयच्चानुपक्रमम् ॥९॥' at https://www.siva.sh/caraka-samhita/sutra-sthana/10/6-10
classical.quote: As regards curable diseases, they are of two kinds, viz., those that are easily curable and those that are curable with difficulty. Incurable diseases, also, are of two kinds, viz., those that are capable of being suppressed, and those that have no treatment.

classical.establishes: Sādhya has three grades (alpa, madhya, utkṛṣṭa); asādhya-anupakrama has none. Sanskrit (siva.sh 10/10): 'साध्यानांत्रिविधश्चाल्पमध्यमोत्कृष्टतांप्रति। विकल्पो, न त्वसाध्यानांनियतानांविकल्पना ॥१०॥'
classical.quote: As regards diseases that are curable, they may again be regarded from three points of view, viz., those that are capable of being cured by the application of means that are easy, those that are curable by means neither easy nor difficult, and lastly those that are curable by means that are difficult. Incurable diseases, which have no treatment, do not admit of being looked upon from different points of view.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita (translator's footnote, NOT the text)
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's own gloss of yāpya and anupakrama; cite as translator's note, not as Charaka.
classical.quote: 'Yapya' means those diseases which without admitting of radical cure can, by medicine and diet and change of air, be kept in a state of partial suppression. 'Anupakramam' is explained by the Commentator as those for which there is no treatment, i.e., those in which treatment is productive of no beneficial consequence.

classical.verse: standard 10/18-20 (10/18-19ab = yāpya features closed by vidyād dvidoṣajam; 10/19cd-20 = pratyākhyeya features from tadvat pratyākhyeyaṃ tridoṣajam); Kaviratna prints 12-14 for the whole
classical.establishes: Features of the pratyākhyeya (to-be-declined) disease, standard Su 10/19cd-20: born of all three doṣas (tridoṣaja), beyond the path of treatment (kriyāpatham atikrānta), running through all the channels (sarvamārgānusārin), causing restlessness, distress and stupefaction, destroying the senses, fully developed in a weak patient, and attended by fatal signs (sāriṣṭa). The opening clauses of Kaviratna's sentence (deep-seated, in many dhātus, lodged in vital parts and joints, continuous, long-standing, born of two doṣas = 10/18-19ab) are in the Sanskrit the description of the yāpya (palliable) disease, closed by vidyāt; Kaviratna merges the two lists into one sentence and renders dvidoṣaja/tridoṣaja as 'two of the three ... or of all the three'.
classical.quote: When the disease is deeply ingrained (into the marrow and such other constituents of the body), when it affects many of the constituent parts, when it is attached to the vital limbs and joints of the body, when it manifests itself continuously, when it is chronic and very old, when it is born of the derangement of two of the three ingredients (of wind, bile, and phlegm) or of all the three, when it is beyond the operation of treatment, when it affects all the organs, when the patient is thoroughly cheerless and despairing, when the disease is characterised by a stupefaction of the mind, when the disease weakens the strength of all the organs (of knowledge and action), when the disease has reached the highest limit of aggravation and the patient has become entirely strengthless, and lastly when the disease exhibits indications of the patient's dissolution, it should be regarded as one that should not be taken up for treatment.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.chapter: 18 (Trishothiya; Kaviratna's colophon 'Thus ends the Eighteenth Lesson, called Tritjothiya')

classical.establishes: The sādhya/asādhya x mṛdu/dāruṇa cross-classification (four kinds). Kaviratna's footnote (not text) adds: 'Among these, Mild and Incurable would mean Yapya or suppressible.'
classical.quote: Diseases are of two kinds, viz., Curable and Incurable. Distributing them according to the considerations of mildness and violence, they become of four kinds.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's threefold scheme, with yāpya as a head of its own rather than a subdivision of asādhya as in Charaka Su 10/9.
classical.quote: All the diseases, whose names have been specifically enumerated before, may be grouped under any of the three different heads as the curable, the suppressible (Yapya) and the incurable (lit: fit to be pronounced as hopeless).

classical.establishes: Operational meaning of yāpya in Sushruta: survival contingent on continued treatment.
classical.quote: A patient laid up with a disease, which only admits of a palliative treatment, lives so long as the course of the medical treatment is continued, and will die almost simultaneously with its discontinuance.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata follows Charaka's 2x2 scheme (susādhya, kṛcchrasādhya; yāpya, anupakrama).

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ITA-1.8.2.7 glosses this sense as 'dependent variable'; same word, Nyaya meaning, unrelated to prognosis.

In Charaka Su 10/9 and AH Su 1 it is a subdivision of asādhya; in Sushruta Su 35 it is a third head alongside sādhya and asādhya. Translating yāpya as 'curable' or lumping it under 'treatable' erases this.
Disease with no treatment / to be declined; WHO treats them as synonyms ('Terminal disease'); Charaka Su 10/19 uses pratyākhyeya for the tridoṣaja type.

classical.establishes: Charaka's fourfold division is by balabheda (difference of strength), and samāgni belongs to those whose vāta, pitta and kapha are equable and in their natural state.
classical.quote: अग्निषु तु शारीरेषु चतुर्विधो विशेषो बलभेदेन भवति। तद्यथा- तीक्ष्णो, मन्दः, समो, विषमश्चेति। ... तत्र समवातपित्तश्लेष्मणां प्रकृतिस्थानां समा भवन्त्यग्नयः

classical.establishes: Public-domain English. Note Charaka's samāgni is defined by conditional vulnerability (it deranges under dietary abuse and recovers under good regimen), which is subtly different from Sushruta's 'digests fully and on time'.
classical.quote: In the fires dwelling in the physical system, a fourfold distinction may be made agreeably to difference of strength. It is as follows: Keen, mild, even, and uneven. ... That fire is said to be even which becomes vitiated by dietary riotousness, but which exists without being deranged when no dietary riotousness is indulged in. ... Amongst these, of those persons that are of equable wind, bile, and phlegm, and that are in their normal state, the (digestive) fires are even.

classical.establishes: Charaka cross-references his own Vimāna 6 classification and declares the four agnis to be grahaṇī-faults 'sama-varjam' — excluding sama. This is the textual warrant for treating samāgni as a state of health and not a diagnosis.
classical.quote: यश्चाग्निः पूर्वमुद्दिष्टो रोगानीके चतुर्विधः। तं चापि ग्रहणीदोषं समवर्जं प्रचक्ष्महे॥७१॥

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa adds a mechanism Charaka and Sushruta do not: agni is sama when samāna vāyu is in its own place, and viṣama when samāna goes astray. Verse numbers confirmed by the file's own internal variant markers (3.74dv, 3.75av).
classical.quote:
samaḥ samāne sthāna-sthe viṣamo 'gnir vi-mārga-ge |
pittābhimūrchite tīkṣṇo mando 'smin kapha-pīḍite || 73 ||

samo 'gnir viṣamas tīkṣṇo mandaś caivaṃ catur-vidhaḥ |
yaḥ pacet samyag evānnaṃ bhuktaṃ samyak samas tv asau || 74 ||
classical.translator: none — no public-domain English translation of Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya exists

distinguishFrom.why: samāgni is a state of agni, not a kind of agni alongside jāṭharāgni/dhātvagni/bhūtāgni. The 13-fold and the 4-fold schemes are orthogonal axes and are routinely presented as if they were one list.

Ca.Vi.6.12 links samāgni to sama-doṣa constitution, but Charaka argues in Vi.6.13 that vāta/pitta/kapha-prakṛti persons are not thereby diseased. Agni state and constitutional type are correlated (PMID 35101333) but not identical.
samāgni is one marker of health, not health itself.
Bhishagratna's own footnote at Su.Sū.35 warns that agni and appetite are different, then he glosses sama as 'normal or regular appetite' in the same passage. The two are not interchangeable.

mistranslations.why: Reverses the doctrine. Excessive strength is tīkṣṇāgni, which is a fault. Sama is adequacy and regularity, not maximum power.
Not wrong, but it smuggles in the doṣa-equilibrium explanation as if it were the definition. Sushruta defines sama by digestive performance and treats doṣa balance as what that reflects.
Charaka's sama is explicitly still derangeable by dietary abuse (Ca.Vi.6.12); 'normal' in English suggests a stable trait rather than a conditional equilibrium.

Do Bhishagratna's and Kaviratna's definitions reflect a real Sushruta/Charaka divergence or translator choice?
Has any instrument demonstrated it can separate samāgni from mild viṣamāgni?

Sutra Sthana 13/23-24' (general sāma features) and '13/26-27' (sāma doṣa and sāma dhātu) was read on the carakasamhitaonline Ama page, i.e. it is a secondary attestation and has NOT been checked against the Ashtanga Hridaya text itself. distinguishFrom.why: THE critical disambiguation for this record. सामदोष (sa-āma, 'with āma') and समदोष (sama, 'equal') are distinct words that become identical when transliterated without diacritics as 'sama dosha'. They are near-opposites: one is a pathological state, the other is the definition of health at Sushruta Sutrasthana 15/41. Any English or romanised source using 'samadosha' must be checked for which is meant.
Āma is the product of incomplete digestion (WHO ITA-4.6.2). Sāmadoṣa is a doṣa that has become associated with it. 'Ama dosha' in loose usage means either.
WHO ITA-4.6.2 also covers āmāvasthā, the stage of a disease. A disease can be in āma stage; a doṣa is sāma. The referents are different.
A doṣa can be aggravated without being sāma. WHO's description makes āma-association a qualitative and functional alteration distinct from increase.
The same prefix applies to tissues and wastes with separate sign-lists (carakasamhitaonline cites Cha.Su.28/9-19 for sāma dhātu). 'Sama' alone does not say which.

mistranslations.why: The direct product of the homograph collapse. Renders समदोष, and applied to सामदोष it states the reverse of the truth.
The commonest popular rendering. WHO ISTA deliberately avoids 'toxin' for āma, describing it as a standstill in digestive and metabolic transformation.
Too literal and too narrow: WHO's āma covers metabolic as well as digestive incompleteness, and includes channel blockade and accumulation of waste.
Common in Indian clinical English but ambiguous between āmadoṣa (āma as a doṣa-like entity) and sāmadoṣa (a doṣa carrying āma).

openQuestions: The Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 13 verse numbers for the sāma/nirāma lakṣaṇas were taken from a secondary source and are UNVERIFIED against the primary text. Wisdomlib's Ashtanga Hridaya Sanskrit page returned HTTP 403 to both curl and WebFetch, and GRETIL's Astangahrdaya file path returned 404 at the URL tried. A human should verify against a printed edition or a working GRETIL path before any of these locators is published.
Whether Charaka states the sāma/nirāma doṣa distinction in its own words anywhere, or whether it is a Vagbhata systematisation, was not established.
No WHO ISTA entry was found that flags the samadoṣa/sāmadoṣa homograph, despite the standard containing both (ITA-4.8.23 and ITA-10.1.1).

classical.establishes: Sushruta seats samāna in āmāśaya and pakvāśaya, joined to agni, and gives it both digestion and the separation of essence (sāra) from waste (kiṭṭa). Corresponding Sanskrit, cross-checked at a separate URL: 'आमपक्वाशयचरः समानो वह्निसङ्गतः | सोऽन्नं पचति तज्जांश्च विशेषान्विविनक्ति हि ||१६|| गुल्माग्निसादातीसारप्रभृतीन् कुरुते गदान् |१७|'.
classical.quote: The Samana Vayu courses in (governs) the stomach (Amashaya) and in the region of intestines (Pakvashaya). Its functions consist in digesting the chyme brought down into the intestines in unison with the digestive ferment (Agni), and especially in disintegrating its essence from its refuse or excreted matter. A deranged or aggravated condition of the Samana Vayu causes dysentery, Gulma, and impaired digestion, etc. 9.

classical.establishes: Charaka's samāna is NOT seated in the stomach. It presides over the srotas carrying sveda (sweat), doṣas and ambu (water), stands beside the internal fire (antaragni), and its defining function is agnibalaprada — giving strength to the digestive fire. It is the fire's bellows, not the digester. This is materially different from Sushruta Ni.1.16 and from every popular rendering that makes samāna 'the digestive vata'.
classical.quote: स्वेददोषाम्बुवाहीनि स्रोतांसि समधिष्ठितः | अन्तरग्नेश्च पार्श्वस्थः समानोऽग्निबलप्रदः ||८||

classical.establishes: Names samāna as one of the five in a lawfully quotable English Charaka. No seat or function given.
classical.quote: It exists in the fivefold form of Prana, Udana, Samana, Vyana, and Apana.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata gives samāna a single self-contained verse: situated near the fire (agnisamīpasthaḥ), ranging throughout the koṣṭha, and performing four sequential acts — it receives food (gṛhṇāti), cooks it (pacati), separates it (vivecayati) and releases it (muñcati). This four-verb formulation is Vagbhata's own and is the tidiest classical definition of samāna anywhere. Sanskrit mūla and verse number verified on the retrieved page; not quoted, as Ashtanga Hridaya has no public-domain English translation.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

classical.verse: 5.27-28; and PK 2 on timing of medicine
classical.establishes: PK 5.27-28 place samāna at the koṣṭha / vahnisthāna (seat of fire). Separately, Purva Khanda 2 uses the full compound समानवाते ('when samāna vāta is disordered') in prescribing that agni-kindling medicine be given when samāna is deranged and agni is weak — the only occurrence of the compound headword form 'samāna vāta' I found in any retrieved classical Sanskrit. Not quoted, as Sharngadhara has no public-domain English translation.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: The single most important distinction for this term. Charaka Ci.28.8 makes samāna agnibalaprada — it gives STRENGTH to the fire. Pācaka pitta is the fire's digesting agency. Samāna moves and fans; pācaka pitta transforms. Sources that define samāna as 'the digestive vata' have quietly absorbed pācaka pitta's job, and WHO's choice of 'Kindling vata' is a deliberate guard against exactly this.

Samāna is adjacent to agni (antaragneḥ pārśvasthaḥ, agnisamīpasthaḥ) — never identical with it. The adjacency is stated in the verse itself in both Charaka and Vagbhata, which suggests the texts were guarding against the conflation.

Both operate in the pakvāśaya region and Sushruta explicitly gives samāna a pakvāśaya range (Ni.1.16). The separation is functional: samāna separates sāra from kiṭṭa; apāna expels the kiṭṭa. Charaka avoids the overlap entirely by moving samāna out of the gut and into the sveda/doṣa/ambu srotas.

In yoga samāna is the equalising current at the navel, often tied to the manipura cakra and to assimilation of prāṇa rather than of food. The Ayurvedic samāna is defined against agni and the koṣṭha, not against a cakra.
Sharngadhara PK 2 prescribes agni-kindling medicine FOR deranged samāna. The indication is not the definition; samāna is not 'the appetite'.

mistranslations.why: Directly contradicts Charaka Ci.28.8, where samāna's function is to give strength to the fire, not to digest. It also silently annexes pācaka pitta's role. Sushruta Ni.1.16 does say samāna digests (pacati), so this rendering is defensible from Sushruta alone — but presenting it as THE definition hides that the two texts disagree.

mistranslations.rendering: the balancing air / the equalising breath
mistranslations.why: A literal etymological reading (sam + ana) imported from the yogic scheme. Neither Charaka nor Sushruta nor Vagbhata defines samāna by equalisation; all three define it by its relation to agni and to the separation of nutrient from waste.
Bhishagratna's 1911 footnote, 'The Samana is same as the energy of the epigastric plexus'. Colonial-era neuroanatomical mapping, still quoted as though it were Sushruta's own.

As given on the Kerala Tourism page. Sweat is textually defensible from Charaka Ci.28.8 (svedavaha srotas); semen and urine are explicitly apāna's at Charaka Ci.28.10 and Sushruta Ni.1.19. The rendering merges two subtypes.

WHO uses it ('responsible for metabolism and transformation') and it is not wrong, but it is a modern abstraction with no classical counterpart term, and it makes samāna indistinguishable from agni in English.

openQuestions: Does Chakrapani reconcile Charaka Ci.28.8's srotas-based seat for samāna with Sushruta Ni.1.16's āmāśaya/pakvāśaya seat, or does he let the disagreement stand?
Why did WHO pick 'Kindling vata' (which follows Charaka's agnibalaprada) but then write a description that follows the gut-seat tradition? Was the inconsistency noticed?
Is there any classical source that assigns semen or urine to samāna, or is the Kerala Tourism rendering wholly unsupported?
Does NAMASTE assign samāna vāta a Sharira Kriya code, and what English term does it use?

classical.establishes: The therapeutic principle: sāmānya causes vṛddhi, viśeṣa causes hrāsa. Sanskrit as retrieved from https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya&action=raw : सर्वदा सर्वभावानां सामान्यं वृद्धिकारणम्| ह्रासहेतुर्विशेषश्च, प्रवृत्तिरुभयस्य तु||४४||. 'A tendency exists towards both' renders 'pravṛttir ubhayasya tu' (the activity/operation belongs to both). Kaviratna's footnote (translator's note) adds the water/heat illustration and calls this 'almost the basis of the Science of Life'.
classical.quote: Of all things, at all times, similarity is the cause of increase; and dissimilarity is the cause of decrease. A tendency exists towards both.

classical.establishes: The definition: sāmānya is ekatvakara (produces oneness) and tulyārthatā. Sanskrit: सामान्यमेकत्वकरं, विशेषस्तु पृथक्त्वकृत्| तुल्यार्थता हि सामान्यं, विशेषस्तु विपर्ययः||४५||. Kaviratna's 'identity of substance' for tulyārthatā is a translator's interpretation; the Sanskrit says 'sameness of artha (purpose/effect/object)'.
classical.quote: Similarity is that which produces oneness; and dissimilarity is that which produces diversity. Therefore, similarity is identity of substance, and dissimilarity is the reverse of this.

classical.establishes: Sāmānya listed first among the six. Sanskrit: सामान्यं च विशेषं च गुणान् द्रव्याणि कर्म च||२८||.
classical.quote: Those great Rishis (then) beheld duly, with the eye of knowledge, similarities, dissimilarities, properties, objects, and operations, as also compositions.

Nigrahasthana. ?*26'); his 27 is the following aphorism, the Vada definition ending 'in a spirit of contradiction' = standard 28. His terms are left untranslated per his footnote on the same page.

classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Su.1.44-45: the paired opposite; sāmānya increases and unifies, viśeṣa decreases and separates.

Sinha renders Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.4's sāmānya as 'Genus'; WHO ITA-1.9.1.1 as 'Generality ... the universal or class-essence'. Charaka's definition (Su.1.44-45) is functional: whatever causes increase and oneness. Same word, two doctrines.
Ordinary likeness; Charaka's sāmānya is defined by its effect (vṛddhi), not by resemblance as such, though Kaviratna's 'similarity' makes them sound identical.
NIA DG0263: a property shared by more than one mahābhūta (guru in pṛthvī and jala). A compound, not the category.
WHO ITA entries 'sāmānyapūrvarūpam' and 'sāmānyajavikāraḥ' use sāmānya in the everyday sense 'general, common', not the category.

mistranslations.why: WHO's headword imports Vaiśeṣika; Charaka Su.1.44 defines sāmānya by its causing increase. The Ayurvedic texts do not discuss class-essences.
Kaviratna's rendering of tulyārthatā (Su.1.45); the Sanskrit says sameness of artha (purpose/effect), not identity of substance.
Ca.Su.1.44 says like INCREASES like; treatment of excess is by viśeṣa (the dissimilar). The homoeopathic slogan inverts the therapeutic direction.
Correct for the Ayurvedic sense but hides the fact that Charaka also places sāmānya among six ontological terms (Su.1.28, Vi.8.27), where 'similarity' is an odd member of a list of categories.

openQuestions: Chakrapāṇi's threefold sāmānya (dravya/guṇa/karma) that WHO ITA-1.9.1.2-4 and NIA presuppose was not retrieved from the commentary; only the WHO/NIA statements were read.
Whether Kaviratna's 'identity of substance' reflects a commentarial gloss on tulyārthatā was not checked.

classical.establishes: The definition: samavāya is the non-separateness (apṛthagbhāva) of earth etc. from their gunas, and it is nitya because wherever the dravya is, the guna is not absent. Sanskrit as retrieved from https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya&action=raw : समवायोऽपृथग्भावो भूम्यादीनां गुणैर्मतः| स नित्यो यत्र हि द्रव्यं न तत्रानियतो गुणः||५०||. '(of scent and the like)' is Kaviratna's gloss (gandha being the characteristic guna of pṛthvī).
classical.quote: The co-existence of objects such as earth, &c., with their corresponding properties (of scent and the like) is styled samavaya. That is permanent, since wherever the substance is, it cannot be that the property is not.

classical.establishes: Samavāya as the relation presupposed by the definitions of dravya (samavāyi-kāraṇa) and guna (samavāyī). Sanskrit: यत्राश्रिताः कर्मगुणाः कारणं समवायि यत्| तद्द्रव्यं समवायी तु निश्चेष्टः कारणं गुणः||५१||. Kaviratna renders 'samavāyi' once as 'inhere' and once as 'inherent' and drops it from 'the cause' for dravya.
classical.quote: That in which actions and attributes inhere, and that which is the cause, is called substance. That, on the other hand, which is inherent, and which is the passive cause, is called attribute.

classical.establishes: Samavāya ('compositions') closing the list of six. Sanskrit: समवायं च तज्ज्ञात्वा तन्त्रोक्तं विधिमास्थिताः| लेभिरे परमं शर्म जीवितं चाप्यनित्वरम्||२९||.
classical.quote: ...as also compositions. Knowing these, and conforming to the ordinances of that Science, they obtained great felicity and even immortal life.

classical.verse: Standard 40.3 region per siva.sh; Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers
classical.establishes: Sushruta's use of samavāyi-kāraṇa for the dravya-guna relation. The Sanskrit retrieved from siva.sh for 40.3 contains 'आश्रयत्वाच्च, द्रव्यमाश्रिता रसादयः' (because of being the substratum; rasa etc. depend on dravya); the compound samavāyi-kāraṇa itself was not located in the siva.sh Sanskrit of 40.3 and may be Bhishagratna's expansion or sit in an adjacent sentence; a human should check.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: Saṁyoga is a guna in the parādi series (Kaviratna's 'union' at Su.1.49) and is separable; samavāya is nitya and apṛthagbhāva (Su.1.50). Kaviratna's 'combination' (Vi.8) and 'compositions' (Su.1.28) both sound like saṁyoga.
The adjective applied to dravya (Ca.Su.1.51; Bhishagratna Su.40): the substratum-cause. Samavāya is the relation; samavāyi-kāraṇa is the relatum.
Vaiśeṣika extends the relation to whole/part, universal/particular, action/substance (WHO ITA-1.9.6.1 includes 'the whole and its parts'); Charaka Su.1.50 names only bhūta/guna.
Kaviratna uses 'co-existence' for these in the dosha context too (e.g. 'Co-existence must be in the form of ... Sannipata'); a different notion of two doshas being deranged together.
Kaviratna renders anubandha as 'co-existence of diseases' in Nidanasthana; same English word, unrelated concept.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's words at Su.1.28 and Vi.8.29; Sinha's 'Combination'. Both suggest things put together (saṁyoga), whereas samavāya is the inseparable relation.
Kaviratna, WHO and NIA all use it, but unqualified it covers saṁyoga too. Ca.Su.1.50's apṛthagbhāva and nitya are the distinguishing content.
WHO ITA-1.9.6.1; in logic 'concomitance' translates vyāpti (invariable accompaniment), a different technical term.

openQuestions: Whether Bhishagratna's '(Samavayi-Karana)' corresponds to an explicit compound in the Sanskrit of Su.Su.40 was not resolved.
Chakrapāṇi on 'apṛthagbhāva' not retrieved.

Those men who are possessed of firm and compact bodies become endued with strength.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO gives asthisaṅghātaḥ / saṅghātaḥ its own anatomical entry at ITA-3.13.64, 'Conglomeration of bones'. So the same word is a synonym of saṃhanana in Vimana 8 and a distinct structure in the śārīra vocabulary.
The next examination item. Pramāṇa measures dimensions in aṅgulas; saṃhanana judges how well the parts are put together.
Sāra grades each tissue's quality; saṃhanana grades the assembly. A person may be māṃsa-sāra and still not susaṃhata.
An indicator from which bala is inferred, not bala itself.

mistranslations.why: Imports somatotype. The three classical criteria are about articulation and distribution, not mass or shape.

A modern medicalisation. samasuvibhaktāsthi is about even distribution of bone, with no claim about density.

classical.establishes: SIX bheda in the Sanskrit compound: saṅkhyā, prādhānya, vidhi, vikalpa, bala, kāla. The retrieved page's own English renders these as five by fusing the last two into 'bala-kala vishesha', which is a live translation disagreement visible within a single source. The page then supplies worked examples at 12.1 (eight jvara, five gulma, seven kuṣṭha for saṅkhyā).

classical.quote: Samprapti, ' jati', and 1 agati' of disease, are words of the same import 'Samprapti' is distinguished by these considerations, viz., number (or enumeration), predominance, kind (or order), solution of doubt, strength](or intensity), and Time.

classical.establishes: THE SIX KRIYĀKĀLA IN A LAWFULLY QUOTABLE ENGLISH TRANSLATION, naming all six with their Sanskrit: sañcaya, prakopa, prasara, sthāna-saṃśraya, vyakti, bheda. This is what modern writing usually means by 'samprāpti as six stages' — but it is Sushruta's kriyākāla, a separate doctrine, and Sushruta does not call it samprāpti here. 'Sth3na' and the unclosed parentheses are OCR artifacts, preserved verbatim. Retrieved and string-matched by me.
classical.quote: The physician, who fully knows about the accumula- tion (Sanchaya), disturbance or aggravation (Prakopa , expansion (Prasaram), and differentiating traits of the deranged humours (Bheda), and is well conversant with the specific localities in which they are respectively confined in the course of their expansion (Sth3na- samshrayam), and with the symptoms which they respec- tively exhibit in connection with the incidental disease (Vyakti), is alone worthy of that epithet.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata DOES define it where Charaka only gives synonyms: the nirvṛtti of the disease by the vitiated dosha as they circulate. And his subtypes number FIVE, not six — saṅkhyā, vikalpa, prādhānya, bala, kāla, omitting Charaka's vidhi. Devanagari mūla and verse numbers sighted on the retrieved page; not quoted per the rule for this text.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

classical.establishes: Madhavakara follows Vagbhata's five subtypes, again without vidhi. So the count is six in Charaka and five in both Vagbhata and Madhavakara, while WHO codes six. Verse numbers from the modern English rendering on the retrieved page.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: THE CENTRAL CONFUSION, and WHO's own ITA-4.5.16 description commits it by saying samprāpti is 'classified into six stages'. Samprāpti is Charaka's member of the pentad, subdivided at Ni. 1.12 into six ASPECTS (number, predominance, kind, and so on). Kriyākāla is Sushruta's six-stage temporal sequence (sañcaya to bheda), quoted here from Bhishagratna. Different texts, different doctrines, different sixes. Modern writing routinely presents the kriyākāla stages AS the content of samprāpti.
Cause versus process. WHO separates them into chapter 4.4 and chapter 4.5.
A modern analytic breakdown into named participant slots (dosha, dūṣya, srotas, agni, and so on). Not classical, and WHO has no entry for it. See that record.
The six aspects at Ca. Ni. 1.12, coded by WHO at ITA-4.5.18-4.5.23. Dimensions along which a samprāpti varies, not components of it and not stages in it.

Declared synonyms at Ni. 1.11 and coded under the same WHO ID, but Kaviratna's footnote treats them as differently-angled: jāti as birth, āgati as coming-in versus going-out. Recording them as bare synonyms loses that.

The standard rendering, and it carries a mechanistic commitment the Sanskrit does not. Samprāpti as classically divided is about counting subtypes, judging dominance and timing severity — closer to a structured characterisation of a disease episode than to a causal mechanism.

mistranslations.why: Conflates samprāpti with ṣaṭ-kriyākāla. WHO's ITA-4.5.16 description makes exactly this error, which means the error now has standards-body authority.
Implies a physiological mechanism specified at the level of function. Ca. Ni. 1.12's six divisions specify no mechanism at all.
Folds nidāna back into samprāpti. The pentad separates them deliberately.
Captures the kriyākāla sense and loses the bheda sense entirely, including saṅkhyā (how many types) and vidhi (curable, difficult, incurable), neither of which is about progression.

mistranslations.rendering: ascertainment of the strength or otherwise of the disease
mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's own gloss, recorded above as a rendering because it is public-domain and historically interesting, but it is wrong: it promotes one of six divisions (bala) into the meaning of the whole.

openQuestions: Whether the six-versus-five subtype count is a genuine doctrinal difference or a textual variant. Charaka's compound at Ni. 1.12 contains vidhi; the Ashtanga Hridaya and Madhava Nidana lists as rendered on the retrieved pages do not. Someone with the Sanskrit of AH Ni. 1.9 should confirm.
Why the retrieved carakasamhitaonline English fuses bala and kāla into one item when its own Sanskrit gives six. Possibly following a commentary. Worth checking Chakrapani.

Whether any paper proposes a measurable correlate for any stage of kriyākāla. Across the three papers recorded here, none does; all three propose future work. PubMed returns 15 records for 'samprapti' and I read the abstracts of the three most relevant.
Whether WHO's ITA-4.5.17 blank description is an error or intentional.

distinguishFrom.why: Samprāpti is the process. Samprāpti-ghaṭaka is an analytic breakdown of it into named slots to be filled in. The ghaṭaka format is how a samprāpti is WRITTEN UP in modern case documentation and dissertations; it is not a second process.

The genuinely classical subdivision (Ca. Ni. 1.12: saṅkhyā, prādhānya, vidhi, vikalpa, bala, kāla, which I verified in the Sanskrit; WHO codes six at ITA-4.5.18-4.5.23). Those are dimensions along which a samprāpti varies. The ghaṭaka are the anatomical and physiological participants. Completely different lists, routinely confused because both are 'the parts of samprāpti'.
The ghaṭaka list describes what is involved INSIDE the pathological process. The causes that set it going are nidāna and sit outside the list.

A staging sequence, quotable from Bhishagratna's Sūtra 21. Kriyākāla is often listed AS ONE of the ghaṭaka slots, which makes the two easy to conflate; the ghaṭaka set is larger and is not temporally ordered.
One component of the list, not the list. WHO codes dūṣya independently.
Two separate slots in most component lists — the channel involved, and the manner of its vitiation. Frequently collapsed into one in write-ups.

mistranslations.why: Reads ghaṭaka as causal agents. They are participants in the pathology, not its causes; the causes are nidāna.
The usual rendering and defensible, but it obscures that these are documentation slots in a modern template rather than a classical enumeration. A lexicon should say which it is.
A ghaṭaka list names the participants; it does not by itself state a mechanism connecting them.
Too vague; loses the specific reference to the samprāpti process.

openQuestions: Does the compound samprāpti-ghaṭaka occur in ANY classical or commentarial Sanskrit text? I could not find it, and my search was not exhaustive: I checked Charaka Nidana Sthana 1 and Vimana 8 (Sanskrit, retrieved and searched), Bhishagratna's Sushruta Sutrasthana volume (full-text search of the OCR), the full WHO 2022 terminology PDF (full-text search of the extraction), and general web search. I did NOT search a Sanskrit corpus such as GRETIL, and did not check Chakrapani, Madhukosha, Dalhana, Sharngadhara or Bhavaprakasha. The correct statement is 'not found', not 'does not exist'.

Which modern author first codified the list. The likeliest candidates are the mid-20th-century Roga Nidana / Vyadhi Vinishchaya teaching texts used in Indian BAMS and MD(Ay) curricula. A human should check Yogesh Chandra Mishra's and Ajay Kumar Sharma's Roga Nidana textbooks and the CCIM syllabus for Roga Nidana evam Vikriti Vigyana.

How many slots the canonical list has, and whether it is stable. Component sets I encountered in secondary sources ran to roughly ten items (doṣa, dūṣya, srotas, sroto-duṣṭi-prakāra, agni, ama, udbhava-sthāna, sañcāra-sthāna, vyakta-sthāna, roga-mārga, sometimes svabhāva and sādhya-asādhyatā), but I verified no single authoritative enumeration from a primary source and so record none here.
Whether NAMASTE codes the construct. namaste.ayush.gov.in answers at the root but its terminologies path 302-redirects and the machine-readable data was not reachable.
Devanagari is left empty deliberately: I did not sight सम्प्राप्तिघटक in any retrieved Sanskrit source.

classical.verse: Standard 1.21 (list) and 1.22 (definition); Kaviratna's printed numbers are OCR-damaged in the retrieved scan (prakriti clause prints 17)
classical.establishes: The canonical definition: karaṇa = abhisaṁskāra of natural substances; saṁskāra = guṇāntarādhāna (conferring other qualities), achieved by water, fire, cleansing, churning, place, time, perfuming, impregnation, duration, vessel. Sanskrit as retrieved: करणं पुनः स्वाभाविकानां द्रव्याणामभिसंस्कारः| संस्कारो हि गुणान्तराधानमुच्यते|| (within ||२२||, https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Rasa_Vimana). The eightfold list is 1.21: प्रकृतिकरणसंयोगराशिदेशकालोपयोगसंस्थोपयोक्त्रष्टमानि.
classical.quote: That, again, is called Karana which is a transmutation or improvement of the products of Nature. Verily, the super-inducing of other attributes is said to be Transmutation or Improvement. Those attributes are induced by the refinement brought about by contact with water and fire, by churning, by (virtue of) place and time, and perfuming, steeping, &c, as also by excellence through length of time, and (use of different kinds of) vessels and the rest.

classical.verse: Standard 26.29-30 (list) and 26.34 (definition); Kaviratna prints 44-45 after the list paragraph (printed p. 305) and 49 after the Parimāna/Saṁskāra/Abhyāsa block (printed p. 306), Lesson XXVI. His 46 belongs to the Yukti definition, not to the list.
classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English for two things: (a) Charaka's list of the ten parādi guṇas (Su 26.29-30), in which 'Sanskara' is ninth, and (b) the one-line definition of saṁskāra in Su 26.34, whose Sanskrit is only संस्कारः करणं मतम् ('saṁskāra is held to be karaṇa, processing'). Membership in the parādi list rests on sentence (a), not on the definition. In (b), 'production of other attributes' follows the Vi.1.22 gloss and 'by admixture' is Kaviratna's own addition: it is his word for saṁyoga in the neighbouring definition ('Admixture or combination is Samyoga') and is not in the Sanskrit of 26.34.
classical.quote: They are Paratwa, Aparatwa, Yukti, Sankhyā, Samyoga, Vibhāga, Prithaktwa, Parimāna, Sanskāra, and Abhyāsa. These are regarded as means for the success of treatment. ... Samskāra is the production of other attributes by admixture.

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Vi.1.22 uses karaṇa as the āyatana and saṁskāra as its definition; Ca.Su.26.34 reverses the direction (saṁskāraḥ karaṇaṁ matam). The two are near-synonyms in Charaka, not two steps.
Combination of two or more substances (Ca.Vi.1.22); saṁskāra changes one substance's qualities. Kaviratna's 'by admixture' blurs this line.
Purification of a toxic drug is one kind of saṁskāra (modern literature: Datura, aconite, Nerium), not the whole concept.
WHO ITA-9.4.24 and following; a social-ritual sense that shares the word.
Kaviratna's note (OCR line 46592) glosses 'Samskaras in this life, meaning tendencies or inclinations' — the yoga/darshana sense.
Impregnation/levigation; listed in Ca.Vi.1.22 as one of the means by which saṁskāra works, not a synonym.

mistranslations.why: Narrows saṁskāra to śodhana; the Vi.1.22 list includes cooking, churning, ageing, perfuming and vessel effects, which purify nothing.
Kaviratna's word; carries alchemical connotations of changing substance, whereas the text says only that qualities are conferred (guṇāntarādhāna).

classical.verse: Standard 1.22 (saṁyoga clause); Kaviratna's printed number OCR-damaged ('t^')
classical.establishes: Definition (saṁhatībhāva of two or more dravyas) plus the doctrine that combination produces a viśeṣa the components lack, with the honey-ghee and honey-fish-milk examples. Sanskrit as retrieved: संयोगः पुनर्द्वयोर्बहूनां वा द्रव्याणां संहतीभावः|| (within ||२२||, https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Rasa_Vimana). The examples' Sanskrit was not retrieved this session.
classical.quote: Samyoga is the state of union of two or more articles. This produces especial consequences which the articles, existing separately, do not produce. As examples may be cited the union of honey and ghee, or of honey, fish, and milk.

classical.establishes: Saṁyoga as a parādi guṇa, threefold (dvandva-, sarva-, eka-karmaja) and anitya (impermanent). Sanskrit as retrieved: सङ्ख्या स्याद्गणितं, योगः सह संयोग उच्यते| द्रव्याणां द्वन्द्वसर्वैककर्मजोऽनित्य एव च||३२|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya). Kaviratna's 'hostile' for dvandva and 'operation or effects' for karma are interpretive.
classical.quote: Admixture or combination is Samyoga. Samyoga may be of three kinds : the combination which arises from the union of the operation or effects of two hostile objects ; that which arises from the union of the operation or effects of many objects ; and that which arises from the union of the operation or effects of two separate objects (not particularly related to each other). Such combinations are not enduring.

distinguishFrom.why: Processing of one substance vs combination of several (both are Vi.1 āyatanas and parādi guṇas).
Mere proximity/contact; Kaviratna's note at OCR line 42422 says a case 'is not samyoga or union. It is only sannikarsha'.
WHO ITA-1.9.6.1 'Inherence ... an intimate and constant relation'; saṁyoga is by definition anitya (Ca.Su.26.32).
The harmful subtype in viruddha-āhāra doctrine; saṁyoga itself is neutral and can be beneficial (honey + ghee in unequal measure).
Kaviratna's note (OCR 44337-44339) on 'ashtmyarthasamyogah' shows saṁyoga also means sense-object contact in the trividha-hetu context (asātmyendriyārtha-saṁyoga).
Division/disjunction, its listed counterpart in the parādi series (Ca.Su.26.33).

mistranslations.why: Modern pharmacology term; Ca.Vi.1.22 says only that combination yields a viśeṣa, which may be harmful (fish + milk) as well as helpful.
Suggests a physical blend; saṁyoga covers co-ingestion and sense-object contact too (asātmyendriyārtha-saṁyoga).
Kaviratna at Su.26 his 47; dvandva is 'pair', not 'enemies'.

openQuestions: Retrieve the Sanskrit of the honey-ghee and honey-fish-milk examples in Vi.1.22.

classical.establishes: Defines sañcaya as doshas accumulating IN THEIR OWN SEATS (doṣasthānāni), lists its signs, and marks it the first kriyākāla. Also attests the variant चय (caya) inside the compound चयकारणविद्वेष — aversion to the causes of accumulation.
classical.quote: एतानि खलु दोषस्थानानि; एषु सञ्चीयन्ते [१३] दोषाः । प्राक् सञ्चयहेतुरुक्तः । तत्र सञ्चितानां खलु दोषाणां स्तब्धपूर्णकोष्ठता पीतावभासता मन्दोष्मता चाङ्गानां गौरवमालस्यं चयकारणविद्वेषश्चेति लिङ्गानि भवन्ति । तत्र प्रथमः क्रियाकालः ॥१८॥

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for the sañcaya passage, including the unmatched parentheses that are in the retrieved text. Verse number assigned by content match to the Sanskrit; not printed on the page.
classical.quote: These are the locations of the deranged humours, which are respectively accumulated in them on account of the aforesaid causes. The deranged humours exhibit such symptoms as, fullness and stuffedness of the abdomen, or of any of the viscera (due to the action of the deranged Vayu); yellowness of the affected part (due to the action of the deranged Pitta, and diminution of the bodily heat, heaviness of the limbs, and a sense of languor (due to the action of the diseased Kapha), and a natural repugnance for causes (factors) which lead to their respective aggravations or accumulations. The medical treatment should be commenced as soon as the symptoms, peculiar to their accumulation, would become manifest.

classical.establishes: The therapeutic rationale for the stage: doshas removed at sañcaya do not reach the later stages; if they do, they become stronger. This is the verse that makes sañcaya the highest-value intervention window.
classical.quote: सञ्चयेऽपहृता दोषा लभन्ते नोत्तरा गतीः । ते तूत्तरासु गतिषु भवन्ति बलवत्तराः ॥३७॥

classical.chapter: Lesson III (Jwara / Treatment of Fever), as numbered in Kaviratna's translation
classical.establishes: Charaka uses accumulation-then-provocation as a SEASONAL sequence, not as a six-stage schema. Re-verified this session: the sentence sits inside LESSON III with the inline aphorism number 40 immediately following, and the boundary 'Thus ends Lesson Third, named Treatment of Fever' is present in the same document. Kaviratna's lesson/verse numbering may not match Chaukhamba editions.
classical.quote: The  phlegm,  accumulating  in  winter,  becomes  greatly  excited  in  the  season  of  spring  (coming  after  winter).  40

classical.chapter: Lesson II ('disparity of race' / Atulyagotriya), as numbered in Kaviratna's translation
classical.establishes: Charaka prescribes seasonal shodhana aimed precisely at accumulated doshas — the Charaka-side parallel to intervening at sañcaya, but framed by season rather than by stage. The inline number 44 is confirmed adjacent in the retrieved text, and the boundary 'Thus ends the second Lesson, called disparity of race' is present in the same document.
classical.quote: By 'removing  effectively  and  without  delay,  in  the  spring, the^faults  accumulated  in  winter,  in  the  ante-rainy  season  the faults  accumulated  in  summer,  and  in  the  autumn  the  faults accumulated  in  the  rainy  season,  one  never  gets  the  diseases that  are  especial  to  the  several  seasons.44

distinguishFrom.why: Vṛddhi is quantitative increase of a dosha or dhatu generally, with no implication about location or about being a stage in a sequence. Sañcaya is specifically increase WITHIN the dosha's own seat, at a stage where it has not yet overflowed. WHO builds the location constraint into its rendering of sañcaya (ITA-4.6.7) but not into vṛddhi.

Āma is undigested or immature metabolic residue from impaired agni; WHO gives it its own staging entry at ITA-4.6.2. Sañcaya is dosha piling up in its own seat. They can co-occur but are different entities, and 'accumulation of toxins' silently swaps one for the other.

Usually treated as a synonym — Su.Su. 21.18 uses चयकारण- alongside सञ्चीयन्ते, and easyayurveda writes 'Sanchaya or Chaya'. But caya is also the first member of Vagbhata's three-fold caya-kopa-praśama cycle, where it carries seasonal rather than six-stage meaning. Do not assume the two usages are interchangeable without checking context.
A general word for build-up or development of form; in Charaka's Indriyasthana it appears in the sense of bodily development, not dosha pathology.

mistranslations.why: Imports āma, which is a different concept with its own WHO term ID. The mula text says doshas accumulate in their own seats; it says nothing about toxins.

At sañcaya there is no disease. The text gives only non-specific signs (fullness, heaviness, languor, aversion to the causes) and the whole therapeutic point of the stage is that no disease has formed yet.
Borrows a Western pathological mechanism (vascular engorgement) that the source does not assert.

openQuestions: Whether any modern paper offers operational, measurable criteria for identifying sañcaya in a live patient.

Whether Charaka anywhere uses sañcaya as a named stage rather than as a seasonal descriptor — the Kaviratna volume retrieved does not contain the Sutrasthana or Nidanasthana, so absence there proves nothing.
Whether WHO intends ITA-4.6.7 (stage) and ITA-5.2.x (disorder) to be the same referent under two headings, or two distinct entities.

alternates: ghana (घन, often treated as synonym; see distinguishFrom)

classical.establishes: Sushruta's karma of sāndra: sthūla-making and bandhakāraka. Sanskrit as retrieved: दशैवान्यान् प्रवक्ष्यामि द्रवादींस्तान्निबोध मे| द्रवः प्रक्लेदनः, सान्द्रः स्थूलः स्याद्बन्धकारकः||५२०|| (https://www.easyayurveda.com/sushruta-samhitha-sutrasthana-46-annapana-vidhi-adhyaya-regimen-of-food-and-drinks/).
classical.quote: Now hear me describe the other ten properties of matter with their specific actions. Fluidity is moistening. Compactness is thickening and obstructive.

distinguishFrom.why: Paired opposite (Ca.Su.25.36 सान्द्रद्रव; Su.Su.46.520).
WHO ITA-7.1.11 'ghanaḥ' is a pharmaceutical form (solid extract), not the guna; textbooks sometimes use ghana as a synonym of sāndra.
Adjacent in the pārthiva list and in Kaviratna ('thick, gross'); Su.Su.46.520 says sāndra makes a thing sthūla, so they are cause and effect, not synonyms.
WHO's 'viscidity' for sāndra invites confusion with picchila (WHO 'Sliminess, murkiness').
Prameha subtypes (WHO ITA-5.41.5-6; Kaviratna's note 'Sandra is condensed'); the urine quality, not the drug guna.
In Ca.Su.22.13 the bṛṁhaṇa list has bahala ('dense, abundant') rather than sāndra; Kaviratna renders it 'exceedingly'.

mistranslations.why: Sāndra is a quality on a continuum with drava (Ca.Su.25.36), applied to thick liquids such as condensed urine; 'solid' is kaṭhina's territory.
WHO's secondary word; viscosity is closer to picchila. Sushruta defines sāndra by bulk-making and binding, not by flow resistance.

openQuestions: Whether Bhishagratna's 'compact' in Su.Su.41 corresponds to sāndra or ghana in the Sanskrit (word order not checked against a Sanskrit Su.41).
Any measured density/specific-gravity study linking to sāndra (a Zenodo record 11044307 surfaced in search; not retrieved).
