classical.establishes: saṅga as the second of the four signs of srotodushti, in the nominative singular saṅgaḥ (sandhi form saṅgo before vā).
classical.quote: अतिप्रवृत्तिः सङ्गो वा सिराणां ग्रन्थयोऽपि वा| विमार्गगमनं चापि स्रोतसां दुष्टिलक्षणम्||२४||

classical.establishes: The independent Sushrutan locus for saṅga, and the single most important verse in this whole term-set: aggravated doshas coursing through the body produce disease AT THE PLACE WHERE THEY ARE ARRESTED (yatra saṅgaḥ) BECAUSE OF A DEFECT IN THE CHANNEL (khavaiguṇyāt). This verse links saṅga and khavaiguṇya in one sentence and is the only verified mula occurrence of khavaiguṇya I found.
classical.quote: कुपितानां हि दोषाणां शरीरे परिधावताम् | यत्र सङ्गः खवैगुण्याद्व्याधिस्तत्रोपजायते ||१०||

classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of Su.Su.24/10. 'Incarcerated' renders saṅgaḥ; 'owing to an obstruction in their natural passage' is his rendering of khavaiguṇyāt, which is a paraphrase rather than a translation of that word.
classical.quote: The deranged and aggravated humours, freely coursing through the body, give rise to a disease at the place in which they are incarcerated owing to an obstruction in their natural passage.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ISTA ITA-4.8.1 lists srotorodhaḥ as its own entry, 'Obstructive pathology', described as complete or partial obstruction leading to malfunction. saṅga is the sign-name within Charaka's four-fold scheme; srotorodha is the general pathological state. They are used interchangeably in practice and WHO's own descriptions barely differ, which is worth flagging rather than resolving.

Occlusion of vata's pathway by another dosha or dhatu, a vata-vyadhi mechanism. It is a cause of obstruction from OUTSIDE the channel's contents, whereas saṅga names the arrest of flow itself. Secondary literature routinely lists them side by side as if parallel.
Clinical entities characterised by retention. They are diseases; saṅga is a pathophysiological sign that may underlie several of them.

distinguishFrom.term: saṅga in its ordinary Sanskrit sense
distinguishFrom.why: Outside medicine saṅga means attachment, clinging, association (a central term in the Gita and in Yoga). A naive dictionary lookup will return that sense. The medical sense is 'sticking, arrest, stasis of flow'.

mistranslations.why: Common and defensible in some contexts but imports a Chinese-medicine flavour (qi/blood stagnation) with different diagnostic criteria and different treatment logic. WHO's 'obstruction with restriction of movement' is more faithful.

Appears in Kaviratna's own rendering but has no counterpart in the received Sanskrit of Ca.Vi.5/24. Attenuation (narrowing/thinning) is close to the opposite of the sirā-granthi sign. Do not carry it forward as a gloss without resolving the recension question.
A single clinical instance (purishavaha saṅga), frequently offered as though it were the definition. Saṅga applies to any of the thirteen channels.
The non-medical Sanskrit sense, wrong here.

openQuestions: Whether Charaka or his commentators anywhere distinguish saṅga from srotorodha, or whether srotorodha is a later coinage.
Whether the 'collateral pathway' consequence WHO attaches to saṅga has a classical source or is an editorial gloss.
The Kaviratna 'attenuation' variant, as above.

renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda
renderings.locator: searched; the compound saptadhātu is not a headword
renderings.assessment: Significant negative finding. WHO ISTA has no entry for the compound. The number is carried inside the definition of dhātuḥ at ITA-2.2.1, whose first sentence begins 'The seven fundamental structural components of the body'. So WHO treats sevenness as part of the definition of dhātu rather than as a term.
renderings.licenceNote: this project's own paraphrase, not the source's words

renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda
renderings.locator: ITA-2.2.1, within the description of dhātuḥ
renderings.assessment: Not a headword, a phrase inside a definition. Recorded because it is the nearest thing WHO offers and because the sub-entries ITA-2.2.4 to ITA-2.2.18 are each numbered 'the first/second/.../seventh of the seven fundamental structural components'.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.english: their seven respective fires / the seven 'dhatus'
renderings.sourceName: Charaka Samhita, tr. Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (1896-1913)
renderings.assessment: Kaviratna never compounds the term. He writes 'the seven dhatus', and his two parenthetical enumerations of what those seven are do not agree with each other.
renderings.licenceNote: Kaviratna's Charaka Samhita, 1896-1913

renderings.english: the six remaining fundamental principles of the body
renderings.sourceName: Sushruta Samhita, tr. Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916)
renderings.assessment: Bhishagratna counts from rasa outward: rasa plus six others. He too never uses a compound.
renderings.licenceNote: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Samhita, 1907-1916

renderings.sourceName: Common English-language textbook usage
renderings.assessment: The standard modern rendering. Carries the same 'tissue' problem as dhātu itself, plus a count the sources do not consistently support.
renderings.licenceNote: this project's own paraphrase, not the source's words

renderings.sourceName: Rasashastra usage
renderings.assessment: An entirely separate referent for the same compound: gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, iron and a seventh variously given. WHO ISTA's metals list (7.2.5) covers these individually. Recorded here as a disambiguation, not as a verified WHO rendering of the compound.
renderings.licenceNote: this project's own paraphrase, not the source's words

classical.establishes: The count of seven, tied to seven fires. Also the clearest evidence of translator drift: this parenthetical lists adeps and marrow before bones, while the chain Kaviratna translates two lines later runs flesh-adeps-bone-marrow-seed.
classical.quote: They who sustain the body, viz., the 'dhatus' (i. e., 'Rasa' or juice, blood, flesh, adeps, marrow, bones, and vital seed), are cooked by their seven respective fires.

classical.establishes: The canonical order of the seven in the Sanskrit, with its verse number: rasa, rakta, mamsa, medas, asthi, majja, shukra. This is the single most citable verse for the sequence.
classical.quote: रसाद्रक्तं ततो मांसं मांसान्मेदः प्रजायते । मेदसोऽस्थि ततो मज्जा मज्ज्ञः शुक्रं तु जायते ॥१०॥

classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of the same verse. Note Bhishagratna renders medas as 'fat' and does not name rasa as the first member, beginning instead with 'chyle'.
classical.quote: The chyle produces blood. From blood is formed flesh. From flesh originates fat which gives rise to bones. From bones originate marrow, which, in its turn, germinates semen.

classical.establishes: That the count is not uniformly seven. Here Charaka's list runs to eight, closing with ojas. Kaviratna's own footnote at Sutrasthana Lesson XXVII states the order as 'fluids, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, vital seed, and Ojas' - eight again.
classical.quote: From, however, that juice which springs from food grow the fluids, blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, vital seed, and that which has been called Ojas

classical.establishes: A third, internally inconsistent enumeration in the same translation: seven members, but medas is dropped and ojas included. Strong evidence that Kaviratna's parenthetical lists are his own gloss and not reliable as the text's enumeration.
classical.quote: the seven 'dhatus' (juice, blood, flesh, bones, marrow, semen, and ojas), grow.

distinguishFrom.why: The same compound names the seven medicinal metals. Any index keyed on the Sanskrit will collide. WHO ISTA flags the ambiguity on dhātuḥ but has no entry for the compound at all, in either sense.
Three regulatory factors, not seven structural constituents. Paired with saptadhātu and trimala in the standard triad of body constituents but categorically different.
The three excreta. Formed as the kiṭṭa fraction of dhātu formation, so downstream of the seven rather than parallel to them.
Five ontological elements. The dhātus are said to be pāñcabhautika (made of the five), so the two are levels of description, not alternatives.
The eight-member enumeration that appears when ojas is counted. Attested in Kaviratna's Charaka as quoted above and in Bhishagratna's footnote to Su.Su.14. Modern teaching almost never mentions it.

mistranslations.why: Two problems compounded. 'Tissue' imports histology, and 'seven' is stated as settled when the retrieved public-domain translations give eight at least three times.

mistranslations.rendering: the seven dhatus, as though the compound were a technical term in the samhitas
mistranslations.why: Searched in full text: the strings 'saptadhatu', 'sapta-dhatu' and 'sapta dhatu' occur zero times across Kaviratna's Charaka and both Bhishagratna Sushruta volumes. The texts say 'seven dhatus'; the compound is later usage. Citing saptadhātu to a samhita verse would be a fabrication.
Correct for the Rasashastra homonym only.

openQuestions: Where and when the compound saptadhātu first appears as a fixed technical term is not established. It is absent from both public-domain samhita translations; the commentaries and the Laghu Trayi were not searched.

Whether the eight-member lists in Charaka Sutrasthana 28 and the phthisis chapter reflect the mula or Kaviratna's glossing could not be settled without a Sanskrit Charaka. Both possibilities are live and they have different consequences for the lexicon.
Why the phthisis-chapter list omits medas is unexplained by anything retrieved.

renderings.assessment: His footnote is unusually candid: 'This long periphrasis becomes inconvenient in rendering such short compounds as "Twak-sara", "Rakta-sara," &c.'

classical.establishes: Eight sāras in order: tvak, rakta, māṁsa, medas, asthi, majjā, śukra, sattva. The stated purpose is knowing the measure of strength.
classical.quote: sārataścēti sārāṇyaṣṭau puruṣāṇāṁ balamānaviśēṣajñānārthamupadiśyantē; tadyathā- tvagraktamāṁsamēdō'sthimajjaśukrasattvānīti||102||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Vi 8/102. 'i.' is an OCR artefact of '1.'.
classical.quote: Next, as to examination according to Sara (predominating essence or element) : there are eight Saras of human beings. We shall lay down instructions about them for exact knowledge of the measure of one's strength. They are i. skin, 2. blood, 3. flesh, 4. fat, 5. bones, 6. marrow, 7. vital seed, and 8. mind,

classical.establishes: Why sāra is examined at all: a physician must not infer strength from body size, the proof being the ant that carries loads far beyond its bulk. The classical warning against exactly the somatotype reading that dominates popular prakṛti writing.
classical.quote: dr̥śyantē hyalpaśarīrāḥ kr̥śāścaikē balavantaḥ; tatra pipīlikābhāraharaṇavat siddhiḥ| ataśca sārataḥ parīkṣētētyuktam||115||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for the ant argument. 'btearing' is an OCR artefact.
classical.quote: It is, indeed, seen that men whose bodies are of small dimensions or whose bodies are lean are still possessed of strength. In this connection, a proof is offered by ants (which are very diminutive creatures) btearing away large weights.

classical.establishes: Sushruta treats sāra in the clinical-examination chapter, runs the list in reverse of Charaka's order, and adds a ranking Charaka does not make: 'In respect of worldly success and longevity, men of each of the aforesaid types should be successively judged inferior to men belonging to the one preceding it'. No verse numbers on the retrieved page.
classical.quote: Now we shall describe the characteristic traits of the different preponderant principles ( Sara ) or temperaments of the human organism.

distinguishFrom.why: Among the twenty gurvādi guṇas, sara means mobile, the opposite of sthira. A dravyaguṇa passage using sara means this.

distinguishFrom.term: sāra as extract or essence of a drug
distinguishFrom.why: Standard in rasaśāstra and bhaiṣajya-kalpanā; WHO carries sāra-viṣaḥ as a separate poison headword on the same stem.
A further pharmacological sense (sāraka, sraṁsana family), distinct from all the above.
The sāras are named after the dhātus, but sāra grades a dhātu's excellence, not its presence. A person can have all seven dhātus and be asāra.
Consecutive, separate items in Vi 8; prakṛti sorts by doṣa, sāra by tissue.
Vi 8/102 says sāra is taught in order to know bala. It is an indicator of strength, not strength itself.
WHO makes sarva-sāra and oja-sāra synonyms, but ojas has its own entry as a substance; equating them goes beyond the retrieved Charaka text.

mistranslations.why: Not wrong, but it loses the gradable character of sāra, which the text grades pravara, madhya and asāra.
A different Ayurvedic term with the same spelling once diacritics are dropped; a search of an unmarked corpus returns both.
The eight sāras are not a typology of body shape, and Vi 8/115 is an explicit argument against reading strength from shape.
Bhishagratna's choice; it makes sāra indistinguishable from prakṛti in English, which is what the examination sequence exists to keep apart.

openQuestions: Is there any modern instrument for sāra assessment? None found.
Sushruta ranks the sāras hierarchically and Charaka does not. Which commentators discuss that?

renderings.english: Agreeable to nature or natural constitution
renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.assessment: Full description continues: 'excellence or abundance of suitable qualities: food that is fully compatible with the individual and which is completely digested and accepted by the body.' WHO places sātmya in the DIETETICS chapter and defines it as a property of food, narrowing a term the samhitas also apply to conduct, place and season.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.assessment: An extraordinary choice. In ordinary English 'homologation' means official certification of a product; it appears to be reaching for 'homologous'. The most opaque rendering in the WHO ten-domain list, and it should not be reproduced without comment.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.english: power of assimilation … assimilable (i. e., suitable to the constitution)
renderings.sourceName: Charaka Samhita, tr. Kaviratna (1896-1913)
renderings.assessment: His heading for Vi 8/118.
renderings.licenceNote: Kaviratna's Charaka Samhita, 1896-1913

renderings.sourceName: Charaka Samhita, tr. Kaviratna (1896-1913)
renderings.assessment: The clearest exposition in any public-domain English: 'A certain article is said to be "satmya" with regard to one, and "asatmya" with regard to another. Continued or habitual use without injury is the basis of "satmyata." … Habitual use may make even a virulent poison "satmya" or agreeable to a person.'
renderings.licenceNote: Kaviratna's Charaka Samhita, 1896-1913

renderings.sourceName: Indian Ayurvedic college usage
renderings.assessment: 'Wholesome' is the standard rendering of hita, not of sātmya — a conflation, not a translation.
renderings.licenceNote: this project's own paraphrase, not the source's words

classical.establishes: The definition: sātmya is that which, used continuously, agrees. The prognostic grading is by breadth of tolerance — those to whom ghee, milk, oil, meat juice and all rasas are sātmya are strong and long-lived; those habituated to dry food and a single rasa are weak and short-lived. The criterion is variety tolerated, not any particular food.
classical.quote: sātmyataścēti sātmyaṁ nāma tadyat sātatyēnōpasēvyamānamupaśētē| tatra yē ghr̥takṣīratailamāṁsarasasātmyāḥ sarvarasasātmyāśca tē balavantaḥ klēśasahāścirajīvinaśca bhavanti, rūkṣasātmyāḥ punarēkarasasātmyāśca yē tē prāyēṇālpabalā alpaklēśasahā alpāyuṣō'lpasādhanāśca bhavanti||118||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Vi 8/118. Kaviratna writes 'all the five tastes' where the Sanskrit has sarvarasa; whether his exemplar read five or he erred is not established, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than smoothed.
classical.quote: Next, as to examination (of the patient) as regards power of assimilation. That is called assimilable (i. e., suitable to the constitution) which, indulged habitually, agrees with the constitution. In this connection, (it should be said that) those persons with whom ghee, milk, oil, juice of flesh, and all the five tastes, agree in consequence of habitual use, are endued with strength, capable of bearing hardship, and long-lived.

classical.establishes: The relativity-of-wholesomeness argument underlying sātmya. Recorded as adjacent and relevant, NOT as a definition: the chapter's own term is hita and the retrieved page does not use sātmya in this passage.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: Hita is what is beneficial, an objective property. Sātmya is what agrees with THIS person through habituation. A thing can be sātmya and not hita — Kaviratna makes the point with poison.
What is prescribed as suiting the disease pathway. Sātmya precedes and constrains it: a physician cannot prescribe against long-established sātmya without consequence.
The habituation subtype, often used loosely as though it were the whole of sātmya.
Sātmya of place and season, both silently dropped by WHO's food-only definition.
Not merely the negation. At Vimana 6/6 the vitiating cause is asātmyendriyārthasaṁyoga, unsuitable contact of sense with object — asātmya operating outside diet altogether.
Both individual-specific baselines, but prakṛti is fixed at conception while sātmya is acquired and can be deliberately changed, which is the point of the pādāṃśika krama (WHO ITA-10.2.5).

mistranslations.why: WHO's own word at ITA-4.7.5. In English it denotes regulatory certification; nothing in Vi 8/118 concerns approval.
That is hita. Using it for sātmya erases the individual-and-habit dependence that is the term's entire content.
Closer, but modern 'tolerance' suggests merely enduring. Vi 8/118 grades people by how WIDE their sātmya is and treats breadth as a marker of strength and longevity.
An immunological reading with no classical warrant; asātmya includes unsuitable sensory contact and season.

openQuestions: Does Kaviratna's exemplar really read 'five tastes' at Vi 8/118 where the Trikamji text reads sarvarasa, or is it a translator's slip?
Why does WHO confine sātmya to food when the samhitas apply it to place, season and sense-contact?

renderings.assessment: The clinical sense, the one the ten-fold examination actually uses.

renderings.assessment: Keeps the Sanskrit as an adjective and supplies a trait list rather than a single English word.

classical.establishes: In the ten-fold examination sattva IS manas, graded only pravara/madhya/avara by strength. Not the guṇa, not a personality type. The most load-bearing quote in this term group.
classical.quote: sattvataścēti sattvamucyatē manaḥ| taccharīrasya tantrakamātmasaṁyōgāt| tat trividhaṁ balabhēdēna- pravaraṁ, madhyam, avaraṁ cēti||119||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Vi 8/119. The clinical criterion follows: the avara-sattva patient cannot be steadied by himself or others and collapses at the sight of blood or flesh.
classical.quote: Next, as to examination (of the patient) in respect of sattwa or mind (or mental energy) : the mind is known by the name of sattwa. It is the ruler of the body, owing to its connection with the soul (or self). It is of three kinds, according to difference of strength, viz., superior, middling, and inferior.

classical.establishes: sattva is the eighth of the eight sāras, alongside the seven dhātus — a third technical use of the word inside one chapter.
classical.quote: sārataścēti sārāṇyaṣṭau puruṣāṇāṁ balamānaviśēṣajñānārthamupadiśyantē; tadyathā- tvagraktamāṁsamēdō'sthimajjaśukrasattvānīti||102||

classical.establishes: Opens the sixteen sattva-bheda at Sharirasthana 4/36 with the mutual-dependence formula.
classical.quote: शरीरं ह्यपि सत्त्वमनुविधीयते, सत्त्वं च शरीरम्||३६||

classical.establishes: The guṇa/temperament sense in Sushruta with its trait list; verse 19 as printed on the retrieved page.
classical.quote: An absence of all killing or hostile propensities, a judicious regimen of diet, forbearance, truthfulness, piety, a belief in God, spiritual knowledge, intellect, a good retentive memory, comprehension, and the doing of good deeds irrespective of consequences, are the qualities which grace the mind of a person of a Sattvika temperament .

classical.establishes: The six categories as Charaka gives them, in Charaka's order (sāmānya, viśeṣa, guṇa, dravya, karma, samavāya), and — crucially — framed as what the sages SAW with the eye of knowledge, i.e. as the content of medical insight, not as an imported metaphysics. Note the word ṣaṭpadārtha does not occur in the verse.
classical.quote: maharṣayaste dadṛśuryathāvajjñānacakṣuṣā / sāmānyaṃ ca viśeṣaṃ ca guṇān dravyāṇi karma ca // car_1,1.28 // samavāyaṃ ca tajjñātvā tantroktaṃ vidhimāsthitāḥ / lebhire paramaṃ śarma jīvitaṃ cāpyanitvaram // car_1,1.29

classical.text: Cakrapāṇidatta, Āyurvedadīpikā on Charaka Samhita Sūtrasthāna 1.28
classical.establishes: That the commentator explicitly counts them as SIX PADĀRTHAS ('ṣaṇṇāṃ padārthānāṃ') and defers their definition to the later passage. This is the textual warrant for treating ṣaṭpadārtha as a term at all, since the mūla verse does not use the word.
classical.quote: eṣāṃ cottaratra lakṣaṇaṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ padārthānāṃ viśvarūpāṇāṃ bhaviṣyati tenaitat tatraiva vyākaraṇīyam

classical.establishes: A complete, lawful English rendering of the six that shares not one word with WHO's rendering of the same six.
classical.quote: Those great Rishis (then) beheld duly, with the eye of knowledge, similarities, dissimilarities, properties, objects, and operations, as also compositions. Knowing these, and conforming to the ordinances of that Science, they obtained great felicity and even immortal life.

distinguishFrom.why: Same six members, DIFFERENT ORDER and different doctrinal role. Kaṇāda enumerates dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, samavāya; Charaka leads with sāmānya and viśeṣa because his use of them is therapeutic (like increases like), not ontological. Calling Charaka's list 'the Vaiśeṣika categories' obscures exactly the thing that makes it medical.

Later Vaiśeṣika adds abhāva as a seventh category. Charaka has six. A reader meeting 'the seven padārthas' in a Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika text and 'the six' in Ayurveda is not meeting a contradiction but two historical stages.

Su. Uttara 65 lists Padārtha as the THIRD of the 32 tantrayuktis, defined by Bhishagratna as 'the meaning implied by a word or an aphorism' — a hermeneutic device, not an ontological category. Two entirely different technical uses of one word, both inside Ayurveda.
WHO ITA-1.8.3.4, 'Object of knowledge, the object of investigation'. Overlapping but distinct: prameya is what enquiry is ABOUT, padārtha is what exists and is nameable.
Five elements, not six categories. The bhūtas are members of dravya, one of the six; the two schemes are constantly conflated in popular writing.

mistranslations.why: Dravya (substance) is ONE of the six. Rendering the whole set as 'substances' makes the list incoherent — sāmānya is not a substance.
Confuses ṣaṭpadārtha with pañcamahābhūta, and there are six of one and five of the other.
Vague to the point of uselessness, and it hides the fact that the list is an ontology with a specific therapeutic payoff (sāmānya increases, viśeṣa decreases).
Seen in low-quality secondary sources; no relation whatever.

openQuestions: Whether Charaka's ordering (sāmānya/viśeṣa first) is deliberate doctrine or inherited from a pre-Vaiśeṣika source — worth checking Chakrapāṇi's fuller comment at Sū. 1.44-52.
Whether any classical Ayurvedic text uses the compound ṣaṭpadārtha itself, as opposed to the count 'ṣaṇṇāṃ padārthānām' in the commentary. Not established.
The relation of Charaka's samavāya definition (co-inherence of dravya and guṇa) to Vaiśeṣika samavāya, which is a broader relation covering whole/part and universal/particular.

classical.establishes: Five causes by which malas move FROM koṣṭha TO śākhā: exercise, sharpness of heat, non-observance of the wholesome, and the swiftness of vāyu. Establishes śākhā and koṣṭha as a functional pair, not merely two of three sites.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.establishes: The return movement: by increase, liquefaction, ripening, clearing of the channel-mouths and restraint of vāyu, malas leave śākhā and go to koṣṭha. This is the verse that underwrites the whole of pre-purificatory therapy, and it is why śākhā cannot be translated as 'limbs'.
classical.quote: vṛddhyā viṣyandanāt pākāt srotomukhaviśodhanāt / śākhā muktvā malāḥ koṣṭhaṃ yānti vāyośca nigrahāt

distinguishFrom.why: The same word, and the sense WHO ISTA standardises (ITA-3.1.23). In CS Sū. 11.48 it denotes a tissue class (rakta onward plus tvak), which is present throughout the body including the trunk. Using the limb sense in a pathology context makes nonsense of śākhāgata doṣa.
Its paired opposite. Doṣas move between them in both directions (CS Sū. 28.31 and 28.33); a therapy that works on one is chosen precisely because the doṣa is in the other.

Śākhā in the rogamārga sense is a COLLECTION of dhātus plus skin, considered as a site. A dhātu is a constituent. Saying 'the disease is in rasa dhātu' and 'the disease is in śākhā' are claims at different levels.
Skin is one member of śākhā, not a synonym for it; bāhya ('external') is the rogamārga's epithet, not the compartment's name.
Unrelated homonym, separately standardised by WHO at ITA-1.5.3. Text searches for 'śākhā' will return both.

mistranslations.why: Correct for the anatomical homonym, wrong for the rogamārga. CS Sū. 11.48 defines śākhā by tissue (rakta and other dhātus, skin), and disorders Charaka assigns to it include skin lesions and swellings that are not limb-confined.
The literal etymology. Kaviratna reports the commentator's plant analogy and then records that 'The analogy, however, is not obvious' — a translated 'branch' conveys nothing clinical.

Śākhā includes asthi and majjā per Kaviratna's own footnote gloss ('it includes flesh, marrow, fat, bones, and seminal fluid'), so 'superficial' is wrong on its face — though note asthi also figures in the madhyama mārga, which is a real tension in the text.
Tvak is one item in the list, mentioned last and with 'ca'.

openQuestions: The apparent overlap: asthi appears within śākhā (as one of 'rakta and the rest of the dhātus') and also within the madhyama rogamārga as asthi-sandhi. How the commentators resolve this was not checked.
Whether any classical text uses śākhā in the rogamārga sense outside Charaka.
Whether WHO ISTA's omission of the pathological sense of śākhā was deliberate.

distinguishFrom.why: Expels doṣas from the body (AH Su. 14.5); śamana settles them in place. Charaka Su. 16.20 makes the recurrence claim that underlies the contrast.
In AH Su. 14.4 both śodhana and śamana are subtypes of laṅghana; in Charaka Su. 22 laṅghana is itself one of six upakramas, so the hierarchy differs between the two texts.
Synonym in Charaka's chikitsā-synonym list (Chi. 1.1, Kaviratna footnote 'alleviation'); NIA 2011 lists it separately as 'palliative therapeutics'.
Modern palliation implies non-curative, end-of-life care; śamana is a curative strategy for doṣas without expulsion.
Two of the seven śamana methods in AH Su. 14.6; not synonyms for śamana.

mistranslations.why: The most common rendering, but 'palliative' in English medicine means symptom relief without cure; śamana is held to resolve the doṣic state.
Implies suppression of symptoms with later rebound; the Sanskrit (śama = calming/equalizing) does not.
Imports surgical vs conservative dichotomy; serviceable, but 'conservative' can also mean 'watchful waiting'.

classical.establishes: All four classes have manas and sharira as their adhishthana (seat). This is the verse that makes sharira function as a SEAT in Sushruta as well as a class name, and it is the root of the ambiguity the lexicon has to flag.

classical.quote: The Mind and the Body are the seats of the abovesaid distempers according as they are restricted to either of them, or affect both of them in unison.

classical.establishes: Charaka's two ashrayas of disease: sharira and sattva (mind). Together with Su.55's preceding verse (dvayāśrayāṇāṃ vyādhīnāṃ, Su.1/54) this is the Charaka anchor for the sharira/manas division of disease by seat.
classical.quote: शरीरं सत्त्वसञ्ज्ञं च व्याधीनामाश्रयो मतः| तथा सुखानां, योगस्तु सुखानां कारणं समः||५५|| / śarīraṁ sattvasañjñaṁ ca vyādhīnāmāśrayō mataḥ| tathā sukhānāṁ, yōgastu sukhānāṁ kāraṇaṁ samaḥ||55||

classical.establishes: The threefold somatic (agneya/saumya/vayavya) and twofold psychic (rajasa/tamasa) division. This is the verse behind WHO ISTA ITA-4.2.7 trividha-śārīrika-rogaḥ, although the verse itself does not use the word śārīrika.
classical.quote: अतस्त्रिविधा व्याधयः प्रादुर्भवन्ति- आग्नेयाः, सौम्याः,वायव्याश्च;-द्विविधाश्चापरे- राजसाः, तामसाश्च||४|| / atastrividhā vyādhayaḥ prādurbhavanti- āgnēyāḥ, saumyāḥ, vāyavyāśca; dvividhāścāparē- rājasāḥ, tāmasāśca||4||

classical.establishes: Quotable English for Cha.Ni.1/4. Kaviratna prints this as his aphorism 2; the verse number 4 is the modern one carried over from the verified Sanskrit.
classical.quote: From these arise three kinds of diseases, viz., those relating to Agni (heat), those relating to moon, and those relating to the wind. There are two other kinds of diseases, viz., those arising from the attribute of 'Rajas', and those from the attribute of 'Tamas.'

distinguishFrom.why: The complementary class by seat. Su.Su.1/26 and Cha.Su.1/55 both make sharira and manas the two seats, so this is the cleanest opposition of the seven terms. But Sushruta lists sharira and manasa as two of FOUR classes at 1/24 while also making both of them seats at 1/26, which is not a contradiction the texts resolve.

Charaka defines nija as śārīra-doṣa-samuttha, so nija is defined via sharira. Sushruta's sharira is defined by dosha-vaishamya, which is Charaka's nija. The two terms are close to coextensive in practice but belong to different classifications (cause vs seat) and should not be recorded as synonyms.
'Bodily' in the sense used in ethics and in kaya-chikitsa. Kaya in Ayurveda also carries the specific sense of agni/metabolism, so 'kayika roga' is not a safe substitute for sharirika roga.

WHO ISTA ITA-2.1.2 gives śārīrikadoṣa as a synonym of tridosha, i.e. sharirika there qualifies the DOSHAS, not the disease. The same adjective doing two jobs is a genuine retrieval hazard in any term index.

mistranslations.why: Reads in modern English as 'not psychological', importing a body/mind dualism that Su.Su.1/26 and Cha.Su.1/55 explicitly reject by allowing diseases that affect both seats 'in unison'. It is also the word Kaviratna used for nija, so it double-books.

A clinical term of art in Western psychiatry meaning 'with demonstrable physical pathology', opposed to 'functional'. Sharirika carries no such implication and the import smuggles in a contested Western distinction.

Sharirika is precisely NOT the psychosomatic category. Confusingly, WHO ISTA attaches 'including all psychosomatic diseases' to a different term, ādhyātmikarogaḥ (ITA-4.2.11), which increases the risk of this slip.

openQuestions: Is śārīrika (with the -ika suffix) attested as a disease-class term in the samhitas, or only śārīra? Every classical instance I retrieved uses śārīra (शारीराः, शारीरदोषसमुत्थः); śārīrika appears in WHO ISTA and modern usage. The headword form may be post-classical.
How do the commentators handle Sushruta listing sharira as a class at 1/24 and as one of two seats at 1/26?

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ITA-4.5.16 gives the English term 'Evolution or natural course of disease' and describes it as 'The sequence of events from etiology to manifestation of a disease, which is classified into six stages .' (Sanskrit column: samprāptiḥ, jātiḥ, āgatiḥ.) Same sequence, but named as pathogenesis. Kriyākāla names that sequence as a series of treatment opportunities. Treating the two as synonyms erases the kriyā (action) element, which is the whole point of Sushruta's term. WHO keeps them as separate term IDs.
The five-fold diagnostic set (nidana, purvarupa, rupa, upashaya, samprapti). Kriyakala is one axis inside it — it expands samprapti — not a parallel diagnostic pentad.

distinguishFrom.term: doṣa-caya / kopa / praśama (Vagbhata's three-fold seasonal scheme)
distinguishFrom.why: A three-member cycle tied to seasons, ending in spontaneous subsidence (praśama). The six-fold kriyakala has no praśama member and is not seasonal. Charaka and Vagbhata work mainly with the three-fold scheme; the six-fold list is Sushruta's.

mistranslations.why: Drops kriyā entirely. The compound names six times for ACTION, not six phases of an illness. Bhishagratna's 'occasion for medical treatment' is the rendering that keeps this; almost every modern source loses it.

mistranslations.rendering: 'Six stages of pathogenesis' used interchangeably with samprapti
mistranslations.why: Conflates the diagnostic description (samprapti) with the therapeutic-window framing (kriyakala). WHO ISTA keeps these as separate term IDs (ITA-4.5.16 vs ITA-4.6.6).

mistranslations.rendering: Presenting ṣaṭkriyākāla as a term used by Sushruta
mistranslations.why: In the retrieved Sanskrit of Sutrasthana 21.16-21.38 the text uses only kriyākāla with ordinals (prathamaḥ ... ṣaṣṭhaḥ). The compound ṣaṭkriyākāla appears in later usage, in WHO ISTA and in modern literature, but was not found in any mula verse retrieved.

openQuestions: Whether ṣaṭkriyākāla occurs anywhere in the Sushruta mula text or only in Dalhana's Nibandhasangraha and later works — still open.

Whether NAMASTE's Ayurveda Standardized Terminologies module carries kriyakala, and under what code. The portal is reachable but every path resolves to the same 60,493-byte homepage and the one form action found (ayurveda_morb_code_downexcel) returns a 302 with no body to an unauthenticated POST. Needs a logged-in human.

Whether ICD-11 TM2 represents kriyakala stages. TM2 (Chapter 26, Module 2, Ayurveda/Siddha/Unani) exists, but the ICD-11 browser serves only an SPA shell and its search endpoint 404s without a token. Since TM2 is a morbidity classification, stage entities are a priori unlikely, but this is unverified either way.
Whether the Devanagari orthography of the compound षट्क्रियाकाल can be confirmed from a clean source — see gathering notes.

classical.establishes: Śīta ('cooling') as a bṛṁhaṇa quality. Sanskrit as retrieved: गुरु शीतं मृदु स्निग्धं बहलं स्थूलपिच्छिलम्||१३|| प्रायो मन्दं स्थिरं श्लक्ष्णं द्रव्यं बृंहणमुच्यते| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Langhanabrimhaniya_Adhyaya). 'Vringhana' is OCR of Vrimhana.

classical.verse: Sanskrit 46.515 per the numbered text on easyayurveda.com; Bhishagratna prints no verse number (vol. 1 p. 567, 'Specific properties of matter')
classical.establishes: Sushruta's karma of śīta per the Sanskrit of Su Su 46.515: hlādana (pleasing), stambhana (styptic), and relieving mūrcchā (fainting), tṛṭ (thirst), sveda (sweating) and dāha (burning); uṣṇa is the reverse and especially pācana. Sanskrit as retrieved: ह्लादनः स्तम्भनः शीतो मूर्च्छातृट्स्वेददाहजित्| उष्णस्तद्विपरीतः स्यात्पाचनश्च विशेषतः||५१५|| (siva.sh 46/515; easyayurveda Su 46). The quoted English is Bhishagratna's rendering: his 'epileptic fits' stands where the Sanskrit has mūrcchā (fainting), and his 'suppuration in boils' is not in the verse, which says uṣṇa is pācana. The English is evidence of how Bhishagratna read the verse, not of a Sushruta claim about epilepsy.
classical.quote: Coldness — is pleasurable, exercises styptic virtues, alleviates epileptic fits, thirst and a burning sensation of the body, and arrests perspiration. Heat is the reverse in its action to coldness.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Sūtrasthāna 42.7, printed ॥ ७ ॥ in Suśrutasaṃhitā with Dalhaṇa's Nibandhasaṅgraha, ed. Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya, 2nd edn 1931, p. 166; Bhishagratna vol. 1 ch. XLII prints the same passage as an unnumbered paragraph beginning 'According to certain authorities'.
classical.establishes: A view Sushruta reports (kecid āhuḥ, 'some say'), not his own statement: that rasas are two-fold by the agnīṣomīya nature of the world, with madhura, tikta and kaṣāya saumya and therefore śīta, and kaṭu, amla and lavaṇa āgneya and therefore uṣṇa. Sanskrit: केचिदाहुः- अग्नीषोमीयत्वाज्जगतो रसा द्विविधाः- सौम्या आग्नेयाश्च । मधुरतिक्तकषायाः सौम्याः; कट्वम्ललवणा आग्नेयाः । ... सौम्याः शीताः, आग्नेया उष्णाः ॥७॥ (siva.sh Su Su 42.7).
classical.quote: According to certain authorities, there are only two kinds of tastes, owing to the two-fold (hot and cold) nature of the temperament of the world. Of these the tastes such as sweet, bitter and astringent are cold in their properties, while the pungent, acid and saline ones exercise fiery or heat making virtues.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: Paired opposite; Su.Su.46.515 'tadviparītaḥ'.

A mistranslation of sasneha; Pitta is uṣṇa (see snigdha record).

Not wrong, but 'cooling' is also used for śīta-vīrya; the lexicon should keep guna and vīrya apart.

Subtlety, also co-occurring in the ākāśa list and the bṛṁhaṇa list.

renderings.locator: ITA-2.1.3.6; printed p. 36 (PDF p. 54). Sanskrit term 'śleṣaka-kaphaḥ'. Description: 'Subtype of kapha seated in the joints which provides lubrication.'
renderings.assessment: WHO records ONLY lubrication. Both mūlas make the primary function SAṂŚLEṢA — binding/holding the joints together — with Suśruta explicitly adding that it opposes their separation. Cohesion, not lubrication, is the root sense of śliṣ-. WHO's gloss keeps the mechanical convenience and drops the structural claim.

classical.establishes: Seat = the joints (sandhi); function = holding them united, favouring the articulation, opposing separation. Cohesion is primary; lubrication is not mentioned.
classical.quote: The Shimeshakam:—The Kapham, situated in the joints, keeps them firmly united, protects their articulation and opposes their separation and disunion.

classical.establishes: The NAME 'śleṣaka' does not appear — the text says 'sandhi-sthaḥ śleṣmā' (the kapha situated in the joints) and gives the function as 'sarva-sandhi-saṃśleṣāt sarva-sandhi-anugrahaṃ karoti': by the binding-together of all joints it favours all joints. Saṃśleṣa (cohesion, adhesion), not lubrication. This sentence carries the ||१४|| verse marker, fixing the verse number for the whole kapha passage.

classical.establishes: Sandhi-saṃśleṣaṇa heads the list of kapha's six functions at Su.Sū. 15.4, confirming that joint-binding is treated as a primary kapha action. The five are not named here.

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa supplies the NAME with its etymology — called śleṣaka FROM sandhi-saṃśleṣa — and agrees with Suśruta on seat and function. Confirms the standard form is ŚLEṢAKA (not śleṣmaka, which is Bhishagratna's spelling).
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.term: sandhi (the joint) and the sandhi-gata doṣa concept
distinguishFrom.why: Sandhi is the anatomical site; śleṣaka is the kapha acting there. 'Sandhigata vāta' (the classical osteoarthritis analogue) is a vāta pathology AT the joint, not a śleṣaka disorder, though the two are constantly discussed together and conflated in clinical writing.

Kledana (moistening) and saṃśleṣa (binding) are distinct actions, but English 'lubricating'/'moistening' are near-synonyms and collapse them. PMID 42492167 glosses KLEDAKA as 'food lubrication' — which is śleṣaka's English label in WHO ISTA. A real, published crossover.
Suśruta gives avalambaka the job of trika-sandhāraṇa, holding the trika joint complex. That overlaps śleṣaka's general joint remit. The division is regional versus universal (sarva-sandhi).
Unctuousness is a general kapha quality and a therapeutic procedure. It is listed separately from sandhi-saṃśleṣaṇa in Su.Sū. 15.4, so oiliness is not the same as śleṣaka's binding action.
Joint pathology in Ayurveda is usually routed through asthi-dhātu-kṣaya and vāta, not primarily through śleṣaka. Attributing all joint disease to śleṣaka depletion is a modern simplification.

mistranslations.why: The near-universal modern equation and purely a hypothesis. Synovial fluid lubricates and nourishes cartilage; śleṣaka's stated action is to BIND the joint and oppose its separation, which is ligamentous/capsular work, not fluid work. No study measures synovial parameters against any śleṣaka assessment.

This is WHO ISTA's own English term and it silently drops the cohesion sense that both mūlas make primary. Bhishagratna's much older rendering ('keeps them firmly united... opposes their separation') is more faithful than the 2022 standard.

mistranslations.rendering: "Shleshmaka" used as the term's standard form
mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's spelling. It is confusable with śleṣmaka as a general word for kapha. Vāgbhaṭa's AH 12.17b-18a gives śleṣaka, which is the standard form and what WHO records.
Not a word. An OCR corruption in the Wikisource transcription of Bhishagratna's chapter 21. Recorded here only so that anyone who encounters it in a digitised corpus can identify it.

openQuestions: Does Dalhaṇa name this kapha in his gloss on Su.Sū. 21.14, and does he spell it śleṣaka or śleṣmaka?
Is the Wikisource 'Shimeshakam' present in the printed Bhishagratna edition or introduced in transcription? Check the archive.org scan.
Is there any imaging or biomechanical study that has attempted to operationalise śleṣaka kapha? PMID 22048545 and PMID 40215578 both invoke it without measuring it.
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 carries any śleṣaka-kapha entry — ICD-11 TM2 does have a 'Bone, joint and muscle disorders (SP00-SP4Z)' block, so this is the most likely of the ten to surface there.

classical.establishes: Shukra's functions run from courage and strength through to impregnation. The first two are constitutional, not reproductive, and are the reason the term cannot simply be read as 'semen'.
classical.quote: The semen gives rise to valour and courageousness, makes a man amorously disposed towards the female sex, increases his strength and amativeness, is the sole impregnating principle in the male organism, and is possessed of the virtue of being quickly emitted.

classical.establishes: Crucially, that rasa becomes śukra in men AND ārtava in women over one month (स्त्रीणां चार्तवं भवति). The mula parallels shukra with menstrual fluid rather than positing a female shukra here. Verified Sanskrit with verse number.
classical.quote: स खलु त्रीणि त्रीणि कलासहस्राणि पञ्चदश च कला एकैकस्मिन् धाताववतिष्ठते; एवं मासेन रसः शुक्रं स्त्रीणां चार्तवं भवति ॥१४॥

classical.establishes: The quotable English of the same verse, with Bhishagratna's bracketed gloss equating menstrual blood with the ovum - a nineteenth-century identification that should be flagged, not adopted.
classical.quote: The Rasa is successively transformed into each of the six remaining fundamental principles of the body, and continues in the shape of each for the period of three thousand and fifteen kalas [five days according to our modern computation]. Thus the Rasa is converted into semen, or into the menstrual blood (ovum) in women, in the course of a month.

classical.establishes: That shukra is held to be present potentially from childhood and to become manifest at puberty. Answers the text's own objection 'how is it that semen is not found in an infant?' and is decisive against reading shukra as simply the ejaculate.
classical.quote: As the perfume in a flower-bud lies latent in its early stage of growth but becomes patent only with the growth of its seed organs, so semen or catamenial blood lies in a potential state in a male or a female child, and appears with the growth of beards and mustaches, or with the enlargement of the breasts, uterus and vaginal canal and the appearance of pubic hair.

classical.establishes: The clinical presentations of śukra-kṣaya and śukra-vṛddhi, including the named entity shukrashmari (seminal calculus).
classical.quote: The loss or waste of semen is marked by pain in the penis and the testes, and by incapacity for sexual intercourse. In such cases the emission of semen but rarely happens, and is then perceptibly deficient in its quantity, the emitted matter consisting of a small quantity of semen marked with shreds of blood. ... An excess of semen in the body is marked by an excessive flow of that fluid and gives rise to the formation of gravels (concretions) in the bladder which are known as Shukrashmari.

classical.establishes: Shukra as terminal member of the chain and source of the foetus. Charaka's chain runs one step further than Sushruta's, to garbha.
classical.quote: from marrow is vital seed : from the vital seed arises the foetus.

classical.verse: 122 in Kaviratna's marginal numbering; sara section cited as Vi 8/102 ff by carakasamhitaonline
classical.establishes: Śukra-sāra as a constitutional type recognised by disposition and appearance, notably the 'milky' eyes that WHO ISTA also records at ITA-2.8.1.8 ('milky-looking eyes').
classical.quote: They who have the vital seed for the predominating element in their constitution become possessed of an amiable disposition, and amiable (or agreeable) looks. Their eyes seem to be full of milk.

classical.verse: translator's footnote to the prose section
classical.establishes: That shukra alone among the dhātus is held to produce no waste fraction, and that its subtle residue is taken by some authorities to be ojas as an eighth principle. Recorded as the translator's footnote, not as mula.
classical.quote: Semen, like gold a thousand times purified, casts off no dregs. Hence certain authorities hold albumen (protoplasmic matter) to be the eighth or the culminating principle of the body.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ISTA gives retas its own headword, 'Semen' (ITA-2.2.19), describing it as 'Part of seminal tissue' that 'generally refers to the ejaculate'. So in the standard's own scheme retas is the ejaculate and śukra is the wider dhātu. Translating śukra as 'semen' collides directly with this.
WHO gives 'Seed' (ITA-2.2.20), 'Male seed' (ITA-2.2.21) and 'Female seed' (ITA-2.2.22) as separate headwords. The generative factors are terminologically distinct from the dhātu.

Sushruta 14.14 parallels shukra in men with ārtava in women, and WHO classes ārtava as an upadhātu of rasa (ITA-2.3.3), not as a female shukra. Modern teaching often posits a female śukra; the mula verse retrieved here does not.

Bhishagratna's footnote derives the eighth principle from shukra's thin fraction. Ojas is the sāra of all seven dhātus per Sushruta Sutrasthana 15; whether it is also specifically shukra's product is the open question.
Virility (WHO ITA-2.2.23) and the therapeutic class that promotes it. Properties and treatments, not the dhātu.
A named disease of śukra excess (seminal calculus), not the dhātu.

mistranslations.why: WHO ISTA assigns 'Semen' to retas, a different headword. Śukra is said to exist latently in children of both sexes, to be formed from rasa over a month, to produce courage and strength, and to pervade the whole body in one of its two forms. None of that is semen.

Narrower still. Sperm is a cell type; śukra in the sources is a bodily principle with constitutional and affective functions. The equation is nonetheless how śukra disorders are measured in practice (PMID 32741654, 39157286).
WHO's own first headword, and better, but it still fixes on fluidity and reproduction and drops the pervasive whole-body form that WHO's description mentions in the same entry.

Bhishagratna's bracketed gloss equating menstrual blood with the ovum. A nineteenth-century error about reproductive biology embedded inside a quotable translation. Quote the sentence if needed; never adopt the gloss.

openQuestions: Whether women have śukra, or whether the female counterpart is ārtava, is stated differently by the sources retrieved here: Su.Su.14.14 parallels shukra with ārtava, WHO calls śukra 'reproductive fluids ... (semen, ovum)', and modern teaching posits a female śukra. Unresolved.

The relationship between śukra and ojas: Bhishagratna's footnote derives the eighth principle from shukra's thin fraction, Sushruta's chapter XV makes ojas the essence of all seven. Not reconciled anywhere retrieved.

No study operationalises śukra as anything other than semen parameters, and no study asks whether the classical śukra-kṣaya presentation (penile and testicular pain, blood-flecked ejaculate) identifies the same patients as oligospermia.
What the 'first form which pervades the entire body' in WHO's description corresponds to, and where WHO drew it from, could not be determined; WHO gives no source references per entry.

classical.establishes: Suśruta's root = BREASTS and testes — not penis. This is the textual hinge that connects śukravaha and stanyavaha (see that record): at Śā.9 Suśruta says the same pair of dhamanīs carries milk in women and śukra in men.
classical.quote: The two semen-carrying Srotas (ducts) have their roots in the breasts and the testes. An injury to any of them leads to loss of manhood, delayed emission of semen, or blood-streaked character of that fluid.

classical.establishes: Explains Suśruta's otherwise baffling 'roots in the breasts': one pair of upward-coursing dhamanīs is milk-carrying in women and śukra-carrying in men.
classical.quote: two of them (ducts), attached to the breasts of a woman, carry milk of her breasts, which, coursing through the breast of a man, convey his seminal fluid.

distinguishFrom.why: śukra is the seventh dhātu, present in both sexes in classical physiology; retas/semen is the ejaculate. WHO's 'structural components of reproduction' is an attempt to preserve this.
Suśruta enumerates both, giving the female reproductive channel separately; śukravaha in Suśruta is nevertheless rooted partly in the breasts, so the two are not simply male/female counterparts.
Su.Śā.9 makes them share a dhamanī pair — sex-differentiated function of one structure, not two structures.
Caraka roots śukravaha in vṛṣaṇa+śepha and mūtravaha in basti+vaṅkṣaṇa; the shared urethra tempts conflation.

mistranslations.why: Caraka's roots are male, but Suśruta's are breasts and testes, and śukra is classically present in both sexes. The gendered reading is Caraka-only.
WHO explicitly avoids it in the anatomy term. śukra is a dhātu, not an ejaculate.

classical.establishes: Charaka does NOT use the compound sirāgranthi. He writes 'sirāṇāṃ granthayaḥ', knots OF the siras, genitive plural plus plural noun. The single-word term sirāgranthi that WHO and every textbook use is a later compression. This is the single most important philological point in this record.
classical.quote: अतिप्रवृत्तिः सङ्गो वा सिराणां ग्रन्थयोऽपि वा|

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English for sirāṇāṃ granthayaḥ. Recorded verbatim; the word 'cystic' is his addition.
classical.quote: or cystic tumours,

classical.establishes: The disease entity. Note the Sanskrit reads 'granthiḥ sirājaḥ' — the granthi BORN OF the siras — not 'sirāgranthi'. Vata, deranged by exertion in a weak person, seizes the network of siras (sirā-pratāna), compresses, contracts and dries them, and quickly makes a raised round knot. Prognosis: painful and mobile = curable with difficulty; painless, fixed, large, or arising at a marma = to be rejected.
classical.quote: व्यायामजातैरबलस्य तैस्तैराक्षिप्य वायुर्हि सिराप्रतानम् | सम्पीड्य सङ्कोच्य विशोष्य चापि ग्रन्थिं करोत्युन्नतमाशु वृत्तम् ||८|| ग्रन्थिः सिराजः स तु कृच्छ्रसाध्यो भवेद्यदि स्यात् सरुजश्चलश्च | अरुक् स एवाप्यचलो महांश्च मर्मोत्थितश्चापि विवर्जनीयः ||९||

classical.verse: 7 (Bhishagratna's numbering; = 8-9 in the Sanskrit editions cited above)
classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of the disease description. NUMBERING WARNING: Bhishagratna prints this as verse 7 of Nidana XI; the Sanskrit editions number it 8-9. Do not assume the two numbering systems agree. Also note Bhishagratna hedges 'veins (Sira) or arteries', undoing his own usual sirā=vein equation.
classical.quote: The bodily Vayu in weak and enfeebled persons, deranged by over-fatiguing physical exercises, straining or exertion or by pressure, presses on, contracts, dries or draws up the ramifications of veins (Sira) or arteries (of the affected locality), and speedily gives rise to a raised knotty formation which is called a Sira-Granthi, In the event of its being shifting and slightly painful, it can be cured only with the greatest difficulty. Whereas a case in which the knotty formation is painless, fixed, large and situated at any of the vital parts of the body (Marmas), should be deemed incurable.

classical.establishes: The genus under which sirāja granthi sits. Sushruta's granthi series is vataja, pittaja, kaphaja, medaja, sirāja, raktaja — so the vascular one is one of six, not a category of its own.

distinguishFrom.why: The disease entity of Sushruta Nidana 11 and WHO ITA-5.49.6. sirāgranthi as used in Ca.Vi.5/24 and WHO ITA-4.8.8 is a channel-pathology SIGN. Same root, two different levels of the system, and WHO deliberately gives them separate codes. Most English writing merges them.

The genus: any round knotty elevated swelling, of which Sushruta names six types by causative dosha or dhatu. WHO ITA-5.49.1 'Nodular swelling, cyst'. Calling sirāgranthi simply 'granthi' loses the vascular specification.
Treated in the same Sushruta chapter but distinguished from granthi by being deep-rooted, slow-growing and non-suppurating (WHO ITA-5.50.1 'Tumour'). Granthi and arbuda are not interchangeable.
Also in Sushruta Nidana 11: a chain or crop of hard glossy painless nodules about the jaw, neck and axilla from meda and kapha. A string of granthis, not a sirā lesion.

Bhishagratna renders the Sushrutan text as 'veins (Sira) or arteries', leaving it open. Anyone building a vascular correlate must decide whether sirā here means veins specifically; Bhishagratna himself would not commit.

mistranslations.rendering: reduction of the lumen of the system
mistranslations.why: In print (IRJAY 2023, section heading) and flatly wrong — granthi is a knot or nodular enlargement, and the same paper's next sentence says 'vein enlargement'. Also incompatible with WHO's own description ('bulging or growth').

Bhishagratna's own parenthesis, but the Sushrutan mechanism is vata compressing, contracting and drying the sirā network, and the prognosis rules (painless, fixed, large, at a marma = incurable) do not match aneurysm's natural history. Aneurysm and varicosity cannot both be the referent.

Widely offered as the modern example (IRJAY 2023 uses exactly this). Atherosclerosis is arterial intimal plaque; sirāja granthi is described as a raised round knot of the sirā network arising from exertion in a weak person. The equation is an analogy, not a translation.
Kaviratna's gloss. Nothing in the Sanskrit implies a cyst.

mistranslations.why: Charaka's phrase is sirāṇāṃ granthayaḥ, plural knots of the siras. It is specifically vascular. Using it as a general term for any nodular channel lesion goes beyond the text.

classical.establishes: The nine gunas Caraka assigns to snehana substances at Su 22.15, 'as a rule' (prayah): drava, suksma, sara, snigdha, picchila, guru, sitala, manda, mrdu. Kaviratna's English (his aphorism 13, p. 245) renders these as liquid, subtile, stable, oily, slimy, heavy, cooling, not pungent or mild, and soft. His 'stable' for saram is a slip: on the same page he renders saram as 'unstable' in the Langhana (his 10) and Swedana (his 14) aphorisms, where sthiram is 'stable', and his footnote glosses 'Sara' as 'moving or unstable'. Sthira does not occur in 22.15. Use the Sanskrit for the guna list; the English is evidence of Kaviratna's rendering only.

classical.establishes: Ḍalhaṇa's Nibandhasaṅgraha on Su.Su. 42.7 passes no judgement on whether Sushruta accepts the kecit two-fold saumya/āgneya division of rasas: he glosses agnīṣomīyatva and reads the two ca-s as implying a further twofold division by sneha/rūkṣa and guru/laghu, and records no dissent. Sushruta's mūla at 42.7 also lacks the rejection marker he uses elsewhere (Su.Su. 36, 'tat tu na samyak'). A Sushruta-voice link between sneha and madhura rasa is available instead at Su.Su. 42.8, third sub-clause, where kapha is characterised by mādhurya, sneha, gaurava, śaitya and paicchilya and madhura is named its samāna-yoni rasa.

classical.establishes: The sentence in which the plural srotāṃsi appears in its most-quoted form. Grammatically the plural is unremarkable; the sentence is the definition of srotas, not of a distinct thing called srotāṃsi.
classical.quote: स्रोतांसि खलु परिणाममापद्यमानानां धातूनामभिवाहीनि भवन्त्ययनार्थेन||३||

classical.establishes: Charaka records the view that the person IS simply the aggregate of the srotas, and rejects it ('na tvetadevam'): the one whose srotas they are, what they carry, and where they are situated are all other than the srotas. He then records the dispute over whether they are countable or uncountable. Directly relevant because the reified plural 'srotamsi' is usually deployed in support of the view Charaka rejects.
classical.quote: अपि चैके स्रोतसामेव समुदयंपुरुषमिच्छन्ति, सर्वगतत्वात् सर्वसरत्वाच्च दोषप्रकोपणप्रशमनानाम्| न त्वेतदेवं, यस्य हि स्रोतांसि, यच्च वहन्ति, यच्चावहन्ति,यत्र चावस्थितानि, सर्वं तदन्यत्तेभ्यः||४|| अतिबहुत्वात् खलु केचिदपरिसङ्ख्येयान्याचक्षते स्रोतांसि, परिसङ्ख्येयानि पुनरन्ये||५||

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English of the rejection. OCR artifacts ('duets' for 'ducts') are in the archive.org text as retrieved and are reproduced unaltered.
classical.quote: Then, again, some sages say that a person is only the sum total- of the ducts, because of the ducts being present in every part of the body,, and because also of the duets being the conduits of both the excitements and the alleviations- of the faults. This, however, is not so. Since he whose ducts they are, that which they develop ( or nourish ), and that in which they are located, — all these are differ- ent from them.

classical.establishes: Charaka's enumeration of the thirteen srotāṃsi: prāṇa, udaka, anna, rasa, rudhira, māṃsa, medas, asthi, majjā, śukra, mūtra, purīṣa, sveda — all as -vahāni compounds. The same verse adds that vata, pitta and kapha move through ALL the channels and have none of their own.

classical.establishes: There are as many kinds of srotas as there are embodied entities in a person; nothing in the person comes into being or wastes away except through the srotas; and the srotas carry (abhivāhīni) the dhatus that are undergoing transformation (pariṇāma), by way of being their pathway (ayanārthena). This is the single most-cited definitional verse for srotas.
classical.quote: यावन्तः पुरुषे मूर्तिमन्तो भावविशेषास्तावन्त एवास्मिन् स्रोतसां प्रकारविशेषाः| सर्वे हि भावा पुरुषे नान्तरेण स्रोतांस्यभिनिर्वर्तन्ते, क्षयं वाऽप्यभिगच्छन्ति| स्रोतांसि खलु परिणाममापद्यमानानां धातूनामभिवाहीनि भवन्त्ययनार्थेन||३||

classical.establishes: The only lawfully quotable English rendering of the core srotas definition. Kaviratna = 'ducts'; 'ingredients of the body' = dhatu; 'development or transformation' = pariṇāma. Retrieved text is OCR of the archive.org scan; spacing and punctuation artifacts are reproduced as found.
classical.quote: Verily, the ducts are the conduits of the ingredients of the body, for bearing them (from one place to another), during the process of their development ( or transformation ),

classical.establishes: The canonical list of synonyms/near-synonyms for srotas: sirā, dhamanī, rasāyanī, rasavāhinī, nāḍī, panthā, mārga, śarīracchidra, saṃvṛta-asaṃvṛta, sthāna, āśaya, niketa. Charaka treats these as names for the perceptible and imperceptible spaces of the bodily dhatus, which is why lexicons that treat sirā/dhamanī/srotas as strictly separate structures are importing a Sushrutan distinction into Charaka.
classical.quote: स्रोतांसि, सिराः, धमन्यः,रसायन्यः, रसवाहिन्यः, नाड्यः, पन्थानः,मार्गाः, शरीरच्छिद्राणि, संवृतासंवृतानि, स्थानानि, आशयाः, निकेताश्चेति शरीरधात्ववकाशानां लक्ष्यालक्ष्याणां नामानि भवन्ति|

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English of the synonym list, rendered collectively as 'the passages or conduits, visible and invisible'. OCR errors are in the source ('Srolas' for Srotas, 'Cariracchidra' for Sharira-cchidra, 'dliatus' for dhatus); his list also carries 'Ayaya' and 'Kshaya' where the Yadavji text has āśayāḥ, so his Sanskrit base text differed.
classical.quote: Srolas, Siras, Dhamani, Rasavahini, Nadi, Pantha Marga, Cariracchidra, covered and uncovered Sthana, Ayaya, Kshaya, and Niketa, — these are the names by which are known the passages or conduits, visible and invisible, of the dliatus ( or constituent elements ) of the body.

classical.establishes: Morphology of srotas: long in form and resembling a creeping/spreading network (pratāna). The immediately preceding half-verse (which I did not capture verbatim) supplies the colour, roundness and gross/subtle attributes.
classical.quote: स्रोतांसि दीर्घाण्याकृत्या प्रतानसदृशानि च||२५||

classical.establishes: Sushruta's definition, which is materially different from Charaka's: for Sushruta srotas is a third category, expressly distinguished from sirā and dhamanī, originating from the heart cavity. This is the root of the Charaka/Sushruta divergence that most English lexicon entries silently flatten. Also confirmed against the wisdomlib page for the same chapter (https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/sushruta-samhita-volume-3-sharirasthana/d/doc142889.html), which carries the identical sentence.
classical.quote: The ducts emanating from the cavity of the heart, other than the Siras (veins), Dhaman is (arteries), and found to course through the whole body, are called Srotas (lit. channels or currents).

classical.establishes: Sushruta enumerates ELEVEN PAIRS of srotas (prana, anna, udaka, rasa, rakta, mamsa, meda, mutra, purisha, shukra, artava) as surgically relevant, against Charaka's THIRTEEN. Sushruta has no asthi-vaha or majja-vaha or sveda-vaha srotas and does have an artava-vaha srotas; Charaka has the reverse. Any lexicon that gives 'the thirteen srotas' as the definition is reporting Charaka only.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: In Charaka Vi.5/9 sirā is listed as one of the names for srotas, i.e. effectively a synonym. In Sushruta Sharira 9/13 srotas is expressly defined as the ducts OTHER THAN sirā and dhamanī. The two texts are not reconcilable on this point and a lexicon must say which one it is following.

Same divergence as sirā. Bhishagratna glosses dhamanī as 'arteries' and sirā as 'veins', which is his 1907 anatomical overlay, not a translation. Sushruta himself records and then rejects the view that dhamanī and srotas are merely modifications of sirā.

nāḍī appears in Charaka's synonym list for srotas as an anatomical conduit. It is NOT the yogic/tantric nāḍī (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumṇā) of the haṭha-yoga corpus, which belongs to a different textual tradition. Conflating them is the single most common error in English-language popular writing.

WHO ISTA files mahāsrotas under Viscera (ITA.3.11.1) as the major inner cavity from mouth to anus, i.e. the gut lumen / koṣṭha, not as a member of the srotas series. It is not 'the great channel' in an abstract sense.
kha is a synonym for srotas in the compound khavaiguṇya, but khavaiguṇya names a DEFECT in the channel, not the channel. See the khavaigunya record.

mistranslations.rendering: arteries and veins / the arterial and venous system
mistranslations.why: This is Kaviratna's own 1890s translator's footnote, not the text, and he hedges it himself ('It probably includes also the nervous system'). Charaka's srotas include annavaha (gut), mutravaha (urinary), purishavaha (colorectal) and svedavaha (sweat) channels, none of which is vascular.

A modern coinage. Charaka Vi.5/25 describes srotas as both sthūla (gross) and aṇu (subtle); restricting the word to the micro scale drops half the definition and imports a capillary-bed reading that the text does not make.
Imports a Chinese-medicine concept with a different anatomy, a different enumeration and a different clinical use. No classical Ayurvedic text supports the equation.

A misspelling, not a translation, but it is endemic in Indian journal literature and in web sources and will defeat a naive search. The correct transliteration is srotas (स्रोतस्), from √sru, to flow.

openQuestions: The derivation 'sravaṇāt srotāṃsi' is attributed by some papers to Charaka himself and by others to Chakrapani's commentary on Ca.Su.30/12. I could not retrieve the commentary text to settle it.
Whether Charaka's thirteen and Sushruta's eleven were ever harmonised in the classical commentarial literature, or whether the discrepancy was simply left standing.

classical.establishes: THE defining verse. The four signs of srotoduṣṭi are atipravṛtti, saṅga, sirāṇāṃ granthayaḥ, and vimārgagamana. Note the text says 'sirāṇāṃ granthayaḥ' (knots OF the siras, genitive plural) — NOT the single compound 'sirāgranthi'. The compound is a later textbook and WHO form. Also note the verse says duṣṭi-LAKṢAṆAM, the SIGNS of vitiation, not the types; the widespread phrase 'four types of srotodushti' is an interpretive step beyond the wording.
classical.quote: अतिप्रवृत्तिः सङ्गो वा सिराणां ग्रन्थयोऽपि वा| विमार्गगमनं चापि स्रोतसां दुष्टिलक्षणम्||२४||

classical.establishes: The only lawfully quotable English of the defining verse. CRITICAL CAVEAT: Kaviratna's rendering does not map cleanly onto the received Sanskrit. He has FOUR items but adds 'or attenuation' alongside 'stoppage' for saṅga, and renders sirāṇāṃ granthayaḥ as 'cystic tumours'. 'diviations' is an OCR artifact for 'deviations'. Kaviratna worked from a Gangadhara-influenced Bengal recension (he repeatedly contrasts 'Gangadhara's reading' with 'the vicious Bengal texts' in this very chapter), so a variant reading is the likely explanation.
classical.quote: Excessive generation (or flow, of food-juice, blood, and other ingredients of the body), or stoppage or attenuation (of these), or cystic tumours, or diviations (of the elements from their own into other channels), are regarded as indications of the vitiation of the ducts.

classical.establishes: The propagation rule: vitiated srotas vitiate other srotas, vitiated dhatus vitiate other dhatus, and the vitiators of all of them are the vitiated vata, pitta and kapha 'by the very nature of dosha'. This is the mechanism clause that most English definitions of srotodushti omit.
classical.quote: तेषां प्रकोपात् स्थानस्थाश्चैव मार्गगाश्च शरीरधातवःप्रकोपमापद्यन्ते, इतरेषां प्रकोपादितराणि च| स्रोतांसि स्रोतांस्येव, धातवश्च धातूनेव प्रदूषयन्ति प्रदुष्टाः| तेषां सर्वेषामेव वातपित्तश्लेष्माणः प्रदुष्टा दूषयितारो भवन्ति, दोषस्वभावादिति||९||

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's English of the propagation rule. He renders dosha as 'faults' and vata/pitta/kapha as 'wind, bile, and phlegm' throughout.
classical.quote: After the same manner, the ducts that become vitiated, vitiate other ducts. Similarly, those constituent elements that become vitiated, vitiate other constituents ( of the body ) Of all those ducts and constituent elements vitiated wind, bile, and phlegm become vitiators in consequence of their very nature as faults.

classical.establishes: The general srotodushti-hetu rule (the passage WHO ISTA labels srotoduṣṭihetuḥ at ITA-4.8.3): whatever is dosha-like in quality and dhatu-hostile vitiates the channels. Preceded in Kaviratna by channel-specific causes for each of the thirteen.
classical.quote: Such food, and such practices, as correspond with the qualities of the faults, and as are hostile to the ingredients (dhdtus) of the body, are vitiators of the ducts.

distinguishFrom.why: The tradition orders them: khavaiguṇya is the pre-existing susceptibility or defect in the channel; srotodushti is what happens when dosha and dushya then combine there. The CSNE Kha vaigunya article states the distinction explicitly ('it is different from the vitiation of body channels (srotodushti)... This process of vitiation takes place at the site where Khavaigunya already exists'). WHO ISTA blurs it by giving srotovaiguṇyam and srotoduṣṭihetuḥ the SAME English term.

WHO ISTA ITA-4.8.1 defines srotorodhaḥ as 'Obstructive pathology: a complete or partial obstruction in the body channels leading to their malfunctioning'. That is one mode of srotodushti (overlapping saṅga), not a synonym for the whole category.

Ca.Vi.5/8 says that the signs of vitiation of the rasa-and-later channels have already been stated in Vividhashitapitiya (Ca.Su.28) as the signs of vitiation of the DHATUS themselves. Charaka deliberately does not give separate channel signs for those. So dhatu-pradoshaja vikara and the corresponding srotodushti are, for Charaka, the same sign set read two ways — not two independent findings.

Sushruta Sharira 9/11-12 deals with a channel PIERCED by a weapon and the symptoms that follow. That is traumatic injury, a surgical category, not the dosha-mediated vitiation Charaka means by srotodushti.

mistranslations.why: In print (IRJAY 2023) but wrong. Histopathology is a tissue-level microscopic diagnostic method; srotodushti is a functional-pathological category defined by four flow behaviours, three of which (excess flow, obstruction, wrong-route flow) are not histological findings at all.

Ca.Vi.5/24 says duṣṭi-LAKṢAṆAM, signs. Charaka does not say they are mutually exclusive types, and clinically more than one is routinely present. WHO's own entry ITA-4.8.4 (srotoduṣṭiprakāraḥ, 'types') is the standards-body version of the same interpretive slide.
Collapses the whole four-fold scheme into its saṅga member. Atipravṛtti is the opposite of blockage and vimārgagamana is orthogonal to it.
No inflammatory sense in duṣṭi; the word is 'spoiling, corruption, vitiation'. Nothing in Ca.Vi.5/24 corresponds to the cardinal signs of inflammation.

openQuestions: Why Kaviratna's text yields 'stoppage or attenuation' where the vulgate has only saṅga — is this a Gangadhara-recension variant, and does any printed edition carry a fifth item?

Stiffness/rigidity as a morbidity term (WHO AF2151 'stambha: Fixedness, stiffness...'); stambhana is the therapy, and svedana is defined as stambha-destroying (Su.22.11).

Victorian materia-medica English (U. C. Dutt via Kaviratna); the Sanskrit covers arresting any flow (bleeding, diarrhoea, vomiting, sweating), not only stool.
Narrows to bleeding; acceptable only for raktastambhana.

classical.establishes: The closest classical warrant for a milk-carrying channel: a pair of upward-coursing DHAMANĪS, milk-bearing in women and śukra-bearing in men. Suśruta does NOT call this a srotas and does not include it in his eleven pairs of srotas later in the same chapter.
classical.quote: Two of the Dhamanis (ducts) carry the fluid of lachrymation, two of them (ducts), attached to the breasts of a woman, carry milk of her breasts, which, coursing through the breast of a man, convey his seminal fluid.

classical.establishes: The Sanskrit behind the Bhishagratna passage above: 'two carry tears; two, situated in the breasts, carry stanya in a woman; those same two carry a man's śukra from the breasts.' Confirms the word used is a dhamanī description, and that stanya is the object carried, not a compounded channel-name.
classical.quote: द्वे चाश्रुवाहिन्यौ, द्वे स्तन्यं स्त्रिया वहतः स्तनसंश्रिते, ते एव शुक्रं नरस्य स्तनाभ्यामभिवहतः

classical.establishes: DECISIVE NEGATIVE: this is the verse NAMASTE cites for 'stanyavaha-srotoduṣṭi', and the word it uses is kṣīravahāḥ SIRĀḤ (milk-carrying veins/vessels), not stanyavaha srotas. The doṣas reach the milk-carrying sirās, vitiate the stanya, and produce eightfold stanya-duṣṭi. I string-searched the whole retrieved chapter: neither 'स्तन्यवह' nor 'आर्तववह' occurs anywhere in Ca.Ci.30.
classical.quote: दोषाः क्षीरवहाः प्राप्य सिराः स्तन्यं प्रदूष्य च| कुर्युरष्टविधं भूयो दोषतस्तन्निबोध मे ||२३६||

classical.establishes: Negative evidence, quoted: stanya-vaha is absent from Caraka's thirteen, as it is from Suśruta's eleven.
classical.quote: तद्यथा प्राणोदकान्नरसरुधिरमांसमेदोस्थिमज्जशुक्रमूत्रपुरीषस्वेदवहानीति

distinguishFrom.why: This is Caraka's actual term (Ci.30/236). Anyone citing Ca.Ci.30 under the head-word 'stanyavaha srotas' is substituting a later coinage for the text's own word.

Su.Śā.9 gives both Suśruta's śukravaha srotas roots in the BREASTS and a breast dhamanī pair that is milk-bearing in women and śukra-bearing in men — so in Suśruta these are one structure with two sex-specific outputs, not two channels.
WHO codes stanyam as an upadhātu of rasa (ITA-2.3.2). The milk exists in the standards; its channel does not.

stanya is classically an upadhātu of rasa, so milk disorders are often routed through rasavaha pathology — NAMASTE in fact files stanyavaha-srotodushti as EC-4.5, i.e. INSIDE its rasavaha (EC) code block.

mistranslations.why: No classical text names such a channel. The Suśruta passage describes systemic dhamanīs running to the breast, explicitly shared with male śukra transport, not intramammary ducts.

mistranslations.rendering: 'the 14th srotas' / 'one of the two extra srotas in women'
mistranslations.why: A textbook convention, not a textual fact. Caraka lists thirteen (no stanya, no ārtava); Suśruta lists eleven pairs (ārtava yes, stanya no). No enumeration in either text contains stanyavaha.
The verses say kṣīravahāḥ sirāḥ. The citation is real but the term is not in it — exactly the kind of inherited reference that looks verified and is not.

openQuestions: Does any pre-modern text actually use the compound stanyavaha srotas, or is it entirely a modern textbook coinage back-formed from stanya + srotas?
If Suśruta's breast dhamanīs are shared between milk and śukra, should stanyavaha be an entry at all, or a cross-reference under śukravaha?

classical.establishes: Defines the stage as doshas reaching particular bodily regions and generating the diseases proper to each, and expressly ties the fourth kriyākāla to the APPEARANCE OF PRODROMES (pūrvarūpaprādurbhāvaḥ ... pūrvarūpagateṣu caturthaḥ kriyākālaḥ). This is the verse behind WHO's inclusion of prodromes in ITA-4.6.10.
classical.quote: अत ऊर्ध्वं स्थानसंश्रयं वक्ष्यामः । एवं प्रकुपितातांस्ताञ् शरीरप्रदेशानागम्य तांस्तान् व्याधीन् जनयन्ति । ते यदोदरसन्निवेशं कुर्वन्ति तदा गुल्म विद्रध्युदराग्निसङ्गानाहविसूचिकातिसारप्रभृतीञ्जनयन्ति; बस्तिगताः प्रमेहाश्मरीमूत्राघातमूत्रदोषप्रभृतीन्; ... तेषामेवमभिसन्निविष्टानां पूर्वरूपप्रादुर्भावः ; तं प्रतिरोगं वक्ष्यामः । तत्र पूर्वरूपगतेषु चतुर्थः क्रियाकालः ॥३३॥

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's opening of the sthanasamshraya section. His disease equivalents here (cholera for Visuchika, dropsy, and syphilis later in the same passage) are 1907 colonial-medicine glosses and must not be carried into a modern lexicon.
classical.quote: Now we shall enumerate the names of the peculiar diseases, which are originated by the deranged and expanded humours, incarcerated in the different parts of the body. These humours, confined in the abdomen, give rise to Gulma (abdominal glands) tumours, internal abscesses ( Vidradhi ), abdominal dropsy, impaired digestion in the bowels, constipation (anaha), cholera (Visuchika) and dysentery.

classical.establishes: The stage-marker in English, confirming that the fourth occasion is defined by the appearance of premonitory symptoms, not by lodgement as such.
classical.quote: The aggravated and expanded humours, thus firmly ensconced in the different parts of the body, exhibit the premonitory symptoms of diseases which will be fully dealt with under their respective heads. The manifestation of these premonitory symptoms should be considered as the fourth occasion for medical treatment.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ITA-4.5.1's English term is 'Prodrome, premonitory symptoms', described as 'Recognition of the prodrome or set of premonitory, precursory symptoms, treatment of which can forestall manifestation of the disease; they are classified into two types depending on their nature.' (Sanskrit column: pūrvarūpam / पूर्वरूपम्, printed p. 109.) Sthānasaṃśraya is the dosha-side event, the lodgement; pūrvarūpa is the clinical output of that event. Su.Su. 21.33 links them (pūrvarūpaprādurbhāvaḥ) but does not equate them.

The pre-existing defect or weakness in a srotas or dhatu that lets the dosha lodge there. It is the enabling condition, not the stage. It is absent from the retrieved verses of Su.Su. 21 and is supplied by commentators and by teaching tradition.
The interaction of dosha with the tissue, often taught as what happens at this stage. It is a separate technical term and is not the compound sthānasaṃśraya.

Migration versus settling. WHO's own wording — 'migrates outside its own location' (ITA-4.6.9) versus 'lodges in a different location ... and gives rise to prodromal symptoms' (ITA-4.6.10) — is the cleanest available statement of the difference.

mistranslations.why: Imports an infectious-disease mechanism. Nothing in the compound or the verse involves an external organism; sthāna is a bodily site and saṃśraya is taking refuge in it.

Not wrong, but incomplete in a way that matters: it omits the prodrome, which is the criterion the text itself uses to mark the fourth kriyākāla (pūrvarūpagateṣu caturthaḥ kriyākālaḥ). WHO includes the prodrome; most short glosses do not.
Collides with vyakti, the fifth stage. At sthānasaṃśraya the disease is not yet manifest, only heralded.

mistranslations.rendering: Reading Bhishagratna's disease equivalents as the referents
mistranslations.why: He renders Visuchika as 'cholera' and gives 'syphilis' in the penile-lodgement list. Those are 1907 identifications, not translations of the Sanskrit, and repeating them would put false modern diagnoses into the lexicon.

openQuestions: Whether khavaiguṇya appears anywhere in Su.Su. 21 itself or only in Dalhana — I could not verify either way from the verses retrieved (21.16-21.38).
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 codes the pūrvarūpa/sthānasaṃśraya stage at all — see the shat-kriyakala record for why both lookups failed again this session.
Whether any source offers a way to tell lodgement from mere presence in a site, clinically.
