classical.quote: विंशतिगुणः, गुरुलघुशीतोष्णस्निग्धरूक्षमन्दतीक्ष्णस्थिरसरमृदुकठिनविशदपिच्छिलश्लक्ष्णखरसूक्ष्मस्थूलसान्द्रद्रवानुगमात्

distinguishFrom.why: Paired opposite in Charaka's twenty (Ca.Su.25.36) and WHO (ITA-1.9.4.2.19 'Instability, mobility'); Kaviratna 'unstable'.
Vata's mobility quality in Ca.Su.1.59 (चल); textbooks treat cala and sara as interchangeable opposites of sthira, but Charaka uses different words in the two places.
The abstract noun and karma ('consistency' in Kaviratna at Su.26 his 22); the effect sthira produces.
Separate guna, co-listed in the pārthiva set; firmness vs immobility.
Co-listed with sthira in Kapha and pārthiva lists; different pair (guru/laghu).
A plant name that dominates Kaviratna's uses of the word; WHO lists the plant under its own synonyms, not as sthira.

Sushruta's enumeration at Su.Su.46.514-525 (as retrieved) lists drava, sāndra, ślakṣṇa, karkaśa, sugandha, durgandha, sara, manda, vyavāyī, vikāsī, āśukārī, sūkṣma in the second ten and names no sthira — a real inter-text difference to flag.

Modern pharmacy sense; the texts mean position-keeping, firmness, resistance to movement (WHO 'maintaining stability and position').

Where the retrieved Sanskrit of 22.15 reads सरं, Kaviratna prints 'stable'; sthira and sara are opposites, so this is either a variant reading or an error and must not be cited as the text calling snehana dravyas sthira.

classical.establishes: Defines sukham āyuḥ by: freedom from bodily and mental disease, youth in particular, strength/vigour/fame/manliness/prowess proportionate to capacity, command of knowledge, science, senses and sense-objects, great affluence and varied enjoyments, success in all undertakings, and moving as one wishes. Then defines its opposite as asukham, by reverse. This is an excerpt of the first portion of verse 24; the hitāyu portion follows in the same verse.
classical.quote: तत्र शारीरमानसाभ्यां रोगाभ्यामनभिद्रुतस्य विशेषेण यौवनवतः समर्थानुगतबलवीर्ययशःपौरुषपराक्रमस्यज्ञानविज्ञानेन्द्रियेन्द्रियार्थबलसमुदये वर्तमानस्य परमर्द्धिरुचिरविविधोपभोगस्य समृद्धसर्वारम्भस्य यथेष्टविचारिणःसुखमायुरुच्यते; असुखमतो विपर्ययेण

classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English of the sukhāyu definition, matching the Sanskrit above clause for clause and in the same order. Note how much of it is circumstantial - wealth, success, freedom of action - which is what makes WHO's 'quotient of happiness' gloss a narrowing.
classical.quote: who  is  not  afflicted  by  any  disease  physical  or  mental,  who  is,  particularly,  possessed  of  youth,  who  is  endued  with  strength,  energy,  manliness,  and  prowess,  proportioned  to  the  capacity  of  his  frame,  who  rests  on  strength  of  knowledge,  of  science,  and  of  the  senses,  as  also  on  all  the  objects  of  the  senses,  who  is  endued  with  great  affluence  and  diverse  agreeable  objects  of  enjoyment,  who  is  crowned  with  success  in  respect  of  all  his  essays,  and  who  moves  and  acts  as  he  pleases,  Life  is  called  happy.

classical.establishes: The first occurrence of sukha as a division of āyu, here as a bare adjective with no content.
classical.quote: हिताहितं सुखं दुःखमायुस्तस्य हिताहितम्| मानं च तच्च यत्रोक्तमायुर्वेदः स उच्यते||४१||

distinguishFrom.why: Sukhāyu is about condition and circumstance (health, youth, wealth, success, freedom); hitāyu is about conduct (truthfulness, restraint, giving, reverence). They are independent axes, and the fourfold scheme exists precisely so that a life can be classified on both.

distinguishFrom.term: sukha (as the counterpart of duḥkha in doṣa/health contexts)
distinguishFrom.why: Sukha is used throughout the Samhitas for pleasant sensation and for the comfortable state of the body. In sukhāyu it qualifies a whole life, assessed by a checklist, not a sensation.
Freedom from disease is only the first item in the sukhāyu list; svastha is the technical term for that item alone. Sukhāyu is broader and includes wealth and success, which svastha does not.
Sukhāyu is worldly and enumerable. Rendering it as bliss slides it toward a soteriological category the verse does not invoke.

mistranslations.why: WHO uses it, so it must be recorded, but it is an import: it carries the apparatus of QoL instruments and a self-report methodology alien to a verse that lists objective circumstances such as affluence and success in undertakings. Recording it as WHO's rendering is correct; adopting it as the definition is not.
Freedom from disease is one of nine or so items in the list.
Understates. The list includes strength, prowess, fame and command of the senses, not merely pleasantness.

openQuestions: Why Su 30.24 uses asukham rather than duḥkham for the negative limb, when Su 1.41 uses duḥkham. This is a real lexical inconsistency in the source and I could not establish whether any commentator addresses it.
Whether NAMASTE codes sukhāyu and whether it followed WHO into 'quality of life'.

distinguishFrom.why: Opposite member of the pair.
Light (easy to digest) is a separate pair; both appear in the Vāta and laṅghana lists, so renderings like 'fine/light' merge them.
Also 'minute'; used of srotas size (WHO 'Sthūla (macro) and Aṇu (micro)') and of manas; not the gurvadi guna.
'Subtle body' (WHO BP0274), a Sankhya-derived philosophical term unrelated to the drug quality.
Both are glossed 'penetrating'; tīkṣṇa is speed/sharpness of action, sūkṣma is fineness of substance (Kaviratna's note).

mistranslations.why: Imports the sūkṣma-śarīra sense into pharmacology; the Charaka passages describe a physical quality of substances and of Vāta.
WHO BP0275's gloss; the retrieved Charaka passages attribute no mass-reducing karma to sūkṣma specifically (that is laṅghana as a whole).

classical.quote: किट्टात् स्वेदमूत्रपुरीषवातपित्तश्लेष्माणः ... पुष्यन्ति| / kiṭṭāt svēdamūtrapurīṣavātaPittaślēṣmāṇaḥ ... puṣyanti| — Kaviratna: 'From the Refuse arise urine, sweat, faeces* wind, bile, and phlegm'

classical.establishes: Sweat is the mala of medas (fat). This is why WHO and NAMASTE class sweat as dhātumala, not āhāramala. Kaviratna's 'sweet' is a misprint for 'sweat' and 'adeps' = medas.
classical.quote: मलः स्वेदस्तु मेदसः / malaḥ svēdastu mēdasaḥ — Kaviratna: 'while sweet forms the ‘Kitta’ of adeps'

classical.establishes: Two statements in one sūtra: medas produces sneha and sveda; and sveda's function is kleda and softness (saukumārya) of the skin. Bhishagratna compresses this to 'moisten the skin' and drops saukumārya.
classical.quote: मेदः स्नेहस्वेदौ दृढत्वं पुष्टिमस्थ्नां च ... स्वेदः क्लेदत्वक्सौकुमार्यकृत् / mēdaḥ snēhasvēdau dr̥ḍhatvaṁ puṣṭim asthnāṁ ca ... svēdaḥ klēdatvaksaukumāryakr̥t — Bhishagratna: 'whereas perspiration tends to moisten the skin.'
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (English); Sanskrit from siva.sh

classical.establishes: Sveda-kṣaya signs (stiff hair follicles, dry skin, altered touch, cessation of sweating) with treatment by abhyaṅga and svedana; sveda-vṛddhi signs (bad odour, itching). Note the Sanskrit itself prescribes sveda(na) therapy for sveda(mala)-kṣaya, which is the root of the English confusion between the two words. Charaka Su 17 has NO sveda-kṣaya verse; Sushruta supplies it.
classical.quote: स्वेदक्षये स्तब्धरोमकूपता त्वक्शोषः स्पर्शवैगुण्यं स्वेदनाशश्च; तत्राभ्यङ्गः स्वेदोपयोगश्च [11] ... स्वेदस्त्वचो दौर्गन्ध्यं कण्डूं च [15] — Bhishagratna: 'Similarly the waste, absence or scanty formation of perspiration is followed by such symptoms as numbness about the pores of the hair, and dryness of the epidermis (skin). The sense of touch is perceptibly affected, and perspiration is entirely stopped. The medical treatment in such a case consists in the application of medicated unguents, lubrications, diaphoretics, and adoption of measures (that tend to produce a copious perspiration).' ... 'Similarly, an increased secretion of perspiration is attended with an itching of the skin which emits a bad odour.'

distinguishFrom.why: Induced sweating / fomentation (WHO ITA-9.2.36; one of the pūrvakarma). Same stem, different category. Sushruta Su 15/11 prescribes svedana FOR sveda-kṣaya, so the two co-occur in one sentence. Over-sudation has its own code (WHO ITA-5.76.8 svedana-atiyogaḥ) distinct from svedavṛddhiḥ (ITA-5.4.11).
The channel (Ca.Vi.5/8); separate record. The earlier record in this corpus found that neither WHO's body-channel block nor NAMASTE SAT-B lists the channel, though both code its disorder.

In Charaka Su 17/23 and 17/33 'svēdaḥ' appears as a SIGN (sweating in pitta-type head and heart disease); PubMed hits for 'sveda ayurveda' are all case reports using the word in this sign sense. Not the mala entry.
The moisture that sweat holds in the skin (AH 11/5 kleda-vidhṛti) and urine carries away (kleda-vāhana); sveda is the agent, kleda the substance.

The textbook 'trimala' (stool, urine, sweat) groups sweat with the food-wastes, but Charaka Chi 15/18, AH Sha 3/63, WHO 2.4.1/2.4.5 and NAMASTE SAT-B.457/462 all make sweat the mala of medas (dhātumala). The grouping and the derivation do not agree.

Kaviratna's footnote at Su 17/63 counts stools, urine and five orifice-secretions as the seven mala-kṣayas; sweat is not among them, and Su 17 has no sveda-kṣaya verse. 'Charaka describes sveda-kṣaya' would be unsupported.

mistranslations.why: No retrieved classical source assigns sweat an eliminative function; Su.Su.15/5 (kleda, saukumārya) and AH Su 11/5 (kleda-vidhṛti) make sweat RETAIN moisture in the skin. Elimination of kleda is assigned to urine, not sweat.
Category error between mala and karma; see distinguishFrom.

mistranslations.rendering: 'moisten the skin' as the whole function (Bhishagratna)
mistranslations.why: Drops tvak-saukumārya (softness of skin) from Su.Su.15/5, and inverts the direction of AH 11/5 (holding moisture in vs applying moisture).

openQuestions: Textual variant at AH Su 11/5c: kleda-vidhṛti vs keśa-vidhṛti (GRETIL records both). Which commentators prefer which was not checked.

Why the 'trimala' grouping (stool, urine, sweat) became standard in teaching when the Bṛhattrayī derive sweat from medas; no primary-text source for 'trimala' as a term was located (PubMed 'trimala' 0 records; WHO and NAMASTE have no trimala headword).
Whether Charaka anywhere states sweat's function (as opposed to origin) was not established.

distinguishFrom.why: A therapeutic procedure, not a channel. The English 'sweating channels' invites the confusion.
Caraka gives BOTH a root in medas — medovaha at vṛkka + vapāvahana, svedavaha at medas + lomakūpa. sveda is classically a mala of medas, which is why they share territory.
Both concern body water; udakavaha is rooted in palate and kloma and governs thirst, svedavaha is rooted in fat and hair follicles and governs perspiration.
Skin and hair follicle are the peripheral root, not the channel; svedavaha is not a synonym for 'the skin'.

mistranslations.why: lomakūpa is the hair follicle; sweat glands are not named in the Sanskrit, and the primary root is medas, not skin.
Imports a system boundary the text does not draw, and drops the medas root entirely.

mistranslations.why: Caraka places svedavaha among the srotas whose vitiation is triggered by anger, grief and fear — i.e. it carries a psychophysiological load that 'excretory channel' erases.

openQuestions: Why do WHO and NAMASTE code the disorder without coding the anatomy? Editorial oversight or a deliberate decision that sweat has no channel?
Does 'medas' as the root here mean subcutaneous fat specifically, given the pairing with hair follicles?

classical.quote: A man of Tamisika-temperament sleeps both in the day and night; one of the Rajasika-temperament sleeps either in the day or in the night; while sleep never visits the eyelids of a man of Sattvika -temperament before midnight.

distinguishFrom.why: Ayurvedic clinical Sanskrit uses tamaḥ-praveśa and related compounds for darkening of vision and syncope. A bare 'tamas' in a symptom list is very likely this, not the guṇa.
The ordinary sense, including the darkness of night relevant to dinacaryā and nidrā physiology.
Popular writing equates them on shared heaviness. Vi 6/5 keeps mental and bodily doṣas separate, and Sushruta Sharira 1/21 assigns tamas to pṛthvī and water.
Sha 4/39 says the tāmasa types are so called from their moha portion. moha is a vikāra of the mental doṣas, not a synonym for tamas.

mistranslations.why: Etymologically accurate, but in English it carries moral overtones that make Vi 6/5 read as theology rather than a classification of disease causes.
Category error; guṇas and doṣas are parallel schemes, not levels of one.
One of WHO's listed characteristics, but the guṇa also covers ignorance, delusion and the physiology of sleep.

classical.quote: Now we shall discourse on the chapter which deals with the technical terms used in this treatise (Tantra-Yukti-Nama-Adhyaya). 1. Names of the technical terms: — There are thirty-two technical terms in this Treatise. They are — (1) Adhikarana, (2) Yoga, (3) Padartha, (4) Hetvartha, (5) Uddes'a, (6) Nirdes'a, (7) Upades'a, (8) Apades'a, (9) Prades'a, (10) Atides'a, (11) Apavarga, (12) Vakya-s'esha, (13) Arthapatti, (14) Viparyaya, (15) Prasanga, (16) Ekanta, (17) Anekanta, (18) Purvapaksha, (19) Nirnaya, (20) Anumata, (21) Vidhana, (22) Anagata-vekshana, (23) Atikranta-vekshana, (24) Sams'aya, (25) Vyakhyana, (26) Sva-samjna, (27) Nirvachana, (28) Nidars'ana, (29) Niyoga, (30) Samuchchaya, (31) Vikalpa, and (32) Uhya. 2.

classical.establishes: The stated PURPOSE: refuting opponents and establishing one's own position, plus the sun/lotus and lamp/room similes. The same similes appear in Charaka Si. 12.46, which is how the two texts are known to share a source.
classical.quote: What is the necessity of the use of these technical terms (Tantra-Yukti) ? The answer is — For connecting words together, i.e., making up sentences and giving a sense or meaning to them. 3. Memorable verses: — By the use of technical terms in a scientific treatise the points of argument of the opposite party are frustrated and the points of one's own argument are established. ... Just as the sun shows a cluster of lotus and a lighted lamp (the inside of) a room at their best, so the technical terms used in a treatise clearly show i.e., explain the intended meaning. 4.

distinguishFrom.term: vāda-mārga / the 44 debate terms of Charaka Vimāna 8
distinguishFrom.why: A different list in a different sthāna, covering disputation (pratijñā, sthāpanā, hetu, dṛṣṭānta, upanaya, nigamana and so on). Kaviratna's translation of Vi. 8 contains items named Viśeṣa and Samavāya too, which makes keyword searching treacherous: the same Sanskrit words occur in the six-padārtha list, the debate list and the tantrayukti list with three different meanings.

WHO ITA-1.5.9 makes tantrayukti one of FIVE components of good technical writing, alongside arthāśraya, kalpanā, tācchīlya and vyākhyā. Treating tantrayukti as the whole of Ayurvedic textual method overstates it.
The faults of a treatise, the complement of the yuktis. Charaka Si. 12.40 says the redacted text is 'free from textual blemishes' (tantradoṣavivarjitam) in the same breath as it counts the yuktis.
Inside this very list, Padārtha means 'the meaning implied by a word or an aphorism' (Bhishagratna, Su. U. 65). Do not cross-link it to the ṣaṭpadārtha entry as if the same concept.

A widely asserted equivalence (e.g. 'adhikaraṇa = research topic', 'pūrvapakṣa = literature review'). It is a mapping proposed in the secondary literature, not an identity, and the primary purpose stated at Su. U. 65.4 is winning a textual argument, not generating new knowledge.

mistranslations.why: Bhishagratna's own rendering, and the reason it persists — but the items are operations and relations (arthāpatti = implication, viparyaya = the contrary case, ūhya = what must be inferred), not vocabulary. WHO's 'devices' is better and the divergence should be flagged wherever Bhishagratna is quoted.
Pure homonym error from 'tantra'. Here tantra means a systematic treatise (WHO ITA-1.5.6: 'a term that means literally to hold together on a thread').
An equation, not a translation. It projects a modern knowledge-production framework onto a set of exegetical and disputational devices.

Not wrong, but incomplete as a definite description: 32 is Sushruta's and the Arthaśāstra's count, 36 is Charaka's. Stating a single number without naming the text is the commonest factual slip on this topic.

openQuestions: Whether Ch.Si.12/40 genuinely reads ṣaḍviṁśatā (26) in printed editions, or whether the retrieved page has a typo for ṣaṭtriṁśatā (36). This must be settled before any number is published.

The five scholarly renderings attributed to Vidyabhushana, Shamasastry, Solomon, Oberhammer and Mittal — each needs checking against the original publication; I have only the attributing page's word for them.
Whether the Arthaśāstra's 32 and Sushruta's 32 are the same 32.

classical.establishes: Seat = head (śiras); function = nourishing/satiating the sense organs by its own unctuous-watery potency. The heading name is the translator's.
classical.quote: The Tarpakam:—The Kapham, situated in the head, cools and bathes the different sense organs with its own humid essence, in virtue of its natural humid attributes.

classical.establishes: The word 'tarpaka' as a NAME does not appear, but the function compound 'sneha-santarpaṇa-adhikṛtatvāt' (being appointed to unctuous satiation) is present and is the source of the later name. Seat śiraḥ-stha; it favours the indriyas by its own potency.
classical.quote: शिरःस्थः स्नेहसन्तर्पणाधिकृतत्वादिन्द्रियाणामात्मवीर्येणानुग्रहं करोत्;

classical.text: Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya (Sanskrit mūla; no public-domain English translation exists, so no translation is quoted)
classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa supplies the NAME with etymology — śiraḥ-saṃstha, called tarpaka FROM akṣa-tarpaṇa (satiating the sense organs). Vāgbhaṭa's 'akṣa' is narrower than Suśruta's 'indriyāṇām' and is sometimes read as the eyes specifically.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: Both are head/brain-region entities. Tarpaka is a kapha subtype performing a nourishing function for the sense organs; majjā is a tissue; mastiṣka is the organ. Modern texts frequently slide tarpaka into 'brain tissue', which is a category error.

A serious homonym trap. Netra-tarpaṇa is a well-known ophthalmic procedure in which medicated ghee is pooled over the eye. It shares the root but is a TREATMENT, not a doṣa subtype. Literature searches on 'tarpaka'/'tarpana' will return large numbers of procedure papers.
Both are nourishing/sustaining principles and both are invoked for resilience and sense function. Ojas is the essence of all dhātus, not a locational kapha subtype.
Both serve sense perception — bodhaka for taste at the tongue, tarpaka for the sense organs of the head generally. PMID 39114320 lumps them together, which blurs the distinction.

mistranslations.why: The dominant modern equation and entirely a hypothesis. CSF does not satiate sense organs in any sense the texts would recognise, and neither mūla describes a fluid compartment. I found no study that tests the equation.
Substitutes an anatomical structure for a functional principle, and conflates tarpaka with majjā dhātu.
Memory (smṛti) is not assigned to tarpaka in either mūla. Vāgbhaṭa gives the cognitive functions (buddhi, medhā) to SĀDHAKA PITTA. Attaching memory to tarpaka crosses the doṣa boundary.
Suśruta says 'indriyāṇām' — the sense organs generally. The narrower 'akṣa' (eye) reading is Vāgbhaṭa's at AH 12.17.

openQuestions: Does Vāgbhaṭa's 'akṣa' mean the eyes specifically or the sense organs generally? The commentaries would settle it, and it changes the term's scope.
The retrieved Suśruta page prints 'करोत्' where 'करोति' is expected — typographical or variant? Needs a critical edition.
Has anyone actually measured slow-wave sleep against a validated tarpaka-kapha assessment? PMID 42739755 proposes the link but I found no primary study.
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 carries any tarpaka-kapha entry.

classical.verse: Kaviratna Sharirasthana Lesson V, his printed aphorism 4 (superscript 4 after '...and the Inner Self is Brahma.', vol. 1 p. 765); standard Trikamji Ca.Sa. 5.5, whose opening sentence Kaviratna folds into his 4 — तस्य पुरुषस्य पृथिवी मूर्तिः, आपः क्लेदः, तेजोऽभिसन्तापः, वायुः प्राणः, वियत् सुषिराणि, ब्रह्म अन्तरात्मा| ... ||५||. The six-dhatu list पृथिव्यापस्तेजो वायुराकाशं ब्रह्म चाव्यक्तमिति is standard 5.4, a separate sentence, and is NOT what this citation quotes.
classical.establishes: Caraka's loka-purusa correspondence gives tejas a bodily correlate: तेजोऽभिसन्तापः, 'tejas [in the body] is abhisantapa' — scorching, bodily heat. The Sanskrit term is abhisantapa; usma does not occur in this passage. Kaviratna renders the clause 'the animal heat is Heat'. His footnote on the English for tejas is translator's voice and belongs in the renderings and mistranslations blocks rather than here; it is also keyed to the preceding six-ingredient sentence (standard 5.4), not to this clause, and what it says is that tejas is generally rendered 'light' or 'heat', that 'properly speaking, Tejas is energy', and that 'in such a connection, what is meant is Fire' — he offers 'energy' as the proper sense and 'Fire' only as what is meant in this context, so 'argues the right English is Fire' overstated him.
classical.quote: the animal heat is Heat
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: Agni is the functional principle of digestion and transformation; tejas is the bhūta. WHO lists agni as an alternate name of the bhūta, which makes the distinction harder, not easier. NAMASTE SAT-D.118 'diminution of agni' is a clinical sign unrelated to the bhūta.
Pitta is the doṣa in which tejas predominates (NIA draft p.21 'dominant of Agni Mahābhūta'); not the bhūta itself.
NAMASTE SAT-D.3674-3675 'fiery', 'person with radiant glow'; a descriptive/clinical sense distinct from the bhūta.

Kaviratna's footnote shows translators oscillating between 'light', 'heat' and 'energy'; the bhūta's guṇa is rūpa (form/colour) and its liṅga uṣṇatva (heat), so neither 'light' nor 'energy' alone is adequate.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's footnote ('Properly speaking, Tejas is energy') is a translator's opinion of 1890s physics; not a textual rendering.
Kaviratna 'fire (or light)'; tejas governs rūpa (visible form), so 'light' captures one guṇa but loses uṣṇatva and digestion.
Bhishagratna 'heat, (fire,)'; Kaviratna 'Heat' in Śā. 5; a liṅga, not the bhūta.
Misprint on the wisdomlib Bhishagratna page; not a Sanskrit form.

classical.establishes: Tīkṣṇa ('keen') as a quality of Pitta. Sanskrit as retrieved: सस्नेहमुष्णं तीक्ष्णं च द्रवमम्लं सरं कटु| विपरीतगुणैः पित्तं द्रव्यैराशु प्रशाम्यति||६०|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya). classical.establishes: Tīkṣṇa as one of the eight vīryas (Kaviratna's 'Energy'). Sanskrit as retrieved: मृदुतीक्ष्णगुरुलघुस्निग्धरूक्षोष्णशीतलम्| वीर्यमष्टविधं केचित्, केचिद्द्विविधमास्थिताः||६४|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya).
classical.quote: Some say that mild and keen, heavy and light, oily and dry, and hot and cooling, are the eight kinds of Energy which objects may have. Others are of opinion that objects have only two kinds of Energy, viz., cooling and hot.

classical.verse: Suśruta Sūtrasthāna 40.5 — 'केचिदष्टविधमाहुः — शीतमुष्णं स्निग्धं रूक्षं विशदं पिच्छिलं मृदु तीक्ष्णं ... एतानि खलु वीर्याणि स्वबलगुणोत्कर्षाद्रसमभिभूयात्मकर्म कुर्वन्ति ... तदेतन्निदर्शनमात्रमुक्तम् ॥५॥' (Trikamji/Dalhaṇa ed. 1938, pp. 175-176). This closes the Su.40 half of the openQuestion 'Sanskrit verse numbers for Sushruta Su.40-41 eight-virya passages'; the Su.41 half was already at 41.11.
classical.establishes: A variant reading placing guru (with laghu, displacing picchila and viśada) in Suśruta's eight-vīrya list at Su.Su. 41.11 is attested: Jadavji Trikamji's apparatus to Dalhaṇa's edition records it as Hāraṇacandra's pāṭha, both in the list itself (fn. 2) and in the dosha-action clause of the same sūtra (fn. 6). Dalhaṇa's own gloss supports the printed list without guru. Bhishagratna's 'heavy' is therefore consistent with an attested variant tradition and should not be recorded as an error, though his exact eight-item sequence reproduces neither the printed text nor that variant. Separately, the Su.40 eight-vīrya passage is Su.Su. 40.5.
classical.quote: तत्र य इमे गुणा वीर्यसंज्ञकाः शीतोष्णस्निग्धरूक्षमृदुतीक्ष्णपिच्छिलविशदास्तेषां तीक्ष्णोष्णावाग्नेयौ, शीतपिच्छिलौ अम्बुगुणभूयिष्ठौ, पृथिव्यम्बुगुणभूयिष्ठः स्नेहः, तोयाकाशगुणभूयिष्ठं मृदुत्वं, वायुगुणभूयिष्ठं रौक्ष्यं, क्षितिसमीरणगुणभूयिष्ठं वैशद्यं; विपाकाद्गुरुलघुगुणौ ॥११॥ — Suśruta Sū. 41.11, mūla as printed in the Dalhaṇa edition (Trikamji, Pandurang Jawaji 1938), p. 183. Variant recorded there: 'गुरुलघुमृदुतीक्ष्णा' (Hāraṇacandra).

A taste, not a guna; Kaviratna's 'pungent' for tīkṣṇa in Su.22 collides with his 'pungent' for kaṭu.
Hot; co-listed with tīkṣṇa in fire-dominant lists and in Pitta, but a separate pair (uṣṇa/śīta).
Rough; Kaviratna renders khara 'keen' (Su.1.59) and 'sharp' (Su.26.11, Wind list), so his 'sharp/keen' is not always tīkṣṇa.
A state of digestive fire (WHO AF2265), not the drug guna.
WHO DG0351 uses it as 'higher potency', a grading of strength rather than the sharpness quality.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's Su.22 choice; 'pungent' is the standard English for kaṭu rasa, so it conflates a taste with a guna.
Tīkṣṇa is speed and penetration of action; the texts pair it with manda (slow), not with cold.

classical.quote: Tikshna'gni: -The digestive heat, which helps the digestion of even a heavy meal within an incredibly short space of time is called " Keen " (Tikshnagni) and which becoming abnormally augmented begets an excessive or voracious appetite (Atyagni), helps a glutton to digest his frequent meals, and produces a parched throat, palate and lips, heat and other discomforts.

classical.quote: यः प्रभूतमप्युपयुक्तमन्नमाशुपचति स तीक्ष्णः स एवाभिवर्धमानोऽत्यग्निरित्याभाष्यते स मुहुर्मुहुः प्रभूतमप्युपयुक्तमन्नमाशुतरं पचति पाकान्ते च गलताल्वोष्ठशोषदाहसंतापाञ्जनयति

classical.quote: A keen (Tikshna) digestive fire brings on bilious (Pittaja) affections ... In a case of abnormally keen digestive fire, the medical treatment should consist in prescribing purgatives and a diet in the composition of which sweet, cooling, and fatty or albuminous matters largely enter.

classical.establishes: Charaka's criterion is tolerance, not speed: tīkṣṇa agni is 'sarvāpacāra-saha' — it withstands all dietary abuse. This is a genuinely different criterion from Sushruta's 'digests a heavy meal fast'.
classical.quote: तत्र तीक्ष्णोऽग्निः सर्वापचारसहः ... पित्तलानां तु पित्ताभिभूते ह्यग्न्यधिष्ठाने तीक्ष्णा भवन्त्यग्नयः

classical.establishes: The harm mechanism: a keen fire with insufficient fuel dries up the dhātus. Kaviratna's English for the same verse (his v.49): 'If, when its force or energy is great, it does not get sufficient fuel (in the shape of food and drink), it consumes the dhatus.'
classical.quote: तीक्ष्णो मन्देन्धनो धातून् विशोषयति पावकः॥५०॥

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa's pitta attribution and speed criterion. NAMASTE cites Ah.Sa.3/75 for tīkṣṇāgni, matching.
classical.quote: pittābhimūrchite tīkṣṇo mando 'smin kapha-pīḍite || 73 || ... tīkṣṇo vahniḥ pacec chīghram a-samyag api bhojanam || 75 ||
classical.translator: none — no public-domain English translation of Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya exists

distinguishFrom.why: Su.Sū.35.24 makes atyagni the intensified continuation of tīkṣṇāgni, not a separate type. NAMASTE codes them separately (DB-3 vs DB-4) and WHO puts the disorder entry under atyagni (ITA-5.11.2) while keeping tīkṣṇāgni as a state (ITA-2.6.9). Three sources, three treatments of the same boundary.

Hunger is a consequence; tīkṣṇāgni is defined by what happens to the food, not by the appetite. Bhishagratna's own footnote at this chapter insists on the distinction and then blurs it by glossing atyagni as 'voracious appetite'.
Often equated in clinical writing. ICD-11 TM2 has a separate SM3A Hyperacidity disorder; no source I retrieved equates it with tīkṣṇāgni.

Ca.Vi.6.12 says pitta-predominant persons tend to tīkṣṇāgni, but constitution and current agni state are different variables (PMID 35101333 treats them as an association to be tested, not an identity).

mistranslations.why: Directly inverts the classical valence. Su.Sū.35.25 lists tīkṣṇāgni as a cause of pittaja diseases and Ca.Ci.15.50 says it consumes the tissues. Only samāgni is the healthy state.

Charaka's criterion is tolerance of dietary abuse, not speed; Sushruta's is speed. 'Fast metabolism' picks one of two classical criteria without saying so, and also implies systemic basal metabolism rather than digestive performance.
A popular biomedical equation with no support in any source I retrieved, and one that cannot account for tīkṣṇāgni being a normal constitutional variant in pitta-predominant persons.

openQuestions: Is atyagni a distinct diagnosis or a severity grade of tīkṣṇāgni? WHO, NAMASTE and Sushruta imply different answers.
Does Ca.Ci.15.219-221 (cited by NAMASTE for atyagni/bhasmaka) actually contain that material?
Is there a physiological correlate — gastric emptying, appetite hormone — that has been tested against tīkṣṇāgni?

classical.establishes: Mahābhūta composition of tikta (vāyu + ākāśa). Sanskrit as retrieved: ...वाय्वाकाशातिरिक्तत्वात्तिक्तः... ||४०|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya).
classical.quote: From a preponderance of the attributes of Wind and Ether arises the taste called Bitter.

classical.verse: Standard 26.43 sub-section 5 per carakasamhitaonline (which prints '(५)' after this paragraph and ||४३|| after the whole six-rasa block; Trikamji may number the block 26.42, not checked); Kaviratna's printed number is OCR'd as '85', but the preceding aphorism reads '84' (for katu, where 64 is expected) and the following kashaya aphorism reads '67', so his print is most likely 65 (unverified against the page image)
classical.establishes: The karma and gunas of tikta rasa (rūkṣa, śīta, laghu). Sanskrit as retrieved: तिक्तो रसः स्वयमरोचिष्णुरप्यरोचकघ्नो विषघ्नः क्रिमिघ्नो मूर्च्छादाहकण्डूकुष्ठतृष्णाप्रशमनस्त्वङ्मांसयोः स्थिरीकरणो ज्वरघ्नो दीपनः पाचनः स्तन्यशोधनो लेखनः क्लेदमेदोवसामज्जलसीकापूयस्वेदमूत्रपुरीषपित्तश्लेष्मोपशोषणो रूक्षः शीतो लघुश्च| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya). 'leprosy' is Kaviratna's rendering of kuṣṭha; 'puss' is OCR.
classical.quote: The Bitter taste is so disagreeable as to produce a disgust for itself, but nevertheless it cures disgust for food. It destroys the action of poisons. It is anthelmintic. It alleviates swoons, burning sensation of the skin, itching, leprosy, and thirst. It causes the skin and the flesh to become tough. It is destructive of fevers. It promotes or sharpens the appetite. It assists the digestion of undigested food. It improves the qualities of the milk in the breast. It removes bad humours and altered constituents of the body by thinning them gradually and thus clearing the system of them. It dries up phlegmonous secretions, fat, serum (or marrow of the flesh), marrow of the bones, saliva, puss, sweat, urine, stools, bile, and phlegm. Its attributes are dry, cool, and light.

classical.establishes: Tikta has kaṭu vipāka. Sanskrit as retrieved: कटुतिक्तकषायाणां विपाकः प्रायशः कटुः| अम्लोऽम्लं पच्यते स्वादुर्मधुरं लवणस्तथा||५८|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya).
classical.quote: Of the Pungent, the Bitter, and the Astringent, the change, upon assimilation, is generally Pungent. The Sour taste changes into the Sour. The Sweet and the Saline change into the Sweet.

classical.verse: Sanskrit verse number not established (Bhishagratna prints none)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's perceptual definition (lakṣaṇa) of tikta; the same chapter states 'The specific attributes of air and sky predominate in a bitter taste', 'The tastes such as sweet, bitter and astringent are cold in their properties' and 'The pungent, astringent and bitter ones are dry and light', agreeing with Charaka on bhūta composition and gunas.
classical.quote: A taste, which gives rise to a sort of sucking sensation at the throat, removes the slimy character of the cavity of the mouth, gives rise to the appearance of goose-flesh on the skin, and increases the relish for food, is called bitter (Tikta).
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Sushruta's karma of tikta, closely parallel to Charaka's; 'brings on a sense of general languor' has no obvious counterpart in Charaka and may reflect a variant reading or translator's gloss.
classical.quote: A bitter taste serves to restore the natural relish of a person for food and brings on a sense of general languor. It is a good appetiser, and acts as a good purifying agent (in respect of ulcers, etc.), and proves curative in itches and urticaria. It removes thirst, swoon and fever, purifies mother's milk, and is possessed of the virtue of drying up urine, ordure, mucous, fat and pus, etc.

classical.establishes: Tikta heads the three rasas that subdue Kapha and is among the three that subdue Pitta. Reference only.
classical.quote: tatrādyā mārutaṃ ghnanti trayas tiktādayaḥ kapham || 15 || kaṣāya-tikta-madhurāḥ pittam anye tu kurvate |

distinguishFrom.why: Pungent; shares kaṭu vipāka and vāyu composition with tikta but is uṣṇa, whereas tikta is śīta.
Astringent; also rūkṣa and śīta with kaṭu vipāka, and Sushruta Su.40 shows a kaṣāya taste 'transformed into a bitter one', so the two are routinely confused in secondary drug lists.
Bitter taste in the mouth as a symptom (WHO AF2267, AF2269), not the rasa of a substance.
WHO DG0352 sense 2 (Parpaṭa); also Tiktaka ghrita etc.

mistranslations.why: Lifts one karma (viṣaghna, lekhana) into the definition; classically tikta is defined by taste perception and elemental composition.

mistranslations.rendering: leprosy (for kuṣṭha in the tikta karma list)
mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's Edwardian nosology; kuṣṭha covers skin disease broadly.

Sanskrit source for Bhishagratna's 'general languor'.

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) numbering 11/34 (enumeration) and 11/35 (elaboration), read from the Devanagari on carakasamhitaonline.com. Kaviratna prints his own numbers 29 and (OCR-read) 36, probably 30, AFTER the respective aphorisms; the two systems are recorded side by side and NOT converted.
classical.establishes: That Charaka names three upastambhas (food, sleep, brahmacarya) which, when properly observed, keep the body endowed with strength, complexion and growth throughout life. Kaviratna's 'restraint of the senses' for brahmacarya is a translator's choice; his footnote gloss ('judicious indulgence or use of our faculties and powers') is a note, not the text. Sanskrit seen (Trikamji 11/35): 'त्रय उपस्तम्भा इति- आहारः, स्वप्नो, ब्रह्मचर्यमिति; एभिस्त्रिभिर्युक्तियुक्तैरुपस्तब्धमुपस्तम्भैः शरीरं बलवर्णोपचयोपचितमनुवर्तते यावदायुः'. Note the Sanskrit uses svapna (sleep), not nidrā; NAMASTE and most textbooks substitute nidrā.
classical.quote: There are three stays (of the body) ; three kinds of strength ; three kinds of causes of disease ; three kinds of disease ; three seats of disease ; three kinds of physicians ; and lastly three kinds of medicines.*29  The three stays (of the body regarded as a column) are eating, sleep, and restraint of the senses. In consequence of the three stays (mentioned above) supporting the body, the latter receives accession of strength and complexion and nourishment. As long as a man lives, he should attend to the causes that support life. Long life becomes his who does not indulge in practices that are injurious to the body. Instructions are being offerred in respect of causes that support and lengthen life.36  [Translator's footnote:] * The word 'upastambha' is used to express the stays which support a column. This sentence is elaborated and explained in the next.— T.

distinguishFrom.term: tristhūṇa / the three doshas as pillars
distinguishFrom.why: Vāta, pitta and kapha are the body's primary 'pillars' (sthūṇa) in the classical metaphor; āhāra, svapna and brahmacarya are upa-stambha, the subsidiary props. Modern writing that calls both 'three pillars' blurs this; the 'sub-' in upastambha is doing real work. The Sushruta locus usually cited for tristhūṇa was not verified in this gathering.

Listed in the very next aphorism of Charaka Su. 11 (Kaviratna 31; Trikamji 11/36) and routinely confused with the three upastambhas in student notes because both are 'three' lists from the same tristhana enumeration (Trikamji 11/34).

The sources themselves disagree: NAMASTE SAT-J.4 'celibacy ... avoidance of sexual act physically, mentally & verbally in all ways'; WHO ITA-10.2.1 'moderation in sensual indulgence including sexual activity'; Kaviratna 'restraint of the senses'. The lexicon should record the spread rather than pick one.

Charaka's Sanskrit in 11/35 reads svapna; NAMASTE, WHO's description and almost all textbooks say nidrā. Both mean sleep here, but a reader searching the Sanskrit for 'nidrā' in this verse will not find it.

mistranslations.why: Upastambha means a subsidiary support (upa-), of the body (śarīra), not of the science. 'Pillars of Ayurveda' is a slogan, not a translation, and it collides with the English phrase's use for other triads (see PMIDs 33528692, 22408293).

mistranslations.rendering: the three pillars of health (as if primary)
mistranslations.why: Drops upa-; the classical metaphor has the doshas as the main pillars and these three as the props that hold the column up. Kaviratna's 'stays' and NAMASTE's 'sub-pillars' preserve this; 'pillars' alone does not.

mistranslations.rendering: celibacy (as the only meaning of brahmacarya in this context)
mistranslations.why: At least two standards (WHO, Kaviratna) render it as regulated or moderated conduct rather than abstinence; presenting 'celibacy' as the settled meaning hides a live disagreement.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's second printed number is OCR-read as '36' but is almost certainly '30' (sequence 29, 3x, 31); a human should check the scan (Lesson XI, p. 16 of that fascicule).
Whether Ashtanga Hridaya or Sushruta use the exact compound trayopastambha was not checked; most secondary sources attribute the term to Charaka Su. 11 only.
The WHO text extraction garbled Devanagari (rendered 'रियोपसतमभः'); the Devanagari recorded here comes from carakasamhitaonline and NAMASTE, not from the WHO PDF.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's scheme is arguably a tetrad, not a triad: rakta is given equal standing with the three doṣas as constitutive of a living organism. Any record that presents 'tridosha' as the unanimous classical position is overstating it.
classical.quote: There can be no organism without Vayu, Pitta, Kapha and blood, which are necessary to constantly maintain its integrity.

classical.establishes: The triad is framed cosmologically as well as physiologically, which is the aspect the 2025 IJME critique calls conjectural.
classical.quote: The vital humours (Vayu, Pitta and Kapha) maintain the integrity of the animated organism by creating, assimilating and diffusing strength in the same way as the moon, the sun, and the winds maintain the integrity of the terrestrial globe.

classical.establishes: Charaka's canonical enumeration. The word used is doṣasaṅgraha ('the collection of doṣas'), not tridoṣa; the compound tridoṣa is later and more common in commentaries and in modern usage than in this verse.
classical.quote: वायुः पित्तं कफश्चोक्तः शारीरो दोषसङ्ग्रहः| / vāyuḥ pittaṁ kaphaścōktaḥ śārīrō dōṣasaṅgrahaḥ|

distinguishFrom.why: A Samkhya psychological/cosmological triad. Two of its members (rajas, tamas) are the mānasa doṣas, which produces a genuine overlap, but sattva is never a doṣa and the triads are not parallel.

Sannipāta is a disease in which all three doṣas are simultaneously vitiated. 'Tridoshic' used of a disease means sannipātaja; used of a person it means a balanced prakṛti. English usage runs the two together constantly.
A constitutional category, not the theory. Saying someone 'is tridosha' is a prakṛti claim.

distinguishFrom.term: Siddha Mukkuṟṟam (Vaḷi, Aẕal, Aiyam) and Unani Akhlāṭ
distinguishFrom.why: ICD-11 TM2 places all three triads in one block with parallel English labels. The labels were chosen to work across three systems, so an ICD-11 English rendering is not evidence about the Ayurvedic term specifically.
Sushruta Sutrasthana 21 gives blood equal constitutive standing. 'Tridosha' is Charaka's framing generalised backwards over Sushruta.

mistranslations.why: Same Galenic problem as for doṣa, compounded: the Greek scheme has four, and the pairing readers reach for (blood/phlegm/yellow bile/black bile) is not the Ayurvedic set.
Confuses tridoṣa with prakṛti classification, and silently drops the two-, three- and seven-fold combination types the texts actually enumerate.
No classical or standardised warrant; 'energy' is not a category in the texts, which speak of guṇas and karmas.

mistranslations.rendering: tridosha theory as a unanimous classical doctrine
mistranslations.why: Not strictly a mistranslation but a framing error: Sushruta Sutrasthana 21 makes it a tetrad with blood, and the compound tridoṣa does not appear in Charaka Sutrasthana 1/57.

openQuestions: When does the compound tridoṣa first appear in the Brihat Trayi as against the commentaries? Not established here.
Whether WHO ISTA anywhere defines the relation between tridoṣa and rakta, given Sushruta's tetrad.

classical.establishes: The locus classicus. The word trisūtraṃ occurs here, and the verse specifies its content in the compound hetu-liṅga-auṣadha-jñānam, 'knowledge of cause, sign and remedy', described as the refuge of both the healthy and the sick (svasthātura-parāyaṇam), eternal and auspicious, first known by the Grandsire.
classical.quote: हेतुलिङ्गौषधज्ञानं स्वस्थातुरपरायणम्| त्रिसूत्रं शाश्वतं पुण्यं बुबुधे यं पितामहः||२४||

classical.establishes: The immediately following verse, using triskandha (three-trunked) of āyurveda rather than trisūtra. The two terms are adjacent but not identical and this pair of verses is the evidence for treating them as distinct.
classical.quote: सोऽनन्तपारं त्रिस्कन्धमायुर्वेदं महामतिः| यथावदचिरात् सर्वं बुबुधे तन्मना मुनिः||२५||

classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English for both verses, showing Kaviratna's 'causes, symptoms, and drugs' for hetu-liṅga-auṣadha and his separate renderings of trisūtra ('three aphorisms') and triskandha ('three trunks'). Hyphenation and the split '2  4' for the verse number are OCR; reproduced as retrieved.
classical.quote: Fraught  with  the  knowledge  of  causes,  symp¬  toms,  and  drugs,  the  refuge  both  of  the  hale  and  the  sick,  consisting  of  three  aphorisms,  eternal  and  auspicious,  which  the  Grandsire  had  (first)  discovered,23  that  limitless  and  shoreless  Science  of  Life,  of  three  trunks,  the  intelligent  ascetic,  with  mind  devoted  to  it,  soon  enough  duly  learnt  in  its  entirety, 2  4

distinguishFrom.why: The adjacent verse's term (Su 1.25). Skandha is a trunk/section; sūtra is a thread or aphorism. WHO merges them under one term ID; Charaka uses them in consecutive verses of different metaphors. Whether they denote the same triad is a question the sources leave open.
The three means of examination (aptopadesha, pratyaksha, anumana) is a different triad about how knowledge is obtained. Trisūtra is about the structure of the subject matter.
Other numbered triads in Charaka Sutrasthana that are routinely confused with trisūtra in teaching material.

A fivefold diagnostic scheme (nidana, purvarupa, rupa, upashaya, samprapti). Hetu and linga appear in both, which is why the two are conflated, but nidāna pañcaka is a diagnostic procedure and trisūtra is a description of the whole science.

mistranslations.why: Reads sūtra as a text-unit and suggests there are three specific aphorisms somewhere in the Samhita. Kaviratna's 'three aphorisms' has the same problem, and is recorded because it is what the quotable translator wrote, not because it is right.
Confuses trisūtra with tristhūṇa/trayopastambha (the three supports of life: āhāra, nidrā, brahmacarya), an entirely different triad. This is the commonest error attached to this term.
Substitutes prognosis for liṅga (sign/symptom). The Sanskrit compound is hetu-liṅga-auṣadha and contains no term for prognosis.

openQuestions: Whether trisūtra and triskandha denote the same triad. Su 1.24 and 1.25 use them of the same body of knowledge in consecutive verses but with different metaphors, and I did not retrieve a commentator on the point.
Whether the triad is actually stated in Sushruta and Ashtanga Hridaya as the 2026 IAMJ title claims. I did not verify this and it should not be repeated without checking.
Whether NAMASTE codes trisūtra.

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for the Sushruta triad; the same chapter continues with examination by hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell and interrogation (sixfold). distinguishFrom.term: trividha roga-viśeṣa-vijñāna (āptopadeśa, pratyakṣa, anumāna) — Ch. Vi. 4.3
distinguishFrom.why: Also called 'trividha pariksha' in textbooks, but it is a theory of valid knowledge sources (testimony, perception, inference), not a bedside sequence. Darśana and sparśana both fall under pratyakṣa; praśna is closer to āptopadeśa/anumāna. A record that cites Charaka for darśana-sparśana-praśna is mis-citing.
Sushruta's sixfold examination by the five senses plus questioning; WHO IST lists it separately as ITA-4.7.3. The threefold triad is a compression of it, not a synonym.

distinguishFrom.term: caturvidha parīkṣā / pramāṇa (pratyakṣa, anumāna, āptopadeśa, yukti) — Ch. Su. 11
distinguishFrom.why: Charaka's fourfold means of examination adds yukti (reasoning); epistemological, not bedside.

distinguishFrom.term: aṣṭasthāna / aṣṭavidha parīkṣā (nāḍī, mūtra, mala, jihvā, śabda, sparśa, dṣk, ākṛti)
distinguishFrom.why: Later (Yogaratnākara-era) eightfold examination of specific sites, WHO ITA-4.7.4; frequently conflated with the threefold method in popular writing.
Tenfold examination of the patient (prakṛti, vikṛti, sāra, saṁhanana, ...), WHO ITA-4.7.5; a different axis (what to assess) from trividha (how to assess).
A.H. Su. 1.22 pairs the threefold ROGI (patient) examination with the fivefold ROGA (disease) examination; the two halves of the verse are often merged in summaries.

mistranslations.why: Sparśana is touch/palpation; percussion and auscultation are additions from modern clinical method, found on textbook websites but not in the Sanskrit.

mistranslations.rendering: 'Trividha pariksha = Charaka's three-fold examination by inspection, palpation, interrogation'
mistranslations.why: Charaka's trividha (Vi. 4.3) is āptopadeśa-pratyakṣa-anumāna. The see-touch-ask triad is Vāgbhaṭa's (A.H. Su. 1.22) and, in prose, Suśruta's (Su.Su. 10).
WHO IST's choice; acceptable, but praśna is simply 'questioning/interrogation'. Not wrong, just softer than the classical sense.

openQuestions: Which printed Sanskrit edition siva.sh follows for Sushruta verse numbering (10.4) is not stated; confirm against the Trikamji/Nirnaya Sagar edition before publishing a verse number.
Does Ashtanga Sangraha carry a parallel verse to A.H. Su. 1.22? Not checked.

classical.establishes: Caraka himself switches to ambu-vāhīni in the metrical section — direct textual warrant that udakavaha and ambuvaha are the same channel.

classical.establishes: Suśruta's roots are identical to Caraka's (palate + kloma) — a rare full agreement between the two texts. ('pieicing' is an OCR artefact of the retrieved page for 'piercing'.)
classical.quote: There are two water-carrying (Udaka-vaha) ducts or channels which have their roots in the palate and the Kloma, and a pieicing of any of these makes the patient thirsty and ends in his instantaneous death (z. e , within seven days).

distinguishFrom.why: kloma is the root organ, not the channel. Its identification is itself unsettled: WHO says 'usually commensurate with the gallbladder, pancreas and right lung'; Bhishagratna leaves it untranslated; other authors read it as lung, pancreas, or trachea (WHO separately codes klomanāḍī as 'Trachea', ITA.3.11.7).
Both are fluid channels; udakavaha governs water/thirst homeostasis and is rooted in palate+kloma, while rasavaha carries the nutrient fluid and is rooted in the heart.
Modern writers mapping udakavaha to 'fluid balance' slide into renal physiology; mūtravaha is separately enumerated with basti and vaṅkṣaṇa as roots.
Not a different channel — an attested synonym, used by Caraka himself at Vi.5/11 and recorded by WHO and NAMASTE as an alternative Sanskrit form.

mistranslations.why: A common modern equation with no classical warrant; the roots given are palate and kloma and the cardinal sign is thirst, not oedema or lymph stasis.
WHO itself hedges ('usually commensurate with the gallbladder, pancreas and right lung'). Stating a single organ presents an unresolved identification as settled.
Bhishagratna's own English is internally contradictory — he immediately glosses it '(z. e , within seven days)'. Quoting 'instantaneous death' without the gloss misreports the source.

openQuestions: What is kloma? Until this is settled the channel cannot be mapped to any biomedical system.
Why does Suśruta rate piercing of this channel as rapidly fatal when the vitiation signs in Caraka are merely dryness and thirst?

classical.establishes: Sushruta defines udāna by DIRECTION (upward) and by DISEASE TERRITORY (ūrdhvajatru, above the clavicles), not by seat, and calls it pavanottama, the foremost of the vāyus. Corresponding Sanskrit, cross-checked at a separate URL: 'उदानो नाम यस्तूर्ध्वमुपैति पवनोत्तमः ||१४|| तेन भाषितगीतादिविशेषोऽभिप्रवर्तते | ऊर्ध्वजत्रुगतान् रोगान् करोति च विशेषतः ||१५||'.
classical.quote: The most important of the vital Vayus, which courses (sends its vibrations) upward, is called the Udana. It produces speech, song, etc. In its deranged state it brings on diseases which are specifically confined to regions lying above the clavicles. 8.

classical.establishes: Charaka seats udāna in nābhi (navel), uras (chest) and kaṇṭha (throat); its karma is vākpravṛtti (initiation of speech), prayatna (effort), ūrjas (vigour), bala (strength) and varṇa (complexion). Note that Charaka gives udāna a navel-to-throat seat, whereas Sushruta gives it none.

classical.establishes: Names udāna as one of the five in a lawfully quotable English Charaka. Gives it no seat or function.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata seats udāna in the chest (uraḥ sthānam udānasya) and has it move in nose, navel and throat (nāsā-nābhi-galān); functions given at the start of 12.6 are speech, effort, vigour, strength, complexion and MEMORY (smṛti). The inclusion of smṛti is Vagbhata's addition over Charaka Ci.28.7. Sanskrit mūla and verse numbering verified on the retrieved page; not quoted, as Ashtanga Hridaya has no public-domain English translation.

classical.establishes: 5.27-28 place udāna at the throat (kaṇṭha). Separately and more strikingly, 5.45 states that the LUNGS (phupphusa) are the ādhāra (support/seat) of udāna vāyu — a claim found in neither Charaka nor Vagbhata, and the clearest classical basis for the modern 'udāna = respiratory' reading. Sanskrit mūla and verse numbers verified on the retrieved page; not quoted, as Sharngadhara has no public-domain English translation.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: The hardest pair in the set, and the texts do not agree on the boundary. Charaka Ci.28.6-7 gives both a chest-and-throat presence; Ashtanga Hridaya Su.12.4-5 puts prāṇa in the head moving to chest/throat and udāna in the chest moving to nose/navel/throat — i.e. they cross. Sushruta gives prāṇa a seat (mouth) and udāna none. Speech is the one function consistently udāna's across all three.

In the yogic scheme udāna is the ascending current used in meditation and at death, associated with the throat cakra. Classical Ayurveda ties it to speech, effort, strength and complexion. The shared name and the shared 'upward' direction make the two collapse into each other in popular writing.

Ashtanga Hridaya Su.12.6 puts the udāna function list and the vyāna definition in the SAME verse, so careless citation attributes vyāna's 'seated in the heart, whole-body-ranging, great velocity' to udāna. Check where the verse break falls before citing AH Su.12.6 for either.

WHO renders udāna 'Ascending vata' and never says respiratory; Kerala Tourism says 'Breathing is controlled by this Vata'. Respiration (śvāsa) belongs to prāṇa at Charaka Ci.28.6. The respiratory reading of udāna rests on Sharngadhara PK 5.45 (lungs), not on Charaka or Sushruta.

distinguishFrom.term: the act of vomiting or emesis (vamana)
distinguishFrom.why: Charaka Ci.28 prescribes upward-moving therapy for udāna morbidity, which leads some writers to define udāna AS emesis. The therapy is not the definition.

mistranslations.why: Neither is in any retrieved classical locus. Both are later organ- or cakra-substitutions imported from modern anatomy and from yoga respectively.

Kaviratna's own footnote says udāna 'rises up either in the form of eructations or passes into the head' — but that is his gloss on a yogic list, and Charaka Ci.28.6 assigns belching (udgāra) and respiration to PRĀṆA, not udāna. The breath reading is yogic, not Ayurvedic.

From Bhishagratna's 1911 footnote, 'the Udana with that of the one which is situated in the speech centre'. A colonial-era neuroanatomical equation. The same footnote is internally corrupt: it then names Udana a SECOND time as 'the energy of the Motor-Sensory Nerves', a slot that context shows must belong to Vyana. Anyone citing that footnote is citing a typo.
Wellness-register expansions of prayatna and ūrjas. 'Utsāha' (enthusiasm) is listed by WHO as a function of vata as a whole (ITA-2.1.1.8), not of udāna specifically.

openQuestions: Does Dalhana supply a seat for udāna where Sushruta gives none, and does it match Charaka's nābhi-uras-kaṇṭha?
Is Sharngadhara PK 5.45 (phupphusa as seat of udāna) the earliest text to link udāna to the lungs, and did WHO consider it?
Why does WHO's 'Ascending vata' description include effort and strength but omit complexion (varṇa) and memory (smṛti), both of which are in Charaka Ci.28.7 / AH Su.12.6?
Does NAMASTE assign udāna vāta a code, and does its English term match WHO's 'Ascending vata'?

classical.verse: 16 in Kaviratna's marginal numbering; carakasamhitaonline cites this content as Cha. Sa. Chikitsa Sthana 15/17
classical.establishes: The locus classicus for the upadhātu list, WITHOUT the word upadhātu. Milk and menstrual blood from rasa; vessels from rakta; vasā and the six skin layers from māṃsa; tendons from medas. Kaviratna frames it as something 'especial' that happens in women, which the standard modern presentation does not.
classical.quote: As regards women, from 'Rasa' are both milk and blood ; from blood are ducts large and small ; from flesh is fat or adeps and six varieties of skin ; and from adeps is the origin of the tendons and muscles.

classical.establishes: Kaviratna's own reading, that the whole upadhātu passage is about what is additional in women. Whether the mula supports that restriction is an open question and it matters, because modern tables present the upadhātus as universal. OCR renders 'flesh' as 'jlesh'; corrected here only in that the intended word is obvious.
classical.quote: The growth of the 'dhatus', as explained in 15, is true in the case of both males and females. In the case of the latter, something especial happens ; that is stated in 16. Thus from blood, besides flesh, are the ducts

classical.establishes: That the text explicitly separates the prasāda transformations (the upadhātu list) from the kiṭṭa list (the malas). The sentence 'The above are the transformations of Prasada' is the textual boundary between the two categories, and it is the strongest evidence in this record set that upadhātu and mala are distinct in the mula even though the mula names neither.
classical.quote: The above are the transformations of 'Prasada.' That which Is called the 'Kitta' (refuse) of the food taken, consists of stools and urine ; the 'Kitta' of 'Rasa is phlegm ; that of blood is bile ; that of flesh are the filths of the body, including the secretions (from the nose, the ears, &c.) ; while sweet forms the 'Kitta' of adeps,

classical.verse: prose section, corresponds to the mula verses on bodily principles
classical.establishes: That Sushruta treats ārtava and stanya alongside the doṣas, dhātus and malas as things whose increase and decrease must be assessed - i.e. as bodily principles in their own right - without assigning them to a named intermediate category.
classical.quote: The Artavam (menstrual blood) is endued with the same properties as its arterial namesake, and is one of the essential factors in a woman which makes impregnation possible. ... The breast-milk in its turn tends to bring about an expansion of the mammae (of a woman), and maintains the life of her child (by supplying it with the necessary and nutritive element of food). These Vayu, etc. should be duly preserved in their normal condition.

classical.establishes: Full kṣaya descriptions for ārtava and stanya, parallel in form to those given for the seven dhātus. Structurally they are treated as members of the same list.
classical.quote: In the case of loss or waste of the catamenial flow, the menses do not appear at the appointed time or are scanty. The vagina seems stuffed and painful. ... The loss or waste of breast-milk is characterised by a shrunken condition of the mammas, and suppression or scanty secretion of the fluid.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's treatment of vasā, which WHO classes as the upadhātu of māṃsa (ITA-2.3.5), but which Sushruta discusses within the medas section.
classical.quote: This fatty matter (Vasa) predominates in the female organism and produces its peculiar softness, beauty and pleasing shape, causes the growth of scanty but soft hair on its surface.

classical.establishes: Cited by carakasamhitaonline as carrying an alternative view on stanya. I did not retrieve the passage itself and assert no verse.

distinguishFrom.why: The defining difference, per WHO ITA-2.3.1, is that upadhātus 'do not undergo further transformation'. They are formed from a dhātu but do not feed the next one. Nothing else in the definition distinguishes them.

The waste fraction (kiṭṭa). Charaka Chikitsasthana 15 lists the two separately and marks the boundary with the sentence 'The above are the transformations of Prasada.' Calling upadhātus 'by-products' collapses exactly this distinction.
The technical term for the waste fraction produced at each stage. Upadhātus come from the prasāda fraction, malas from the kiṭṭa fraction.
Charaka Sutrasthana 28 names 'the essence of the Dhatus' as what supplies the sense organs. Whether that is the same category as upadhātu is not established anywhere retrieved.

Classed by WHO as an upadhātu of rasa (ITA-2.3.3), but Sushruta 14.14 makes ārtava the female terminus of the whole chain, parallel to śukra. The two placements are not compatible and both are in retrievable sources.

Also derived from the dhātus without being one of them, but classed as their sāra rather than as an upadhātu. WHO places ojas at ITA-2.2.25, inside the fundamental-components section, not in the supportive-components section.

mistranslations.why: 'Secondary' imports a ranking the category does not assert. The criterion is that these products do not transform further, not that they matter less. Breast milk and menstrual blood are hardly secondary in the tradition's own reckoning.
That is mala. The mula distinguishes prasāda transformations from kiṭṭa explicitly, and this rendering erases the distinction.
Same ranking problem, compounded by 'tissue'.

mistranslations.rendering: citing upadhātu to a samhita verse
mistranslations.why: The most damaging error available here. The word occurs zero times in Kaviratna's Charaka and zero times in both Bhishagratna Sushruta volumes. The CONTENT is at Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.16-17; the TERM is later. Any citation of the form 'upadhātu, Ca.Ci.15.16' asserts something the retrieved sources do not support.

openQuestions: When and where upadhātu becomes a fixed technical term is not established. It is absent from both public-domain samhita translations and present as a headword in WHO ISTA 2022. The commentaries (Chakrapanidatta, Dalhana) and the Laghu Trayi are where to look, and none of them is quotable in English.

Whether the Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.16 list is universal or, as Kaviratna's footnote reads it, specific to women, is a real interpretive fork with consequences for every modern upadhātu table. It cannot be settled without the Sanskrit and a commentary.

The membership of the list is unstable across sources: WHO names seven in a prose description but gives entries to only four. Charaka's Ci.15.16 yields milk, menstrual blood, vessels, skin (six layers), vasā and tendons. Whether tvak and snāyu belong, and to which parent dhātu, differs between WHO and Charaka.
Whether ārtava is an upadhātu of rasa (WHO) or the female terminus of the chain (Su.Su.14.14) is directly contradictory between two retrievable sources and is not reconciled by either.
Whether Charaka's dhātu-prasāda (the essence of the dhātus supplying the senses, Ca.Su.28) is the same category as upadhātu is undetermined.

classical.establishes: Charaka's definition, with three structural elements: the object (auṣadha, āhāra, vihāra — drug, diet AND conduct, not drug alone); the relation (viparīta to hetu or vyādhi, or viparītārthakārī); and the criterion (sukhānubandha, relief following). Nothing in the verse says the purpose is treatment. Retrieved and string-matched by me.
classical.quote: उपशयः पुनर्हेतुव्याधिविपरीतानां विपरीतार्थकारिणां चौषधाहारविहाराणामुपयोगः सुखानुबन्धः||१०||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English. 'upagaya', the hyphen in 'prac-tices' and the stray quote marks before 'to cause' are all scan artifacts, preserved verbatim. Kaviratna's aphorism number here is 4 where the Sanskrit edition numbers the same sentence 10.
classical.quote: In this connection, 'upagaya', again, is the prescribing, followed by happiness (or recovery) as the result, of medicines, diet, and prac- tices, that are contrary '"to cause and disease, or contrary, as regards their effects, to the same.

classical.establishes: THE KEY DISAMBIGUATION, in the public domain and explicit: upaśaya is diagnostic, not therapeutic. The same footnote supplies worked examples on the same page: dry ginger in cold/phlegmatic fever as viparīta to cause; Stephania hernandifolia in diarrhoea as viparīta to disease; Randia dumetorum fruit in small doses checking nausea as viparītārthakārī; milk in measured quantity in certain diarrhoeas. Retrieved and string-matched by me.
classical.quote: The object of 'upacaya' is the ascertainment of disease, with a view to its cure, by experi- mental prescriptions in respect of drugs and diet and practices. It is one of the five methods of diagnosis or ascertainment of disease, and should not be mistaken for treatment. — T.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata adds what Charaka does not: upaśaya is identified with SĀTMYA for the given disease, and anupaśaya with asātmya. Verse numbers and Devanagari mūla sighted on the retrieved page (6 defines the viparīta/viparītārthakārī use, 7 carries the sātmya equation and the anupaśaya clause); not quoted per the rule for this text.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

classical.establishes: Madhavakara follows Vagbhata including the sātmya/asātmya equation. The same retrieved page records that Madhava Nidana compiles the pañcaka for each disease 'with exception of Upashaya and Anupashaya' — these two are defined in chapter 1 and then never supplied disease by disease.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: Kaviratna's footnote states it outright: upaśaya 'should not be mistaken for treatment'. The same drug, diet or conduct is given, but the endpoint is a diagnostic inference. WHO's ITA-4.5.7 calls it 'the trial-and-error method of diagnosis'.

Vagbhata and Madhavakara equate upaśaya with sātmya FOR A GIVEN DISEASE. Elsewhere sātmya means habituation or suitability for a person or region, a constitutional notion. The equation is local to this chapter.

Withdrawal of the causative factor (WHO ITA-9.1.56), prescribed as a treatment principle. If relief follows it is evidence about the nidāna, but the purpose differs: parivarjana aims to cure, upaśaya to find out.

What the patient reports makes them better is history-taking. Charaka's verse specifies the physician's upayoga of an agent chosen for a defined viparīta relation. WHO's own ITA-4.3.2 gloss blurs exactly this line.
Its paired opposite, coded separately at WHO ITA-4.5.15. Not merely the absence of upaśaya; see that record.

A SUBTYPE of upaśaya, not a synonym: an agent not opposite to cause or disease that nonetheless produces the opposite effect. Kaviratna's emetic-fruit-in-small-dose example. WHO codes the variants across ITA-4.5.8 to 4.5.14.
The tempting modern analogue, but an n-of-1 trial is randomised and blinded and aims at treatment effect; upaśaya is neither and aims at classification. Draw the analogy only with that caveat.

mistranslations.why: Directly contradicted by Kaviratna's public-domain footnote. Relief is the readout, not the goal.

Reduces a physician-initiated probe to a line in the history. WHO itself uses the looser phrase at ITA-4.3.2 while defining the term strictly at ITA-4.5.6, so the error has a standards-body precedent.
Half right: the intervention is therapeutic in form, the endpoint diagnostic. WHO's 'trial-and-error method of diagnosis' is more accurate.
In oncology and psychiatry that is an outcome measure. Upaśaya is a classification device. WHO's head term avoids the trap by naming the inference rather than the response.
Seen in sceptical writing. Nothing in the classical definition concerns expectancy; the classification turns on the viparīta relation of the agent.

openQuestions: Whether Sushruta treats upaśaya at all. I full-text searched Bhishagratna's Sūtrasthāna volume and did not locate a definition; Sushruta's framework is the six kriyākāla and upaśaya may simply be absent. That negative needs confirming properly rather than by keyword search of an OCR text.

How many subtypes the classical texts give. Kaviratna's examples imply six (three viparīta plus three viparītārthakārī); WHO codes entries across ITA-4.5.8 to 4.5.14; some textbooks teach six and some eighteen. The eighteen-fold scheme needs tracing.
Whether WHO's ITA-4.5.11 (viparītārthakārī) is deliberately blank or a production error in the 2022 PDF. ITA-4.5.17 is likewise blank in my extraction, so blank descriptions do occur in the document.
No study reports how long to observe before calling a response, or any sensitivity or specificity for the procedure.

"If duly taken, the Vaji-karana remedies make a man sexually as strong as a horse (Vaji), and enable him to cheerfully satisfy the heat and amorous ardours of young maidens, a fact which has determined the nomenclature of this class of (medicinal) remedies. 2-B." distinguishFrom.why: Charaka Chi.1 pairs them as the two urjaskara (vitalising) therapies for the healthy, but rasayana aims at longevity/tissue quality and vajikarana at shukra and progeny; Kaviratna's note that vrishya drugs 'are also called Rasayana' is a translator's conflation.
Drug-class adjective (aphrodisiac/semen-promoting); PMID 23858267 treats 'Vrishya chikitsa' as a synonym of the branch, which is loose.
WHO ITA-6.2.6.20-21 drug actions (semen-producing, increasing semen); vajikarana is the branch/therapy, of which these are pharmacological components (cf. Bhishagratna's three-kind note).
Kaviratna's footnote records a ritual sense 'bringing an enemy under control'; unrelated to the medical branch.
Modern usage means libido enhancement; Charaka Chi.1.1/9-12 defines the aim as progeny, strength and social standing as much as sexual capacity.

mistranslations.why: Drops the progeny/fertility and strength components explicit in Charaka Chi.1.1/9-12 and WHO 9.9.1 ('male and female fertility').
Imports a psychotherapeutic discipline; vajikarana is primarily dietary-pharmacological with conduct rules.
Non-standard English coinage; also male-only, whereas WHO 9.9.1 includes female fertility.

openQuestions: Whether Sushruta's own text (as opposed to Bhishagratna's note) contains the threefold shukra classification was not checked in Sanskrit.
NAMASTE and ICD-11 TM2 coverage not verified.

classical.verse: Standard 1.4 (Sanskrit only; Kaviratna's archive edition does not extend to Kalpasthana)
classical.establishes: Charaka's definition: removal of dosha by the upward route is called vamana, by the downward route virechana; and both may be called virechana because both purge bodily malas. Sanskrit verbatim from a retrieved numbered edition; no public-domain English available for Kalpasthana.
classical.quote: "तत्र दोषहरणमूर्ध्वभागं वमनसञ्ज्ञकम्, अधोभागं विरेचनसञ्ज्ञकम्; उभयं वा शरीरमलविरेचनाद्विरेचनसञ्ज्ञां लभते||४||"

classical.verse: Bhishagratna section 2; Sanskrit 33.3-4 per siva.sh edition
classical.establishes: Sushruta ranks vamana and virechana as the principal means of dosha removal (nirharana), after stating the general therapeutic maxim (33.3).
classical.quote: Bhishagratna: "The principal maxims to be followed are to augment the loss or deficiency, to pacify the aggravation and reduce the increment of the Doshas and maintain them in a state of healthy equilibrium. Emetics and purgatives are the principal remedies in cleansing the system of all the Doshas (morbific principles). Now hear me, therefore, discourse on the mode of their administration. 2." Sanskrit 33.4: "प्राधान्येन वमनविरेचने वर्तेते निर्हरणे दोषाणाम् । तस्मात्तयोर्विधानमुच्यमानमुपधारय ॥४॥"

classical.establishes: Sequence snehana-svedana-utkleshana before vamana. Bhishagratna's parenthesis '(Kapha-producing)' is his gloss and carries footnote [1] on a variant reading.
classical.quote: Bhishagratna: "An emetic medicine does its fullest action, when given to a man after having applied a Sneha and Sveda (to him) and after having stirred up the Doshas of his body with the help of a soft mucilaginous (Kapha-producing) fluid and emollient food so as to accelerate their easy expulsion from the system 4." Sanskrit: "भवति चात्र- पेशलैर्विविधैरन्नैर्दोषानुत्क्लेश्य देहिनः । स्निग्धस्विन्नाय वमनं दत्तं सम्यक् प्रवर्तते ॥६॥"

classical.establishes: Signs of inadequate (dushchardita) and excessive (ativanta) emesis.
classical.quote: Bhishagratna: "The symptoms of an imperfect emesis are water-brash (Kaphapraseka), sticking secretion or sensation of impurity in the regions of the Hridaya (heart) and itching sensations." Sanskrit: "कफप्रसेकं हृदयाविशुद्धिं कण्डूं च दुश्छर्दितलिङ्गमाहुः । पित्तातियोगं च विसञ्ज्ञतां च हृत्कण्ठपीडामपि चातिवान्ते ॥८॥"

classical.establishes: Contraindications to vamana. Bhishagratna's 'cataract' for timira is a translator's identification.
classical.quote: Bhishagratna: "Emesis or the exhibition of emetics is forbidden in cases of Timira (cataract, upward determination of the Vayu in the body (Urdhva-vata), Gulma, Udavarta, abdominal dropsy, enlargement of the spleen, worms (in the intestines) and urinary complaints, as well as in respect of fatigued, corpulent, thirsty, hungry, emaciated and too old persons and of infants, Kshata- kshina patients and those suffering from a loss of voice and in respect of those also who are of studious habits or are capable of being treated with a strong emetic and that only with the greatest difficulty."

classical.establishes: Charaka classes vamana (with virechana, shirovirechana, niruha) under langhana; important for taxonomy. Standard verse number assumed from Kaviratna's '18' and the chapter sequence but not separately confirmed in Sanskrit.
classical.quoteWithheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

distinguishFrom.why: Downward-route counterpart (Ca.Ka.1.4); Charaka notes both can be called virechana in the wide sense.
Pathological emesis; vamana is induced, staged, with snehana-svedana preparation and samyak signs (Su.Chi.33.6, 33.8).
Umbrella terms; vamana is one of the five, and WHO 6.2.6.10 defines it by reference to preparatory panchakarma.
Charaka Su.22.18 classes vamana under langhana (reducing therapy); it is not a separate upakrama in the sixfold scheme.
Marketing or research glosses for shodhana with no classical equivalent; they obscure the specific route (urdhva) and dosha target (kapha, pitta).

mistranslations.why: Loses the therapeutic apparatus (preparation, dose, samyak/ayoga/atiyoga signs) that defines vamana as karma.
Non-classical; dosha are not 'toxins'.
Translator's gloss for utkleshana foods; the Sanskrit says peshala/various foods that provoke (utkleshya) dosha.

classical.establishes: The five canonical functions of vāta, each named in Sanskrit in the translation itself. Crucially the definition is functional (motion, conduction, propulsion, separation, retention), which is what makes 'wind' inadequate.
classical.quote: The imparting of motion to the body (Praspandana), the carrying of the sensations of the respective sense organs (Udvahana), the passing down of food to its proper receptacles (Purana), the separation of excretions from the assimilated food matter (Viveka), and the retention and evacuation of urine and semen, etc. (Dharana) should be ascribed to the functions of the five kinds of Vayu (nerve force) which support the body.

classical.establishes: Vāta is the agent of prasara for all three doṣas, giving it an asymmetric role in the pathogenesis sequence that the phrase 'one of the three doshas' obscures.
classical.quote: The Vayu, which is possessed of locomotion or extreme mobility, should be looked upon as the cause of their expansion or over-flowing.

classical.establishes: The seven guṇas of vāta in a lawfully quotable English form, together with the viparīta (opposite-quality) treatment principle.
classical.quote: Wind, which may be dry, cold, light, subtile, unstable, clear, keen, is cured by objects which have adverse attributes.

classical.establishes: States the prākṛta/vaikṛta duality for vāta specifically: normal vāta is prāṇa and is responsible for all activity; the same vāta produces disease and death. This is the verse that makes 'vata as pathogen' untenable.
classical.quote: सर्वा हि चेष्टा वातेन स प्राणः प्राणीनां स्मृतः| तेनैव रोगा जायन्ते तेन चैवोपरुध्यते||११८|| / sarvā hi cēṣṭā vātēna sa prāṇaḥ prāṇīnāṁ smr̥taḥ| tēnaiva rōgā jāyantē tēna caivōparudhyatē||118||

distinguishFrom.why: Air as one of the five elements. WHO ISTA says air and space predominate in vāta, i.e. vāta is not identical with the air element but weighted towards it. The texts use vāyu for both, which is the root of the confusion.

Prāṇa is a subtype of vāta (WHO ITA-2.1.1.2) and, per Charaka Sutrasthana 17/118, also a name for vāta in its normal state; in yoga literature prāṇa is a separate and broader concept. Three overlapping senses, routinely merged.
A disease category (the nervous/musculoskeletal disorders of Charaka Chikitsa 28), not the doṣa. 'Vata disorder' in English is ambiguous between vāta-vyādhi and vātaprakopa.
A constitutional type. 'She is vata' is a prakṛti statement; 'her vata is aggravated' is a vikṛti statement.

distinguishFrom.term: vāyu (the deity) and vāta in Vedic usage
distinguishFrom.why: Pre-medical Sanskrit uses vāta for the wind and the wind god. Etymological arguments drawn from Vedic usage do not settle the medical sense.
The five subtypes are not interchangeable with vāta as a whole; ICD-11 and WHO both code them separately (e.g. WHO ITA-5.2.1.3 prāṇavātakopaḥ).

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's rendering and the commonest one. Reduces a functional principle governing motion, sensory conduction and cognition to a gas in the gut; cannot account for prāṇa-vāta governing intellect.
Confuses the doṣa with the mahābhūta. WHO ISTA is explicit that air is only one of two predominant elements in vāta.
Bhishagratna's 1907 gloss. A Victorian neurological identification that the Sanskrit does not support and that no modern standard repeats.
Common in clinical translation from Indian sources; it renders one effect of vitiated apāna as the name of the whole doṣa.

mistranslations.rendering: the air element of the body
mistranslations.why: Same error as 'air', dressed up; it also implies the doṣas map one-to-one onto elements, which none of them do.

openQuestions: Whether NAMASTE renders vāta differently from WHO ISTA; not retrievable.
Whether any published instrument measures a vāta quantity as opposed to classifying vāta prakṛti. Nothing of the kind was located.
