classical.establishes: vayas is a state of the body indexed to elapsed time; three stages bāla, madhya, jīrṇa; bāla runs to sixteen with immature dhātus and kapha predominance, with a sub-stage to thirty. The same verse continues: madhya to sixty with pitta predominance, then jīrṇa to a hundred with vāta predominance.
classical.quote: vayastaścēti kālapramāṇaviśēṣāpēkṣiṇī hi śarīrāvasthā vayō'bhidhīyatē| tadvayō yathāsthūlabhēdēna trividhaṁ- bālaṁ, madhyaṁ, jīrṇamiti| tatra bālamaparipakvadhātumajātavyañjanaṁ sukumāramaklēśasahamasampūrṇabalaṁ ślēṣmadhātuprāyamāṣōḍaśavarṣaṁ||122||

classical.establishes: Public-domain English for Vi 8/122, including the stage boundaries at 16, 30, 60 and 100 years.
classical.quote: That condition of the body which is dependent on the measure of Time (for which the body has existed) is called Age. This Age, according to difference of duration, is of three kinds, viz., Boyhood, Manhood, and Decrepitude. Amongst these, Boyhood is (the period characterised by) immaturity of the constituent elements (of the body), non-appearance of hirsute appendage, delicacy (of constitution both physical and mental), incapacity to bear fatigue (and the pain it brings about), non-development of strength, and predominance of phlegm.

classical.establishes: The stage boundaries are proportional, not absolute: for a person whose estimated lifespan is not a hundred years, the physician rescales the three periods. Kaviratna's footnote works the arithmetic — for a 120-year life, boyhood ends at 36 and manhood at 72. This proportionality is almost never reproduced in modern summaries, which quote 16/30/60/100 as fixed.
classical.quote: In this epoch {kali), the measure of (human) life, is a century. There are men who live more than a hundred years or less than that period. As regards this last class of persons, disregarding all incidents that are abnormal, noting only the diversities of the strength of Nature and the rest, the physician should ascertain the measure of life from the (usual) indications, and divide it into the three periods (named).

classical.establishes: Sushruta gives sex-differentiated maturity ages where Charaka's Vi 8/122 boundaries are undifferentiated. A second independent disagreement between the samhitas on this term. No verse numbers on the retrieved page.
classical.quote: An intelligent physician should regard the organism of a man of twenty-five or of a woman of sixteen years of age, as fully developed in respect of the maturity of the seven fundamental principles of the body such as, serum, blood, etc.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's own examination list includes age among a dozen factors but is not the same list as Charaka Vi 8/94 and is not called daśavidha parīkṣā. Modern writing that presents the ten-fold examination as pan-classical should be checked against this.
classical.quote: A physician should first observe the vital condition (Ayu) of the patient before commencing the medical treatment. After that, the nature of the disease, the country and season of the year in which it has made its appearance, as well as the state of digestion, age, body, strength, disposition, habit, previous medicine, natural temperament and the power of endurance of the patient, etc. should be observed and carefully examined.

distinguishFrom.why: Lifespan, the quantity; vayas is the stage. Sushruta Sutrasthana 35 tells the physician to assess āyu first and lists age separately.

WHO pairs vayaḥ/kālaḥ as one headword, but Vimana 8 distinguishes them: after the vayas section the text says time is of two kinds, the year and the age of the patient. Collapsing them loses the seasonal axis.
The third stage and its pathology. WHO describes vārdhakyam fully while leaving vayaḥ empty, inverting the classical emphasis.
Purely a transliteration hazard: vaya and vayu differ by one letter in unmarked Latin script and both are common headwords.
Kaumārabhṛtya's bāla is a patient category with its own therapeutics; Vi 8/122's bāla is a stage of any patient's life used to modulate dose.

mistranslations.why: Vi 8/122 defines vayas as a state of the body indexed to time and then makes the boundaries proportional to estimated lifespan. It is not a count of years.
Drops the sub-stage to thirty and, more importantly, the rescaling instruction for people whose lifespan is not a century.
Kaviratna's word for jīrṇa; pejorative in modern English where the Sanskrit is descriptive.

mistranslations.rendering: childhood is kapha, adulthood pitta, old age vata as a constitutional fact
mistranslations.why: Vi 8/122 says these doṣas predominate in the STAGES. That is not a statement about a person's prakṛti, and the two are separate examination items.

openQuestions: Charaka's stages are undifferentiated by sex; Sushruta gives 25 and 16. Do the commentators reconcile these?
Does any modern work test the proportional-rescaling rule, or is it universally ignored?

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints '25' (OCR '26') after this sentence; standard 26.11 (prose unit; Sanskrit clause लघुशीतरूक्षखरविशदसूक्ष्मस्पर्शगुणबहुलानि वायव्यानि per carakasamhitaonline.com)
classical.establishes: Caraka's vāyavya dravya profile: laghu, śīta, rūkṣa, khara, viśada, sūkṣma, sparśa-guṇa-bahula. Kaviratna's 'sharp' renders khara (rough).
classical.quote: Those that are principally light, cold, dry, sharp, clear, subtile, and largely endued with the attribute of touch, are regarded as appertaining to Wind.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; Sanskrit at siva.sh places this in verse 4 (see pañcamahābhūta record for the caveat)
classical.establishes: Suśruta's vāyavya dravya profile including taste (astringent with bitter), which Caraka's parallel omits.
classical.quote: A thing or substance, which is subtle in its essence, and is dry, rough, light, cold and non-slimy, increases tactual sensation and is endued with a largely astringent taste marked by a shade of bitter, is called a substance of the dominant principle of air (Vayaviyam).

classical.verse: Bhishagratna section 20; Sanskrit verse 19 per siva.sh: वायव्यास्तु- स्पर्शः स्पर्शेन्द्रियं सर्वचेष्टासमूहः सर्वशरीरस्पन्दनं लघुता च
classical.establishes: Vāyu-derived bodily features: touch, tactile organ, all movements, pulsation, lightness. Matches the Sanskrit; 'etherin' is the translator's word.
classical.quote: The properties Vayu (etherin) are touch, the skin, all functional activities of the organism, throbbing of the whole body (Spandana) and lightness.

classical.verse: Caraka Śārīrasthāna 5.5 confirmed against a printed, numbered Sanskrit edition (Trikamji 1941, p. 325), not only against carakasamhitaonline; 5.4 closes at 'एत एव च षड्धातवः समुदिताः "पुरुष" इति शब्दं लभन्ते ॥४॥' and the correspondence list opens 5.5, exactly as the earlier repair stated.
classical.establishes: Ca. Śā. 5.5 reads वियत् सुषिराणि in the printed Trikamji/Cakrapāṇi edition (1941, p. 325) as well as on carakasamhitaonline, with no variant recorded at that word. वियत् is a synonym of ākāśa and stands in the ākāśa slot of the six-dhātu list given at Śā. 5.4; Kaviratna's 'the hollow places are Ether (or Space)' therefore renders the received text correctly and implies no different base text. The fuller loka-puruṣa correspondence list can be quoted without the caveat.
classical.quote: तस्य पुरुषस्य पृथिवी मूर्तिः, आपः क्लेदः, तेजोऽभिसन्तापः, वायुः प्राणः, वियत् सुषिराणि, ब्रह्म अन्तरात्मा । — Caraka Śārīrasthāna 5.5, as printed in Carakasaṃhitā with Āyurvedadīpikā, ed. Jadavji Trikamji, Nirṇayasāgara 1941, p. 325 (the unit closes at ॥५॥). Preceding at 5.4: ... तद्यथा — पृथिव्यापस्तेजो वायुराकाशं ब्रह्म चाव्यक्तमिति ... ॥४॥
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

distinguishFrom.why: The central confusion. Vāta is a doṣa (NAMASTE SAT-B.393 vāyu-karma 'functions of vātadoṣa'; the NIA draft's SK0210 actually defines vāyu as 'A synonym of Vāta'); vāyu mahābhūta is the bhūta whose guṇa is sparśa and liṅga is calatva. Texts use vāyu for both, so context decides.

distinguishFrom.term: prāṇa / the five vāyus (prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna, apāna)
distinguishFrom.why: Subtypes of vāta doṣa, not of the bhūta (NIA draft p.51, 239, 273, 334, 377 list them as 'subtypes of Vāta (Vāyu)').
Bhishagratna's footnote equivalence; the bhūta is defined by touch and motion, not by phase.
Kaviratna's 'Wind' and ordinary 'air' invite the meteorological sense; the bhūta is the principle of motion and tangibility.

mistranslations.why: Even a WHO-commissioned draft (NIA 2011, SK0210) made this slip; the 2022 WHO ISTA and NAMASTE correct it with separate 'Air element' entries.
Bhishagratna's coinages (Su.Śā. 1 section 20; footnote to Su.Sū. 41), period science rather than translation.
Kaviratna's Sū. 26 choice; acceptable for marut/anila etymologically, but in a mahābhūta list 'wind' reads as weather and blurs into vāta.

openQuestions: Whether the 2022 WHO ISTA has a separate vāta doṣa entry that cross-references the bhūta was not checked.

classical.chapter: 7 (Na Vegan Dharaniya Adhyaya; Kaviratna: 'the lesson on the inadvisability of suppressing the urgings of nature')
classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 7/3-4 for the list of non-suppressible urges, read from Devanagari on carakasamhitaonline.com: 'न वेगान् धारयेद्धीमाञ्जातान् मूत्रपुरीषयोः| न रेतसो न वातस्य न छर्द्याः क्षवथोर्न च||३|| नोद्गारस्य न जृम्भाया न वेगान् क्षुत्पिपासयोः| न बाष्पस्य न निद्राया निःश्वासस्य श्रमेण च||४||'. Kaviratna prints his own numbers 1 and (OCR) 3, almost certainly 2, after these two aphorisms; he does not number the two opening formula sentences that Trikamji counts as 7/1-2. Both systems recorded; no conversion applied.
classical.establishes: Charaka's list of thirteen adhāraṇīya vegas: urine, faeces, semen, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, eructation, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, and breathing on exertion (niḥśvāsa śrameṇa). Note: no kāsa (cough) and no hikkā in Charaka's list as read here; cough appears in the Ashtanga Hridaya list (see gatheringNotes).
classical.quote: We shall now expound the lesson on the inadvisability of suppressing the urgings of nature. Thus said the illustrious son of Atri.  One endued with intelligence should not suppress urgings, that have become pronounced, in respect of urine and faeces ; as also of the semen and the wind, and of vomitting and sneezing.1  The urgings also in respect of eructations, of yawns, of hunger and of thirst, of tears, of sleep, and of heavy breathing induced by toil (should not to be suppressed). Listen now to me as I discourse (to you) on the topic of treating the several diseases that are generated of the person who suppresses the urgings of these when they appear in pronounced forms.3

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 7/25-27 (vega-nigraha-ja rogāḥ; dhāraṇīya vegas), Devanagari read on carakasamhitaonline.com: '||२५|| वेगनिग्रहजा रोगा य एते परिकीर्तिताः| इच्छंस्तेषामनुत्पत्तिं वेगानेतान्न धारयेत्', '||२६|| इमांस्तु धारयेद्वेगान् हितार्थी प्रेत्य चेह च| साहसानामशस्तानां मनोवाक्कायकर्मणाम्', '||२७|| लोभशोकभयक्रोधमानवेगान् विधारयेत्| नैर्लज्ज्येर्ष्यातिरागाणामभिध्यायाश्च बुद्धिमान्'. Kaviratna prints 24 and (OCR) 26, probably 25, after the corresponding aphorisms. Both systems recorded; not converted.
classical.establishes: That the same chapter prescribes dhāraṇa (suppression) of the dhāraṇīya vegas (greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, shamelessness, envy, excessive attachment, covetousness, and rash acts of mind, speech and body). 'Vega-dhāraṇa' is therefore not uniformly harmful in Charaka; the harmful act is dhāraṇa of the adhāraṇīya vegas, which Charaka names vega-nigraha in 7/25. The first sentence of the quote begins mid-aphorism because the OCR page break fell inside it; a human should read the scan for the opening words.
classical.quote: suppress these impulses also, viz., those of (ill-regulated) courage and all fruitless impulses of thought, word, and deed.*24  The man of intelligence should also suppress the impulses of cupidity, grief, fear, wrath, pride, shamelessness, envy, violent propensities of every kind, and covetousness.26

classical.verse: Suśruta Uttaratantra 55.3-6 (chapter title उदावर्तप्रतिषेध; Trikamji/Dalhaṇa ed., Pandurang Jawaji 1938, pp. 776-777). 55.3 = the 'wise man' verse; 55.6 = the 'thirteen types' verse.
classical.establishes: Suśruta Uttaratantra 55.1-6 established from a printed, numbered Sanskrit edition. The citation's 'wise man valuing his life shall never repress any natural urging' = Su.U. 55.3; the udāvarta definition from the nine urges = 55.4; hunger, thirst, breath and sleep = 55.5; 'of thirteen different types ... over and above the apathyaja one' = 55.6. Thirteen = nine urges in 55.4 + four in 55.5; apathyaja is a further type named in 55.6. Dalhaṇa glosses इन्द्रिय at 55.4 as शुक्र, corroborating Bhishagratna's 'discharge of semen'. The chapter-level address can now be replaced by Su.U. 55.3-6, and the openQuestion's guess of 55.3-5 corrected.
classical.quote: अधश्चोर्ध्वं च भावानां प्रवृत्तानां स्वभावतः ॥ न वेगान् धारयेत् प्राज्ञो वातादीनां जिजीविषुः ॥३॥ वातविण्मूत्रजृम्भाश्रुक्षवोद्गारवमीन्द्रियैः ॥ व्याहन्यमानैरुदितैरुदावर्तो निरुच्यते ॥४॥ क्षुत्तृष्णाश्वासनिद्राणामुदावर्तो विधारणात् ॥ तस्याभिधास्ये व्यासेन लक्षणं च चिकित्सितम् ॥५॥ त्रयोदशविधश्चासौ भिन्न एतैस्तु कारणैः ॥ अपथ्यभोजनाच्चापि वक्ष्यते च तथाऽपरः ॥६॥
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: 4/1 (adhāraṇīya list: 'वेगान्न धारयेद्वातविण्मूत्रक्षवतृट्क्षुधाम् । निद्राकासश्रमश्वासजृम्भाश्रुच्छर्दिरेतसाम् ॥ १ ॥') and 4/24 (dhāraṇīya: 'धारयेत्तु सदा वेगान् हितैषी प्रेत्य चेह च । लोभेर्ष्याद्वेषमात्सर्यरागादीनां जितेन्द्रियः ॥ २४ ॥'), numbers as printed on easyayurveda.com and ahsutrasthana.blogspot.com; not checked against a printed Sanskrit edition.
classical.establishes: Vagbhata's adhāraṇīya list includes kāsa (cough), which Charaka's Su. 7/3-4 list does not; it is this AH list that most modern '13 urges' tables actually follow.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: The urges Charaka says SHOULD be held (greed, grief, fear, anger, etc.; Su. 7/26-27). 'Vega-dhāraṇa' as a harm applies only to the adhāraṇīya vegas; applied to dhāraṇīya vegas, dhāraṇa is the prescribed conduct. English 'suppression of urges' without the qualifier conflates the two.

Forcibly initiating an urge that has not arisen (straining to pass stool, inducing vomiting). The opposite error to dhāraṇa; both appear in the Sushruta Udāvarta framing ('whether upward or downward') and in PMID 33218848 ('Udiran' vs 'Dhaaran').
The disease outcome in Sushruta Ut. 55 (thirteen types), not the act. Modern writing sometimes uses 'udavarta' loosely for any effect of suppression.

Near-synonyms. Charaka's own disease label in 7/25 is vega-nigraha-ja; WHO and NAMASTE use vegāvarodha as the head term; Tripathi 1981 uses vega-vidharan. A lexicon entry under 'vega-dharana' should cross-reference all of them, since a PubMed search on one spelling misses the others (counts on 2026-10-07: 'vegadharana' 1, 'vega dharana' 1, '"natural urges" ayurveda' 3).
Vega also names the propulsive attribute of vāta (PMID 33218848 'Vata has unique attribute of Vega (locomotion)'); in the swasthavritta sense it is the arisen urge itself.

mistranslations.why: Charaka explicitly prescribes suppression of the dhāraṇīya vegas in the same chapter; the harmful act is suppression of the adhāraṇīya vegas only. The unqualified phrase reverses half the chapter's teaching.

mistranslations.rendering: 13 natural urges (as a fixed canonical list)
mistranslations.why: The lists differ by text and standard: Charaka Su. 7/3-4 as read here (urine, faeces, semen, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, eructation, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, exertional breathing); Ashtanga Hridaya Su. 4/1 adds kāsa; Sushruta Ut. 55 counts thirteen udāvartas including an apathyaja type; NAMASTE SAT-J.57 lists 12; NAMASTE morbidity codes add hikkā. Present 'the 13 urges' as a textual list with its source, not as a single fact.
Bhishagratna's 'retention' fits urine and stool but not sneezing, yawning or tears; 'holding back' or 'withholding' generalises better.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's printed numbers OCR-read as '3' and '26' are almost certainly '2' and '25' (sequence); a human should read the scan (Lesson VII, pp. 73-77 of the fascicule).

Standard Sanskrit verse numbers for Sushruta Ut. 55 (the 'wise man' verse and the 'thirteen types' verse) were not established; NAMASTE's reference column cites 'Su.U.55/12', 'Su.U.55/16', 'Su.U.55/17' for individual urges but these were not verified.
Whether ICD-11 TM2 codes vegāvarodha-related disorders was not checked.

distinguishFrom.why: The popular pair treats vikṛti as a present doṣa reading against a birth reading. Vi 8/101 equates vikṛti with vikāra and lists prakṛti as one of eight parameters for grading it.
This is the prakṛti WHO opposes to vikṛti. Anyone citing WHO for the prakriti/vikriti pair is citing the normal/abnormal pair, not the constitution pair.
Not a distinction at all in Vi 8/101, which says they are the same; but WHO treats them separately and later usage often reserves vikāra for the manifest disease.
An evolute of prakṛti; carries no disorder sense.
Aggravation of a specific doṣa is a mechanism; vikṛti is the resulting disordered state examined as a whole.

mistranslations.why: The most widespread error in this group. It makes vikṛti a second constitutional reading; Vi 8/101 makes it the disease.
Too weak. vikāra in Charaka covers jvara, atīsāra, śoṣa, śvāsa, meha, kuṣṭha — named diseases.
A legitimate anatomical sense, wrong for Vi 8/101 where the word is being defined as morbidity in general.

classical.establishes: vimārgagamana as the fourth sign of srotodushti. The only verified classical occurrence of the term I located.
classical.quote: विमार्गगमनं चापि स्रोतसां दुष्टिलक्षणम्||२४||

classical.establishes: The lawfully quotable English. His parenthesis makes explicit what WHO's 'displacement of contents' leaves vague: it is the dhatus/contents leaving their proper channel for another channel.
classical.quote: or diviations (of the elements from their own into other channels), are regarded as indications of the vitiation of the ducts.

distinguishFrom.why: Movement against the normal direction (retrograde), as in pratiloma vata. That is reversal along the SAME path. vimārgagamana is departure onto a DIFFERENT path. Textbook renderings that say 'opposite direction flow' conflate the two.

The third stage of shatkriyakala, in which aggravated doshas overflow their own seats and spread through the body. That is a normal-for-pathology stage of dosha movement; vimārgagamana is a sign of the CHANNEL being vitiated. They are described at different levels of the model.

Frequently the cause of vimārgagamana rather than an alternative to it — WHO's own saṅga entry notes obstruction 'sometimes resulting in the formation of a collateral pathway'. The four signs are not independent.
Terms occasionally used in secondary literature for mixing of tissue elements. Not the same as a content travelling a wrong channel.

mistranslations.why: The commonest error. vi-mārga is 'wrong road', not 'reverse road'. Retrograde flow is pratiloma. Vomiting is often cited as the example, but vomiting is only one instance and not the paradigm case.
A vascular-specific biomedical term. vimārgagamana applies across all thirteen channels including annavaha and purishavaha, where extravasation is meaningless.
Attractive because WHO's saṅga entry mentions collateral pathways, but shunt implies an anatomically defined abnormal connection, which the Sanskrit does not assert.

openQuestions: Whether Chakrapani or any commentator gives worked examples of vimārgagamana, and whether they include reversal as a case.
Whether the term occurs anywhere in Sushruta. I did not find it, but my Sushruta full-text search covered only the Nidana and Sharira sthanas of the Bhishagratna scan, so absence is not established.
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 carries any code whose definition depends on this concept.

classical.establishes: The definitional verse distinguishing rasa, vipāka ('Assimilation') and vīrya ('Energy') by when each is known. Sanskrit as retrieved: रसो निपाते द्रव्याणां, विपाकः कर्मनिष्ठया| वीर्यं यावदधीवासान्निपाताच्चोपलभ्यते||६६|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya).
classical.quote: That is called the Taste of objects which is perceived as soon as the objects are brought into contact (with the tongue.) That is called Assimilation which is ascertained from the completion of the action. That is called Energy which is ascertained from the retention of the object within the body and its first contact with the tongue.

classical.establishes: Charaka's three vipākas and their mapping from the six rasas. Sanskrit as retrieved: कटुतिक्तकषायाणां विपाकः प्रायशः कटुः| अम्लोऽम्लं पच्यते स्वादुर्मधुरं लवणस्तथा||५८||.
classical.quote: Of the Pungent, the Bitter, and the Astringent, the change, upon assimilation, is generally Pungent. The Sour taste changes into the Sour. The Sweet and the Saline change into the Sweet.

classical.verse: Standard 26.61; Kaviratna prints 17 (second run; his OCR'd '17' follows 'increases phlegm and semen')
classical.establishes: The karma of kaṭu and madhura vipāka (the observable signs Jadoun 2013 later used as endpoints). Sanskrit as retrieved: शुक्रहा बद्धविण्मूत्रो विपाको वातलः कटुः| मधुरः सृष्टविण्मूत्रो विपाकः कफशुक्रलः||६१||. Here Kaviratna switches to 'after effects' for vipāka; 'tate' is OCR of taste.
classical.quote: The Pungent taste, in respect of its after effects, is destructive of the semen ; leads to retention of faeces and urine, and to increase of wind. The Sweet tate, in respect of its after effects, leads to easy and copious discharges of urine and stools, and increases phlegm and semen.

classical.establishes: The hierarchy rasa < vipāka < vīrya < prabhāva. Sanskrit as retrieved: द्रव्यं गुणेन पाकेन प्रभावेण च किञ्चन| रसं विपाकस्तौ वीर्यं प्रभावस्तानपोहति||७२||. Note Kaviratna's 'Potency' = prabhāva.
classical.quote: In cases where there is uniformity of attributes in Taste and the others (viz., in Energy, Assimilation, and Potency), Taste is subjugated by Assimilation ; both of them, again, are subjugated by Energy ; and all three are subjugated by Potency. Even such is the natural force of each of these.

classical.verse: Sanskrit verse number not established (Bhishagratna prints none)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's two-vipāka doctrine (madhura/guru and kaṭu/laghu), explicitly rejecting the three-vipāka view earlier on the same page ('the theory that only three tastes, such as sweet, acid, and pungent are developed through digestive reaction, appears to be untenable'). A primary inter-text disagreement.
classical.quote: Only two kinds of digestion (digestive reactionary tastes) have been noticed in the Shastras, such as, the sweet and the pungent, the first being heavy and the second light.

classical.establishes: Sushruta grounds the two vipākas in mahābhūta composition; introduced on the page as 'Authoritative verses on the subject'.
classical.quote: Of substances under the process of digestion, those, which are characterised by attributes, specifically belonging to earth and water, are called substances of sweet (heavy) digestion; while those which are permeated with the specific properties of air, fire and sky are called substances of pungent (light) digestion (easily digestible articles of food).

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa follows Charaka's three vipākas (sweet, sour, pungent). Reference only.
classical.quote: tri-dhā vipāko dravyasya svādv-amla-kaṭukātmakaḥ || 17 ||

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Su.26.66: vīrya is known from administration to excretion, vipāka from the completed action; Ca.Su.26.72 ranks vīrya above vipāka.
The unaccountable specific effect (Ca.Su.26.67); Kaviratna's 'Potency' is prabhāva, which readers may confuse with vipāka/vīrya.
Vipāka is the final (niṣṭhā) state after digestion, not the digestive process; Bhishagratna's bare 'digestion' blurs this.
A secondary taste perceived at the end of tasting, not after digestion.
Clinical indigestion (WHO SK0039), a different word-sense.

mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's choice, by his own footnote made for 'scientific dignity'; in modern English it names nutrient uptake, not a post-digestive taste-category.
Bhishagratna; conflates the process (pāka) with its resulting classification (vipāka).

Analogies offered in modern papers; not what the Samhitas say, and vipāka is classified by rasa not by chemistry.

classical.establishes: Contraindications to virechana, including the rule that it follows prior snehana. Sanskrit verse number not retrieved for this passage.
classical.quote: Bhishagratna: "Exhibition of purgatives are prohibited in respect of persons of impaired digestion, or of those treated with an excessive application of any emulsive remedy (Sneha- Karma), or of those who are exceedingly corpulent, too old, fatigued, thirsty or intoxicated, or of those suffering from any ulcer. They are similarly prohibited in respect of frightened persons and Kshata-kshina patients or of those afflicted with hemorrhage from the downward orifices of the body or of persons with any dart or foreign matter (salya) lying imbedded in the organism as well as in respect of infants and enciente. A purgative medicine should not be administered before the digestion of a meal previously taken, neither in the diseases due to an abuse of wine, nor in acute catarrh and acute fever or to a newly parturient woman and persons not previously treated with a Sneha (oil or Ghrita)."

The oils prepared from (the seeds of) Jimutaka, Kutaja, Kritave-dhana, Ikshvaku (bitter gourd), Dhamargava and of Madana act as emetics. The expressed oils prepared from (the seeds of) Vidanga, Khara manjari, Madhu-shigru, Surya-valli, Pilu, Siddharthaka and of Jyotishmati act as errhines (Shiro-virecana). 5." classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 26/85, Devanagari read on carakasamhitaonline.com: 'भवन्ति चात्र श्लोकाः- यत् किञ्चिद्दोषमास्राव्य न निर्हरति कायतः| आहारजातं तत् सर्वमहितायोपपद्यते||८५||'. Kaviratna prints his own number 21 after this verse, having restarted his count at 1 for the prose viruddha block (his footnote: 'This and the following aphorisms are in prose. Hence I number them anew, beginning with 1.— T.'). Both systems recorded; no conversion applied.
classical.establishes: Charaka's general definition of viruddha/ahita āhāra: food that provokes the doshas (Kaviratna: 'faults') without expelling them from the body. This is the verse NAMASTE SAT-J.84 paraphrases. Note Kaviratna's 'faults' = doṣa, an Edwardian rendering; not a doctrine of moral fault.
classical.quote: (Here occurs a verse.)  Whatever diet excites the faults without being able to dispel or drive them out of the system, becomes a source of affliction or disease.21

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 26/81 for the prose definition ('देहधातुप्रत्यनीकभूतानि द्रव्याणि देहधातुभिर्विरोधमापद्यन्ते; परस्परगुणविरुद्धानि कानिचित्, कानिचित् संयोगात्, संस्कारादपराणि, देशकालमात्रादिभिश्चापराणि, तथा स्वभावादपराणि||८१||'), 26/82 for fish-with-milk, 26/84 for the long list of pairs ending with honey-and-ghee in equal parts. Kaviratna's renumbered prose block: 3 (introduction), 4 (fish and milk), 5-6 (Bhadrakapya exchange), 7-20 (pairs). WARNING: Trikamji 26/84 is a single prose unit that spans Kaviratna's paragraphs 12-20, so there is no one-to-one mapping in this block; do not convert.
classical.establishes: The paradigm examples (fish with milk; honey and ghee in equal parts) and Charaka's reasoning by vīrya opposition and abhiṣyandi quality. 'Energy' is Kaviratna's word for vīrya and 'assimilation' for vipāka; both are translator's choices, not Ayurvedic doctrine about 'energy'.
classical.quote: Fish should never be taken with milk. Both of these are sweet in taste. They are, again, sweet in assimilation. Being highly emollient, they retain the secretions (without allowing them to escape) and thus cause a heaviness or fulness of the body. One of them (milk) is of cooling energy ; the other (fish) of heating energy ; they are thus of opposite energies. In consequence of their being thus of opposite energies, they corrupt or defile the blood. In consequence, again, of their being highly emollient, they stop the pores and passages through which all impurities escape.4  [...]  Honey and Ghee in equal portions, honey and rain water mingled in equal measures, honey and Pushkara seeds, warm water drink after the taking of honey, Bhallataka and warm water, Kampillaka boiled in whey, stale Kakamachi, the flesh of Bhasa roasted on a spit, are incompatible combinations. (Hence, if these be taken, disease and even death may be produced). We have thus laid down (what kinds of food are incompatible) agreeably to your question.20

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 26/86-87 (list of the 18 types: deśa, kāla, agni, mātrā, sātmya, doṣa/anila-ādi, saṁskāra, vīrya, koṣṭha, avasthā, krama, parihāra, upacāra, pāka, saṁyoga, hṛt, sampad, vidhi) and 26/88-101 (one-line definitions), Devanagari read on carakasamhitaonline.com, e.g. '||८६|| यच्चापि देशकालाग्निमात्रासात्म्यानिलादिभिः| संस्कारतो वीर्यतश्च कोष्ठावस्थाक्रमैरपि', '||८७|| परिहारोपचाराभ्यां पाकात् संयोगतोऽपि च| विरुद्धं तच्च न हितं हृत्सम्पद्विधिभिश्च यत्'. Kaviratna's translation of these verses was not located in the OCR text read (the block between his 21 and 22 appears to omit or compress them); a human should check the scan.
classical.establishes: The canonical enumeration of 18 types of viruddha that NAMASTE codes as SAT-J.85 to SAT-J.102. Confirmed first (86) and last (101) verses independently.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 26/102-103 (disease list) and 26/104-105 (management), Devanagari read on carakasamhitaonline.com: '||१०२|| षाण्ढ्यान्ध्यवीसर्पदकोदराणां विस्फोटकोन्मादभगन्दराणाम्| मूर्च्छामदाध्मानगलग्रहाणां पाण्ड्वामयस्यामविषस्य चैव', '||१०३|| किलासकुष्ठग्रहणीगदानां शोथाम्लपित्तज्वरपीनसानाम् | सन्तानदोषस्य तथैव मृत्योर्विरुद्धमन्नं प्रवदन्ति हेतुम्'. Kaviratna prints (OCR) 23 after the disease list, almost certainly 22, then 23 after the remedies paragraph and 24 after the summary verse. Both systems recorded; not converted.
classical.establishes: The disease list and the three-fold management (vamana, virecana, śamana/neutralising agents, plus prior habituation to wholesome articles). Kaviratna's English list does not map one-to-one onto the Sanskrit: 'Pulmonary consumption' and 'Bilious hemorrhage' have no obvious counterpart in 26/102-103 (which has śotha and amlapitta), while 'Leprous blotches, Leprosy' = kilāsa, kuṣṭha. Treat his disease names as period English, not identifications. Also 26/106 (unaffected persons: those habituated, taking small amounts, with strong agni, young, unctuous, exercising, strong) was seen in Sanskrit but Kaviratna's rendering of it was not located in the OCR read.
classical.quote: Diet that is incompatible is said to be the cause of the following diseases, viz.. Impotence, Blindness, Erysipelas, abdominal dropsy, malignant Boils, Lunacy, Fistula-in-ano, Swoons, Vertigo, Flatulence, choaking of the throat (with suppression of the voice), chlorosis and anaemia, acidity of the stomach (such that no food is capable of being retained), Leprous blotches, Leprosy, diseases that affect the Grahani, Pulmonary consumption, Bilious hemorrhage, Fever, Inflammation of the schneidenian membrane, with loss of the sense of smell, incapacity to beget healthy offspring, as also death itself.  [...]  (Here occurs a verse.)  All diseases that are generated by the taking of incompatible food are destroyed by purging, and vomitting, and neutralising agents, and by the previous administration or use of such articles as are beneficial.24

classical.chapter: 20 (Hitāhitīya Adhyāya; Bhishagratna: 'the salutary and non-salutary effects of regimen')
classical.verse: Sushruta Sutrasthana 20 (Hitahitiya). Bhishagratna prints no Sanskrit verse numbers; the standard numbers are confirmed against the printed Sanskrit edition (Susrutasamhita with Dalhana's Nibandhasangraha, ed. Jadavji Trikamji Acharya, Nirnaya Sagar Press, Bombay 1915, Sutrasthana adhyaya 20, pp. 81-83, page images on archive.org): Valli-fruit list with milk = 20.8; all fish, especially Chilichima, with milk, and plantain with Tala fruit, milk or whey = 20.13; two oils, or honey and an oil, in equal measure (manaviruddha) = 20.15; the rasa / virya / vipaka couples = 20.16; the 'disease, weakness of the sense-organs, death' verse = 20.19. Quoted segments appear here in chapter order. Note that visatulyani occurs twice in this chapter: 20.4 announces the category ('samyogad aparani visatulyani bhavanti') and 20.8 gives the Valli list; Dalhana on 20.4 records a variant 'tesam eva samyogatas tv aparani', which is why the two read so alike.
classical.establishes: Sushruta's parallel treatment of incompatibilities (notably milk with fish, and oils/honey in equal parts), framed by rasa, vīrya and vipāka ('tastes, potencies and digestive transformation'), and his 'deadly poisons' comparison, which anticipates the Ashtanga Hridaya's viṣa-gara simile.
classical.quote: The Valli fruit, the Karaka, the Karira, the Amla-phala, the salt, the Kulattha, the Pinyaka, curd, oil, Virohi, cakes, the dried pot-herbs, goat's flesh, mutton, wine, the Jamboline fruit, the Chilichima fish, the flesh of the Godha, and the Varaha (wild boar) being eaten simultaneously with milk, furnish an example of articles which may act as deadly poisons through incompatible combinations.  [...]  All fish, specially those of the Chilichimi species, should not be taken with milk, nor the fruit of a plantain tree should be simultaneously eaten with Tala fruit, milk or whey.  [...]  Two oily substances (such as oil and clarified butter) or honey and any of the oily substances, mixed in equal proportions, should not be taken  [...]  By taking substances which are incompatible to one another as regards their tastes, potencies and digestive transformation, a greedy and intemperate person becomes afflicted with disease and weakness of the sense-organs, and ultimately meets with his doom.

classical.verse: 7/29 ('विरुद्धमपि चाहारं विद्याद्विषगरोपमम्') through 7/51, with 7/47 for persons unaffected ('व्यायामस्निग्धदीप्ताग्निवयःस्थबलशालिनाम्'), numbers as printed on easyayurveda.com; not checked against a printed Sanskrit edition.
classical.establishes: Vagbhata treats viruddha āhāra as comparable to viṣa and gara (poison and artificial/slow poison), which is why modern Agada Tantra literature (PMIDs 33773882, 30254386) files it under toxicology.

distinguishFrom.why: Generic unwholesome or contraindicated food. Charaka 26/85 defines viruddha by a specific mechanism (provokes doshas without expelling them); not every ahita item is viruddha, though NAMASTE's definition and Kaviratna's 'incompatible' both lean on the 26/85 verse, which in Sanskrit actually says 'ahitāya' (unwholesome).

Unsuitability to the individual's habituation. It is one of the 18 types (sātmya-viruddha, SAT-J.89) and also one of the conditions that neutralise viruddha (26/106: the habituated person is unaffected). Confusing the whole with the part is common.
Incompatibility by combination is only one of 18 types (SAT-J.99). Almost all popular 'wrong food combinations' lists describe this type alone and call it viruddha āhāra.
Ashtanga Hridaya Su. 7/29 compares viruddha to viṣa and gara ('viṣa-garopamam'); it is a simile, not an identification. Modern toxicology papers (PMIDs 33773882, 30254386) build on the simile.

Immunological or enzymatic reactions in an individual. Viruddha is defined by the properties of the food and its combination, processing, dose, place, time and sequence, and is said to be neutralised by habituation, exercise and strong agni (26/106), which is not how allergy behaves.
Charaka 26/104 calls the resulting disorders 'vairodhika-nimitta'; vairodhika is sometimes used as the noun for viruddha āhāra itself. Same concept, different grammatical form.

mistranslations.why: Covers only saṁyoga-viruddha; omits the other 17 types (place, time, agni, dose, habituation, dosha, processing, potency, bowel, condition, order, contraindication, treatment sequence, cooking, palatability, quality, rules of eating).
Imports an immunological or chemical mechanism absent from the texts; the classical mechanism is dosha provocation without elimination (26/85), neutralised by habituation and strong agni (26/106).

mistranslations.why: Edwardian disease labels for kuṣṭha, unmāda etc.; two items in his list have no clear counterpart in the Sanskrit of 26/102-103. Use them as evidence of his reading, not as identifications.
Translator's period vocabulary; 'energy' in particular invites a modern 'energetic' reading that is not in the text.

classical.verse: Standard 26.13 (prose unit ending ||१३||); Kaviratna's corresponding passage sits at his 27-28 and renders vīrya loosely (not quoted here)
classical.establishes: The six-fold analysis of drug action in Ca.Su.26.13: karma is what drugs do (yat kurvanti), vīrya is that by which they act (yena kurvanti), adhikaraṇa is where (yatra), kāla is when (yadā), upāya is how (yathā), phala is what they accomplish (yat sādhayanti). The enumeration is the second half of a single prose unit whose opening clause ('na tu kevalaṃ guṇaprabhāvādeva dravyāṇi kārmukāṇi bhavanti') states its premise: drugs act not by quality alone but by dravyaprabhāva, guṇaprabhāva and dravyaguṇaprabhāva, in a given time and site. 'कुर्विन्ति' is carakasamhitaonline's typo; GRETIL's Trikamji-based text and the printed Sen & Sen 1897 edition both read कुर्वन्ति. Cakrapāṇi's Āyurvedadīpikā on this unit glosses vīrya as śakti, 'and that belongs to a substance or to a quality' (vīryaṃ śaktiḥ sā ca dravyasya guṇasya vā). Sushruta Su.41 (Bhishagratna) defines the same six, kāla first: 'The principle, in virtue of which the action is performed, is called its potency or Viryam.'
classical.quote: न तु केवलं गुणप्रभावादेव द्रव्याणि कार्मुकाणि भवन्ति; द्रव्याणि हि द्रव्यप्रभावाद्गुणप्रभावाद्द्रव्यगुणप्रभावाच्च तस्मिंस्तस्मिन् काले तत्तदधिकरणमासाद्य तां तां च युक्तिमर्थं च तं तमभिप्रेत्य यत् कुर्वन्ति, तत् कर्म; येन कुर्विन्ति, तद्वीर्यं; यत्र कुर्वन्ति, तदधिकरणं; यदा कुर्वन्ति, स कालः; यथा कुर्वन्ति, स उपायः; यत् साधयन्ति, तत् फलम्||१३||

classical.establishes: The eight-fold vs two-fold vīrya and the functional definition (yena kriyate yā kriyā). Sanskrit as retrieved: मृदुतीक्ष्णगुरुलघुस्निग्धरूक्षोष्णशीतलम्| वीर्यमष्टविधं केचित्, केचिद्द्विविधमास्थिताः||६४|| शीतोष्णमिति, वीर्यं तु क्रियते येन या क्रिया| नावीर्यं कुरुते किञ्चित् सर्वा वीर्यकृता क्रिया||६५|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya).
classical.quote: Some say that mild and keen, heavy and light, oily and dry, and hot and cooling, are the eight kinds of Energy which objects may have. Others are of opinion that objects have only two kinds of Energy, viz., cooling and hot. That is called the Energy of an object in consequence of which the object acts or operates on the system. An object which has no Energy can have no action (upon the system.) Every action proceeds from Energy.

classical.establishes: How vīrya is known (yāvad adhīvāsāt nipātāc ca). Sanskrit as retrieved: रसो निपाते द्रव्याणां, विपाकः कर्मनिष्ठया| वीर्यं यावदधीवासान्निपाताच्चोपलभ्यते||६६||. Kaviratna's footnote (editorial) adds Chakrapani's gloss of adhivāsa as 'lying of the object within the body'.
classical.quote: That is called Energy which is ascertained from the retention of the object within the body and its first contact with the tongue.

classical.establishes: Inference of vīrya from rasa and vipāka, with exceptions following (his 4-6: hot sweets such as Mahat Panchamula; Amalaka sour but not heating). Sanskrit as retrieved: शीतं वीर्येण यद्द्रव्यं मधुरं रसपाकयोः| तयोरम्लं यदुष्णं च यद्द्रव्यं कटुकं तयोः||४५||.
classical.quote: That object which is sweet in Taste and Assimilation, should be known as cooling in Energy. That which is sour in Taste and Assimilation, should be known as heating in Energy. So also that object which is pungent in Taste and Assimilation, should be known as heating in energy.

classical.verse: Sanskrit: Sutrasthana 40, sutra 5 (siva.sh numbering) 'तच्च वीर्यं द्विविधमुष्णं शीतं च, अग्नीषोमीयत्वाज्जगतः । केचिदष्टविधमाहुः- शीतमुष्णं स्निग्धं रूक्षं विशदं पिच्छिलं मृदु तीक्ष्णं चेति'; Bhishagratna (wisdomlib doc141670, Chapter XL) prints no number
classical.establishes: Sushruta's two-fold vīrya (uṣṇa and śīta, 'owing to the agni-soma nature of the world') and the eight-fold view he attributes to 'some' (kecit): śīta, uṣṇa, snigdha, rūkṣa, viśada, picchila, mṛdu, tīkṣṇa (Su.40/5, siva.sh numbering). His eight differ from Charaka's 26.64 by having viśada and picchila where Charaka has guru and laghu. Su.41/11 repeats the identical eight ('य इमे गुणा वीर्यसञ्ज्ञकाः शीतोष्णस्निग्धरूक्षमृदुतीक्ष्णपिच्छिलविशदाः') and treats guru and laghu as pāka, not vīrya ('गुरुपाको वातपित्तघ्नः, लघुपाकः श्लेष्मघ्नः'); the 'heavy' in Bhishagratna's Su.41 rendering ('cooling, thermogenetic, oleaginous, heavy, parchifying, plastive, keen and slimy') is his insertion, not a third Sanskrit variant. 'Expansive' for viśada is also Bhishagratna's gloss.
classical.quote: The potency of a drug is either cooling or heat-making owing to the twofold (hot and cool) nature of the temperament of the world. According to several authorities the potency of a medicinal drug may be classed as either hot or cool, emollient or dry, expansive or slimy, mild or keen, so as to embrace the eight different attributes in all.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's functional definition, parallel to Ca.Su.26.13 yena kurvanti tad vīryam.

classical.verse: 12-14 (GRETIL, Das and Emmerick numbering); the eight-vs-two discussion continues to 9.17; Su.1.17 for the two-fold statement
classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa reports the eight-fold vīrya (guru, snigdha, hima, mṛdu, laghu, rūkṣa, uṣṇa, tīkṣṇa) as the view of 'some' (eke) and attributes the functional definition to Caraka by name ('carakas tv āha vīryaṃ tat kriyate yena yā kriyā'), 9.12-14. 9.15-16 then give his reasons for applying the name vīrya to guru and the rest ('vivakṣyate rasādyeṣu vīryaṃ gurv-ādayo hy ataḥ'), and 9.17 reports the two-fold uṣṇa/śīta view as that of others ('uṣṇaṃ śītaṃ dvi-dhaivānye vīryam ācakṣate 'pi ca'). The two-fold vīrya in Vāgbhaṭa's own summary is at Su.1.17 'uṣṇa-śīta-guṇotkarṣāt tatra vīryaṃ dvi-dhā smṛtam'. Reference only.
classical.quote: vīryaṃ punar vadanty eke guru snigdhaṃ himaṃ mṛdu || 12 || laghu rūkṣoṣṇa-tīkṣṇaṃ ca tad evaṃ matam aṣṭa-dhā | carakas tv āha vīryaṃ tat kriyate yena yā kriyā || 13 || nā-vīryaṃ kurute kiñ-cit sarvā vīrya-kṛtā hi sā | gurv-ādiṣv eva vīryākhyā tenānv-artheti varṇyate || 14 ||

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Su.26.67: the specific effect when rasa, vīrya and vipāka are alike; Kaviratna calls prabhāva 'Potency' and vīrya 'Energy', inverting the modern convention.
Known from the completed action, whereas vīrya is known during the drug's stay in the body (Ca.Su.26.66).
The eight vīryas are themselves gurvadi gunas; AH Su.9.14 says the name vīrya is given to gurvādi qualities when they dominate action ('gurv-ādiṣv eva vīryākhyā').
WHO SK0217 sense 2; Ca.Su.26 'bala-varṇa-tejo-vīrya' uses it as bodily vigour; Kaviratna's 'sexual potency' passages are this sense.
WHO's 'tīkṣṇa/madhya/mṛdu vīrya = higher/moderate/mild potency' grades strength, a derived usage not in Ca.Su.26.

mistranslations.why: In English pharmacology potency is dose-response position; vīrya is a qualitative mode of action (hot/cold etc.), as Ca.Su.26.64 shows.
Kaviratna's 'Potency' is prabhāva; his vīrya is 'Energy'.

mistranslations.rendering: energy (read as caloric or vitalistic energy)
mistranslations.why: Kaviratna's and Gilca's 'energy/energetic' invite a vitalist reading the texts do not support; the Sanskrit defines vīrya purely by agency.
WHO DG0408's own analogy; a chemical-constituent reading the Samhitas do not make.

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 6/4, Devanagari read on carakasamhitaonline.com: 'इह खलु संवत्सरं षडङ्गमृतुविभागेन विद्यात्| तत्रादित्यस्योदगयनमादानं च त्रीनृतूञ्छिशिरादीन् ग्रीष्मान्तान् व्यवस्येत्, वर्षादीन् पुनर्हेमन्तान्तान् दक्षिणायनं विसर्गं च||४||'. Kaviratna prints his number 2 after this passage (he numbers the opening verse 1). Both systems recorded; not converted.
classical.establishes: Charaka's definition: the year has six seasons; the sun's northern course (udagayana) is ādāna and comprises śiśira, vasanta, grīṣma; the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is visarga and comprises varṣā, śarad, hemanta. Kaviratna's parenthetical glosses ('sucks up the liquid portion', 'yields moisture') are his, not the text; his footnote on the Indian calendar months is a translator's note.
classical.quote: For the purposes of this lesson, the year should be known as consisting of six portions, divided according to the seasons. Of these, the three seasons commencing with the season of dews and ending with summer constitute the period when the Sun travels in the region lying to the north of the equinoctial. That is again the period when the Sun takes (i. e., sucks up the liquid portion of every earthly object). The three other seasons commencing with the season of rains and ending with Hemanta constitutes the period of the Sun's southerly course. That is, besides, the time when the Sun gives (or yields moisture to all earthly objects).*2

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 6/5, Devanagari read on carakasamhitaonline.com: 'विसर्गे पुनर्वायवो नातिरूक्षाः प्रवान्ति, इतरे पुनरादाने; सोमश्चाव्याहतबलः शिशिराभिर्भाभिरापूरयञ्जगदाप्याययति शश्वत्, अतो विसर्गः सौम्यः| आदानं पुनराग्नेयं; तावेतावर्कवायू सोमश्च कालस्वभावमार्गपरिगृहीताः कालर्तुरसदोषदेहबलनिर्वृत्तिप्रत्ययभूताः समुपदिश्यन्ते||५||'. Kaviratna splits this one Trikamji unit into his aphorisms 3 ('...Hence the period of Giving is mild (and agreeable).') and 4 ('The period of Taking is fiery...'). No one-to-one mapping; both recorded.
classical.establishes: Visarga is saumya (Kaviratna: 'mild (and agreeable)'), ādāna is āgneya ('fiery'); the moon is unimpaired in visarga. 'Moisture' = rasa and 'faults' = doṣa are Kaviratna's words.
classical.quote: During the period when the Sun gives, the winds are not very dry; they also blow (without being deprived of motion). The winds of the period when the Sun takes have opposite virtues. The Moon, during the former period, appears with unabated vigor and, filling the universe with cool rays gladdens it every day. Hence the period of Giving is mild (and agreeable).3  The period of Taking is fiery. These two periods, the Sun and the winds, and the Moon also, as the learned instruct us, are subject to the influences of Time, of their own respective natures, and of track, and become the determining causes of time, season, moisture, faults, and strength of body.4

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji) 6/7 (prose on strength increasing in varṣā-śarad-hemanta) and 6/8 (verse on strength at the start/middle/end of visarga and ādāna), Devanagari read on carakasamhitaonline.com: '||७|| वर्षाशरद्धेमन्तेषु तु दक्षिणाभिमुखेऽर्के ... तत्र बलमुपचीयते नृणामिति', '||८|| भवन्ति चात्र- आदावन्ते च दौर्बल्यं विसर्गादानयोर्नृणाम्| मध्ये मध्यबलं, त्वन्ते श्रेष्ठमग्रे च निर्दिशेत्'. Kaviratna prints 6 after the prose and restarts his count at 1 for the verse. Both recorded; not converted.
classical.establishes: The physiological point of the term: in visarga, unctuous (arūkṣa) sour, salty and sweet rasas increase and human strength accumulates; strength is lowest at the start of visarga (varṣā) and end of ādāna (grīṣma), highest at the end of visarga (hemanta) and start of ādāna (śiśira). The season names in parentheses in the verse are Kaviratna's insertions. OCR renders ś as 'Ç' ('Çarat', 'Çiçira').
classical.quote: In the season, however, of rains, of Çarat, and of Hemanta, when the Sun begins his southerly course, and his powers become weakened by time, by the virtue of his track itself, by the winds generated by the clouds, and by the downpours (from the cloudy regions), when the Moon also appears with unabated vigor, and (lastly) when the heat of the universe becomes cooled by the water that falls from the clouds, moisture that is cool, sour, saltish, and sweet, increases gradually, and the strength of human beings increases.6  On this topic are the following verses :—  It should be said that during the first season of the Giving period, (viz., the season of rains), and the last season of the Taking period, (viz., summer), men become weak. In the two intermediate seasons of both the periods, (viz., Çarat and Vasanta), men become neither very weak nor very strong. During the last season of the Giving period, (viz., Hemanta), and the first of the Taking period, (viz., Çiçira), the strength of men is at its highest.1

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers (chapter-level). The Sanskrit sūtra is Sushruta Sutrasthana 6.7, confirmed in a printed edition: Suśrutasaṃhitā with Dalhaṇa's Nibandhasaṃgraha, ed. Jādavji Trikamji Āchārya, Nirnaya Sagar Press, Bombay 1915, Sūtrasthāna adhyāya 6, p. 23, where the mūla ends 'uttarottaraṃ ca sarvaprāṇināṃ balamupahīyate ७' and Dalhaṇa's gloss on it closes ॥७॥; the edition's table of contents lists '7 dakṣiṇottarabhedenāyanavibhāgaḥ, p. 23'. (तयोर्दक्षिणं वर्षाशरद्धेमन्ताः ... उत्तरं च शिशिरवसन्तग्रीष्माः ...)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's parallel: the dakṣiṇa ayana (rains, autumn, hemanta) strengthens the moon (soma), makes the sour-salty-sweet rasas strong and progressively increases the strength of all beings; the uttara ayana (śiśira, spring, summer) strengthens the sun and progressively diminishes strength. Bhishagratna's 'Summer Solstice (Uttarayana)' and 'Tropic of Capricorn / Winter Solstice (Dakshinayana)' are his astronomical glosses, not in the Sanskrit, and doctrinally odd (uttarāyaṇa begins at the winter solstice); do not record them as what the text says. His 'bitter, pungent and sour' for the ādāna rasas is a slip: the printed Trikamji edition reads tikta-kaṣāya-kaṭuka (bitter, astringent, pungent) and Dalhaṇa re-quotes the same, agreeing with Charaka Su 6/6. Dalhaṇa also notes that most copies read the sūtra with the uttarāyaṇa first ('te śiśiravasantagrīṣmavarṣāśaraddhemantāḥ'), and defends his text's dakṣiṇāyana-first order on the ground that visarga is what gives beings strength; so the order in which the two halves are printed is itself a known variant.
classical.quote: The rains, autumn and Hemanta follow one another in succession when the sun is over the Tropic of Capricorn or is in the Winter Solstice (Dakshinayana) and the moon gains in strength in this part of the year. Rasas (Serum or sap) possessed of acid, saline and sweet tastes, grow strong and become dominant when the sun is over the Tropic of Capricorn (Dakshinayana) and all beings gain in strength and energy more and more. Winter, spring and summer mark the passing of the sun over the Summer Solstice (Uttarayana). The sun grows stronger in heat and light, and saps (rasas) of bitter, pungent and sour tastes increase in intensity, and all animals gradually begin to lose strength and energy.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Verses 1-4 as numbered on ahsutrasthana.blogspot.com (verse 3 incipit: 'ऋतवो दक्षिणायनम् । वर्षादयो विसर्गश्च यद्बलं विसृजत्ययम् । सौम्यत्वादत्र सोमो हि बलवान् हीयते रविः'); not checked against a printed Sanskrit edition.
classical.establishes: Vagbhata supplies the etymology behind the modern rendering 'release': visarga is so called because it releases (visṛjati) strength to beings. The 'Ashtanga Hridaya' etymology should not be attributed to Charaka, whose 6/4-5 gives no etymology.
classical.checked: address only, nothing quoted to check

distinguishFrom.why: Charaka 6/4 equates them ('दक्षिणायनं विसर्गं च') but they are not synonyms in sense: dakṣiṇāyana names the sun's southward half-year (astronomical; NAMASTE SAT-G.109 'ayanam'), visarga names its physiological character (the half in which the earth and bodies are 'given' moisture and strength; saumya). Sushruta as translated by Bhishagratna uses only dakṣiṇāyana.

The opposite half (śiśira, vasanta, grīṣma), āgneya, in which the sun 'takes' (Kaviratna) moisture and strength declines. Confusion arises because hemanta (early winter) belongs to visarga while śiśira (late winter) belongs to ādāna, and strength peaks across that boundary (6/8).

Visarga spans three seasons (varṣā, śarad, hemanta). Treating it as 'the rainy season' or 'monsoon' truncates it; strength is in fact lowest in varṣā and highest in hemanta within the same visarga (6/8).
The Sanskrit phoneme ḥ is also called visarga; the WHO PDF's only 'Visarga' hit is in its transliteration key. Unrelated sense, same word.
The 'seasonal strength' of Charaka 11/36 (WHO ITA-2.2.30; NAMASTE SAT-B.464) is the strength acquired in visarga-kāla; the term names the effect, not the period.

mistranslations.why: Ayana is a six-month course of the sun, not an instant; Bhishagratna's 'Winter Solstice (Dakshinayana)' and 'Summer Solstice (Uttarayana)' misplace both (uttarāyaṇa begins at the winter solstice). Record as the translator's gloss.
Only the first of visarga's three seasons.

The etymology 'yad balaṃ visṛjati' is Vagbhata's (AH Su. 3); Charaka 6/4-5 defines visarga by the sun's course and its saumya character without that etymology. Kaviratna's 'Giving' is a literal rendering of vi-sṛj, not a claim about strength.
Period English; 'moisture' for rasa in 6/5-7 obscures that the text is about the six tastes becoming dominant, not humidity alone.

openQuestions: Standard Sanskrit verse numbers for Sushruta Su. 6 were not established; a numbered Sanskrit edition is needed before any 'Su.Su. 6/x' citation.
Bhishagratna's 'bitter, pungent and sour' for the ādāna rasas vs Charaka's tikta-kaṣāya-kaṭu: check the Sushruta Sanskrit.
AH Su. 3 verse numbers come from a blog transcription and need checking against a printed edition.

Whether WHO ISTA contains visarga/ādāna under a rendering my text search did not anticipate (e.g. 'southward movement of the sun') is possible; a human should check the ṛtucaryā block around ITA-10.3.x on pp. 473-474.

classical.establishes: Viśada ('clear') as the sixth quality of Vāta. Sanskrit as retrieved: रूक्षः शीतो लघुः सूक्ष्मश्चलोऽथ विशदः खरः| विपरीतगुणैर्द्रव्यैर्मारुतः सम्प्रशाम्यति||५९|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya).
classical.quote: Wind, which may be dry, cold, light, subtile, unstable, clear, keen, is cured by objects which have adverse attributes.

classical.establishes: Viśada ('not slimy') as a laṅghana quality. Sanskrit as retrieved: लघूष्णतीक्ष्णविशदं रूक्षं सूक्ष्मं खरं सरम्||१२|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Langhanabrimhaniya_Adhyaya).
classical.quote: Such things as are light, warm, pungent, not slimy, dry, subtile, rough, unstable, and hard, are generally Langhana.

classical.verse: Standard 26.11 (single prose unit); Kaviratna prints 22, 24, 25 after the earth, fire and wind sentences
classical.establishes: Charaka lists viśada among earth-, fire- and air-dominant substances, and vaiśadya among the effects of air-dominant ones. Sanskrit as retrieved: गुरुखरकठिनमन्दस्थिरविशदसान्द्रस्थूलगन्धगुणबहुलानि पार्थिवानि ... उष्णतीक्ष्णसूक्ष्मलघुरूक्षविशदरूपगुणबहुलान्याग्नेयानि ... लघुशीतरूक्षखरविशदसूक्ष्मस्पर्शगुणबहुलानि वायव्यानि, तानि रौक्ष्यग्लानिविचारवैशद्यलाघवकराणि ||११|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Atreyabhadrakapyiya_Adhyaya). The ellipsis omits the Water sentence (his 23). This contradicts WHO's 'akash & pṛthvī'.
classical.quote: Amongst objects those that are principally heavy, sharp or pungent, hard, mild, immobile, clear, thick, gross, and possessed of scent, are regarded as appertaining to Earth. ... Those that are principally hot, keen, subtile, light, dry, and clear, and largely endued with the attribute of form, are regarded as appertaining to Fire. Those that are principally light, cold, dry, sharp, clear, subtile, and largely endued with the attribute of touch, are regarded as appertaining to Wind.

classical.verse: Sanskrit verse number not established (Bhishagratna prints none)
classical.establishes: Sushruta assigns vaiśadya to earth + air and (same page) 'Keenness, parchifying and non-slimy potencies conquer the deranged Kapha'; also 'The properties of sliminess and its opposite may be perceived by the eyes and touch.' Bhishagratna names the Sanskrit (Vaishadyam) here, so the rendering is anchored.
classical.quote: parchifying potency, to the excess of the attributes of air; non-slimy potency (Vaishadyam), to the predominance of the attributes of earth and air; and heavy and light digestion, to the same cause.

classical.establishes: Viśada named explicitly among the ten gunas whose opposites complete the twenty (its opposite picchila is unnamed). Reference only.
classical.quote: guru-manda-hima-snigdha-ślakṣṇa-sāndra-mṛdu-sthirāḥ | guṇāḥ sa-sūkṣma-viśadā viṃśatiḥ sa-viparyayāḥ || 18 ||

distinguishFrom.why: Opposite member (Kaviratna's note 'Vishada in Pichcchila'; Bhishagratna 'sliminess and its opposite').
Dejection/depression (WHO AF2569 'Dejection; Depression'); identical in common transliteration 'vishada' and the only sense PubMed returns.
Dry; co-listed with viśada in Vāta and laṅghana lists and both oppose unctuous/slimy, so 'clear/dry' are blurred in textbooks.
Smooth; a separate pair (with khara); WHO's 'Lucid' and 'Transparent' drift toward smoothness/clarity of appearance rather than non-adhesion.
The abstract noun (effect), used by Charaka 26.11 of air-dominant substances and by Bhishagratna 'Vaishadyam'.

mistranslations.why: WHO DG0411's wording; the classical use is tactile (non-sticky, non-slimy), perceived 'by the eyes and touch' per Sushruta, and opposed to picchila.
Bhishagratna's Su.40 pair 'expansive or slimy'; no obvious basis for 'expansive' as viśada.
Homograph; different word.

openQuestions: Reconcile the bhūta attribution: WHO (ākāśa + pṛthvī), Sushruta Su.41 (earth + air), Charaka Su.26.11 (earth, fire and air lists), easyayurveda (earth, air, fire, ether).
Why carakasamhitaonline prints विषद in 26.43(5) (खरविषदस्वभावाच्च) against विशद elsewhere; orthographic variant or edition error.
Sanskrit behind Bhishagratna's 'expansive' in Su.40.

classical.establishes: The defining feature is alternation, not deficiency: it sometimes digests properly and sometimes produces this symptom set. WHO's ITA-5.11.3 symptom list is recognisably a modernisation of this same list.
classical.quote: The digestive heat which is irregular in its action, and which sometimes helps the process of complete digestion, and produces distension of the abdomen, colic pain, constipation of the bowels, dysentery, ascites, heaviness of the limbs, rumbling in the intestines, and loose motions (diarrhoea) at other times, is called Vishamagni.

classical.establishes: Sanskrit for the definition, fixing the verse number and showing that Bhishagratna's 'ascites' renders udara/jaṭhara-gaurava (heaviness of the abdomen), i.e. that his rendering over-reads.
classical.quote: यः कदाचित् सम्यक् पचति कदाचिदाध्मानशूलोदावर्तातिसारजठरगौरवान्त्रकूजनप्रवाहणानि कृत्वा स विषमः

classical.establishes: Doṣa attribution (vāta) and the management principle (snigdha, amla, lavaṇa), both public domain.
classical.quote: The digestive fire of the Vishama kind brings on diseases characterised by the derangement of the Vayu. ... The one known as Vishama (irregular) should be corrected by a diet consisting of emollient, acid or saline substances.

classical.establishes: Charaka defines viṣama purely negatively — 'having characteristics opposite to sama' — and attributes it to vāta overwhelming agni's seat. He gives no symptom list here; Sushruta does.
classical.quote: समलक्षणविपरीतलक्षणस्तु विषम इति। ... वातलानां तु वाताभिभूतेऽग्न्यधिष्ठाने विषमा भवन्त्यग्नयः

classical.establishes: The downstream consequence: viṣamāgni, cooking unevenly, produces dhātu-vaiṣamya (tissue disequilibrium). This is the link from agni state to systemic pathology.
classical.quote: विषमो धातुवैषम्यं करोति विषमं पचन्। तीक्ष्णो मन्देन्धनो धातून् विशोषयति पावकः॥५०॥

classical.establishes: Vāgbhaṭa's mechanism (samāna vāyu off its path) and his behavioural criterion (digests improper food quickly, or proper food only after long delay). NAMASTE cites Ah.Sa.3/75 for viṣamāgni, matching.
classical.quote: samaḥ samāne sthāna-sthe viṣamo 'gnir vi-mārga-ge || 73 || ... viṣamo '-samyag apy āśu samyag vāpi cirāt pacet || 75 ||
classical.translator: none — no public-domain English translation of Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya exists

distinguishFrom.why: Sushruta's viṣama alternates between adequate and inadequate; manda is uniformly slow. WHO's ITA-2.6.10 muddies this by including 'diminished' inside the definition of erratic.
Ca.Ci.15.71 makes viṣamāgni a grahaṇī-doṣa, but grahaṇī-roga is the manifest disease with its own symptom set; the agni state is the functional substrate.
Same adjective, unrelated referent. NAMASTE has a whole series of viṣamajvara codes (EC-3.10.x) that a naive string match will confuse with DB-2.
Irregular eating — a cause listed among the aetiologies (Ca.Ci.15.42 viṣamāśanāt), not the state itself.
A tempting biomedical mapping given the symptom overlap, but no study has tested the correspondence, and viṣamāgni is defined by digestive performance rather than by symptom duration criteria.

mistranslations.why: Confuses viṣama with manda. The defining feature is variability, not deficiency.
An unvalidated diagnostic equation. Sushruta's symptom list overlaps IBS but includes ascites/abdominal heaviness and the definition rests on inconsistent digestion, not on Rome criteria.
Loses the gastrointestinal specificity that both Sushruta's symptom list and WHO's disorder entry (ITA-5.11.3) carry.

openQuestions: Why does WHO define viṣamāgni twice with materially different emphases?
Is there any study correlating viṣamāgni with objective gastric emptying or transit measures?
Does Aṣṭāṅga Saṅgraha 6/32 and 6/70 (cited by NAMASTE) contain parallel definitions? I could not retrieve Aṣṭāṅga Saṅgraha.
