renderings.assessment: 'Genus/Species' is Aristotelian; in Vaiśeṣika viśeṣa is the ultimate individuator of eternal substances, which 'species' misrepresents too.
renderings.licenceNote: Sinha 1923, pre-1930 and probably clear, but outside the two translations this project has cleared and never confirmed by a human

renderings.sourceName: PubMed abstract, PMID 30401500 (J Ayurveda Integr Med 2018)
renderings.assessment: Modern Ayurvedic academic usage.
renderings.licenceNote: "PubMed abstract, PMID 30401500 (J Ayurveda Integr Med 2018)" is not a source this project has cleared for quotation

classical.establishes: Viśeṣa as hrāsahetu (cause of decrease). Sanskrit as retrieved from https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Deerghanjiviteeya_Adhyaya&action=raw : सर्वदा सर्वभावानां सामान्यं वृद्धिकारणम्| ह्रासहेतुर्विशेषश्च, प्रवृत्तिरुभयस्य तु||४४||.
classical.quote: Of all things, at all times, similarity is the cause of increase; and dissimilarity is the cause of decrease. A tendency exists towards both.

classical.establishes: Viśeṣa as pṛthaktvakṛt (producing separateness) and the viparyaya (reverse) of sāmānya. Sanskrit: सामान्यमेकत्वकरं, विशेषस्तु पृथक्त्वकृत्| तुल्यार्थता हि सामान्यं, विशेषस्तु विपर्ययः||४५||. Kaviratna's 'diversity' renders pṛthaktva (separateness).
classical.quote: Similarity is that which produces oneness; and dissimilarity is that which produces diversity. Therefore, similarity is identity of substance, and dissimilarity is the reverse of this.

classical.establishes: Viśeṣa second among the six. Sanskrit: सामान्यं च विशेषं च गुणान् द्रव्याणि कर्म च||२८||.
classical.quote: Those great Rishis (then) beheld duly, with the eye of knowledge, similarities, dissimilarities, properties, objects, and operations, as also compositions.

classical.establishes: Viśeṣa referred back to its Sutrasthana definition in the debate chapter. Sanskrit: द्रव्य-गुण-कर्म-सामान्य-विशेष-समवायाः स्वलक्षणैः श्लोकस्थाने पूर्वमुक्ताः||२९|| (https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php?title=Rogabhishagjitiya_Vimana&action=raw).
classical.quote: Dravya (substance), Guna (attribute), Samanya (similarity), Vigesha (dissimilarity), and Samavaya (combination), — these have been explained, by means of their respective indications, in the Place of flokas Sutrasthana before.

distinguishFrom.why: Ca.Su.1.44-45: the paired opposite; viśeṣa decreases and separates, sāmānya increases and unifies.
Sinha's 'Species' and WHO's 'unique individuality' belong to Vaiśeṣika, where viśeṣa individuates eternal atoms. Charaka's viśeṣa is functional (hrāsahetu). Same word, different doctrine.
Su.Su.41 title 'Dravya-Vishesha-Vijnaniya' (Bhishagratna: 'specific properties of drugs'), WHO 'viśeṣapūrvarūpam' (specific prodrome), NIA 'Specialty'. Everyday adjective, not the category.

Treatment by opposites is the application of viśeṣa, but 'opposite' is stronger than 'dissimilar'; Charaka's term is viśeṣa (difference), and NIA BP0241's 'Doctrine of similar and Opposites' silently upgrades it.
Specific unexplained action of a drug; sometimes loosely called its 'viśeṣa'. Different term.

mistranslations.why: Vaiśeṣika reading; Ca.Su.1.44 defines viśeṣa as the cause of decrease.
NIA DG0412's first gloss; a false friend from the adjective viśeṣa 'special'.
Sinha 1923; Aristotelian taxonomy has no counterpart in Charaka's usage.
Charaka says dissimilar (viśeṣa, pṛthaktva), not contrary; 'opposites' is an interpretive strengthening found in NIA BP0241 and WHO ITA-1.9.2.3 ('opposing actions').
NIA DG0412; hrāsa is decrease, which is therapeutic when a dosha is in excess, not 'negative'.

openQuestions: Chakrapāṇi on viparyaya at Su.1.45 and on the threefold viśeṣa not retrieved.
Whether Sushruta uses viśeṣa in the categorial sense anywhere (Su.Su.41 uses it adjectivally) was not established.

renderings.english: Disease, a condition which causes various types of pain and distress to the body and mind
renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.locator: ITA-4.2.1, English term 'Disease'. vyādhiḥ is listed as sense 1 of nine Sanskrit terms sharing this entry (vyādhiḥ, āmayaḥ, gadaḥ, ātaṅkaḥ, yakṣmā/samuccaya, jvara, vikāraḥ, roga, pāpmā).
renderings.assessment: WHO does not give vyadhi its own entry. It bundles nine Sanskrit terms under one English headword 'Disease' and assigns each a numbered sense. vyadhi gets sense 1; roga gets sense 8 ('Disorder, ailment'). The bundling follows Cha.Ni.1/5.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.locator: ITA-4.2.3, vyādhibhedaḥ (व्याधिभेदः): 'The categorization of diseases based on various established criteria.'
renderings.assessment: One of several places WHO uses vyādhi rather than roga as the compounding element.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.locator: ITA-4.2.2, vyādhisaṅkaraḥ (व्याधिसङ्करः): 'A disease that gives rise to another disease while continuing to exist; it may also signify two or more diseases which coexist owing to a similarity of etiology or pathogenic mechanism.'
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.english: the words 'Vyadhi', 'amaya', 'gada', 'atanka', 'yakshman', 'jwara', 'vikara', and 'roga', are of the same import.
renderings.sourceName: Charaka Samhita, trans. Avinash Chandra Kaviratna
renderings.assessment: Kaviratna leaves the terms untranslated and asserts synonymy, which is what the Sanskrit says (anarthāntaram).
renderings.licenceNote: Kaviratna's Charaka Samhita, 1896-1913

renderings.english: 'Vyadhi' comes from the root 'vyadh', to beat or belabour. Disease, owing to the pain it causes, is regarded as 'beating' or 'belabouring' the person who is afflicted by it.
renderings.sourceName: Charaka Samhita, trans. Avinash Chandra Kaviratna
renderings.locator: translator's footnote to Nidana Sthana ch. 1
renderings.assessment: Kaviratna's etymological note. The apostrophe before 'Disease' in the scan reads as a stray mark; otherwise verbatim.
renderings.licenceNote: Kaviratna's Charaka Samhita, 1896-1913

renderings.english: anything that afflicts either the body or the living personality—self, or both, is called disease
renderings.sourceName: Sushruta Samhita, trans. Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna
renderings.locator: Sutrasthana ch. XXIV (Vyadhi-Samuddheshiya), opening, back-reference to Su.Su.1
renderings.assessment: Bhishagratna's compressed definition. Chapter XXIV is the chapter literally named for vyadhi.
renderings.licenceNote: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Samhita, 1907-1916

renderings.english: The Purusha (man) is the receptacle of any. particular disease, and that which proves a source of torment or pain to him, is denominated as a disease.
renderings.sourceName: Sushruta Samhita, trans. Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna
renderings.assessment: Quoted exactly as retrieved, including the stray full stop after 'any.' which is an OCR/typesetting artifact on the retrieved page, not an editorial change.
renderings.licenceNote: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Samhita, 1907-1916

renderings.sourceName: common BAMS/textbook rendering
renderings.assessment: 'Disease' is near-universal; 'disorder' is used where a non-pathological reading is wanted.
renderings.licenceNote: this project's own paraphrase, not the source's words

classical.establishes: THE central verse for this record and for roga. Charaka declares vyadhi, amaya, gada, atanka, yakshma, jvara, vikara and roga to be anarthantaram, not different in meaning. Any lexicon that distinguishes vyadhi from roga must do so against this verse, not in ignorance of it.
classical.quote: तत्र व्याधिरामयो गद आतङ्को यक्ष्मा ज्वरो विकारो रोग इत्यनर्थान्तरम्||५|| / tatra vyādhirāmayō gada ātaṅkō yakṣmā jvarō vikārō rōga ityanarthāntaram||5||

classical.establishes: Sushruta's definition: that which is a duhkha-samyoga (association with suffering) for the purusha is called vyadhi. A suffering-based, patient-centred definition rather than a lesion-based one.
classical.quote: तद्दुःखसंयोगा व्याधय उच्यन्ते ||२३||

classical.establishes: Quotable English for Su.Su.1/23. Verse numbers are not printed on this page.
classical.quote: The Purusha (man) is the receptacle of any. particular disease, and that which proves a source of torment or pain to him, is denominated as a disease.

classical.establishes: The Vyadhi-Samuddheshiya chapter's definition plus the tapa-traya and the seven-fold bala-pravritta classification. This is the source of most of WHO ISTA's section 4.2 disease-class entries (ITA-4.2.11 to 4.2.36). Verse numbers are not printed on the retrieved page.
classical.quote: It has been stated before that anything that afflicts either the body or the living personality—self, or both, is called disease. This pain or affliction may be either physical in its character (Adhyat-mika), or due to any disturbance in the physical environments of a man (adhibhautika), or to the acts of God (adhidaivika) etc. This three-fold pain may be ultimately transformed into any of the seven kinds of diseases such as, the adi-vala-pravritta, Janma-vala-pravritta, Dosha-vala-pravritta, Sanghata-vala-pravritta, Kala-vala-pravritta, Daiva-vala-pravritta and Svabhava-vala-pravritta.

classical.establishes: Sushruta subordinates every classification of vyadhi to the doshas, including the agantu and svabhavika classes. Relevant to any claim that agantu diseases lie outside dosha theory.
classical.quote: The deranged bodily humours such as, Vayu, Pitta and Kapha should be looked upon as the primary sources of all diseases, inasmuch as symptoms characteristic of each of them may be detected in the case of a disease of whatsoever type, (which usually abates with their corresponding subsidence), and also because the Shastras have ascribed to them the fatherhood of all maladies that assail the human frame.

classical.establishes: The two ashrayas of vyadhi. Note the verse uses vyādhi, not roga, for the general term.
classical.quote: शरीरं सत्त्वसञ्ज्ञं च व्याधीनामाश्रयो मतः| तथा सुखानां, योगस्तु सुखानां कारणं समः||५५||

distinguishFrom.why: Declared anarthantaram (not different in meaning) at Cha.Ni.1/5. Any distinction drawn between them is post-classical usage, not textual. See the roga record for the one asymmetry that is observable: which term each source prefers as a compounding element.

Also on the Cha.Ni.1/5 synonym list, but vikara has a second life as the general term for 'modification/change' in dravyaguna and in the dhatu-vaishamya definition of disease, so it is not safely interchangeable outside a nidana context.

Kaviratna's Charaka Vimana 6 passage (see the roga record) states explicitly that the same word roga is applied both to the faults (dosha) and to the disorders, which means the vyadhi/dosha boundary is not as clean in the text as textbooks present it.
WHO ISTA ITA entries use vyādhikṣamatvam for resistance/immunity. A string search for 'vyadhi' in any index will surface it; it is about the host's capacity, not about disease.
'Ulcer/wound'. Sushruta Su.21 ends by deriving vrana from the root vri, and Su.24 divides all disease into surgical and medical. Vrana is a disease kind, not a synonym for disease.

mistranslations.why: Appears in WHO ISTA's own ITA-4.2.1 gloss list as one of the nine senses, but as the gloss for yakṣmā/samuccaya, not for vyādhi. Lifting 'syndrome' onto vyadhi misreads the numbered senses.
Confuses the condition with the study or mechanism of it. The mechanism word is samprapti.
Imports a structural requirement. Sushruta's definition at Su.Su.1/23 is duhkha-samyoga, association with suffering, which is explicitly experiential.
A wellness-industry softening. Dhatu-vaishamya is a cause of vyadhi in Charaka's frame, not a translation of it, and 'imbalance' erases the suffering criterion that both samhitas make definitional.

openQuestions: What are the printed verse numbers for the Bhishagratna Sushruta Sutrasthana chapter XXIV passages? The retrieved page carries no verse numbers at all, only footnote markers.
Does any samhita passage distinguish vyadhi from roga in extension, as against Cha.Ni.1/5's declaration of synonymy? Nothing retrieved suggests one, but the commentators are unchecked.

alternates: bala (WHO pairs the two under one ID)

renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.locator: ITA-2.2.27 (Sanskrit term given as 'balam, vyādhikṣamatvam'); description: 'This is classified into three types: innate strength, acquired strength and seasonal strength'
renderings.assessment: WHO merges bala and vyādhikṣamatva into a single entry here, which is a substantive lexical decision, not a neutral gloss.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.english: Inherent capacity of the body to resist diseases
renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.locator: ITA-4.8.25; description: 'The inherent resisting power of the body, which strives to arrest the occurrence, progress and re-occurrence of diseases.'
renderings.assessment: WHO gives the SAME English head-term to three different Sanskrit words (ITA-4.8.25 vyādhikṣamatvam, ITA-4.8.26 vyādhibalavirodhitatvam, ITA-4.8.27 vyādhyutpādapratibandhakatvam), separating what Chakrapāṇi treats as synonyms.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2022)
renderings.locator: ITA-10.3.9 (health-promotion chapter), Sanskrit 'vyādhikṣamatva', no description text given
renderings.assessment: Third WHO entry for the same word, in a third chapter, with a third English term. The same term is rendered three ways inside one document.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.english: Immunity; ... the power of the body which prevents the development of diseases or resists a developed disease
renderings.sourceName: National Institute of Ayurveda / WHO-APW glossary, 'Standardization of non-clinical terminologies of Ayurveda'
renderings.assessment: Draft Indian glossary prepared under a WHO agreement; predates and differs in framing from the 2022 WHO ISTA. Provenance of the local copy of this PDF was not re-established this session, so treat the locator as indicative.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.english: capable of resisting diseases / incapable of resisting diseases (of bodies)
renderings.sourceName: Charaka Samhita, tr. Avinash Chandra Kaviratna
renderings.locator: Sūtrasthāna ch. 28, his verses 13-14; 'These bodies which are the reverse of those described above are capable of resisting diseases.'
renderings.assessment: Kaviratna has no noun for vyādhikṣamatva; he renders it only predicatively, of bodies.
renderings.licenceNote: Kaviratna's Charaka Samhita, 1896-1913

renderings.english: All bodies, again, are not equally liable to disease.
renderings.sourceName: Charaka Samhita, tr. Avinash Chandra Kaviratna
renderings.locator: Sūtrasthāna ch. 28, his verse 11 (= CS Sū. 28.7 in modern numbering)
renderings.assessment: This renders 'na ca sarvāṇi śarīrāṇi vyādhikṣamatve samarthāni bhavanti'. Kaviratna inverts the polarity: the Sanskrit says bodies are not all CAPABLE of resistance; he writes they are not all LIABLE to disease. Semantically close, logically not identical.
renderings.licenceNote: Kaviratna's Charaka Samhita, 1896-1913

renderings.english: immunity / disease resistance / resistance to disease
renderings.sourceName: Standard Indian BAMS textbook and journal usage
renderings.locator: ubiquitous in Ayurvedic periodical literature, e.g. PMID 24501524 title uses the untranslated term
renderings.assessment: The commonest working rendering; carries immunological baggage the classical term does not.
renderings.licenceNote: this project's own paraphrase, not the source's words

classical.establishes: The locus classicus. The word appears not as a defined entity but inside a triple denial: not all unwholesome things are equally harmful, not all doṣas equally strong, and not all bodies capable of vyādhikṣamatva.
classical.quote: na hi sarvāṇyapathyāni tulyadoṣāṇi na ca sarve doṣāstulyabalā na ca sarvāṇi śarīrāṇi vyādhikṣamatve samarthāni bhavanti

classical.text: Cakrapāṇidatta, Āyurvedadīpikā commentary on Charaka Samhita Sūtrasthāna 28.7
classical.establishes: Chakrapāṇi EQUATES vyādhikṣamatva with vyādhibalavirodhitva and with vyādhyutpādapratibandhakatva. WHO ISTA splits these same three words into three separate term IDs with different definitions. This is the single most important disagreement in the record.
classical.quote: vyādhikṣamatvaṃ vyādhibalavirodhitvaṃ vyādhyutpādapratibandhakatvamiti yāvat

classical.establishes: The earliest English rendering available for lawful quotation; shows the term was not treated as a technical noun in 1900.
classical.quote: All bodies, again, are not equally liable to disease. ... are incapable of resisting diseases.13 These bodies which are the reverse of those described above are capable of resisting diseases.

distinguishFrom.why: WHO ISTA ITA-2.2.27 lists both words under one entry, but bala is the positive capacity (classified sahaja / yuktikṛta / kālaja) while vyādhikṣamatva in CS Sū. 28.7 is specifically the body's competence to withstand disease. Every bala is not vyādhikṣamatva; Chakrapāṇi defines the latter by what it obstructs.

Chakrapāṇi says they are the same thing (see quote). WHO ISTA ITA-4.8.26 makes it a separate entry, 'A natural, nonspecific type of immunity which defends the body whenever any disease occurs for the first time' — an innate-immunity reading with no classical warrant given. A lexicon must not silently adopt either position.
Again a Chakrapāṇi synonym, but WHO ISTA ITA-4.8.27 defines it separately as 'The defence mechanism of the body which intervenes to resist the occurrence or re-occurrence of diseases'.
Ojas is a substance-like entity (the essence of the dhātus); vyādhikṣamatva is a capacity predicated of the śarīra. Modern papers routinely conflate them; CS Sū. 28.7 does not mention ojas.

The biomedical term denotes a specific organ-system. CS Sū. 28.7's account of bodies unable to resist is anatomical and nutritional (too fat, too thin, undeveloped flesh/blood/bone, weak, sustained on unsuitable food, on very little food, of little vitality) — nothing immunological.

mistranslations.why: Turns a capacity into an anatomical system. Nothing in CS Sū. 28.7 or in Chakrapāṇi's gloss individuates a system; the qualifying factors listed are body habitus, tissue quality, diet and sattva.

Defensible as shorthand and used by WHO ISTA, but it imports specificity/memory/antigen concepts. The classical term also covers resistance to non-infectious causation (apathya āhāra, prajñāparādha), which 'immunity' excludes.
Marketing usage. It treats vyādhikṣamatva as a quantity that can be raised by a product, whereas the classical passage treats it as a standing property of the constituted body.
Narrows the term to infectious disease; the Charaka context is about vyādhi in general arising from diet and other rogaprakṛtis.

openQuestions: Does any classical text other than Charaka use the word vyādhikṣamatva? Not found in the GRETIL Charaka-parts corpus beyond Sū. 28.7 and its commentary; Sushruta was not searched exhaustively for it.
Whether WHO ISTA's three-way split (ITA-4.8.25/26/27) rests on any commentarial authority, or is an editorial invention contradicting Chakrapāṇi.
Whether NAMASTE assigns a code to vyādhikṣamatva (portal unreachable this session).

renderings.english: Stage of clinical manifestation of a disease
renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda
renderings.assessment: WHO description, verbatim: 'The fifth stage of disease manifestation, when a disease or condition becomes clinically manifest.' Re-read from the PDF this session. WHO adds 'clinical', which is not in the Sanskrit but is the intended sense.
renderings.licenceNote: the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda

renderings.english: the symptoms which they respectively exhibit in connection with the incidental disease ( Vyakti )
renderings.sourceName: Sushruta Samhita, tr. Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907)
renderings.assessment: Bhishagratna again paraphrases rather than giving a term. In the prose for the stage itself he writes 'the full development or manifestation of a disease' and 'the complete development of the characteristic symptoms'.
renderings.licenceNote: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Samhita, 1907-1916

renderings.english: Vyakta or Vyakteebhava – Stage of manifestation of disease
renderings.sourceName: easyayurveda.com (Dr Raghuram Y.S. / Dr J.V. Hebbar)
renderings.assessment: String-matched on the retrieved page. Note this source does not use 'vyakti' at all for the stage — it uses vyakta / vyaktībhāva, and lists 'Vyakta' in its own contents list of the six. The naming of the fifth stage is genuinely unsettled between sources.
renderings.licenceNote: "easyayurveda.com (Dr Raghuram Y.S. / Dr J.V. Hebbar)" is not a source this project has cleared for quotation

renderings.sourceName: siva.sh (machine-generated English layer)
renderings.assessment: LOW AUTHORITY. The same site's Hindi layer for this verse renders व्यक्तिं as 'व्यक्तित्व' (personality) — a documented machine-translation failure of exactly the kind this record warns about.
renderings.licenceNote: a machine-generated English layer

classical.establishes: Critical lexicographic point, re-confirmed this session: the prose of the fifth stage does NOT use the word vyakti. It says vyādher darśanam (the appearing of the disease) and pravyaktalakṣaṇatā (the state of having fully manifest signs). The name 'vyakti' for this stage comes only from the summary verse 21.36.
classical.quote: अत ऊर्ध्वं व्याधेर्दर्शनं वक्ष्यामः- शोफार्बुदग्रन्थिविद्रधिविसर्पप्रभृतीनां प्रव्यक्तलक्षणता ज्वरातीसारप्रभृतीनां च । तत्र पञ्चमः क्रियाकालः ॥३४॥

classical.establishes: Bhishagratna's English for the fifth stage, and his 1907 disease equivalents (Granthi as 'aneurism', Visarpa as 'erysipelas') which should be treated as period glosses, not as identifications.
classical.quote: Now we shall deal with the full development or manifestation of a disease. The full manifestation of a disease, such as a swelling, tumour, aneurism (Granthi), Vidradhi (abscess) and erysipelas ( Visarpa ) etc., fever or dysentery, signifies the complete development of the characteristic symptoms, which should be regarded as the fifth occasion for medical treatment.

classical.establishes: The only place in the retrieved verses where the stage is named vyakti. Grammatically vyaktiṃ ... doṣāṇām — the manifestation OF THE DOSHAS, which is a subtly different claim from 'manifestation of the disease' used by WHO and by textbooks.
classical.quote: व्यक्तिं भेदं च यो वेत्ति दोषाणां स भवेद्भिषक् ॥३६॥

distinguishFrom.why: These name the signs and symptoms themselves. WHO ITA-4.5.5 groups the sign-and-symptom synonyms under one entry, noting that 'Ayurveda uses several terms as synonyms for signs and symptoms, based on the different perspectives under which they are understood'. Vyakti names the stage at which those signs are fully present. A symptom is not a stage.
Prodromes belong to the previous stage (sthānasaṃśraya). The vyakti/pūrvarūpa boundary is the diagnostic boundary between 'about to have' and 'has' the disease.

In Samkhya philosophy, which Charaka's Sharirasthana engages with at length, vyakta means the manifest as opposed to avyakta, the unmanifest prakriti. Unrelated to pathology, and a live source of confusion in translated Samhita passages.

distinguishFrom.term: vyakti in ordinary Sanskrit and modern Hindi
distinguishFrom.why: व्यक्ति in current Hindi standardly means 'a person, an individual'. This is the single most dangerous false friend in the whole kriyakala set, and it is not hypothetical: an AI translation layer on a Sanskrit text site rendered व्यक्तिं in this very verse as व्यक्तित्व, personality.
Alternative names used for the same stage by practitioner sources. If a source names the stage vyakta rather than vyakti, that is a naming difference, not a different stage.

mistranslations.why: Reads the ordinary-language sense of vyakti into a technical staging term. Observed in the wild in a machine-generated Hindi layer on a Sanskrit text site, and it makes the verse say something about constitutional individuality that the text does not say.
Conflates the patient's state with the clinician's act. The disease manifests at vyakti whether or not anyone diagnoses it.

Imports an acute/chronic axis the text does not use. Sushruta explicitly includes long-running conditions such as jvara and atisara in the later stages, and 21.35 makes long duration a feature of the SIXTH stage, not a contrast with the fifth.

openQuestions: Whether commentators (Dalhana) justify naming the fifth stage vyakti when the prose uses vyādher darśanam and pravyaktalakṣaṇatā.
Which of vyakti / vyakta / vyaktībhāva is the dominant form in current BAMS curricula — WHO uses vyakti, a major practitioner reference uses vyakta/vyaktībhāva.
Whether NAMASTE or ICD-11 TM2 carry this term — both lookups failed again this session; see the shat-kriyakala record.

renderings.sourceName: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda
renderings.assessment: WHO's description: 'Subtype of vata seated in the cardiac region (hrdaya), which circulates or diffuses through the body. It performs the function of circulating of fluids through heart to all parts of the body, as well as transporting various materials from one body part to another.' Follows Ashtanga Hridaya Su.12.6 (hṛdi sthitaḥ) rather than Sushruta, which gives vyāna no seat. Note WHO's description is entirely about transport and omits the motor functions (flexion, extension, blinking) that Charaka Ci.28.9 makes central. Lemma is bare vyānaḥ.

classical.establishes: Sushruta gives vyāna NO seat — only whole-body range — and three function groups: conveyance of rasa, outflow of blood and sweat, and five kinds of bodily movement. Corresponding Sanskrit, cross-checked at a separate URL: 'कृत्स्नदेहचरो व्यानो रससंवहनोद्यतः ||१७|| स्वेदासृक्स्रावणश्चापि पञ्चधा चेष्टयत्यपि | क्रुद्धश्च कुरुते रोगान् प्रायशः सर्वदेहगान् ||१८||'. Bhishagratna's footnote [5] specifies the five movements as 'expansion, flexion, lowering down and lifting up or lateral thrusting of any part of the body'.
classical.quote: The Vayu known as the Vyana courses (acts) through the whole organism, and its functions consist in sending the lymph chyle, etc. all through the body and in helping the out-flow of blood (Asrik) and perspiration. Five kinds of muscular movements are ascribed to the action of the Vyana Vayu, a deranged condition of which is generally attended with diseases which are not confined to any particular region, member, or organ of the body, but are found to affect the whole organism (such as, fever, etc). 10.

classical.establishes: A rare classical statement of a COMBINED subtype pathology (vyāna + apāna together producing prameha and śukra disorders), and of the prognosis when all five are simultaneously deranged. Corresponding Sanskrit: 'शुक्रदोषप्रमेहास्तु व्यानापानप्रकोपजाः ||२०||'.
classical.quote: An aggravated condition of both the Vyana and Apana Vayus may produce Prameha and disorders of the seminal fluid, while a simultaneous excitement of the five vital Vayus leads to a sure and speedy termination of life.

classical.establishes: Charaka's vyāna pervades the whole body and is śīghragati (swift-moving); its functions are gati (locomotion), prasāraṇa (extension), ākṣepa (flexion/throwing), nimeṣa (closing of the eyelids) and the like. Charaka's vyāna is therefore primarily a MOTOR subtype, not a circulatory one — the circulatory emphasis in WHO and in modern writing comes from Sushruta's rasasaṃvahana and from Vagbhata's hṛdi sthitaḥ.
classical.quote: देहं व्याप्नोति सर्वं तु व्यानः शीघ्रगतिर्नृणाम् | गतिप्रसारणाक्षेपनिमेषादिक्रियः सदा ||९||

classical.establishes: Names vyāna as one of the five in a lawfully quotable English Charaka. No seat or function given.
classical.quote: It exists in the fivefold form of Prana, Udana, Samana, Vyana, and Apana.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata seats vyāna in the HEART (vyāno hṛdi sthitaḥ), has it range the entire body with great velocity (kṛtsnadehacārī mahājavaḥ), and at 12.7 assigns it gati, apakṣepaṇa (downward movement), utkṣepa (upward movement), nimeṣa and unmeṣa (closing and opening of the eyelids), adding that 'nearly all the activities of embodied beings are bound up in it'. Vagbhata's hṛdi sthitaḥ is the source of WHO's 'seated in the cardiac region'. Sanskrit mūla and verse numbering verified on the retrieved page; not quoted, as Ashtanga Hridaya has no public-domain English translation.

classical.establishes: Sharngadhara's seat list at 5.27 ends with sarvāṅgadeśeṣu (all parts of the body), which the naming verse 5.28 maps to vyāna. Consistent with Charaka and Sushruta on range; unlike Vagbhata, Sharngadhara does not seat vyāna in the heart. Sanskrit mūla verified on the retrieved page; not quoted, as Sharngadhara has no public-domain English translation.

distinguishFrom.why: Vyāna is the mover, not the thing moved. Sushruta Ni.1.17b has it 'rasasaṃvahanodyata' — engaged in conveying rasa. Modern writing routinely slides from 'vyāna circulates the blood' to 'vyāna IS the circulation', which erases the doṣa/dhātu distinction.

The yogic vyāna is the pervasive current linking the other four and is often tied to coordination and to the nāḍī network. The Ayurvedic vyāna is defined by Charaka Ci.28.9 through specific motor acts (locomotion, extension, flexion, blinking), not through a subtle-body network.

Vagbhata seats vyāna in the heart (AH Su.12.6) while WHO's prāṇa entry says prāṇa controls 'the intellect, heart, sensory and motor organs'. Both end up at the heart. Charaka keeps them apart cleanly: prāṇa is above the diaphragm and ingestive; vyāna is everywhere and motor.

A citation hazard rather than a conceptual one: in Ashtanga Hridaya, verse 12.6 contains the END of udāna's function list and the BEGINNING of vyāna's definition. A bare 'AH Su.12.6' citation can be read as supporting either. Check the hemistich.

distinguishFrom.term: vyāna in the context of svedavaha srotas
distinguishFrom.why: Both Sushruta (svedāsṛksrāvaṇa) and Charaka's samāna verse (svedavaha srotas) involve sweat. Sushruta assigns the OUTFLOW of sweat to vyāna; Charaka Ci.28.8 seats samāna in the sweat-carrying channels. Sweat is contested between the two subtypes across the two texts.

mistranslations.why: WHO's 'Circulating vata' invites it, but Charaka Ci.28.9 makes vyāna's functions motor (gati, prasāraṇa, ākṣepa, nimeṣa) with no mention of circulation at all. The circulatory reading rests on Sushruta and Vagbhata only. Rendering vyāna as 'circulation' silently picks a side in a textual disagreement.

From Bhishagratna's 1911 footnote [3]. Worse, that footnote is internally corrupt: it assigns 'the energy of the Motor-Sensory Nerves' to UDANA, naming Udana twice and omitting Vyana entirely. Anyone quoting that footnote for vyāna is quoting a printing error, and anyone quoting it for udāna is quoting a colonial neuroanatomical equation. I inspected the footnote text directly and it reads exactly this way on the retrieved page.

mistranslations.rendering: the autonomic nervous system / all involuntary actions
mistranslations.why: As on the Kerala Tourism page. Charaka's function list includes both voluntary locomotion and reflex blinking, so the voluntary/involuntary distinction is not the one the text is drawing.
Bhishagratna's rendering of rasa. Accurate to 1911 physiology, misleading now — rasa is the first dhātu, not lymph or chyle. Quote it as his wording, never as a modern equivalence.

Follows from the hypertension literature (PMID 29153383) treating vyāna vāta as the operative factor in blood pressure. That paper proposes the link; it does not establish it, and no classical locus mentions anything answering to blood pressure.

openQuestions: Does Chakrapani read rasa circulation into Charaka Ci.28.9, or does Charaka genuinely omit it and confine vyāna to motor function?
Which text first seats vyāna in the heart — is Ashtanga Hridaya Su.12.6 the earliest, given that Sushruta, Charaka and Sharngadhara all give it whole-body range instead?
Is Bhishagratna's footnote [3] corrupt in the 1911 printing itself, or only in the wisdomlib transcription? A physical copy would settle it.
Does NAMASTE assign vyāna vāta a code, and does its English term follow WHO's 'Circulating vata'?

classical.establishes: The fourfold prognostic scheme: sādhya is twofold (sukha-/kṛcchra-sādhya); asādhya is twofold, yāpya and anupakrama. Yāpya is here a subdivision of asādhya.
classical.quote: सुखसाध्यं मतं साध्यं कृच्छ्रसाध्यमथापि च| द्विविधं चाप्यसाध्यं स्याद्याप्यं यच्चानुपक्रमम् ||९||

The asterisked footnote is the TRANSLATOR'S: "'Yapya' means those diseases which without admitting of radical cure can, by medicine and diet and change of air, be kept in a state of partial suppression. 'Anupakramam' is explained by the Commentator as those for which there is no treatment, i.e., those in which treatment is productive of no beneficial consequence. — T." OCR text; spacing normalized.
classical.quote: As regards curable diseases, they are of two kinds, viz., those that are easily curable and those that are curable with difficulty. Incurable diseases, also, are of two [OCR: tw©] kinds, viz., those that are capable of being suppressed, and those that have no treatment.*3

classical.establishes: The marks of a yāpya disease: incurable yet kept going by wholesome regimen because life-span remains (śeṣatvād āyuṣaḥ); little relief obtained, quickly provoked by a slight cause; deep-seated, in many dhātus, lodged in marma and joints, constantly recurring, long-standing.
classical.quote: शेषत्वादायुषो याप्यमसाध्यं पथ्यसेवया| लब्धाल्पसुखमल्पेन हेतुनाऽऽशुप्रवर्तकम्||१७|| गम्भीरं बहुधातुस्थं मर्मसन्धिसमाश्रितम्| नित्यानुशायिनं रोगं दीर्घकालमवस्थितम्||१८||

CAUTION (translator's word choice, not doctrine): 'exhaustion of one's allotted period of life' inverts the Sanskrit śeṣatvād āyuṣaḥ, 'because of the remainder of life-span', i.e. the patient survives BECAUSE life remains. Do not record 'yāpya = incurable because life is exhausted'.
classical.quote: Even diseases that are incurable in consequence of the exhaustion of one's allotted period of life may be kept in a suppressed state by means of regulated diet and (proper) nursing.*8-11

"Yatrakaram" is "competent to make the patient live on."' A second footnote glosses the fourfold mild/violent × curable/incurable scheme and says 'Mild and Incurable would mean Yapya or suppressible' — this mapping is Kaviratna's, not Charaka's.
classical.quote: Some, again, (though incurable) are capable of being suppressed. In diseases of this latter kind, well-applied treatment assists the patient to live on.*44

classical.establishes: The verb yāpayet ('should make [them] go on / maintain') applied to yāpya diseases, confirming the sense 'to be kept going' rather than 'to be cured'.
classical.quote: एवमभिसमीक्ष्य साध्यान् साधयेत्, याप्यान् यापयेत्, असाध्यान्नैवोपक्रमेत, परिसंवत्सरोत्थितांश्च विकारान् प्रायशो वर्जयेत् ॥६॥

distinguishFrom.why: In Charaka Su. 10.9 yāpya is one of the two kinds of asādhya; in Sushruta Su. 35.18 and WHO IST (ITA-4.2.41/42) yāpya and asādhya/pratyākhyeya sit side by side. A lexicon entry must state which scheme it follows; 'yāpya is not asādhya' is true only in the Sushruta/WHO arrangement.

The truly untreatable class ('having no treatment' / 'to be refused'). Charaka Su. 10.9 uses anupakrama, Ni. 8.34 and Sushruta use pratyākhyeya; both contrast with yāpya, where treatment is worthwhile though non-curative.
Still curable; yāpya is never cured (Ni. 8.34 'yāti na aśeṣatām'). Clinical papers (e.g. PMID 22131763) blur the two when outcomes are poor.
Same root yā-/yāpana, 'sustaining', but a class of enemas; adjacency in alphabetical lists causes confusion.

Modern palliative care is end-of-life symptom relief; yāpya covers lifelong chronic management (WHO's own examples are diabetes and asthma), and Kaviratna's 'suppressible' is closer to 'controllable'.

mistranslations.why: Grammatically off: palliative describes a treatment. 'Palliable' (can be palliated) or 'controllable/manageable' is what the Sanskrit gerundive yāpya (fit to be made to go on) means.

mistranslations.rendering: 'incurable in consequence of the exhaustion of one's allotted period of life' (Kaviratna, Su. 10.17ab)
mistranslations.why: Translator's rendering inverts śeṣatvād āyuṣaḥ, which gives the REMAINING life-span as the reason the patient survives on regimen. Not a doctrine of Charaka.

mistranslations.rendering: 'Mild and Incurable would mean Yapya' (Kaviratna footnote, Su. 18)
mistranslations.why: An editorial mapping of yāpya onto the mṛdu/dāruṇa × sādhya/asādhya grid; Charaka Su. 18.41 names the four kinds without equating any to yāpya. Quote as translator's note only.
Dīrghakālam avasthitam (long-standing) is one sign of yāpya (Su. 10.18), but many chronic diseases are kṛcchrasādhya; chronicity alone does not make a disease yāpya.
WHO IST reserves 'terminal' for pratyākhyeya (ITA-4.2.43); applying it to yāpya collapses the distinction the classification exists to make.

Does Ashtanga Hridaya carry its own yāpya definition (A.H. Su. 1 or Ni. 1)? Discussed in secondary literature (PMID 22131763 cites Vagbhata) but not located here.
NAMASTE terminology/morbidity codes for yāpya not retrieved (portal is a JS application).
ICD-11 TM2 coverage not checked; TM2 codes disorders and patterns, and a prognostic class may have no code — unestablished.

classical.verse: Standard (Trikamji / carakasamhitaonline) Sutrasthana 11.54 (verified: 53 'प्रयोगज्ञानविज्ञानसिद्धिसिद्धाः...' before, 55 'शरीरदोषप्रकोपे खलु...' after); Kaviratna aphorism 55, printed AFTER the passage as '*55' on p. 130 of Lesson XI (archive.org BIUSante_47357 leaf 193; the djvu OCR misreads it as '*56'), with his 54 closing the preceding aphorism
classical.establishes: The locus classicus: aushadha is threefold (daivavyapashraya, yuktivyapashraya, sattvavajaya); yuktivyapashraya is 'yojana' (planned deployment) of diet and drug substances. Kaviratna numbers this aphorism 55 against standard 54: he runs one ahead through the close of this chapter (from S50 on), and the number is read from the page image, not the OCR, which prints '*56'.
classical.quote: Sanskrit 11.54: "त्रिविधमौषधमिति- दैवव्यपाश्रयं, युक्तिव्यपाश्रयं, सत्त्वावजयश्च| तत्र दैवव्यपाश्रयं- मन्त्रौषधिमणिमङ्गलबल्युपहारहोमनियमप्रायश्चित्तोपवासस्वस्त्ययनप्रणिपातगमनादि, युक्तिव्यपाश्रयं- पुनराहारौषधद्रव्याणां योजना, सत्त्वावजयः- पुनरहितेभ्योऽर्थेभ्यो मनोनिग्रहः||५४||" Kaviratna: "Medicines are of three kinds; those that depend for their action upon the deities and invisible influences ; those that depend for their application and action upon knowledge and reason ; and those that appertain to the subjugation of the mind. Among these, mantras, herbs and plants of invisible virtue ( if kept in contact with the body), gems, auspicious rites, offerings in sacrifices, offers of articles to the deities in course of worship or religious rites, libations of meat and ghee on the sacred fire, practice of vows, expiatory ceremonies and rites, fasts, propitiatory rites, bows to the deities, and pilgrimage to sacred waters and shrines, constitute medicines of the first kind. Diet and articles of medicinal virtue that are applied with the aid of knowledge and reason are medicines of the second kind. The subjugation of the mind by withdrawing it from every kind of injurious or harmful acts and objects of the senses, constitutes medicine of the third kind.*55"
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Standard 11.17 and 11.23-25 (yukti as fourth pariksha); 11.32 (definition of yukti)
classical.establishes: In the same chapter yukti is also one of four means of examination (pariksha), defined by multi-causal reasoning. The therapy class yuktivyapashraya borrows this epistemic sense; the two uses should be cross-referenced, not merged.
classical.quote: Sanskrit 11.17: "द्विविधमेव खलु सर्वं सच्चासच्च; तस्य चतुर्विधा परीक्षा- आप्तोपदेशः, प्रत्यक्षम्, अनुमानं, युक्तिश्चेति||१७||" Sanskrit 11.32: "युक्तिश्चैषा- षड्धातुसमुदयाद्गर्भजन्म, कर्तृकरणसंयोगात् क्रिया; कृतस्य कर्मणः फलं नाकृतस्य, नाङ्कुरोत्पत्तिरबीजात्;कर्मसदृशं फलं, नान्यस्माद्बीजादन्यस्योत्पत्तिः; इति युक्तिः||३२||"
classical.translator: none (Sanskrit); Kaviratna's rendering of these verses not extracted

distinguishFrom.why: The first of the three (mantra, gems, rites, fasting, pilgrimage); WHO 9.1.14 'Therapeutic rituals'. Note Charaka lists upavasa (fasting) under daiva, not yukti.
The third: restraint of mind from unwholesome objects (manonigraha); modern writers call it psychotherapy.
Same word as the fourth means of examination in Su.11.17, 11.32; the therapy class is 'what rests on yukti', not yukti itself.
WHO gives it as a synonym; the daivī/mānuṣī pairing is a later convention and is not in Charaka Su.11.54.
WHO's gloss; EBM is a 1990s methodology, whereas yukti is the physician's reasoned combination (yojana) of diet and drug for the case.

mistranslations.why: WHO ITA-9.1.26 imports the term; Charaka defines yuktivyapashraya as planned use of ahara and aushadha dravya, with no notion of trial evidence.

mistranslations.rendering: rational medicine (as opposed to the rest of Ayurveda)
mistranslations.why: Implies the other two classes are irrational; Charaka presents all three as aushadha. Kaviratna's 'knowledge and reason' is accurate for yukti but 'medicines' for all three preserves the parity.
Omits ahara (diet), which Charaka names first in the definition.

openQuestions: Kaviratna's number '*56' versus the standard 54 at this point of Sutrasthana 11 should be checked on the scan image for other passages in the chapter before any claim about his offset here.
Whether Sushruta uses the yukti/daiva split at all was not checked.
